CHG:4.150.0.release_notes:
Pages that quote when a quantum computer might arrive now stick to what their sources say: the Threats page drops the range this site had worked out itself and shows the Global Risk Institute survey in its own words, the Assess steps no longer claim a 2030–2040 expert range, and the FAQ, Simulation, report and Learn exercises say that these figures are published estimates, still open to debate. The Confidential Computing workshop also now prints the real ML-DSA key sizes.

### Added

- **Notes that estimates are still open, on more pages**: the FAQ answers that quote a quantum-computer year or qubit count, the Simulation's years-to-Q-Day figure in the report, and the Learn exercises where you set a quantum-computer year now say that these are published estimates or example figures, not settled answers. The 2029 year the Simulation and the assessment report plan against is now labelled as this site's own planning anchor, not a figure from a source.

### Changed

- **The Threats page no longer shows a CRQC range of its own**: the expanded source list used to show a 2029–2036 range that this site had worked out from a Google Quantum AI paper, but the paper gives no arrival date. The list now states what the paper does estimate (at most 1,200 logical qubits, fewer than half a million physical qubits on the stated machine assumptions) and says plainly that no reliable estimate of when such a machine could exist is established.
- **The Assess steps no longer claim a 2030–2040 expert range**: the data-retention and credential-lifetime steps now say that 2029 is this site's own planning anchor for a first CRQC, not a source figure, and quote the Global Risk Institute's 2025 survey of 26 experts, which found a CRQC "quite possible" (28–49%) within 10 years. The AI security scale-encryption exercise now calls its risk bands an example planning window instead of a range of estimates.
- **The Threats headline shows the Global Risk Institute survey in its own words**: the headline card used to show a "2030–2041 expert forecast" that this site had worked out itself. It now reports what the 2025 survey of 26 experts actually says: a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is "quite possible" (28–49%) within 10 years and "likely" (51–70%) within 15. The years 2030–2041 are now called a planning range set by this site, in the calculators and in the Quantum Threats module. A note that a majority expect a CRQC by 2035, which the survey does not support, is removed.

### Fixed

- **The trusted-channel steps show the real ML-DSA key sizes**: the key-provisioning steps in the Confidential Computing workshop used to print two fixed sizes (about 2.5 KB for an ML-DSA public key and about 4.5 KB for a wrapped private key) that did not match the algorithm of the chosen integration. They now print the FIPS 204 sizes for that algorithm (for example 1,952 bytes public and 4,032 bytes private for ML-DSA-65), plus the 28 bytes that AES-GCM wrapping adds to the private key.

CHG:4.151.0.full: The Privacy and Terms pages now say plainly that analytics run on every visit; Homomorphic Encryption becomes its own Learn module with fourteen new quiz questions; the assessment report keeps the frameworks you selected and names any it leaves out; every Crypto Lab tool, planning tool and Learn module has a page that search engines can read; and the About page, README, tour and manual quote the real counts.
CHG:4.151.0.release_notes:
The Privacy and Terms pages now say plainly that analytics run on every visit; Homomorphic Encryption becomes its own Learn module with fourteen new quiz questions; the assessment report keeps the frameworks you selected and names any it leaves out; every Crypto Lab tool, planning tool and Learn module has a page that search engines can read; and the About page, README, tour and manual quote the real counts.

### Added

- **Homomorphic encryption now has its own module**: the section and the "FHE + HSM Flows" workshop on computing on encrypted data, which used to sit inside Confidential Computing & TEEs, are now the module "Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody". It has five learn sections, the six-scenario workshop, five guided exercises, a check-your-understanding question and a poster. It sits right after Confidential Computing & TEEs in the Hardware Infrastructure track.
- **Quiz questions on homomorphic encryption**: a new "Homomorphic Encryption & HSM Key Custody" topic with fourteen questions: how FHE differs from a TEE, noise and bootstrapping, the four ISO/IEC 28033 draft schemes, which keys are public, why AES needs transciphering, what the quantum threat does and does not touch, how an HSM holds the key, and why it must not decrypt on request. Each question links to the section it comes from.
- **The report names the frameworks you selected that were left out**: when a framework you selected does not apply to your country or industry, the assessment report now says which ones it left out, by name, instead of dropping them silently. Shared report links show this too, but links made before this release do not have that line. The compliance section now says "among the frameworks you selected that apply to you", and the list of what applies to your industry and country explains that "mandatory" there includes guidance and drafts.
- **Every Crypto Lab and Business tool has its own page for search engines**: each of the 99 tools now has its own title, description and readable page, and the saved copy of each page that search engines read holds its real content: what you will do, a worked example, and whether it runs in your browser or needs a separate sandbox. The Crypto Lab cards are real links to those pages. An address that matches no tool now shows a "Crypto Lab tool not found" page with a link back, instead of silently jumping to the Crypto Lab start page, and is kept out of search results.
- **A short introduction on the Report page**: before you complete an assessment, the Report page now says what the report is, an executive-ready view of cryptographic exposure, prioritized remediation work and next steps, and invites you to read the example first.
- **Link to one Transition row, one landscape standard, a KAT variant or a coverage case**: shared links can now open a single classical→PQC transition row, an industry standard on the Landscape tab (with Share on each), the SLH-DSA test-vector variant, or the coverage matrix's case polarity.
- **Who maintains an open-source product**: product details list the open-source maintainers, linked to their Community profiles where we have one.
- **Certificates on phones**: the phone Records section adds a searchable list of certification records, and a certificate opens with the same details as on a computer.
- **Share and "open on its page" from more places**: Community cards and revision-history panels can be shared, and Library, threat and timeline pop-ups inside "For You" link to their own page; on phones, the Migrate catalog filter now travels in shared links too.
- **The FHE service installed in the shipped board image**: a new validated run in the FHE + HSM workshop, with the encrypted-computation service installed in the KV260 board's own system image instead of copied onto the board by hand. A 7-step encrypted program ran on the board in 48.6 s, with the key held in a software token on a Mac: the token released 5 of 6 results, all correct, and refused the 64-bit one by policy, and a tampered server key was refused. The service starts only after its three pinned values are written, and they are kept in memory, so they are lost on reboot. This run was slower than the earlier 42.7 s run, probably because the installed service uses three of the four cores; that was not isolated. This is an educational test on a software token whose attestation uses its own test root, not hardware custody.

### Changed

- **The Privacy and Terms pages now say plainly that analytics run on every visit**: the Terms page and the About page's privacy section used to say that no personal data is collected and that we never know you visited. They now say that Google Analytics 4 runs on every visit, that there is no consent prompt or on/off switch yet, what it records (page views, interaction events, the role, region and industry you pick, summary labels, basic browser details and a random cookie identifier), that Google also receives your IP address, and how to block it. The Terms date is now October 4, 2026.
- **The privacy text on the About, Terms and README pages matches what the site does**: the Terms storage paragraph, the Data Privacy and Cloud Sync text on the About page and the README no longer say that nothing leaves your browser or that no data is collected. They now say that your learning progress, preferences, saved assessments and, if you add one, your AI provider key stay on your device and that we do not receive them; that they leave your browser only if you share a report link or use the Gemini cloud mode of the PQC Assistant, which sends your chat messages and page context to Google; that Google Drive sync is built into the code but not currently available; and that "no personal data" describes the sync feature, not the whole site. Section 10 of the Terms is now titled Privacy and Analytics. The search index and the PQC Assistant's page summaries for About, Terms and the home page now say the same.
- **The About page, README, tour and user manual quote the real counts**: they now say 73 learning modules, 37 planning tools, 888 products in the migration catalog, 1,125 quiz questions in 79 categories and 13 assessment steps, taken from the real catalogs instead of older fixed numbers. The offline-mode banner, the guided tour and the user manual use the same module and quiz figures, and their product, glossary and library figures are updated (880+ products, 630+ glossary terms, 1,200+ library documents).
- **The About page counts Timeline countries from the data**: the About page used to say the Timeline covers 37 countries, a figure that also counted blocs and bodies such as the EU, the G7 and NATO. It now counts only sovereign countries (United Nations members), which is 28 today, and follows the data when it changes.
- **The user manual describes the Compliance and Learn pages as they are**: the Compliance section of the manual now describes the eight views (Rules & Standards, Requirements, Progress, Products, Landscape, Product Records, For You and CSWP.39 Agility) and says that old links to the earlier tabs still work; the Learn section lists the nine tracks and the module tabs. Two lines promising automatic data updates, one of them daily, are removed.
- **The role boards call the quantum-computer year our own planning year**: the home boards for Executive, Researcher, Curious and Cert Engineer used to present the 2035 (2030–2041) year as an "expert forecast", a "consensus estimate" or a date the machine "arrives". They now say it is this site's own planning year, with the range it plans across, and the Researcher board points to the published survey for what the experts said.
- **Automated reviews show as "maintainer (automated)"**: the "reviewed by" badge, the revision lists and the published compliance data files (OSCAL) now use that name for the earliest automated reviews instead of the tool's own name. The stored revision history is unchanged.
- **The Quantum Threats lesson's search summary matches its sources**: the short summary that search and the PQC Assistant read said there is a "33% chance by 2033" and that ANSSI "mandates hybrid for government by 2025", neither of which the sources support. It now states the published positions of NIST, the NSA, the Global Risk Institute, BSI and ANSSI.
- **The Quantum Threats lesson shows what each source says about a quantum-computer estimate**: for each estimate it now shows who said it, the reason it stands, the sources with their quotes and when they were last checked. Where sources disagree, or the question cannot be settled today, it says "open question" instead of choosing.
- **The Threats page shows the same behind each estimate's Sources button**: opening Sources now shows who said it, why, the quoted sources and the date they were last checked, with the newest statement first and the earlier one a click away. The page never averages the figures or picks one source. On a phone the Threats page shows the same, folded under "What each source says, in its own words" until you open it.
- **Every Library document shows one of six labels**: Released, Draft, Expired, Historical, Research Paper or Misc. On a computer, the Library page's Lifecycle filter lists the same six, and links shared with the old names (Published, Proposed, Superseded) still open and show the matching new label. On a phone, each document shows its label on its card and in its detail sheet.
- **Products whose PQC status is unknown no longer show a plain "Verified" badge**: a product whose evidence was reviewed but whose post-quantum status is unknown used to show the same green "Verified" badge as a product with confirmed PQC support, which read as "PQC verified". It now shows "Evidence reviewed: PQC unknown", with a tooltip saying that the cited evidence does not establish PQC support either way. Products with a known PQC status keep the plain Verified badge.
- **Extracted passages and obligations name "automated extraction" as their source**: the source-evidence drawer, the governance obligations on a Library document and the CSWP.39 requirements panel used to name the tool that extracted the text. They now say "automated extraction", and curated entries still read "human".
- **Confidential Computing & TEEs is back to its five TEE steps**: the module is now 60 minutes (it was 90 with the FHE material), has its five TEE steps, and points to the new Homomorphic Encryption module. Old links to the FHE workshop step or the FHE section open the new module. If you had finished the FHE step or read that section, it now counts in the new module, and if you had finished the five TEE steps the module now shows as complete.
- **Learning paths list Homomorphic Encryption after Confidential Computing & TEEs**: the developer, architect, researcher and IT ops paths include the new module right after Confidential Computing & TEEs, so each path's estimated time is 15 minutes longer, and the modules after it in the Hardware Infrastructure track move down one place.
- **Very long pages are saved smaller for search engines, without dropping anything**: search engines read only the first 2 MB of a page, and the saved copies of the Library (5.3 MB) and the Changelog (over 3 MB) had grown past that, with the Community page close behind (1.8 MB). Beyond the first items, the repeated list is now stored without presentation details, so the Library falls to about 1.2 MB with all 1,275 items and all 1,243 of their links kept, and the Changelog to about 1.5 MB. Every build checks that no link, heading or visible word was lost and stops if one was, and fails any saved page above 1.9 MB. What visitors see is unchanged.

### Fixed

- **The report keeps the frameworks you selected that apply to your industry and country**: the assessment report no longer leaves out frameworks you selected. Before, a framework could vanish from the compliance section if its industry or country was worded differently in our framework list than in the assessment questions: PCI DSS for banks, HIPAA for hospitals, FERPA for schools, and EU rules such as DORA for organizations in EU member countries. These now appear, and none that appeared before has been removed.
- **Typed search text is cleaned before our analytics events count it**: text typed into the Leaders search, the Migrate workbench asset search and the Timeline text filter is now cleaned before it is counted: email addresses, web addresses, IP addresses and long key-like strings are replaced and the rest is cut to 80 characters. A search term that also appears in the page address (the Leaders ?q=) can still be recorded by an automatic Google Analytics feature; the Terms page says so.
- **The page address we send to Google Analytics no longer includes anything after a "?"**: our page views and events used to carry the full address, including a Leaders search term and the data in a shared-report link. They now carry only the site and the page path, and the same applies to the previous page. Two automatic Google Analytics features (site search and navigation tracking) read the browser's own address instead and can still record text after a "?"; the Terms page says so.
- **Highlight links tint only the algorithm named**: a link that highlights 3DES no longer also highlights DES, and ML-KEM-768 no longer tints its composite variants.
- **The Entropy Evidence Lab shows the recorded commands without local file paths**: the command shown for the Mac baseline dataset used to include a local temporary folder path, and the dataset list named where its private source file is kept. Local paths are now reduced to the file name (board paths, which are part of the recorded procedure, stay). The datasets and their hashes are unchanged.
- **The PQC Assistant can link to every Learn module and every business planning tool**: the assistant used to be given typed lists, 51 Learn modules and 17 of the 37 planning tools, so it could not point you to the rest. Its lists and its counts (73 modules, 37 planning tools, and 58 Crypto Lab tools: 34 that run in the browser and 24 that need the Docker sandbox) now come from the same registries the pages use, with no typed numbers, so a new module or tool is available to it as soon as it exists.
- **The assistant's links use the exact filter values on the Algorithms, Threats, Timeline, Leaders and OpenSSL pages**: the PQC Assistant's links now use the exact filter values those pages accept, including the Skeptic/Critic category on Community and the MENA region on the Timeline. It also links to the Sponsor, Editorial Independence, Revisions and Navigate pages.
- **More leaders appear when you filter the Community page by region**: leaders whose country is spelled another way in our data ("United States", "United Kingdom", Brazil, Estonia, Norway and others) used to drop out of the region filter and of region links: 95 of 402 were missing, including NIST's Dustin Moody and Lily Chen. They now appear under Americas, Europe and the other regions, and those countries have flags.
- **Twelve more Learn modules can be found through search**: CBOM, SBOM, SLH-DSA, PQC GRC, Skills and team structure, SOC implementation for PQC, the CycloneDX cryptography registry, cryptographic management modernization, MLS group messaging, PKI enrollment protocols, PQC candidates and lifecycle, and decommissioning and program closure were in the Learn catalog but missing from the pages search engines read, so their addresses could not be found. Each now has its own title and description, with its real duration and level.
- **Each Learn module page's study time matches the module**: the study time published for search engines disagreed with the module's own duration on 44 of 60 pages (for example the vendor-risk page said 90 minutes where the module says 30, and the quantum-threats page said 60 where the module says 40), and one module had none. Each figure now comes from the module itself.
- **Learn, Explore and the home page quote the real number of modules**: the titles and descriptions of Learn and Explore, the Learn course data and the home page's feature list said 62 modules, and the course's total study time was a typed number. All of them now come from the module pages themselves, so adding a module updates them everywhere.
- **The Business Tools page description quotes the real number of tools**: in search results it said "34 interactive business planning tools"; there are 37, and the number now comes from the tool list.
- **The Migrate page's search description says 9 infrastructure layers, as the page groups them**: it used to say 7 technology layers.
- **Clicking anywhere on a Crypto Lab card opens its preview again**: the card opens the preview when clicked anywhere, not only on the Preview button. The tool name stays a real link to the tool's page, and following it does not also open the preview.
- **Long workshop titles no longer overflow the page header**: on narrow screens a long title pushed the buttons beside it off the screen in the PKCS#11 HSM playground, the KMIP control plane and the Learn workshops. The title is shortened with an ellipsis again.

### Data

- **Library documents carry their lifecycle label**: 975 more documents now show Released, Draft, Expired, Historical, Research Paper or Misc instead of an unset status.
- **The Threats page's BSI, NSA and ANSSI entries now point at the current statements**: the saved copies behind the three entries match the renamed entries (BSI TR-02102-1 of January 2026, the NSA's 2022 announcement with its December 2024 FAQ, and ANSSI's current FAQ), each with its address and checksum.
- **Library dates and status corrected**: the three parts of the TCG TPM 2.0 specification, version 185, now show as published instead of draft; thirteen "last updated" dates and one first-publication date were corrected to the documents' own dates (for example IBM Quantum Safe Research, the UK NCSC PQC whitepaper, Signal's PQXDH specification, RFC 9901 and the NIST CMVP lists); and the tfhe-rs, Lattigo, OpenFHE and fhe.rs entries now point to the Homomorphic Encryption module, so its References tab lists them.
- **Migrate catalog corrections for 13 products**: versions, release and proof-publication dates, PQC support wording, verification status and proof links were corrected after review. WhatsApp and Azure Dedicated HSM now cite their current proof documents, the WhatsApp Encryption Overview white paper (Version 9, February 2026) and the Thales Luna HSM firmware 7.9.2 release notes.
- **Trust tiers of 20 sources corrected**: after review, 20 sources moved to the tier that fits them (for example 4 from Core to Authoritative and 6 from Core to Supporting), which changes the trust level shown next to the assistant's citations and feeds the trust scores shown on the Library, Compliance, Threats and Algorithms pages.
- **One Timeline source date corrected**: a timeline entry's source date now matches its source.

CHG:4.152.0.full: A mistyped or outdated address now shows a clear "Page not found" page instead of the home page; on phones every page has one main heading, shared Library links keep their status filter and the About page explains analytics; and the Simulation offers the new Homomorphic Encryption module.
CHG:4.152.0.release_notes:
A mistyped or outdated address now shows a clear "Page not found" page instead of the home page; on phones every page has one main heading, shared Library links keep their status filter and the About page explains analytics; and the Simulation offers the new Homomorphic Encryption module.

### Added

- **The Simulation offers the Homomorphic Encryption module**: the "Defense-in-Depth & Data-at-Rest Strategy" activity (phase 5) now lists Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody as an optional deep dive next to Confidential Computing, where this material used to sit, and the module opens inside the Simulation instead of leaving it. It is optional, so what you need to finish the activity and your maturity results are unchanged.

### Changed

- **An unknown address shows "Page not found"**: a mistyped or outdated address used to take you to the home page without telling you anything was wrong. It now shows a "Page not found" page with links to the main sections, and search engines are told not to index it. Links to pages that exist, including embedded and older addresses, work as before.

### Fixed

- **Each page on a phone has exactly one main heading**: on a phone, the "PQC Today" header was marked as a main heading on top of each page's own title, so screen readers and search engines found two on almost every page. Each page now has one, its own title. The Crypto-Agility Control Plane tool page could also show a second one while its in-browser engine started; that is fixed too. Pages on a computer are unchanged.
- **On a phone, a shared Library link keeps its status filter**: a Library link that names a status (one of the six labels, or an older name such as Published) now narrows the list on a phone as it does on a computer, with a Status chip to remove it. The phone used to ignore it.

CHG:4.153.0.full: The Report now says which compliance frameworks are binding and which are guidance, phone visitors see the page they asked for instead of a role question, and the Merkle Tree Certificates workshop proves the tree you built.
CHG:4.153.0.release_notes:
The Report now says which compliance frameworks are binding and which are guidance, phone visitors see the page they asked for instead of a role question, and the Merkle Tree Certificates workshop proves the tree you built.

### Added

- **The Report separates laws from guidance**: for the frameworks from your own country's bodies, the Report no longer calls them all "Mandatory". Each one now sits under Binding (a law, regulation or enforceable rule that applies to organisations like yours), Guidance and drafts (recommendations, goals and drafts nobody is required to follow), or Not yet classified, and the same label appears beside each framework you selected. 171 of the 191 active frameworks are classified so far; the other 20 stay Not yet classified until their documents settle, and a blank is never treated as guidance.

### Fixed

- **On a phone, the page you asked for opens straight away**: a first-time visitor on a phone used to be asked "Who's asking?" on every page before seeing anything. The role picker now takes over the home page only. Every other page opens normally with a one-line "Pick your role" prompt above it, which you can dismiss for good. Visitors who have already chosen a role, and the computer layout, are unchanged.
- **Merkle Tree Certificates: the proof steps now use the tree you built**: in the Learn workshop, Step 2 (Inclusion Proof) and Step 3 (Verify Proof) used to start from eight sample certificates even after you built your own tree in Step 1. They now prove and verify the certificates you added, with a note that your tree is loaded. If you skip Step 1, they say so and use the sample set. Resetting the workshop clears the tree.

### Security

- **Dependency updates**: the HTML sanitising library (DOMPurify) moves from 3.4.13 to 3.4.16.

CHG:4.154.0.full: The OT & Industrial Control Systems module now shows the three ways attackers reach a plant, and its Zone & Conduit Planner separates firmware signing from command authentication and adds industrial IoT.
CHG:4.154.0.release_notes:
The OT & Industrial Control Systems module now shows the three ways attackers reach a plant, and its Zone & Conduit Planner separates firmware signing from command authentication and adds industrial IoT.

### Added

- **OT attack surface: three paths in**: a new Learn section shows how attackers reach industrial control systems. They move from the office network through the industrial DMZ into the plant, come in over remote access and internet-connected industrial IoT devices, or get on site, where most installed field equipment accepts commands from anyone. Each path gets its own fix, from separate OT accounts and a guarded DMZ to hybrid post-quantum key exchange on remote links and classical authentication at the field level. The December 2015 Ukraine grid attack is worked through as an example that used all three paths.

### Changed

- **Zone & Conduit Planner: industrial IoT and command authentication**: the planner adds an "IIoT & cloud connectors" zone on its own segment next to the industrial DMZ, and shows a cloud link that skips the DMZ as a connection that should not exist. Each zone now has separate settings for firmware and project signing and for command authentication; controllers and field devices start with unauthenticated commands, which the planner flags as a gap to fix today rather than a quantum risk. Every conduit is labelled with its attack path and can be filtered by it. The exercise on zone ranking is now "Where attacks start vs where they hurt".
- **IoT module: where industrial IoT sits in a plant**: a short note explains that industrial IoT gateways should connect through the plant's industrial DMZ, and links to the new OT section.

### Data

- **Four new OT security documents in the Library**: CISA's 2026 study "Barriers to Secure OT Communication: Why Johnny Can't Authenticate", the CISA, FBI, EPA and DOE fact sheet "Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology", CISA advisory AA21-131A on the 2021 pipeline ransomware incident, and CISA's alert on the 2015 attack on Ukrainian power distribution.

CHG:4.155.0.full: Certification engineers now start the Library on the documents their work depends on, the Glossary gains twelve terms for module validation, the Timeline records when FIPS 140-2 validations move to NIST's historical list, and the Migrate page no longer shows certificates that belong to other products.
CHG:4.155.0.release_notes:
Certification engineers now start the Library on the documents their work depends on, the Glossary gains twelve terms for module validation, the Timeline records when FIPS 140-2 validations move to NIST's historical list, and the Migrate page no longer shows certificates that belong to other products.

### Added

- **Twelve Glossary terms for module validation and certification**: entropy source validation, known-answer test, cryptographic algorithm self-test, pairwise consistency test, sensitive security parameter, security policy, cryptographic boundary, Protection Profile, Security Target, target of evaluation, the CMVP Modules In Process list and the testing laboratory. Each definition is taken from the NIST or Common Criteria document it cites, with the section and page given, and the Modules In Process entry notes that appearing on the list does not imply or guarantee FIPS 140 validation.
- **Timeline: FIPS 140-2 validations move to NIST's historical list**: a new entry records NIST's statement that FIPS 140-2 validations move to the historical list on 21 September 2026, and that the CMVP still supports buying and using those modules for existing systems.

### Changed

- **The Library opens on certification documents for certification engineers**: the three starting documents are now the FIPS 140-3 implementation guidance for post-quantum cryptography, the CMVP Management Manual and NIST's public ACVP reference samples, in place of three documents chosen by citation count.
- **Migrate: certificates that belong to other products are gone**: Bouncy Castle Java LTS, Google Cloud HSM, Citrix Virtual Apps and Desktops and Cisco IOS XR no longer list a certificate that belongs to a different product, and each row says which one. STSAFE-V100-TPM now shows its FIPS 140-3 certificate, which names the same module under its former name. The Oracle OpenSSL FIPS Provider is shown as CAVP-validated, because its only FIPS 140-3 certificate covers the OpenSSL 3.0.7 build on Oracle Linux 9, not the 3.5.4 provider. The page now counts 84 FIPS 140-3 certified products and 53 that are CAVP-validated only.

### Data

- **Twenty certification-programme documents filed under Compliance & Certification**: NIST's CMVP, CAVP, ACVP and entropy-validation pages, the CMVP and entropy-validation certificates, ISO/IEC 15408-1, NIAP and two protection-profile documents now appear under Compliance & Certification, where they were previously hidden from the certification view unless you searched for them.

CHG:4.156.0.full: The Homomorphic Encryption module is reorganised into nine sections and gains measured key-streaming results, workshop views and sourced sections on operations, standards and market position; the Library gains thirteen primary papers behind it. The Executive's first Library suggestion shows the right document, two Migrate rows describe their certification and post-quantum status accurately, and a bundled sanitiser library is brought up to date.
CHG:4.156.0.release_notes:
The Homomorphic Encryption module is reorganised into nine sections and gains measured key-streaming results, workshop views and sourced sections on operations, standards and market position; the Library gains thirteen primary papers behind it. The Executive's first Library suggestion shows the right document, two Migrate rows describe their certification and post-quantum status accurately, and a bundled sanitiser library is brought up to date.

### Added

- **New hands-on workshop step: FHE concepts**: four interactive views, namely noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, a program turned into an FHE circuit, and key streaming with a chunk-size control backed by measured times.
- **CKKS evaluation keys scale when streamed, measured on Mac and MX95 boards**: an HSM token produced the full 3.94 GB bootstrappable key set as 1,001 bounded calls, never holding more than about 16 MB. On one MX95 core this took about 8 minutes; it was limited by the CPU, not the network. Chunk size trades memory for time, and every limb matched the reference exactly.
- **Decryption results are noisy: how to read them, and the decryption limits**: CKKS gives approximate fixed-point values that you read by rounding, while TFHE decrypts exactly. Explains why anyone allowed to ask for decryption can recover the key, what the HSM's decryption policy controls, and the value and limits of threshold decryption, all with sources.
- **Where FHE is used, what it costs, and how it is positioned**: use cases ranked by evidence (in production for private lookups; peer-reviewed or pilots for genomics, biometrics, AI inference and financial crime); compute overhead next to enclaves, MPC, differential privacy and federated learning; GPU, FPGA, chip and algorithm speedups; and FHE's market position among privacy technologies, with analyst estimates labelled.
- **Standards and compliance status of FHE**: no FHE scheme is FIPS-approved, in CNSA 2.0 or Common Criteria-certified, and ISO/IEC 28033 is still in ballot. What can be validated today is the conventional cryptography around FHE.
- **Operations, encoding and turning programs into FHE circuits**: what CKKS, TFHE and BFV/BGV support natively, how inputs are encoded and results decoded, why programs must avoid secret-dependent branches, and which compilers automate the conversion.

### Changed

- **FHE module reorganised into nine sections in learning order**: what FHE is and what "fully homomorphic" does and does not promise; schemes, data types and noisy results; where FHE is used; what it costs; keys; quantum; standards and compliance; the HSM's role; implementations. Each section opens with key takeaways, and one grouped reference list closes the page.

### Fixed

- **The Executive's first "Start here" suggestion in the Library shows the right document**: the card now names NIST CSWP 39, Considerations for Achieving Cryptographic Agility, with its status, instead of a retired entry with a different title.

### Data

- **Thirteen primary papers on homomorphic encryption**: the CKKS and TFHE scheme papers; the two CKKS bootstrapping papers behind the Lattigo library; the Li-Micciancio decryption-oracle attack on CKKS and the differential-privacy countermeasure; the later attacks on exact schemes (BFV, BGV, TFHE) and on threshold decryption; the chosen-ciphertext and verifiability papers; and a preliminary threshold-FHE document. Each entry gives the authors, dates and venue as the IACR archive page shows them and links to the homomorphic-encryption module. Eleven name a peer-reviewed venue; one is a preprint and one shows no venue.
- **Migrate: Google Cloud HSM and Bouncy Castle Java say only what their sources say**: Google Cloud HSM's text no longer calls it a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 service that supports ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; Google's pages say FIPS 140-2 Level 3, with a quantum-safe Cloud HSM listed for 2028. Bouncy Castle Java's certification line now says the validated module is the separate BC-FJA, FIPS 140-3 Level 1, certificate #4943, version 2.1.1. The Migrate counts do not change.

### Security

- **Dependency updates**: the code editor package carried its own older copy of the DOMPurify sanitising library (3.4.8) with five published advisories; it now uses 3.4.16, the same as the rest of the site.

CHG:4.157.0.full: Bouncy Castle's three Migrate rows move to the current releases, the Singapore handbook draft is backed by its own saved copy, and a broken Timeline source link is repaired.
CHG:4.157.0.release_notes:
Bouncy Castle's three Migrate rows move to the current releases, the Singapore handbook draft is backed by its own saved copy, and a broken Timeline source link is repaired.

### Fixed

- **A broken source link on the Timeline is repaired**: the Australian ASD milestone on quantum-vulnerable algorithms (Diffie-Hellman, ECDH, ECDSA and RSA not approved beyond 2030) linked to a web page that no longer exists. It now links to the June 2025 Guidelines for cryptography PDF it describes.

### Data

- **Migrate: Bouncy Castle at the current releases**: Java moves to 1.86 (announced 15 September 2026), Java LTS to 2.73.13 (22 September) and C# .NET to 2.7.0 (7 August), each with the vendor's own announcement as the proof page. The capability text now matches those announcements: C# .NET 2.7.0 adds hybrid ML-KEM key exchange and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA authentication for TLS 1.3, Java 1.86 names post-quantum and hybrid key encapsulation across CMS/S-MIME, HPKE and TLS, and the Java LTS row no longer says composite signatures are unconfirmed. The Migrate counts do not change.
- **Singapore Quantum-Safe Handbook: the draft is backed by the draft**: the Library entry for the October 2025 draft for public consultation shared a saved file with the final V1 handbook of 16 July 2026. It now has its own copy of the draft; the entry for the final handbook is unchanged.

CHG:4.158.0.full: The Homomorphic Encryption module corrects its figures for releasing CKKS results to others and adds key rotation and shared decryption as interactive views. The certificate records behind Compliance and Migrate are refreshed, six classical-only FIPS 140-3 modules show their certificates again, and twelve NIST certification documents in the Library carry checked details.
CHG:4.158.0.release_notes:
The Homomorphic Encryption module corrects its figures for releasing CKKS results to others and adds key rotation and shared decryption as interactive views. The certificate records behind Compliance and Migrate are refreshed, six classical-only FIPS 140-3 modules show their certificates again, and twelve NIST certification documents in the Library carry checked details.

### Added

- **Key rotation and shared decryption as interactive views**: a step-through of replacing an HSM key without decrypting stored data (who may start it, what the token refuses, 31.5 MB key, about 1.5 bits of precision lost, old key no longer decrypts), and a two-board shared-decryption view with switches for "approvals independent" and "noise on or off" that show the measured outcome. Both are in the workshop and in the HSM flow diagrams.
- **Releasing CKKS results to others: the corrected result at a thin margin**: with the published noise sizing, today's default parameters cannot release results to third parties, while a second parameter set (higher-precision bootstrapping, scale 2^90) keeps 11.1–11.4 bits against a bar of 10, on a Mac and with the token on both MX95 boards, for programs of 0, 1 and 3 multiplications after a refresh. The margin is about 1 bit; the section says so, and states the costs: refreshes take about twice as long, 3 multiplications fit between refreshes instead of 9, and the key set is about 12 % larger.
- **Cross-checks against OpenFHE, Microsoft SEAL and TFHE-rs**: OpenFHE's own CKKS keys at comparable 128-bit settings take 80 keys and 13.26 GB, and keys in Lattigo's layout ran in OpenFHE with equal precision; Lattigo decrypted all seven SEAL ciphertexts exactly as SEAL did; TFHE-rs 1.8.1 reproduced 28 of its 36 published test vectors byte for byte on the Mac and both boards (the other 8 differ in floating-point rounding but are identical across our platforms and decrypt correctly).

### Changed

- **Key streaming on the MX95 boards is 2–6 times faster**: the full 3.94 GB key set takes 214 s on one MX95 core (was 473 s) and 72–84 s on six MX95 Pro cores (was 451 s on one core), byte-identical. The cost is token memory, 65–124 MB instead of about 16 MB, or about 16 MB at twice the time with the cache off. Still limited by the CPU, at about half of a 1 Gb/s link. The key-streaming view shows runs before and after.
- **Shared decryption across two boards: what it gives and what it does not**: joint keys bootstrap at 24.3–24.5 bits against 24.9 for one key, at about 4.1 GB uploaded per token. A crafted request to one token still returns that token's whole share, so the two approvals must be independent. Notes a 2026 preprint reporting attacks on t-of-N threshold decryption.
- **HSM steps of the CKKS scenario show "in engine"**: key generation, evaluation-key export, public key, decryption under policy and release are now shown as built, citing the merged commits.

### Fixed

- **Figures for releasing CKKS results to others corrected**: an earlier version of the module (and its measurement records) quoted 22.6–22.8 bits for the second parameter set. Those runs used a noise width about 10 bits narrower than the published analysis requires; the figures are corrected above and the old records are marked as superseded.
- **What was measured with OpenFHE is stated accurately**: the module said or implied that CKKS evaluation-key sizes had been measured with OpenFHE. It now says OpenFHE v1.6.0 CKKS was measured separately on 2026-10-11 and that the HSM's own key set has not been run in OpenFHE.
- **Run logs listed in the measurement records can be opened**: eight log files were listed but not published; they are now available as text files, and a test checks that every listed file is published.

### Security

- **Dependency updates**: the maths library that the diagram package (Mermaid) uses, KaTeX, moves from 0.16.47 to 0.18.2, which closes its open advisory (prototype pollution that could bypass the trust option). One open security alert on a logging helper (sprintf-js), which has no published fix and is not part of the deployed site, was reviewed and dismissed as accepted risk.

### Data

- **New measurement records for homomorphic encryption**: faster board streaming, the second parameter set on the Mac and both MX95 boards at the corrected noise sizing, key rotation, the two-token threshold run, and the OpenFHE, SEAL and TFHE-rs reference runs. Each record names the commits it was measured at; Mac runs are labelled as reference runs.
- **Compliance: certificate records refreshed**: 38 new records (19 FIPS 140-3 module validations dated 28 September to 10 October, and 19 algorithm validations that include ML-KEM or ML-DSA), no removals, and three status changes: two FIPS 140-3 modules (Palo Alto PAN-OS and Apple corecrypto v12.0) move to Historical and one Common Criteria record to Archived. NIST's list of modules in process grows from 197 to 204 and its implementations-under-test list from 229 to 234.
- **Migrate: certificate links brought up to date**: 17 new algorithm validations are linked (AWS-LC, Apple, OpenSSL, Thales CipherTrust and others) and four superseded links are retired. Six classical-only FIPS 140-3 modules (CGI Momentum, CTERA, HID Global, Radiant Logic, Tellabs Panorama PON Manager and Trend Micro) show their certificates again, labelled as having no post-quantum algorithms. Oracle OpenSSL FIPS Provider and NetApp CryptoMod now show "module in process", because NIST lists their modules.
- **Twelve NIST certification documents in the Library carry checked details**: the entropy-validation program page and its announcements, five entropy certificates, two module certificates, the module-package page, the automated validation workstream and the NCCoE automation project now state the correct title, publisher, status and last-update date; first-published dates are left empty where the page gives none.
- **Singapore Quantum-Safe Migration Handbook entry names its document**: the Library entry for Singapore's final handbook (Version 1, 16 July 2026, by CSA, GovTech and IMDA) now carries that title, those authors and those dates; before, it carried a different title and a last-update date of 2024.

CHG:4.159.0.full: The Homomorphic Encryption module adds the HSM key set running in OpenFHE and an encrypted risk-scoring service, its workshop now works on phones and its HSM scenario shows what the engine already does; the build now pins the compiled engine files the site ships and fails loudly when one differs.
CHG:4.159.0.release_notes:
The Homomorphic Encryption module adds the HSM key set running in OpenFHE and an encrypted risk-scoring service, its workshop now works on phones and its HSM scenario shows what the engine already does; the build now pins the compiled engine files the site ships and fails loudly when one differs.

### Added

- **The HSM's own key set now works in OpenFHE**: a third CKKS parameter set follows OpenFHE's own 128-bit settings, so the 79 keys the token streams out (6.56 GB in 17.8 s on a Mac) bootstrap in OpenFHE with no keys of its own, at the same precision (13.28 bits against 13.20 with OpenFHE's keys). Results go to the data owner only, and it has not run on the boards yet.
- **An encrypted risk-scoring service, measured end to end**: a reference service scores 32,768 customers' encrypted credit records per request in about 200 ms and ranks them exactly as the plaintext model does (AUC 0.717298 against 0.717299, the same decision for every customer). It accepts only token-signed keys, uses post-quantum TLS 1.3 with a client certificate, never holds a secret key, and only the data owner can read a score. Its limits are stated alongside: test certificates, one tenant, memory only, one Mac.

### Changed

- **The Homomorphic Encryption workshop now works on phones**: the Workshop tab opens on a phone instead of the "not built for mobile yet" note. All eight HSM flow scenarios step through to the end, the key-rotation and shared-decryption views respond to touch, and the six concept views open and work, with no horizontal scrolling.
- **"What can run in the HSM?" shows what the merged engine already does**: five steps that said "planned" now say "in engine today": key generation, streaming the evaluation-key set as bounded calls, the application's decrypt request, decryption under policy, and the release. The streaming step now states the second parameter set (4.41 GB in 1,201 calls, generated in 96.9 s on the MX95 Pro and 99.2 s on the MX95), the 31.5 MB rotation key that only the security officer may request, and that the key generator is frozen, so the same seed gives the same bytes. Shared decryption and replication stay "planned"; homomorphic evaluation inside the HSM stays "refused by design".
- **Corrected OpenFHE key count**: the cross-check now says that OpenFHE's bootstrapping needs 79 keys (13.09 GB); the 80 keys and 13.26 GB reported earlier included one test rotation.

### Security

- **The engine files the site ships are pinned**: the site contains 18 compiled engine files (OpenSSL, strongSwan and the PKCS#11 engines, in 6 bundles). Their checksums and sizes are now recorded in a lock list, and the build fails, naming the bundle and file, if one changes, goes missing or is added without being listed. The KMIP engine's record now names its seven generated files instead of a whole folder that also holds code written here. Four existing checks that used to skip quietly when the HSM project is not checked out next to the site now fail with a clear message unless skipping is switched on deliberately. The leak scan of the source and of the built site that was added after 4.158.0 runs on every build.

CHG:4.16.0.full: A cross-page accuracy and trust release touching Report, Business tools, Revisions, Changelog, FAQ, Playground, OpenSSL Studio, Terms, About, and Migrate: shared report links now show the sender's real score, breach-cost defaults finally agree across three business tools, the revisions feed surfaces corrections that were previously invisible, the Playground and OpenSSL Studio get clearer status indicators and fewer dead ends, the Migrate workbench now shows which products are still awaiting verification proof, and several dead links and stale numbers are fixed across the site.
CHG:4.16.0.release_notes:
A cross-page accuracy and trust release touching Report, Business tools, Revisions, Changelog, FAQ, Playground, OpenSSL Studio, Terms, About, and Migrate: shared report links now show the sender's real score, breach-cost defaults finally agree across three business tools, the revisions feed surfaces corrections that were previously invisible, the Playground and OpenSSL Studio get clearer status indicators and fewer dead ends, the Migrate workbench now shows which products are still awaiting verification proof, and several dead links and stale numbers are fixed across the site.

### Fixed

- **Shared and example report links now show the exact score the sender saw**: previously, opening a shared link recomputed the score from scratch, so a scoring-logic update after a link was shared could silently show the recipient a different result than the sender intended. Older links already in circulation still open, now with a note that they're an approximate view.
- **Viewing someone else's shared report can no longer overwrite your own saved assessment**: a partial safeguard only covered visitors who already had a saved assessment; first-time visitors opening a shared link were having their own (not-yet-started) assessment silently populated with the sender's data. Every input a shared report displays — industry, country, current cryptography, persona, and more — is now drawn strictly from the sender's snapshot.
- **ROI and vendor-risk figures now flag when they're using default estimates**: the fast-track assessment path skips some inputs (like vendor dependency), so those sections were quietly falling back to neutral assumptions with no indication. They now show a "uses default estimates" note.
- **Breach-probability defaults now agree across the ROI Calculator, Breach Cost Model, and Cost of Inaction tools**: two of the three tools were using an unsourced flat 15% instead of the sourced, size-tiered default (from Cyentia's 2025 breach research) the site had already adopted elsewhere, so the same organization could get three different breach-cost estimates depending which tool they used. All three now share one sourced default, with a simple small/average/large organization picker to adjust it.
- **Fixed a stale year in the ROI Calculator's source citation**: it cited a 2024 report; the figures themselves were already the 2025 update.
- **The Roadmap Builder now cites the actual federal order and deadlines behind the PQC transition mandate**: added a sourced callout with the order number and both key-establishment and signature deadlines, verified against the official published text.
- **The "data" category on the Revisions feed was invisible**: a filtering bug hid every entry logged under the data-corrections category (28 entries) from the page entirely; it's now visible like every other category, and empty categories now auto-hide instead of sitting there as a dead click.
- **The Revisions feed was missing about seven weeks of real corrections**: several dataset updates had shipped without being logged. Backfilled with accurate before/after summaries tied to the actual changes, and the feed's signature was re-verified.
- **Freshness date labels on the Changelog page were showing the wrong file's date**: a pattern-matching bug meant some "last updated" chips (Compliance, Timeline) skipped past the newest snapshot to an older one. Also fixed the Software freshness chip, which had been pointing at a renamed file and so never appeared at all.
- **Cleaned up mislabeled role tags on several changelog entries** so each one now correctly routes to the researcher, developer, ops, or architect "For me" filter instead of a generic catch-all.
- **Fixed a dead reference link on the FAQ page**: a NIST document link had gone stale after the underlying reference was renamed; FAQ links to renamed references now resolve automatically instead of opening an empty page.
- **Merged two near-duplicate FAQ questions about the Cryptography Bill of Materials** into one clearer answer.
- **Fixed an inconsistent step count on the FAQ page**: the risk assessment wizard's step count was quoted as both 13 and 14 in different places; confirmed the real count (13) and made every mention match.
- **Fixed the project's GitHub repository name** where it had been quoted incorrectly.
- **Replaced a few exact module/document/product counts on the FAQ page with wording that won't go stale** (e.g. "dozens of modules" instead of a fixed number that was already out of date).
- **The Docker-based playground tool no longer shows a dead, unresponsive embedded window when the sandbox isn't reachable**: it now checks whether the sandbox is actually reachable and shows a clear "request access" link instead of a blank iframe pointed at a local address that only works for the sandbox's own operators.
- **Renamed the KMIP control-plane tool consistently across the Playground** so its name, banner, and page heading all match instead of showing three different names for the same tool.
- **Replaced a personal email link for sandbox-access requests with a trackable request form**.
- **Fixed OpenSSL Studio's documentation links**: every "view docs" link across all OpenSSL commands pointed at a broken or outdated page (wrong version, malformed URL); all now go to the correct, current OpenSSL documentation.
- **Removed a non-functional option from OpenSSL Studio's configuration-file helper command** that produced an "unknown option" error when used, and clarified that the command itself requires OpenSSL 3.6 or newer.
- **OpenSSL Studio's post-quantum key/signature tools now note the OpenSSL version they require** (3.5 or newer for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA), so it's clear up front rather than discovered via an error.
- **Fixed OpenSSL Studio's key-decapsulation example, which was using the wrong output flag** and silently producing empty results in some cases.
- **OpenSSL Studio now shows a clear error and retry option if the underlying engine fails to load**, instead of leaving the page stuck on "Initializing..." indefinitely.
- **Marked two OpenSSL Studio example commands as reference-only** since they use shell piping the in-browser tool can't run directly, and running them now shows a clear message instead of a confusing partial result.
- **Fixed the Terms page's binding-acceptance clause, which pointed to a retired mirror site that no longer resolves**: it now correctly references the live production site.
- **Added a table of contents with jump-to-section links to the Terms page**, plus a note on when the terms were last substantively updated.
- **Added plain-language summaries above the Terms page's export-control section and its "don't use generated keys in production" guidance**, so the legal text now has a plain-English preview.
- **The About page's platform statistics (module counts, dataset sizes, and similar figures) are now computed from the live data** instead of hand-typed numbers that could silently drift out of date as datasets grew.
- **Fixed an overstated "refreshed weekly" claim about compliance data on the About page**; it now shows the actual last-updated date.
- **Fixed the About page's "last security audit" date, which no longer matched the actual audit report it was describing**.
- **The About page's changelog link now navigates within the app instead of triggering a full page reload**.
- **The Migrate workbench now labels NIST IR 8547 as a draft** everywhere it's cited, rather than implying it's a finished standard.
- **Vendor roadmap entries in Migrate now show when they were last verified, plus a "new" or "updated" marker**, so it's clear how current each vendor's stated plans are.
- **Fixed a duplicate Migrate workbench address** that could show two different URLs for the same page; both now lead to the same place.
- **Each migration wave in the Migrate planner now explains why it's sequenced where it is**, and the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk term is explained in plain language the first time it appears.
- **Fixed a handful of product records in the migration catalog with inconsistent verification labels** so their status now displays correctly.

### Added

- **Search on the Changelog page**: a free-text box now filters entries by title and body, on top of the existing category and role filters.
- **Explanatory tooltips on the Changelog page's freshness indicators** clarifying what each date measures and what a stale marker means.
- **Filters by zone, phase, and audience on the Business tools grid**, in addition to the existing category and text search.
- **FAQ questions aimed at your role now float to the top of their section** with a small "For you" marker, when you've selected a persona (executive, developer, architect, ops, or researcher).
- **The Business Center's learning module list now collapses by default for advanced users**, keeping its header visible so it's a one-click expand rather than taking up space unasked.
- **The Playground's algorithm picker now shows a "Draft" badge with an explanatory tooltip for algorithms that aren't yet finalized standards**, so it's clear at a glance which selections are backup candidates rather than production-ready standards.
- **Executive-persona guidance banners added to three more Playground tools** (the interactive, HSM, and KMIP control-plane tools), pointing toward the business-focused Command Center and Compliance views instead of leaving executives on a developer-oriented tool.
- **Products in the Migrate workbench now show a verification badge and last-verified date**, and the page now tells you how many catalog entries are hidden because they're still awaiting verification proof, instead of leaving that count invisible.
- **The Migrate workbench's asset guidance is now tailored for executive and developer views**, highlighting the systems (cloud key management, TLS, code signing, databases) most relevant to each role instead of showing the same generic list to everyone.

CHG:4.160.0.full: Five certification modules now name the official document behind ten more of their statements. The Homomorphic Encryption module adds a two-round refresh that restores precision, runs the encrypted scoring service on an x86 machine and an MX95 Pro board, and generates the OpenFHE key set on both boards. The playground retires the Step-CA scenario, and the TPM emulator now comes from a tagged release.
CHG:4.160.0.release_notes:
Five certification modules now name the official document behind ten more of their statements. The Homomorphic Encryption module adds a two-round refresh that restores precision, runs the encrypted scoring service on an x86 machine and an MX95 Pro board, and generates the OpenFHE key set on both boards. The playground retires the Step-CA scenario, and the TPM emulator now comes from a tagged release.

### Added

- **Certification modules name their sources for ten more statements**: five modules now list the document that states each of these sentences:
  - PCI: the PCI SSC announcement of PIN Security Standard v3.1.
  - EUCC: ENISA's EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography page, the CMVP Management Manual, ENISA's 2024 State of Cybersecurity report and NIAP's CCEVS Policy 33.
  - FIPS 140-3: NIST's CMVP FIPS 140-3 standards page and a published CMVP certificate.
  - Product certification: NIST's CMVP FIPS 140-3 standards page and ETSI EN 319 411.
  - ACVP lab workflow: NIST's ACVP ML-DSA test specification.

  The module text is unchanged; only the reference lists grow.

- **OpenFHE's two-round refresh lifts precision from about 13 to about 32 bits with the HSM's own keys**: one refresh keeps 13.2 bits. Two rounds at OpenFHE's recommended setting give 21.1 bits, and the best setting gives 31.7–31.8 bits, close to a fresh ciphertext's 32.1. The cost is about twice the time and one level. This was measured on one Mac with one test input, not on a board.
- **The encrypted risk-scoring service runs on an x86 virtual machine and on an MX95 Pro board, with the token on a second board**: each batch scores 32,768 customers. A batch takes 277 ms on the virtual machine and 4.29 s on the MX95 Pro, about 21 times the Mac's 0.2 s. Peak memory is 1,311 MiB and 1,870 MiB. Both machines give identical scores (21.00 bits, AUC 0.717298). The runs use test certificates and a published test seed, so they show time, memory and correctness only.
- **The OpenFHE key set is also generated on both MX95 boards**: the token exports the 79-key, 6.56 GB set in 145 s on the MX95 and 142 s on the MX95 Pro. Streaming it to a Mac takes about 3 minutes. All 1,565 pieces match the reference and the token-signed manifest, and the token uses 89–91 MiB of memory.

### Changed

- **The Automated CA (Step-CA) sandbox scenario is retired**: the lab now issues post-quantum certificates with EJBCA and OpenBao. The playground lists 23 sandbox scenarios, and two Industry Landscape use cases no longer link to the retired one. Product entries that describe step-ca as a real product are unchanged.
- **The TPM playground's emulator is built from the pqctoday-tpm v0.10.1 release**: the browser emulator now comes from a tagged release, and the software bill of materials names it.
- **The Homomorphic Encryption figures say which refresh they mean**: "about 13 bits" now refers to the default single refresh. The release figure reads 30.5 bits with the exact scale applied, or 27.0 at face value. The scoring-service box covers three machines, and fact tables stack on phones.
- **Every engine the site ships is checked against its lock before release**: the check now also covers the TPM emulator, the LMS/HSS module and the entropy estimators, including their loader files. The engines built in pqctoday-hsm are pinned to their published release.

### Fixed

- **A Homomorphic Encryption record headline is corrected**: it no longer says the HSM's key set was never run in OpenFHE.
- **The playground lists the certificate-discovery lesson, and two lesson summaries match their lessons**: the OpenSSL Studio summary now says `openssl kdf` arrived in OpenSSL 3.0, and the TPM 2.0 summary uses the lesson's current wording.

### Data

- **Four new Library entries**:
  - the PCI PIN Security Standard v3.1 announcement;
  - ENISA's EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography page;
  - NIST's ACVP ML-DSA test specification;
  - NIST's CMVP FIPS 140-3 standards page.
- **Thirteen homomorphic-encryption papers in the Library are read in full**: their summaries, key points and search results now come from the complete paper, not its abstract page.
- **Three new homomorphic-encryption measurement records**: the two-round refresh, the scoring service on the MX95 Pro, and the scoring service on the x86 virtual machine. Two board records cover the key-set generation.

CHG:4.161.0.full: The site now links the exact source code of the version you are viewing and lists the licence of every third-party package and engine it ships. The repository no longer redistributes full copies of third-party documents, and one Library title is corrected.
CHG:4.161.0.release_notes:
The site now links the exact source code of the version you are viewing and lists the licence of every third-party package and engine it ships. The repository no longer redistributes full copies of third-party documents, and one Library title is corrected.

### Added

- **A "Source code" link on every page**: the footer links to the exact source of the version you are viewing, and the About page shows that link next to the version number.
- **Open-source licences at /licenses/**: the page gives the licence text of every npm package in the site's production bundle and a notices file for each WebAssembly engine. strongSwan is listed under GPL-2.0-or-later, with a link to its exact source.
- **Credit for adapted framework material**: Learn pages that adapt CC BY 4.0 framework material now credit it on the page.

### Changed

- **No more full copies of third-party documents in the repository**: the 11 reference PDFs and two copied texts are removed. A list now gives each one's publisher link and checksum, and our own extracted data stays. The KMIP test cases carry the OASIS notice.
- **How to contribute**: feedback is welcome through GitHub issues; code changes are made by the maintainer.

### Fixed

- **/report shows a sample report instead of an empty page**: visitors who have not run the assessment yet see the sample report, under a banner that marks it as a sample, with a button to start their own. Its link no longer changes between releases.
- **Two broken links fixed**: the SOC Implementation guide now links Quantum Threats, and the KMIP playground's "Docker sandbox" link opens the Docker sandbox.
- **A Library paper shows its correct title**: IACR ePrint 2010/560 is "On CCA-Secure Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption" (it read "Fully").

CHG:4.162.0.full: Each role now starts from its own questions and downloads (including a new operations pack for IT Ops), beginner pages keep their qualifiers, Library labels say what stage a document is at and how far to trust it, and 20 new certificates join the certification records. The Terms of Service now cover the website only.
CHG:4.162.0.release_notes:
Each role now starts from its own questions and downloads (including a new operations pack for IT Ops), beginner pages keep their qualifiers, Library labels say what stage a document is at and how far to trust it, and 20 new certificates join the certification records. The Terms of Service now cover the website only.

### Added

- **Engineering migration plan download**: developer and IT ops reports can download one ZIP with the algorithm backlog, the products you bookmarked (each with its FIPS state, whether its post-quantum algorithms are inside the certificate, and an evidence link), your latest saved Crypto API Refactor Audit, and a release test checklist.
- **Language runtimes table**: a new tab shows, for Go, Python, .NET, Java, Windows, OpenSSL and Bouncy Castle, which of ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each supports, from which version, with an official source and the date it was checked.
- **An architecture pack in the Command Center**: download your scope, saved architecture artifacts, decision records and test plan as one Markdown or PDF document. Sections you haven't produced yet are listed, and each cited Library source shows its current status.
- **A three-step quick run on the KMIP Migration tab**: create a signing key by name, change the policy, use the key again, and compare the old and new key. You can copy the result, which states its limits: an in-browser software token and a committee-draft protocol.
- **An operations pack for IT Ops**: the Command Center now builds one document for a change board or on-call team from what you have saved: scope, renewal and refresh windows, HSM and certificate capacity, configuration fragments, roadmap, deployment playbook, a VPN rehearsal, test plan, KPI thresholds and closure evidence, each with its review status. Missing sections link to the tool that produces them. Download it as Markdown, PDF, or a zip that adds every table as a CSV.
- **Save results to the operations pack**: the HSM and certificate capacity calculators, the SSH and TLS config generators and the VPN simulator can save their current result into the pack. Capacity plans mark each rate as an estimate or a value you entered; VPN runs can be saved only with the settings that established the tunnel.
- **FHE key custody over KMIP**: the Homomorphic Encryption lesson adds two runs with the key custodian on a separate hardware token reached over KMIP — an encrypted risk-scoring service (32,768 customers per batch, the same scores as the earlier run) and a TFHE loan pre-qualification (1,016 applicants, no mismatches) — and explains how the lab's HSM serves FHE keys as vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms and which refused decryptions spend the budget.
- **Record a lesson as an architecture decision**: the Hybrid Cryptography, KMS, HSM and PKI Workshop lessons end with a link that opens the decision-record editor on the matching template.
- **Save what a TLS demo run showed**: after a run, one button downloads a small file with the settings, the negotiated cipher, key exchange and signature, whether the key exchange was post-quantum, the byte counts and round trips, and what the run does not prove. Nothing is uploaded.
- **Download a record of what you ran**: the SP 800-90A DRBG check, Entropy Testing, Source Combining and the Entropy Evidence Lab can now save a JSON record of each run: the site version and commit, every test case and negative control, the test vectors used, and what the run does not prove. The Library can export your bookmarks or the current list as BibTeX or CSL-JSON for a citation manager.
- **Sources on beginner home facts**: facts on the Curious home boards can link to the document behind them; the "who decides" card links each row to FIPS 203, the NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ and the PQC Community page.
- **Evidence bundle and research workspace**: save a run from the DRBG, Entropy Testing, Source Combining and Entropy Evidence tools to your evidence and download a bundle: a zip of your saved runs with a list of what is missing. A saved research question, a claim table (fact, estimate, scenario or recommendation, with supporting and contrary sources) and a side-by-side comparison of two saved runs of the same tool travel with the bundle, and a reviewer can open it read-only. The workspace is best on a larger screen, and a collection cannot yet be restored from a re-imported bundle.
- **Library collections and "Changed since you saved"**: keep a note on each record in a collection, and a list flags records whose revision, stage, replacement or removal changed since you saved them.
- **Follow Library documents by research topic**: follow and filter documents by 12 research topics. The topic filter stays hidden until documents are tagged.
- **The source of every figure in the board pack**: the Board Pack and the GRC Compliance Pack now list every figure they state with whether it is a fact, an estimate, a scenario or a recommendation, where it comes from, how it was worked out, its date and what to bear in mind before quoting it. A figure with no published source is still shown, marked as an estimate with no published source.
- **How each answer moved your risk score**: "How this was calculated" has a second table showing, for each question, how many points the score would change had you answered "don't know", largest first, and where each value came from. It appears only when your stored answers reproduce the report's score.
- **Executive boards lead with one next step**: each of the six board questions shows one next step and one "after that" link, with the rest under a collapsed "More for this question". Progress labels name decisions: Briefed, Mandated, Funded, Governing.
- **The Simulation says how long a run takes**: the landing states the length of the Executive Overview and the intro, what a finished run gives you (a maturity score, a run grade and a roadmap you can save), and every board screen shows whether it uses sample data or your assessment.

### Changed

- **Each role starts from its own questions**: in the Command Center, developers open on four engineering questions and a tool sequence, GRC on what applies, who owns each control, what evidence is missing and how exceptions close, and researchers on four research questions — instead of board questions and return on investment.
- **Command Center for architects**: opens on four architecture questions (dependencies, transition mode, key custody, the KMIP rekey) and a link to the architecture learning path. "Start Executive Learning" now shows only to executives.
- **Review status without WIP logos**: WIP logos are removed from modules and workshops, including the PKCS#11 workshop. Review badges still say whether a person or an automated agent approved an LLM-drafted change.
- **Playground and Threats say what you are looking at**: the Playground counts in-browser tools and Docker scenarios separately. The Mosca calculator marks its default result as example values until you enter your own.
- **Plainer time and filter labels**: home boards give hours with units ("6 hours 20 minutes of essentials, not the full 39¾ hours"). Filters read "All selected" when nothing is filtered out.
- **Report downloads that fit the role**: developer and IT ops reports offer "Download report (PDF)" and "Export CSV"; GRC's "Compliance Pack ZIP" adds a spreadsheet of every framework in scope for your country and sector, with why it applies, its binding status, whether it requires PQC, the cited basis and the source; researchers no longer see the executive brief and board pack.
- **GRC's example report is a full assessment**: the worked example GRC is pointed to now answers the comprehensive questions, so its HNDL/HNFL windows and domain scores are filled in.
- **Leadership and GRC modules share a "Governance & Risk" track**: risk management, PQC GRC, compliance strategy, governance, vendor risk, verification & closure and the other leadership modules used to carry an "Executive" badge, even on the GRC learning path. The track is now named for its topic.
- **Researchers start from the evidence**: the researcher home points to recent standards changes instead of the readiness assessment, keeps the learning path as optional, and every page gives the same module count. The board also shows its Evidence-Ready capstone.
- **Roles no longer assume a region or sectors**: you choose your own.
- **Threats asks for your sector instead of counting every sector**: when you have not picked a sector, the exposure card offers a sector picker instead of "N threats apply to all sectors"; picking one narrows the page and sets your sector across the site, and a sector reads by its name ("apply to Finance & Banking"). Phones get the same picker.
- **A shorter Curious Explorer path**: the Essentials are now PQC 101, Quantum Threats and TLS Basics (about 1½ hours). Candidates, risk and compliance stay on the full path, and the capstone quiz still opens after the Essentials.
- **From Explore to a real handshake**: for Curious Explorers, Home leads to Explore and Explore leads to the TLS 1.3 simulator, not the organisational readiness assessment. The Playground features the simulator first and explains in plain words what a run shows and doesn't.
- **A beginner Library shelf**: the start picks open with the CISA/NSA/NIST Quantum-Readiness factsheet, then FIPS 203, then NIST IR 8547, labelled an initial public draft.
- **PQC GRC and Vendor Risk separate example policy from requirements**: the KRI, risk-tolerance, vendor-tier and audit-cadence cards carry an "Illustrative policy template" label; asking vendors for a CBOM is a procurement control you choose, not an external mandate; and the insurance advice tells you what to ask your broker instead of claiming underwriters already price quantum readiness.
- **Clearer Terms of Service**: the terms apply to the website, while your rights to the source code come only from its licence. The "You must not" lists are now plain disclaimers (not certified, not for production keys, not professional advice), and the export section is a notice about the law.
- **Flags with a known licence**: country and organisation flags now come from the open flag-icons set (MIT), credited at /licenses/. G7, NATO and "international" are shown as simple labelled badges.
- **Contact by email**: the welcome banner's contact link is now pqctoday@proton.me.
- **Engines from a published release, with their notices**: all six browser engines are taken from the engines-2 release, and each ships its full third-party licence notices. OpenSSL Studio uses the engine built in the public HSM repository; the other engines are unchanged.
- **The roadmap lists every upcoming milestone and who set it**: besides the country's next milestone, the migration roadmap groups upcoming dates by the body that set them (for the United States: federal civilian agencies, national security systems, certified products), each marked binding or guidance, with a note that a date applies only to what its issuing body covers.
- **The Compliance drawer says how binding a framework is**: the framework drawer has a "Binding" line worded as in the report: binding for its scope, with the framework's own words for who it applies to (and our translation where the original is not in English), binding, or guidance or draft, followed by its basis. The report quotes who a scoped framework binds in the same way.

### Fixed

- **The report says who a rule binds**: a framework you selected shows "Binding" only when it applies to you; one that binds only certain systems, such as FIPS 140-3, says "Binding for its scope" and shows its legal basis; one outside your country or sector says "Binding for others".
- **The report's milestones and applicability follow your country**: the roadmap shows the country's next upcoming milestone and its name instead of a past year (a US report used to show "deadline: 2025"), the applicability list follows the report's own country and industry, and board decks call a date a binding deadline only when it is one.
- **Pick your country and sector right on an empty Rules & Standards page**: the empty register offers a country picker and a sector picker itself, asks only for what is still missing, and lists the instruments as soon as both are set. Phones get the same step.
- **Executive and compliance lessons state what each rule requires**: rules that set PQC deadlines (CNSA 2.0, US Executive Order 14412, the EU PQC roadmap) are kept apart from general cyber-resilience duties (NIS2, DORA); the SEC cyber-disclosure rules are described accurately (disclosure four business days after an incident is found material, and an annual risk-management description, with no PQC requirement and nothing on personal liability); and insurance and competitive effects are presented as questions to ask, without unsourced figures.
- **Hybrid cryptography, country by country**: ANSSI recommends hybrid and makes it mandatory only inside France's regulated perimeter, BSI recommends it, and NSA does not require it — in the Compliance Strategy, Hybrid Cryptography and Standards Bodies lessons and on the Algorithms CNSA 2.0 panel ("Hybrid required" now reads "Hybrid expected").
- **Researcher and healthcare facts corrected**: data-retention periods come from the rule that actually sets them (FDA Part 11 sets none; HIPAA's documentation rule is six years), unsourced claims about future GA4GH, DARPA and grant requirements are gone, long-term signatures are explained as timestamps and evidence renewal rather than one algorithm choice, and the NIST additional-signature candidates are labelled Round 3.
