The modules' questions and answers now state the "harvest now, decrypt later" window the right way round and cite expert-survey timelines as the survey states them.
- **PQC Candidates: HAWK withdrawn**: HAWK was withdrawn from NIST's process in July 2026; NIST expects the third round to last about two years and has set no standardisation year.
- **Language support in the Crypto APIs lesson**: the lesson no longer says Go, Python, .NET, Java or Windows lack post-quantum support; all of them ship ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and the lesson says from which version. It no longer recommends the broken SIDH scheme or names a .NET class that never existed, and its Q&A is brought up to date.
- **HelloRetryRequest explained correctly**: a retry asks for a missing key share of a group both sides support, and no shared group ends the handshake. The two retry exercises now run a real retry and a real failure.
- **TLS downgrades and references**: TLS 1.3 detects an attacker who deletes the post-quantum option; the real risk is a client's own classical retry. The simulator and two lessons cite RFC 9846, RFC 9954 and RFC 10024, show each source as Released or Draft, and list the ML-KEM and ML-DSA TLS drafts as awaiting publication.
- **Hybrid key exchange details**: the lessons give the real order in which X25519MLKEM768 combines its two parts (ML-KEM first), and the workshop states once what its key combination guarantees.
- **One FIPS label everywhere**: products no longer show "FIPS" just for implementing a FIPS standard, or "FIPS Partial" for FedRAMP. Validated products say whether their post-quantum algorithms are inside the certificate.
- **Beginner summaries keep their qualifiers**: the short summaries for fourteen modules no longer say quantum computers break encryption "instantly" or that post-quantum cryptography is "unbreakable". The welcome tour and summaries say CNSA 2.0 applies to U.S. National Security Systems, call NIST IR 8547 a draft, and note FN-DSA (FIPS 206) is not yet published.
- **"Show advanced controls everywhere" now works**: once chosen, the Playground shows its workbench tabs, engine choice, ACVP and conformance suites and KMIP developer tools. The Explore card lists exactly what changes.
- **All three standards on the beginner Algorithms page**: the preview no longer filters to key exchange, so ML-DSA and SLH-DSA show beside ML-KEM.
- **Classic McEliece carries the BSI's 1 October advice**: Germany's BSI now advises against Classic McEliece for new developments. The Algorithms page and the Playground key picker show a "BSI: not for new use" badge that links to the notice, and the KMIP playground's BSI policy examples say the same. Classic McEliece is still an ISO standard and still listed in TR-02102-1, so its status is unchanged.
- **Library: stage and trust are no longer confused**: each card shows the document's own stage (Draft, Released, Expired…) apart from its trust score, so a current draft no longer reads "Released"; an unreviewed or unrecognised status reads "Unverified"; the trust word says High trust, Moderate trust or Needs review instead of "Authoritative"; the filter for documents mapped to NIST CSWP 39 is named that way; and Russia appears by name in the country filter.
- **Corrected the cyber-insurance source on the insurance lens**: the coverage grid cited a Lloyd's bulletin as a "quantum exclusion clause" at a dead link. That bulletin (Y5258, 2019) is the rule that policies must affirm or exclude cyber cover, and we found no insurer that has published a quantum-specific exclusion. Every scenario is now marked Ambiguous, and the note links the two Lloyd's bulletins that do bear on it.
- **KMIP policy defaults no longer say "denied" when everything is allowed**: under the permissive policy, signing and key exchange show "any (no default)". The KMIP control plane now has one address (/playground/cacp-kmip redirects), and the guided tour's operation count comes from the code.
- **Corrected architecture facts across 17 Learn modules**: the AWS KMS lab no longer teaches a policy condition that does not exist (it now teaches restricting new keys to ML-DSA, and explains that post-quantum TLS is a client setting); cloud KMS examples use only documented commands; Google Cloud KMS status is current (signing generally available, KEMs in Preview, software level only); HSM pages say what differs by vendor instead of "full PQC support"; composite certificates are no longer called backward compatible; one stated certificate-chain size replaces "18–36 KB"; the 47-day rule is scoped to public TLS certificates; NIST IR 8547 dates are marked as draft proposals; and two quotations their cited sources do not contain were removed or replaced.
- **Demo links open at the right place**: links to an About section and to an OpenSSL command now open at the right place.
- **Validation links land on the right section**: links to the known-answer tests and coverage sections scroll the section to the top of the page, and the certification-schemes view's Validation link opens the known-answer tests directly.
- **Algorithm status filter says what it means**: the "Certified" filter is now "Standardised or selected", because algorithms aren't certified, and the bucket includes NIST selections whose FIPS is still pending.
- **Implementation attack profiles corrected**: FN-DSA is marked as selected but not yet a FIPS standard; SLH-DSA, LMS and XMSS note side-channel and fault-injection risks, citing FIPS 205 and SP 800-208; hybrid and composite rows state when the combination is at least as strong as its parts (SP 800-227).
- **Cloud HSM and PKCS#11 facts brought up to date**: the HSM, key-management, confidential-computing and crypto-modernisation lessons reflect AWS CloudHSM's ML-DSA support in the HSM and PKCS#11 v3.2 as a published OASIS Standard.
- **Caddy settings that Caddy accepts**: the TLS config generator no longer tells Caddy users to install OpenSSL. Caddy 2.10+ gets post-quantum key exchange from Go and uses it by default, the generated Caddyfile uses Caddy's own curve names, and "pure PQC" explains that Caddy offers only the hybrid group.
- **SSH configs OpenSSH accepts**: the SSH config generator no longer writes an ML-KEM key exchange name that OpenSSH rejects. Hybrid now offers mlkem768x25519-sha256 first, and "Pure PQC" is renamed "PQC only (no classical fallback)", because both OpenSSH PQC methods combine with X25519.
- **History links open where items were made**: saved architecture-pack and operations-pack items, and KMIP quick runs, now open their pack or tab instead of an empty Learn page.
- **A lesson you have opened but not progressed in now says "Start"**, not "Resume".
- **The sample organisation reads as sample data**: loading the fictional bank no longer labels it "Your assessment", and the landing says "the 10-minute intro".

### Data

- **Certification records refreshed**: 20 new certificates — 14 Common Criteria, 3 EU EUCC, 2 FIPS 140-3 and 1 ANSSI CSPN — and none removed.
- **Two modules in FIPS 140-3 testing**: Migrate adds Isidore Mini Core (Forward Edge-AI) and QiSpace SDK Cryptographic Module (Quantropi), both on NIST's Implementation Under Test list.
- **ISO/IEC 19790:2025 in the Library**: the security requirements for cryptographic modules, cited by the FIPS 140-3 certification module for its eleven requirement areas and four security levels.
- **US timeline: real deadlines only**: five US entries that were issuance or not-before dates are no longer listed as deadlines, so the readiness report and board decks show the next real US deadline. The Singapore MAS quantum advisory no longer shows a 2028 deadline; MAS has set none, and the advisory is guidance. Summaries filed under an entry's old title are no longer published once the entry has a current one.
- **Honest Home boards for Curious Explorers**: the Essentials list matches the three-module path, the boards say "every page is open" and name the one gate (the capstone quiz). OpenSSL is described as one widely used TLS library, not the one your browser uses. The capstone is "PQC Foundations".
- **Quiz corrections**: answers about compliance frameworks, hybrid cryptography, FIPS 140-3 validation and lattice-based homomorphic encryption are corrected.
- **Library entries completed and kept current**: sixteen entries gained status, dates, summaries, categories and links to the documents they cite; the BSI's notice advising against Classic McEliece for new systems is added; NIST CSWP 39 is listed and cited as "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility: Strategies and Practices" (updated June 2026); superseded editions (FIPS 140-2, ISO 11898-1:2015, FDA's 2023 device guidance) point to their replacements, and the Automotive lesson cites the current ISO 11898-1 edition; duplicate entries are retired.
- **Product links to Learn modules**: 139 products link to the Learn modules that cover them, and modules list them under Tools & Products.
- **Compliance sources and binding status**: more frameworks show whether they bind the organisations they cover; UN-ECE WP.29 and CISA's PQC initiative cite their own documents; an entry with no post-quantum source (Bahrain) is retired. PCI DSS and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 now keep their own texts as evidence.
- **Two threat entries cite their sources**: a cloud threat entry now names its at-risk cryptography and replacement from NIST and Australian guidance, and an entropy entry cites NIST's validation certificate.
- **58 Library documents re-checked**: each live link was fetched and its identity confirmed; verification dates and confidence scores are updated. The PCI DSS Quick Reference Guide now carries its real title (v3.0), and PCI Card Production Logical Security points to PCI SSC's own page.
- **TFHE evidence notes**: twelve TFHE evidence records note that their parameter fingerprint label was computed from a mistyped library commit; keys, measurements and results are unaffected.
- **Reviewer name on review records**: review records name the PQC Today account as reviewer.
- **One Library title correction recorded**: the change record for the corrected IACR ePrint 2010/560 title, shipped in 4.161.0, is now marked as shipped.
- **Microsoft's post-quantum features in Windows added to its roadmap**: post-quantum algorithms are generally available in Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025, with ML-DSA certificates in AD Certificate Services; hybrid TLS key exchange and composite algorithms in the APIs are in preview.
- **Roadmap summaries filled in for AWS and Futurex**.
- **Compliance bases and scope**: DISA STIG, Brazil's BACEN Resolution 4.893, UN Regulation No. 155 (UN-ECE WP.29) and PCI DSS now say who they apply to in their own words and name their basis; the evidence for DISA STIG, PCI DSS and the DoD instruction names where its saved copy came from.
- **Library: a research-topics field**: each Library entry now has a research-topics field, empty until entries are tagged.
- **ARINC 653P0-4 in the Library**: the current edition of ARINC 653 Part 0 replaces the earlier one.
- **Quiz and lesson answers corrected**: two quiz explanations and three lesson Q&A answers (VPN and SSH, operations) are corrected.

CHG:4.163.0.full: The KMIP protocol workshop now runs its own local engine with a real audit trail, entropy and certification lessons separate test results from compliance claims, and workshop controls and results fit phone screens.
CHG:4.163.0.release_notes:
The KMIP protocol workshop now runs its own local engine with a real audit trail, entropy and certification lessons separate test results from compliance claims, and workshop controls and results fit phone screens.

### Changed

- **Open gaps explain the lesson before the investigation history**: the coverage register now separates what a finding means, why it limits a claim, its scope and disposition, and the underlying technical record. General readers start with a guided overview; certification engineers start with structured evidence. Status explanations, search, filters and expandable history replace the previous walls of text, including on phones.
- **Entropy learning paths for both audiences**: general practitioners get a concepts-first route while certification engineers get the validation and evidence route. The random-generation workshop now makes a predictable generator visibly different, recovers its parameters as an exercise, and separates statistical observations from claims about entropy.
- **Validation workbenches fit the role and screen**: certification engineers open on technical evidence and traces; other roles get plain-language interpretation with raw details available. Phones get a compact ACVP runner, readable KAT results and an ordered KMIP policy-to-protocol-to-PKCS#11 timeline instead of compressed desktop panes.
- **The KMIP lesson now runs the local engine**: the protocol workshop executes browser-local KMIP requests and shows their real result and audit trail. Cloud-provider commands and cross-provider states are clearly marked as teaching examples, and the wrap and rotation exercises name where their runnable analogue differs from the exact KMIP operation.

### Fixed

- **The Entropy Evidence Lab opens and explains each dataset choice**: both learning paths can now open the six-screen SP 800-90B lab, including from a direct workshop link. The first screen makes clear that its choices are stored evidence datasets rather than live entropy sources, marks the selected dataset, and explains that estimation begins only after the learner inspects its provenance, chooses a track and runs the tool.
- **Entropy exercises distinguish randomness tests from entropy evidence**: the module no longer treats visual plots, health tests, estimators and primitive self-checks as one pass score. Hex input is checked consistently, deterministic-generator recovery is verified, DRBG and entropy-source responsibilities are stated separately, and lag plots no longer spill into adjacent columns.
- **Certification lessons match the current validation boundaries**: ACVP response artifacts distinguish local demonstrations from NIST submissions, FIPS level planning no longer turns physical-security examples into automatic level claims, and Common Criteria/EUCC exercises distinguish assurance claims, national certification and scheme recognition.
- **Workshop controls and results stay inside phone layouts**: long workshop titles and methodology controls wrap without shifting the page sideways, KMIP inspector actions wrap, and mobile KAT cards show their explanatory result instead of only a pass icon.

CHG:4.164.0.full: Algorithms now distinguish standards, validation, maturity and measured evidence; Compliance is framed as an educational reference with visible evidence limits; and the FHE module offers a general path plus optional advanced key custody. Current ANSSI and BSI material is included from official sources.
CHG:4.164.0.release_notes:
Algorithms now distinguish standards, validation, maturity and measured evidence; Compliance is framed as an educational reference with visible evidence limits; and the FHE module offers a general path plus optional advanced key custody. Current ANSSI and BSI material is included from official sources.

### Changed

- **Algorithm comparisons now separate facts, maturity, missing evidence, and measured hardware results**: standards are no longer called validations; published standards, pending selections, drafts, candidates, regional recommendations, non-selected schemes, non-standardized schemes, and unverified evidence are distinct filters. Migration rows are taught as candidate paths rather than drop-in replacements, and blanks say whether a field is not applicable, not specified, not measured, or not researched. Heterogeneous catalogue performance estimates are withheld from comparisons and exports; a scoped same-engine hardware case study shows measured signing throughput on M4 Pro, i.MX 95, and KV260—including which KV260 rows used FPGA acceleration. Phones can compare up to three algorithms, old filter links normalize to current terminology, and filtered exports include their source snapshot, scope, caveats, maturity, and provenance.
- **Compliance lessons say exactly what their evidence proves**: the page is explicitly an educational reference, not a GRC system or applicability decision. Binding classifications require a reviewed basis instead of a regulator-name match; ACVP, FIPS module validation and algorithms named in evaluated product documentation have distinct labels; certification and GRC views use guided evidence questions; source freshness and extraction-review gaps are visible; and phones include compact date, evidence and role-lens lessons. Extracted source material is called practices rather than legal requirements, and the CSWP 39 sequence is clearly labelled as a PQC Today synthesis.
- **FHE now starts with the general lesson and offers custody as an advanced path**: the full module starts with schemes, noise, precision, threat models and parameter choices. Developers, architects, researchers and operators may then opt into HSM custody, while certification engineers start there by default; Executive and GRC roles stay on foundations, and Curious learners keep their distilled summary with custody explicitly left out. The workshop now asks learners to predict outcomes before revealing explanations, distinguishes measured lab evidence from product or certification claims, and keeps its controls readable on phones. References follow the selected path, current and locally tested implementation versions are distinguished, and the empty products tab is no longer shown.

### Fixed

- **Every role can reach the FHE foundations without being sent into advanced custody material**: role learning paths, search metadata and study-time estimates now agree with the redesigned 105-minute module. Executive, GRC and Curious learners receive the foundations path; technical roles can continue into advanced HSM custody.
- **Algorithm evidence stays honest and readable on small screens**: the catalogue now distinguishes its file snapshot date from a row-level review and says when reviewer, method and next-review evidence are not recorded. Unparseable performance text no longer becomes a baseline result, phone Industry and implementation-attack views retain sources and limitations, and wide Coverage Matrix tables scroll inside a labelled region instead of widening the page. Automated checks now cover 320- and 390-pixel layouts plus cold and warm production loading.
- **The phone migration wizard keeps key exchange and signatures apart**: choosing an algorithm such as RSA under key establishment could suggest a signature scheme as its replacement. The wizard now only offers paths for the function you chose, calls them candidate paths rather than replacements, and skips rows with no reviewed path.
- **Government positions on post-quantum algorithms are stated accurately**: the CNSA 2.0 panel now follows NSA's October 2026 guidance. NSA does not require hybrids and counts only the ones it has identified, the 2027, 2030 and 2031 policy dates set the mandate, and 2033 is no longer called the final deadline. BSI's hybrid recommendation is shown separately from ANSSI's requirement, the federal Executive Order 14412 timeline is included, and transition dates are credited to NIST's draft guidance only where NIST is their source.
- **Attack severity labels and executive heatmap colours are visible again**: severity and evidence badges on Implementation Attacks, and the colours of the executive readiness heatmap, had lost their backgrounds and were close to invisible. They now render clearly in light and dark themes, and "No recorded evidence" is shown as a neutral badge rather than a green one.
- **Missing key sizes are no longer shown as zero**: the phone detail sheet showed "0 B" for about 30 algorithms whose sizes are not recorded, and comparisons could mark a missing size as the smallest. Each size now shows its own value or says why it is missing, and missing values sort last.
- **Withdrawn and unverified algorithms are labelled for what they are**: withdrawn, broken, not-selected and unverified schemes no longer carry a "Draft" badge; badges and status chips now use the same wording as the status filter.
- **Protocol Support describes deployment evidence instead of giving production advice**: the "Recommended for production use today" panel is now "Reviewed deployment evidence", explains that it summarises public evidence rather than advising any organisation, and cites specifications and independent deployments. KMIP 3.0, still a committee draft, leaves the panel.
- **Compliance actions no longer overstate their result**: the developer inventory gate now fails on a finding without falling through to a success message, the executive download is a learning worksheet rather than an audit or management register, the FIPS progress track excludes Common Criteria evaluations, and an in-force date asks learners what to verify instead of declaring work overdue.
- **Known-answer checks report honestly and are easier to follow**: the run button now says "Run known-answer checks", a run where nothing passed is no longer shown in green, results are announced to screen readers and keyboard focus returns to the button.
- **Coverage and gap counts add up**: the Open Gaps heading and chips count the entries the list can show and say when generated entries are folded away, and the "untested" filter now finds every group with an untested cell.
- **Implementation attack advice is phrased as considerations**: mitigations no longer suggest that a validated module proves side-channel resistance, and the phone view explains that severity is a qualitative reading, not a CVSS score.
- **Comparisons and exports show the same values everywhere**: the table, drawer, comparison and CSV now agree for each size and missing-data state, approximate values keep their "~", the Transition tab exports the transition rows you see, and exported text cannot be read as a spreadsheet formula.
- **Filters say what they are doing**: a role's default status filter is shown as a removable chip instead of hiding rows behind "Everything", phone comparisons name the picks they leave out, and search finds results for multi-word queries such as "lattice KEM".
- **Protocol, industry and catalogue wording avoids claims of absence**: "no deployment" and "no PQC path" now read "no reviewed evidence", the protocol heatmap separates published, draft and absent work, industry examples carry their context note on desktop too, and the catalogue says how many rows it withholds and why.
- **Standards labels match their current state**: NIST's Round 4 outcome, the May 2026 additional-signature round, HQC's selection status, the latest IETF composite drafts, the KpqC final selection, NIST's dates for 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman and ANSSI's position on SLH-DSA are now stated as their sources say.

### Data

- **Algorithm statuses match the latest standards news**: the TLS hybrid key exchanges (X25519MLKEM768 and its P-256/P-384 siblings) are shown as published in RFC 10024 and the SSH hybrids as RFC 10042; HAWK, withdrawn by its authors in July 2026, is no longer listed as an active candidate; and FrodoKEM-640 and two Classic McEliece parameter sets no longer claim a BSI recommendation they do not have.
- **Current BSI and ANSSI guidance joins the Library evidence set**: the Library adds ANSSI’s 2026 crypto-agility guidance and refreshes the derived learning fields and evidence-grounded maturity requirements for it and BSI TR-02102-1. The older 2021 ANSSI algorithm-selection guide is deliberately excluded from the current guidance set. Only official publisher links and derived records are public; source files remain private.

CHG:4.165.0.full: Compliance source labels now explain who published an item, why it appears for the selected profile, and what its evidence can establish. Official publications open at their publisher; copied third-party documents are excluded from the public Library.
CHG:4.165.0.release_notes:
Compliance source labels now explain who published an item, why it appears for the selected profile, and what its evidence can establish. Official publications open at their publisher; copied third-party documents are excluded from the public Library.

### Changed

- **Compliance source relationships are explained instead of guessed**: domestic, foreign, international and unclassified sources now come from reviewed organization records. Government guidance, regulators, standards bodies, certification schemes, professional bodies and industry groups keep distinct labels, while legal force remains a separate fact. The same “Why this is shown” evidence is available in compact assessment, report and export views.
- **Certification engineers have a tested evidence journey**: the role-specific path moves from local validation and known-answer tests through the product-certification workshop to jurisdiction-aware guidance and product records. Recorder instructions identify every click, wait and scroll for producing the matching explainer video.

### Fixed

- **U.S. organizations are no longer described as foreign in a U.S. profile**: NIST NCCoE, CISA, NIAP and AICPA now use their reviewed U.S. organization type and relationship. CCRA is identified as an international recognition arrangement, and unresolved metadata uses a neutral prompt to verify the primary source rather than inventing a foreign authority.
- **NIST CSWP 39 opens at its official source**: the broken local PDF route is removed. Public Library builds retain official publisher URLs and educational extractions, and a release gate prevents third-party source documents from being copied into the deployable Library.

CHG:4.166.0.full: Library, Threats, Migrate, Assess, Report, Timeline, Community and Navigate now teach learners how to interpret their evidence without turning source records, estimates or planning inputs into applicability, certification, readiness or ranking claims.
CHG:4.166.0.release_notes:
Library, Threats, Migrate, Assess, Report, Timeline, Community and Navigate now teach learners how to interpret their evidence without turning source records, estimates or planning inputs into applicability, certification, readiness or ranking claims.

### Changed

- **Library records distinguish source facts from PQC Today teaching notes**: source scope, lifecycle, access, freshness and trust language have been reconciled across desktop and phone views. Reviewed records retain official publisher links and educational extractions without publishing locally held third-party documents, while inferred categories and purpose counts are identified as navigation aids rather than authoritative classifications.
- **Threat records now say what kind of evidence they are**: a short primer explains harvest-now-decrypt-later and harvest-now-forge-later, while every card, table row and detail view distinguishes threat scenarios, implementation vulnerabilities, migration constraints, policy signals, adoption milestones, quantum-capability evidence and educational guidance. A shareable record-type filter prevents unlike entries from being compared as though they were equivalent threats.
- **CRQC evidence is taught as uncertain source claims, not a smooth forecast**: the former continuous trajectory graphic is replaced by discrete demonstrations and roadmap markers with their scope and comparability limits. Source cards retain their individual estimates and lineage instead of being turned into a percentage-complete story.
- **Candidate responses are framed as questions to validate**: catalogue suggestions no longer read as prescribed mitigations. Detail views explain that each response is site-derived educational guidance and prompt the learner to verify maturity, applicability and evidence before using it.
- **Migrate presents evidence and planning inputs instead of product verdicts**: capability, certification, roadmap and replacement signals now state their evidence boundary; missing evidence is not treated as proof of absence; role guidance and phone views follow the same model; and planning exports identify assumptions rather than presenting generated paths as approved migration decisions.
- **Assess and Report explain their educational model before showing results**: assessment tracks, review navigation and portable reports now agree on what was answered. CRQC estimates, policy milestones and internal planning anchors remain separate; inventory answers are self-reported rather than scans; and scores, costs, compliance prompts and board outputs are labelled as learning and planning aids rather than audits, forecasts, certifications or approved business cases.
- **Timeline, Community, and Navigate explain what their evidence can establish**: Timeline now presents published records without implying personal applicability or false month-level precision; Community is an evidence-linked directory rather than an influence ranking; and Navigate teaches its graph encoding, offers direct guided and keyboard paths, and keeps controls inside phone screens.

### Fixed

- **Certification engineers now get a focused learning journey**: the unrelated invitation to contribute a validation test has been removed from the role journey, leaving the five steps that teach algorithm testing, entropy evidence, module interfaces, certificate stages and hardware validation.
- **Unscoped visitors no longer receive made-up personal exposure figures**: the page first explains what a sector and role selection will change, keeps the catalogue available in neutral mode, and only calculates a personal exposure summary after the learner supplies the needed context.
- **Threat navigation remains usable on phones and from shared links**: the phone view adds purpose-built search and progressive loading, preserves record-type and threat deep links, expands far enough to reveal a linked record, and returns to that record after its detail sheet closes. Desktop sort controls use real buttons and announce their sort state to assistive technology.
- **CNSA 2.0 and NSM-10 dates are no longer conflated**: NSA's current 2027 acquisition, 2030 phase-out and 2031 NSS algorithm-mandate milestones replace the superseded category schedule. The separate NSM-10 objective to mitigate as much federal quantum risk as feasible by 2035 remains clearly identified as a different claim.

### Data

- **The Library review queue is closed with scoped, source-linked records**: high-impact policy, certification, protocol, research, vendor and product records were checked against their stated sources. Overbroad mandates, product claims, ecosystem claims and certification implications were narrowed, and records without sufficient current evidence remain visibly qualified instead of being upgraded by inference.
- **Current threat-source claims carry explicit freshness and provenance states**: all published records now identify their source-link quality and registered source, stale future-tense statements were revised or bounded by date, and the open-claims lineage preserves the superseded CNSA material instead of deleting its history.

CHG:4.167.0.full: The browser Playground and Business Tools now tell learners what each result represents, what it can establish, and where an educational demonstration or planning artifact stops short of certification, compliance, approval or production evidence. Role journeys, phone layouts, standards references, exports and exercises follow the same evidence-first model.
CHG:4.167.0.release_notes:
The browser Playground and Business Tools now tell learners what each result represents, what it can establish, and where an educational demonstration or planning artifact stops short of certification, compliance, approval or production evidence. Role journeys, phone layouts, standards references, exports and exercises follow the same evidence-first model.

### Changed

- **Every browser tool explains the strength of its evidence**: cards and tool pages identify real cryptographic execution, protocol models, calculators and simulations before learners interpret a result. Certification-shaped experiences state that a local pass is not an ACVP, CAVP, CMVP or product-certification verdict, and downloaded run records carry the same evidence class, assumptions, implementation identity, time and limitation.
- **Each role gets one coherent Playground journey**: desktop and phone now agree on the first tools, why they matter and which Learn module should follow. Executive and GRC learners receive a short demonstration before returning to role-appropriate education; certification engineers begin with entropy and test evidence.
- **Exercises ask learners to predict, run and explain**: correct answers are no longer always in the first position, and prompts distinguish an observed result from the broader conclusions it cannot support.
- **Business Tools identify the kind of artifact they produce**: all 37 tools now distinguish financial and threat scenarios, planning worksheets, draft templates, evidence organizers and technical design worksheets. Each tool says what its output can show and what it cannot prove, including explicit boundaries around forecasts, legal advice, audits, certification, compliance and security approval.
- **Every role gets an intentional Business Tools starting sequence**: architect, certification-engineer, operations and curious paths no longer fall back to a generic ROI-first journey, and the selected role's short sequence is now available on phones as well as laptops.
- **Breach-cost estimates disclose their source age in the page and export**: the retained IBM 2025 per-sector table is visibly labelled one edition behind the July 2026 global report and remains an assumption because the current per-sector report is registration-gated.
- **Cost of Inaction compares transparent scenarios instead of inventing penalties**: the ten-year workshop now shows its source age, model assumptions and slow-to-fast quantum range before the result; regulatory dates remain planning context, while only a learner-entered, organization-verified consequence can affect the calculation. Positive and negative results use accurate language, and the full reproducible scenario follows the learner into the board-pitch handoff and export.
- **Executive quantum-impact and KPI lessons preserve uncertainty**: the workshop now records Yes, No and Unknown evidence questions instead of inventing a Low/Moderate/High exposure rating. The dashboard separates global catalogue context from explicitly selected organizational products, withholds its combined score until enough evidence exists, identifies value origins and saves dated browser-local snapshots for trend comparison.
- **KPI observations retain their evidence lineage**: every measure can now record its numerator, denominator, unit, reporting period, as-of date, evidence owner, reference and declared verification state. The same structured record appears in browser-local snapshots, saved artifacts and exports, while missing fields remain visibly unprovided and PQC Today does not claim to verify learner-entered evidence.
- **The About page describes review evidence more precisely**: desktop and phone distinguish recorded updates, source checks, human decisions, signed audit entries and freshness limits instead of implying that every fact has already received the same review or that records update themselves.
- **The About page no longer presents an outdated Trust Score methodology**: the standalone dimension table and formula explainer have been removed. Role guidance and citation labels now direct learners to the cited source and public audit trail instead of treating a composite badge as proof that a claim is correct.

### Fixed

- **Current standards and implementation boundaries are stated accurately**: TPM object attributes and hierarchies no longer borrow PKCS #11 terminology; final TPM Version 185 is separated from the browser engine's earlier snapshot; SSH points to RFC 10042; and current TLS and RSA-OAEP references use RFC 9846 and RFC 8017.
- **Opening the Playground no longer probes a local Sandbox**: the browser contacts a local Sandbox only after the learner explicitly asks it to check, avoiding an unexplained private-network request during an ordinary visit.
- **Wide Playground content remains usable on phones and at high zoom**: tab rails, tables, diagrams, long values and protocol traces wrap or scroll inside labelled regions with visible cues and keyboard access instead of widening or silently clipping the page.
- **MLS Group Messaging and PKI Enrollment show their real scope instead of a generic WIP warning**: both working educational tools are now version 1.0.0 and distinguish the operations they execute from the protocol or external interoperability they model.
- **Business Tool cards are usable with touch, keyboard and assistive technology**: standards provenance is no longer nested inside the card's Open button, removing 36 conflicting interactive controls from the phone catalogue. A release gate now loads every Business Tool on desktop and phone, checks role journeys and evidence boundaries, and rejects serious accessibility or page-width regressions.
- **Navigate guidance and connected records now follow the learner's actions**: the introductory guide can be dismissed and reopened, connected records omitted from the initial graph are drawn when selected, the camera follows the selected connection, Escape closes the record drawer, Reset view returns to the full graph, and patent labels no longer expose search-highlight markup.

CHG:4.168.0.full: The repository entry point now reflects the current educational product, its evidence boundaries and its actual maintenance process. Generated facts and documentation checks prevent release, dataset and navigation claims from silently becoming stale again.
CHG:4.168.0.release_notes:
The repository entry point now reflects the current educational product, its evidence boundaries and its actual maintenance process. Generated facts and documentation checks prevent release, dataset and navigation claims from silently becoming stale again.

### Changed

- **The project guide now starts learners and contributors in the right place**: the README replaces its historical feature ledger with role-specific routes, clear browser and optional-service boundaries, reproducible setup instructions and the explicit statement that PQC Today is an education and demonstration platform rather than a production cryptographic, certification or GRC system.
- **Published evidence follows the official-source boundary**: repository guidance now explains that public records retain official publisher URLs and reviewed educational extractions without publishing downloaded third-party documents or private maintenance artifacts.

### Fixed

- **Repository facts can no longer drift silently**: release, module, catalogue, glossary and assistant-corpus figures are derived from the committed sources. Local and pull-request checks reject stale figures, broken repository links, product routes that would misdirect GitHub readers and superseded claims about GRC, scraping, archives or unfinished-tool badges.
- **Testing guidance matches the gates that actually run**: the contributor and testing guides now distinguish fast pre-push checks, full local suites, the final release gate and manual KMIP/CACP checks without promising repeated work that is not wired into the workflow.

CHG:4.17.0.full: A cross-page accuracy release covering Timeline, Compliance, Threats, Patents, Leaders, Learn, and the Library: deadline mandates on the Timeline are now individually sourced and labeled instead of guessed, the Compliance page covers the actual federal executive order behind the 2030/2031 deadlines, the Threats page's quantum-computer arrival estimate is now the same number everywhere it appears, Patents share links no longer lose your filters, Leaders profiles are split into a curated set and the full contributor list, several Learn modules got corrected facts and real quiz coverage, and dozens of Library references were re-verified, fixed, or retired.
CHG:4.17.0.release_notes:
A cross-page accuracy release covering Timeline, Compliance, Threats, Patents, Leaders, Learn, and the Library: deadline mandates on the Timeline are now individually sourced and labeled instead of guessed, the Compliance page covers the actual federal executive order behind the 2030/2031 deadlines, the Threats page's quantum-computer arrival estimate is now the same number everywhere it appears, Patents share links no longer lose your filters, Leaders profiles are split into a curated set and the full contributor list, several Learn modules got corrected facts and real quiz coverage, and dozens of Library references were re-verified, fixed, or retired.

### Fixed

- **Every deadline on the Timeline now shows whether it's a binding legal mandate, informal guidance, or still-draft language**: most rows previously had no label at all. All deadline and CNSA 2.0 migration rows are now individually labeled from their own primary source, and the popover and the headline deadline banner now agree with each other instead of computing "binding" two different ways.
- **The Timeline's chart no longer clips future or historical entries to a fixed 2024–2035 window**: the year axis now scales to whatever data is actually in view.
- **Malformed dates in the Timeline's underlying data no longer silently render as blank bars**: bad values are now excluded with a logged warning instead of failing invisibly.
- **The Compliance page now covers the actual U.S. executive order behind the post-quantum migration deadlines**: the operative order (with its 2030 key-establishment and 2031 digital-signature deadlines) previously only appeared on the Timeline page, not in the Compliance framework list.
- **Several "plain-English summary" blurbs on the Compliance page were overstating what their underlying framework actually requires** (including DORA, CNSA 2.0, ANSSI, and BSI guidance): rewritten to match what's actually in the framework record, including the difference between a binding deadline and a staged recommendation.
- **The Compliance Records tab no longer shows a live-sounding "Refresh Data" button that does nothing on the deployed site**: it's now disabled with an explanation, and the freshness date reflects the actual data snapshot instead of the moment you loaded the page.
- **The Compliance page's "New to PQC compliance?" intro banner no longer reappears every visit** once you've already seen it.
- **Threat-horizon (Q-Day) estimates now agree across the whole Threats page**: the hero summary, the trajectory chart, the economics calculator, and the capability strip previously each computed their own version of "when could a quantum computer break today's encryption," and could disagree with each other. All four now derive from one shared calculation.
- **Fixed a false-positive bug in the Threats page's "harvest-now" vs. "forge-now" risk classification**: threats whose description merely mentioned a post-quantum replacement algorithm's name (like ML-KEM or ML-DSA) were sometimes being misclassified based on that mention alone. Threats that genuinely can't be classified from available data now say so honestly instead of defaulting to a guess.
- **The Threats page now shows why each threat was vetted the way it was**: peer-review status, confidence level, the body that vetted it, and any data-quality notes are now visible in the threat detail view, and CRQC arrival-estimate citations are now clickable links to their sources.
- **Merged two near-duplicate industry categories on the Threats page** ("Critical Infrastructure" and "Energy / Critical Infrastructure") that were splitting the same sector's threats across two filter buckets.
- **Threat classification definitions are now readable on touchscreens**: they previously only appeared on hover, which doesn't work on mobile; tapping now opens the same explanation.
- **Fixed a data-loading bug that could conflate "this patent has no post-quantum relevance score" with "this patent scored zero"**.
- **Sharing a filtered Patents view now preserves what you were actually looking at**: the corpus scope (post-quantum only vs. everything) and your chosen columns weren't part of the shareable link, so recipients could land on a different view than the one you sent. Also added a Share button to the page, which it didn't previously have.
- **Corrected the classification of Classic McEliece across the Patents catalog**: it was mislabeled as a classical (pre-quantum) algorithm; it's actually a NIST post-quantum Round 4 candidate, recommended by Germany's BSI. Fixed on all 13 affected records.
- **Patent search now finds algorithms by either their original filing-era name or their finalized NIST name** (e.g. "Kyber" and "ML-KEM," or "Dilithium" and "ML-DSA," now both work).
- **Added a small glossary for patent-specific terms** (CPC classification codes, priority/filing/issue dates, independent claims), available as inline tooltips.
- **The Leaders page now separates the curated, individually-vetted profile set from the larger auto-imported contributor list**: it previously showed all 332 profiles mixed together with no way to tell which had been individually reviewed. The default view now shows the 208 curated profiles, with a toggle to see everyone.
- **Refreshed and spot-checked Leaders profile data**, fixing two out-of-date entries and adding a visible "verified as of" date to each profile.
- **Fixed a bug where an executive's explicit "sort by name" choice on the Leaders page was silently overridden back to a relevance-based order**.
- **Added a Skeptic/Critic filter category to the Leaders page** and a couple of previously-missing sourced entries to that category and to Industry Adopter.
- **Fixed two overstated claims in Learn module content**: a national security algorithm mandate was described as a blanket 2030 government-wide requirement (it's staged and scoped to national security systems), and a post-quantum certificate size comparison significantly overstated the size difference versus real measured figures (it said certificates are 10–50x larger; they're actually roughly 4–7x larger).
- **Learn checkpoints now only count as "passed" once you've actually scored well enough on them**: previously, simply opening every module in a section marked its checkpoint as passed regardless of quiz performance. Existing progress isn't reset; you'll see a one-time notice explaining the change.
- **Fixed a Learn progress-tracking bug where browsing a "curious mode" module's workshop steps counted as completing them**: viewing now only marks a module as viewed; workshop credit requires actually doing the workshop.
- **Three previously-orphaned Learn modules (governance/risk, team staffing, and SOC incident response) now have quiz coverage and are properly routed into the relevant role-based learning path**, instead of being reachable only by direct link with no way to test your understanding.
- **Retired a redundant Learn module that duplicated a newer, fuller one on team staffing**, and retired the old five-mode Learn dashboard (old links now redirect to the current Learn experience).
- **Learn module reference panels now show when each module's content was last reviewed**.
- **Filled in missing descriptions for 29 Library entries** that previously just repeated the document's title with no summary of what it actually covers.
- **Re-checked every Library link that was flagged as broken or unverified**: of the 100+ flagged links, the large majority were confirmed live and corrected (including a wrong ETSI document version), and the remainder that are genuinely unreachable (or fabricated document numbers that don't exist in the issuing standards body's catalog) are now retired instead of sitting in the catalog unresolved.
- **Fixed a Library entry that incorrectly implied FN-DSA (FIPS 206) has already been published**; it remains in draft.
- **Corrected a mismatched document title on a Library reference** that had been carrying an unrelated draft's title instead of its own.
- **Normalized a handful of Library confidence scores that were on the wrong 0–1 scale** instead of the 0–100 scale used everywhere else, and surfaced the confidence score in the document detail view.
- **The Library can now be filtered by why you're looking something up** (reference material vs. general education), corrected for about 40 entries that a keyword-based guess had filed under the wrong purpose.

### Data

- Refreshed the Timeline, Compliance, Patents, Leaders, and Library datasets with new dated snapshots and re-verified sourcing; added quiz question coverage for previously-untested Learn topics (software bill of materials, cryptography bill of materials, crypto-algorithm registry naming, and post-quantum verification/closure).

CHG:4.170.0.full: The certification engineer journey has been reviewed source by source and its five certification modules were reviewed end to end: its Learn modules, Library entries, Timeline milestones, maturity requirements and citations now match the current standards and documents. The browser HSM gains a PKCS#11 v3.3 working-draft track and more ACVP test coverage, certificate records are refreshed, and the Sources panel links each source to its trusted-source record.
CHG:4.170.0.release_notes:
The certification engineer journey has been reviewed source by source and its five certification modules were reviewed end to end: its Learn modules, Library entries, Timeline milestones, maturity requirements and citations now match the current standards and documents. The browser HSM gains a PKCS#11 v3.3 working-draft track and more ACVP test coverage, certificate records are refreshed, and the Sources panel links each source to its trusted-source record.

### Added

- **A PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft) lesson track in the browser HSM**: six lessons run real PKCS#11 calls for composite ML-DSA and ML-KEM, external µ, signatures remaining on stateful keys, and renamed identifiers. Each lesson has a quiz, glossary terms and plain-English log lines. The draft is unpublished, and the engine still reports Cryptoki 3.2.0.
- **A v3.3 test bench and a separate "v3.3 draft features" compliance group**: pick any of the 30 composite parameter sets and run IETF LAMPS known-answer checks in the browser. Draft results are kept apart from the v3.2 profile results, and the key inspector and PKCS#11 log decode composite keys, ciphertexts and signatures.
- **The ACVP lab runs the NIST test groups that need an optional test input**: deterministic ML-DSA and SLH-DSA signing with a given random value, internal verification, and ML-KEM encapsulation with a given seed now run through a clearly marked test-only extension. All 909 cases pass on both browser engines, and a new lesson section explains why a production module must never accept these inputs.
- **Ten new Library entries for certification work**: the SOG-IS notice on the end of national certificates under the agreement (27 February 2026), the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v3 draft, composite ML-KEM draft -23, RFC 10042, RFC 9955, RFC 10033, the COSE HPKE post-quantum draft, Google's Chrome ML-KEM post and two PCI SSC posts.
- **A France milestone for buying products with PQC from 2030**: ANSSI's FAQ advises that from 2030 it will not be reasonable to buy products without post-quantum cryptography. It is shown as a recommendation, not an obligation.
- **Four Timeline entries are published after review**: BSI's 2030 milestone for very-high-protection systems, the UK NCSC's 2035 target, the Monetary Authority of Singapore's announced quantum-resilience work, and NIST's working drafts for post-quantum PIV credentials.
- **New Library documents for certification and telecom**: NIAP's Protection Profile for Application Software v2.0, ISO/IEC 24759:2025 (test requirements for cryptographic modules, the companion to ISO/IEC 19790:2025), and GSMA's PQ.06 (hybrid key exchange for base stations and security gateways) and PQ.07 (post-quantum cryptography for non-terrestrial networks).

### Changed

- **Common Criteria and EUCC are taught separately**: what changed in Europe in 2025–2026, what EUCC takes from Common Criteria and what it adds, and separate planning guidance, each claim cited to its source.
- **Hybrid cryptography positions in one dated table**: NIST, the ECCG ACM v3 draft, BSI, ANSSI and the IETF are compared side by side "as of 22 October 2026", and the EU hybrid rule is stated once.
- **A leaner certification engineer journey**: FHE, Crypto APIs, PQC Candidates and Hardware Acceleration leave the path (they stay on the site), PCI certification joins the essentials, and HSM PQC becomes an optional section.
- **Payment network roadmaps and capacity calculators show their assumptions**: the Payment Network Comparator separates each network's official stance, public evidence and tentative plans. The certificate and HSM calculators state their chain, utilisation and redundancy assumptions, keep fictional performance profiles labelled, and no longer predict signing capacity without benchmarks.
- **Protocol status follows the latest IETF work**: X.509, EST/CMP, Kerberos, EAP/RADIUS and JOSE rows reflect current drafts and RFCs, and composite JWS examples move to draft -06.
- **Maturity requirements cite the current version of each document**: requirements drawn from documents that have since been updated now point at the newer version where the same requirement appears there word for word. Requirements whose wording changed are replaced with the new wording, and duplicates of a requirement the newer document already carries are retired. Requirements that could not be matched in the newer version keep citing the earlier one, which states them.
- **About 200 Library entries now show their key details**: entries that were added without a description, status, publisher, region or urgency now carry values taken from their own documents and checked against them. Security levels appear only on documents that define or test algorithms, mapped from the parameter sets the document names, and migration urgency appears only where the document's own wording supports it.
- **The protocol table reflects current IETF drafts**: draft revisions are updated, expired drafts are marked, the TLS hybrid key-exchange draft now points to its published RFC 10024, and the hybrid-signature cells cite RFC 9955 for the range of hybrid signature designs.
- **Product records match their vendors' current releases**: OpenVPN shows version 2.7.8; OPNsense shows 26.7.7 (13 October 2026) with hybrid post-quantum key exchange for IPsec since 26.7.4; pfSense Community Edition 2.9.0 shows post-quantum key exchange in its SSH daemon.
- **Certificate records are refreshed**: the catalogue now holds 2,330 FIPS 140-3, algorithm-validation and Common Criteria records, including new certifications, with nothing removed.
- **Five certification modules reviewed and corrected against their source documents**: FIPS 140-3, the ACVP lab workflow, PCI, CC/EUCC and product certification were read end to end and their explanations corrected against the source documents; each now shows it was reviewed on 22 October 2026.
- **The certification engineer page starts with learning**: the role page now opens on the Learn path, with the tools and references after it.
- **More ACVP test cases run in the browser, and the known limits are listed**: 56 more ML-DSA and SLH-DSA pre-hash cases (SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256), 49 AES-CTR encrypt cases and 30 HKDF multi-expansion cases (every expansion compared with NIST's) now run on both engines. The AES-CTR cases use NIST's sample IV as the counter block, and the page says so: the module's own IV generation isn't tested. A local check also runs all 1,000 NIST multi-expansion cases on both engines. The ACVP page lists what isn't run and why: tests with no PKCS#11 v3.2 mechanism (RSA SHAKE, some ECDSA hash combinations), AES-CTR cases whose length isn't a whole number of bytes, curves neither engine supports, primitives not in the engine yet, and the 1 GiB long-message hash tests.
- **Rule-based confidence scores are labelled**: 43 Library entries that showed no confidence score now have one set by a rule for their document type, and their Key facts say so: "set by document-type rule, not assessed per document".
- **NIST CSWP 37B (final) is in the Library**: the final report on automating the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (published 30 September 2026) replaces its initial public draft and is cited by the FIPS 140-3 module.

### Fixed

- **Certification facts corrected against their primary sources**: across FIPS 140-3, Entropy & Randomness, Hybrid Cryptography, Stateful Signatures, SLH-DSA, PQC Testing, HSM PQC, Standards Bodies, Secure Boot and PCI. For example, RFC 9794 is Informational terminology, the TVLA 4.5 threshold comes from Goodwill et al. (2011), CNSA 2.0 milestones are stated as published, and CAVP and CMVP are told apart.
- **The EUCC exercise names the right issuer**: an accredited certification body issues EUCC certificates; ENISA supports the scheme, and the ECCG agrees the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms.
- **India's and France's Timeline entries match their documents**: India's critical infrastructure must complete PQC adoption by 31 December 2029 and other enterprises by 2033. The national roadmap recommends mandating CBOM submissions rather than imposing them. ANSSI's three phases use ANSSI's own wording and are shown as recommendations.
- **Citations follow documents to their current versions**: quiz and Q&A answers that cited RFC 8446 now cite RFC 9846, retired drafts point to their RFCs or newer editions, and dead links are removed.
- **The JOSE known-answer suite counts all published examples**: the workshop runs 12 vectors, including all seven composite examples from the draft.
- **CROSS and LESS show their actual status**: both are marked as not advancing to NIST's third round of additional signatures, so neither is shown as on a standardization track.
- **Superseded and unverifiable records are retired**: concepts that existed once per draft version now appear once per standard, pointing at its current document, and three Community profiles whose only source no longer exists are retired.

### Security

- **Dependency advisories fixed**: vite moves to 7.3.7 (five high advisories) and the pinned dompurify to 3.4.17 (three critical advisories).

### Data

- **Oracle's Java post-quantum roadmap and OpenSSH 10.6p1 in the product catalog**: Oracle's published roadmap for post-quantum cryptography in Java is added to the vendor roadmaps, and the catalog lists OpenSSH at its current release, 10.6p1.
- **Sources link to their trusted-source records**: in the Sources panel (the Sources button in each page header), 73 source-directory entries now link to the trusted-source record behind them, and 69 details were filled from each organization's own pages: 67 regions and descriptions, plus two websites (six more organization pages were read for this release); one entry that could not be confirmed is retired.
- **Five new trusted sources, two re-verified**: the UK FCA, the US OCC, EIOPA, the EPO's Espacenet and Thailand's PDPC are added, and NERC and X9 are re-verified.
- **Browser engines published as release engines-5**: the site's engine files are pinned to a published release, and the licence notices shipped with each engine are refreshed.

CHG:4.171.0.full: The certification engineer journey now follows what the standards and vendors actually say: wrong statements in the Learn modules, quizzes and answers are corrected against their sources, the Product Records and validation workbench pages are easier to read, and HSM post-quantum statements are re-checked against each vendor's newest release notes.
CHG:4.171.0.release_notes:
The certification engineer journey now follows what the standards and vendors actually say: wrong statements in the Learn modules, quizzes and answers are corrected against their sources, the Product Records and validation workbench pages are easier to read, and HSM post-quantum statements are re-checked against each vendor's newest release notes.

### Added

- **"What the lab tests" panels and real NIST test cases in the certification modules**: Stateful Signatures, SLH-DSA, Secure Boot and HSM PQC show which checks a validation lab runs, and a hybrid panel explains what the validated-module guidance allows. The SLH-DSA, LMS, ML-KEM and ML-DSA known-answer panels replay published NIST cases through the in-browser engines, and the remaining round trips are labelled as round trips.
- **A new Library paper on card and PIN handling**: the post-quantum PCI use cases for ATMs and point-of-sale devices, with three matching maturity requirements for terminal keys, device certificates and boot code.

### Changed

- **Product Records open on the search and the table**: the page says plainly that the table is a snapshot, labels retrieval dates in UTC, shows a one-line PQC summary on phones, and no longer shows an internal identifier as a Common Criteria certificate number.
- **The validation workbench opens with one algorithm family ticked**: it explains what "test groups" and "test cases" mean, fits its results table to the panel, and lets you filter result rows by status and by evidence class.
- **The certification engineer path is shorter and its page matches it**: PQC Network Testing leaves the six essentials (it stays on the full path with a short certification route), Product Certification shows its measured 90-minute duration, the module header shows the duration of the path you are on, the Standards Bodies module is optional orientation at the start, and the "Testing & validation" line on the role page states the real order of the path.
- **The welcome notice is a slim strip**: on the desktop home page the first-visit notice sits above the role cards instead of covering them; the text, links and button are unchanged.
- **Library cards show both dates, and search finds exact standards first**: a card shows the record's update date beside the first-publication date, and a search for a standard's exact number or title lists that document first.
- **Migrate shows FIPS 140-2 certificates as historical**: a product whose certificate names only FIPS 140-2 is no longer shown with a current FIPS badge, because the CMVP moved those certificates to its historical list on 21–22 September 2026.
- **Silithium is described as its paper does**: it targets Strong Non-Separability, and the table and Playground card say so.

### Fixed

- **Wrong statements in the certification modules corrected against their sources**: for example the ACVP lab names the protocol-draft revision it checked, Secure Boot reflects TPM 2.0 Library v185 adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA and HashML-DSA, a fixed-versus-random TVLA test is explained correctly, EUCC certificates are issued by accredited certification bodies rather than by ENISA, the Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement is typed as governmental, and the ACM v2 date reads April 2025.
- **Quiz and answer corrections**: the Stateful Signatures question on SHA-256/192 no longer says national security systems are excluded (NSA prefers LMS with SHA-256/192), the ANSSI questions state that hash-based signatures are the algorithms it does not recommend hybridising systematically, and 18 quiz questions and 14 answers in all now match the corrected modules, and the quiz questions carry their sources.
- **HSM PQC statements follow each vendor's release notes**: nShield exposes ML-DSA through PKCS #11 from Security World v13.9.0, ML-KEM from v13.9.3 and SLH-DSA from v13.9.5; the LMS signature size is 2,828 bytes (H=20, W=4); AWS CloudHSM shows both its FIPS-mode statement and the NIST security policy side by side; unsourced side-channel and cloud-isolation statements were replaced.
- **One vendor's website address corrected in Sources**: the Kryotech Software entry now points at its current website in both source lists.

### Data

- **Six new products and eight corrected status flags in the product catalog**: six products are added and marked "Pending Verification" until their vendors' own documents are read, and eight existing entries whose post-quantum status showed as unknown beside a stated level of support now show the matching status.
- **Four new vendors in the catalog**: the vendors behind the new products are registered, so their products group under the right company.
- **Products linked to their NIST validations**: five newly catalogued products link to their NIST validation entries, and the Samsung Evan FW Crypto Engine now lists both of its NIST certificates (A8889 and A8900).
- **Qrypt is a supporting source**: in the Sources panel, Qrypt moves from a contextual source to a supporting source.
- **HSM post-quantum facts, source by source, and six refreshed library matches**: the product data now holds 55 facts for the 11 HSM products in the lessons (algorithm available or not, standard or vendor-defined PKCS #11 mechanism, certificate, FIPS mode), each with its source and the date it was read; pages do not show them yet. Six library matches to product records carry a refreshed verified date.

CHG:4.172.0.full: Three new lessons for certification engineers explain what a FIPS 140-3 certificate shows about side-channel and fault attacks, how a hybrid appears in a certificate's scope, and what carries over to a new platform. The change analyzer's Common Criteria and EUCC answers are corrected.
CHG:4.172.0.release_notes:
Three new lessons for certification engineers explain what a FIPS 140-3 certificate shows about side-channel and fault attacks, how a hybrid appears in a certificate's scope, and what carries over to a new platform. The change analyzer's Common Criteria and EUCC answers are corrected.

### Added

- **A lesson on side-channel and fault attacks in FIPS 140-3**: it explains that non-invasive security has no CMVP test metrics yet, what a lab does check under "Mitigation of other attacks", where attack testing does exist (Common Criteria vulnerability analysis) and what to ask a vendor. Passages that are the module's own reading of the sources are marked "Module analysis". Study time goes from 60 to 65 minutes.
- **Two lessons on hybrids and new platforms in Cryptographic Product Certification**: "Reading a hybrid in a certificate's scope" maps each part of a hybrid key exchange to where it shows on paper and what is tested; "A new platform, chip or accelerator: what carries over?" covers vendor affirmation, the operational environment, revalidation, processor acceleration and the Common Criteria view. Study time goes from 90 to 95 minutes, and the role learning-path totals follow.

### Fixed

- **The change analyzer answers Common Criteria and EUCC cases correctly**: adding ML-KEM is shown as a typical major change under Common Criteria and EUCC, beside the CMVP answer that now uses the Management Manual's own limits (under 30% overall and no category above 30%). Random number generator, tamper-sensor, new isolation and exploitable-vulnerability changes are shown as major, the FIPS enclosure route is limited to enclosure-only changes with no operational impact, the FPGA case names the bitstream and hardware-description rules, and an Intel-to-Arm move is rated as ENISA rates it.
- **The CCRA assurance-continuity document is named CCDB-015**: the lessons called it CCDB-014; its own front page gives 015. The document and its links are unchanged.

CHG:4.173.0.full: A new lesson in Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification explains what NIAP's protection profiles offer and require for post-quantum cryptography, and 15 NIAP documents join the Library.
CHG:4.173.0.release_notes:
A new lesson in Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification explains what NIAP's protection profiles offer and require for post-quantum cryptography, and 15 NIAP documents join the Library.

### Added

- **A lesson on NIAP and post-quantum cryptography**: "NIAP and post-quantum cryptography: what its profiles require" leads with the Dedicated Security Component profile, explains that NIAP's Technical Decisions add the CNSA rule for the Product Compliant List so post-quantum is one allowed route rather than the only one, separates a NIAP certificate from a CMVP module certificate, and ends with questions to put to the lab. A table lists the 11 NIAP documents that carry post-quantum selections beside the classical ones, with the algorithms, the classical choices still allowed, the date NIAP shows for each and a quote from each. Passages that are the module's own reading are marked "Module analysis". The Common Criteria path goes from 70 to 76 minutes and the module from 60 to 66; the role learning-path totals follow.
- **15 NIAP documents in the Library**: the protection profiles and modules for dedicated security components (with their Supporting Document), network devices, general-purpose computing platforms, full-drive encryption, virtualization, VPN clients, hardcopy devices and file encryption; NIAP Technical Decisions 1010, 1011 and 1064; and NIAP's announcements notice on its Policy 33 decisions.

### Changed

- **Patents in the certification engineer's main page list**: certification engineers now see Patents in their main page list, next to Leaders, instead of only under More.
- **Recent Library entries show their key details**: NIAP's Protection Profile for Application Software v2.0 (published 16 June 2025) and the FS-ISAC paper on post-quantum risk in ATM and card-terminal PIN handling now carry a description, publisher, region, category and urgency taken from the documents themselves, instead of appearing as unverified entries. NIAP's Policy Letter 26 and its CCEVS manual are tagged for government and defense readers.
- **The NSA CSfC post-quantum addendum is shown as a draft**: its status read Published; the document is still a draft.
- **Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification shows its review date again**: the module reads reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 23 October 2026, after the ACM v2 date correction and the new lesson.

CHG:4.174.0.full: Rosenpass and WireGuard are now described correctly across the Learn modules, the Library, the product catalogue and the glossary, the VPN simulator says clearly when it is not ready, and the Migrate page gains a Vulnerabilities tab with refreshed data for cryptographic libraries.
CHG:4.174.0.release_notes:
Rosenpass and WireGuard are now described correctly across the Learn modules, the Library, the product catalogue and the glossary, the VPN simulator says clearly when it is not ready, and the Migrate page gains a Vulnerabilities tab with refreshed data for cryptographic libraries.

### Added

- **A Vulnerabilities tab on the Migrate page**: after "Evidence gaps", it lists the known vulnerabilities (CVEs) for the products you selected, the top 20 per product at Medium severity and above, with a link to the full NVD list. Products whose data was refreshed after the snapshot show a "refreshed" date. With nothing selected it points back to the Replace tab. It is shown on desktop; the Business Center tool is unchanged.

### Fixed

- **Rosenpass uses Classic McEliece and Kyber-512, not ML-KEM**: the VPN and SSH module, its Q&A, the glossary, the protocol table, the Library entry and the product catalogue now say that Rosenpass pairs Classic McEliece 460896 with the pre-standard round-3 Kyber-512, not the standardized ML-KEM of FIPS 203. Its message sizes come from its white paper (four messages, 2,464 bytes in total) and WireGuard's normal handshake is 240 bytes (148 + 92) from WireGuard's own paper; the earlier 6,800-byte and "22x" figures had no source and are removed. WireGuard's catalogue entry now says the protocol has no post-quantum algorithm of its own and that Rosenpass supplies it.
- **OpenSSH and strongSwan hybrid key exchange details corrected**: OpenSSH made sntrup761x25519 its default from 9.0, added mlkem768x25519-sha256 in 9.9 and made it the default in 10.0; strongSwan's configuration uses the mlkem768 prefix. Planning timeframes in the Operations lesson are now marked as estimates, and the certificate size comparison is tied to its worked example. The Hybrid Cryptography summary now names RFC 10024 for hybrid TLS.
- **The 2030 RSA and ECC deprecation date names its document**: the Migration Program lesson attributes the date to the NIST IR 8547 initial public draft (November 2024) instead of presenting it as final.
- **The VPN simulator works in headless browsers and shows clear states**: it recognises headless Chromium, shows an honest idle state instead of a misleading badge, reports strongSwan load failures within 150 seconds and offers Retry.

### Data

- **Rosenpass records corrected**: the Library entry lists the algorithms Rosenpass really uses, the source-directory description names Classic McEliece and Kyber-512, and the Rosenpass and WireGuard product records carry the corrected descriptions, each checked against the vendor's white paper.
- **Vulnerability data for cryptographic libraries refreshed, four product mappings corrected**: the vulnerabilities shown for the cryptographic libraries in the Migrate catalog are refreshed from NIST's NVD. Four products pointed at the wrong NVD product and now show their own: Mbed TLS (20 of 40 shown), Bouncy Castle Java (20 of 42), BoringSSL (1) and CIRCL (1). OpenSSL 3.5.0 and wolfSSL counts are updated and Bouncy Castle Java LTS is included. Other products' data is unchanged.

CHG:4.175.0.full: Entropy source validation certificates get their own tab in the Compliance records, the Migrate Vulnerabilities tab now finds far more vulnerabilities for products that NIST lists without a version, and a round of fixes from a certification engineer's review corrects statements, wording and phone layouts across the certification lessons and the Library.
CHG:4.175.0.release_notes:
Entropy source validation certificates get their own tab in the Compliance records, the Migrate Vulnerabilities tab now finds far more vulnerabilities for products that NIST lists without a version, and a round of fixes from a certification engineer's review corrects statements, wording and phone layouts across the certification lessons and the Library.

### Added

- **An Entropy (ESV) tab on the Compliance records**: 361 NIST entropy source validation certificates, each with its noise-source type, entropy claims, validation history and lab, and a link to NIST's page. FIPS 140-3 modules whose Security Policy names entropy certificates now link to them, and each certificate lists the modules that rely on it. Open it from the record-type strip; on a phone it is one of the record-type chips.
- **The FIPS 140-3 track counts on the phone Compliance page**: one line under the PQC summary gives the same stage counts the desktop chart shows (prerequisite met, in progress, certified).
- **Four documents in the Library**: the ACVP specifications for ML-KEM, SLH-DSA and the SHA family, and NIST's SP 800-90B entropy assessment tool, cited from the ACVP Lab Workflow and Entropy lessons.
- **A document's own dates in the Library detail drawer**: the drawer shows when a document was first published and last updated, with the date we last checked the catalog entry labelled separately, so the FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance and Management Manual no longer look newer or older than they are.

### Changed

- **The ACVP Lab Workflow lesson sits with the other certification lessons**: it is now filed under Hardware Infrastructure, Phase 7, next to FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria and Cryptographic Product Certification, instead of Protocols, Phase 6, so its Related modules list leads with the certification lessons.
- **Certification engineers get a more focused quiz**: the Module & Scheme checkpoint no longer draws eight questions about network scanning and infrastructure tools, the Data & Asset Sensitivity subject drops off the role's list, and the Testing & Validation lesson now points on to FIPS 140-3 Certification. Other roles keep all of these questions.
- **Lesson headers that offer several paths show the range**: with no path chosen, Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS says "35–76 min, depending on your path" instead of a total shorter than its longest path. The certification engineer card on Home says 95 min, matching the first lesson.
- **The FIPS 140-3 record's deadline says whose deadline it is**: the cell now reads that the NIST IR 8547 initial public draft would deprecate 112-bit classical public-key parameter sets after 2030, and the record's notes add that the same draft would disallow the listed quantum-vulnerable public-key schemes after 2035. FIPS 140-3 itself sets no 2030 deadline.
- **The validation gaps register is written in plain words**: twenty generated failure lines became two clear entries (one PBKDF2 sample fails on both engines; eighteen RSA-OAEP samples fail on the Rust engine), more entries lost internal wording, and the technical ids stay under Show technical evidence.

### Fixed

- **Fifteen statements corrected in the certification lessons**: statements in the FIPS 140-3, Cryptographic Product Certification and Common Criteria lessons were checked against the NIST, NIAP and IETF documents they cite and corrected where they went further than the source (the Management Manual section, the hybrid key combiner, the NIAP profile count and a VPN client's curve, among others).
- **The fault-injection card quotes FIPS 204**: it no longer gives a reason for hedged signing that the standard does not give, and says what section 3.4 actually says about the deterministic variant. The HSM simulator code panels also match the calls the live HSM runs.
- **The hybrid known-answer panel says what it does not test**: no published test vector for a hybrid key exchange is run, because NIST's ACVP does not cover hybrids yet.
- **The Vulnerabilities tab says plainly when there is no data**: a selected product with no vulnerability data shows "No vulnerability data yet" and is listed last, instead of looking like a product with no vulnerabilities.
- **The PCI dates table fits a phone**: below 640 px each date becomes a stacked block, so the right-hand column is no longer cut off. Phone lesson headers no longer print an internal module code.
- **Plain words in the Entropy lesson's device datasets**: the boards are described by what they are and what ran on them, without internal image or service names.
- **TPM 2.0 v185 and NIAP Policy Letter 26 described accurately in the Library**: the four TPM v185 parts no longer state a release candidate, a buffer-size change or algorithm numbers their documents do not contain, and Policy Letter 26 is described as the 2019 letter on products barred from national security systems, not the latest letter.
- **Panels with a NIST sample no longer say NIST twice**: the subtitle of the ML-KEM, SLH-DSA and LMS sample panels reads cleanly.

### Data

- **Vulnerability counts cover every version for 52 products**: NIST files most vulnerabilities against version ranges, so products listed without a version showed far too few (OpenSSL showed 73 where 316 are on record, AWS-LC showed none where 3 are). The refreshed data covers every version, and no product lost an entry it had. Fourteen more widely used cryptographic libraries now have a vulnerability lookup.
