CHG:4.180.0.full: More statements in the certification lessons and the Library are checked against their sources, the certification role gets clearer pages on phones and a better path from lesson to lesson, and the Stateful Hash Signatures lesson gains a "Which scheme for which use" section.
CHG:4.180.0.release_notes:
More statements in the certification lessons and the Library are checked against their sources, the certification role gets clearer pages on phones and a better path from lesson to lesson, and the Stateful Hash Signatures lesson gains a "Which scheme for which use" section.

### Fixed

- **The FIPS 140-3 lesson prints the real number of Active certificates**: the older "about 712" is replaced by the count in the site's own certificate data, with the date it was read.
- **The HSM lesson names the message-based signing calls the simulator shows**: Exercise 2 and the ML-DSA row now say C_MessageSignInit with C_SignMessage and C_MessageVerifyInit with C_VerifyMessage.
- **The Testing & Validation lesson lists every document its text cites, and its performance figures say where they come from**: four missing documents are on the References tab, the session-resumption figure is credited to VIAVI's white paper, and an unsourced LAN figure was removed.
- **LMS public-key size and the HSS signature header size are right**: the public key is 24 bytes plus the hash output length (48 bytes for the SHA-256/192 sets, 56 for the SHA-256 sets), and the header no longer counts the 4 bytes per level twice.
- **An SLH-DSA exercise cites the right FIPS 205 section**: the Pure and Hash signing procedures are in section 10.2, not the parameter-set section.
- **The Standards Bodies lesson prints the ISO/IEC SC 27 member counts with their source and date**: 56 participating and 38 observing members, read from the ISO committee page on 25 October 2026.
- **The DRBG page says which random bit generators are seeded from entropy sources**: in SP 800-90C an RBG2 or RBG3 seeds from entropy sources validated under SP 800-90B, and an RBG1 is seeded once by another generator.
- **The hybrid signatures page describes concatenation as the standard does and marks blocked constructions plainly**: the concatenation card says it is bare concatenation with no label, cites RFC 9955, and the vague "Non-Separable" badge and "IETF draft" labels are replaced.
- **A maintainer quote in the OpenSSL lessons is marked as a paraphrase**: three places put a paraphrase in quotation marks.
- **The Library role note matches the real category order**: the note no longer says the categories lead with Compliance & Certification.
- **Secure Boot figures are measured or sourced**: the "8 KB to 40+ KB" database figure and the "about 1.2 KB per certificate" figure are replaced by measured minimal certificate sizes (809 bytes for RSA-2048, 5,538 bytes for ML-DSA-65, OpenSSL 3.6.3), the UEFI Forum box now quotes the white paper of 29 April 2026, and the unsourced Granite Rapids and Zen 6 dates are shown as "TBD".
- **A quiz explanation gives the right date for PKCS#11 v3.2**: the OASIS Standard is dated 3 June 2026.
- **The Library points at the right documents**: the 3GPP cryptographic inventory report starts in June 2025 (its first approved version), the ANSSI entry is the April 2022 position paper (the 2023 follow-up has its own entry), the Microsoft roadmap entry opens the article, the Spherity entry is the research paper (published 21 May 2026, updated 7 September 2026), the TCG TPM entries describe what the specifications define, and the Deloitte, FrodoKEM and CA/Browser Forum entries say what they are.
- **The OpenPGP persistent symmetric keys draft has its own Library entry instead of being filed as RFC 9581**: the old entry now says it was listed by mistake and points to the draft (version 04 of 15 September 2026).
- **A Library note about NIST's FIPS 140-3 transition page says what the page says**: the page lists two different milestones, not a contradiction, and one quoted sentence that is not on the page was replaced by one that is.
- **NIAP Policy #33 is typed as a compliance framework, and Navigate uses the Compliance page's labels**: FIPS 140-3 now reads "Certification scheme" in both places, and the CMVP source lists its products apart from other references with a note that a link is not a validation.

### Changed

- **On a phone, a lesson's header shows the minutes of your learning path**: it no longer shows the whole module's length, and the "Start here" box is hidden when your path skips that step.
- **Tables in the ACVP, Common Criteria, PCI and SLH-DSA lessons read well on a phone**: below 640 pixels each row becomes a block with its column headings, so no column is hidden and no table scrolls sideways inside a narrow box.
- **Lessons on the certification path end with a card for the next lesson on that path**: five lessons and tools sent the role to a planner or an unrelated lesson, and a test now keeps the cards in step with the path.
- **The learning path pages read more clearly**: the role card counts the first lesson in its six, the Essentials / Full buttons show a space before the time, checkpoints say how many quiz topics they cover, the Full track note says the essentials start at the certificate, and lesson descriptions name other lessons by title.
- **The Testing & Validation lesson on the certification route shows only what belongs to it**: one exercise (the IoT firmware leakage assessment) and the side-channel tool; other routes keep all six exercises and all fifteen products.
- **The SLH-DSA tool, the validation workbench and the conformance runner explain themselves**: the SLH-DSA tool carries the standard validation disclaimer under its NIST sample panels, the greyed engine selector says why, the results legend says what an unbadged row means, and the conformance runner's empty state no longer points to a list that is not on a phone.
- **The phone Community page shows the role note the computer shows**
- **The phone Validation page links to the coverage matrix and the register of open gaps**: the coverage page is exactly screen-width on a phone and a browser test keeps it so.
- **The role text for Secure Boot and Stateful Hash Signatures points to "What the lab tests"**
- **The certification Stages board says entropy source certificates are kept apart from the module stages**

### Added

- **The Stateful Hash Signatures lesson has a "Which scheme for which use" section**: five uses (firmware, code signing, secure boot, document signing, timestamping), each with an example parameter set, the number of signatures it can ever make (worked out from the tree height), where the state must live, and the NSA CNSA 2.0 position. NSA approves only LMS and XMSS, and only for firmware and software.
- **The Secure Boot lesson opens "What the lab tests" with a three-row summary**: code that only verifies needs algorithm validation, a signer that is a National Security System needs hardware validated by CMVP, and a product under a NIAP profile that only verifies needs algorithm validation only.
- **The Hybrid lesson says what NIST's guidance does not cover**: the Implementation Guidance (updated 19 August 2026) has no section on composite or hybrid signatures; ask the lab.
- **The OpenSSL Studio lessons explain the FIPS provider**: only a FIPS provider built from a certified OpenSSL version is validated, and this in-browser build is not.
- **The Entropy Testing workshop points to the entropy source certificates**: NIST entropy source validation certificates are listed under Compliance, Entropy (ESV).
- **Step 2 of the ACVP lab workshop says how to choose for each test group**: a box above the test groups explains that a standard PKCS#11 call can carry a key, a ciphertext, a message or a signature, but not a value the module normally chooses for itself (such as the random input of ML-KEM encapsulation), and has no call for the key checks.
- **The Library lists NIST's ACVP specification for LMS**: the draft of 2 October 2026 is the algorithm test specification for the LMS signature scheme.

CHG:4.180.1.full: Library entries now name the organisation that published them, and seven certification lessons carry a second review after the 4.180.0 changes.
CHG:4.180.1.release_notes:
Library entries now name the organisation that published them, and seven certification lessons carry a second review after the 4.180.0 changes.

### Fixed

- **Almost 200 Library entries now link to their real publisher**: entries with no linked publisher scored "No linked trusted source", which lowered the trust score of documents from NIST, the IETF, ISO, arXiv and many others. Each entry now points to the organisation that published it, and 39 publishers that were missing from the list of trusted sources were added.
- **Seventeen Library entries no longer link to the wrong publisher**: eleven documents from Czech, Canadian, Indian, US and international bodies had been linked to the European Commission, and six others to a neighbouring organisation. They now link to the publisher that issued them.
- **The 4.180.0 note on Testing & Validation counts the products right**: other routes list fifteen products, not sixteen.

### Changed

- **Seven certification lessons were reviewed again after the 4.180.0 changes**: the owner went through every change to the ACVP lab workflow, PCI, entropy, SLH-DSA, stateful signatures, secure boot and testing lessons and confirmed their review of 25 October 2026 for the text as it now reads.

CHG:4.181.0.full: The PQC Hardware Acceleration lesson now compares seven platforms on the same measurements, and two Library links, the PCI Quick Reference Guide entry, a Nokia product name and the Entropy board are corrected.
CHG:4.181.0.release_notes:
The PQC Hardware Acceleration lesson now compares seven platforms on the same measurements, and two Library links, the PCI Quick Reference Guide entry, a Nokia product name and the Entropy board are corrected.

### Added

- **The PQC Hardware Acceleration lesson now has one set of results for seven platforms**: a new results view in the workshop compares an AMD AI X1 Pro, two NXP i.MX 95 boards, an AMD Kria KV260 (CPU cores only), a Ventuno Q, an Apple M4 Pro and an Apple M5 Max on the same signing, key-agreement and key-encapsulation operations, including the hybrid mechanisms of PKCS#11 v3.3, with the speed of one worker and of the whole board side by side. The lesson also gains sections on Arm platforms and core types, on what the AMD64 instruction sets did and did not help on the AI X1 Pro, and on measuring hybrid mechanisms as whole HSM operations, and it has a new infographic.

### Fixed

- **Two ISO links in the Library now open the right standard**: ISO/IEC 27005:2022 opened the page for a different standard (ISO/IEC 15408-2:2022), and ISO/IEC 7816-4:2020 opened the 2013 edition.
- **The PCI Quick Reference Guide entry no longer contradicts itself**: its description named PCI DSS v4.0 while the guide it links to is the 2014 version 3.0. The entry now says so and is marked superseded.
- **A Nokia product is spelled correctly in the certification records**: the EUCC record for the Nokia Lightspan Access Node MF-2 read "Lightstpan"; it now matches the ENISA certificate page.

### Changed

- **The Entropy board for certification engineers now links to the entropy source certificates**: a new card, "See the entropy source certificates", opens the entropy tab of the certification records. The standards-community card it replaced now sits on the Hardware board, in place of the card for the hardware-acceleration lesson.

CHG:4.182.0.full: Forty-four corrections on the certification engineer's path: wrong figures and unsourced claims replaced with what the standards say, phone tables that were cut off now stack, the certificates page has an EUCC tab and finds EUCC numbers, and the certificate data is refreshed.
CHG:4.182.0.release_notes:
Forty-four corrections on the certification engineer's path: wrong figures and unsourced claims replaced with what the standards say, phone tables that were cut off now stack, the certificates page has an EUCC tab and finds EUCC numbers, and the certificate data is refreshed.

### Added

- **The Certificates page has its own EUCC (ENISA) tab**: the 112 European EUCC certificates now sit under one tab, and the search finds a certificate by the EUCC number the table shows. Common Criteria Portal rows whose product name ends with an EUCC number now show that number instead of "No scheme number in the listing".
- **A "Go to Algorithm checks" button in the SLH-DSA workshop**: the three workshop steps share one demo page, so the button takes you to the checks the role line points to.
- **The phone quiz tells you how long each length takes**: each choice shows its question count and time, a line above says what the quiz covers, and "Quick pick" now means 20 questions on phone and desktop alike (the desktop 5-minute run is called "Short run").

### Changed

- **Four lesson tables that were cut off on a phone now stack**: the random-input rules, the four HSM tables (including the "FIPS Recert" column), the SLH-DSA parameter table and the key-hierarchy table show every column as a block per row.
- **The Navigate panel names a link in plain words**: a record such as FIPS 140-3 now reads "Applies to these industries", "Governed by" or "Cited by" instead of "Governs (from) 4: Public Administration, Finance and Insurance".
- **The Stages board button says where it goes**: "See the migration programme's closure gate" replaces "See the evidence closure gate".
- **The first checkpoint quiz on My Path is named for what it covers**: "Certificates, FIPS 140-3, ACVP & Entropy" replaces "Algorithms & Entropy". Long lesson titles on the phone path list wrap to two lines.
- **On the certification route, the Network Testing lesson ends with the two workshops that apply**: TVLA leakage analysis and ACVP validation.
- **The first-visit notice no longer floats over the home page**: after you pick a role it sits in the page, above the board on a desktop and below it on a phone.
- **Crypto Lab no longer shows the same three tools twice**: tools already shown for your role are left out of the recommended list, and the phone note counts the Docker scenarios from the same list as the desktop header.
- **The Validation Workbench heading is shown in full**: the page title wraps instead of being cut to "PKCS#11 HSM Play...", and the page now points to the ACVP Lab Workflow lesson that teaches it.
- **The PCI Certification lesson ends by sending you to the final quiz**.
- **A lesson's Tools and Products tab no longer calls every product PQC-ready**: when a module lists products that are there for their certificates and carry no PQC support, the header says each badge shows its PQC support.

### Fixed

- **The Network Testing lesson no longer says a TCP handshake adds six round trips**: a TCP connection costs one round trip and a TLS 1.3 handshake one more; the unsourced "6x" figure is gone, and the lesson summary, the benchmark designer and the lesson's answer in search say the same.
- **The Hybrid lesson no longer says NIST's ACVP does not cover hybrids, or that the FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance uses "hybrid" only for hybrid modules**: the workshop now names the X-Wing tests on the CAVP prerequisites page, and the lesson says the guidance names a hybrid key-establishment scheme that uses ML-KEM and that a hybrid module is a different thing. The lesson's references now list RFC 10024 instead of the superseded TLS draft.
- **The Secure Boot and OS lessons agree on Linux**: ML-DSA kernel module signing is in mainline Linux from 7.0 and ML-DSA verification of IMA/EVM signatures from 7.2; the unsourced "production 2027+" is gone. The key-hierarchy text names the CNSA 2.0 / NSS column it describes.
- **The Firmware Signing Migrator compares like with like**: key sizes say which encoding they use, and the headline comparison uses certificate-form public keys (RSA-2048 294 bytes, ML-DSA-65 1,974 bytes).
- **The FIPS 140-3 lesson says which numbers are as of its review date**: the certificate count is read from the site's own CMVP data.
- **The Standards Bodies lesson cites its membership numbers**: ITU (194 Member States and more than 1,000 other members), ETSI (over 950 members) and 3GPP (no direct membership, through seven Organizational Partners) now carry the source and the date they were read, and a garbled sentence in the Korea card is fixed.
- **The SLH-DSA demo warns when a category 3 or 5 set uses a SHA-256 or SHAKE128 pre-hash**: FIPS 205 allows those pre-hash functions only for category 1 parameter sets.
- **The entropy tests' monobit cutoff scales with the sample length, and the rollback warning reads correctly**: the pass limit follows SP 800-22 instead of a fixed 0.05, a one-leaf rollback reads "leaf 2" rather than "leaves 2 to 2", and the LMS signature size and XMSS speed statements follow RFC 8554 and RFC 8391.
- **OpenSSL Studio says why LMS is refused**: this build was not configured with enable-lms; OpenSSL 3.6 supports LMS verification only when that option is on. The glossary and lesson 10 now agree with the Explore panel about the PKCS#11 provider, and the role hint points to the Validation tab on the Algorithms page.
- **Two quiz explanations are corrected**: LMS signature sizes (1,776 bytes shrinking to 1,144 for h=20, w=8, RFC 9858 Table 3) and the ML-KEM noise sampling, which produces the secret and error vectors from a seed derived from the secret seed.

### Data

- **Library entries tidied**: ISO/IEC 15408-1:2022 shows as withdrawn on 19 May 2026 and replaced by the 2026 edition, NIST CSWP 37B shows as final with its real authors, RFC 10024 is listed as published, the Debian SSLkeys page names its publisher and a book is no longer labelled a standard. The FIPS 140-3 record on Navigate now links to the standard, the Implementation Guidance, the CMVP Management Manual and the SP 800-140 series.
- **Certificate data refreshed**: NIST FIPS 140-3 certificate #5562 (Ergotron Cryptographic Module) and six new NIST CAVP validations for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA or LMS (Versa Networks, Microchip, KIOXIA, Citrix and Chipsea) are added, and the validity end date of EUCC certificate EUCC-3087-2026-000013-I-00 now reads 16 July 2031, as ENISA states. Every record shows when it was last read.

CHG:4.183.0.full: NIST published the final IR 8547 on 27 October 2026, and the site now uses its dates everywhere. Certification lessons say exactly what NIST's CMVP documents say, the Certificates page shows when ENISA has withdrawn a certificate, Java's post-quantum support is shown as it is after Oracle's October 2026 update, X-Wing is named and checked correctly, the PKCS#11 call log folds routine calls so the cryptographic ones stand out, and the Industry Landscape gets a first pass of source corrections.
CHG:4.183.0.release_notes:
NIST published the final IR 8547 on 27 October 2026, and the site now uses its dates everywhere. Certification lessons say exactly what NIST's CMVP documents say, the Certificates page shows when ENISA has withdrawn a certificate, Java's post-quantum support is shown as it is after Oracle's October 2026 update, X-Wing is named and checked correctly, the PKCS#11 call log folds routine calls so the cryptographic ones stand out, and the Industry Landscape gets a first pass of source corrections.

### Added

- **The Certificates page shows ENISA withdrawals**: an EUCC certificate that ENISA has withdrawn is marked Withdrawn, its detail view quotes ENISA's own sentence, and it no longer counts as current.
- **Common Criteria Portal rows say where an EUCC number stands with ENISA**: when a Portal listing names an EUCC certificate, the number links to ENISA's certificate page if ENISA lists it, and otherwise reads "not on ENISA's certificate list". Each ENISA document is now named by ENISA's own title (Certificate, Certification Report, Security Target) instead of "ENISA document".

### Changed

- **The site follows the final NIST IR 8547**: NIST published the final report on 27 October 2026, replacing the November 2024 draft. Quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, DH and ECDH at 112 bits of security or more; EdDSA at 128 bits or more) are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. The draft had deprecated only the 112-bit sets, so the Algorithms transition table now gives 61 rows both steps, including RSA-3072/4096, P-256/384/521, X25519, X448, Ed25519, Ed448 and DH-3072/4096. The Library, Compliance, timeline, threat and industry records, the FAQ, glossary, search descriptions, Business Center, Migrate workbench, Sandbox scenarios, Learn lessons and quiz no longer call these dates a draft proposal.
- **The PKCS#11 call log is readable again**: attribute reads, object searches and session setup fold into one expandable row, so the calls that run a mechanism stand out; Expand all and Collapse support sit in the toolbar, and errors and the calls a lesson asks for never fold. This applies to the HSM Playground, Learn lessons and workshops, OpenSSL Studio and the VPN/SSH simulators.
- **Every PKCS#11 call in the log can be opened**: multi-part encrypt, decrypt and verify, the v3.x message API, single-shot verify, sign and verify with recovery, random generation, named-user login (PIN never shown) and the library, slot, token and session information now open a decoded view. X-Wing and the other HPKE hybrid KEMs show their KEM, KDF, AEAD, mode and info, and multi-part composite ML-DSA signatures are split into their two parts. Ten functions that showed wrong argument labels now follow the PKCS#11 headers.
- **The welcome notice is a slim strip on every page**: the same text and "I Understand" button now sit at the top of the page instead of a sheet covering the lower half of a phone screen.
- **Smaller reading fixes**: OpenSSL Studio links straight to the Validation tab on the Algorithms page; the Crypto Lab no longer shows an empty "Recommended" heading; the phone quiz length screen has side margins; long Learn path titles wrap on narrow phones; and the Firmware Signing Migrator explains why its raw and certificate-form key-size ratios differ.
- **Eleven certification lessons, OpenSSL Studio and two quiz explanations were reviewed again by the owner**: nine lessons (PQC Network Testing, Hybrid, Secure Boot, OS PQC, Standards Bodies, SLH-DSA, Entropy, HSM, Stateful Signatures), OpenSSL Studio and two quiz explanations after the 4.182.0 changes, and FIPS 140-3 Certification and Cryptographic Product Certification after this release's corrections.

### Fixed

- **Learn lessons no longer call NIST IR 8547 a draft**: nineteen lessons give the final dates. Their timelines label 2030 as the deprecation of quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography, not only "RSA-2048 and 112-bit ECC". The Talking About PQC lesson now says the dates are final NIST guidance, not a ban, and the PQC Risk Management lesson quotes the final report's own wording. Six lesson Q&A answers are corrected too, including two that credited IR 8547 with a QKD position and a seven-phase framework it does not contain.
- **Twelve quiz questions follow the final IR 8547**: two answers change. "What is the status of those dates?" is now "final NIST guidance", and "IR 8547 has been published in final form" is now true. The others drop "draft" and "proposed" and say "after 2030 / after 2035".
- **X-Wing is named and computed correctly**: the HSM key-wrap tool no longer labels an HKDF construction as X-Wing, the KMS explorer shows X-Wing's real SHA3-256 combiner, and the TLS examples no longer confuse the X25519MLKEM768 TLS group with standalone X-Wing. A new reference check runs X-Wing's published test vectors, NIST ML-KEM-768 samples and a published X25519 example in your browser; draft test vectors stay marked as such, and nothing claims certification.
- **The Cryptographic APIs lesson no longer says JDK 21 lacks ML-KEM and ML-DSA**: Oracle added both to Oracle JDK 21.0.13 and 17.0.21 on 20 October 2026, and plans JDK 11 and 8 for the second half of 2027. The support table, migration step, code notes, exercise answer and lesson answers now say so, and the timeline adds JDK 27 and the October backports. Other OpenJDK builds are not assumed: the lesson tells you to check your vendor's release notes.
- **Hybrid post-quantum TLS in Java is dated correctly**: the JDK's own TLS stack negotiates X25519MLKEM768 by default from JDK 27 (September 2026) and from Oracle JDK 25.0.5 (October 2026); Oracle plans it for JDK 21 and 17 in the first half of 2027. The Java product records no longer say JDK 27 is unreleased.
- **Two more lessons give the current Java picture**: the Crypto Modernization refactoring checklist points to the JDK's built-in ML-DSA instead of "waiting for JDK 25", and the IAM lesson no longer credits JDK 21 with hybrid TLS for WildFly.
- **FIPS 140-3 self-test history is stated correctly**: the Crypto Management Modernization lesson, its workshop and a quiz answer no longer say the September 2025 Implementation Guidance "retroactively" imposed post-quantum self-tests. NIST added those self-tests in August 2024; in September 2025 it let the key-generation tests check against the private key only. The lesson also explains how the CMVP Management Manual decides, route by route, which requirements a revalidation must meet.
- **"In progress" no longer means "on NIST's list"**: the Modules In Process and Implementation Under Test lists are voluntary and may omit modules, as the Management Manual says. The FIPS 140-3 summary, the Certificates chart note and the certification role board now say so.
- **Historical FIPS modules are described in NIST's words**: instead of "no longer valid for new procurement", the lessons, glossary, HSM notes and three quiz questions say that Federal Agencies should not include Historical modules in new systems, that NIST still supports buying and using them for existing systems, and that the certificates are not revoked.
- **A certificate becomes Historical at its sunset date**: an exercise and the risk engine no longer say an Implementation Guidance update moved a certificate to the Historical list, and the risk engine no longer calls the Active Bouncy Castle certificate #4943 Historical.
- **Smaller CMVP corrections**: the Implementation Guidance is one document, last updated 19 August 2026; the queue state is "Pending Resubmission", with NIST Billing and the lab named where they act; the interim-validation route is shown as closed to new cases (NIST's two cut-off dates have passed); the FIPS 140-3 "as of" date covers only its own section; and the Hybrid lesson names the TLS draft the Implementation Guidance cites, with RFC 10024 as its published successor.
- **Playground links on a phone say when they can't open the exact algorithm**: a "Try in playground" link from the Algorithms page, or a shared one, now tells you on a phone that the algorithm you picked needs the Key Store on a wider screen, instead of opening the phone screen as if it were that algorithm.
- **Industry Landscape cites the published TLS hybrid key-agreement RFC**: nine industry standards chips now show RFC 10024 (Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Key Agreement for TLS 1.3, published August 2026) as published, instead of the IETF draft it replaced, and the use cases that relied on that draft now cite the RFC.
- **Industry Landscape use cases now match their sources**: about 40 use-case and standards entries were corrected so each claim says only what its cited document says. Among them: the aviation data-link entry is complete; national-security entries follow NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ version 2.2 and its 2027, 2030 and 2031 milestones; V2X no longer claims a post-quantum amendment that does not exist, and no longer says FIPS 140 is required; SSH cites RFC 9941 and RFC 10042 and notes OpenSSH 10.0's ML-KEM default; and the banking, cloud key-management, HSM, medical-device, DRM, broadcast, rail and payment-terminal entries now cite the right documents.
- **Certification requirements in the Industry Landscape are sourced**: Common Criteria and FIPS 140 requirements shown on industry tiles are now backed by a cited document; two that were not (satellite communications and cloud HSM roots of trust) no longer claim Common Criteria is mandated, and payment terminals now show the FIPS 140 Level 3 or PCI-approved HSM requirement from PCI PIN.
- **Source notes on six Algorithms entries name their reference**: the size and status notes for two composite signatures, two hybrid KEMs, Covercrypt and HPKE-PQ now name the curated April 2026 algorithm reference. The facts in the notes are unchanged.

### Data

- **Library, timeline, compliance, threat and industry records follow the final IR 8547**: the NIST IR 8547 Library entry opens the October 2026 report and lists the 2024 draft as its earlier version. The timeline adds the final publication (27 October 2026) and a 2030 deprecation milestone, and the 2035 milestone now covers every quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithm, not only 112-bit sets. The NIST IR 8547, FIPS 140-3 and FISMA compliance entries describe the final, with the earlier federal deadlines from Executive Order 14412 and OMB M-26-15 named separately. Two cross-industry threat records and four Industry Landscape use cases cite the final report.
- **The Java runtime product is renamed "Java SE (JDK) PQC Runtime"**: it covers JDK 24 to 27 and the Oracle LTS updates rather than one version; links that use the old name "Java 24 PQC Runtime" still open it.
- **Oracle Jipher is in the product catalog**: Oracle's Java provider for FIPS-regulated environments added ML-KEM (512, 768, 1024) and ML-DSA (44, 65, 87) in Jipher 20 (September 2026). The entry says plainly that Oracle cites no FIPS 140-3 certificate for it yet.
- **Oracle's Java LTS roadmap is described on the Vendor roadmaps page**: which LTS release gets ML-KEM, ML-DSA and hybrid TLS, and when. Thanks to the community member who pointed us to it.
- **Library, quiz and role board follow the same NIST wording**: the retired "September 2025" Implementation Guidance entry no longer says it applies retroactively, and the CSWP 37B entry is completed (final, 30 September 2026).
- **EU certificate data checked against ENISA**: all 112 EUCC certificates were read again from ENISA; one (NXP MF0AES(H)x0, NT2H2xy1G and NT2H2xy1S, release B0, EUCC-3100-2026-7001701) is now marked Withdrawn after its re-assessment, and of the 75 Common Criteria Portal listings that name an EUCC number, 65 now link to ENISA's certificate page and 10 are marked as not on ENISA's list. NIST's lists were read again in full as well: one new CAVP validation (A9204, Arista's BC-FJA on CloudVision Appliance, LMS) is added, and the FIPS 140-3 and entropy-source records are unchanged.
- **PQC Community, Compliance and maturity entries cite RFC 10024**: the TLS 1.3 hybrid key-agreement draft was published as RFC 10024. Five PQC Community profiles, the IETF and IETF Hybrid ML-KEM compliance entries, and five maturity-model requirements now cite the RFC instead of the draft.
- **Two new Library documents**: the OpenSSH 10.0 release notes and NSA's draft CNSA 2.0 profile for TLS 1.3 (draft-becker-cnsa2-tls-profile-05).

### Security

- **Development tools updated with security fixes**: build-time dependencies are updated; nothing changes on the site.

CHG:4.184.0.full: The Industry Landscape tab covers 31 more use cases and 54 more standards documents across two new sectors, the Validation tab explains every algorithm's implementation attacks with a source for each Yes, and the Algorithms page names NIST's additional-signature candidates by their Round 3 outcome.
CHG:4.184.0.release_notes:
The Industry Landscape tab covers 31 more use cases and 54 more standards documents across two new sectors, the Validation tab explains every algorithm's implementation attacks with a source for each Yes, and the Algorithms page names NIST's additional-signature candidates by their Round 3 outcome.

### Added

- **Industry Landscape: 31 new use cases, including two new sectors**: Government Identity & Travel Documents and Semiconductors / Secure Elements join the sector list, with 54 new cited standards across the sectors. Each cell says only what its source says; a vendor's own statement is worded as the vendor's statement.
- **Industry Landscape summaries were re-read against their sources**: every use-case summary was checked sentence by sentence against its source document, and 52 summaries were reworded or shortened where the source did not support a statement.
- **Industry Landscape: unsupported certification details were removed**: certification details that no source backed were taken out of 18 use cases and will return when a source supports them. The source copies for 15 use cases were refreshed or added.
- **The certification-engineer home starts with validation**: the home page for certification engineers now opens with the validation tests, with learning as the secondary action.
- **HSM, management and confidential-computing lessons share one set of product-specific capability records**: each record shows availability, approved mode and certificate inclusion separately, with its source, its date and any pending review, and the vendor comparison's status label now reads Available instead of Production. Long mechanism identifiers wrap inside the evidence cards.
- **27 new documents in the Library**: the Cloudflare, Signal and Chromium posts on post-quantum deployment, the Algorand roadmap and technical brief, the ITU X.509 Day talk on IEC 62351, Nacha's payments readiness road map, the Toppan/NICT/ISARA smart-card trial, ICP-Brasil's Normative Instruction 35, the 3GPP SA3 overview, APRA's remarks to the AFIA Risk Summit, the ICAO ID4Africa talk, Infineon's post-quantum page, and four avionics software-loading documents (AIA, DLR/CEAS, EASA AMC 20 and SAE ARINC 835-2). Search finds passages from each. Open Metering System Group is added to the trusted sources.
- **The implementation-attack table covers every algorithm in the catalogue**: it grew from 51 rows to 133, so each of the 127 algorithms has its own row with its own check date. A cell says Yes only when a published paper supports it; the table lists the papers, and a cell with no supporting paper now reads Unknown instead of Yes.
- **Each Yes now points to a paper, and says how far the paper reaches**: the table records whether the evidence concerns the whole algorithm family or one parameter set. Hybrid and composite constructions stay Unknown unless a paper names the combination; their row shows what is known about the component schemes.
- **A short note on low-order public keys in X25519 and X448**: the Validation tab's RNG and API misuse card now explains what RFC 7748 and RFC 9180 require, how Project Wycheproof grades the matching test cases, and how the Hub's engines handle them today.

### Changed

- **The Algorithms page names NIST's additional-signature candidates by their Round 3 outcome**: UOV, MAYO, SQIsign, FAEST and SNOVA are Round 3 candidates, HAWK entered Round 3 and was withdrawn, and CROSS and LESS did not advance from Round 2. The Candidate filter's banner says Round 3.
- **HQC's status states only what NIST has announced**: HQC was selected for standardization on 11 March 2025. The earlier "draft in about a year, final in 2027" was NIST's plan of that day, not a current schedule.
- **Side-channel, fault, randomness, secret-handling and misuse columns reflect current research**: 63 papers and records now back the table, 14 of them first posted since 6 May 2026 (for example on SQIsign, MAYO, SNOVA, LESS, HQC, SMAUG-T, FAEST and Falcon). The randomness and misuse columns, which were marked Yes for almost every algorithm, now show Yes only where a paper reports it.
- **Corrections on the algorithm cards**: the HQC timing attack is described as needing the attacker on the same physical core, not as network-remote; the masked-Kyber attack is described as run on an ARM Cortex-M4; the hybrid key-exchange card now follows NIST SP 800-227 on how combiners can lose chosen-ciphertext security; UOV is described as having short signatures and large public keys.
- **Statements on the algorithm cards were checked against their sources**: each summary line, cell detail and design consideration on the 14 cards was compared with the papers and standards it relies on. Those the sources support were kept, those they contradict were reworded to what the source says, and those no source could be found for were removed. The impact labels remain an editorial reading, as the page already says.
- **Validation coverage shows the HPKE single-call tests and the accepted gaps**: the 58 tests of the single-call HPKE mechanism (Rust engine) are registered as round-trip evidence for HPKE key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation, and show as registered, not as passed, until a result is recorded. The SLH-DSA pre-hash waiver is gone because NIST test cases now cover those cells on both engines; the mechanisms with no test yet are listed as accepted gaps with a review date of 31 January 2027.
- **The Stateful Signatures workshop calls its XMSS key-generation check a repeatability check**: RFC 8391 publishes no test vectors for it.
- **The IETF Hybrid ML-KEM card cites RFC 10024**: the compliance card now cites RFC 10024 (Proposed Standard, August 2026) instead of the expired draft, and is classed as a recommendation rather than a draft.
- **The KMIP policy presets match the engine's policy files**: seven presets (FIPS-only and the PQC migration 2030 family) were brought back in line with the policy files they are copied from.
- **Scrollable editors keep their native accessibility behaviour**: scrollable native controls keep their built-in accessibility semantics, and the YAML editor stays an editable textbox.
- **The Migrate catalogue's Trident entry says what the vendor's specification lists**: the post-quantum line now names SPHINCS+, the algorithm the vendor's published specification lists, and says ML-KEM and ML-DSA support is not confirmed.
- **The Revisions page lists four earlier changes once**: PT-011, API Security JWT, Quantum Threats and the ACVP lab workflow were each listed twice on their own page.

### Fixed

- **The 5G lesson shows the correct Profile A example key**: the ephemeral private key in the GSMA test-data window had two extra hex digits (33 bytes). It now shows the 32-byte value printed in 3GPP TS 33.501 Annex C, which gives the published ephemeral public key; the other Annex C.4 values were checked against version 19.7.0 and match.

CHG:4.185.0.full: The certification-engineer path now opens with the validation tests, fifteen lessons were corrected against their sources, the Industry Landscape's badges and wording were checked again, and the Library gained ten documents.
CHG:4.185.0.release_notes:
The certification-engineer path now opens with the validation tests, fifteen lessons were corrected against their sources, the Industry Landscape's badges and wording were checked again, and the Library gained ten documents.

### Added

- **10 new documents in the Library**: the AUTOSAR R25-11 specifications for the TCP/IP stack, secure onboard communication, secure hardware extensions and the security overview, the Uptane standard 2.1.0, ETSI TS 103 097 V2.2.1 on ITS security headers and certificates, the FuSeCar report selecting candidate post-quantum algorithms for connected cars, IOG's Cardano Vision 2026 research article, Cardano problem statement CPS-0030 on a quantum-secure settlement layer, and a CIGRE paper on IEC 61850 and IEC 62351 substations.

### Changed

- **The certification-engineer path starts with the validation tests everywhere**: the Learn page's next step, the My Path page and the Journey panel now open the validation workbench first, as the home page already does, and the lessons follow from the certificate. The home page's main button opens the workbench with both engines (C++ and Rust) selected, so the comparison is ready to run.
- **Industry Landscape summaries were rewritten from newly added source documents**: In-Vehicle Networks, Secure Boot, Energy SCADA and Cardano Signing now follow the AUTOSAR specifications, the Uptane standard, the FuSeCar report, the CIGRE paper, IOG's article and CPS-0030; the V2X summary follows ETSI TS 103 097.
- **Industry Landscape badges say only what the source shows**: the "Adopted" badge was lowered to "Standardised" on six use cases whose sources show a standard but not the sector running it, and four use cases whose sources name no post-quantum route no longer claim one. The rows for health records, medical devices, supply chain, identity, credentials, VPN, federal PKI and IoT firmware each name the post-quantum route their badge rests on.
- **Industry Landscape wording was corrected where a source did not back a sentence**: 39 use cases were updated (EMV, PIN key management, SATCOM certification, the air interface and others); web TLS and streaming now cite Cloudflare's October 2025 measurement; the National Security Systems rows state the CNSA 2.0 dates as the NSA's FAQ words them; and qualified electronic signatures follow ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1. The EUDI Wallet row names the framework edition on file (v2.9.0).
- **Two Industry Landscape standards entries were corrected**: GSMA PQ.04 is recorded as an industry report, and the ONC (d)(7) criterion now belongs to the electronic-health-record use case.
- **Industry lessons keep their statements within their sources**: Aerospace describes EASA AMC 20-42 as an accepted means of compliance rather than a mandate and states the FAA rule as the notice of proposed rulemaking it is; Automotive says no post-quantum amendment to IEEE 1609.2 or the ETSI V2X specifications is identified and adds ETSI TR 103 949; EMV payments label card-replacement figures as estimates and add the measured card-chip findings; Digital Assets describes BIP-360 as it stands, a Pay-to-Merkle-Root output with no post-quantum signature of its own.
- **Health, government, telecom, trust-services, identity, OT and IoT lessons were corrected against their sources**: HIPAA encryption reads as an addressable requirement and the FDA guidance as nonbinding; federal civilian systems show Executive Order 14412's own 2030 and 2031 dates, separate from the NSA's dates for National Security Systems; 5G no longer implies that post-quantum algorithms already protect session-key derivation and signalling integrity (TS 33.501 uses symmetric algorithms for both); the EUDI Wallet text says only what the framework and regulation say; OT and IoT add the IEC 62351 migration work, RFC 9019's bootloader advice and the TPM profile's post-quantum requirement.
- **The Compliance Strategy lesson states the eIDAS 2.0 position from its sources**: each Member State must provide at least one EUDI wallet within 24 months of the entry into force of the implementing acts; eIDAS 2.0 does not yet mandate post-quantum cryptography, and the earlier claim that ENISA names wallet providers as early adopters was removed.
- **Certificate records in the HSM lessons were corrected**: the Luna Network HSM 7 uses the K7 module, certificate #4684, which lists no post-quantum algorithm; Marvell's LS2 HSM family shows both certificates (#4703 and #5502) with no post-quantum algorithm among their approved algorithms; and the HSM example cards show the same availability label as the vendor tiles.
- **The Azure Dedicated HSM card follows Azure's own pages**: Azure documents FIPS 140-2 Level 3 firmware 7.0.3 and lists no post-quantum algorithm; Thales documents ML-KEM and ML-DSA from Luna firmware 7.9, customers administer the firmware themselves, and the service is retiring (no new onboardings, existing customers supported until 31 July 2028). A legend under the HSM table says the colour is PQC availability and the certificate column is separate.
- **Five HSM entries in the Migrate catalogue follow each vendor's pages**: Crypto4A's QxHSM and QxEDGE point to certificate #5497 (their QASM module, Active, FIPS 140-3 Level 3, listing ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS; the certificate names the module, not the products); Google's entry says it lists post-quantum algorithms for software keys and none for HSM-protected keys; Fortanix's says DSM supports ML-KEM, ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS, outside its FIPS 140-2 certificate; Azure Dedicated HSM names firmware 7.0.3 and needs a customer firmware upgrade for post-quantum algorithms, and its entry notes that CMVP #4684 covers only Luna firmware 7.8.4 and 7.8.5.
- **The Standards Bodies lesson dates NIST's competition correctly**: the call for proposals was in December 2016, round three had 7 finalists and 8 alternates, the first algorithms were selected in July 2022 and HQC in March 2025.
- **OpenSSL Studio no longer calls `openssl kdf` new in 3.6**: the lesson and the glossary say it was added in OpenSSL 3.0; only `configutl` is new in 3.6.
- **Five quiz questions and five lesson Q&A answers match the corrected lessons**: the 5G, Digital ID, IoT, OT and Compliance Strategy questions and the 5G, Digital ID and IoT answers were brought in line with the sourced lesson text.
- **The BIP-360 and Solana SIMD glossary entries match the Digital Assets lesson**: BIP-360 is described as Pay-to-Merkle-Root with no post-quantum signature, and SIMD-0461 as closed on 17 June 2026.

### Fixed

- **The simulation page no longer waits on the sandbox status check**: the three sandbox health checks now release their response as soon as the status is known, so the page reaches idle while a sandbox is answering.

CHG:4.186.0.full: Two new Learn modules (Media, Entertainment & DRM and Software Supply Chain), a protected backup for post-quantum keys in the HSM playground, finite-field Diffie-Hellman on the Algorithms page, and lesson corrections that follow the final NIST IR 8547 and a second reading against sources.
CHG:4.186.0.release_notes:
Two new Learn modules (Media, Entertainment & DRM and Software Supply Chain), a protected backup for post-quantum keys in the HSM playground, finite-field Diffie-Hellman on the Algorithms page, and lesson corrections that follow the final NIST IR 8547 and a second reading against sources.

### Added

- **New lesson: Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC**: a 60-minute intermediate lesson on the Industries track. It reads the AACS key ladder, CI Plus broadcast protection, the MovieLabs ECP specification, streaming licences and transport, and C2PA Content Credentials link by link, and says which public-key primitive each one uses and what each edition states, or leaves unstated, about quantum computing. It comes with a key-ladder explorer, an infographic and 10 quiz questions.
- **New lesson: Software Supply Chain PQC**: a 40-minute intermediate lesson on the Industries track. It maps where each signature link stands on post-quantum signatures (Sigstore, the CA/Browser Forum code signing requirements, UEFI, COSE, CMS, X.509, OpenPGP, SUIT), then covers the TUF and Uptane update frameworks, SLSA v1.2 and in-toto provenance, and what changes when a verifier has already shipped. Two workshop steps (roles and thresholds, a provenance chain check), an infographic and 8 quiz questions come with it, and 37 cited Library documents now list it in their References.
- **8 new documents in the Library**: CISA alert AA20-352A and Mandiant's report on the 3CX compromise for the Code Signing lesson, and the SLSA v1.2 build pages, the in-toto attestation statement, the TUF specification and NIST SP 800-204D for the Software Supply Chain lesson.
- **Finite-field Diffie-Hellman has its own family**: the catalogue gains the 2048, 3072 and 4096-bit groups of RFC 3526 (127 to 130 algorithm records), ML-KEM lists the family among those it replaces, and six Industry Landscape use cases that rely on finite-field Diffie-Hellman now show it instead of elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman.
- **Protected backup of ML-KEM and ML-DSA keys in the HSM playground**: the Key Wrap panel can back up ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 keys in both Seed and Expanded forms as a protected package, using the replication profile of the Rust engine. Files written by the earlier prefix scheme cannot be recovered there, and the panel says so.

### Changed

- **The lessons follow the final NIST IR 8547 on deprecation**: RSA-2048 and DH Group 14 (112-bit security) are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035, not "by 2030" as in the 2024 draft. PQC 101, the TLS scenarios, the testing exercises, the regulatory timeline and one lesson Q&A answer were corrected.
- **The Code Signing lesson says only what its sources say**: CNSA 2.0 lists LMS and XMSS for firmware signing but does not mandate them, the algorithm cards and comparison table say the same, the ML-DSA parameter set CNSA 2.0 approves is named, and the SolarWinds signing point and the 3CX chain are quoted from the CISA and Mandiant documents.
- **The SLH-DSA and Stateful Signatures lessons match the standards**: four statements the standards contradict were corrected, the context string and the whole public key are described as FIPS 205 does, section numbers and the BSI TR-02102-1 recommendation are stated precisely, and LMS and XMSS are no longer described as resting on collision resistance. The XMSS key-generation check is described as a repeatability check.
- **The AI Security lesson separates forgery from harvest-now-decrypt-later**: certificate and signature risk is described as forgery, lattice schemes are described as believed rather than inherently quantum-safe, and C2PA 2.4 is described as allowing seven signature algorithms, none post-quantum. The glossary entry for Content Credentials says the same.
- **The Platform Engineering lesson corrects SLSA and signing-tool details**: SLSA names no signature algorithm and its build track ends at L3, Docker Content Trust is described as retired, and the OpenPGP post-quantum schemes are described as RFC 9980 does, here and in the Crypto Management, Ops and Developer impact lessons.
- **Network Security and PQC Risk Management lessons state vendor facts as the vendors publish them**: the pfSense sentence follows Netgate's 2.9.0 release notes, OPNsense ML-KEM maturity reads "Not stated", the Juniper rows say only what Juniper publishes, and the VPN scenarios credit the ML-KEM exchange to the right document. Unsourced vendor details elsewhere were removed or shown as "not stated".
- **The 5G, Digital Assets and MLS lessons state security levels and the MLS combiner as their sources do**: ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 are described as NIST security category 3 instead of "128-bit" security (FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 say a single number does not describe it), and the MLS lesson says a post-quantum session combines with the classical one by exporting a secret and importing it as a pre-shared key, not by XORing application keys.
- **The PKI Enrollment and Email Signing lessons label CMP RFCs correctly and state the ML-KEM key usage from RFC 9935**: RFC 9811 is described as CMP over HTTP rather than an HSM profile and RFC 9480 as CMP Updates, and the Email Signing lesson says that when a certificate carries the key usage extension, keyEncipherment is the only key usage set for ML-KEM certificates, instead of calling it undecided.
- **The Data Asset Sensitivity lesson follows the CNSA 2.0 FAQ on software signing**: the code-signing scenario names ML-DSA-87, because CNSA 2.0 specifies it for all classification levels, with ECDSA P-384 as the optional classical half (NSA does not require hybrid). The Developer impact lesson cites RFC 9964 for the ML-DSA JOSE algorithm identifiers.
- **The Database Encryption lesson no longer lists SLH-DSA as approved in the CNSA 2.0 row**: the CNSA 2.0 FAQ does not approve SLH-DSA for national security systems, so the row now lists ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 only. The Platform Engineering exercise on container signing says Docker is retiring Docker Content Trust and the Notary v1 service.
- **The Confidential Computing lesson no longer calls the Marvell HSM an Azure product, and cites RFC 9052**: the COSE_Sign1 citation now names the RFC that defines it.
- **The SSH workshop compares like with like**: the live handshake in Step 2 and the table it is compared with now use the same framing, with the share names per specification and the sntrup761 server share at 1071 bytes.
- **The Industry Landscape explains its PQC mark and fixes the Media/DRM row**: the legend says what the PQC mark on a standards chip means, and the Media and DRM row cites AACS Revision 0.953.
- **Quiz answers use the standards' names and sizes**: SLH-DSA, SPHINCS+, Falcon and Kyber are named as the standards and the held drafts name them, a code-signing question was added, the ML-DSA-65 signature is 3309 bytes (FIPS 204), the JWK key type for ML-DSA is AKP (RFC 9964), and F5 BIG-IP's first hybrid ML-KEM support is 17.5.0.
- **Two Migrate catalogue entries name the second Marvell certificate**: the HSM capability notes now list Marvell LS2 certificate 5502 next to the first.
- **The Rust engine in the Playground is the engines-6 build**: the validation results were recorded again against it, and the open-gap list is unchanged from 4.185.0 (71 entries).

CHG:4.187.0.full: A line-by-line reading of the Learn lessons against the documents they cite: 62 lessons now say what their sources say (or label a statement as this site's own estimate), the PCI lessons follow PCI SSC's public pages, 14 documents join the Library, and 90 quiz questions and 19 lesson answers were rechecked. This is the first part of that reading; the remaining lessons and questions follow in a later release.
CHG:4.187.0.release_notes:
A line-by-line reading of the Learn lessons against the documents they cite: 62 lessons now say what their sources say (or label a statement as this site's own estimate), the PCI lessons follow PCI SSC's public pages, 14 documents join the Library, and 90 quiz questions and 19 lesson answers were rechecked. This is the first part of that reading; the remaining lessons and questions follow in a later release.

### Added

- **14 new documents in the Library**: the SD-JWT VC specification draft, NERC CIP-013-2 and CIP-015-1, Sigstore and post-quantum cryptography (2025), NIST's CMVP page on programmatic transitions, the Bouncy Castle Java 1.81 and C# 2.6.1 announcement, the HIPAA Security Rule proposed rule, Regulation (EU) 536/2014, Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2444 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2977, the EPA memorandum withdrawing its 2023 cybersecurity memo, and the ANSSI certificates and certification report for the Samsung S3SSE2A secure element. Each cited lesson lists them under References.

### Changed

- **The PCI lessons follow PCI SSC's public pages**: statements are tied to the pages that were read (dated 30 October 2026), the PCI DSS and PTS HSM wording says what the announcements say and no more, and where the public pages are silent the lessons say so instead of stating a deadline. The PCI 3DS Core and PCI DSS v4.0.1 Library entries now rest on the public pages. Lessons whose wording changed after the owner's last sign-off say they await re-sign-off.
- **The HSM, FIPS 140-3 and Common Criteria lessons follow the certificates and release notes**: nShield firmware is given per algorithm (v13.8 or later; v13.8.3 or later for ML-KEM) and used through PKCS#11, Luna statements are bounded to the pages that were read, Azure Dedicated HSM is described as being retired when its Luna firmware upgrade is mentioned, the FIPS 140-3 sub-chip and interim-validation dates follow the CMVP pages, NIAP Policy 33 names its AES-128 Bluetooth exception, and the ACVP lesson says what the specification text and the module's own test show for the ML-KEM key checks.
- **The Hybrid Cryptography lessons follow SP 800-227, RFC 9180 and the composite drafts**: Encaps, HPKE and domain separation are described as their specifications do, the draft cipher-suite and status statements are dated and name where to check, Ed25519 lengths are credited to RFC 8032, and the ~2035 key-size rule of thumb is marked as not coming from a standard.
- **The Code Signing, Secure Boot and Standards Bodies lessons follow the CNSA 2.0 FAQ and the RFCs**: LMS and XMSS, RFC 9980, RFC 9882 and SP 800-208 are cited for what they say, the ANSSI phase dates are 2022 as published, and the FedRAMP forecast is labelled as this site's expectation.
- **The Platform Engineering, Crypto Management, Crypto Developer APIs, Secrets and KMS lessons keep to the product documentation**: certificates are described as authentication assets whose quantum risk is forgery, not harvest-now-decrypt-later; Vault, cert-manager and HSM statements follow their documentation; the KMS lesson says AWS KMS offers ML-KEM key specs, that a KEM output needs no further key derivation (the HKDF step is this lesson's design), and that Google Cloud KMS offers its KEMs at the software protection level with its two differing launch-stage statements side by side; the AES-KWP wrap of a 32-byte key is 40 bytes; and figures nobody published are removed or marked as the lesson's own assumptions.
- **The Database Encryption, IAM, Confidential Computing, Healthcare and Homomorphic Encryption lessons say what vendors have published**: Microsoft statements follow its quantum safe program roadmap, vendor dates nobody published are replaced by "we found no published date" or by what the product catalogue records, the RTS 2024/1774 paraphrases keep the regulation's wording, and RAM, power and device figures are labelled as the lesson's own model.
- **The industry lessons separate sources from assumptions**: aerospace memory budgets and service-life statements, automotive ASIL scope and TPM edition, OT standards status and trip-message times, the 5G key split, Digital ID attestations, Bitcoin and Ethereum details, the EMV certificate chain and the registry's curve fields now follow their sources or are marked as planning assumptions.
- **The Network, OS, Web Gateway and Hardware Acceleration lessons state vendor and standards facts as published**: Ubuntu and RHEL expectations are labelled as the lessons' own, unpublished roadmap clauses are removed, the ML-DSA certificate size is stated from FIPS 204, and the gateway vendor rows quote what each post says.
- **The Compliance Strategy, Governance and Business Case lessons state EO 14412, the ASD and G7 CEG positions as their sources do**: the executive order dates apply to high-value assets and high-impact systems, the Israel row says the national strategy document held here does not mention quantum, the HIPAA proposal and PCI SSC's HSM v5.0 announcement are quoted as published, the EU research entry keeps to the roadmap and GSMA sentences, and the Governance KPI dashboard says which KPIs cannot be scored yet.
- **The Quantum Threats, QKD, Stateful Signatures, SLH-DSA, Developer and Ops Quantum Impact, PKI Workshop and Testing lessons follow the standards**: qubit estimates cite their tables, classical sizes name one scheme each, ML-DSA signature sizes come from FIPS 204, GSMA handshake sizes and NIST SP 1800-38C results are quoted from their tables, and the certificate validity schedule follows the CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements by issue date.
- **Quiz answers and lesson Q&A follow their sources**: 90 quiz questions and 19 lesson answers were rechecked against the cited documents; explanations that stated more than the source (for example CMVP durations, hybrid key wrapping and CNSA 2.0, vendor post-quantum status) were corrected.
- **The Industry Landscape tab cites final documents**: 33 use cases were reread (the cloud tenant TLS source is the final NIST IR 8547, and certification verdicts the page no longer asserts are left blank rather than shown).
- **The executive role board and journey wording was reviewed**: role-board cells use the reviewed sample-worksheet wording, journey milestones are phased, and coverage and budget wording says "KPIs that can be scored" and notes the modelled total in every ROI case.

### Fixed

- **The validation register's twist-point entry is an accepted limitation**: the entry moves from open to accepted limitation, matching the shipped engine.
- **The Migrate catalogue follows the vendor and certificate pages**: the Samsung S3SSE2A secure element and the Microsoft Azure entry were corrected to what the certificate and vendor pages state.
- **The protocol matrix, glossary and timeline carry small corrections**: the OpenPGP post-quantum row names the composites RFC 9980 defines, the Bouncy Castle C# glossary entry says which CMS signature algorithms it covers, and two timeline rows were updated.

The next part of the line-by-line reading of the Learn lessons against the documents they cite: 32 lessons drop statements that no document backs, or label them as this site's own assumption or reading.

### Changed

- **Learn lessons keep to what their documents say**: across 32 lessons, figures, dates, version claims and vendor or standards statements that no cited document supports were removed, and judgements, advice and modelled inputs are now marked as the lesson's own reading or assumption.
- **OpenSSL's post-quantum start version is corrected**: the OS lesson now says post-quantum algorithms are built into OpenSSL from 3.5.0, as OpenSSL's own release notes state, not from 3.4.

CHG:4.189.0.full: The rest of the line-by-line reading that could be finished safely: 48 more lessons and 8 quiz explanations follow their documents, and usage analytics now cover search, algorithm views and exports.
CHG:4.189.0.release_notes:
The rest of the line-by-line reading that could be finished safely: 48 more lessons and 8 quiz explanations follow their documents, and usage analytics now cover search, algorithm views and exports.

### Changed

- **More Learn lessons keep to what their documents say**: across 48 more lessons, including the HSM, Secure Boot, IoT, Stateful Signatures, KMS, Secrets Management, Hybrid Cryptography, Healthcare and Standards Bodies lessons, figures, dates, version claims and vendor or standards statements that no cited document supports were removed, and judgements, advice and modelled inputs are marked as the lesson's own reading or assumption.
- **Quiz explanations stay within their sources**: eight quiz explanations lost claims that no document supports or are now marked as this lesson's own reading. The RSA-2048 question no longer says how many physical qubits are needed and keeps its 4,000 logical qubits statement.
- **Usage analytics cover search, algorithm views and exports**: searches in the Library and Compliance pages, algorithm views, Library downloads and Business tool exports are now counted, together with the role and experience level a visitor has chosen. Page views on Library, Compliance, Algorithms and Timeline are counted once per page visit, not once per search or filter change, so their totals read lower than before. The About page now says that exported files are recorded by the tool that made them and their file type, never their contents.

### Fixed

- **CNSA 2.0 deadlines in two lesson summaries match their notes**: the Crypto Management lesson shows 2030 and 2031 as the NSS equipment and algorithm dates its note cites, and the Data Asset Sensitivity lesson shows 2035 for the National Security Memorandum 10 transition.
- **Leftover gaps from removed statements are closed**: empty table cells, a sentence that began in lower case, a stray space and an empty summary field in several lessons now read correctly.

CHG:4.19.0.full: A hands-on release for the KMIP playground, the Report page, the Business
CHG:4.19.0.release_notes:
A hands-on release for the KMIP playground, the Report page, the Business
Center, and the Simulation board: the in-browser KMIP engine is rebuilt from
the real 0.13.1 engine with eight more operations now genuinely executed
instead of simulated, the report gains a Cryptographic Bill of Materials
section built on the new CycloneDX 1.7 standard, the Simulation board's
framework references were audited line by line against what actually ships,
and a sourcing sweep across the Business Center tools corrected several
citation and data errors.

### Added

- **Three new KMIP lessons with a guided tour, glossary, and knowledge checks**: the CACP Learn track now continues past the basics with three new walkthroughs (lessons 7–9), a guided tour of the KMIP 3.0 tab, an in-context glossary, and knowledge checks so you can confirm what you learned.
- **A rollback recipe for batch key migrations**: the KMIP workbench now ships a batch-Undo rollback recipe plus validated pass/fail scenarios for each migration policy, so you can see what a safe abort looks like before trying one for real.
- **The Report page now includes a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) section**: your report can now show the site's machine-readable inventory of cryptographic assets alongside the existing risk and compliance sections.

### Changed

- **The site's CBOM now follows CycloneDX 1.7**: upgraded from 1.6, adopting the new Cryptography Registry identifiers and adding classical (non-PQC) crypto assets, so the inventory names algorithms the same way scanning tools do.
- **Eight KMIP operations promoted from simulated to real**: the in-browser KMIP engine was rebuilt from engine release 0.13.1; operation labels are now honest about which commands execute for real versus which are simulated, and the OASIS test-corpus replay is aligned to the exact engine baseline it runs against.
- **Reorganized the Report page's internal code for easier maintenance**: the report's sections (risk breakdown, compliance impact, recommended actions, threat landscape, and others) now each live in their own file instead of one large file. This is an internal, behind-the-scenes change — the report itself looks and behaves exactly the same, including sharing a report link and viewing a sample report.

### Fixed

- **Corrected several sourcing and citation errors across Business Center tools**: the Cost Model Explorer's breach-probability default now uses the same sourced, size-tiered figure as the ROI Calculator and Breach Cost Model instead of an older unsourced flat estimate; the CRQC Scenario Planner's "Software/Firmware Signing" compliance deadline was corrected from 2025 to 2030 to match the actual exclusive-use date (2025 was NSA's earlier "prefer by" milestone, not the deadline); the Policy Template Generator no longer cites NIST SP 800-88 (a media-sanitization standard) as if it were a key-destruction standard; the Supply Chain Risk Matrix no longer claims NIST's crypto-agility guidance defines a specific "six asset class" taxonomy (it doesn't — this is the tool's own simplified classification); the Audit Readiness Checklist's citation for CMVP/CAVP validation evidence was corrected to the right section; and several tools' references to NIST's crypto-agility guidance were updated to the current, non-withdrawn version of that document.
- **Simulation framework references now match what actually ships**: corrected gate approval authorities, stale live/gap labels on linked tools and reports, and drift in each phase's list of produced artifacts.
- **Simulation jargon is now explained where it appears**: terms like TNFL and the governance vocabulary get plain-language glosses, activities surface their teaching text, and the board now shows which phases run in parallel instead of implying a strict sequence.
- **Closed topical gaps in Simulation phase content**: fixed Phase 5 wave content, filled Phase 1 and 2 topical gaps, corrected the Phase 3 risk-scoring label, and added the missing Foundations F.5 coverage.
