In May 2026 ICAO stated that it is in the process of specifying post-quantum cryptography for inclusion in Doc 9303, and an ISO/IEC SC17/WG3 update to the ICAO Facilitation Conference gives 2027 as the target for specifications of PQC algorithms in X.509 certificates and CMS. ICAO's NTWG and ISO WG 3 have identified Passive Authentication as the protocol most vulnerable to quantum computing, and the same deck calls the threat to the ICAO PKI urgent given the 10-year validity of eMRTDs now being issued.
Industry: Government Identity & Travel Documents
Migration status: draft

IL:id-eudi-wallet.full:
The EUDI Wallet is specified in the Architecture and Reference Framework: wallet units support ISO/IEC 18013-5 and SD-JWT VC attestations (both mandatory; W3C VCDM v2.0 support is optional), with OpenID4VP for remote presentation and OpenID4VCI for issuance. Algorithm choices appear in those specifications: OpenID4VP names ECDSA with SHA-256, and RFC 9901 requires SHA-256 support. RFC 9901 leaves post-quantum JWS algorithms to the application 'when they are ready'; ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 states that it is incomplete for the needs of the EUDI-Wallet and that an update is in preparation.
Industry: Government Identity & Travel Documents
Migration status: none

IL:id-mobile-driving-licence.full:
ISO/IEC 18013-5 defines the mobile driving licence as an mdoc: CBOR data secured with COSE, which a reader checks through issuer data authentication, mdoc authentication of the holder's device and, where the mDL requires it, reader authentication. OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI profile the format and, in their examples, use ECDSA with SHA-256 on a P-256 key for the issuer signature (issuerAuth), and ECDSA on P-256 or HMAC 256/256 over an ECDH-derived key for the device. The cited documents describe no post-quantum profile.
Industry: Government Identity & Travel Documents
Migration status: none

IL:id-national-eid.full:
The BSI eIDAS token specification TR-03110 v2.21 (December 2016), whose examples include the German ID card, maps PACE, Terminal Authentication and Chip Authentication to ECDH, RSA and ECDSA. For US PIV cards, NIST SP 800-78-5 (July 2024) sets RSA, ECDSA and ECDH and states that post-quantum algorithms will be specified in a future revision; NIST's initial working drafts of 12 June 2026 identify the changes expected to be needed to use ML-DSA and ML-KEM with PIV, and an April 2026 draft Federal PKI profile specifies ML-DSA PIV authentication certificates for a test environment.
Industry: Government Identity & Travel Documents
Migration status: draft

IL:ins-cyber-underwriting.full:
Munich Re's 2025 cyber-insurance report says RSA will in future be vulnerable to quantum-based decryption but should still offer sufficient protection through at least 2030.
Industry: Insurance
Migration status: none

IL:ins-policyholder-data.full:
Insurers hold decades-sensitive policyholder and claims data behind TLS and classically-encrypted stores; Munich Re's 2025 cyber-trends report flags harvest-now-decrypt-later theft and the NIST PQC transition (RSA vulnerable to quantum decryption, protection horizon ~2030) as a sector concern.
Industry: Insurance
Migration status: none

IL:ins-regulator-crypto-expectations.full:
In a speech published on 24 June 2026, an APRA member said APRA wants to see its regulated entities at least starting to map where cryptography is relied upon across their systems, data and third-party providers, including long-lived data and critical infrastructure. APRA oversees general insurance and reinsurance companies, life insurance and private health insurers, among others. The speech says APRA intends to step up its supervisory engagement on this over the coming year and will want evidence that boards understand the risk and are advancing plans to meet the ASD's recommended timeline: a plan to transition to post-quantum cryptography by the end of 2026 and a transition commenced by the end of 2028. These are expectations stated in a speech, not a rule, and the speech names no algorithm.
Industry: Insurance
Migration status: none

IL:iot-esim-provisioning.full:
GSMA PQ.04 states that RSP for IoT is vulnerable to quantum attacks because of its recommended use of TLS, DTLS and cipher suites that include asymmetric cryptography such as ECDHE and ECDSA.
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Migration status: draft

IL:iot-firmware.full:
RFC 9019 recommends that unchangeable bootloader code in ROM use post-quantum secure signature schemes such as hash-based signatures, because RSA and ECC signatures may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated key extraction. RFC 8778 specifies the conventions for using the HSS/LMS hash-based signature algorithm with COSE. RFC 9964 specifies COSE serializations for ML-DSA, a post-quantum digital-signature scheme defined in FIPS 204.
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Migration status: draft

IL:iot-industrial.full:
IEC's page on the IEC 62443 series notes that operational technology (OT) systems often have a long lifecycle, so they may not be updated or replaced as frequently as IT systems.
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Migration status: none

IL:iot-matter-attestation.full:
Each Matter device holds a number of certificate chains. Its device attestation certificate (DAC) proves the authenticity of the manufacturer and is used by the commissioner during commissioning. The attestation chapter refers to ECDSA with SHA-256 on the elliptic curve secp256r1 (NIST P-256). A note in the Matter 1.6 text says that PQC Phase 1 will likely soon replace the AttestationCryptoInfo mechanism in the onboarding payload with an equivalent mechanism using the Operational Credentials cluster.
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Migration status: none

IL:iot-provisioning.full:
NISTIR 8259A defines an IoT device cybersecurity capability core baseline: a set of device capabilities generally needed to support common cybersecurity controls that protect an organization's devices as well as device data, systems, and ecosystems.
Industry: Internet of Things (IoT)
Migration status: none

IL:it-composite-certs.full:
RFC 10073 combines ML-DSA with a traditional signature algorithm in one X.509 signature. Both components must verify. Resistance to forgery of new messages depends on an unforgeable component and a collision-resistant pre-hash. Resistance to a quantum adversary depends on the ML-DSA component. For TLS, check the endpoints’ certificate and handshake-signature support separately. Publicly trusted TLS issuance also has separate CA/Browser Forum requirements for CA key protection.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: none

IL:it-identity.full:
SAML assertions, OAuth/OIDC tokens (JOSE), and FIDO2/WebAuthn attestation all sign with RSA/ECDSA; the FIDO Alliance has a PQC roadmap and JOSE/COSE composite drafts exist. RFC 9964 specifies JOSE and COSE serializations for ML-DSA, a post-quantum digital-signature scheme defined in FIPS 204.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: draft

IL:it-kerberos.full:
Kerberos' core ticket exchange is symmetric and not directly quantum-exposed, but PKINIT — the public-key path used for smart-card and certificate-based initial authentication — relies on RSA and ECDH key transport; an active draft specifies ML-KEM encapsulation for that exchange.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: none

IL:it-libraries.full:
OpenSSL 3.5 shipped ML-KEM natively and changed its default TLS key shares to offer X25519MLKEM768 — the hybrid group RFC 10024 standardised in August 2026 — putting PQC key exchange into the default dependency graph of most software; legacy pre-3.5 estates are the migration tail. PQC signatures in the same libraries are on their own row because the protocol bindings are at a different stage.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: production

IL:it-libraries-signatures.full:
OpenSSL 3.5 also ships ML-DSA and SLH-DSA as native signature algorithms, but using them for TLS and SSH authentication is still on the IETF standards track (draft-ietf-tls-mldsa) — the libraries expose the primitives while the protocols that would carry them are not yet published RFCs.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: pilot

IL:it-ssh.full:
RFC 10042 defines the SSH hybrid key exchange method mlkem768x25519-sha256, which pairs ML-KEM-768 with Curve25519 (X25519). RFC 9941 states that OpenSSH's sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com became the default key exchange algorithm in OpenSSH in 2022.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: production

IL:it-supplychain.full:
The Sigstore algorithm registry lists ECDSA and Ed25519 as sign/verify algorithms and lists ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 as experimental, with the warning that they are currently not operational within Sigstore. SLSA v1.2 asks at Build level 2 for signed provenance generated by a hosted build platform and, at level 3, for a hardened build platform that keeps the secret material used to sign the provenance away from user-defined build steps; its pages name no signature algorithm.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: draft

IL:it-webpki.full:
CA root and intermediate keys (RSA-4096/ECDSA) anchor the web PKI under CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements; ML-DSA certificate profiles are advancing through IETF LAMPS. Chrome's February 2026 post says it has no immediate plan to add traditional X.509 certificates containing post-quantum cryptography to the Chrome Root Store and is developing Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) in the IETF PLANTS working group instead, with a planned phase 3 (Q3 2027) for onboarding additional CAs into a new Chrome Quantum-resistant Root Store that only supports MTCs; Chrome's Q3 2026 security update reports buy-in on MTCs from other organizations, including commitments to participate from five of the largest CAs, Apple and Edge. Let's Encrypt (June 2026) says it is planning to support MTCs, targeting late 2026 for a staging environment and 2027 for a production-ready environment.
Industry: IT Industry / Software
Migration status: pilot

IL:leg-icp-brasil.full:
Instrução Normativa ITI nº 35, dated 30 January 2026, amends DOC-ICP-01.01, the ICP-Brasil document of cryptographic standards and algorithms, and approves its version 6.0. The amended entries add ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for certificate-authority key generation (ML-DSA-65 or 87) and for end-user keys (ML-DSA-44), and list ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 for key-agreement schemes and ML-KEM-768 or 1024 for the safekeeping of the holder's private key and its backup. The instruction takes effect on publication and the RSA, elliptic-curve and EdDSA options stay in the amended entries; the text does not say whether any certificate has yet been issued with ML-DSA or ML-KEM.
Industry: Legal / Notary / eSignature
Migration status: draft

IL:leg-pdf-signing.full:
Distinct from the EU eIDAS/AdES-weighted rows elsewhere in this sector: in May 2025, PDF vendor BFO and Adobe (which operates the Adobe Approved Trust List) exchanged the first PDFs signed with ML-DSA, followed shortly by SLH-DSA — leading to an agreement at PDF Days 2025 to formally add both algorithms to the PDF specification. This is real, already-happened vendor interoperability testing, not yet a ratified PDF/ISO 32000 specification change — the formal spec text had not landed as of this citation. Certification rules for qualified electronic signatures apply to qualified trust services and qualified signature creation devices (eIDAS Article 30), not to PDF signing in general.
Industry: Legal / Notary / eSignature
Migration status: draft

IL:leg-qes.full:
ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) lists cryptographic suites used for the creation and validation of digital signatures, electronic timestamps, electronic registered delivery services, electronic archiving, electronic ledgers and related certificates. It says it incorporates requirements for the transition to post-quantum cryptography, including hybrid cryptographic schemes and the phasing out of legacy mechanisms. It says that where protection against attacks leveraging quantum computers is required, for example where the long-term validity of a signature extends beyond 2030, RSA shall be used in a hybrid scheme or replaced by a quantum-safe algorithm. It says that, for hybrid signatures, implementations shall combine a classical signature and a post-quantum signature, and that acceptance requires both signatures to be valid. Its recommended hybrid combinations (Table 3.3) include RSA-PSS (≥ 3 000 bit) with ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87, ECDSA (P-256/P-384) with ML-DSA-65, and ECDSA or EdDSA with SLH-DSA for time-stamps and firmware signing. It says that ML-DSA as specified in NIST FIPS 204 shall be used as a recommended mechanism. It says that SLH-DSA as specified in NIST FIPS 205 shall be used as a recommended mechanism. It says that LMS as specified in IETF RFC 8554 and XMSS as specified in IETF RFC 8391 shall be used as recommended mechanisms, subject to the condition specified in its note. It adds that the use of LMS and XMSS is therefore restricted to deployment environments where state management can be strictly enforced. Annex A of the document sets requirements for the hash function and the signature algorithm used in CAdES and PAdES signatures.
Industry: Legal / Notary / eSignature
Migration status: draft

IL:leg-timestamp.full:
In ETSI EN 319 422, a time-stamp is data in electronic form that binds other electronic data to a particular time, establishing evidence that the data existed at that time.
Industry: Legal / Notary / eSignature
Migration status: none

IL:leg-wallet.full:
Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 says European Digital Identity Wallets should enable users to identify themselves electronically and to authenticate online and in offline mode, across borders, to access public and private services.
Industry: Legal / Notary / eSignature
Migration status: none

IL:media-broadcast.full:
CI Plus, the content-protection layer for DVB conditional-access modules, authenticates the module and host receiver with certificates signed using RSASSA-PSS (2048-bit RSA keys) and negotiates content-control keys with Diffie-Hellman, protecting content once it leaves the CA module and re-enters the host. This describes CI Plus Specification v1.3.2 (March 2015).
Industry: Media / Entertainment / DRM
Migration status: none

IL:media-content-provenance.full:
The C2PA Technical Specification 2.4 requires digital signatures to use its allowed list: ECDSA (ES256, ES384, ES512), RSASSA-PSS (PS256, PS384, PS512) and EdDSA (Ed25519 only). The deprecated list is empty.
Industry: Media / Entertainment / DRM
Migration status: none

IL:media-drm.full:
In AACS, a device uses its Device Keys to decrypt elements of a Media Key Block and extract a secret Media Key. All digital signatures in AACS use the ECDSA digital signature scheme. In AACS Drive Authentication, the host calculates the Bus Key from a point on an elliptic curve.
Industry: Media / Entertainment / DRM
Migration status: none

IL:media-streaming.full:
Streaming platforms deliver content keys and licenses over TLS. Cloudflare reported in October 2025 that the majority of human-initiated traffic with Cloudflare is using post-quantum encryption, mitigating the threat of harvest-now/decrypt-later.
Industry: Media / Entertainment / DRM
Migration status: draft

IL:pci-ecommerce.full:
RFC 10024 defines three hybrid key-agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3 that combine post-quantum ML-KEM with ECDHE. Early production example: Toss Payments, a Korean payment gateway, announced on 3 April 2026 that it had deployed ML-KEM-based hybrid key exchange across all segments of its payment data; the sector as a whole stays at pilot.
Industry: Payment Card Industry
Migration status: pilot

IL:pci-emv.full:
An FS-ISAC paper on the impact of quantum computing on payments says that RSA 2048 is in use for multiple use cases such as EMV cards and remote key loading, that elliptic curve cryptography is available with the latest EMV asymmetric specifications, and that none of the asymmetric algorithms it lists is quantum resilient.
Industry: Payment Card Industry
Migration status: none

IL:pci-pboc-cards.full:
Chinas PBOC 3.0 card specification runs a dual-algorithm design: international EMV cards use RSA/ECDSA, while domestic-scheme (UnionPay) cards may authenticate with SM2, the State Cryptography Administrations national elliptic-curve signature algorithm (GM/T 0003). A certified PBOC 3.0 smart card product (ACS ACOSJ-P) lists "SM2/SM3/SM4" as a cryptographic feature directly alongside its "Compliant with PBOC 3.0 Debit/Credit" certification line, confirming real deployment rather than a paper option.
Industry: Payment Card Industry
Migration status: none

IL:pci-terminals.full:
The PCI SSC announcement of PIN Security v3.1 (12 March 2021) says the PCI PIN Security Standard provides requirements and testing procedures for the secure management, processing and transmission of PIN data at ATMs and attended and unattended point-of-sale terminals.
Industry: Payment Card Industry
Migration status: none

IL:pci-tokenization-3ds.full:
The PCI SSC page for the PCI 3DS Core Security Standard says it offers security requirements, validation methods and implementation guidance to protect environments where specific ACS, DS and/or 3DS functions are performed, as defined in the EMV 3-D Secure Protocol and Core Functions Specification, to enable secure consumer authentication with their payment card issuers when making card-not-present purchases.
Industry: Payment Card Industry
Migration status: none

IL:rail-etcs.full:
UNISIG SUBSET-137 chooses the TLS protocol to give the distributed KMAC key material confidentiality, authenticity and integrity.
Industry: Rail / Transit
Migration status: none

IL:rail-frmcs.full:
FRMCS, the 5G successor to GSM-R, takes a layered cybersecurity approach in its ETSI TS 103 764 architecture, including a TLS-backed, mutually authenticated control-plane link (Local Binding) between applications and the On-Board FRMCS or the Trackside Gateway; the architecture names no specific signature or key-exchange algorithms.
Industry: Rail / Transit
Migration status: none

IL:rail-ptc.full:
US Positive Train Control mandated by 49 CFR 236 Subpart I relies on PKI-authenticated wireless messaging between locomotives, wayside units, and back offices.
Industry: Rail / Transit
Migration status: none

IL:retail-checkout.full:
RFC 10024 defines three hybrid key-agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3 that combine post-quantum ML-KEM with ECDHE.
Industry: Retail & E-Commerce
Migration status: draft

IL:retail-digital-wallet.full:
Digital-wallet checkout (Apple Pay): Apple's own developer docs name 'calculating an SHA-1 hash... and performing elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange' for payment-token processing, plus 'a PKCS #7 signature' without naming which signature algorithm. W3C's Secure Payment Confirmation spec (WebAuthn-based strong customer authentication) separately names ES256/RS256 — the JOSE aliases for ECDSA/RSA — in its authentication examples, informationally noted here though not used as a structured mechanism citation. No post-quantum work found for either.
Industry: Retail & E-Commerce
Migration status: none

IL:retail-pin-keys.full:
PCI SSC's Key Blocks 101 page says key blocks may be used to protect both Triple Data Encryption Algorithm (TDEA), sometimes referred to as 3DES or TripleDES, and Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) keys. The page does not mention quantum computing.
Industry: Retail & E-Commerce
Migration status: none

IL:semis-euicc.full:
GSMA's eUICC protection profile (SGP.25 v2.1, 3 February 2025; registered as BSI-CC-PP-0100) sets the assurance level at Common Criteria EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2 and AVA_VAN.5 and names ECDSA signature verification, elliptic-curve key agreement (ECKA) and AES. Neither the profile, GSMA SGP.24 v2.4.4 nor ENISA's EUCC specification for eUICC names a post-quantum mechanism. SGP.24 says the IC/hardware platform on which the eUICC is based 'shall be certified to either PP-0084 or PP-0035'; ENISA's specification (version 1.0, public consultation, June 2024) calls certification voluntary and sets EAL4 augmented where an eUICC is certified. GSMA PQ.03 v2.0 says all migration strategies will require post-quantum cryptography on eUICCs at some point, and PQ.04 v1.0 (25 November 2024) says the GSMA eSIM group is actively working on a PQC version of RSP.
Industry: Semiconductors / Secure Elements
Migration status: draft

IL:semis-payment-card-chip.full:
An IDEMIA research paper, written after NIST's July 2022 selection of a first set of post-quantum algorithms, builds post-quantum and hybrid versions of two EMV payment protocols on a banking smart-card (an Arm Cortex-M3 derivative with a basic "toy" application profile), using NTRU or Kyber512 as the key-encapsulation mechanism and Falcon or Dilithium in the certificates. It reports that Dilithium-5 data reached the application's maximum capacity and could not be loaded, that most of the transaction time is the transmission of the card certificate chain to the terminal, and that such products are possible but several issues remain. EMVCo's position statement (8 March 2024, published September 2024) names no post-quantum mechanism: it says its Security Working Group will monitor and support standards development of quantum resistant solutions, and the quantum threat is on current projections unlikely prior to 2040. Mastercard's white paper cites a Banque de France report estimating 4 to 6 times more chip RAM for post-quantum algorithms and calls combining chip cards and quantum resistance a work in progress.
Industry: Semiconductors / Secure Elements
Migration status: draft

IL:semis-security-ic-certification.full:
The NIAP collaborative Protection Profile for Dedicated Security Component, version 2.1 (17 November 2025), covers one or more hardware components with their controlling operating system or firmware, and its revision history lists post-quantum cryptography for the v2.1 final publication. The NIAP Protection Profile for General Purpose Computing Platforms, version 2.0, gives a TPM or other secure element as an example of an on-platform dedicated security component. The cPP's allowed choices for signature generation and verification include LMS, XMSS, ML-DSA and HashML-DSA beside RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA, and ML-KEM is among its allowed choices for key encapsulation. NIAP Technical Decision TD1011 (26 March 2026) states that, to be listed on the NIAP product compliant list, each applicable cryptographic requirement must include at least one selection conforming to CNSA suite 1.0 or 2.0. NIAP Policy Letter #33 (31 August 2026) states that products not meeting CNSA 2.0 requirements for every cryptographic function will not be accepted into NIAP evaluation from 1 January 2028. The Security IC Platform Protection Profile, version 2.0 (16 December 2025), is a separate profile for security ICs.
Industry: Semiconductors / Secure Elements
Migration status: draft

IL:semis-tpm.full:
TCG's TPM 2.0 Library Specification Version 185 (published 12 March 2026) introduced support for ML-DSA, HashML-DSA, ML-KEM and EdDSA; its algorithm table ties ML-KEM and ML-DSA to NIST FIPS 203 and 204, with ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 and ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87 as parameter sets. The PC Client Platform TPM Profile Version 1.07 (published 23 March 2026) makes ML-KEM (768 or 1024) and ML-DSA (65 or 87) support mandatory beside RSA 3072 and ECC, adds a buffer-chunking mechanism for the larger commands and responses anticipated with post-quantum algorithms, and requires a TPM that ships with EK certificates to carry RSA 3072 or ECC P-384 together with ML-KEM. The EK Credential Profile Version 2.7 (published 16 March 2026) defines ML-KEM (storage) and ML-DSA (signing) EK templates beside the RSA and ECC ones.
Industry: Semiconductors / Secure Elements
Migration status: draft

IL:supply-customs.full:
The WCO SAFE Framework of Standards says digital signatures, or Public Key Infrastructure arrangements, can play an important role in securing the electronic exchange of information.
Industry: Supply Chain / Logistics
Migration status: none

IL:supply-ebl.full:
The DCSA Information Model 3.0 defines an EBL Endorsement Chain entity for title transfers whose Signature attribute holds the digital signature of the previous title holder.
Industry: Supply Chain / Logistics
Migration status: none

IL:supply-maritime.full:
The IMO maritime cyber risk management guidelines recommend implementing policies and procedures regarding the use of cryptography.
Industry: Supply Chain / Logistics
Migration status: none

IL:telco-air-interface.full:
In TS 33.501 the UE and the gNB must provide the null algorithms NEA0 and NIA0 (NIA0 must not be used for user-data integrity protection) plus the 128-NEA1/NIA1 (SNOW 3G based) and 128-NEA2/NIA2 (128-bit AES based) ciphering and integrity algorithms (identifiers defined for 5G NAS and New Radio), while 128-NEA3/NIA3 (ZUC based) is optional: the UE and the gNB may implement or support it. The 128-NEA and 128-NIA algorithms are all symmetric, so none carry a NIST PQC KEM/signature component; their quantum exposure is purely Grover's-algorithm key-length erosion.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: none

IL:telco-certs.full:
3GPP TS 33.310 certificate profiles for network functions and base stations use RSA/ECDSA today; ML-DSA profiles track the LAMPS certificate work.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: draft

IL:telco-roaming-sepp.full:
5G roaming signalling crosses the N32 interface between security edge protection proxies (SEPPs): directly over TLS on N32-c, or through PRINS (JOSE message protection) when an IPX provider is in the path. ATIS analyses SEPP-to-SEPP communications as exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later. ATIS says the following upgrades are necessary for SEPP-to-SEPP communications to maintain robust security against future quantum threats: mTLS 1.3 with PQC-compliant crypto-suites (e.g. ML-KEM) for key establishment, and PKI certificates with PQC-compliant digital signature algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA).
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: none

IL:telco-routing.full:
RPKI route-origin authorisations, certificates, CRLs, and CMS signed objects currently use RSA-2048/SHA-256 (RFC 7935); BGPsec per-hop path signatures separately use ECDSA P-256 (RFC 8608). A proposed post-quantum migration design introduces a composite ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 suite for the RPKI side, with signature size and per-hop verification cost as the binding constraints.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: none

IL:telco-subscriber.full:
In GSMA FS.35, LTE and 5G require a 3G authentication and key agreement (AKA) algorithm such as MILENAGE or TUAK. GSMA FS.35 says the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman component of ECIES could be broken very efficiently by a large-scale quantum computer running Shor's algorithm. GSMA PQ.03 expects the interfaces between 5G core components, and between 4G core components, to be protected using IPsec. GSMA PQ.03 notes that all mandatory and recommended TLS cipher suites use ECDHE or DHE for key agreement, in its section on TLS between 5G core network components.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: none

IL:telco-suci.full:
5G SUCI conceals subscriber identifiers with ECIES under two standardised protection schemes: Profile A (scheme ID 1, Curve25519/X25519) and Profile B (scheme ID 2, secp256r1/P-256). 3GPP TS 33.501 sizes the SUCI scheme output to allow later quantum-resistant protection schemes but defines none; ATIS recommends that 3GPP specify quantum-resistant key encapsulation such as ML-KEM for SUPI protection, and an ML-KEM (Kyber-512) Profile C has been published only as a research proposal, not a 3GPP profile.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: none

IL:telco-transport.full:
In GSMA PQ.03, the security gateway terminates IPsec tunnels from the gNodeBs, each of which encapsulates the N2 and N3 interfaces. GSMA PQ.03 says TLS is required on all service-based interfaces between network functions inside a PLMN and on the N32 interface between the vSEPP and hSEPP. GSMA PQ.03 presents a phased approach to migration that allows the actions required to be prioritised. RFC 8784 describes an extension of IKEv2 that makes it resistant to a quantum computer by using preshared keys.
Industry: Telecommunications
Migration status: pilot

IL:water-ami.full:
The European Open Metering System (OMS) specification, whose scope includes water meters, defines a TLS-based security mode in which each OMS end-device (meters, sensors and actuators) holds its own certificate and key pair for TLS authentication and key agreement. In that European OMS mode an end-device shall be able to handle X.509v3 certificates, clients and servers shall support ECDSA, and at least brainpoolP256r1 and NIST P-256 shall be supported for ECDHE and ECDSA keys. NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) says that where the code that checks signatures cannot be updated after manufacture, devices should be designed to require quantum-resistant signatures on the executable code if they may still be in use once cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers exist; this is a general statement, not specific to meters.
Industry: Water / Wastewater
Migration status: none

IL:water-dams.full:
The FERC Security Program for Hydropower Projects checklist asks whether vendors or third parties have remote access to the project's network and, if so, whether access controls prevent and monitor unauthorized access.
Industry: Water / Wastewater
Migration status: none

IL:water-scada.full:
Water utility SCADA authentication and remote-monitoring VPNs fall under America's Water Infrastructure Act assessments; OT asset lifecycles stretch decades.
Industry: Water / Wastewater
Migration status: none

LIB:Avalanche-Docs-What-is-ICM-Warp-Mess.full:
Official Avalanche developer documentation for Interchain Messaging (ICM, formerly Avalanche Warp Messaging). ICM messages are verified with BLS signatures, and every validator on the Avalanche network holds its own BLS key pair. Validators of the origin L1 each sign a message; a signature aggregator, for example a relayer, combines the signatures into one BLS multi-signature and records the signers in a bit set. The destination L1 accepts the message only if the signers hold at least the configured quorum of the origin L1's stake weight (67% by default). This is an aggregated multi-signature checked against a stake quorum; the page does not describe a threshold signature over a shared key.

LIB:BSI TR-02102-1.full:
German federal technical guideline on cryptographic mechanisms and key lengths, Version 2026-01 (January 2026 edition). It recommends quantum-safe key agreement (FrodoKEM, Classic McEliece and ML-KEM) only in hybrid use with a classical mechanism, and quantum-safe signatures (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and the stateful XMSS and LMS) only together with a classical signature, except that hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS) can in principle also be used alone if their implementation security is carefully considered; sole use of classical key agreement is recommended only until the end of 2031. HQC is not yet part of the recommendations: BSI intends to add it after the NIST standard is published. A BSI notice dated 29 September 2026 advises that Classic McEliece should no longer be used in new developments or new cryptographic applications, says the guideline's current recommendation for it is limited to hybrid use, and expects a revised guideline in early 2027.

Authors: BSI; ANSSI; NLNCSA Netherlands; SNCSA Sweden
Publication Date: 2024-04-01
Last Updated: 2024-04-01
Document Status: Published
Main Topic: Joint position paper concluding that QKD is insufficient for most government communications and recommending PQC as the primary quantum-safe approach with QKD as a complementary niche solution.
Quantum Threats Addressed: Shor's algorithm; store-now-decrypt-later scenario
Migration Timeline Info: First selection of NIST standards will be available sometime in 2024
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Bodies: French Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI); Federal Office for Information Security (BSI); Netherlands National Communications Security Agency (NLNCSA); Swedish National Communications Security Authority, Swedish Armed Forces; European Commission

Key Takeaways: QKD is currently only viable for niche use cases due to technological limitations and high costs; migration to post-quantum cryptography and symmetric keying should be the clear priority for quantum-safe key establishment; QKD implementations lack rigorous standardization and comprehensive security proofs compared to PQC; practical QKD systems cannot achieve end-to-end security over long distances without trusted nodes; claims of absolute security for QKD do not apply to actual implementations due to device imperfections
Hybrid & Transition Approaches: Use of pre-shared symmetric keys in combination with classically secure public-key cryptography; use of post-quantum signature schemes with an associated public-key infrastructure for QKD authentication

QKD Protocols & Quantum Networking: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD); prepare-and-measure QKD; quantum communication networks; EuroQCI project; quantum channel; quantum-physical phenomena
QRNG & Entropy Sources: random number generators (RNGs) as part of QKD modules
Constrained Device & IoT Suitability: unsuitable for mobile devices, cannot be deployed to every individual user
Supply Chain & Vendor Risk: high acquisition and maintenance costs over life cycle, proprietary equipment requirements
Deployment & Migration Complexity: migration to post-quantum cryptography; hybrid solutions with traditional symmetric keying or classically secure public-key cryptography; deployment in classical communication infrastructures
Financial & Business Impact: very large costs for equipment acquisition and maintenance, significant costs for satellite infrastructure
Organizational Readiness: need for standardised protocols with comprehensive security proofs, requirement for rigorous evaluation before confidence in security

Reference ID: Bech32m-format-for-v1-witness-addresses
Title: Bech32m format for v1+ witness addresses
Authors: GitHub
Publication Date: 2020-12-16
Document Status: Deployed
Main Topic: BIP 350 defines Bech32m, a Bech32 variant with a modified checksum constant, and amends BIP173 so native segregated witness outputs of version 1 and later use Bech32m while version 0 keeps Bech32.
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Regions: None detected; Bodies: None detected
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: Pieter Wuille (author of BIP 350); Greg Maxwell (did most of the computation for code selection and analysis, and commented); Mark Erhardt (helped write and edit the document); Rusty Russell (contributed to the bitcoin-dev discussion on intentionally breaking compatibility with existing senders)
Protocols Covered: Bitcoin segregated witness (BIP141); Bech32 (BIP173); Bech32m
Key Takeaways: Bech32 has a weakness where inserting or deleting 'q' characters before a final 'p' does not invalidate the checksum; Bech32m fixes this by xoring the constant 0x2bc830a3 instead of 1 into the checksum; Witness version 0 addresses (P2WPKH, P2WSH) keep Bech32 while versions 1 through 16 use Bech32m; Decoders must verify the encoding matches the witness version (Bech32 for 0, Bech32m for others); Forward-compatibility with v1+ senders is intentionally broken to prevent software from burning funds
Security Levels & Parameters: Checksum constant 0x2bc830a3; Witness programs between 2 and 40 bytes; Witness versions 0 through 16; HRP 'bc'
Hybrid & Transition Approaches: Combined decoder supporting both Bech32 and Bech32m simultaneously; Intentional break of forward-compatibility for sending to v1+ witness addresses

Deployment & Migration Complexity: Breaks forward-compatibility for sending to v1+ witness addresses intentionally; No receiver-side compatibility issues as no wallets create v1 addresses yet; Software must decode with both Bech32 and Bech32m and check encoding against witness version
Financial & Business Impact: Prevents funds from being burned when sending to version 1 addresses

LIB:Bitcoin-BIP360-P2QRH.full:
Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (status Draft, version 0.12.1) for a new output type, Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), activated by a soft fork. It works like a Taproot (P2TR) output with the key-path spend removed, uses SegWit version 2 and has addresses that start with bc1z. This makes outputs resistant to long-exposure quantum attacks, where a public key is exposed for longer than needed to confirm a spending transaction; it does not protect against short-exposure attacks on keys exposed in the mempool. The proposal introduces no post-quantum signature scheme; the authors say post-quantum signatures would be a separate future proposal. Earlier drafts were titled P2QRH and then P2TSH.

LIB:BoringSSL-xwing-h.full:
BoringSSL public C header declaring the X-Wing (MLKEM768-X25519) hybrid KEM API: key generation, encapsulation, decapsulation and key serialization.
Authors: The BoringSSL Authors
Status: Unverified — needs review
Document type: Reference
Published: 2025
passages: This implements the hybrid key encapsulation mechanism "MLKEM768-X25519" from // https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems-02 // which is also known as "X-Wing".
XWING_private_key contains an X-Wing private key. The contents of this object // should never leave the address space since the format is unstable.
XWING_PUBLIC_KEY_BYTES is the number of bytes in an encoded X-Wing public // key. #define XWING_PUBLIC_KEY_BYTES 1216
XWING_encap encapsulates a random shared secret for `encoded_public_key`, // writes the ciphertext to `out_ciphertext`, and writes the random shared // secret to `out_shared_secret`.
XWING_decap decapsulates a shared secret from `ciphertext` using // `private_key` and writes it to `out_shared_secret`. Returns one on success // and zero on error.

passages: This publication identifies and describes recommended cryptographic algorithms and appropriate methods of use that organizations can implement to protect sensitive information.

The RSA modulus length should be increased to at least 3072 bits by the end of 2030. The use of RSA without a post-quantum key establishment scheme should be phased out by the end of 2035.

SLH-DSA does not require state management but has inferior performance and larger signatures than ML-DSA and the stateful hash-bashed signature schemes.

LIB:CAB-Forum-SC-081v3.full:
CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3, which amends the TLS Baseline Requirements to reduce the maximum validity of publicly trusted TLS certificates from 398 days to 47 days and the reuse period for validation data (from 398 days to 10 days for domain and IP (SAN) validation data, and from 825 days to 398 days for other validation data), with the reductions starting in March 2026 and concluding in March 2029. The ballot does not address post-quantum key exchange or algorithms; it argues that a reduced maximum validity period supports transitioning between deployed and supported cryptography.

The base CI Plus technical specification (313 pages) governing CICAM/Host mutual authentication and link encryption in DVB conditional access. Reference ID: CRYSTALS-Dilithium-Spec-v31
Title: CRYSTALS-Dilithium Algorithm Specifications v3.1
Authors: KU Leuven COSIC; Ruhr University Bochum; INRIA France; ETH Zurich
Publication Date: 2021-02-08
Last Updated: 2021-02-08
Document Status: Final
Main Topic: Official algorithm specification for CRYSTALS-Dilithium covering lattice-based digital signature schemes with EUF-CMA security and parameter sets Dilithium2/3/5.
PQC Algorithms Covered: CRYSTALS-Dilithium, ML-DSA
Migration Timeline Info: Years mentioned: 2021
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Regions: United States, Germany, France, Bodies: NIST
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: Shi Bai; Léo Ducas; Eike Kiltz; Tancrède Lepoint; Vadim Lyubashevsky; Peter Schwabe; Gregor Seiler; Damien Stehlé

Key Takeaways: Dilithium uses uniform sampling instead of discrete Gaussian to avoid side-channel vulnerabilities; The scheme offers both randomized and deterministic signing options with deterministic as the default; Public key compression is achieved by omitting low-order bits of t and including hints in the signature; Security levels are varied by adjusting operations over a fixed ring rather than changing the ring parameters; Implementation efficiency relies on Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) for polynomial multiplication.
Security Levels & Parameters: NIST level 2; NIST level 3; NIST level 5; Dilithium2; Dilithium3; Dilithium5; q = 2^23 - 2^13 + 1; n = 256; 4x4 public key matrix for level 2; 192 bits entropy for level 2; 225 bits entropy for level 3
Performance & Size Considerations: Signature size reduced by 8 bytes via two-stage challenge sampling; Public key size slightly increased by decreasing dropped bits from 14 to 13; Expected signing loop repetitions around 4; Public key compression shrinks bit-representation of t by factor slightly larger than two at expense of increasing signature by less than 100 bytes
Target Audience: Developer; Security Architect; Researcher

Implementation Attack Surface: side-channel attacks (branch tracing, electromagnetic emanations), fault attacks (deterministic signature schemes), constant time implementation requirements
QRNG & Entropy Sources: uniform sampling, discrete Gaussian distribution (avoided), seed generation, SHAKE expansion
Constrained Device & IoT Suitability: embedded systems viability
Deployment & Migration Complexity: deterministic version as default option, randomized version for side-channel scenarios, public key compression, signature size reduction

Title: 1.1.1.1 now supports post-quantum DNSSEC, all 2,420 bytes of it

Publication Date: 2026-09-10
Document Status: Published
Main Topic: Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 resolver now validates DNSSEC signatures made with ML-DSA-44, with a local policy that prevents downgrade to conventional signatures and an analysis of the operational challenges of large post-quantum signatures.
PQC Algorithms Covered: ML-DSA
Quantum Threats Addressed: Quantum computers breaking RSA and ECDSA signing keys; forged DNSSEC signatures; "break once, forge everywhere" attack on root zone signing key; downgrade to conventional signatures; no harvest-now-decrypt-later risk for DNSSEC (authenticity, not confidentiality)
Migration Timeline Info: Milestones: Cloudflare plans full post-quantum security by 2029; possible sufficiently powerful quantum computer in 2030; next steps are ML-DSA-44 signing in Cloudflare Authoritative DNS and DS record support in Cloudflare Registrar; migration must extend to the DNS root
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Regions: None detected; Bodies: NIST, IANA, IETF (RFCs, Internet-Draft)

Protocols Covered: DNSSEC; DNS; EDNS(0); DNS over UDP; DNS over TCP; DNS over TLS (DoT); DNS over HTTPS (DoH); TLS
Infrastructure Layers: DNS resolvers; Authoritative DNS servers; DNS root and delegation chain; Registries and registrars; Chain of trust and trust anchors
Standardization Bodies: NIST; IETF; IANA

Key Takeaways: ML-DSA-44 signatures (2,420 bytes) exceed common DNS-over-UDP limits, so responses must fall back to TCP; Publishing conventional and post-quantum signatures together creates a downgrade path if validators accept any single valid path; 1.1.1.1 uses a parent-published DS record as an authenticated signal and then requires a valid ML-DSA-44 path; A complete post-quantum chain of trust needs signing, registrar and registry support through every parent zone up to the DNS root; Resolver-side validation lets Cloudflare measure TCP use, bandwidth and signature verification cost at Internet scale
Security Levels & Parameters: ML-DSA-44; DNSSEC algorithm number 18; ML-DSA-44 public key 1,312 bytes; ML-DSA-44 signature 2,420 bytes
Hybrid & Transition Approaches: Publishing conventional and post-quantum keys and signatures together in the same zone for older resolvers; Local resolver policy requiring a valid ML-DSA-44 path when the DS RRset contains a supported post-quantum algorithm; Downgrade protection extended from the trust anchor through every delegation

Key Takeaways: Supply chain risk and COTS use should be addressed through supplier vetting, diversification, SBOMs and pre-production analysis and hardening; Apply security by design/default, zero trust, network segmentation, regular patching and hardening across the whole satellite lifecycle; Deploy validated cryptographic mechanisms and ensure crypto agility, considering PQC and hybrid approaches for the quantum era; Strengthen human-factor resilience through training, insider-threat controls and information sharing (e.g. EU Space ISAC, NIS2 incident reporting); Use risk scenarios and the 125-control framework mapped to the threat taxonomy to tailor protections to a specific mission
Hybrid & Transition Approaches: Combination of quantum-resistant asymmetric cryptography (PQC) with pre-quantum asymmetric cryptography (hybrid); FPGAs to allow reconfiguring encryption algorithms; crypto agility to adapt to new cryptographic standards; QKD with reliable alternative communication methods

Financial & Business Impact: Financial losses from satellite service disruption; downtime and delays in transport, logistics and remote monitoring; fines and reputational damage for operators; Viasat 2022 hack as example impact

LIB:Ethereum-EIP7702.full:
Ethereum EIP (status Final) that adds a transaction type letting an externally owned account (EOA) set its code to a delegation indicator pointing at a smart contract, using authorization tuples signed with secp256k1; the delegation is persistent until the account sets another or clears it by delegating to the zero address. The EIP text does not mention post-quantum cryptography and has no mechanism that disables the account's secp256k1 key: an authorized account can still invalidate an authorization by increasing its nonce or sweep assets out of the account. Any post-quantum use is outside the EIP: a delegate contract that verifies a post-quantum signature would only cover operations routed through that contract, and the secp256k1 key keeps its authority over the account unless other account or protocol changes are made.

passages: The new crypto/mlkem package implements ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024. ML-KEM is a post-quantum key exchange mechanism formerly known as Kyber and specified in FIPS 203 .

MLKEM768X25519 returns a KEM implementing MLKEM768-X25519 (a.k.a. X-Wing) from draft-ietf-hpke-pq.

Seal instantiates a single-use HPKE sending HPKE context like NewSender , and then encrypts the provided plaintext like Sender.Seal (with no aad).

LIB:HAWK-Round2-Spec.full:
Lattice signature that eliminates FN-DSA's floating-point Gaussian-sampling pain — pure integer arithmetic on a rank-2 module lattice with a Gram matrix as the public key. Compact 555 B signatures at NIST L1 — smaller than both ML-DSA and FN-DSA — and dramatically easier to implement in constant time on constrained hardware. Security rests on newer assumptions: the Search Module Lattice Isomorphism Problem (smLIP) and the One-More-Shortest-Vector Problem (omSVP). NIST flagged these for further community analysis; Round 2 included a refined omSVP definition addressing a discrepancy found during evaluation. The HAWK team withdrew HAWK from NIST's additional signatures process on 29 July 2026 after a new key-recovery attack; its site now says Hawk is insecure and should not be used.

LIB:IETF-Token-Status-List.full:
IETF draft (draft-ietf-oauth-status-list) defining a compact bit-array status list for checking the validity state of tokens such as SD-JWT VCs (valid, revoked, suspended). Its privacy considerations (Section 12) assign each property to a specific actor. Because one list covers many tokens, the Issuer or Status Provider serving the list does not learn which token a Relying Party is checking (herd privacy, 12.1), and privacy improves as the list grows. The Relying Party itself learns the token's list URI and index and can re-request the list to profile the token's status over time (12.3). Colluding Relying Parties or a Status Issuer can link transactions by the token's status claim, so the draft recommends one-time-use batch tokens, non-sequential indices and decoy entries (12.5). Status List Tokens carry exp and ttl claims that govern how long a list may be cached (13.7).

ML-KEM The Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) as defined in FIPS 203 . This algorithm supports keys with ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 parameter sets.
ML-DSA The Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) as defined in FIPS 204 . This algorithm supports keys with ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87 parameter sets.

LIB:NIST IR 8547.full:
NIST's final transition plan (October 2026) for moving from quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms to post-quantum standards. Every quantum-vulnerable signature and key-establishment parameter set in NIST standards (RSA, ECDSA and finite-field or elliptic-curve DH and MQV at 112 bits of classical security or more; EdDSA at 128 bits or more) is deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. ML-KEM-768 is the recommended default ML-KEM parameter set, HQC becomes approved once its FIPS is published, and a hybrid key-establishment scheme can be FIPS 140-validated when at least one input comes from an approved scheme. It supports Executive Order 14412 and OMB M-26-15, which set earlier federal deadlines for the most sensitive systems: post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and signatures by 31 December 2031.

LIB:NIST-SP-800-132.full:
NIST SP 800-132 (December 2010) specifies password-based key derivation for protecting stored data or data protection keys, using PBKDF2 with HMAC and an approved hash. It recommends a minimum iteration count of 1,000, chosen as large as is acceptable to users, with 10,000,000 given as possibly appropriate for especially critical keys or powerful systems, and requires a derived key length of at least 112 bits. These figures date from 2010: SP 800-63B-4 (July 2025) says the cost factor should be as high as practical and increased over time, with a salt of at least 32 bits, and NIST's page for SP 800-132 says NIST is planning to revise it. OWASP currently suggests 600,000 or more iterations for PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 where FIPS 140 compliance is required. The document does not address quantum computers, and a PBKDF only slows dictionary and brute-force guessing, which is less likely to succeed against random passwords.

LIB:NIST-SP-800-140F.full:
NIST SP 800-140F (March 2020) is the CMVP document that replaces ISO/IEC 19790 Annex F and ISO/IEC 24759 paragraph 6.18 for non-invasive attack mitigation test metrics. In the published document the section that lists approved test metrics reads "No additional requirements at this time", so it adds no test method of its own. LIB:NIST-SP-800-209-R1-IPD.full:
NIST SP 800-209r1 (Initial Public Draft) provides security guidelines and a structured catalog of security controls for enterprise and cloud storage infrastructure, revising NIST SP 800-209 (2020). LIB:NIST-SP-800-63B-4.full:
Sets FIPS 140 validation requirements for authentication, by assurance level. Cryptography used by verifiers operated by or on behalf of federal agencies must be validated to FIPS 140 Level 1 at AAL1 and AAL2 (at AAL2 unless otherwise specified) and to Level 1 or higher at AAL3 (Sections 2.1.2, 2.2.2, 2.3.2). For authenticators, AAL1 requires approved cryptography but no FIPS 140 validation; cryptographic authenticators procured by federal agencies must be validated to Level 1 at AAL2; single-factor and multi-factor authenticators used at AAL3 must be validated to Level 1 or higher overall. The July 2025 revision lowers the validation level required for AAL3 authenticators compared with SP 800-63B-3.

passages: Composite KEM is a mechanism for key encapsulation, following the key encapsulation algorithm defined in [COMP_KEM].
The CKA_PARAMETER_SET attribute value selects a predefined set of parameters specified by [COMP_KEM]. The parameter set will select the security level and public key sizes.
Note that when generating a Composite KEM private key, the parameter set is not specified in the key’s template.
The Composite KEM key pair generation mechanism, denoted CKM_COMP_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN , is a key pair generation mechanism defined in section 3.1 of [COMP_KEM].
When used in C_EncapsulateKey , this mechanism generates a secret key and an encapsulated ciphertext from a Composite KEM public key using section 3.2 of [COMP_KEM].

LIB:OpenJDK-JEP-452-KEM-API.full:
A Java Enhancement Proposal introducing a standard API in the Java Platform for key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs), used to secure symmetric keys with public key cryptography.
Authors: Weijun Wang
Status: Final
Document type: Standard
Published: 2023-01-25
passages: Introduce an API for key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs), an encryption technique for securing symmetric keys using public key cryptography.
A key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) instead uses properties of the public key to derive a related symmetric key, which requires no padding.
The encapsulate() method returns a key containing the full shared secret, with an algorithm name of "Generic" . This key is usually passed to a key derivation function.
For example, Hybrid TLS Key Exchange concatenates two key encapsulation messages into a single key_exchange field, and RSA-KEM concatenates the key encapsulation message with the wrapped keying data.
However, a Java security provider might be backed by a native-code implementation and the shared secret might not be extractable.

LIB:OpenJDK-JEP-510-KDF-API.full:
OpenJDK JEP finalizing the javax.crypto.KDF API for key derivation functions such as HKDF in Java 25.
Authors: Kevin Driver
Status: Final
Document type: Standard
Published: 2025-03-31
passages: Introduce an API for Key Derivation Functions (KDFs), which are cryptographic algorithms for deriving additional keys from a secret key and other data.
We proposed the KDF API as a preview feature in JEP 478 and delivered it in JDK 24. We here propose to finalize the API in JDK 25, without change.
Enable applications to use KDF algorithms such as the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF, RFC 5869 ) and Argon2 ( RFC 9106 ).
Enable an implementation of Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) in the JDK to use KDFs in its key schedule setup and secret export.
The HKDF algorithm, which is the only KDF we intend to include at this time, does not require a KDFParameters object. Other algorithms, however, such as SHAKE , may need it.

LIB:OpenJDK-JEP-527-PQ-Hybrid-TLS13.full:
OpenJDK JEP specifying post-quantum hybrid key exchange (ML-KEM combined with ECDHE) for TLS 1.3 in the javax.net.ssl APIs.
Authors: Jamil Nimeh
Status: Final
Document type: Standard
Published: 2025-06-03
passages: Enhance the security of Java applications that require secure network communication by implementing hybrid key exchange algorithms for TLS 1.3.
A hybrid key exchange scheme combines a quantum-resistant algorithm with a traditional algorithm, and is secure as long as one of the algorithms remains unbroken.
By default, the JDK’s TLS 1.3 implementation will place the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid scheme at the front of that list, making it the most preferred.
The complete default list of schemes will be: X25519MLKEM768 , x25519 , secp256r1 , secp384r1 , secp521r1 , x448 , ffdhe2048 , ffdhe3072 and ffdhe4096 .
The hybrid groups SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 are not enabled by default. You can change the default list of schemes by setting the system property jdk.tls.namedGroups .

LIB:PI-PROFINET-Security-Whitepaper-V105.full:
PROFIBUS & PROFINET International white paper (V1.05, Feb 2019) setting out the security concept for PROFINET protocol extensions, aligned with IEC 62443. Defines three PROFINET Security Classes - 1 Robustness (e.g. changeable SNMP default strings, read-only DCP, signed GSD files), 2 Integrity + Authenticity (cryptographically protected cyclic and acyclic communication, confidential configuration data), 3 Confidentiality (adds encryption) - using device certificates for start-up key negotiation and a MAC over cyclic frames (HMAC-SHA256 best performer, not finally selected).

LIB:PKCS-11-Cryptographic-Token-Interfac.full:
Defines the conformance profiles that PKCS#11 v3.2 conformance is measured against. Section 7 of the base specification states that an implementation is a conforming Provider only if it meets one or more provider profiles specified here, so the base spec mandates no mechanism on its own. Specifies Baseline Provider, Complete Provider, Extended Provider, Authentication Token, Public Certificates Token and HKDF TLS Token, plus Baseline and Extended Consumer. Baseline Provider requires a CKO_PROFILE object with CKP_BASELINE_PROVIDER and explicitly requires no mechanisms. Edited by Tim Hudson (Cryptsoft); supersedes Profiles v3.1.

LIB:PKCS11-V3-OASIS.full:
PKCS#11 v3.0 is the HSM programming interface standard. It adds CKM_HKDF_DERIVE and CKM_HKDF_KEY_GEN mechanisms for TLS 1.3 and CKM_SP800_108_COUNTER_KDF / FEEDBACK_KDF / DOUBLE_PIPELINE_KDF for NIST SP 800-108 derivation. Essential for HSM-based QKD integration workflows where QKD secrets are imported as non-extractable keys and used to derive session keys. Superseded by PKCS#11 v3.1 and v3.2.

LIB:PKCS11-V32-OASIS.full:
PKCS#11 v3.2 adds post-quantum cryptography mechanisms: ML-KEM (CKM_ML_KEM 0x00000017, CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000000f), ML-DSA (CKM_ML_DSA 0x0000001d, CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000001c, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_*), and SLH-DSA (CKM_SLH_DSA, CKM_SLH_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN). Introduces C_EncapsulateKey() and C_DecapsulateKey() functions for KEM operations. New key types: CKK_ML_KEM (0x49), CKK_ML_DSA (0x4a), CKK_SLH_DSA (0x4b). New attributes: CKA_PARAMETER_SET, CKA_ENCAPSULATE, CKA_DECAPSULATE, CKA_SEED.

PKCS#11 v3.2 finalized as an OASIS Standard (3 June 2026), technically identical in content to the prior Committee Specification Draft 01 / Committee Specification 01 — no substantive changes after Working Draft 13 (16 April 2025) per the spec's own Appendix C Revision History. Adds post-quantum mechanisms: ML-KEM (CKM_ML_KEM 0x00000017, CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000000f), ML-DSA (CKM_ML_DSA 0x0000001d, CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000001c, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_*), and SLH-DSA (CKM_SLH_DSA, CKM_SLH_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN). Introduces C_EncapsulateKey() and C_DecapsulateKey() for KEM operations, and C_WrapKeyAuthenticated()/C_UnwrapKeyAuthenticated(). New key types: CKK_ML_KEM (0x49), CKK_ML_DSA (0x4a), CKK_SLH_DSA (0x4b). New attributes: CKA_PARAMETER_SET, CKA_ENCAPSULATE, CKA_DECAPSULATE, CKA_SEED.

Title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) Algorithms
Authors: IETF
Publication Date: 2003-08-01
Last Updated: 2003-08-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: This document specifies the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms, including RSA, DSA, Diffie-Hellman, SHA-1, MD5, Triple-DES, and RC2, with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS).
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: Russell Housley; Author of the document

Infrastructure Layers: Key Management; PKI (implied via certificates and key identifiers)
Standardization Bodies: IETF; Internet Society; RSA Laboratories

Key Takeaways: Implementations supporting specified algorithms must adhere strictly to the conventions defined in this document; RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks in interactive applications, requiring mitigation via OAEP or oracle protection; Cryptographic algorithms weaken over time, necessitating modular implementations for easy algorithm updates; Key wrap algorithms for ciphers other than Triple-DES or RC2 must be separately defined; Private keys and encryption keys must be protected to prevent masquerade and content disclosure
Target Audience: Developer; Security Architect; Protocol Designer
Implementation Prerequisites: Support for ASN.1 BER-encoding; Modular algorithm implementation architecture; Protection mechanisms for private and encryption keys
Relevant PQC Today Features: Algorithms; crypto-agility; email-signing; pki-workshop
Implementation Attack Surface: adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks; compromise of signer's private key; compromise of key management private key; compromise of key-encryption key; compromise of content-encryption key
Deployment & Migration Complexity: modular implementations allowing new algorithms to be readily inserted; regular updates to the set of algorithms; separation of protocol and algorithm specifications to allow independent updates

Authors: IETF

Last Updated: 2003-07-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: Specifies the conventions for using the RSAES-OAEP key transport algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) to address vulnerabilities in PKCS #1 Version 1.5.

LIB:RFC 4253.full:
Defines the SSH transport layer: protocol version exchange, algorithm negotiation, key exchange, server authentication, encryption and integrity protection. Key exchange methods are negotiated by name in the kex_algorithms list of the SSH_MSG_KEXINIT message, which is how later methods, including hybrid post-quantum ones, are added to SSH. Authors: IETF

LIB:RFC 6176.analysis:
Reference ID: RFC 6176
Title: Prohibiting Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) Version 2.0
Authors: IETF
Publication Date: 2011-03-01
Last Updated: 2011-03-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: This document formally prohibits the negotiation of Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) version 2.0 in Transport Layer Security (TLS) connections due to known security deficiencies.
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: Sean Turner and Tim Polk are the document authors; Peter Saint Andre and Simon Josefsson inspired the idea; Michael D'Errico, Paul Hoffman, Nikos Mavrogiannopoulos, Tom Petch, Yngve Pettersen, Marsh Ray, Martin Rex, Yaron Sheffer, and Glen Zorn provided reviews and comments.
Protocols Covered: TLS, SSL 2.0, SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2
Standardization Bodies: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG)
Classical Algorithms Referenced: MD5
Key Takeaways: TLS clients MUST NOT send SSL version 2.0 compatible CLIENT-HELLO messages; TLS servers MUST NOT reply with an SSL 2.0 SERVER-HELLO with a protocol version less than { 0x03, 0x00 }; SSL 2.0 is prohibited due to deficiencies including unprotected handshake messages and weak message authentication using MD5; The prohibition updates backward compatibility sections in TLS standards to phase out legacy protocol support.
Target Audience: Developer, Security Architect
Relevant PQC Today Features: tls-basics, crypto-agility
Implementation Attack Surface: Man-in-the-middle attacks exploiting unprotected handshake messages; Session termination via TCP FIN insertion; Weak cipher suite selection due to lack of handshake protection.
Deployment & Migration Complexity: Backward compatibility sections in TLS are updated to prohibit SSL 2.0 negotiation; Servers may continue to accept version 2 CLIENT-HELLO format but must not negotiate SSL 2.0; The number of servers supporting the "MAY accept" option is declining.

LIB:RFC 6749.full:
Defines the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework enabling delegated access using access tokens. The token format is not specified: the access token string is usually opaque to the client, and it may be an identifier used to retrieve the authorization information or may carry that information in a verifiable (signed) form. ID tokens are defined by OpenID Connect, not by this RFC. Post-quantum migration affects signed tokens such as JWT access tokens (the authorization server's signing algorithm and resource servers' signature validation); a reference token validated by lookup does not depend on a token signature.

Key Takeaways: A RawPublicKey Certificate entry carries a DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo instead of an X.509 certificate chain. Authentication still requires proof of private-key possession and a securely established identity-to-key binding. Omitting the chain therefore changes trust handling as well as byte counts; successful key parsing alone does not authenticate the peer.

RSA-2048 uses a 294-byte SPKI and 307-byte handshake versus 1,642 bytes (81.30%). Totals include empty context, list/entry lengths, empty entry extensions and the four-byte handshake header. The root stays local in the X.509 baseline. These selected profiles have different security strengths; neither result is a universal savings rate or a measurement of the whole connection.

A JWT is always a JWS or a JWE in compact serialization: a signed or MAC-protected JWT has three dot-separated parts (header.payload.signature), an encrypted JWT has five, and an Unsecured JWT (alg none) has an empty signature. Title: Deprecating Secure Sockets Layer Version 3.0
Authors: IETF
Publication Date: 2015-06-01
Last Updated: 2015-06-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: Formal deprecation of Secure Sockets Layer version 3.0 (SSLv3) due to comprehensive security flaws, requiring its prohibition in favor of more secure TLS versions.
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: R. Barnes, M. Thomson, A. Pironti, A. Langley
Protocols Covered: SSLv3, TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2, DTLS
Standardization Bodies: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG)
Classical Algorithms Referenced: RC4, SHA-1, MD5, SHA-256, ECDH, ECDSA
Key Takeaways: SSLv3 MUST NOT be used and negotiation of SSLv3 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted; SSLv3 is comprehensively broken due to flawed CBC padding, weak stream ciphers, and vulnerable key exchange mechanisms; TLS servers MUST accept any record layer version number for ClientHello but MUST NOT negotiate SSLv3; SSLv3 lacks support for modern security features such as AEAD modes, ECDH, and stateless session tickets; Custom cryptographic primitives in SSLv3 rely on weak hash algorithms like SHA-1 and MD5.
Target Audience: Security Architect, Developer, Compliance Officer
Relevant PQC Today Features: tls-basics, crypto-agility, migration-program
Implementation Attack Surface: POODLE attack, man-in-the-middle attacks during renegotiation or session resumption, non-deterministic padding in CBC construction, biases in RC4 stream cipher
Deployment & Migration Complexity: Backward compatibility issues noted as TLS implementations historically permitted SSLv3 negotiation; prohibition of fallback to SSLv3 required.

Authors: IETF
Publication Date: 2017-12-01
Last Updated: 2017-12-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: This document defines additional Modular Exponentiation (MODP) Diffie-Hellman key exchange groups for the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol using SHA-2 hashes to address security concerns with smaller groups and SHA-1.
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: M. Baushke
Protocols Covered: Secure Shell (SSH)

Security Levels & Parameters: 110 bits of security; 310 bits of security; 2048 bits; 3072 bits; 4096-8192 bit groups
Target Audience: Developer; Security Architect

QRNG & Entropy Sources: Deterministic random-bit generator (DRBG); Sufficient entropy

Title: TLS Certificate Compression
Authors: IETF TLS
Publication Date: 2020-11-01
Last Updated: 2020-11-01
Document Status: Proposed Standard
Main Topic: Defines a TLS 1.3 extension for compressing certificate chains using algorithms like zlib, brotli, and zstd to reduce handshake overhead.
Migration Timeline Info: Years mentioned: 2020
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Regions: International
Leaders Contributions Mentioned: A. Ghedini (Author); V. Vasiliev (Author); Adam Langley (Original design of certificate compression in QUIC); Wan-Teh Chang (Original design of certificate compression in QUIC)
PQC Products Mentioned: Signal
Protocols Covered: TLS 1.3
Infrastructure Layers: PKI
Standardization Bodies: IETF
Key Takeaways: TLS 1.3 certificate compression is negotiated and compresses the Certificate message body, not its four-byte handshake header. It preserves the same certificates and trust checks after decompression. The worked chain examples below show different savings for different certificate bytes; compression does not change their algorithms or security strengths.
Pure PQC KEM Support: Not Applicable
Hybrid PQC KEM Support: Not Applicable
Pure PQC Signature Support: Not Applicable
Hybrid PQC Signature Support: Not Applicable
PQC Heatmap Protocols Covered: TLS-1.3
PQC Heatmap Protocols Evidence: TLS-1.3: "This extension is only supported with TLS 1.3"
Lifecycle State: Released
Performance & Size Considerations: Retained fictional leaf-plus-intermediate samples, with the root kept local: ML-DSA-65 Certificate handshake 11,100 bytes becomes a 10,913-byte CompressedCertificate (1.68% smaller); RSA-2048/SHA-256 1,642 becomes 1,453 bytes (11.51%). With leaf only, the corresponding reductions are 0.09% and 2.01%. Measurements use zlib 1.2.12 level 6 and the same verified sample bytes: compressed totals include the four-byte handshake header plus two-byte algorithm, three-byte uncompressed length and three-byte compressed-vector length. Record/TCP/IP overhead and latency are excluded. Fresh keys/signatures or another chain/compressor can change these results.
Target Audience: Developer; Security Architect
Implementation Prerequisites: TLS 1.3 endpoints must negotiate a matching compression algorithm (zlib in this example), bound decompression and verify the resulting certificate chain normally. The sample checks exact decompression and rejects corrupt or truncated input, inconsistent lengths and output beyond its size cap. Byte framing and local decode tests do not establish endpoint interoperability.
Relevant PQC Today Features: tls-basics; crypto-agility
Implementation Attack Surface: Memory usage bounds during decompression; Message size limits to prevent abuse; Length inference attacks via compression
Constrained Device & IoT Suitability: constrained IoT devices
Deployment & Migration Complexity: Evaluate transmitted chain composition, actual serialized bytes, negotiated compressor and receiver resource limits together. Repeat measurements on the intended endpoints and test both compressed and uncompressed paths; RFC 8879 does not define this TLS 1.3 extension as a TLS 1.2 compression mechanism.
PQC Round: Not Applicable
Extraction Note: carry-forward (DS05p2): record not iterated this run; preserved from prior enrichment
LIB:RFC 8879.full:
Defines negotiated TLS 1.3 Certificate-body compression with normal certificate validation after decompression. A retained fictional ML-DSA-65 leaf-plus-intermediate sample shrinks from 11,100 to 10,913 handshake bytes using zlib level 6 (1.68%); the stated RSA-2048 sample shrinks from 1,642 to 1,453 bytes (11.51%). These sample-specific counts include handshake/compression framing, exclude transport overhead, and do not establish a latency benefit.

Implementation Attack Surface: Timing side channels; Replay attacks; Packet tampering; Header protection bypass

LIB:RFC 9449.full:
Defines DPoP for binding OAuth 2.0 tokens to a client key pair using a signed proof-of-possession JWT. The proof's alg header must identify a JWS asymmetric digital signature algorithm from the IANA JOSE registry (not none or a MAC); the RFC's examples use ES256 and PS256, and a server can list the algorithms it accepts in an algs parameter. Proofs signed with ECDSA or RSA are quantum-vulnerable. The IANA JOSE registry now lists ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 (RFC 9964), so a post-quantum proof is possible where client and server both support them; ML-DSA-signed DPoP proofs result in significantly larger proof headers per request.

LIB:RFC 9711.full:
Defines the Entity Attestation Token (EAT), a CWT- or JWT-based framework of attestation claims that describe the state and characteristics of an entity such as a device.
Authors: L. Lundblade (Security Theory LLC); G. Mandyam; J. O'Donoghue (Qualcomm Technologies Inc.); C. Wallace (Red Hound Software, Inc.)
Status: Standards Track
Document type: RFC
Published: 2025-04
passages: provides an attested claims set that describes the state and characteristics of an entity, a device such as a smartphone, an Internet of Things (IoT) device, network equipment, or such.
This claims set is used by a relying party, server, or service to determine the type and degree of trust placed in the entity.
An EAT is either a CBOR Web Token (CWT) or a JSON Web Token (JWT) with attestation-oriented claims.

Main Topic: Defines Composite ML-DSA, a PQ/T hybrid signature scheme combining ML-DSA with RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5, RSASSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519 and Ed448 for use in X.509/PKIX, including key generation, encodings, OIDs and security considerations.
PQC Algorithms Covered: ML-DSA
Quantum Threats Addressed: Traditional signature algorithms (RSA, DSA, elliptic curve variants) becoming vulnerable to quantum attacks; hedging against breaks or catastrophic bugs in ML-DSA implementations
Applicable Regions / Bodies: Regions: None detected; Bodies: US NIST, BSI, ANSSI, NLNCSA, Swedish National Communications Security Authority/Swedish Armed Forces, CA/Browser Forum, European Parliament/Council of the European Union (eIDAS)

LIB:RFC-7924.full:
Defines the TLS cached_info extension, also applicable to DTLS, so peers can identify previously cached certificate or certificate-request data by fingerprint and omit unchanged handshake payloads. It reduces repeat-handshake bandwidth but does not change the certificate's signature algorithm or make a classical certificate post-quantum secure. LIB:RFC-9345.full:
Defines a TLS 1.3-or-later mechanism allowing a certificate holder to issue a short-lived delegated credential for TLS or DTLS authentication while retaining compatibility with peers that do not support it. The credential is bound to the end-entity certificate, is normally limited to seven days absent another application profile, and has no independent early-revocation mechanism. It can decouple an endpoint signature algorithm from CA issuance support, but the RFC does not itself define a PQ algorithm or PQ migration requirement.

Published: 2023-12
passages: An Oblivious Pseudorandom Function (OPRF) is a two-party protocol between a client and a server for computing the output of a Pseudorandom Function (PRF).
At the end of the protocol, the client learns the PRF output without learning anything about the PRF private key, and the server learns neither the PRF input nor output.
A VOPRF ensures clients can verify that the server used a specific private key during the execution of the protocol.

Defines the Rosenpass protocol for adding post-quantum key exchange to WireGuard. Runs a separate handshake that combines Classic McEliece 460896 (static keys) with Kyber-512 (ephemeral keys), both NIST round-3 submissions rather than the FIPS 203 ML-KEM standard, and passes the resulting key to WireGuard as a pre-shared key (PSK). Handshake packages are 1092, 1132 and 176 bytes, plus a 64-byte EmptyData acknowledgement. Security is analysed symbolically with ProVerif; a CryptoVerif proof is in progress.

LIB:SQIsign-Round2-Spec.full:
Isogeny-based signature scheme — the only post-quantum candidate built on supersingular elliptic-curve isogenies. Smallest combined public-key+signature of any PQC candidate by a wide margin: SQIsign-I (NIST L1) is pk=64 B, sig=177 B (up from 148 B in Round 1, traded for a 20× signing speedup). Safe's checkNSignatures reference documents validation of a caller-supplied number of signatures. LIB:Simple-Proof-of-Security-of-the-BB84.full:
Physical Review Letters 85, 441 (2000). Proves BB84 secure against any physical operation quantum mechanics permits, by reducing it to an entanglement-purification protocol built on CSS codes. In the paper's asymptotic analysis the key-distribution protocol works as long as the measured bit and phase error rates are below about 11%, the point at which the Shannon rate for the code reaches zero. This is the highest error rate the analysis tolerates, not a test for detecting an eavesdropper: channel noise and an attack both show up as errors. The paper notes that no proof then known covered the weak coherent sources that most experimental systems use.

Original UOV construction by Kipnis-Patarin-Goubin (1999). Public key is a system of multivariate quadratic polynomials with the secret oil/vinegar partition hidden inside. passages: registers IANA values in the TLS Supported Groups registry for use in TLS 1.3 to achieve post-quantum (PQ) key establishment.
For all parameter sets, the client MUST check if the ciphertext length matches the selected parameter set, and abort with an illegal_parameter alert if it fails.

An IRTF CFRG Internet-Draft defining concrete hybrid post-quantum/traditional KEM instances (MLKEM768-P256, MLKEM768-X25519, MLKEM1024-P384) built on the CFRG hybrid KEM framework, with test vectors.

Status: Internet-Draft

Published: 2026-07-06
passages: PQ/T Hybrid Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) combine "post-quantum" cryptographic algorithms, which are safe from attack by a quantum computer, with "traditional" algorithms, which are not.
Such KEMs are secure against a quantum attacker as long as the PQ algorithm is secure, and remain secure against traditional attackers even if the PQ algorithm is not secure.
MLKEM768-P256: A hybrid KEM composing ML-KEM-768 and P-256 using the CG framework, with SHAKE256 as the PRG and SHA3-256 as the KDF.
This hybrid KEM combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519 using the CG framework from [ HYBRID-KEMS ] . It is identical to the X-Wing construction from [ XWING-SPEC ] .
When the C2PRI combiner is used (as it is here), the PQ KEM also needs to satisfy the C2PRI property. ¶ KDFs need to be indifferentiable from a random oracle, even by a quantum attacker.
