# Hybrid Cryptography — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Transitioning a massive network to brand-new, cutting-edge cryptographic algorithms introduces risk. "Hybrid Cryptography" is the strategy of combining a highly trusted classical algorithm (like X25519) with a new quantum-safe algorithm (like ML-KEM) simultaneously.

## Why It Matters

It is a hedge. If a flaw is found in the new quantum-safe algorithm or in its new code, the classical algorithm still protects the data against today's attackers, provided the two are combined soundly. The hedge has costs: two algorithms to implement, test and negotiate, larger messages, and a second transition later when the classical part is removed. For signatures, every verifier must insist on both signatures, or an attacker can strip one.

## Who Recommends It

Agencies disagree. France (ANSSI), Germany (BSI), the Netherlands and the EU certification group ask for hybrid during the transition. The US NSA, the UK NCSC and the Czech NÚKIB accept post-quantum algorithms on their own, and the NSA warns that hybrids add complexity that can introduce their own flaws. Canada's Cyber Centre recommends the new algorithms without saying either way.

## The Key Takeaway

Whether to use hybrid depends on whose rules apply to you and on what you protect. For key exchange in TLS, hybrid is already the common default on the web. For signatures and certificates the formats are newer and the advice is more divided.

## Hybrid in a Validated Module

A security product certified under FIPS 140-3 can offer a hybrid key exchange as an approved service even though one half, such as X25519, is not an approved algorithm. The NIST/CMVP guidance (IG D.S) sets five conditions: an approved ML-KEM, another key exchange (approved or not), an approved way to combine the two secrets, a fixed list of allowed hybrid pairs that the module enforces itself, and module control over the order in which the secrets are joined. The non-approved half is allowed but "no security claimed": the hybrid's claimed strength comes from ML-KEM. If any condition is missing, the hybrid cannot be an approved service. The guidance says the TLS hybrid groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) may qualify, while the X-Wing hybrid cannot yet, even though NIST's algorithm-testing page lists X-Wing tests. A separate rule, IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules", is about firmware plus hardware in one module and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange.

## What's Happening

Major tech companies, including Google and Cloudflare, have already deployed hybrid TLS key exchange (X25519MLKEM768, standardized as RFC 10024, replacing the earlier X25519Kyber768Draft00) across Chrome and web infrastructure at scale; Chrome reported about a 4% slower TLS handshake. On the certificate side, Composite ML-DSA is now published as RFC 10073, while Composite ML-KEM (`draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23`) is in the RFC Editor queue.

A compliant ML-KEM deployment is more than “call the library.” SP 800-227 §3.2 covers the required input checks, and FIPS 203 specifies implicit rejection: if the re-encrypted ciphertext does not match the one received, decapsulation returns a key derived from the ciphertext and a secret value stored in the decapsulation key (Algorithm 18) instead of reporting an error. SP 800-227 §3.3 says KEM modules should be designed with appropriate countermeasures against side-channel attacks, including constant-time implementations and protecting memory from leakage.
ML-KEM is the key-encapsulation algorithm defined in FIPS 203. Alice uses Bob's public encapsulation key to produce a shared secret and a ciphertext. Bob uses his private decapsulation key and that ciphertext to recover the same secret. A protocol can then derive encryption and authentication keys from it.
For example, an ML-KEM-768 ciphertext must be 1,088 bytes long. A 1,087-byte ciphertext fails the length check, and decapsulation must not run. FIPS 203 also requires checks on the decapsulation key. Normal library argument and operational errors still apply.
For inputs that pass those checks, ML-KEM decrypts and re-encrypts internally, then compares the reconstructed ciphertext with the received one. If they differ, it selects a fallback shared secret derived from the secret rejection value
and the received ciphertext. The implementation returns that secret without exposing the mismatch as an error or through timing. This is implicit rejection.
What happens to the encrypted data?
Suppose an attacker changes Alice's ciphertext without changing its length and triggers implicit rejection. Bob obtains a different secret. If the protocol derives an AES-GCM key from it, authentication of Alice's encrypted message fails, and the receiver rejects the message without releasing unauthenticated plaintext. Successful decapsulation alone does not confirm that both parties share a key; the protocol needs authentication or key confirmation.
Why hide the mismatch if authentication fails later?
A specific decapsulation error would answer an attacker's repeated queries about the internal ciphertext check, creating a validity oracle. Implicit rejection conceals that answer. A later authentication failure only says that the message did not authenticate with the resulting key; a wrong tag can cause the same failure even after valid decapsulation. The protocol must preserve this distinction in its error handling and timing.

Correct results alone do not show that an implementation protects its secrets. Attackers may learn information by measuring execution time or observing memory access. Constant-time techniques help prevent these behaviours from revealing secret values; they do not mean every call takes exactly the same number of milliseconds. NIST recommends appropriate protections against these attacks. Their effectiveness depends on the implementation and the device running it.

Combining the two secrets in application memory means reading them out of the token, and anything that can read that memory can rebuild the session key. Combining inside the token is possible, but only as a chain the application drives.

A v3.2 token can concatenate two secret keys (CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_KEY), append public data (CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_DATA) and hash the result (CKM_SHA3_256_KEY_DERIVATION, or CKM_HKDF_DERIVE). Upgrading the world's computers to use entirely new Post-Quantum math isn't like flipping a simple light switch; it takes years of meticulous testing and auditing.
To stay safe during this long transition, security architects are using "Hybrid Cryptography". This means they lock their sensitive data using both the tried-and-true old math AND the brand new Post-Quantum math simultaneously. For encryption, if either method turns out to have a hidden, fatal flaw, the data stays protected by the other lock, as long as the two locks are joined in a well-designed way (as the TLS hybrid design and X-Wing do). For signatures, a forger must break both methods, as long as the checker insists that both signatures are valid.
Hybrid has costs too: two algorithms to build and test, bigger messages, and a second switch-over later when the old math is retired. That is why some agencies (France, Germany) ask for hybrid while others (the US NSA, the UK NCSC) accept the new math on its own.

Hybrid Cryptography — In Simple Terms
It is a hedge. If a flaw is found in the new quantum-safe algorithm or in its new code, the classical algorithm still protects the data against today's attackers, provided the two are combined soundly. The hedge has costs: two algorithms to implement, test and negotiate, larger messages, and a second transition later when the classical part is removed. For signatures, every verifier must insist on both signatures, or an attacker can strip one.

NIST SP 800-227 describes how to combine key-establishment mechanisms securely (§4.6): a suitably designed classical/PQC combination can retain security if one component remains secure. §3.3 recommends appropriate side-channel protections such as constant-time implementations; migration to pure PQC is driven by algorithm maturation rather than calendar deadlines alone
Hybrid combiner construction (SP 800-227 + SP 800-56C-Rev2): concatenation order is fixed per protocol (TLS 1.3 per RFC 10024 §4.3: X25519MLKEM768 uses `ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss`, while SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 use `ECDHE_ss || ML-KEM_ss`; per its §5, SP 800-56C-Rev2 approves this when the first secret comes from a FIPS-approved scheme, so ML-KEM goes first where X25519 is used, and ECDHE goes first for the NIST curves, whose certified implementations are more widely available; SP 800-227 §4.6.2, September 2025, approves its key combiner when at least one shared secret in any position comes from an approved scheme); SP 800-56C permits either HKDF (HMAC-based extractor with SHA-256/384/512) or KMAC128/256 as the combiner; dual-PRF assumption means the combined secret is safe as long as _either_ input looks uniform to the attacker, so a future break of ML-KEM or of X25519 alone does not break the session key; SP 800-227 §4.6.3 says the domain-separation input should be used to uniquely identify the composite scheme in use (for example the two component schemes, order of composition, choice of parameter set, key combiner, KDF)
What makes X-Wing different: it leaves out the ML-KEM ciphertext and public key, relying on the specifics of ML-KEM-768's Fujisaki-Okamoto transform; the draft warns the combiner "cannot be assumed to be secure, when used with different KEMs"; if SHA3-256, SHA3-512 and SHAKE-256 are modelled as random oracles its IND-CCA security is bounded by ML-KEM-768's and the gap-CDH security of Curve25519; it claims MAL-BIND-K-PK and MAL-BIND-K-CT, which ML-KEM alone does not achieve; its private key is a 32-byte seed expanded with SHAKE256 into both component keys (public key 1,216 bytes, ciphertext 1,120 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes), the reason FIPS 140-3 IG D.S says it cannot yet meet Scenario 2; the composite ML-KEM draft calls X-Wing and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry "largely interchangeable", the one difference being X-Wing's joint seed keygen, so an X-Wing implementation is a compliant composite implementation but not the reverse
ML-KEM decapsulation and implicit rejection (FIPS 203 §§6.3 and 7.3): input checks can fail; for example, ML-KEM-768 requires a 1,088-byte ciphertext. After the required checks pass, an internal re-encryption mismatch selects a fallback shared secret derived from the secret rejection value `z` and the received ciphertext, without exposing the mismatch through an error or timing. Normal library argument and operational errors still apply. If tampering triggers this path, the receiver obtains a different secret; in a protocol deriving an AES-GCM key from it, authentication fails and unauthenticated plaintext must not be released. Implicit rejection conceals the internal ciphertext-validity result; a later authentication failure can also occur after valid decapsulation and does not directly disclose that result. Protocol error handling and timing must preserve this distinction. Successful decapsulation alone does not confirm a shared key: use protocol authentication or key confirmation.
CNSA 2.0 (NSA): its FAQ (v2.2, October 2026) quotes CNSSP 15 as requiring CNSA 2.0 algorithms in all new NSS acquisitions by 1 January 2027, says that by 31 December 2030 NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception, and that by 31 December 2031 CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted; it also says specific deadlines depend on equipment type; NSA will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes, although product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions in specific cases
Seven certificate formats in the main comparison (five signature formats + two KEM formats): - Pure PQC (ML-DSA) — standard single-algorithm X.509 using ML-DSA signatures; OIDs standardized in RFC 9881; the workshop is tested with OpenSSL 3.6.3 - Pure PQC (SLH-DSA) — hash-based signature X.509 certificates; OIDs in RFC 9909; ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for hash-based signatures such as SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS - Composite (dual-algorithm) — single composite OID identifies the algorithm pair; both signatures must verify; defined in RFC 10073 (November 2026) - Alt-Sig / Catalyst — classical primary cert with PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions (SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo 2.5.29.72, AltSignatureAlgorithm 2.5.29.73, AltSignatureValue 2.5.29.74); legacy verifiers ignore the extensions; defined in ITU-T X.509 (2019) §7.2.2 and §9.8; relying-party policy decides whether one or both signatures are required - Related Certificates (RFC 9763) — a NEW certificate (Cert B) carries a RelatedCertificate extension holding the hash of the complete final DER of an EXISTING certificate (Cert A); the binding is one-way and Cert A is never modified; the CA issues Cert B only after a relatedCertRequest proves possession of Cert A's key; a protocol may use either certificate or both — RFC 9763 does not require both - Pure PQC KEM (ML-KEM, RFC 9935) — an ML-KEM public key in X.509; if keyUsage is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit; the certificate is CA-issued, never self-signed; the key is used e.g. in CMS KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629, ML-KEM in CMS: RFC 9936) - Composite KEM — ML-KEM plus a classical KEM under one OID, ML-KEM first; defined in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23, approved by the IESG and in the RFC Editor queue since 2026-10-12 (not yet an RFC)
Advanced examples (outside the main comparison): Certificate Discovery (draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-06, active LAMPS WG draft) lets a primary certificate advertise in subjectInfoAccess where a related secondary certificate can be fetched, which algorithms it uses and, optionally, its hash (certHash); after fetching, those fields must match the retrieved certificate, and it must still pass full path validation; -06 removed the earlier 'intent' field and gives no way to say why two certificates are related; the draft's OIDs are TBD, so the workshop uses documentation-arc placeholders (1.3.6.1.4.1.32473) and its encoding is illustrative. RFC 9925 unsigned certificates use id-alg-unsigned (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.36), a zero-length signature and a placeholder issuer (id-rdna-unsigned); they suit keys trusted by other means and are never valid in a certification path
Historical design — Chameleon Certificates: a single cert with a DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension encoding the differences needed to rebuild a paired cert; draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07 is an expired individual draft never adopted by the LAMPS working group; kept for study only and not recommended for new deployments
Watchlist: FN-DSA (planned FIPS 206, not yet final) has an IETF certificate draft, draft-ietf-lamps-fn-dsa-certificates, whose OIDs are still TBD — no deployable FN-DSA certificate exists yet
Other hybrid KEM variants: SecP256r1MLKEM768 (P-256 + ML-KEM-768, FIPS-approved classical curve), SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (P-384 + ML-KEM-1024, NIST Level 5)
HPKE standards status (November 2026): The successor of RFC 9180, draft-ietf-hpke-hpke-06, removes the Auth and AuthPSK modes. The IETF Datatracker lists it in the RFC Editor queue (state on 8 November 2026). The draft is dated 29 October 2026. It adds a framework for single-stage KDFs, requires that applications not derive an AEAD key and nonce from an exported secret without fresh per-derivation input, and requires implementations to support info values of at least 64 bytes (recommending at least 16,384). It does not specify Auth and AuthPSK but reserves mode values 0x02 and 0x03 and does not deprecate them, so RFC 9180 deployments can keep using them. draft-ietf-hpke-pq (-05, 6 July 2026) is a working-group draft registering ML-KEM, the PQ/T hybrid KEMs and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE KDFs. Users of HPKE: draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt-22 (RFC Editor queue), draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt-02 (working-group draft), draft-ietf-cose-hpke-27 (IESG, waiting for AD go-ahead), draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-07 (publication requested)

A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is a one-sided primitive: the sender gives Encaps the receiver's public key and gets back a shared secret and a ciphertext, rather than supplying a key of its own choosing.

If a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer (CRQC) breaks X25519 via Shor's algorithm, the ML-KEM shared secret remains secret.
If ML-KEM-768 has an unforeseen algebraic weakness, the X25519 shared secret remains secret.
What this construction does and does not do: its combiner has the form CMVP IG D.S accepts (both secrets concatenated and fed into an SP 800-56C KDF, HKDF included), but it mixes in only the two secrets and a fixed label, not the exchanged key shares or public keys. Deployed combiners bind those too (X-Wing hashes the X25519 key share and public key into its output; TLS 1.3 feeds the whole handshake transcript into its key schedule). A validated module must also enforce a fixed set of hybrid schemes and control the concatenation order itself, which this demo does not, so treat it as the idea, not a design to copy.

qa.answer: Hybrid cryptography ensures that security holds even if one component (either the classical or the PQC algorithm) is broken. This defense-in-depth strategy mitigates the risk during the quantum transition period where PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical ones.
qa.question: What is the primary security benefit of combining classical and post-quantum algorithms in a hybrid approach?

qa.answer: ANSSI (Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information) requires hybrid mode during the PQC transition. They do not accept PQC-only implementations until the algorithms have sufficiently matured, with exceptions for specific hash-based signatures.
qa.question: Which French agency mandates the use of hybrid mode during the PQC transition period?

qa.answer: The leading hybrid KEM combining these algorithms is named X25519MLKEM768. It derives a combined shared secret using a Key Derivation Function (KDF) applied to the concatenation of the X25519 and ML-KEM shared secrets.
qa.question: What is the specific hybrid KEM combination that integrates Curve25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768?

qa.answer: NIST Special Publication 800-227 (SP 800-227) recommends the use of hybrid key exchange mechanisms. This guidance supports the adoption of combined classical and PQC algorithms to secure protocols like TLS while PQC standards mature.
qa.question: Which NIST publication recommends hybrid key exchange for TLS and other protocols during the transition?

qa.answer: Composite signatures are approximately 3.4 KB in size, whereas a standard ECDSA signature is only about 72 bytes. This significant increase in size is a trade-off for the enhanced security provided by combining two distinct algorithms.
qa.question: What is the approximate size difference between a composite signature and a standard ECDSA signature?

qa.answer: RFC 9794 standardizes the terminology for hybrid schemes, defining 'composite' as a single OID where both algorithms must verify, and 'non-composite' as parallel independent algorithms. It also establishes the 'PQ/T' naming convention.
qa.question: Which RFC standardizes the terminology distinguishing between 'composite' and 'non-composite' hybrid schemes?

qa.answer: A hybrid approach is recommended because PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical ones, creating a fundamental dilemma. Waiting for full maturity exposes systems to HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threats, while hybridization provides immediate defense in depth.
qa.question: Why is a hybrid approach recommended despite the existence of pure PQC algorithms?

qa.answer: In the Composite format, a single OID identifies the algorithm pair, and both signatures must verify for the certificate to be valid. In contrast, the Parallel format uses a primary PQC signature with classical keys/signatures in X.509 extensions, maximizing backward compatibility.
qa.question: How does the 'Composite' certificate format differ from the 'Parallel (alt-sig)' format in terms of verification?

qa.answer: Integrating X25519MLKEM768 causes the ClientHello key_share extension to grow from 32 bytes to 1,216 bytes, representing a 38-fold increase. This expansion may push the ClientHello message beyond a single TCP packet, potentially affecting network performance.
qa.question: What is the impact of using X25519MLKEM768 on the size of the ClientHello message in TLS 1.3?

qa.answer: ANSSI allows hash-based signatures like SLH-DSA, LMS, and XMSS to be used in standalone mode without hybridization. This exception exists because these specific algorithms are considered mature enough or distinct enough from the lattice-based approaches that require hybrid defense.
qa.question: Why are hash-based signatures like SLH-DSA, LMS, and XMSS treated differently by ANSSI compared to other PQC algorithms?

qa.answer: NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2) sets dates for national security systems (new national security system acquisitions from 1 January 2027, phase-out of equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 by 31 December 2030 (exceptions possible), and CNSA 2.0 algorithms mandated by 31 December 2031 unless otherwise noted) but does not require hybrid key exchange: NSA states it "will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes". Hybrid is a separate matter for jurisdictions such as France (ANSSI) and Germany (BSI), whose published guidance expects it during the transition.
qa.question: How does the CNSA 2.0 mandate from the NSA relate to hybrid key exchange?

qa.answer: Using a single OID for composite signatures simplifies handling and prevents downgrade attacks by ensuring both algorithms must verify. This contrasts with parallel approaches where independent algorithms might be processed separately, potentially allowing an attacker to bypass one component.
qa.question: What is the primary advantage of using a single OID for composite signatures over parallel algorithms?

qa.answer: A hybrid key exchange: a classical Diffie-Hellman exchange combined with a post-quantum KEM such as ML-KEM. ANSSI's FAQ says hybridisation is mandatory inside the French regulated perimeter (defence-classified and Diffusion Restreinte information, vital information systems, ANSSI-certified or qualified products), and its TLS 1.3 fact sheet (ANSSI-FT-115) recommends hybridisation for both key exchange and signature authentication, treating a pre-shared key as a possible but temporary measure. ANSSI expects standalone PQC only in a later phase (probably not before 2030). Outside the perimeter its PQC recommendations, including on hybridisation, are not a regulatory obligation today.
qa.question: In a scenario where an organization falls inside ANSSI's regulated perimeter, what is the minimum acceptable configuration for its TLS key exchange?

qa.answer: The architect should account for an additional ~0.1–0.3 ms per handshake due to ML-KEM encapsulation/decapsulation. Real-world measurements show this results in less than a 1% latency increase at P50, which is generally acceptable for most applications.
qa.question: How should a system architect handle the latency increase observed in hybrid KEM handshakes?

qa.answer: The team must monitor the size of the ClientHello message, as it grows from 32 bytes to 1,216 bytes. This 38x increase may cause the packet to exceed a single TCP segment, potentially triggering fragmentation or requiring Path MTU discovery adjustments.
qa.question: If a team is deploying X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3, what specific network constraint must they monitor?

qa.answer: The CNSA 2.0 dates (31 December 2030 phase-out of unsupported equipment (exceptions possible), 31 December 2031 mandated use) require national security systems to transition to CNSA 2.0 algorithms, but CNSA 2.0 itself does not require hybrid key exchange -- it permits pure PQC. Hybrid is expected separately by ANSSI and BSI in their published guidance (binding only inside their regulated perimeters), not by the NSA's CNSA 2.0. Organizations targeting only the CNSA 2.0 deadline can plan for pure PQC; those also subject to ANSSI or BSI requirements need hybrid specifically because of that guidance, not because of CNSA 2.0.
qa.question: What is the strategic implication of the CNSA 2.0 dates for national security systems?

qa.answer: Pure PQC uses standard single-algorithm X.509 with PQC signatures (e.g., ML-DSA in RFC 9881) and is ready today, but lacks defense-in-depth if the PQC algorithm fails. Composite formats use a single OID for both algorithms, offering stronger security by requiring dual verification, though they rely on draft standards like draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs.
qa.question: Compare the trade-offs between 'Pure PQC' and 'Composite' certificate formats regarding standardization and security.

qa.answer: In a high-assurance environment, Parallel (alt-sig) certificates pose a higher risk because the PQC component sits in an X.509 extension field, with the classical signature as the primary, default-parsed signature -- legacy verifiers process only the classical signature, while PQC-aware verifiers check both. Unlike Composite signatures that enforce dual verification via a single OID, the parallel approach could theoretically allow a downgrade if an implementation only checks the primary classical signature and never inspects the PQC extension.
qa.question: Analyze the risk of using 'Parallel (alt-sig)' certificates in a high-assurance environment where downgrade attacks are a concern.

qa.answer: Composite signatures are approximately 3.4 KB, which is significantly larger than the 72 bytes of ECDSA alone. In constrained IoT environments with limited bandwidth or storage, this size increase could be prohibitive, necessitating a careful evaluation of whether the security benefits outweigh the resource costs.
qa.question: How does the size of composite signatures impact the deployment of hybrid certificates in constrained IoT environments?

qa.answer: One hybrid posture does not satisfy both, because the two apply to different scopes. ANSSI recommends hybridisation and makes it mandatory only inside the French regulated perimeter; hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS) are the exception. CNSA 2.0 applies to US national security systems and does not require hybrid: NSA "will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes", and where it has issued public guidance on a hybrid, only the hybrid it identified counts as CNSA 2.0 compliant. For PKI it says NSS "should not use novel mechanisms to support multiple algorithms within a single certificate", so composite certificates are not the CNSA 2.0 route. A global enterprise should therefore keep per-jurisdiction profiles (hybrid key establishment where ANSSI's perimeter applies, CNSA 2.0 algorithms such as ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 for NSS work); sharing one design for operational simplicity is a choice, not a rule that both regimes impose.
qa.question: Synthesize the requirements for a global enterprise to achieve compliance with both ANSSI and CNSA 2.0 simultaneously.

qa.answer: The integration adds approximately 0.1–0.3 ms per handshake due to ML-KEM operations, resulting in a real-world latency increase of less than 1% at P50. While the ClientHello size increases significantly (38x), the computational overhead remains minimal, making it feasible for widespread deployment.
qa.question: How does the integration of X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 affect the overall handshake performance compared to pure classical ECDH?

qa.answer: No. ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism and cannot sign. Under RFC 9935 an ML-KEM certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA, ...): the ML-KEM subject key performs encapsulation and decapsulation, and only the issuer key signs the certificate. The subject public-key algorithm and the certificate signature algorithm are independent.
qa.question: Can an ML-KEM key sign its own X.509 certificate?

qa.answer: If the keyUsage extension is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit set (RFC 9935 §5). RFC 9935 itself says nothing about criticality; RFC 5280 recommends marking keyUsage critical, which is what the workshop does.
qa.question: What key usage does RFC 9935 allow in an ML-KEM certificate?

qa.answer: The new certificate (Cert B) carries a non-critical RelatedCertificate extension holding a hash of the complete final DER of the existing certificate (Cert A), using the hash named by Cert A's signature algorithm. Before issuing Cert B, the CA verifies a relatedCertRequest CSR attribute signed with Cert A's key. The link is one-way: Cert A is never modified and RFC 9763 does not require reciprocity, nor that a protocol use both certificates.
qa.question: How does an RFC 9763 Related Certificate bind a new certificate to an existing one, and is the binding reciprocal?

qa.answer: draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23 (14 October 2026) is the current revision. The IESG has approved it and it has been in the RFC Editor queue since 21 October 2026 — still an Internet-Draft, not yet an RFC. Its id-MLKEM768-X25519-SHA3-256 identifier is 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.58, unchanged from earlier revisions.
qa.question: What is the current status of the Composite ML-KEM certificate draft?

qa.answer: No. FIPS 206 is not final, and the IETF certificate draft draft-ietf-lamps-fn-dsa-certificates (revision 00, an active LAMPS working-group draft) still has TBD object identifiers, so no deployable FN-DSA certificate exists yet.
qa.question: Is FIPS 206 (FN-DSA) published, and can FN-DSA certificates be deployed?

qa.answer: draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-06 is an active LAMPS working-group draft that lets a primary certificate advertise, in a subjectInfoAccess entry, where a related secondary certificate (for example one with a PQC key) can be fetched and which signature and public-key algorithms it uses. A fetched secondary must still pass full certification path validation. Its OIDs are still TBD, so the workshop shows it as an illustrative Advanced example.
qa.question: What is Certificate Discovery in LAMPS?

qa.answer: No. draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07 is an expired individual draft that the LAMPS working group never adopted. The workshop keeps it in a separate Historical designs section for study only; it is not recommended for new deployments.
qa.question: Is the Chameleon certificate design still active in the IETF?

qa.answer: RFC 9925 (February 2026) defines id-alg-unsigned (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.36) for certificates that carry no signature: a zero-length signature BIT STRING and a placeholder issuer such as the id-rdna-unsigned RDN, so the certificate is not self-signed. It suits keys trusted by other means, such as trust anchors. Validators must never accept id-alg-unsigned as a signature in a certification path.
qa.question: What is an RFC 9925 unsigned certificate, and can it be used in a certification path?

qa.answer: The developer should choose the Parallel (alt-sig) format. This approach places the PQC primary signature alongside classical keys and signatures in X.509 extensions (OIDs 2.5.29.73/74), maximizing backward compatibility with systems that only recognize classical algorithms.
qa.question: If a developer needs to support legacy systems that do not understand PQC OIDs, which certificate format should they choose?

qa.answer: The Composite (dual-algorithm) format is preferred for high-security environments. It uses a single composite OID to identify the algorithm pair and requires both signatures to verify, providing the strongest security model against component failures.
qa.question: When generating a hybrid certificate for a high-security environment requiring the strongest security model, which format is preferred?

qa.answer: Following Workshop Step 3 ('CA Setup'), you generate two separate root CAs — a classical ECDSA P-256 CA and a PQC ML-DSA-65 CA — rather than a single combined 'hybrid CA'. The sandbox uses these two independent roots side by side so learners can compare classical and PQC certificate issuance directly, rather than modeling a true hybrid-key certificate authority.
qa.question: How would you configure a hybrid CA to support both classical and PQC root keys according to the workshop steps?

qa.answer: The 'Related Certs' approach links separate certificates via a binding hash, whereas the 'Composite' approach embeds both classical and PQC signatures within a single certificate using a composite OID. The Related Certs method offers flexibility but requires managing multiple artifacts compared to the unified Composite model.
qa.question: How does the 'Related Certs' approach (RFC 9763) differ from the 'Composite' approach in terms of certificate structure?

qa.answer: Alt-Sig and Related Certificates (RFC 9763) both leave a classical certificate that legacy validators can verify on its own: Alt-Sig carries the PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions that legacy validators ignore, and Related Certificates issue a separate PQC certificate linked to the classical one by a hash. Composite certificates (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19) give the strongest binding because both signatures must verify, but systems that do not recognise the composite OIDs cannot use them at all. Chameleon certificates are not an option: draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07 is an expired individual draft, shown in the workshop only as a historical design.
qa.question: Which hybrid certificate format gives a system maximum backward compatibility, and why is Composite not the answer?

LM-006.summary:
# Hybrid and Composite Cryptography

## Overview

The Hybrid Cryptography module teaches how to combine classical and post-quantum algorithms during the quantum transition, and what that choice costs. It runs in this order: why hybrid; the risks of hybrid compared with pure PQC, for key establishment and for signatures; which national agencies, standards bodies and companies recommend hybrid or accept pure PQC; hybrid KEM construction (X25519MLKEM768, combiners); hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3; implementation and validation (SP 800-227, FIPS 140-3 IG D.S); HPKE; hybrid signatures (non-separability, Silithium); and finally hybrid certificates (seven X.509 formats plus chameleon certificates as a historical design).

## Key Concepts

- **Hybrid cryptography** combines classical and PQC algorithms so that security holds even if one component is broken
- **Pure PQC risks (what hybrid guards against)**: young schemes can fall to classical cryptanalysis (SIKE and Rainbow, per the Czech NÚKIB annex); in 2026 the BSI advised against Classic McEliece in new developments after new structural cryptanalysis and noted that a hybrid with Classic McEliece still keeps at least classical security; new implementations can carry exploitable bugs (Bernstein 2026: a small change in ML-DSA software is exploitable in 1 second on 1 laptop core, and far fewer Ed25519+ML-DSA keys than ML-DSA-only keys are estimated to be breakable for years after the first quantum attack)
- **Risks of hybrid KEMs**: an unsound combiner (ETSI TR 103 966: a "concatenation only" hybrid key is not secure against active adversaries; SP 800-227 approves specific combiners); fallback to classical-only when a client retries after a failed hybrid attempt (backwards-compatible hybrids can be open to downgrade, ETSI TR 103 966); larger messages (X25519MLKEM768 key share 1,216 bytes vs 32) and, in IKEv2, extra pre-authentication key exchanges raising denial-of-service risk; HPKE Auth modes cannot use ML-KEM or hybrids containing it; FIPS 140-3 approval only under the five IG D.S conditions (X-Wing cannot yet meet them)
- **Risks of hybrid signatures**: stripping one signature when verifiers accept either component (ETSI TR 103 966: such a backwards-compatible hybrid can be less secure than the PQC algorithm alone; fix: require both, or a non-separable construction per RFC 9955); certificate rollback where a server keeps classical certificates (individual draft draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity proposes clients remember PQC support); more complex and less researched than hybrid confidentiality (UK NCSC); a PKI that issues both signature types or two parallel PKIs (NCSC prefers a single migration to a fully post-quantum PKI; the NSA tells national security systems to use a parallel PKI, not several algorithms in one certificate); no universally accepted hybrid certificate format (GSMA PQ.03 finds recommending hybrid certificates premature); composite ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 signatures of about 3.4 KB; no FIPS 140-3 IG section on composite signatures
- **Risks common to both**: added complexity and attack surface (NSA: more products fail through implementation or configuration errors than through algorithms; Dutch PQC Migration Handbook: hybridisation may increase attack surface); every party must support all components and the same combination method; removing the classical part later is a second transition; for some formal properties hybrids may be no stronger, or even weaker, than their components (NSA: a matter of significant debate); something marketed as hybrid is not necessarily quantum resistant; overhead of two algorithms, judged low when hybrid only sets up a session key (Dutch handbook)
- **Who recommends hybrid**: ANSSI (France) insists on hybrid wherever PQC is deployed in the short and medium term, mandatory in the French regulated perimeter, except hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS); its recommendations are not a regulatory obligation elsewhere. BSI (Germany) TR-02102-1 currently recommends quantum-safe methods only in hybrid use (signatures only together with a classical signature), except hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS), which it says can in principle also be used alone if implementation security is carefully considered; classical-only key agreement is recommended until the end of 2031. The Dutch AIVD/CWI/TNO handbook recommends hybrid especially when deploying before mature implementations exist. The EU ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2.0 recommends hybrid mode for long-term confidentiality (the v3 draft adds that lattice mechanisms should not be used standalone); ENISA's 2026 hybridization report is explicitly not a recommendation
- **Who accepts pure PQC**: the NSA will not require hybrid for national security systems and counts only NSA-identified hybrids (such as its IKEv2 profile) as CNSA 2.0 compliant; the UK NCSC uses hybrid only where needed (interoperability, implementation security, protocol constraints); the Czech NÚKIB accepts hybrid or standalone ML-KEM and ML-DSA at security level 5; NIST approves ML-KEM and ML-DSA on their own and says combining can be advantageous during migration (SP 800-227); Canada's Cyber Centre (ITSP.40.111 version 5) recommends ML-KEM and ML-DSA and phases out classical schemes used without a post-quantum scheme by the end of 2035, without discussing hybrid
- **Standards bodies and industry**: ETSI specifies hybrid key exchange (TS 103 744) and describes trade-offs (TR 103 966) without mandating it; the IETF standardizes both hybrid TLS groups (RFC 10024) and pure ML-KEM groups (draft) and does not choose for deployers; Google Chrome, Cloudflare and AWS deploy X25519MLKEM768; Cloudflare targets 2029 for full post-quantum security including authentication
- **NIST SP 800-227** describes how to combine key-establishment mechanisms securely (§4.6): a suitably designed classical/PQC combination can retain security if one component remains secure. §3.3 recommends appropriate side-channel protections such as constant-time implementations; migration to pure PQC is driven by algorithm maturation rather than calendar deadlines alone
- **SP 800-227 approved KEM parameter sets**: ML-KEM-512 → NIST Category 1 (AES-128 equivalent, constrained/IoT, short-lived sessions); ML-KEM-768 → Category 3 (AES-192 equivalent, default for TLS 1.3 and most internet traffic); ML-KEM-1024 → Category 5 (AES-256 equivalent, CNSA 2.0 and high-assurance/federal systems). This module's advice: HNDL risk and data-retention window should drive the choice, and ciphertext that must stay secret past ~2035 should use Category 3 or 5 rather than Category 1
- **Hybrid KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validated module (CMVP IG D.S, last modified 9 April 2026)**: IG D.S "Scenario 2" is a hybrid of an approved ML-KEM plus one or more non-ML-KEM schemes combined through an approved key combiner (SP 800-227 §4.6.2); the non-ML-KEM may be approved or non-approved (examples: X25519, X448). To claim Scenario 2, a module must implement at a minimum all five of: (1) an approved ML-KEM; (2) one or more non-ML-KEM (approved or non-approved); (3) an approved key combiner (a concatenation of the shared secrets fed into an SP 800-56C one-step or two-step KDF, HKDF included, or an SP 800-133 §6.3 method: concatenation, XOR, or key extraction using HMAC; the IG describes the §6.3 route only for combining ML-KEM shared secrets with those of approved key-agreement schemes, IG D.F Scenario 1 or 2); (4) the module does not offer arbitrary hybrid combinations but enforces a pre-defined set of hybrid schemes (e.g., SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024); (5) for each set, the module controls at minimum the shared-secret sequencing logic (e.g., concatenation order). If any is missing (e.g., a library with an approved ML-KEM and X25519 but no approved key combiner, or one with the first three items that does not enforce a set of combinations or control sequencing), Scenario 2 cannot be claimed and any non-approved non-ML-KEM scheme offered must be restricted to the non-approved mode only. A non-approved component such as X25519 is classified as a "non-approved but allowed algorithm with no security claimed" (IG 2.4.A; listed in the Security Policy, not on the certificate); it may be used only inside the approved hybrid, enforced by the module itself (not used for other purposes in approved mode, not offered as an independent approved service such as a separate API call in a software library; operator guidance in the Security Policy cannot enforce it). The claimed security strength of the hybrid comes from the ML-KEM, and the hybrid service is then an approved security service. The Security Policy records the claim in the Security Function Implementation table as "KEM-Hybrid" or "KEM-Hybrid-Full" (entry names such as "KEM-Hybrid X25519MLKEM768"); the non-approved half is listed with the caveat "no security claimed" citing IG D.S Scenario 2 and IG 2.4.A (CMVP KEM Hybrid guidance, last updated 8 April 2026). "KEM-Hybrid" applies when a module meets items 1 to 5 but not the extra conditions for "KEM-Hybrid-Full", and it can still be an approved service, even for a software library offering it to a calling application. IG D.S Additional Comment 8: the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange (draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem-01, now RFC 10024) may meet Scenario 2 using the SP 800-56C HKDF as the approved combiner with one of SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (the specifications may still be in draft form); the X-Wing hybrid KEM "cannot yet meet the requirements of Scenario 2" even though it uses an SP 800-56C one-step KDF, because at a minimum SP 800-133 needs an update to approve the X-Wing seed generation method (seed expansion using SHAKE is not currently in SP 800-133). Separately, the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests; CAVP states that acquiring validations for each implemented algorithm does not by itself meet the FIPS 140 module requirements. Self-tests: every approved scheme in the hybrid must be self-tested individually under IG 10.3.A; for the ML-KEM part, under IG 10.3.A (known-answer self-tests for each ML-KEM function implemented: encapsulation, decapsulation, key generation; decapsulation tests cover both the implicit-rejection and non-rejection paths; on at least one of ML-KEM-512, -768 or -1024 as implemented in approved mode); IG D.S says there is currently no separate self-test for the approved key combiner or for the non-approved half, beyond self-testing any approved algorithms used within (e.g., KDFs). CAVP testing: the IG lets the approved pieces be tested separately (the ML-KEM and, with a non-approved other half, the approved algorithms beneath it such as KDFs), or end-to-end tests of the full hybrid scheme "if available within CAVP", with the IG to be updated after they become available; no hybrid-KEM specification appears in the ACVP specification index (pages.nist.gov/ACVP) as of 23 October 2026. Do not confuse with IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules" (new 19 August 2026), which concerns a module whose boundary combines a software or firmware component with a disjoint hardware component and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange
- **Hybrid combiner construction (SP 800-227 + SP 800-56C-Rev2)**: concatenation order is fixed per protocol (TLS 1.3 per RFC 10024 §4.3: X25519MLKEM768 uses `ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss`, while SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 use `ECDHE_ss || ML-KEM_ss`; per its §5, SP 800-56C-Rev2 approves this when the first secret comes from a FIPS-approved scheme, so ML-KEM goes first where X25519 is used, and ECDHE goes first for the NIST curves, whose certified implementations are more widely available; SP 800-227 §4.6.2, September 2025, approves its key combiner when at least one shared secret in any position comes from an approved scheme); SP 800-56C permits either HKDF (HMAC-based extractor with SHA-256/384/512) or KMAC128/256 as the combiner; dual-PRF assumption means the combined secret is safe as long as _either_ input looks uniform to the attacker, so a future break of ML-KEM or of X25519 alone does not break the session key; SP 800-227 §4.6.3 says the domain-separation input should be used to uniquely identify the composite scheme in use (for example the two component schemes, order of composition, choice of parameter set, key combiner, KDF)
- **Combiners compared**: TLS 1.3 hybrid groups (RFC 10024) feed the concatenated secrets into the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule and rely on the handshake transcript to bind the key shares; X-Wing (draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-11) computes SHA3-256(ss_M || ss_X || ct_X || pk_X || XWingLabel), hashing the X25519 ciphertext and public key but not the ML-KEM ones; composite ML-KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23) uses the same shape, SHA3-256(mlkemSS || tradSS || tradCT || tradPK || Label), for twelve pairings, and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry uses the X-Wing label (hex 5c2e2f2f5e5c); the CFRG concrete hybrid KEMs (draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems-04) use SHAKE256 as PRG and SHA3-256 as KDF and state that MLKEM768-X25519 is identical to X-Wing; ETSI CatKDF (TS 103 744) forms psk || k1 || k2 and runs one KDF (HMAC, KMAC or HKDF) with a context holding all public keys and ciphertexts of both components, which the composite draft calls the more conservative choice, while CasKDF chains one KDF stage per component
- **What makes X-Wing different**: it leaves out the ML-KEM ciphertext and public key, relying on the specifics of ML-KEM-768's Fujisaki-Okamoto transform; the draft warns the combiner "cannot be assumed to be secure, when used with different KEMs"; if SHA3-256, SHA3-512 and SHAKE-256 are modelled as random oracles its IND-CCA security is bounded by ML-KEM-768's and the gap-CDH security of Curve25519; it claims MAL-BIND-K-PK and MAL-BIND-K-CT, which ML-KEM alone does not achieve; its private key is a 32-byte seed expanded with SHAKE256 into both component keys (public key 1,216 bytes, ciphertext 1,120 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes), the reason FIPS 140-3 IG D.S says it cannot yet meet Scenario 2; the composite ML-KEM draft calls X-Wing and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry "largely interchangeable", the one difference being X-Wing's joint seed keygen, so an X-Wing implementation is a compliant composite implementation but not the reverse
- **ML-KEM decapsulation and implicit rejection (FIPS 203 §§6.3 and 7.3)**: input checks can fail; for example, ML-KEM-768 requires a 1,088-byte ciphertext. After the required checks pass, an internal re-encryption mismatch selects a fallback shared secret derived from the secret rejection value `z` and the received ciphertext, without exposing the mismatch through an error or timing. Normal library argument and operational errors still apply. If tampering triggers this path, the receiver obtains a different secret; in a protocol deriving an AES-GCM key from it, authentication fails and unauthenticated plaintext must not be released. Implicit rejection conceals the internal ciphertext-validity result; a later authentication failure can also occur after valid decapsulation and does not directly disclose that result. Protocol error handling and timing must preserve this distinction. Successful decapsulation alone does not confirm a shared key: use protocol authentication or key confirmation.
- **Implementation considerations**: correct results alone do not show that an implementation protects its secrets; constant-time techniques help prevent execution time or memory access from revealing secret values, but do not mean every call takes the same number of milliseconds (SP 800-227 §3.3 recommends appropriate protections; effectiveness depends on the implementation and device). ML-KEM encapsulation requires fresh, unpredictable random input: an attacker who knows the 32-byte `m` can reproduce the encapsulation with the recipient's public key and recover the shared secret (FIPS 203 §3.3). In an X25519 + ML-KEM hybrid, a leak of only the X25519 secret can still be covered by a suitable combiner through the uncompromised ML-KEM secret; a leak of both secrets or the final session key loses that protection. For HSM/TPM devices, check the manufacturer's documentation for which protections exist and which settings affect them — do not assume a PQC-protection switch exists
- **CNSA 2.0** (NSA): its FAQ (v2.2, October 2026) quotes CNSSP 15 as requiring CNSA 2.0 algorithms in all new NSS acquisitions by 1 January 2027, says that by 31 December 2030 NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception, and that by 31 December 2031 CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted; it also says specific deadlines depend on equipment type; NSA will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes, although product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions in specific cases
- **RFC 9794** standardizes terminology for hybrid schemes — "composite" (single OID, both-must-verify) vs "non-composite" (parallel independent algorithms); establishes "PQ/T" (Post-Quantum / Traditional) naming
- **Subject key vs. certificate signature**: the subject public-key algorithm and the certificate-signature algorithm are independent. An ML-KEM key cannot sign, so an ML-KEM certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA). The ML-KEM subject key performs encapsulation/decapsulation; the issuer key signs the certificate
- **Seven certificate formats in the main comparison** (five signature formats + two KEM formats):
  - **Pure PQC (ML-DSA)** — standard single-algorithm X.509 using ML-DSA signatures; OIDs standardized in RFC 9881; the workshop is tested with OpenSSL 3.6.3
  - **Pure PQC (SLH-DSA)** — hash-based signature X.509 certificates; OIDs in RFC 9909; ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for hash-based signatures such as SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS
  - **Composite (dual-algorithm)** — single composite OID identifies the algorithm pair; both signatures must verify; defined in RFC 10073 (November 2026)
  - **Alt-Sig / Catalyst** — classical primary cert with PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions (SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo 2.5.29.72, AltSignatureAlgorithm 2.5.29.73, AltSignatureValue 2.5.29.74); legacy verifiers ignore the extensions; defined in ITU-T X.509 (2019) §7.2.2 and §9.8; relying-party policy decides whether one or both signatures are required
  - **Related Certificates (RFC 9763)** — a NEW certificate (Cert B) carries a RelatedCertificate extension holding the hash of the complete final DER of an EXISTING certificate (Cert A); the binding is one-way and Cert A is never modified; the CA issues Cert B only after a relatedCertRequest proves possession of Cert A's key; a protocol may use either certificate or both — RFC 9763 does not require both
  - **Pure PQC KEM (ML-KEM, RFC 9935)** — an ML-KEM public key in X.509; if keyUsage is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit; the certificate is CA-issued, never self-signed; the key is used e.g. in CMS KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629, ML-KEM in CMS: RFC 9936)
  - **Composite KEM** — ML-KEM plus a classical KEM under one OID, ML-KEM first; defined in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23, approved by the IESG and in the RFC Editor queue since 2026-10-12 (not yet an RFC)
- **Advanced examples (outside the main comparison)**: Certificate Discovery (draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-06, active LAMPS WG draft) lets a primary certificate advertise in subjectInfoAccess where a related secondary certificate can be fetched, which algorithms it uses and, optionally, its hash (certHash); after fetching, those fields must match the retrieved certificate, and it must still pass full path validation; -06 removed the earlier 'intent' field and gives no way to say why two certificates are related; the draft's OIDs are TBD, so the workshop uses documentation-arc placeholders (1.3.6.1.4.1.32473) and its encoding is illustrative. RFC 9925 unsigned certificates use id-alg-unsigned (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.36), a zero-length signature and a placeholder issuer (id-rdna-unsigned); they suit keys trusted by other means and are never valid in a certification path
- **Historical design — Chameleon Certificates**: a single cert with a DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension encoding the differences needed to rebuild a paired cert; draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07 is an expired individual draft never adopted by the LAMPS working group; kept for study only and not recommended for new deployments
- **Watchlist**: FN-DSA (planned FIPS 206, not yet final) has an IETF certificate draft, draft-ietf-lamps-fn-dsa-certificates, whose OIDs are still TBD — no deployable FN-DSA certificate exists yet
- **X25519MLKEM768** — the leading hybrid KEM combining Curve25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768; enabled by default in Chrome 131 (November 2024), protecting most human traffic to Cloudflare by October 2025, and supported on AWS KMS, ACM and Secrets Manager endpoints (launched on non-FIPS endpoints in April 2025; AWS's PQ readiness page now lists FIPS and non-FIPS endpoints for AWS KMS in commercial and US GovCloud Regions, while its Infrastructure security in AWS KMS page says AWS KMS supports hybrid post-quantum TLS in all Regions except the China Regions and does not support it on AWS GovCloud (US) FIPS endpoints); its shares and shared secret put the ML-KEM part first (ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss, RFC 10024 §4.3), unlike SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, which put ECDHE first
- **Other hybrid KEM variants**: SecP256r1MLKEM768 (P-256 + ML-KEM-768, FIPS-approved classical curve), SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (P-384 + ML-KEM-1024, NIST Level 5)
- **Composite signatures** combine ML-DSA with ECDSA or Ed25519 in a single operation; both must verify; single OID simplifies handling; prevents downgrade attacks
- **Size trade-offs**: composite signatures are approximately 3.4 KB versus 72 bytes for ECDSA alone
- **Hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3**: X25519MLKEM768 integrates via the key_share extension; ClientHello key_share grows from 32 bytes (X25519) to 1,216 bytes (38× increase); may push ClientHello beyond a single TCP packet; Chrome reported about a 4% slowdown in TLS handshake time (as cited by Cloudflare, October 2025), and AWS measured a 0.05% (connection reuse) to 2.3% (new handshake per request) throughput drop for KMS (April 2025)
- **Hybrid TLS negotiation downgrade risk**: TLS 1.3's signed and MACed transcript detects an active MITM that removes the ML-KEM key_share from the ClientHello, but an attacker can make PQC attempts fail so that a client configured for compatibility fallback retries classical-only — even when both endpoints support hybrid; client-side memory of prior PQC support (PQ Lock, and the individual draft `draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity`) limits this after a first successful PQC connection, covered in depth in the TLS 1.3 Basics module; composite signatures (single composite OID) prevent the analogous downgrade of authentication because both signature halves must verify together

- **Hybrid in crypto APIs and HSMs (application-composed vs one algorithm)**: an application either composes a hybrid itself (a classical API call plus a pure-PQC API call, combined by its own code) or uses one algorithm the library or token offers (a TLS named group, X-Wing, composite ML-KEM, composite ML-DSA). Most libraries offer hybrid key exchange only inside TLS, so hybrids outside TLS are usually application-composed: in Java an X25519 KeyAgreement, an ML-KEM KEM and the KDF API's HKDF (JEP 527 adds hybrid only for TLS 1.3; Bouncy Castle: "the order is part of the protocol and must be fixed by both parties in advance"); on a PKCS#11 v3.2 HSM CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE, CKM_ML_KEM through C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey, then either reading both secrets out or chaining CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_KEY, CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_DATA and CKM_SHA3_256_KEY_DERIVATION in the token; signatures as two separate signatures with an application policy requiring both
- **Limits of application-composed hybrid, especially with an HSM**: the application owns the combiner and can get it wrong (a concatenation-only key is not secure against active adversaries, ETSI TR 103 966; Microsoft says native composites reduce "the risk of incorrect integrations"); in PKCS#11 v3.2 C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey create secret keys whose CKA_EXTRACTABLE defaults to true unless the template says otherwise, with CKA_ALWAYS_SENSITIVE and CKA_NEVER_EXTRACTABLE set to false, so combining in application memory exposes both secrets; an in-token chain is driven step by step by the application and the token checks none of the order, label or hash; FIPS 140-3 IG D.S approves a hybrid KEM only when the module itself enforces the scheme set and order; C_SignInit takes one key, so a composed hybrid signature is two keys nothing ties together, verified by the application's own policy
- **HPKE standards status (November 2026)**: The successor of RFC 9180, draft-ietf-hpke-hpke-06, removes the Auth and AuthPSK modes. The IETF Datatracker lists it in the RFC Editor queue (state on 8 November 2026). The draft is dated 29 October 2026. It adds a framework for single-stage KDFs, requires that applications not derive an AEAD key and nonce from an exported secret without fresh per-derivation input, and requires implementations to support info values of at least 64 bytes (recommending at least 16,384). It does not specify Auth and AuthPSK but reserves mode values 0x02 and 0x03 and does not deprecate them, so RFC 9180 deployments can keep using them. draft-ietf-hpke-pq (-05, 6 July 2026) is a working-group draft registering ML-KEM, the PQ/T hybrid KEMs and the SHAKE and TurboSHAKE KDFs. Users of HPKE: draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt-22 (RFC Editor queue), draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt-02 (working-group draft), draft-ietf-cose-hpke-27 (IESG, waiting for AD go-ahead), draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-07 (publication requested)
- **PKCS#11 v3.3 working draft**: key types CKK_COMP_KEM and CKK_COMP_SIG and mechanisms CKM_COMP_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_COMP_KEM (through C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey, secret returned as a key handle), CKM_COMP_SIG_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_COMP_SIG and CKM_COMP_SIG_EXTERNAL_HASH; identifiers approved by the OASIS PKCS 11 TC in October 2026, no v3.3 specification published; X-Wing or HPKE mechanisms still under discussion; runnable in the PKCS#11 workshop's v3.3 tab
- **Support across libraries (1 November 2026)**: hybrid TLS 1.3 groups are default in OpenSSL 3.5+ (X25519MLKEM768; 4.x also SecP256r1MLKEM768), Java JDK 27 and 25.0.5 (X25519MLKEM768), Go 1.24+ (all three since 1.26), AWS-LC, BoringSSL, rustls (aws-lc-rs provider), NSS/Firefox (since Firefox 132), wolfSSL and Bouncy Castle BCJSSE; Windows SChannel supports all three but not by default. Hybrid KEM as one algorithm: Windows CNG Composite-ML-KEM (July 2026), .NET 11 CompositeMLKem (experimental), SymCrypt, Bouncy Castle (composite ML-KEM experimental, X-Wing in the lightweight API), BoringSSL (X-Wing), Go crypto/hpke (X-Wing and P-256/P-384 hybrids), PKCS#11 v3.3 draft. Composite signature as one algorithm: Windows CNG Composite-ML-DSA (four ECDSA sets), .NET CompositeMLDsa (experimental), SymCrypt, Bouncy Castle (18 combinations), PKCS#11 v3.3 draft. Not offered by OpenSSL, AWS-LC, NSS, rustls, wolfSSL, the JDK or liboqs/oqs-provider

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 7 hands-on steps:

1. **Hybrid Key Generation** — generate and compare classical, pure PQC, and hybrid key pairs, observing key size differences across categories. Its Known Answer area has a NIST ACVP panel for ML-KEM-768 (encapsulation with NIST's random value m, valid and modified-ciphertext decapsulation, and the FIPS 203 encapsulation-key and decapsulation-key checks, each answer compared with NIST's) and a table of further checks. Rows tagged "Functional" are round trips (the engine accepts its own output) with no published expected value; rows tagged "NIST ACVP sample" or "Standard KAT" compare with a published answer. None of it establishes a validation.
2. **Hybrid Encryption and Signing Demo** — after the key-establishment run, a comparison panel feeds the same two secrets through the demo's HKDF, the X-Wing / composite ML-KEM SHA3-256 combiner and a concatenation-only counter-example (which ETSI TR 103 966 says is not secure against active adversaries), and notes that the demo reads both secrets out of the token to show them, whereas a token can combine them with handles only (CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_KEY, CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_DATA, CKM_SHA3_256_KEY_DERIVATION). perform KEM encapsulation and digital signature operations in hybrid mode, comparing classical and PQC outputs. The key-establishment demo concatenates the two shared secrets, ML-KEM first (the RFC 10024 §4.3 order for X25519MLKEM768), and feeds the 64 bytes into HKDF-SHA-256 with no salt: the combiner form CMVP IG D.S accepts (a concatenation fed into an SP 800-56C KDF, HKDF included). Putting one secret in the HKDF salt and the other in the input is not that form. The demo binds no key shares or transcript and enforces no fixed set of hybrid schemes, so it is an illustration, not a validated design.
3. **HPKE** — RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption composed from PKCS#11 v3.2 primitives, shown beside the PKCS#11 v3.3 draft composite KEM (CKM_COMP_KEM, three hybrid suites) and a PQCToday single-call proposal that is part of no standard: pick a KEM (classical DHKEM, ML-KEM or a PQ/T hybrid), KDF, AEAD and mode, and run Encap, KeySchedule, Seal and Open (the Auth and AuthPSK modes are labelled "RFC 9180 only" because the successor draft does not specify them)
4. **Hybrid Signatures** — concatenation, nesting and a local shared-binding model (inspired by Silithium, not the published scheme and not a proof) side by side, comparing executed component checks
5. **Hybrid CA Setup** — set up a hybrid certificate authority with both classical and PQC keys
6. **Hybrid Certificate Formats** — generate and compare seven X.509 formats: Pure PQC (ML-DSA-65), Pure PQC (SLH-DSA-128s), Composite (ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA), Alt-Sig/Catalyst (ECDSA primary + ML-DSA extensions), Related Certs (RFC 9763), Pure ML-KEM-768 (RFC 9935) and Composite ML-KEM; Chameleon is available separately under Historical designs. End-entity certificates for ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and both KEM formats are issued by a workshop CA in the browser HSM, and every result is checked (signatures, issuer chain, key usage) by an implementation other than the one that signed it
7. **Certificate Inspector** — deep-dive into generated certificates with Tree, Raw, and Size views; also inspect real IETF Hackathon reference certificates from the pqc-certificates test vector repository

## IETF Reference Certificates

The Certificate Inspector (Step 7) includes a toggle to view real DER-encoded hybrid certificates from trusted sources. Five test vectors are embedded:

- **Composite (MLDSA65-ECDSA-P256-SHA512)** — OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.45, generated by Bouncy Castle (IETF Hackathon r5); demonstrates composite OID backward incompatibility (OpenSSL shows "UNKNOWN")
- **Alt-Sig / Catalyst (ECDSA-P256 + ML-DSA-44 alt-sig)** — generated by Bouncy Castle (IETF Hackathon r5); uses alt-sig extensions 2.5.29.72 (SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo), 2.5.29.73 (AltSignatureAlgorithm), 2.5.29.74 (AltSignatureValue); classical primary with PQC in extensions
- **Pure ML-DSA-65** — OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.18, generated by OpenSSL 3.5 (IETF Hackathon r5); reference for FIPS 204 cert format
- **Pure SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s** — OID 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.20, from RFC 9909 Appendix C.3; hash-based signature cert (8,241 bytes); ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for it (ANSSI PQC FAQ 2025)
- **Chameleon (ECDSA-P256 outer + ML-DSA-44 delta)** — historical design (expired draft); generated by Bouncy Castle (IETF Hackathon r5); uses DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension 2.16.840.1.114027.80.6.1

Note: No official test vector exists for Related Certificates (RFC 9763) — the format is purely structural (a binding hash in an extension), not a cryptographic algorithm, so no KAT is applicable. The workshop generates RFC 9763 pairs programmatically.

LM-006.topic:
**Scope.** Hybrid cryptography combines classical and PQC algorithms for defense-in-depth during the quantum transition: if either component is broken, security holds. Covers why hybrid approaches are mandated (or recommended) by ANSSI and NIST SP 800-227, eight X.509 certificate format approaches — six carrying signatures (pure PQC ML-DSA per RFC 9881, pure PQC SLH-DSA per RFC 9909, composite dual-algorithm under a single OID, alt-sig/catalyst per ITU-T X.509 (2019) §9.8, related certificates per RFC 9763, and chameleon certificates from an expired individual draft) plus two carrying KEM keys (pure PQC ML-KEM per RFC 9935 and composite KEM), and hybrid KEM construction (X25519MLKEM768). Details the fundamental dilemma that PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical ones, yet HNDL threats make waiting dangerous. Covers NIST SP 800-227 §4 implementation requirements: implicit rejection, constant-time decapsulation, DRBG quality, side-channel resistance, and domain-separated hybrid combiners. Out of scope: Pure PQC architectures, standalone hash-based signature deployment without hybrid partners, and algorithm replacements for non-KEM key agreement.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Hybrid cryptography, composite signatures, dual-algorithm certificates, X25519MLKEM768, RFC 9794 hybrid terminology, hybrid KEM combiner, ANSSI hybrid mandate, NIST SP 800-227, HKDF HMAC-based extractor, KMAC conditional, domain separation, implicit rejection, constant-time decapsulation, DRBG quality, side-channel resistance, certificate chain size, backward compatibility, related certificates RFC 9763, chameleon certificates, alt-sig catalyst, SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo extension.

Why Hybrid Certificates? Migration Without Breaking Relying Parties
Two quantum risks reach certificates differently. "Harvest now, decrypt later" is a confidentiality risk: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer can break the classical key exchange, so key establishment must move to PQC first. Signatures are different: a future quantum computer could forge new RSA/ECDSA signatures, but it cannot reach back and undo authentication that already happened. Certificates need PQC signatures before that computer exists, and relying parties upgrade at different speeds.

LM-006/s:composite.full:
standardizes terminology for hybrid schemes — distinguishing “composite” (single OID, both-must-verify) from “non-composite” (parallel independent algorithms) and establishing naming conventions such as “PQ/T” (Post-Quantum / Traditional).
IG D.S covers key encapsulation only. The IG (last updated 19 August 2026) has no section on composite or hybrid signatures. It does name one hybrid key-establishment scheme that uses ML-KEM (IG D.S, “Hybrid scheme that uses an approved ML-KEM”); a hybrid module (IG 1.B) is a different thing, about how a module is built, not about combining algorithms. What the IG does say applies to each algorithm on its own: a module that implements ML-DSA signing or verification needs the self-tests of IG 10.3.A. Whether a composite signature can be offered as an approved service is not answered in the published guidance; ask the lab.
A single composite OID identifies the algorithm pair. Both signatures must verify. Under
Hybrid & composite signatures for software supply chain
If a verifier accepts the hybrid when either component is valid, an attacker can remove the post-quantum signature and present the classical one. ETSI notes that such a backwards-compatible hybrid can be less secure than the post-quantum algorithm used alone. Requiring both signatures, or a non-separable construction (RFC 9955), closes this. The same applies one level up: a TLS server that keeps classical certificates for legacy clients can face a rollback in which an attacker strips the PQC or composite certificate; an individual draft proposes that clients remember the server’s PQC support.
No hybrid certificate format is universally accepted yet: composite certificates are not backward compatible, and GSMA PQ.03 considers it premature to recommend hybrid certificates. A composite ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 signature is about 3.4 KB, of which 64 bytes are the ECDSA part. The FIPS 140-3 IG has no section on composite signatures.
For some formal security properties, hybrids may be no stronger, or even weaker, than their components; the NSA calls this a matter of significant debate. A product marketed as hybrid or composite is not necessarily quantum resistant.
Standardizes both options: hybrid groups for TLS 1.3 (RFC 10024) and composite signatures in X.509 (RFC 10073), and pure ML-KEM groups for TLS 1.3 (still a draft). It does not choose between them for deployers.
Both classical and PQC keys/signatures under a single composite OID, each stored as a raw concatenation with the ML-DSA component first. Both must verify.
Composite certificates bind both algorithms under a single OID (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.45) and require both signatures to verify — if either fails, the certificate is rejected. Both the public key and the signature are RAW CONCATENATIONS with the ML-DSA component first (§4.1, §4.3); there is no ASN.1 wrapper, so a verifier splits at ML-DSA's fixed length. Both components sign a shared message representative M' = Prefix || Label || len(ctx) || ctx || PH(TBS), and ML-DSA takes the signature label as its FIPS 204 context — a stripped ML-DSA signature fails verification with an empty context, because it was signed with the composite Label as context; a stripped traditional signature still verifies over M', with the static Prefix remaining as evidence of the original composite (RFC 10073 §9.2.3). Legacy validators cannot process composite OIDs at all: composite is NOT backward compatible.
draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem defines composite KEM public keys binding ML-KEM-768 with a classical KEM (X25519, P-256, P-384, RSA-2048/3072/4096, brainpoolP256) under a single OID (encoded ML-KEM component first, then the classical component — §4.1). Encapsulation runs both KEMs and combines shared secrets via a KDF — both must succeed. Like composite signatures, the wire format is parsed only by composite-aware libraries: stock OpenSSL 3.6.3 registers no composite algorithms at all and fails to load a composite public key, so composite certificates are NOT backward compatible. KEM certs are encryption-only (RFC 9935 §4); signing requires a separate CA. This card shows the certificate encoding only — it does not run composite encapsulation.
The Internet-Draft "Preventing Key Reuse and Cross-Key Forgeries in Composite ML-DSA" says that reusing component keys or combining component signatures across keys can enable mix-and-match forgeries, and that binding both signatures to a hash of the exact composite public-key bytes prevents cross-key recombination.
RFC 9180 Hybrid Public Key Encryption: composed from PKCS#11 v3.2 pieces, shown beside the v3.3 draft composite KEM and a PQCToday single-call proposal.
Risks of hybrid signatures: stripping one signature when verifiers accept either component (ETSI TR 103 966: such a backwards-compatible hybrid can be less secure than the PQC algorithm alone; fix: require both, or a non-separable construction per RFC 9955); certificate rollback where a server keeps classical certificates (individual draft draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity proposes clients remember PQC support); more complex and less researched than hybrid confidentiality (UK NCSC); a PKI that issues both signature types or two parallel PKIs (NCSC prefers a single migration to a fully post-quantum PKI; the NSA tells national security systems to use a parallel PKI, not several algorithms in one certificate); no universally accepted hybrid certificate format (GSMA PQ.03 finds recommending hybrid certificates premature); composite ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 signatures of about 3.4 KB; no FIPS 140-3 IG section on composite signatures
RFC 9794 standardizes terminology for hybrid schemes — "composite" (single OID, both-must-verify) vs "non-composite" (parallel independent algorithms); establishes "PQ/T" (Post-Quantum / Traditional) naming
Composite signatures combine ML-DSA with ECDSA or Ed25519 in a single operation; both must verify; single OID simplifies handling; prevents downgrade attacks
Size trade-offs: composite signatures are approximately 3.4 KB versus 72 bytes for ECDSA alone
Hybrid TLS negotiation downgrade risk: TLS 1.3's signed and MACed transcript detects an active MITM that removes the ML-KEM key_share from the ClientHello, but an attacker can make PQC attempts fail so that a client configured for compatibility fallback retries classical-only — even when both endpoints support hybrid; client-side memory of prior PQC support (PQ Lock, and the individual draft `draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity`) limits this after a first successful PQC connection, covered in depth in the TLS 1.3 Basics module; composite signatures (single composite OID) prevent the analogous downgrade of authentication because both signature halves must verify together

LM-006/s:hybrid-risks.full:
Hybrid is a trade-off rather than a free upgrade. The next two sections set out what it risks compared with pure PQC, for key establishment and for signatures, and how national agencies, standards bodies and industry have decided. The rest of the lesson then builds from the primitives up: hybrid KEMs, hybrid signatures, and finally the certificates that carry them.

Both choices carry risk. Pure PQC relies on algorithms with a shorter record of cryptanalysis and on new implementations. Hybrid adds a second algorithm and the machinery to combine the two. Each item below names the document that states it.
Authorities weigh the same risks differently. France, Germany, the Netherlands and the EU certification group ask for hybrid during the transition; the NSA, the UK NCSC and the Czech NÚKIB accept post-quantum algorithms on their own. A recommendation applies only within its own scope, such as a national regulated perimeter or national security systems.
Pure PQC risks (what hybrid guards against): young schemes can fall to classical cryptanalysis (SIKE and Rainbow, per the Czech NÚKIB annex); in 2026 the BSI advised against Classic McEliece in new developments after new structural cryptanalysis and noted that a hybrid with Classic McEliece still keeps at least classical security; new implementations can carry exploitable bugs (Bernstein 2026: a small change in ML-DSA software is exploitable in 1 second on 1 laptop core, and far fewer Ed25519+ML-DSA keys than ML-DSA-only keys are estimated to be breakable for years after the first quantum attack)
Risks common to both: added complexity and attack surface (NSA: more products fail through implementation or configuration errors than through algorithms; Dutch PQC Migration Handbook: hybridisation may increase attack surface); every party must support all components and the same combination method; removing the classical part later is a second transition; for some formal properties hybrids may be no stronger, or even weaker, than their components (NSA: a matter of significant debate); something marketed as hybrid is not necessarily quantum resistant; overhead of two algorithms, judged low when hybrid only sets up a session key (Dutch handbook)

LM-006/s:kem.full:
, a KDF, and an AEAD — combined through a standard KeySchedule so any KEM/KDF/AEAD triple, plus one of four RFC 9180 modes (Base, PSK, Auth, AuthPSK), yields an interoperable construction. "Hybrid" in HPKE's own name refers to this KEM+KDF+AEAD composition, not to a PQC+classical pairing — that is a separate, additional meaning layered on top by draft-ietf-hpke-pq (below), and easy to conflate with the certificate-level hybrid formats covered earlier on this page.
Silithium adapts the Fiat-Shamir transform to produce a fused hybrid signature from EC-Schnorr (classical, secp256k1) and ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204). Both components share a single challenge μ derived from both public keys, the EC commitment R, and the message. Neither component verifies on its own with the standard challenge. The paper targets Strong Non-Separability (SNS) and reports no separability issues for its construction; this page demonstrates the idea and does not prove the property.
HPKE (RFC 9180) is a public-key encryption scheme built from three swappable components — a KEM, a KDF, and an AEAD — combined through a standard KeySchedule so any KEM/KDF/AEAD triple, plus one of four RFC 9180 modes (Base, PSK, Auth, AuthPSK), yields an interoperable construction. The successor of RFC 9180, draft-ietf-hpke-hpke-06, removes the Auth and AuthPSK modes. The IETF Datatracker lists it in the RFC Editor queue (state on 8 November 2026). The draft is dated 29 October 2026 and adds a framework for single-stage KDFs. It is not itself a hybrid-vs-classical choice: RFC 9180's own KEM registry is all-classical (DHKEM over P-256/P-384/P-521/X25519/X448). The PQC angle comes from draft-ietf-hpke-pq, which registers PQ and PQ/T hybrid KEM IDs (pure ML-KEM, and MLKEM768-X25519 / MLKEM768-P256 / MLKEM1024-P384 hybrids) that plug into the exact same KeySchedule and Seal/Open — still an Internet-Draft (working-group draft, revision -05 of 6 July 2026), not yet an RFC.
