LM-006/s:kem-implementation.full:
X-Wing pairs only ML-KEM-768 with X25519. Its private key is a 32-byte seed that SHAKE256 expands into both component keys; the public key is 1,216 bytes, the ciphertext 1,120 bytes and the shared secret 32 bytes. That seed expansion is why the FIPS 140-3 guidance says X-Wing cannot yet be an approved hybrid service (see Implementation & Validation).
The CFRG's concrete MLKEM768-X25519 is stated to be identical to X-Wing. The composite ML-KEM draft calls X-Wing and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry “largely interchangeable”: the one difference is that X-Wing generates both private keys from the same seed, while composite ML-KEM assumes independently generated components, for example separately validated ones. An X-Wing implementation counts as compliant composite ML-KEM, but not the other way round.
Implementation and Validation (SP 800-227, FIPS 140-3)
Consider X25519 and ML-KEM combined to derive a session key. If a leak exposes only the X25519 shared secret, a suitable combiner can still protect the session key through the uncompromised ML-KEM secret. If the leak exposes both secrets or the final session key, that protection is lost. Assess what information the implementation leaks, including during combination and key handling.

The IG calls an approved ML-KEM combined with one or more non-ML-KEM schemes “Scenario 2”. The non-ML-KEM part may be approved or non-approved (the IG's examples are X25519 and X448).
The module records the claim in the Security Function Implementation table as “KEM-Hybrid” or “KEM-Hybrid-Full”, with entry names such as “KEM-Hybrid X25519MLKEM768”. In short: SP 800-227 sets out certain requirements and recommendations for KEM implementation and use in FIPS 140-validated modules, and gives guidance to vendors that choose to combine keying material securely.

Every hybrid KEM merges two shared secrets, but designs differ in what else goes into the final key. Hashing the exchanged values (ciphertexts, public keys) ties the key to this exchange; TLS gets the same effect from its transcript.

A classical key exchange (for example X25519) and a post-quantum KEM (ML-KEM) run side by side, and a key combiner merges the two shared secrets. The session key stays secret as long as either component is unbroken, provided the combiner is a sound one (for example the TLS hybrid design or X-Wing).

Naïve constructions can be less secure than their components: a "concatenation only" hybrid session key is not secure against active adversaries, whatever the strength of each part. SP 800-227 approves specific key combiners (see Hybrid KEMs below).
Hybrid cryptography solves the dilemma of PQC being newer (less cryptanalysis) while the HNDL threat is real now. For key exchange, the shared secret stays secret as long as either component KEM is unbroken, provided the combiner is a sound one (for example the TLS hybrid design or X-Wing). For signatures, a forgery requires breaking both algorithms, provided the verifier requires both signatures to be valid.
Whether to use hybrid depends on whose rules apply to you and on what you protect. For key exchange in TLS, hybrid is already the common default on the web. For signatures and certificates the formats are newer and the advice is more divided.
A security product certified under FIPS 140-3 can offer a hybrid key exchange as an approved service even though one half, such as X25519, is not an approved algorithm. The NIST/CMVP guidance (IG D.S) sets five conditions: an approved ML-KEM, another key exchange (approved or not), an approved way to combine the two secrets, a fixed list of allowed hybrid pairs that the module enforces itself, and module control over the order in which the secrets are joined. The non-approved half is allowed but "no security claimed": the hybrid's claimed strength comes from ML-KEM. If any condition is missing, the hybrid cannot be an approved service. The guidance says the TLS hybrid groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) may qualify, while the X-Wing hybrid cannot yet, even though NIST's algorithm-testing page lists X-Wing tests. A separate rule, IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules", is about firmware plus hardware in one module and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange.
Major tech companies, including Google and Cloudflare, have already deployed hybrid TLS key exchange (X25519MLKEM768, standardized as RFC 10024, replacing the earlier X25519Kyber768Draft00) across Chrome and web infrastructure at scale; Chrome reported about a 4% slower TLS handshake. On the certificate side, Composite ML-DSA is now published as RFC 10073, while Composite ML-KEM (`draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23`) is in the RFC Editor queue.
RFC 9954 — Hybrid Key Exchange in TLS 1.3, 2026-07
The Hybrid Cryptography module teaches how to combine classical and post-quantum algorithms during the quantum transition, and what that choice costs. It runs in this order: why hybrid; the risks of hybrid compared with pure PQC, for key establishment and for signatures; which national agencies, standards bodies and companies recommend hybrid or accept pure PQC; hybrid KEM construction (X25519MLKEM768, combiners); hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3; implementation and validation (SP 800-227, FIPS 140-3 IG D.S); HPKE; hybrid signatures (non-separability, Silithium); and finally hybrid certificates (seven X.509 formats plus chameleon certificates as a historical design).
Risks of hybrid KEMs: an unsound combiner (ETSI TR 103 966: a "concatenation only" hybrid key is not secure against active adversaries; SP 800-227 approves specific combiners); fallback to classical-only when a client retries after a failed hybrid attempt (backwards-compatible hybrids can be open to downgrade, ETSI TR 103 966); larger messages (X25519MLKEM768 key share 1,216 bytes vs 32) and, in IKEv2, extra pre-authentication key exchanges raising denial-of-service risk; HPKE Auth modes cannot use ML-KEM or hybrids containing it; FIPS 140-3 approval only under the five IG D.S conditions (X-Wing cannot yet meet them)
Standards bodies and industry: ETSI specifies hybrid key exchange (TS 103 744) and describes trade-offs (TR 103 966) without mandating it; the IETF standardizes both hybrid TLS groups (RFC 10024) and pure ML-KEM groups (draft) and does not choose for deployers; Google Chrome, Cloudflare and AWS deploy X25519MLKEM768; Cloudflare targets 2029 for full post-quantum security including authentication
SP 800-227 approved KEM parameter sets: ML-KEM-512 → NIST Category 1 (AES-128 equivalent, constrained/IoT, short-lived sessions); ML-KEM-768 → Category 3 (AES-192 equivalent, default for TLS 1.3 and most internet traffic); ML-KEM-1024 → Category 5 (AES-256 equivalent, CNSA 2.0 and high-assurance/federal systems). This module's advice: HNDL risk and data-retention window should drive the choice, and ciphertext that must stay secret past ~2035 should use Category 3 or 5 rather than Category 1
Combiners compared: TLS 1.3 hybrid groups (RFC 10024) feed the concatenated secrets into the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule and rely on the handshake transcript to bind the key shares; X-Wing (draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-11) computes SHA3-256(ss_M || ss_X || ct_X || pk_X || XWingLabel), hashing the X25519 ciphertext and public key but not the ML-KEM ones; composite ML-KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23) uses the same shape, SHA3-256(mlkemSS || tradSS || tradCT || tradPK || Label), for twelve pairings, and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry uses the X-Wing label (hex 5c2e2f2f5e5c); the CFRG concrete hybrid KEMs (draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems-04) use SHAKE256 as PRG and SHA3-256 as KDF and state that MLKEM768-X25519 is identical to X-Wing; ETSI CatKDF (TS 103 744) forms psk || k1 || k2 and runs one KDF (HMAC, KMAC or HKDF) with a context holding all public keys and ciphertexts of both components, which the composite draft calls the more conservative choice, while CasKDF chains one KDF stage per component
X25519MLKEM768 — the leading hybrid KEM combining Curve25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768; enabled by default in Chrome 131 (November 2024), protecting most human traffic to Cloudflare by October 2025, and supported on AWS KMS, ACM and Secrets Manager endpoints (launched on non-FIPS endpoints in April 2025; AWS's PQ readiness page now lists FIPS and non-FIPS endpoints for AWS KMS in commercial and US GovCloud Regions, while its Infrastructure security in AWS KMS page says AWS KMS supports hybrid post-quantum TLS in all Regions except the China Regions and does not support it on AWS GovCloud (US) FIPS endpoints); its shares and shared secret put the ML-KEM part first (ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss, RFC 10024 §4.3), unlike SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, which put ECDHE first
Hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3: X25519MLKEM768 integrates via the key_share extension; ClientHello key_share grows from 32 bytes (X25519) to 1,216 bytes (38× increase); may push ClientHello beyond a single TCP packet; Chrome reported about a 4% slowdown in TLS handshake time (as cited by Cloudflare, October 2025), and AWS measured a 0.05% (connection reuse) to 2.3% (new handshake per request) throughput drop for KMS (April 2025)
Support across libraries (1 November 2026): hybrid TLS 1.3 groups are default in OpenSSL 3.5+ (X25519MLKEM768; 4.x also SecP256r1MLKEM768), Java JDK 27 and 25.0.5 (X25519MLKEM768), Go 1.24+ (all three since 1.26), AWS-LC, BoringSSL, rustls (aws-lc-rs provider), NSS/Firefox (since Firefox 132), wolfSSL and Bouncy Castle BCJSSE; Windows SChannel supports all three but not by default. Hybrid KEM as one algorithm: Windows CNG Composite-ML-KEM (July 2026), .NET 11 CompositeMLKem (experimental), SymCrypt, Bouncy Castle (composite ML-KEM experimental, X-Wing in the lightweight API), BoringSSL (X-Wing), Go crypto/hpke (X-Wing and P-256/P-384 hybrids), PKCS#11 v3.3 draft. Composite signature as one algorithm: Windows CNG Composite-ML-DSA (four ECDSA sets), .NET CompositeMLDsa (experimental), SymCrypt, Bouncy Castle (18 combinations), PKCS#11 v3.3 draft. Not offered by OpenSSL, AWS-LC, NSS, rustls, wolfSSL, the JDK or liboqs/oqs-provider

LM-006/s:protocol-design-principles.full:
This section introduces protocol design considerations for adapting cryptographic protocols for a quantum-capable threat landscape.
Protocol design also extends to protecting handshake authentication and preparing implementations for future algorithm transitions.

LM-006/s:who-recommends.full:
TR-02102-1 currently recommends quantum-safe methods only in hybrid use with classical methods. Classical-only key agreement is recommended until the end of 2031.
Recommends hybrid particularly for organisations that must deploy before mature implementations exist, for example when data is exposed to store-now-decrypt-later. Notes the overhead and the added attack surface.
ITSP.40.111 recommends ML-KEM and ML-DSA for general use, and says classical key establishment and signatures used without a post-quantum scheme should be phased out by the end of 2035. It does not discuss hybrid constructions.
Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2.0 recommends rolling out PQC in hybrid mode where confidentiality must hold for the long term, and agrees the CatKDF and CasKDF combiners. ENISA’s 2026 report on hybridization surveys standards and is explicitly not a recommendation.
ANSSI recommends hybrid mode for PQC deployments and makes it mandatory inside the French regulated perimeter (classified and Diffusion Restreinte data, vital information systems, certified or qualified products). Exception: for hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS) ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation (ANSSI PQC FAQ 2025).
Agencies disagree. France (ANSSI), Germany (BSI), the Netherlands and the EU certification group ask for hybrid during the transition. The US NSA, the UK NCSC and the Czech NÚKIB accept post-quantum algorithms on their own, and the NSA warns that hybrids add complexity that can introduce their own flaws. Canada's Cyber Centre recommends the new algorithms without saying either way.
Who recommends hybrid: ANSSI (France) insists on hybrid wherever PQC is deployed in the short and medium term, mandatory in the French regulated perimeter, except hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS); its recommendations are not a regulatory obligation elsewhere. BSI (Germany) TR-02102-1 currently recommends quantum-safe methods only in hybrid use (signatures only together with a classical signature), except hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS), which it says can in principle also be used alone if implementation security is carefully considered; classical-only key agreement is recommended until the end of 2031. The Dutch AIVD/CWI/TNO handbook recommends hybrid especially when deploying before mature implementations exist. The EU ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2.0 recommends hybrid mode for long-term confidentiality (the v3 draft adds that lattice mechanisms should not be used standalone); ENISA's 2026 hybridization report is explicitly not a recommendation
Who accepts pure PQC: the NSA will not require hybrid for national security systems and counts only NSA-identified hybrids (such as its IKEv2 profile) as CNSA 2.0 compliant; the UK NCSC uses hybrid only where needed (interoperability, implementation security, protocol constraints); the Czech NÚKIB accepts hybrid or standalone ML-KEM and ML-DSA at security level 5; NIST approves ML-KEM and ML-DSA on their own and says combining can be advantageous during migration (SP 800-227); Canada's Cyber Centre (ITSP.40.111 version 5) recommends ML-KEM and ML-DSA and phases out classical schemes used without a post-quantum scheme by the end of 2035, without discussing hybrid
Implementation considerations: correct results alone do not show that an implementation protects its secrets; constant-time techniques help prevent execution time or memory access from revealing secret values, but do not mean every call takes the same number of milliseconds (SP 800-227 §3.3 recommends appropriate protections; effectiveness depends on the implementation and device). ML-KEM encapsulation requires fresh, unpredictable random input: an attacker who knows the 32-byte `m` can reproduce the encapsulation with the recipient's public key and recover the shared secret (FIPS 203 §3.3). In an X25519 + ML-KEM hybrid, a leak of only the X25519 secret can still be covered by a suitable combiner through the uncompromised ML-KEM secret; a leak of both secrets or the final session key loses that protection. For HSM/TPM devices, check the manufacturer's documentation for which protections exist and which settings affect them — do not assume a PQC-protection switch exists

Index: 1
List: workshop_steps
Module: hybrid-crypto
defines ML-KEM public keys in X.509. An ML-KEM key cannot sign, so its certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA, …). If keyUsage is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit. Because the CA cannot check a self-signature from a KEM key, proof of possession uses a KEM-based exchange instead. The key is then used, for example, in CMS KEMRecipientInfo (
C_SignInit takes one key handle, so an application-composed hybrid signature is two C_Sign calls on two key objects. PKCS#11 v3.2 has no mechanism that binds the keys or requires both signatures; the verifier’s policy must insist on both, or one signature can be stripped. The two keys also need their own lifecycle, attributes and backup, kept in step by the application.
The PKCS#11 v3.3 working draft adds key types CKK_COMP_KEM and CKK_COMP_SIG and five mechanisms: CKM_COMP_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN and CKM_COMP_KEM (run through C_EncapsulateKey / C_DecapsulateKey, returning the combined secret as a key handle), and CKM_COMP_SIG_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_COMP_SIG and CKM_COMP_SIG_EXTERNAL_HASH (one C_Sign call for one composite signature from one key object holding both halves). The combiner then runs inside the token, as the composite ML-KEM and ML-DSA drafts define it. The OASIS PKCS 11 TC approved these identifiers in October 2026, together with identifiers for KMAC and the SHAKE functions; no v3.3 specification has been published. The draft has no HPKE mechanism, only an open request for one. For three combinations (MLKEM768-X25519, which is X-Wing, MLKEM768-P256 and MLKEM1024-P384) the composite KEM computes the same secret as the matching HPKE hybrid KEM, so it can do the key-agreement step of HPKE.
A CA-issued end-entity certificate whose subject key is ML-KEM-768. The ML-KEM key encapsulates and decapsulates; it cannot sign, so a separate ML-DSA-65 CA signs the certificate.
RFC 9935 (March 2026) defines X.509 algorithm identifiers for ML-KEM-512/768/1024. KEM certificates are encryption-only per §4 — they cannot self-sign. This workshop generates an ML-KEM-768 key and issues a CA-issued ML-KEM end-entity certificate from a separate ML-DSA-65 workshop CA: the subject key does encapsulation and decapsulation, and only the issuer key signs. A CA cannot check a self-signature from a KEM key, so the workshop CA injects the public key directly. KEM certs enable PQ-safe key encapsulation at the X.509 layer (CMS, S/MIME, IKE certificate-based modes).
Seven certificate formats make up the main comparison — five that carry signature keys and two that carry KEM (encryption) keys. Signature formats: Pure PQC (ML-DSA, RFC 9881), Pure PQC (SLH-DSA, RFC 9909), Composite (single OID, both-must-verify, RFC 10073), Alt-Sig (a PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions, ITU-T X.509 (2019)), and Related Certificates (RFC 9763: a new certificate carries a hash of an existing one). KEM formats: Pure PQC KEM (ML-KEM, RFC 9935) and Composite KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23, in the RFC Editor queue). The subject key and the certificate signature are independent: an ML-KEM key cannot sign, so a KEM certificate is always signed by a separate signing-capable CA. Only Alt-Sig and the classical certificate of a Related Certificates pair remain verifiable by a validator that does not understand PQC; composite is not backward compatible. Two Advanced examples sit outside the main comparison: Certificate Discovery (draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-06, an active draft whose OIDs are still TBD, so its encoding is illustrative) and the RFC 9925 unsigned certificate (no issuer signature, never valid in a certification path). Chameleon certificates (an expired individual draft, never adopted by the LAMPS working group) are shown separately as a historical design.
PKCS#11 v3.2 has no CKM_HPKE mechanism (checked against the canonical v3.2 header — no HPKE entry exists at all), and the v3.3 working draft has none either: the standards committee has only an open request for one. A real HSM deployment of HPKE composes it from mechanisms the spec does define: CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE / CKM_ML_KEM for the KEM leg, CKM_HKDF_DERIVE plus C_Sign(CKM_SHA*_HMAC) for LabeledExtract/LabeledExpand, and CKM_AES_GCM / CKM_CHACHA20_POLY1305 for Seal/Open. The Step 3 workshop below shows that composed way first, cross-checked byte-for-byte against RFC 9180 Appendix A, beside the PQCToday single-call proposal and the v3.3 draft's CKM_COMP_KEM path (hybrid suites only).
Subject key vs. certificate signature: the subject public-key algorithm and the certificate-signature algorithm are independent. An ML-KEM key cannot sign, so an ML-KEM certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA). The ML-KEM subject key performs encapsulation/decapsulation; the issuer key signs the certificate
Limits of application-composed hybrid, especially with an HSM: the application owns the combiner and can get it wrong (a concatenation-only key is not secure against active adversaries, ETSI TR 103 966; Microsoft says native composites reduce "the risk of incorrect integrations"); in PKCS#11 v3.2 C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey create secret keys whose CKA_EXTRACTABLE defaults to true unless the template says otherwise, with CKA_ALWAYS_SENSITIVE and CKA_NEVER_EXTRACTABLE set to false, so combining in application memory exposes both secrets; an in-token chain is driven step by step by the application and the token checks none of the order, label or hash; FIPS 140-3 IG D.S approves a hybrid KEM only when the module itself enforces the scheme set and order; C_SignInit takes one key, so a composed hybrid signature is two keys nothing ties together, verified by the application's own policy
ML-KEM private key: CKA_DECAPSULATE set, no CKA_SIGN
PKCS#11 v3.2 defines no CKM_HPKE mechanism (checked against the canonical v3.2 header — no HPKE entry exists). Encap is composed from CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE (classical) or CKM_ML_KEM + CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE (PQ-hybrid), then RFC 9180’s LabeledExtract/LabeledExpand built from CKM_HKDF_DERIVE and C_Sign(CKM_SHA*_HMAC).
PKCS#11 v3.2 has no CKM_HPKE mechanism, and the v3.3 draft has none either. This composes HPKE's KeySchedule, DHKEM/hybrid-KEM, and Seal/Open from CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE / CKM_ML_KEM / CKM_HKDF_DERIVE / C_Sign(HMAC) / CKM_AES_GCM / CKM_CHACHA20_POLY1305 primitives, byte-exact against

Module: hybrid-crypto
The IG says the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange (the IG cites an early version of the IETF draft that was later published as RFC 10024) may meet Scenario 2 with the SP 800-56C HKDF as the approved combiner, if one of SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 is used, and notes that these specifications may still be in draft form. It also says the X-Wing hybrid KEM “cannot yet meet the requirements of Scenario 2” even though it uses an SP 800-56C one-step KDF as its combiner: at a minimum, SP 800-133 needs an update to approve X-Wing's seed generation, because seed expansion using SHAKE to generate the key pairs is not currently in SP 800-133. Separately, the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests. Both statements are published; CAVP itself says that acquiring a validation for each implemented algorithm does not by itself meet the FIPS 140 module requirements.
Every approved scheme in the hybrid must be self-tested individually under IG 10.3.A. For the ML-KEM part that means known-answer self-tests for each ML-KEM function the module implements (encapsulation, decapsulation and key generation), with the decapsulation tests covering both the implicit-rejection and the non-rejection path, on at least one of ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 as implemented in approved mode. The IG currently has no separate self-test for the approved key combiner or for the non-approved half, beyond self-testing any approved algorithms used within, such as KDFs.
Compare classical, PQC, and hybrid key generation.
Hybrid KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validated module (CMVP IG D.S, last modified 9 April 2026): IG D.S "Scenario 2" is a hybrid of an approved ML-KEM plus one or more non-ML-KEM schemes combined through an approved key combiner (SP 800-227 §4.6.2); the non-ML-KEM may be approved or non-approved (examples: X25519, X448). To claim Scenario 2, a module must implement at a minimum all five of: (1) an approved ML-KEM; (2) one or more non-ML-KEM (approved or non-approved); (3) an approved key combiner (a concatenation of the shared secrets fed into an SP 800-56C one-step or two-step KDF, HKDF included, or an SP 800-133 §6.3 method: concatenation, XOR, or key extraction using HMAC; the IG describes the §6.3 route only for combining ML-KEM shared secrets with those of approved key-agreement schemes, IG D.F Scenario 1 or 2); (4) the module does not offer arbitrary hybrid combinations but enforces a pre-defined set of hybrid schemes (e.g., SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024); (5) for each set, the module controls at minimum the shared-secret sequencing logic (e.g., concatenation order). If any is missing (e.g., a library with an approved ML-KEM and X25519 but no approved key combiner, or one with the first three items that does not enforce a set of combinations or control sequencing), Scenario 2 cannot be claimed and any non-approved non-ML-KEM scheme offered must be restricted to the non-approved mode only. A non-approved component such as X25519 is classified as a "non-approved but allowed algorithm with no security claimed" (IG 2.4.A; listed in the Security Policy, not on the certificate); it may be used only inside the approved hybrid, enforced by the module itself (not used for other purposes in approved mode, not offered as an independent approved service such as a separate API call in a software library; operator guidance in the Security Policy cannot enforce it). The claimed security strength of the hybrid comes from the ML-KEM, and the hybrid service is then an approved security service. The Security Policy records the claim in the Security Function Implementation table as "KEM-Hybrid" or "KEM-Hybrid-Full" (entry names such as "KEM-Hybrid X25519MLKEM768"); the non-approved half is listed with the caveat "no security claimed" citing IG D.S Scenario 2 and IG 2.4.A (CMVP KEM Hybrid guidance, last updated 8 April 2026). "KEM-Hybrid" applies when a module meets items 1 to 5 but not the extra conditions for "KEM-Hybrid-Full", and it can still be an approved service, even for a software library offering it to a calling application. IG D.S Additional Comment 8: the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange (draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem-01, now RFC 10024) may meet Scenario 2 using the SP 800-56C HKDF as the approved combiner with one of SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (the specifications may still be in draft form); the X-Wing hybrid KEM "cannot yet meet the requirements of Scenario 2" even though it uses an SP 800-56C one-step KDF, because at a minimum SP 800-133 needs an update to approve the X-Wing seed generation method (seed expansion using SHAKE is not currently in SP 800-133). Separately, the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests; CAVP states that acquiring validations for each implemented algorithm does not by itself meet the FIPS 140 module requirements. Self-tests: every approved scheme in the hybrid must be self-tested individually under IG 10.3.A; for the ML-KEM part, under IG 10.3.A (known-answer self-tests for each ML-KEM function implemented: encapsulation, decapsulation, key generation; decapsulation tests cover both the implicit-rejection and non-rejection paths; on at least one of ML-KEM-512, -768 or -1024 as implemented in approved mode); IG D.S says there is currently no separate self-test for the approved key combiner or for the non-approved half, beyond self-testing any approved algorithms used within (e.g., KDFs). CAVP testing: the IG lets the approved pieces be tested separately (the ML-KEM and, with a non-approved other half, the approved algorithms beneath it such as KDFs), or end-to-end tests of the full hybrid scheme "if available within CAVP", with the IG to be updated after they become available; no hybrid-KEM specification appears in the ACVP specification index (pages.nist.gov/ACVP) as of 23 October 2026. Do not confuse with IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules" (new 19 August 2026), which concerns a module whose boundary combines a software or firmware component with a disjoint hardware component and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange

# Crypto Agility — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Crypto agility is the engineering capability to rapidly switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and provider implementations without rewriting the underlying application code. Larger keys and signatures, new encodings and new call patterns (a KEM is not an encryption function) still need review and testing.

## Why It Matters

Migrating to new algorithms requires locating every piece of cryptography in an enterprise via a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM). Without agility patterns—like relying on Provider Models, Service Meshes, or External HSMs—replacing these broken algorithms forces massive, expensive code rewrites.

## The Key Takeaway

The transition demands architectural patterns that decouple cryptographic choices from application logic. For example, a hybrid TLS client key share combines X25519 and ML-KEM-768 material and is 1,216 bytes, compared with 32 bytes for X25519 alone. Application code still needs to handle the larger share and related encoding changes.

## What's Happening

NIST's current crypto-agility white paper is CSWP 39-upd1. Google Chrome and Apple's iMessage have deployed hybrid post-quantum key agreement in phased rollouts.

The Crypto Agility module teaches how to design systems that can switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations with as little change as possible to the applications that use them. Callers can be insulated from the primitive, but credentials, encodings, key/signature/ciphertext sizes, negotiation, storage, rollback and tests still change with each algorithm. Crypto agility is the ability to switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations without rewriting the applications that call them. Three dimensions of agility: Algorithm agility — select algorithms in configuration rather than hard-coding them; moving from RSA encryption to ML-KEM still changes the call pattern (a KEM cannot encrypt data directly — NIST SP 800-227) and key and ciphertext sizes. Protocol agility — support multiple protocol versions simultaneously (TLS 1.2/1.3, hybrid key exchange). Implementation agility — switch between crypto providers (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC) without changing application call sites.

Think of Crypto-Agility like designing a high-tech building with universal plug sockets instead of wiring your electronics directly into the walls. When a television breaks, you just unplug it and plug a new one in. In software design, "Crypto-Agility" means building apps so that their security locks can be swapped out without rewriting the whole program. The new locks are bigger and work a little differently, so some parts around them still need checking and testing.
This strategy is absolutely crucial today. Because we know that the current mathematical locks defending our data will eventually be broken by quantum computers, companies have to find every single outdated lock in their massive networks. If those locks are hardcoded strictly into the apps, replacing them takes years of painstaking rewrites.
By adopting "Crypto-Agility", network engineers can seamlessly upgrade to the new, massive Post-Quantum locks overnight. This ensures businesses can protect their data against future threats immediately, without causing disruptive crashes or slowing down their services.

# Crypto Agility and Architecture Patterns

## Overview

The Crypto Agility module teaches how to design systems that can switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations with as little change as possible to the applications that use them. Callers can be insulated from the primitive, but credentials, encodings, key/signature/ciphertext sizes, negotiation, storage, rollback and tests still change with each algorithm. NIST's current crypto-agility white paper is CSWP 39-upd1 (Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility: Strategies and Practices); the previous CSWP 39 edition was withdrawn and superseded. The module covers three dimensions of agility (algorithm, protocol, and implementation), three architecture patterns (provider model, service mesh, and external KMS/HSM), the Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) concept for discovering all crypto assets in an organization, and a 7-phase PQC migration framework aligned with NIST IR 8547, CISA guidance, and NSA CNSA 2.0 timelines. It also presents real-world case studies from Cloudflare, Google Chrome, and Apple iMessage.

## Key Concepts

- **Crypto agility** is the ability to switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations without rewriting the applications that call them
- **Three dimensions of agility**:
  - **Algorithm agility** — select algorithms in configuration rather than hard-coding them; moving from RSA encryption to ML-KEM still changes the call pattern (a KEM cannot encrypt data directly — NIST SP 800-227) and key and ciphertext sizes
  - **Protocol agility** — support multiple protocol versions simultaneously (TLS 1.2/1.3, hybrid key exchange)
  - **Implementation agility** — switch between crypto providers (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC) without changing application call sites
- **Three architecture patterns**:
  - **Provider Model** — applications use abstraction APIs (JCA, OpenSSL Providers) and select backends in config, per application
  - **Service Mesh / Proxy** — crypto for data-in-transit (mTLS) offloaded to infrastructure proxies (Envoy, Istio); no crypto code changes for the application behind the proxy
  - **External KMS / HSM** — crypto operations outsourced to a central service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault); callers are insulated from the primitive, but each caller still adopts new key types, handles larger outputs and is tested — upgrading the service does not migrate the enterprise instantly
- **CBOM (Cryptographic Bill of Materials)** — uses the CycloneDX standard to inventory all cryptographic algorithms, key sizes, usage locations, security levels, and compliance requirements across an organization
- **CBOM generation tools**: IBM Quantum Safe Explorer, Keyfactor CBOM Generator, InfoSec Global AgileSec, Cryptosense Analyzer, manual audit and code scanning
- **7-Phase Migration Framework**: (1) Assessment and Inventory, (2) Risk Prioritization, (3) Preparation and Tooling, (4) Testing and Validation, (5) Hybrid Migration, (6) Production Deployment, (7) Monitoring
- **Industry case studies**: Chrome reports about a 4% slowdown in TLS handshake time from deploying post-quantum key agreement (Cloudflare, 2025); Google Chrome enabled hybrid PQC by default in Chrome 124, upgraded to standardized X25519MLKEM768 in Chrome 131; Apple iMessage adopted PQ3 protocol (P-256 ECDH + Kyber-1024 initial keys and a Kyber-768 rekeying ratchet — Kyber-1024 is ML-KEM-1024-level per FIPS 203) in iOS 17.4

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 4 interactive steps:

1. **Abstraction Layer Demo** — interactive demonstration of how algorithm-agnostic APIs keep call sites unchanged when the backend changes, and what still changes around them; select different crypto providers and see how the same API calls produce results from different algorithm implementations
2. **CBOM Scanner** — scan a sample enterprise architecture to discover and catalog all quantum-vulnerable cryptographic algorithms in use; produces a CycloneDX-format CBOM with risk assessments
3. **Migration Planning Exercise** — walk through the 7-phase PQC migration framework step by step, making decisions about prioritization, tooling selection, and deployment strategy
4. **Agility Readiness Assessment** — score your organization across four crypto agility dimensions (Algorithm Agility, Protocol Agility, Implementation Agility, Inventory & Visibility); each dimension has three yes/partial/no questions with actionable guidance; produces an overall maturity rating (Not Started → Foundational → Developing → Advanced) and highlights the weakest dimension as the recommended focus area

## Related Standards

- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards)
- NSA CNSA 2.0 (Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0)
- CISA Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative
- CycloneDX CBOM Specification
- NIST SP 800-227

**Scope.** This module teaches designing crypto-agile systems that can rapidly swap cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations without code or infrastructure rewrites. Covers three dimensions of agility (algorithm, protocol, implementation), three architecture patterns (provider model, service mesh, external KMS/HSM), the CBOM (Cryptographic Bill of Materials) concept for discovering all crypto assets, and NIST's recommended 7-phase migration framework (Assessment, Risk Prioritization, Preparation, Testing, Hybrid Migration, Production, Monitoring). Includes real-world case studies from Cloudflare (~4% TLS handshake time increase with hybrid), Google Chrome (X25519MLKEM768 default since Chrome 131), and Apple iMessage (P-256 + Kyber-1024 initial keys, now standardized as ML-KEM-1024/768 per FIPS 203). Out of scope: Protocol-specific implementation details, cryptanalysis of individual algorithms, and hardware-only crypto agility approaches.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Crypto agility, algorithm agility, protocol agility, implementation agility, provider model, service mesh, external KMS HSM, CBOM cryptographic bill of materials, CycloneDX, 7-phase migration framework, assessment inventory, risk prioritization, hybrid migration, production deployment, monitoring, abstraction layer, crypto-agile APIs, JCA OpenSSL providers, configuration-driven algorithm selection, performance overhead, latency budget.

LM-007/s:abstraction.full:
Applications link to a crypto library through an abstraction API (like JCA or OpenSSL Providers). The algorithm is selected in config, one application at a time.
Explore abstraction layers, scan a sample CBOM, and plan a PQC migration.
Three architecture patterns: - Provider Model — applications use abstraction APIs (JCA, OpenSSL Providers) and select backends in config, per application - Service Mesh / Proxy — crypto for data-in-transit (mTLS) offloaded to infrastructure proxies (Envoy, Istio); no crypto code changes for the application behind the proxy - External KMS / HSM — crypto operations outsourced to a central service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault); callers are insulated from the primitive, but each caller still adopts new key types, handles larger outputs and is tested — upgrading the service does not migrate the enterprise instantly

The Crypto Agility module teaches how to design systems that can switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations with as little change as possible to the applications that use them. Callers can be insulated from the primitive, but credentials, encodings, key/signature/ciphertext sizes, negotiation, storage, rollback and tests still change with each algorithm. NIST's current crypto-agility white paper is CSWP 39-upd1 (Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility: Strategies and Practices); the previous CSWP 39 edition was withdrawn and superseded. The module covers three dimensions of agility (algorithm, protocol, and implementation), three architecture patterns (provider model, service mesh, and external KMS/HSM), the Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) concept for discovering all crypto assets in an organization, and a 7-phase PQC migration framework aligned with NIST IR 8547, CISA guidance, and NSA CNSA 2.0 timelines. It also presents real-world case studies from Cloudflare, Google Chrome, and Apple iMessage.
7-Phase Migration Framework: (1) Assessment and Inventory, (2) Risk Prioritization, (3) Preparation and Tooling, (4) Testing and Validation, (5) Hybrid Migration, (6) Production Deployment, (7) Monitoring

The encrypt()/keyExchange() calls never change: the abstraction layer maps the same API to different algorithm implementations. What still changes around them is the algorithm identifier, key and ciphertext sizes (buffers, storage and message formats), key encodings, negotiation with peers, and the error path when a peer does not support the new algorithm.
Applications statically or dynamically link to a cryptography library (like OpenSSL or BouncyCastle) through an abstraction layer (like JCA). The design goal is that the algorithm is selected in configuration, so call sites do not change. It must still be done per application, and key and signature sizes, encodings, storage and tests still change with the algorithm.
Toggle between the RSA-2048, ML-KEM-768 and X25519MLKEM768 backends in the Abstraction Layer demo: the call sites never change while the backend config flips to quantum-safe, and the key-size line shows what still has to change around them.

This RSA-2048 configuration is vulnerable to quantum attack. To migrate, the algorithm choice changes in the configuration file — but check that buffers, storage and peers can handle the larger PQC keys and ciphertexts.
ML-KEM-768 provides NIST Level 3 quantum resistance. The keyExchange() call site stays the same because the abstraction layer maps it to KEM encapsulation. What the layer cannot hide: the 1,184-byte public key and 1,088-byte ciphertext must fit your buffers, storage and messages, and peers must support ML-KEM. Code that used RSA to encrypt data directly needs a new call pattern, because a KEM cannot encrypt data directly (NIST SP 800-227).
X25519MLKEM768 provides both classical and quantum security. If ML-KEM is broken, X25519 still protects. If X25519 is broken by a quantum computer, ML-KEM still protects.

Can you select cryptographic algorithms in configuration, and absorb the size, encoding and call-pattern changes that come with them?
Algorithm choices are externalized — stored in config files, environment variables, or a feature flag system rather than hardcoded in application source code.
Hardcoded imports like `import { rsaEncrypt }` score No. Config-driven provider selection scores Yes.
Your systems can run multiple algorithm variants simultaneously (e.g., RSA-2048 alongside ML-KEM-768) — useful for gradual rollout and rollback.
Check if your key management system supports heterogeneous algorithm families in the same namespace.
Key material storage and transmission buffers are not hard-capped to classical sizes (e.g., no VARCHAR(256) for public keys, no fixed 32-byte shared secret assumptions).
PQC public keys range from 32 bytes (SLH-DSA-128s/f) and 800 bytes (ML-KEM-512) up to 1,357,824 bytes (Classic McEliece-8192128) — over a megabyte, and 261,120 even at the smallest McEliece parameter set. Check DB schema, HSM slot config, and network MTU handling.
Can your services negotiate and serve multiple protocol versions at once?
TLS endpoints are configured to offer both classical and hybrid key-exchange groups (e.g., X25519MLKEM768 alongside X25519), letting clients negotiate based on capability. The symmetric cipher suite (e.g., TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384) is a separate setting.
Hybrid key exchange is negotiated through the supported_groups and key_share extensions, not the cipher suite list (in TLS 1.3 a cipher suite names only the AEAD algorithm and the HKDF hash). Inspect the groups your server and library list and prefer, which groups the peers offer in their ClientHello, and which group the handshake actually selects.
Adding a new protocol version or cipher suite to production does not require service downtime — configuration reload or feature-flag toggle is sufficient.
This tests your deployment agility as much as your crypto stack. Hot-reload nginx/envoy configs, or in-process provider hot-swapping.
Hybrid key exchange (classical + PQC in the same TLS handshake) has been tested in a non-production environment and a rollout plan exists.
X25519MLKEM768 is no longer a draft: RFC 10024 (August 2026) defines it Standards Track for TLS 1.3, which RFC 9846 now specifies. Chrome has defaulted to it since Chrome 131 (November 2024); Cloudflare runs it in production across its edge.
Can you swap the crypto library or provider without changing application call sites?
A cryptographic abstraction layer is in place — applications call a unified internal API (e.g., cryptoService.encrypt()) and are not directly coupled to a specific library.
JCA (Java), OpenSSL Providers, PKCS#11, or an internal crypto service are all valid abstraction patterns.
You have changed (or can change) the underlying crypto library — e.g., from legacy OpenSSL 1.x to OpenSSL 3.x, or from Java Sun provider to BouncyCastle — without changing application call sites.
This is the acid test for implementation agility. If changing the library meant rewriting call sites, your abstraction layer is incomplete. Expect build, configuration, test and rollback work even when the call sites stay the same.
Your HSM or KMS vendor has committed to PQC support on your current hardware (or a hardware upgrade path is budgeted) — ensuring your crypto infrastructure is not the bottleneck.

LM-008.curious:
### What This Is About

TLS 1.3 secured the internet by enforcing modern forward secrecy and 1-RTT handshakes. Upgrading it for PQC involves integrating lattice-based Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (ML-KEM) and signatures (ML-DSA). Running old and new algorithms side by side during the transition also creates a new question: could a connection end up classical-only when both sides support PQC?

### Why It Matters

Post-quantum algorithms demand much larger ciphertexts and keys than classical ECDH (like X25519). Notably, replacing classical certs with ML-DSA certificate chains adds several kilobytes to every handshake, threatening the scalability of billions of daily web connections.

TLS 1.3 signs and MACs the whole handshake, so an attacker who deletes the post-quantum option from the client's message is detected and the connection fails. The real downgrade risks are elsewhere: products that retry without post-quantum after a failed attempt, clients that don't know whether a server supports PQC, and settings that accept a classical-only connection.

### The Key Takeaway

The industry is already deploying "Hybrid" key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) to protect traffic from Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later attacks. To stop deliberate fallbacks from being abused, clients can remember that a server supported PQC on a previous visit. Browsers do this locally ("PQ Lock"), and PQC Continuity is an individual Internet-Draft (one proposal, not adopted by the TLS working group) for a TLS extension that lets a client cache a server's declared commitment to present PQC or composite certificates for a specified duration. Neither can protect the very first visit.

### What's Happening

Major browsers and CDN providers are already deploying hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) in production TLS 1.3, and the IETF published it as RFC 10024. Downgrade-memory proposals such as `draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity` are still individual drafts under discussion, while the IETF PLANTS working group develops Merkle Tree Certificates to address certificate bloat.

Client advertises key_share entries: X25519 + ML-KEM-768 (hybrid X25519MLKEM768). Both classical and PQC options offered.
Server selects X25519MLKEM768. Responds with its own key_share using both X25519 and ML-KEM-768 encapsulated key.
Both sides derive the same shared secret: KDF(ML-KEM_ss ∥ X25519_ss) — concatenated in that order per RFC 10024 §4.3. Session is quantum-safe — breaking X25519 alone is insufficient.
Handshake completes. Session uses AES-256-GCM-SHA384 with a hybrid-derived key. Protected against both classical and quantum adversaries.
Client sends a key_share with X25519MLKEM768. Client supports PQC and intends a hybrid connection.
Attacker drops or resets every connection offering a PQC key_share. Note: silently rewriting the ClientHello in flight would NOT work — the server signs the transcript as it received it (CertificateVerify, RFC 9846 §4.5.2), so the client, hashing its original ClientHello, would detect the mismatch and abort. The attacker can only make the PQC attempt fail.
After the failure, the client retries in "maximum compatibility" mode: a fresh ClientHello with no ML-KEM key_share — classical X25519 only. This retry is the client's own genuine message, so the new handshake is fully self-consistent. TLS has nothing left to detect.
Server sees only X25519 offered and selects it. From the server's view this is a normal classical client — it cannot know a PQC attempt was sabotaged moments earlier.
Session key derived from X25519 only. No ML-KEM contribution. This session is vulnerable to Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later: an adversary recording the handshake can decrypt it with a quantum computer.
Attacker records the ciphertext. Today it is unreadable — but once a CRQC (cryptographically-relevant quantum computer) exists, the X25519 key exchange can be broken and all session data decrypted.
Client has PQ Lock cached from a prior session: server previously signalled PQC support. ClientHello includes the X25519MLKEM768 key_share as before.
Attacker drops the PQC connection attempt to push the client into classical fallback. Same induced-failure attack as before.
The client is about to retry without ML-KEM, but PQ Lock is cached for this server. The cached signal says: "this server supports PQC." Downgrading the retry to classical-only would be inconsistent with that promise.
An active adversary blocks every TLS connection that offers a PQC key_share, pushing the client into its classical "maximum compatibility" fallback retry — so both endpoints end up on a classical-only session even though both support PQC. TLS 1.3 transcript integrity prevents in-flight tampering with the ClientHello, but it cannot stop the client from downgrading itself on retry. This is distinct from passive HNDL harvesting: the attack actively prevents PQC from being used.
Analysis by Bas Westerbaan (Cloudflare Research) · PQCrypto 2025 · Root Causes Podcast ep. 614
Both client and server negotiate X25519MLKEM768. The session is quantum-safe: an adversary recording the ciphertext cannot break it without both a classical compute break of X25519 AND a quantum break of ML-KEM-768.
Downgrade attack — induced fallback to a classical ClientHello
: when a handshake fails, the client retries with a more conservative ClientHello that omits the ML-KEM key_share. The attacker only has to make PQC attempts fail (drop, reset, timeout) — the client downgrades itself, and the resulting classical retry is self-consistent, so neither endpoint can detect it. The session is quantum-vulnerable.

7. HelloRetryRequest — Missing Key Share
The client supports both X25519 and X25519MLKEM768 but lists X25519 first, so its ClientHello carries a key share only for X25519. The server supports only X25519MLKEM768. Because the client did list the hybrid group in supported_groups, the server replies with a HelloRetryRequest naming X25519MLKEM768, and the client resends its ClientHello with a hybrid key share.
Look for the "HRR" badge and the 2-RTT indicator in results. The Protocol Log shows two ClientHellos: a small first one (X25519 key share only) and a larger retry carrying the ML-KEM-768 + X25519 key share (in the Hub's sample capture the ClientHello was 159 B offering only X25519 and 1,337 B offering only the hybrid group; the simulator's own sizes may differ). 8. No Common Group — Handshake Failure
The client offers only pure ML-KEM-1024; the server supports only the hybrid X25519MLKEM768. These are different group codepoints, so the two sides share no group at all. A HelloRetryRequest cannot fix this — the server can only ask for a group the client listed — so the server aborts with a handshake_failure alert.
The handshake fails with no HRR: the Protocol Log shows one ClientHello, then a fatal handshake_failure alert from the server ("no suitable key share"). A hybrid group does not match a pure ML-KEM or a pure X25519 offer. To fix it, add X25519MLKEM768 to the client groups: listed first it negotiates in 1-RTT; listed after ML-KEM-1024 it triggers an HRR, as in Scenario 7.

TLS 1.3 sends the ClientHello, including the
, in plaintext, so an on-path observer can see
a user is connecting to. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH, RFC 9849) lets the client encrypt the real ("inner") ClientHello to an ECH public key that the server normally publishes in DNS, and send a decoy ("outer") ClientHello. This hides the SNI and other sensitive fields such as the ALPN list among the sites that share the same ECH configuration. RFC 9849 states that ECH is not in itself sufficient to protect the identity of the server: the target may still be visible through plaintext DNS queries or the server's IP address.
Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), published as RFC 9849, encrypts the inner ClientHello with HPKE under the server's ECH key.
ECH and a hybrid key exchange such as X25519MLKEM768 protect different things. The hybrid group protects the key exchange of the TLS session. The inner ClientHello is encrypted separately with HPKE (RFC 9180) under the server's ECH key, using the KEM named in the ECH configuration. RFC 9180 defines only Diffie-Hellman KEMs (P-256, P-384, P-521, X25519, X448) and acknowledges that a non-quantum-resistant KEM used with HPKE can be broken by a quantum computer; the
lists ML-KEM-based identifiers that come from Internet-Drafts. RFC 9849 also states that ECH provides no forward secrecy for the inner ClientHello, because the server's ECH key is static. So a hybrid TLS key exchange does not by itself keep ECH-protected metadata private against a future quantum computer: that depends on the KEM in the site's ECH configuration, which this lesson does not assume is post-quantum.

TLS 1.3 secured the internet by enforcing modern forward secrecy and 1-RTT handshakes. Upgrading it for PQC involves integrating lattice-based Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (ML-KEM) and signatures (ML-DSA). Running old and new algorithms side by side during the transition also creates a new question: could a connection end up classical-only when both sides support PQC?
The industry is already deploying "Hybrid" key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) to protect traffic from Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later attacks. To stop deliberate fallbacks from being abused, clients can remember that a server supported PQC on a previous visit. Browsers do this locally ("PQ Lock"), and PQC Continuity is an individual Internet-Draft (one proposal, not adopted by the TLS working group) for a TLS extension that lets a client cache a server's declared commitment to present PQC or composite certificates for a specified duration. Neither can protect the very first visit.

PQC in TLS & Hybrid Modes
Set the client and server panels — identity certificates and key exchange groups — then press Start Full Interaction: the handshake runs and a summary plus the negotiated results appear below.

HelloRetryRequest (HRR) — per RFC 9846 §4.2.4, the server sends an HRR when client and server share a supported group but the ClientHello carried no key_share for the group the server selects; the client retries with that key share (2-RTT). If no group is supported by both sides, no HRR is possible and the server aborts with a handshake_failure alert. A hybrid such as X25519MLKEM768 is its own NamedGroup codepoint (RFC 10024): a classical-only client matches only if the server also supports plain X25519 as a separate group, and that classical fallback needs a policy that prevents silent downgrade
HKDF key schedule: derives all session keys through Extract and Expand operations — Early Secret (from PSK), Handshake Secret (from ECDHE/KEM shared secret, producing client and server handshake traffic secrets), and Master Secret (producing application traffic secrets)
Forward secrecy — TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral key exchange for every connection; session keys cannot be recovered even if long-term keys are compromised
HNDL threat — adversaries can record TLS-encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers break the ECDH key exchange, recovering the symmetric session keys
PQC size trade-off — ML-KEM-768 public keys are approximately 1,184 bytes versus 32 bytes for X25519, increasing handshake overhead; in the Hub's measured sample capture (seven handshake-layer messages, leaf and intermediate certificates) the handshake is 2,233 bytes for X25519 with RSA-2048, 4,499 bytes for X25519MLKEM768 with RSA-2048 and 16,944 bytes for ML-KEM-768 with ML-DSA-65; no handshake time was measured
Quantum downgrade attack (Westerbaan/Cloudflare) — an active MITM adversary cannot silently remove the ML-KEM key_share from a TLS 1.3 ClientHello (the handshake transcript is signed and MACed, so tampering is detected); instead it makes PQC connection attempts fail so that a client configured for compatibility fallback retries with a classical-only ClientHello; distinct from passive HNDL harvesting because it actively prevents PQC even when both endpoints support it
Maximum compatibility mode — the default server posture during transition: serve a classical certificate to any client, PQC only to capable clients; eliminates breakage but provides zero protection against downgrade attacks, and is fundamentally incompatible with PQC Continuity enforcement
PQ Lock / PQC HSTS — an HTTP-layer signal where a server tells the browser it supports PQC key exchange; the browser caches this signal and refuses future connections that omit PQC (implemented in Chromium, analogous to HSTS); provides session-level downgrade protection once the first PQC connection succeeds

qa.answer: TLS 1.3 was first defined by RFC 8446 and is now defined by RFC 9846, which obsoletes it. TLS 1.3 removed RSA key exchange and CBC cipher modes, requires forward-secret (EC)DHE key exchange and simplifies the full handshake to a single round trip.
qa.question: Which RFC standard defines the TLS 1.3 protocol improvements discussed in the module?

qa.answer: TLS 1.3 supports exactly five cipher suites: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, and TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256. These suites specify only symmetric encryption and hash algorithms, as key exchange is negotiated separately.
qa.question: What are the five specific cipher suites supported in TLS 1.3 according to the module?

qa.answer: ML-KEM is standardized under FIPS 203, while ML-DSA is standardized under FIPS 204. These standards define the post-quantum cryptographic primitives used for key encapsulation and digital signatures respectively.
qa.question: Which FIPS standards correspond to the ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms mentioned in the module?

qa.answer: The HKDF key schedule uses Extract and Expand operations to derive all session keys. It progresses from an Early Secret (derived from PSK) to a Handshake Secret (from ECDHE/KEM), which produces client and server handshake traffic secrets, and finally to a Master Secret for application traffic.
qa.question: How does the HKDF key schedule in TLS 1.3 derive session keys from the initial shared secret?

qa.answer: The hybrid approach combines classical X25519 with post-quantum ML-KEM, ensuring security even if one of the algorithms is broken. This provides a defense-in-depth strategy against both current computational attacks and future quantum computer threats.
qa.question: Why is the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange considered more secure than using classical ECDH alone?

qa.answer: The primary trade-off is the significant increase in key size, with ML-KEM-768 public keys being approximately 1,184 bytes compared to 32 bytes for X25519. This larger size increases handshake overhead and bandwidth consumption during the connection establishment.
qa.question: What is the primary trade-off when migrating from classical X25519 to pure PQC ML-KEM-768 in TLS handshakes?

qa.answer: The HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threat describes an adversary recording encrypted traffic now with the intent to decrypt it later once quantum computers are capable of breaking the classical ECDH key exchange. This would allow the recovery of symmetric session keys and the decryption of past communications.
qa.question: In a scenario where an adversary records TLS-encrypted traffic today, what specific threat does the HNDL concept describe?

qa.answer: TLS 1.3 removed static RSA key exchange to mandate ephemeral ECDHE, ensuring forward secrecy where session keys cannot be recovered if long-term keys are compromised. However, since classical ECDH is vulnerable to quantum attacks, migrating to PQC algorithms like ML-KEM is necessary to maintain this forward secrecy against future quantum adversaries.
qa.question: Synthesize the relationship between TLS 1.3's removal of RSA key exchange and the necessity of PQC migration for forward secrecy.

qa.answer: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) provides post-quantum key encapsulation to establish a shared secret for symmetric encryption, ensuring confidentiality against quantum decryption. FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) provides post-quantum digital signatures for the CertificateVerify message, ensuring the integrity and authenticity of the handshake participants.
qa.question: Analyze how the integration of FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) into a TLS 1.3 handshake addresses both confidentiality and integrity.

qa.answer: Deploying hybrid X25519MLKEM768 offers immediate quantum resistance while maintaining compatibility with classical systems, but it introduces a significant bandwidth overhead due to the 1,184-byte ML-KEM keys. Organizations must weigh this increased handshake size against the critical need to protect long-term sensitive data from HNDL attacks.
qa.question: Evaluate the operational impact of deploying hybrid X25519MLKEM768 in production environments considering both security and performance.

qa.answer: A connection using pure classical ECDH is vulnerable to the HNDL threat, as recorded traffic can be decrypted once quantum computers break the ECDH algorithm. In contrast, a hybrid X25519MLKEM768 connection remains secure even if ECDH is broken, because the ML-KEM component provides quantum resistance, preventing the recovery of session keys.
qa.question: Compare the security posture of a TLS 1.3 connection using pure classical ECDH versus one using hybrid X25519MLKEM768 in the context of the HNDL threat.

qa.answer: The organization should configure servers to prioritize hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange groups while maintaining classical ECDH as a fallback for legacy clients. By leveraging TLS 1.3's simplified cipher suite negotiation, the server can automatically select the strongest supported algorithm (hybrid) for modern clients and fall back to classical only when necessary.
qa.question: Design a migration strategy for an organization that needs to support legacy clients while preparing for PQC, utilizing the concepts of cipher suite negotiation and hybrid modes.

qa.answer: In a mutual TLS configuration, the client must present a valid certificate to the server for authentication, just as the server presents one to the client. The simulator supports this by allowing the configuration of client certificates and verifying them against the server's trust store.
qa.question: If a developer configures the TLS simulator to use mutual authentication (mTLS), what additional requirement must be met by the client?

qa.answer: To test post-quantum authentication, you must configure the server panel to use pre-loaded ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87 certificates instead of classical RSA or ECDSA. The simulator includes these specific PQC certificates to demonstrate signature verification in the handshake.
qa.question: How would you configure the TLS simulator to test post-quantum authentication using ML-DSA?

qa.answer: The TLS simulator currently runs its handshake using bundled PEM certificates and keys with native OpenSSL signing — an earlier HSM-backed mode (live SoftHSM keygen and cert-minting at session start, signing through pkcs11-provider) was removed because it never produced a successful handshake for end-users. The module does still include a separate, disconnected side demo — a SoftHSMv3/PKCS#11 v3.2 panel that runs a standalone ML-DSA-65 sign operation — but that panel is not part of the handshake simulation itself, so it doesn't reflect how keys are actually used in the live handshake demo.

# TLS 1.3 Basics

## Overview

The TLS Basics module provides a comprehensive introduction to Transport Layer Security 1.3 (RFC 9846, which obsoleted RFC 8446 in July 2026) and its post-quantum cryptography integration. It covers the TLS 1.3 protocol improvements over TLS 1.2, the 1-RTT handshake process, cipher suite simplification, key exchange mechanisms (classical ECDH, pure PQC ML-KEM, and hybrid X25519MLKEM768), the HKDF-based key schedule, and the trade-offs of PQC migration in TLS. The module also covers active quantum downgrade attacks that threaten the transition period — where an adversary suppresses PQC negotiation entirely — and the layered mitigations developed by Bas Westerbaan (Cloudflare Research) and the IETF: maximum compatibility mode, PQ Lock/PQC HSTS, and PQC Continuity. The module includes a live TLS handshake simulator powered by OpenSSL WASM that demonstrates real handshake operations with configurable client and server parameters, including a downgrade attack scenario.

## Key Concepts

- **TLS 1.3 improvements**: removed RSA key exchange (no forward secrecy), CBC cipher modes, renegotiation, and compression; added mandatory ECDHE forward secrecy, 0-RTT early data, and encrypted handshake messages; simplified to 5 cipher suites and 1-RTT handshake
- **TLS 1.3 cipher suites** specify only symmetric encryption and hash (key exchange negotiated separately): TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256
- **Key exchange approaches**:
  - **Classical (ECDH)** — X25519, P-256, P-384; fast with small keys (~32 bytes); quantum-vulnerable
  - **PQC (ML-KEM)** — ML-KEM-512/768/1024; quantum-resistant; larger keys (~1,184 bytes for ML-KEM-768)
  - **Hybrid** — X25519MLKEM768 (RFC 10024, TLS NamedGroup codepoint `0x11EC`) combines X25519 and ML-KEM-768; already deployed in Chrome and Firefox; secure even if one algorithm is broken
- **HelloRetryRequest (HRR)** — per RFC 9846 §4.2.4, the server sends an HRR when client and server share a supported group but the ClientHello carried no key_share for the group the server selects; the client retries with that key share (2-RTT). If no group is supported by both sides, no HRR is possible and the server aborts with a handshake_failure alert. A hybrid such as X25519MLKEM768 is its own NamedGroup codepoint (RFC 10024): a classical-only client matches only if the server also supports plain X25519 as a separate group, and that classical fallback needs a policy that prevents silent downgrade
- **HKDF key schedule**: derives all session keys through Extract and Expand operations — Early Secret (from PSK), Handshake Secret (from ECDHE/KEM shared secret, producing client and server handshake traffic secrets), and Master Secret (producing application traffic secrets)
- **Forward secrecy** — TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral key exchange for every connection; session keys cannot be recovered even if long-term keys are compromised
- **HNDL threat** — adversaries can record TLS-encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers break the ECDH key exchange, recovering the symmetric session keys
- **PQC size trade-off** — ML-KEM-768 public keys are approximately 1,184 bytes versus 32 bytes for X25519, increasing handshake overhead; in the Hub's measured sample capture (seven handshake-layer messages, leaf and intermediate certificates) the handshake is 2,233 bytes for X25519 with RSA-2048, 4,499 bytes for X25519MLKEM768 with RSA-2048 and 16,944 bytes for ML-KEM-768 with ML-DSA-65; no handshake time was measured
- **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** — the simulator supports both standard TLS and mutual authentication where both client and server present certificates
- **PQC certificate support** — the simulator includes pre-loaded ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 certificates for testing post-quantum authentication
- **Quantum downgrade attack** (Westerbaan/Cloudflare) — an active MITM adversary cannot silently remove the ML-KEM key_share from a TLS 1.3 ClientHello (the handshake transcript is signed and MACed, so tampering is detected); instead it makes PQC connection attempts fail so that a client configured for compatibility fallback retries with a classical-only ClientHello; distinct from passive HNDL harvesting because it actively prevents PQC even when both endpoints support it
- **Maximum compatibility mode** — the default server posture during transition: serve a classical certificate to any client, PQC only to capable clients; eliminates breakage but provides zero protection against downgrade attacks, and is fundamentally incompatible with PQC Continuity enforcement
- **PQ Lock / PQC HSTS** — an HTTP-layer signal where a server tells the browser it supports PQC key exchange; the browser caches this signal and refuses future connections that omit PQC (implemented in Chromium, analogous to HSTS); provides session-level downgrade protection once the first PQC connection succeeds
- **PQC Continuity** (`draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity`, an individual Internet-Draft by Sheffer et al., not adopted by the TLS working group) — a TLS extension that allows a TLS client to cache a server's declared commitment to present PQC or composite certificates for a specified duration (draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity-02); like PQ Lock it needs one prior successful PQC connection, so it cannot protect a first visit

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop is a live TLS handshake simulator with the following features:

- **Client Configuration Panel** — configure TLS version, cipher suites, key exchange groups, supported signature algorithms, and client certificates
- **Server Configuration Panel** — configure server certificates (classical RSA/ECDSA or PQC ML-DSA), cipher preferences, mutual TLS settings, and trust store management

LM-009.curious:
### What This Is About

VPN and SSH protocols are upgrading their key exchanges to Post-Quantum Cryptography using ML-KEM. For instance, recent OpenSSH versions already ship with hybrid modes like `mlkem768x25519-sha256` to secure sessions against future decryption.

### Why It Matters

PQC keys are vastly larger than classical ones. Integrating ML-KEM-768 adds over 1KB per exchange. In highly optimized, lightweight protocols like WireGuard, adding post-quantum protection via Rosenpass (which uses Classic McEliece and the round-3 Kyber, not FIPS 203 ML-KEM) adds four extra Rosenpass messages of 2,464 bytes in total (per the Rosenpass white paper), which raises the risk of UDP IP fragmentation.

### The Key Takeaway

This complex migration strictly targets the "Control Plane" (Key Exchange and Authentication). The "Data Plane" (the actual encrypted tunnel) uses symmetric ciphers like AES-GCM or ChaCha20, which are affected by Grover's algorithm rather than Shor's; per NIST, AES with a minimum key length of 128 bits can continue to be used, and a longer key can be considered for data that must remain secure for many years.

### What's Happening

OpenSSH 10.0+ ships with hybrid PQC key exchange (`mlkem768x25519-sha256`, added in 9.9) as the default, and the IETF drafts for ML-KEM and ML-DSA in IKEv2 are in the RFC Editor queue (October 2026). WireGuard users can add quantum protection through the Rosenpass companion tool.

LM-009.summary:
# VPN/IPsec and SSH PQC

## Overview

The VPN/IPsec and SSH PQC module explores how post-quantum key exchange is being integrated into the three major tunnel and remote-access protocols: IKEv2 (for IPsec VPNs), SSH, and WireGuard. It covers the IKEv2 two-phase handshake and how the multiple key exchanges framework (RFC 9370) enables hybrid ML-KEM integration, the evolution of PQC in OpenSSH from sntrup761 to ML-KEM-768, protocol size impacts of PQC key exchange, and the distinction between control plane migration (key exchange and authentication) and the already quantum-resistant data plane (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). It also covers WireGuard's crypto agility challenge and the Rosenpass add-on.

## Key Concepts

- **IKEv2 handshake** (RFC 7296) — two-phase process: IKE_SA_INIT (Diffie-Hellman key exchange with KE payload, nonces, and SPIs) and IKE_AUTH (identity verification with encrypted auth payloads); derives SKEYSEED from shared secret
- **ML-KEM in IKEv2** — draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem uses the multiple key exchanges framework (RFC 9370) to add ML-KEM encapsulation in IKE_INTERMEDIATE with RFC 9370 limiting its changes to the exchanged messages and the IKEv2 state machine; encapsulation key is 1,184 bytes; combined SKEYSEED derived from both DH and KEM shared secrets via PRF
- **ML-DSA in IKEv2** — draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth updates IKE_AUTH to support ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for post-quantum certificate-based authentication
- **SSH PQC evolution**: OpenSSH 8.5 (2021) added sntrup761x25519-sha512; OpenSSH 9.0 (2022) made it the default KEX; OpenSSH 9.9 (2024) added mlkem768x25519-sha256, OpenSSH's hybrid of ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203, standardised by NIST) and X25519, in the default KexAlgorithms list; OpenSSH 10.0 (2025) made it the preferred default KEX
- **SSH hybrid KEX** works by concatenating classical and PQC public keys in SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT and combining shares in SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY
- **WireGuard** uses a fixed cipher suite (X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s) with zero crypto agility — algorithms cannot be negotiated
- **Rosenpass** — a companion daemon that runs a separate post-quantum key exchange (Classic McEliece-460896 for the static keys, round-3 Kyber-512 for the ephemeral keys; this is not FIPS 203 ML-KEM) and injects the resulting PSK into WireGuard's pre-shared key slot; WireGuard's classical security holds even if Rosenpass is compromised, but the post-quantum protection does not
- **Protocol size impact** (this workshop's message model): IKEv2 classical 1,400 B to hybrid 3,784 B (+170%); SSH 984 B to 3,296 B (+235%); WireGuard is not in the comparison: adding Rosenpass means four extra Rosenpass messages totalling 2,464 B (InitHello 1,092, RespHello 1,132, InitConf 176, EmptyData 64; Rosenpass white paper, Figure 2), the paper gives no WireGuard comparison, and the McEliece public keys are exchanged out of band; TLS 1.3 1,200 B to 3,500 B (+192%)
- **Control plane vs data plane** — PQC migration applies only to the control plane (key exchange and authentication); the data plane's symmetric algorithms (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) are affected by Grover's algorithm rather than Shor's; per NIST (cited in RFC 9370), applications can continue using AES with a minimum key length of 128 bits, and a longer key size can be considered for data that must remain secure for many years
- **IKEv2 fragmentation** — handled explicitly via RFC 7383 over UDP, but only for encrypted messages (not IKE_SA_INIT); SSH handles larger payloads natively via TCP transport
- **Pure ML-KEM in IKEv2 limits** (draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem-09 §2.1) — pure PQC puts ML-KEM in IKE_SA_INIT, which cannot be IKEv2-fragmented; ML-KEM-512 MAY be used there as a quantum-resistant-only key exchange; implementations transporting IKE over UDP and not performing PMTU discovery SHOULD NOT use ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 in IKE_SA_INIT on networks where the PMTU is unknown or restricted, and MAY use any ML-KEM parameter when reliable transport (for example RFC 9329) is used or a sufficient PMTU is guaranteed. CNSA 2.0 lists ML-KEM-1024 for key establishment; the hybrid route (Appendix A) carries ML-KEM in IKE_INTERMEDIATE where RFC 7383 applies

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 3 simulation steps:

1. **IKEv2 Handshake Simulator** — step through the full IKEv2 handshake in three modes: Classical (ECP-256 DH), Hybrid (ECP-256 + ML-KEM-768 additional key exchange), and Pure PQC (ML-KEM-768 only); shows packet sizes, round trips, and key derivation at each stage
2. **SSH Key Exchange Simulator** — compare SSH KEX algorithms side by side: curve25519-sha256 (classical), sntrup761x25519-sha512 (NTRU hybrid), and mlkem768x25519-sha256 (ML-KEM hybrid); shows key sizes, exchange messages, and derived session keys
3. **Protocol Comparison Table** — comprehensive comparison of IKEv2 vs SSH vs WireGuard vs TLS 1.3 covering handshake sizes, round trips, key exchange mechanisms, authentication methods, crypto agility, and PQC readiness

## Related Standards

- RFC 7296 (IKEv2)
- RFC 9370 (Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2)
- draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem-09 (ML-KEM for IKEv2; in the RFC Editor queue, October 2026)
- draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth-12 (Post-Quantum Authentication in IKEv2 using ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; in the RFC Editor queue, October 2026)
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM)
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA)
- OpenSSH 9.9 & 10.0 Release Notes (mlkem768x25519-sha256 added in 9.9, default in 10.0)
- Rosenpass white paper (protocol specification)

Covers IKEv2 (RFC 7296) KEM payload structure with ML-KEM-768 encapsulation (~1,088 bytes ciphertext vs ~256 bytes RSA), RFC 9370 (Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2) for hybrid support, OpenSSH KexAlgorithms negotiation (OpenSSH 9.0+ supports mlkem768x25519-sha256), and Rosenpass post-quantum handshake for WireGuard (adds post-quantum rekeying to classical VPN). Covers IKEv2 handshake size growth (classical ~800 bytes → hybrid ~2,200 bytes), SSH handshake growth (classical ~200 bytes → hybrid ~4,500 bytes), and vendor roadmaps (strongSwan, libreswan, OpenVPN). Out of scope: IPsec protocol mechanics beyond key exchange, WireGuard cryptography details, and SSH protocol layers below key exchange.

The draft also requires a fresh ML-KEM key pair and fresh encapsulation randomness for every exchange. The responder must check the initiator's encapsulation key (FIPS 203 §7.2) before encapsulating, and should reject a bad key with INVALID_SYNTAX to limit resource-exhaustion attacks. The draft further warns that an on-path attacker with a quantum computer could steer peers onto a classical-only group unless local policy forbids one. None of this makes the draft a dead end. It sits in the RFC Editor queue, and several firewall vendors already ship hybrid ML-KEM IKEv2. Only pure-PQC IKEv2 at the higher security levels over plain UDP remains an open engineering problem.
Hybrid IKEv2 per draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem Appendix A, using RFC 9370 multiple key exchanges over an RFC 9242 IKE_INTERMEDIATE round. Classical ECP-256 runs in IKE_SA_INIT; ML-KEM follows as Additional Key Exchange 1 in IKE_INTERMEDIATE. Because IKE_INTERMEDIATE is encrypted, the large ML-KEM payloads can use RFC 7383 fragmentation, which IKE_SA_INIT cannot. HNDL-safe: the chained SKEYSEED requires breaking both algorithms. Tradeoff: 1 extra round trip.
Pure post-quantum IKEv2 with ML-KEM alone in IKE_SA_INIT — no classical DH (draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem, Key Exchange Methods 35/36/37). HNDL-safe from the first exchange.
