CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT.
2. The module certificate (CMVP) and its Security Policy
An algorithm certificate does not make a product validated. The CAVP overview page states the relationship:
For an algorithm implementation to be listed on a cryptographic module validation certificate as an Approved security function, the algorithm implementation must meet all the requirements of FIPS 140 and must successfully complete the cryptographic algorithm validation process. However, a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms.
A Security Policy keeps approved and non-approved items apart. The Security Policy of CMVP certificate #4703 (an HSM), for example, has “Table 10 Approved Services” and “Table 11 Non-Approved Services”, and lists the non-approved algorithms the module also offers in its Tables 4, 5 and 6. For algorithms that are allowed with no security claimed, the IG says:
the algorithm shall be included in the Security Policy's list of non-approved algorithms allowed in the approved mode of operation with no security claimed (see SP 800-140B). However, the module's certificate shall not include these algorithms as they do not claim any security and are not used to meet any requirement of FIPS 140-3.
So the question to put to a certificate is not “does the vendor sell ML-DSA?” but “is ML-DSA among the approved algorithms of this certificate, and which approved services use it?”
3. Self-tests inside the module (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A)
IG 10.3.A (last modified 19 August 2026) sets when the self-tests run and what they must cover. Timing, and what happens outside the approved mode:
The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm.
IG 10.3.A, General Notes, p. 115
GeneralNote8: For all algorithms that require a CAST (e.g., approved algorithms, allowed algorithms with a claim of security as permitted by an IG, and legacy algorithms per IG C.M), a CAST shall be performed prior to first time algorithm execution in the approved mode; but CASTs are NOT required (but are certainly permissible) prior to first time algorithm execution in the non-approved mode.
So firmware that runs ML-KEM or ML-DSA in a non-approved mode need not carry the CASTs that a validated approved mode needs. For ML-KEM:
IG 10.3.A, item 14, p. 110
if the module implements ML-KEM encapsulation, the module shall have a CAST for the ML-KEM encapsulation mechanism.
IG 10.3.A, item 14, Note21, p. 111
The ML-KEM decapsulation CASTs shall cover both the implicit rejection and (unnamed) non-rejection paths.
For ML-DSA signing, the CAST may use either variant from the hedged-signing section above:
IG 10.3.A, item 15, p. 111
if the module implements digital signature generation, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature generation CAST for either the ‘hedged’ or ‘deterministic’ algorithm (per FIPS 204 Section 5.2).
IG 10.3.A, item 5, p. 106
If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation.
A key pair the HSM generates is also tested once, by a PCT, which is not a CAST:
IG 10.3.A, Additional Comments 1, p. 115
Though not a CAST, a pairwise consistency test (PCT) shall be conducted for every generated public and private key pair for the applicable approved algorithm (per ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3).
IG 10.3.A, Additional Comments 1, p. 116
For key pairs generated for use with approved KEMs in FIPS 203, the PCT (described by the tester in TE10.35.01) shall consist of applying the encapsulation key ek to encapsulate a shared secret K leading to ciphertext c, and then applying decapsulation key dk to retrieve the same shared secret K. The PCT passes if the two shared secret K values are equal.
An HSM that stores a seed and rebuilds the key pair from it later is covered by a separate sentence:
For key pairs generated from stored seeds per FIPS 203 (section 3.3) or FIPS 204 (section 3.6.3), a PCT is only required to be performed on the key pair prior to the first exportation of the seed or key pair or prior to the first operational use of the key pair after the seed has been generated within the module.
For an approved ML-KEM, IG D.S (last modified 9 April 2026) ties the algorithm certificate to the module checks:
IG D.S, CAVP testing, Scenario 1, p. 225
ML-KEM shall be CAVP tested via ‘ML-KEM EncapDecap’ for all implemented parameter sets (ML-KEM-1024, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768) and functions (Decapsulation, Encapsulation). The module shall implement the encapsulation and decapsulation key checks specified in FIPS 203 Sections 7.2 and 7.3
4. Adding PQC to a validated HSM: which submission?
The FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual (version 2.7, 9 April 2026) decides how a changed module is submitted. It lists twelve submission scenarios (section 7.1), among them the full submission (FS) and several revalidation routes. The starting point:
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1, p. 50
An updated version of a previously validated cryptographic module can be considered for a revalidation rather than a full validation depending on the extent of the modifications from the previously validated version of the module.
If no revalidation scenario fits, the module is treated as new:
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1.2, p. 52
If modifications are made to hardware, software, or firmware components that do not meet any of the below revalidation criteria, then the cryptographic module shall be considered a new module and shall undergo a full validation testing by a CSTL and submitted as a FS.
Some revalidation scenarios cannot carry new cryptography. Algorithm Update (ALG) is for algorithms that became CAVP-testable after validation, and Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) is for security fixes:
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1.6, p. 55
Code or configuration changes are not permitted under this revalidation scenario.
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1.11, p. 60
Changes shall not introduce new features or cryptography
The scenario that allows security-relevant changes is Update (UPDT), up to a limit:
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1.10, pp. 58-59
An updated cryptographic module can be considered in this scenario if less than a 30% of security changes were made to the module. Security changes include impacts to: approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM. None of these, assessed individually, can exceed 30% of changes.
CMVP Management Manual 2.7, section 7.1.10, p. 59
The CMVP upon review, may determine that the changes are >30% and shall be submitted as an FS.
The Manual's summary table (section 7.1.14, p. 65) gives UPDT a new certificate and a new sunset date, requires the latest guidance, and requires CAVP testing and, where IG 9.3.A applies, entropy source validation (ESV) testing (not sourced in the Library). Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA changes the approved algorithms, the approved services and the self-tests, which are categories the Manual counts toward the 30% limit; whether a particular firmware release is an UPDT or an FS is decided by the CMVP on the lab's submission, not something this page can state in advance.

For every signing request, the HSM must write the updated state counter to NVRAM before the signature leaves the module. A power failure around this write can result in state loss, causing the same leaf to be used twice. NIST SP 800-208 §8.1 requires that LMS/XMSS key and signature generation

the standard fixes the order of operations, not the recovery procedure. How a particular product behaves when it finds incomplete state after a power loss, for example whether it refuses to sign with that key until an operator checks it, is product behaviour: read its Security Policy and administrator guide. NIST SP 800-208 section 8.1 says:
NIST SP 800-208, section 8.1, p. 28
In order to prevent the possible reuse of an OTS key, when the cryptographic module accepts a request to sign a message, the cryptographic module shall increment the leaf index of the private key (q in LMS, idx in XMSS, idx_sig in XMSSMT) and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value or accepting another request to sign a message.
FIPS 140-3 IG C.N Resolution 12 has the lab check it: “the tester shall confirm that the state information for the key (at minimum the leaf index value) is updated in the non-volatile memory before exporting a signature value or accepting a request to sign another message.”

Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are essentially heavily armored, military-grade computer servers built solely to protect the world's most sensitive digital master keys. They are designed to intentionally self-destruct and erase all data if a hacker tries to physically break into them.
Because they hold these incredibly sensitive keys, engineers are racing to physically swap out these remote bunkers worldwide or install massive software updates, ensuring they can mathematically defend against future quantum attacks before the hardware becomes completely obsolete.

HSM & PQC Operations — In Simple Terms
Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are physical, highly secure, tamper-resistant devices that protect a network's most sensitive cryptographic keys (meeting standards like FIPS 140-3). PKCS#11 v3.2, an OASIS Standard since June 2026, defines how these devices handle Post-Quantum Cryptography.
Classical cryptography used tiny memory buffers. For example, ECDSA uses roughly 64 bytes, while ML-KEM-768 requires 1,184 bytes. If an HSM isn't specifically upgraded to handle PQC, its internal buffers will instantly overflow. Additionally, new stateful signatures (like LMS) require atomic NVRAM writes to track every single signature made, making HSMs the only truly safe platform to run them.
Checking a PQC-capable HSM means checking four different things: NIST's algorithm tests (CAVP), the module's own certificate and its Security Policy (CMVP), the self-tests the module runs on its own algorithms and key pairs, and the submission route a firmware update takes. Passing the algorithm tests does not make a product validated, and firmware that runs ML-KEM or ML-DSA in a non-approved mode does not need the self-tests a validated approved mode needs. Under NIST's CMVP Management Manual, adding PQC to a validated module is an Update only if each category of security change stays under 30%; otherwise it is a full submission.
PKCS#11 v3.2, an OASIS Standard since June 2026, standardizes how applications call HSMs for ML-KEM encapsulation, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA signatures, and stateful hash-based signatures, while vendors add each algorithm to their firmware and then to their programming interface release by release.

Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) operations in lattice-based algorithms show data-dependent power consumption patterns. An attacker with physical access can measure power traces to recover secret coefficients.
Polynomial multiplication in lattice operations generates electromagnetic emanations that correlate with secret data. Near-field EM probes can extract information even through shielding.
EM shielding in HSM enclosure, randomized operation scheduling, hardware masking. FIPS 140-3 Level 3 requires tamper detection and response and either environmental failure protection (EFP) or environmental failure testing (EFT).
Hash-based signature schemes rely heavily on hash function calls. Variable-time hash implementations can leak information about the message or key through timing measurements.
Constant-time hash implementations (SHA-256, SHAKE). HSMs typically use hardware-accelerated constant-time hash units.
Table lookups in NTT or hash operations can be observed through CPU cache timing. Flush+Reload or Prime+Probe attacks can recover secret values in shared-hardware environments.
Cache-timing attacks need an attacker who can run code that shares a cache with the victim. An HSM that runs only its own firmware on dedicated crypto processors removes that route; a shared or multi-tenant platform needs its own isolation argument. Check the Security Policy of the module and the documentation of the provider for what applies to the product.
Inducing faults during ML-DSA signing (e.g., voltage glitching, laser fault injection) can cause the signer to produce a faulty signature that leaks the secret key. FIPS 204 §3.4 makes the hedged variant the default, and says the deterministic variant makes the risk of side-channel attacks, particularly fault attacks, more difficult to mitigate.
ML-DSA hedged signing mode (FIPS 204 §3.4): the rnd parameter is random, not zero. FIPS 204 says "The use of fresh randomness during signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks" and that the deterministic variant makes fault attacks "more difficult to mitigate". FIPS 140-3 Level 3 requires tamper-resistant enclosures.
If an HSM loses track of which one-time signature leaves have been used (e.g., power failure during NVRAM write), the same leaf may be used twice. Two signatures from the same leaf completely compromise the key.
Atomic NVRAM state updates, write-ahead logging, pre-reservation of signature indices. NIST SP 800-208 §8.1 requires LMS/XMSS key and signature generation to be validated only within hardware cryptographic modules at Level 3 or higher physical security (see FIPS 140-3 IG C.N).

C_EncapsulateKey( hSession, &mechanism, // CKM_ML_KEM hPublicKey, // ML-KEM public key (encapsulation key) sessionTemplate, // CKA_CLASS=SECRET_KEY, CKA_KEY_TYPE=CKK_GENERIC_SECRET, CKA_VALUE_LEN=32 ulAttributeCount, ciphertext, // Output: KEM ciphertext (1,088 bytes) &ciphertextLen, &hSharedSecretKey // Output: handle to new secret key object holding the shared secret )
Use ML-KEM encapsulation to derive a 32-byte shared secret, created as a secret key object on the token.
PKCS#11 v3.2 adds C_EncapsulateKey specifically for KEM operations. Unlike C_WrapKey (which wraps an existing key), C_EncapsulateKey derives a NEW key object from the KEM shared secret and simultaneously outputs the KEM ciphertext. The 1,088-byte ciphertext is sent to the private key holder; the derived 32-byte secret is created as a generic secret key on the token (CKA_EXTRACTABLE follows the template and defaults to CK_TRUE), which an application then uses as AES-256 key material (for example through a key-derivation step).
CKR_OK Derived Key Handle: 0x00000044 (CKK_GENERIC_SECRET) Mechanism: CKM_ML_KEM KEM Ciphertext: 1,088 bytes Shared Secret: 32 bytes (derived key object)
CKM_RSA_PKCS_OAEP → 256-byte ciphertext (direct encryption)
No cloud HSM supports native PKCS#11 KEM encapsulation yet
C_DecapsulateKey( hSession, &mechanism, // CKM_ML_KEM hPrivateKey, // ML-KEM private key (decapsulation key) sessionTemplate, // CKA_CLASS=SECRET_KEY, CKA_KEY_TYPE=CKK_GENERIC_SECRET, CKA_VALUE_LEN=32, CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE ulAttributeCount, ciphertext, // Input: KEM ciphertext from step 3 ciphertextLen, &hRecoveredKey // Handle to the recovered shared-secret key )
Decapsulate to recover the same 32-byte shared secret (usable as AES-256 key material).
PKCS#11 v3.2 C_DecapsulateKey takes the KEM ciphertext, performs ML-KEM decapsulation with the private key (its CKA_DECAPSULATE attribute must be CK_TRUE) and creates the recovered shared secret as a new key object. The spec sets CKA_EXTRACTABLE on the new key to the value in the input template, with a default of CK_TRUE if not provided, so set CKA_EXTRACTABLE to CK_FALSE in the template if the shared secret must not leave the token.
CKR_OK Recovered Key Handle: 0x00000044 Key Type: CKK_GENERIC_SECRET (use as AES-256 key material) Key Size: 256 bits CKA_SENSITIVE: TRUE CKA_EXTRACTABLE: FALSE (as set in the template)
CKM_RSA_PKCS_OAEP decrypt → recovers plaintext DEK directly
All three on-prem vendors support ML-KEM decapsulation in firmware; check the API each exposes for the exact release (nShield: PKCS#11 from Security World v13.9.3)
AWS CloudHSM: no ML-KEM, so no decapsulation. Azure Dedicated HSM (Thales Luna 7) can take the Luna firmware upgrade for existing customers, but the service is being retired and accepts no new customers (Microsoft supports existing customers until July 31, 2028). Google Cloud HSM: no PQC at the HSM level
// Message-based signing, as the live HSM runs it (PKCS#11 v3.0+) C_MessageSignInit(hSession, &mechanism, hSignKey) // mechanism = CKM_ML_DSA C_SignMessage( hSession, &params, // CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT (hedge variant, context string) paramsLen, data, // Message to sign dataLen, // Message length signature, // Output buffer (must be >= 3,309 bytes) &signatureLen // ML-DSA-65: 3,309 bytes ) C_MessageSignFinal(hSession)
Create a digital signature using ML-DSA-65.
ML-DSA-65 produces 3,309-byte signatures (vs 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256).
CKR_OK Signature Length: 3,309 bytes Algorithm: ML-DSA-65 NIST Level: 3 Hedged Signing: YES (rnd ≠ 0, per FIPS 204 §3.4) Note: Hedged mode recommended for side-channel protection
CKM_ECDSA with P-256 → 64-byte signature (51x smaller)
All vendors: native ML-DSA with hedged signing. Entrust also supports SLH-DSA
AWS CloudHSM: ML-DSA via vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms. Azure Dedicated HSM (Thales Luna 7) can take the Luna firmware upgrade for existing customers, but the service is being retired and accepts no new customers (Microsoft supports existing customers until July 31, 2028). Google Cloud HSM: no PQC at the HSM level
// Message-based verification, as the live HSM runs it (PKCS#11 v3.0+) C_MessageVerifyInit(hSession, &mechanism, hVerifyKey) // mechanism = CKM_ML_DSA C_VerifyMessage( hSession, &params, // CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT, same as step 5 paramsLen, data, // Original message dataLen, signature, // Signature from step 5 signatureLen // 3,309 bytes ) C_MessageVerifyFinal(hSession)
Verify the ML-DSA-65 signature against the original data.
CKR_OK Verification: VALID Algorithm: ML-DSA-65 Public Key Size: 1,952 bytes Signature Valid: TRUE
CKM_ECDSA verify — same API, 64-byte signature input
Public-key verification does not need the private key, so it can run outside the HSM; check each service’s documentation for HSM-side verification
Generate Classical and PQC Key Pairs (Grouped)
// Step 7a: Generate classical keypair C_GenerateKeyPair(hSession, &ecMechanism, // CKM_EC_KEY_PAIR_GEN (P-256) ecPubTemplate, ecPrivTemplate, &hEcPub, &hEcPriv) // Step 7b: Generate PQC keypair C_GenerateKeyPair(hSession, &mlkemMechanism, // CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN mlkemPubTemplate, mlkemPrivTemplate, &hMlkemPub, &hMlkemPriv) // Grouping convention only: give both pairs the same CKA_ID so the // application can find them together (the token does not combine them)
Generate a classical key pair and a PQC key pair as two separate operations, grouped by an application convention.
These are two independent C_GenerateKeyPair calls. Giving both pairs the same CKA_ID is only a grouping convention: PKCS#11 v3.2 says the key identifier of a public key and its private key should be the same, describes CKA_ID as intended to distinguish among multiple keys, and states that Cryptoki does not enforce these associations. The convention is not a hybrid requirement, and linking the keys neither combines them nor adds security. The metadata only helps an application find the pairs: set the same CKA_ID on both and read it back with C_GetAttributeValue. PKCS#11 v3.2 defines no composite or hybrid PQC key type. The security of a hybrid scheme comes from the standard or protocol that defines how its components are used together, so a real design must follow that standard’s combiner, context and authentication rules. For example, composite ML-DSA (Internet-Draft draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs, the successor of draft-ounsworth-pq-composite-sigs) keeps the component keys in one composite private key and signs a message representative that prepends a fixed prefix, an algorithm-specific label and the application context to a hash of the message; composite ML-KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem) defines a KEM combiner over both shared secrets.
CKR_OK EC Public Key: 0x00000050 (65 bytes, P-256) EC Private Key: 0x00000051 ML-KEM Public Key: 0x00000052 (1,184 bytes) ML-KEM Private Key: 0x00000053 CKA_ID (both pairs, application convention): "pair-group-001"
C_GenerateKeyPair for each algorithm, as for any classical key pair; combining the components is a protocol or standard step, not a token operation
Support for composite or hybrid objects, and for any single combined key type, varies by product and release; not verified here, so check each vendor’s release notes and mechanism list
Not verified here: check each cloud HSM service’s documentation for supported hybrid or composite mechanisms
// Query remaining one-time signatures C_GetAttributeValue( hSession, hLmsKey, // LMS signing key handle stateTemplate, // CKA_HSS_KEYS_REMAINING 1 ) // CRITICAL: State must persist to NVRAM after every sign
Check remaining one-time signatures for an LMS/HSS stateful key.
LMS/HSS and XMSS are stateful hash-based schemes: each leaf can only sign ONCE. The HSM must atomically update NVRAM state after every signing operation. Power failure during state update can brick the key. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 FAQ says to implement signing and state management in hardware, such as an HSM, approves only LMS and XMSS for use in NSS, and does not allow the multi-tree HSS and XMSSMT; NIST SP 800-208 requires key and signature generation in hardware cryptographic modules that do not allow secret keying material to be exported. PKCS#11 v3.2 defines CKA_HSS_KEYS_REMAINING for HSS private keys.
CKR_OK Key Type: CKK_HSS Tree Height: H=20 (1,048,576 total signatures) Signatures Used: 12,847 Remaining: 1,035,729 State Storage: NVRAM (atomic write) WARNING: State loss = key compromise
N/A — classical signatures are stateless (unlimited per key)
Thales Luna: LMS/HSS with NVRAM state. Entrust: LMS + XMSS. Utimaco: LMS + XMSS
No cloud HSM supports stateful signatures — state management too risky for shared infrastructure

AWS CloudHSM (hsm2m.medium, CMVP #4703, Marvell LS2 HSM Family, FIPS 140-3 Level 3): ML-DSA-44/65/87 keys are generated and used in the HSM through vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms (CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA, CKM_CLOUDHSM_EXT_MU_ML_DSA); AWS's PKCS#11 library is documented as compliant with PKCS#11 version 2.40. The SDK repository says "This project is still under development and is not yet ready for deployment", and Microsoft's announcement gives FIPS 140-3 Level 3 as what the project is designed to enforce. Microsoft describes Tessera as an evolution of the Azure Integrated HSM; facts about the earlier Azure Integrated HSM are not facts about Tessera. Certificates read: Thales Luna T7 #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS; Kryptus (ASI-HSM) #5282 lists ML-KEM and ML-DSA; Crypto4A #5497 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS; Sansec #5503 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; Luna M7 #5300 lists only LMS; Luna K7 #4684 (firmware 7.8.x), nShield 5s #5329 and #4745 and Marvell LS2 #4703 list no PQC algorithm.
ML-DSA hedged signing, FIPS 204 section 3.4: hedged is the default variant; "The use of fresh randomness during signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks"; the deterministic variant "should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED, so which variant a given HSM uses by default is a property of that product (module documentation and Security Policy).
NIST SP 800-208 section 8.1 (p. 28): "In order to prevent the possible reuse of an OTS key, when the cryptographic module accepts a request to sign a message, the cryptographic module shall increment the leaf index of the private key (q in LMS, idx in XMSS, idx_sig in XMSSMT) and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value or accepting another request to sign a message." IG C.N Resolution 12 has the tester confirm it. How a product recovers after a power failure is product behaviour (Security Policy and administrator guide).
A PQC-capable HSM is checked in four places. CAVP is NIST's algorithm validation program (tests specified in ACVP documents). CMVP is the cryptographic module validation program whose Validation Authority is a joint effort of NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: a module's certificate lists its approved algorithms and the Security Policy published with it lists its services. A CAST is a cryptographic algorithm self-test run by a validated module; a PCT is a pairwise consistency test on a generated key pair; a CSTL is an accredited testing laboratory.
Algorithm certificates (CAVP): NIST's ACVP specification drafts (2 October 2026) cover ML-KEM (keyGen, encapDecap), ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer). CAVP overview page: "Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation." and "Due to this structure, ACVTS testing is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP in order to receive a validation certificate." ML-KEM draft section 6.1: "For the encapsulation key check, the server will generate a potentially valid or invalid encapsulation key ek. The IUT SHALL determine if the provided ek is valid based on [FIPS203] Section 7.2." Not covered (ML-DSA draft section 6.2.2): "An ACVP server will not test the zeroization of intermediate values, security strength of the deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs), or incorrect length signatures or public keys." LMS draft section 6.2.2: "ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation." IG C.N Background (last modified September 2024): "CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT." No ACVP specification is published for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS (October 2026).
Module certificate (CMVP) and Security Policy: CAVP overview page: "For an algorithm implementation to be listed on a cryptographic module validation certificate as an Approved security function, the algorithm implementation must meet all the requirements of FIPS 140 and must successfully complete the cryptographic algorithm validation process. However, a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms." A Security Policy keeps approved and non-approved items apart (the policy of CMVP #4703 has "Table 10 Approved Services" and "Table 11 Non-Approved Services" and lists non-approved algorithms in its Tables 4, 5 and 6). IG 2.4.A: "the algorithm shall be included in the Security Policy's list of non-approved algorithms allowed in the approved mode of operation with no security claimed (see SP 800-140B). However, the module's certificate shall not include these algorithms as they do not claim any security and are not used to meet any requirement of FIPS 140-3." The question to put to a certificate is whether ML-DSA (or ML-KEM, SLH-DSA, LMS) is among its approved algorithms and which approved services use it.
Self-tests (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A, last modified 19 August 2026): "The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm." GeneralNote8: "For all algorithms that require a CAST (e.g., approved algorithms, allowed algorithms with a claim of security as permitted by an IG, and legacy algorithms per IG C.M), a CAST shall be performed prior to first time algorithm execution in the approved mode; but CASTs are NOT required (but are certainly permissible) prior to first time algorithm execution in the non-approved mode." ML-KEM: "if the module implements ML-KEM encapsulation, the module shall have a CAST for the ML-KEM encapsulation mechanism." and Note21: "The ML-KEM decapsulation CASTs shall cover both the implicit rejection and (unnamed) non-rejection paths." ML-DSA: "if the module implements digital signature generation, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature generation CAST for either the 'hedged' or 'deterministic' algorithm (per FIPS 204 Section 5.2)." LMS: "If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation." Pairwise consistency test (Additional Comments 1): "Though not a CAST, a pairwise consistency test (PCT) shall be conducted for every generated public and private key pair for the applicable approved algorithm (per ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3)." For ML-KEM the PCT encapsulates a shared secret K with ek and decapsulates with dk, and passes if the two K values are equal. For key pairs generated from stored seeds (FIPS 203, FIPS 204) a PCT is only required prior to the first exportation of the seed or key pair or prior to the first operational use of the key pair after the seed has been generated within the module. IG D.S Scenario 1 (last modified 9 April 2026): "ML-KEM shall be CAVP tested via 'ML-KEM EncapDecap' for all implemented parameter sets (ML-KEM-1024, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768) and functions (Decapsulation, Encapsulation). The module shall implement the encapsulation and decapsulation key checks specified in FIPS 203 Sections 7.2 and 7.3".
Which submission for a firmware update (CMVP Management Manual version 2.7, 9 April 2026, section 7.1; twelve submission scenarios): "An updated version of a previously validated cryptographic module can be considered for a revalidation rather than a full validation depending on the extent of the modifications from the previously validated version of the module." Full Submission (FS): "If modifications are made to hardware, software, or firmware components that do not meet any of the below revalidation criteria, then the cryptographic module shall be considered a new module and shall undergo a full validation testing by a CSTL and submitted as a FS." Algorithm Update (ALG): "Code or configuration changes are not permitted under this revalidation scenario." CVE: "Changes shall not introduce new features or cryptography". Update (UPDT): "An updated cryptographic module can be considered in this scenario if less than a 30% of security changes were made to the module. Security changes include impacts to: approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM. None of these, assessed individually, can exceed 30% of changes." and "The CMVP upon review, may determine that the changes are >30% and shall be submitted as an FS." The summary table (section 7.1.14) gives UPDT a new certificate and a new sunset date and requires the latest guidance, CAVP testing and, where IG 9.3.A applies, ESV testing. Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA changes the approved algorithms, approved services and self-tests, which are categories counted toward the 30% limit; whether a given release is an UPDT or an FS is decided by the CMVP on the lab's submission.

qa.answer: FIPS 140-3 validation ensures the cryptographic module's security, while PKCS#11 v3.2 provides the interface standard; together they ensure that PQC algorithms like ML-KEM are implemented securely and compliantly in HSMs.

---
module_id: hsm-pqc
title: HSM & PQC Operations
track: Hardware Infrastructure
difficulty: advanced
duration: 60 min
workshop_steps: 5

# HSM & PQC Operations

## Topics Covered

- HSM architecture for PQC (FIPS 140-3 levels, on-prem vs cloud side-by-side)
- PKCS#11 v3.2 PQC mechanisms (`CKM_ML_KEM`, `CKM_ML_DSA`, `CKM_SLH_DSA`, and `CKK_ML_KEM`, `CKK_ML_DSA`, `CKK_SLH_DSA` key types)
- On-prem HSM deep dive (Thales Luna 7.9.0 or newer, Entrust nShield v13.8+ (ML-KEM: v13.8.3+), Utimaco Quantum Protect, Securosys Primus HSM CyberVault)
- Cloud HSM deep dive (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Cloud HSM, Azure Managed HSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, Google Cloud HSM), and Tessera as a specification with no product or certificate yet
- Side-channel attack surfaces (NTT power analysis, EM emanation, fault injection, ML-DSA hedged signing)
- HSM firmware migration (upgrade paths, dual-partition strategy, FIPS re-validation)
- What the lab tests for an HSM (CAVP algorithm certificates, the CMVP module certificate and Security Policy, IG 10.3.A self-tests and pairwise tests, CMVP submission scenarios)
- Stateful signature state management (LMS/HSS NVRAM persistence, CNSA 2.0)
- FIPS 140-3 (CMVP) and CAVP PQC validation tracking

## Workshop

1. PKCS#11 PQC Simulator — 8 operations with classical comparison and on-prem vs cloud notes
2. Vendor Comparison — Interactive matrix with PQC Maturity Score (0-100)
3. HSM Migration Planner — 4-phase firmware migration wizard
4. FIPS Validation Tracker — CMVP/CAVP PQC validation status per vendor
5. HSM Capacity Calculator — Size an HSM fleet across enterprise use cases and compare classical vs next-gen HSM throughput and quantum-crypto impact

## Vendor statements on the Learn tab (checked 23 October 2026 unless stated)

- Entrust nShield (CMVP #5329 and #4745, nShield 5s, FIPS 140-3 Level 3): the approved-algorithm lists of both certificates contain no PQC algorithm. The PKCS#11 interface gained the PQC algorithms one release at a time; ML-KEM and SLH-DSA were available through nCore before PKCS#11. Security World v13.9.0 release notes (revision 1.4, 14 September 2026): section 3.9 adds ML-DSA to the nShield PKCS#11 API (CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_ML_DSA, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA and the _SHA256, _SHA512, _SHAKE128 and _SHAKE256 variants; firmware v13.8 or later and the PostQuantum feature enabled). Section 3.4 (ML-KEM) and section 3.5 (SLH-DSA) each say "This functionality is currently only available via nCore." Later releases changed that: v13.9.3 (12 December 2025) section 3.4 adds ML-KEM to PKCS#11 (CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN and CKM_ML_KEM; firmware v13.8.3 or later) and v13.9.5 (24 April 2026) section 3.8 adds SLH-DSA to PKCS#11 (12 parameter sets). v13.9.6 (29 July 2026) adds FPGA acceleration of ML-KEM on mid- and high-speed models. CAVP certificate A7990 (PQSDK 1.4.1) lists LMS KeyGen, SigGen and SigVer; the Entrust pages read do not describe HSS or XMSS. An nShield 5s module is on the CMVP Modules in Process list, which is a queue position, not an outcome.
- Thales Luna and Utimaco (SLH-DSA): Thales's Luna Network HSM 7 "Post Quantum Algorithms" page says "ML-DSA and ML-KEM algorithms are available using Luna HSM Firmware 7.9.0 or newer" and that LMS-HSS is available in Luna HSM Firmware 7.8.9 and newer; that page and Thales's Luna HSM Firmware v7.9 release post do not list SLH-DSA. Utimaco's Quantum Protect page offers ML-KEM, ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS (with HSS and XMSS-MT) and says "More algorithms such as SLH-DSA are on the roadmap."; its algorithm list shows "SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) in progress". Entrust's v13.9.0 release notes describe SLH-DSA as available via nCore.
- AWS CloudHSM (hsm2m.medium, CMVP #4703, Marvell LS2 HSM Family, FIPS 140-3 Level 3): ML-DSA-44/65/87 keys are generated and used in the HSM through vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms (CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA, CKM_CLOUDHSM_EXT_MU_ML_DSA); AWS's PKCS#11 library is documented as compliant with PKCS#11 version 2.40. No ML-KEM mechanism is documented (the CloudHSM CLI key generate-asymmetric-pair category lists only ec, ml-dsa and rsa). Two statements are unreconciled and the page prefers neither. AWS documentation: "Starting September 1, 2026, ML-DSA is available in FIPS mode for hsm2m.medium clusters." and, on cluster modes, "In FIPS mode, only Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) validated keys and algorithms can be used." The NIST Security Policy for CMVP #4703 (dated January 29, 2026) lists "ML-DSA (non-compliant)" (use "Key generation, sign, verify") and "ML-KEM (non-compliant)" (use "Key generation, Asymmetric key encapsulation and un-encapsulation") in Table 6, "Non-Approved Algorithms Not Allowed in the Approved Mode of Operation", lists the services CN_PQC_GENERATE_KEY_PAIR, CN_PQC_CRYPTO_SIG_GEN and CN_PQC_CRYPTO_SIG_VERIFY in Table 11, "Non-Approved Services", and the note under the table says "The indicator is success for all non-approved services only when the partition is operated in the non-approved mode. The non-approved services will fail FIPS POLICY MISMATCH when partition is operated in the approved mode." The certificate lists no PQC algorithm among its approved ones and its latest update on NIST's page is 26 February 2026. "Available in FIPS mode" (an AWS cluster setting) and "listed on the certificate" are different claims; ask AWS which statement applies to a given cluster. AWS-LC 3 (CMVP #5298 and #5314) is a separate Level 1 software module that approves ML-KEM but not ML-DSA and does not change the HSM certificate.
- Google Cloud: the Cloud KMS algorithms page lists its PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA-44/65/87 including external-mu, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S) and key encapsulation algorithms (ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, X-Wing) for the software protection level; its tables for the HSM and single-tenant HSM protection levels list none. Google's Cloud HSM architecture page says Cloud HSM uses Marvell LiquidSecurity HSMs (certificate #4399) in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified hardware.
- Azure Cloud HSM (Microsoft Learn overview and FAQ, read 8 Nov 2026): a single-tenant service with a customer-owned cluster of three HSMs and a customer-specific security domain; the customer holds administrative authority, and the service takes care of high availability, patching and maintenance; Microsoft oversees the firmware on Marvell LiquidSecurity hardware. FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated. Interfaces: PKCS#11, OpenSSL, Java (JCA and JCE), CNG and a key storage provider. No PQC algorithm is listed on the overview or the FAQ. The Azure Dedicated HSM overview (read 8 Nov 2026) says Microsoft calls Azure Cloud HSM the successor to Azure Dedicated HSM, which is being retired (no new customer onboardings; existing customers supported until 31 July 2028).
- Azure Managed HSM (Microsoft Learn, Key Vault Managed HSM about keys, read 8 Nov 2026): a fully managed, single-tenant service; each instance has its own security domain on hardware that other Managed HSM instances share; FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated hardware; every key is HSM-protected. Key types are RSA-HSM, EC-HSM and oct-HSM, with a data-plane endpoint per instance; no PQC algorithm is listed, and Microsoft notes that 256-bit AES (oct-HSM) keys are quantum-resistant. Microsoft says it can attest that a key was generated and resides inside an HSM that Microsoft operates; keys can be generated in the HSM or imported by bring-your-own-key. Both services give the customer administrative control of the keys (Managed HSM through local RBAC, per the Managed HSM overview; Cloud HSM through HSM users) while Microsoft runs patching and maintenance, and, for Managed HSM, provisioning, configuration; a Cloud HSM cluster is customer-owned and provisioned by the customer.
- Securosys Primus HSM CyberVault (Securosys X2 fact sheet, version FS-E03, and the firmware v3.x algorithm list, read 8 Nov 2026): sold as a 1U rack appliance (X2 models) that supports clustering, load balancing and failover. Securosys lists ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, ML-KEM, HSS-LMS and XMSS, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 as in certification and Common Criteria EAL4+. Interfaces: JCE/JCA, PKCS#11, OpenSSL v3, Microsoft CNG/KSP, a RESTful API and a KMIP API. NIST's CAVP pages (not a module certificate) name Securosys SA and the Primus HSM firmware implementation, version 3.1.0, first validated 7 Nov 2024: A6129 (ML-KEM key generation and encapsulation/decapsulation), A6130 (ML-DSA key generation, signature generation and verification) and A6131 (SLH-DSA key generation, signature generation and verification); a passed algorithm test is a prerequisite of a module validation, not a substitute for it. The firmware v3.x algorithm list gives each algorithm a separate status for the Common Criteria evaluated configuration and for FIPS mode: for example, HSS-LMS is listed as approved in FIPS mode and not allowed in the Common Criteria configuration.
- Tessera (specification stage): a specification for a workload-attached integrated HSM with open firmware and an open hardware design; the sources read describe no product and no certificate. The SDK repository says "This project is still under development and is not yet ready for deployment", and Microsoft's announcement gives FIPS 140-3 Level 3 as what the project is designed to enforce. Microsoft describes Tessera as an evolution of the Azure Integrated HSM; facts about the earlier Azure Integrated HSM are not facts about Tessera. Tessera's Chip Requirements say it "MUST have a Caliptra 2.2 subsystem root of trust"; the Caliptra specifications and figures in this module and in PQC Hardware Acceleration come from the Caliptra 2.1 documentation, and Microsoft's 13 October 2026 post says Caliptra 2.2 is "scheduled for release in December". Compare it with the other trust hardware in Step 6 of Architect Quantum Impact (/learn/arch-quantum-impact?tab=workshop&step=5).
- Certificates read: Thales Luna T7 #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS; Kryptus (ASI-HSM) #5282 lists ML-KEM and ML-DSA; Crypto4A #5497 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS; Sansec #5503 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; Luna M7 #5300 lists only LMS; Luna K7 #4684 (firmware 7.8.x), nShield 5s #5329 and #4745 and Marvell LS2 #4703 list no PQC algorithm.

## Side channels and hedged signing

- The vector cards describe attack classes and the countermeasure techniques discussed for them. Whether a given HSM implements a technique is stated, if at all, in the vendor's documentation and the module's Security Policy. NIST SP 800-140F section 6.2 (March 2020) reads in full "No additional requirements at this time", so CMVP has no approved non-invasive test metrics. FIPS 140-3 IG 12.A: "If a cryptographic module has been purposely designed, built and publicly documented to mitigate one or more specific attacks, this section is applicable and AS12.01 through AS12.04 (as applicable) shall be addressed regardless if the vendor of the module wishes to address the claim or not."
- ML-DSA hedged signing, FIPS 204 section 3.4: hedged is the default variant; "The use of fresh randomness during signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks"; the deterministic variant "should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED, so which variant a given HSM uses by default is a property of that product (module documentation and Security Policy).

## Stateful signatures in an HSM

- NIST SP 800-208 section 8.1 (p. 28): "In order to prevent the possible reuse of an OTS key, when the cryptographic module accepts a request to sign a message, the cryptographic module shall increment the leaf index of the private key (q in LMS, idx in XMSS, idx_sig in XMSSMT) and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value or accepting another request to sign a message." IG C.N Resolution 12 has the tester confirm it. How a product recovers after a power failure is product behaviour (Security Policy and administrator guide).

## What the lab tests (Learn > HSM Firmware Migration)

A PQC-capable HSM is checked in four places. CAVP is NIST's algorithm validation program (tests specified in ACVP documents). CMVP is the cryptographic module validation program whose Validation Authority is a joint effort of NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: a module's certificate lists its approved algorithms and the Security Policy published with it lists its services. A CAST is a cryptographic algorithm self-test run by a validated module; a PCT is a pairwise consistency test on a generated key pair; a CSTL is an accredited testing laboratory.

- Algorithm certificates (CAVP): NIST's ACVP specification drafts (2 October 2026) cover ML-KEM (keyGen, encapDecap), ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer). CAVP overview page: "Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation." and "Due to this structure, ACVTS testing is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP in order to receive a validation certificate." ML-KEM draft section 6.1: "For the encapsulation key check, the server will generate a potentially valid or invalid encapsulation key ek. The IUT SHALL determine if the provided ek is valid based on [FIPS203] Section 7.2." Not covered (ML-DSA draft section 6.2.2): "An ACVP server will not test the zeroization of intermediate values, security strength of the deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs), or incorrect length signatures or public keys." LMS draft section 6.2.2: "ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation." IG C.N Background (last modified September 2024): "CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT." No ACVP specification is published for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS (October 2026).
- Module certificate (CMVP) and Security Policy: CAVP overview page: "For an algorithm implementation to be listed on a cryptographic module validation certificate as an Approved security function, the algorithm implementation must meet all the requirements of FIPS 140 and must successfully complete the cryptographic algorithm validation process. However, a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms." A Security Policy keeps approved and non-approved items apart (the policy of CMVP #4703 has "Table 10 Approved Services" and "Table 11 Non-Approved Services" and lists non-approved algorithms in its Tables 4, 5 and 6). IG 2.4.A: "the algorithm shall be included in the Security Policy's list of non-approved algorithms allowed in the approved mode of operation with no security claimed (see SP 800-140B). However, the module's certificate shall not include these algorithms as they do not claim any security and are not used to meet any requirement of FIPS 140-3." The question to put to a certificate is whether ML-DSA (or ML-KEM, SLH-DSA, LMS) is among its approved algorithms and which approved services use it.
- Self-tests (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A, last modified 19 August 2026): "The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm." GeneralNote8: "For all algorithms that require a CAST (e.g., approved algorithms, allowed algorithms with a claim of security as permitted by an IG, and legacy algorithms per IG C.M), a CAST shall be performed prior to first time algorithm execution in the approved mode; but CASTs are NOT required (but are certainly permissible) prior to first time algorithm execution in the non-approved mode." ML-KEM: "if the module implements ML-KEM encapsulation, the module shall have a CAST for the ML-KEM encapsulation mechanism." and Note21: "The ML-KEM decapsulation CASTs shall cover both the implicit rejection and (unnamed) non-rejection paths." ML-DSA: "if the module implements digital signature generation, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature generation CAST for either the 'hedged' or 'deterministic' algorithm (per FIPS 204 Section 5.2)." LMS: "If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation." Pairwise consistency test (Additional Comments 1): "Though not a CAST, a pairwise consistency test (PCT) shall be conducted for every generated public and private key pair for the applicable approved algorithm (per ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3)." For ML-KEM the PCT encapsulates a shared secret K with ek and decapsulates with dk, and passes if the two K values are equal. For key pairs generated from stored seeds (FIPS 203, FIPS 204) a PCT is only required prior to the first exportation of the seed or key pair or prior to the first operational use of the key pair after the seed has been generated within the module. IG D.S Scenario 1 (last modified 9 April 2026): "ML-KEM shall be CAVP tested via 'ML-KEM EncapDecap' for all implemented parameter sets (ML-KEM-1024, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768) and functions (Decapsulation, Encapsulation). The module shall implement the encapsulation and decapsulation key checks specified in FIPS 203 Sections 7.2 and 7.3".
- Which submission for a firmware update (CMVP Management Manual version 2.7, 9 April 2026, section 7.1; twelve submission scenarios): "An updated version of a previously validated cryptographic module can be considered for a revalidation rather than a full validation depending on the extent of the modifications from the previously validated version of the module." Full Submission (FS): "If modifications are made to hardware, software, or firmware components that do not meet any of the below revalidation criteria, then the cryptographic module shall be considered a new module and shall undergo a full validation testing by a CSTL and submitted as a FS." Algorithm Update (ALG): "Code or configuration changes are not permitted under this revalidation scenario." CVE: "Changes shall not introduce new features or cryptography". Update (UPDT): "An updated cryptographic module can be considered in this scenario if less than a 30% of security changes were made to the module. Security changes include impacts to: approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM. None of these, assessed individually, can exceed 30% of changes." and "The CMVP upon review, may determine that the changes are >30% and shall be submitted as an FS." The summary table (section 7.1.14) gives UPDT a new certificate and a new sunset date and requires the latest guidance, CAVP testing and, where IG 9.3.A applies, ESV testing. Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA changes the approved algorithms, approved services and self-tests, which are categories counted toward the 30% limit; whether a given release is an UPDT or an FS is decided by the CMVP on the lab's submission.

## Key Standards

- FIPS 140-3 (Cryptographic Module Validation), FIPS 140-2 Historical transition (September 2026), and FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG 10.3.A, IG D.S, IG C.N, IG 12.A)
- CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual (version 2.7, 9 April 2026)
- PKCS#11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard, 3 June 2026)
- FIPS 203/204/205 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)
- NIST SP 800-208 (Stateful Hash-Based Signatures)
- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards, final October 2026)
- CNSA 2.0 (NSA FAQ v2.2 for NSS), EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15 (US federal civilian), and EU PQC Roadmap v1.1

Vendor algorithm availability and validation evidence are shown from shared, product-specific capability records with source links, checked dates and the recorded review state. Availability, approved mode and inclusion on a named CMVP certificate are separate facts; missing records remain unknown. Version-specific documentation examples and integration scenarios do not establish support for another firmware, parameter set or environment.

1. PKCS#11 Key Generation — Generate ML-KEM-768 keypair and compare buffer sizes
In the PKCS#11 Simulator workshop, step through the key generation operation. Observe C_GenerateKeyPair with CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN. Compare the 1,184-byte ML-KEM-768 public key with the 256-byte RSA-2048 modulus.
The raw ML-KEM-768 public key is about 4.6 times the width of the RSA-2048 modulus. Measure the serialized key before sizing the application buffer. The HSM keeps this private key sensitive and non-extractable.
2. ML-DSA Signing in HSM — Sign and verify with ML-DSA-65
Continue through the PKCS#11 Simulator to the signing operations (Steps 5-6). Observe the message-based signing calls (C_MessageSignInit / C_SignMessage and C_MessageVerifyInit / C_VerifyMessage) using CKM_ML_DSA. Note the hedged signing output and the 3,309-byte signature size. Expand the on-prem vs cloud notes to see vendor support status.
ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes (vs 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256 — a 51x increase). Hedged signing (rnd drawn from a random source instead of all zero) is the default variant in FIPS 204 section 3.4, which says the deterministic variant "should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose (CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED), so which variant a given HSM uses by default is a product property: look for it in the module documentation and Security Policy rather than assuming it.
3. Vendor Selection — Given requirements, identify matching vendors
Open the Vendor Comparison workshop. Filter vendors by "production" status. For a regulated financial institution requiring FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and ML-KEM + ML-DSA support, identify which vendors meet those criteria. Expand each vendor row to check hybrid support and side-channel countermeasures.
Thales Luna 7 and Entrust nShield 5 both offer ML-KEM and ML-DSA in firmware on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware, but the module certificates differ: Luna T7 #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS among its approved algorithms, while the nShield 5s certificates #5329 and #4745 list no PQC algorithm. # KMS & PQC Key Management — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

In classical cryptography, algorithms like RSA served dual purposes—they could handle both encrypting data and signing documents. The post-quantum standards split these roles by algorithm: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is for key establishment, while ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are for signatures.

## Why It Matters

In this module's reading, organizations use ML-KEM for key encapsulation (envelope encryption) and ML-DSA for digital signatures, so one key no longer does both jobs as an RSA key could. This fundamentally complicates how large enterprises manage their secret keys.

## The Key Takeaway

Because post-quantum algorithms cannot share one key pair between encryption and signing, organisations that used dual-purpose keys will need more keys, and must upgrade their centralized Key Management Systems (KMS) architecture. This infrastructure must be capable of generating, storing, and transmitting these new, significantly larger quantum-safe keys.

## What's Happening

Cloud providers and Hardware Security Module (HSM) vendors are redesigning their platforms to support the massive throughput required to manage millions of these new, specialized Post-Quantum keys securely.

Some key services also hold back a key until the program asking for it proves what it is running. Azure Key Vault's Secure Key Release and AWS KMS used with Nitro Enclaves both work this way: the service checks a signed attestation against a policy before it releases or allows use of the key.

FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), NIST SP 800-227 (KEM recommendations), NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 (Rev. 5 final; Rev. 6 IPD), NIST IR 8547 (final Oct 2026), NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 (NSS), EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15 (US federal civilian), EU PQC Roadmap v1.1, FIPS 140-3 (CMVP; FIPS 140-2 Historical Sept 2026), PKCS#11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard, June 2026), KMIP 2.1 / v3.0 draft, RFC 9180 (HPKE), RFC 10024.

In classical cryptography, algorithms like RSA served dual purposes—they could handle both encrypting data and signing documents. The post-quantum standards split these roles by algorithm: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is for key establishment, while ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are for signatures.
In this module's reading, organizations use ML-KEM for key encapsulation (envelope encryption) and ML-DSA for digital signatures, so one key no longer does both jobs as an RSA key could. This fundamentally complicates how large enterprises manage their secret keys.
Cloud providers and Hardware Security Module (HSM) vendors are redesigning their platforms to support the massive throughput required to manage millions of these new, specialized Post-Quantum keys securely.

Enterprise key escrow and key recovery
Scope of key backup and recovery
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 defines backup storage as storing copies of key information that is also available in normal operational storage during a key's cryptoperiod.
Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General (Revision 6), 2025-12
Section 7.2.2.1 Backup Storage, PDF p. 129
Section 8.5.2 Key Recovery, PDF p. 147
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 states that private signature keys generally shall not be archived and are usually undesirable to back up because of non-repudiation concerns, though backing up a CA's private signature key may be justified in some circumstances.
Appendix B.2.1 Private Signature Key, PDF p. 167
Access controls, auditing, and multiparty custody
Once an organization decides which keys are eligible for recovery, operational controls govern how recovery systems restrict access, record activity, and divide custody.
PCI PIN Security Requirements v3.1 requires unencrypted secret or private keys, including keys loaded from individual key components or shares, to be entered using dual control and split knowledge.
PCI PIN Security Requirements v3.1 — ROC Reporting Template, 2021-03
Control Objective 4, Requirement 12 and 12-1, PDF p. 62
NIST SP 800-152 describes key splitting as a multiparty control technique in which n key splits are provided to n trusted entities so the key cannot be formed unless k entities agree.
A Profile for U.S. Federal Cryptographic Key Management Systems, 2015-10
Section 6.7.5 Key Splitting, PDF p. 76
Recovering older keys also involves rules for using expired keying material and unwrapping keys protected under legacy mechanisms.
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 requires that recovered archived keys with expired cryptoperiods must not apply cryptographic protection, must be erased from the cryptographic process after use, and must remain archived as long as needed.
Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths (Rev 3), 2024-10
Section 10 Key Wrapping, PDF p. 36

# KMS & PQC Key Management

## Topics Covered

- PQC key management fundamentals (algorithm separation, key size explosion)
- NIST SP 800-227 KEM guidance for key wrapping
- Envelope encryption with ML-KEM vs RSA-OAEP
- Complete envelope sizes in the module's HKE1 project sample format (not a standard): 284 bytes for RSA-2048, 1,191 bytes for ML-KEM-768 and 1,218 bytes for X25519+ML-KEM-768, counted from one layout (18-byte header, key ID, salt, info, ephemeral key, KEM ciphertext, 40-byte AES-KW wrapped DEK); the older 1,088 + 40 = 1,128 and 32 + 1,088 = 1,120 figures count data fields only, not a complete envelope
- Hybrid key wrapping (X25519+ML-KEM-768, ECDH P-256+ML-KEM-768, ECDH P-384+ML-KEM-1024, X-Wing); these KMS key-wrap combiners differ from the TLS hybrid groups of RFC 10024
- KMS provider PQC landscape (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, OpenBao, Thales CipherTrust, Fortanix DSM)
- PQC key rotation strategies and compliance deadlines (CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 for NSS, NIST IR 8547 final Oct 2026, EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15 for US federal civilian, EU PQC Roadmap v1.1)
- Enterprise architecture patterns for multi-cloud PQC key management
- KMIP v3.0 (Committee Specification Draft 02; KMIP 2.1 is the OASIS Standard) protocol operations and PQC key type enumerations; Re-key vs Re-key Key Pair and the key lifecycle
- Cross-provider key sync via KMIP orchestration
- Exchanging keys with a third-party HSM or KMS: AWS KMS import is RSA wrapping only, ML-KEM Decapsulate returns the secret to the caller, Google Cloud KMS quantum-safe import uses HPKE (Preview), Azure BYOK uses CKM_RSA_AES_KEY_WRAP; no quantum-safe import path is described for AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault
- AWS KMS policy controls for PQC keys (kms:KeySpec, kms:KeyUsage on CreateKey); hybrid post-quantum TLS to KMS is a client setting, verified in CloudTrail (tlsDetails.keyExchange)
- Key release to an attested workload: Azure Key Vault Secure Key Release (Managed HSM and Premium) releases an HSM-protected, exportable key to an attested trusted execution environment when the Microsoft Azure Attestation claims satisfy a release policy set when the key is created; AWS KMS works with AWS Nitro Enclaves, and its key-policy condition keys (kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384 and kms:RecipientAttestation:PCR) make KMS allow operations with a key only if the enclave provides a signed attestation document whose measurements match the policy. In both cases the key service relies on the attestation and on the hardware behind it (see the Confidential Computing module). Compare the other trust hardware in Step 6 of Architect Quantum Impact (/learn/arch-quantum-impact?tab=workshop&step=5).

Do not confuse these key-wrap combiners with the TLS hybrid groups. X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (RFC 10024) protect a live connection: the two secrets are concatenated and fed to the TLS 1.3 key schedule. KMIP 3.0 (Committee Specification Draft 02, 7 May 2026) adds the FIPS 203, 204 and 205 algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) and includes Encapsulate and Decapsulate operations; KMIP 2.1 is the OASIS Standard. Use KMIP as the abstraction layer for cross-provider key operations: Create Key Pair, Get (with a wrapping specification), Re-key Key Pair, Revoke and Destroy. KMIP has no Wrap, Unwrap or Rotate operation. Re-key replaces a symmetric key; Re-key Key Pair replaces a key pair, which is what an ML-KEM or ML-DSA key needs. A key moves Pre-Active, Active, Deactivated, Destroyed (Compromised is a further state), and Destroy applies only to Pre-Active or Deactivated objects, so an Active key is first deactivated with Revoke.

// AWS KMS — PQC: ML-KEM key establishment aws kms create-key \ --key-spec ML_KEM_768 \ --key-usage ENCAPSULATE_DECAPSULATE aws kms get-public-key --key-id alias/kem-key // The third party encapsulates with its own library (AWS-LC, OpenSSL, // Bouncy Castle): encapsulation key -> ciphertext + 32-byte shared secret. aws kms decapsulate \ --key-id alias/kem-key \ --encapsulation-algorithm ML_KEM \ --shared-secret-ciphertext-blob fileb://ct.bin // Decapsulate returns the 32-byte secret in plaintext to your application. // In the application: wrapping_key = HKDF-SHA-256(secret, salt, info) // wrapped_dek = AES-256-KW(wrapping_key, DEK)

This is the KMS-wrap combiner of this module, one of the choices SP 800-227 Section 4.6 allows. TLS's X25519MLKEM768 group (RFC 10024) concatenates the same two secrets, ML-KEM first, and feeds them to the TLS 1.3 key schedule, so it is a different construction.
HKE1 Sample Envelope: Every Byte Counted
HKE1 is this module's own binary layout. It is not HPKE, X-Wing, a TLS structure or any provider's wrapped-key format. It is the complete stored or transmitted object: an
-byte header (magic, mode, suite and six field lengths) followed by the fields below. Recipient key provisioning, private keys, shared secrets, HTTP/TLS framing and any hex or base64 text encoding are outside it, and a hex or base64 length is a different number. A receiver parses these bytes alone and unwraps the DEK; the sizes here are counted from the same layout it parses.
The 40-byte wrapped DEK is AES-256-KW (RFC 3394): the 32-byte key plus an 8-byte integrity block, with no separate nonce or tag. The hybrid feeds ML-KEM secret first, then X25519, into HKDF-SHA-256. This section introduces enterprise key backup and recovery.
Skill in implementing enterprise key escrow systems
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 defines key recovery as retrieving or reconstructing a key from key backups or archives to process cryptographically protected information.
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 recommends deciding whether key recovery is required on a case-by-case basis, weighing continuity of operations against the risk of exposing keying material and protected information.
Section 7.2.2.2 Key Recovery Function, PDF p. 132
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 requires a federal key-recovery system to protect key-recovery information against unauthorized disclosure, verify request sources, provide only requested and authorized information, and limit access to key-recovery information, audit trails, and authentication data.
Appendix B.1.4 Key-Recovery Systems, PDF pp. 165-166
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 6 requires a federal key-recovery system to provide an audit trail that prohibits modification and must not contain recovered keys or passwords used by the system.

Key rotation with PQC algorithms introduces significant bandwidth and storage overhead. Enterprises must plan phased rotation aligned with compliance deadlines from
At 300 TLS certificates, comparing the 256-byte RSA-2048 modulus with the 2,017 raw bytes of an ML-DSA-65 public key and an uncompressed P-256 point gives a difference of about 528 KB. Measure the complete encoded certificate chains, including signatures, to budget rotation bandwidth.

KMIP has no Rotate operation. Re-key creates a replacement for a symmetric key, and Re-key Key Pair creates a replacement key pair, which is what an ML-KEM or ML-DSA key needs. Providers expose rotation in their own ways, so existing wrapped data keeps working only while the old key or version is kept.
Key Vault key auto-rotation applies to the key types the service offers (RSA and EC); it has no post-quantum key type to rotate.

A post-quantum algorithm counts as FIPS-validated only if the module's own FIPS 140-3 validation covers it. The CMVP implementation guidance for FIPS 140-3 says a module's ML-KEM shall show compliance with FIPS 203 and SP 800-227, and treats a hybrid scheme as an approved ML-KEM plus one or more other algorithms combined through an approved key combiner (SP 800-227 Section 4.6.2). Whether a hybrid counts as FIPS-approved depends on the module's validated algorithms and the current guidance, so check both and the Security Policy of the module that runs your keys. The AWS KMS HSM certificate (CMVP #4884) lists no ML-DSA or ML-KEM algorithm, and a key service's FIPS level does not carry over to a newer key type by implication.
A key service can also decide when a key is used: only after the workload shows what it is running. Two documented examples. Azure Key Vault Secure Key Release (Managed HSM and Premium) releases an HSM-protected, exportable key to an attested trusted execution environment when the Microsoft Azure Attestation claims satisfy a release policy set when the key is created. Some key services also hold back a key until the program asking for it proves what it is running. Azure Key Vault's Secure Key Release and AWS KMS used with Nitro Enclaves both work this way: the service checks a signed attestation against a policy before it releases or allows use of the key.

Large enterprises use millions of digital 'keys' to lock and unlock their data constantly. Managing all of these keys is handled by a central, highly secure brain called a Key Management System (KMS).
To rapidly prepare for the quantum computing threat, this entire central brain must be fully upgraded. It needs to securely generate and flawlessly track completely new, mathematically heavy Post-Quantum keys alongside the older ones. Upgrading a KMS guarantees that a sprawling company won't lose absolute control of its massive digital key ring during the transition.
KMS & PQC Key Management — In Simple Terms
Because post-quantum algorithms cannot share one key pair between encryption and signing, organisations that used dual-purpose keys will need more keys, and must upgrade their centralized Key Management Systems (KMS) architecture. This infrastructure must be capable of generating, storing, and transmitting these new, significantly larger quantum-safe keys.

RSA-OAEP transports a key chosen by the sender. ML-KEM Encaps outputs a shared secret key that is ready to use; a key-derivation method may be applied if the keying material needed differs from the KEM output (SP 800-227 Sec. 4.3).
OAEP (RFC 8017 §7.1) as a general construction has never been proven secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA2), and Victor Shoup showed that no such proof exists in the general case, but RSAES-OAEP itself was later proved CCA2-secure by Fujisaki, Okamoto, Pointcheval, and Stern.
Never use PKCS#1 v1.5 for key transport — it is broken by the 1998 Bleichenbacher padding oracle attack, which lets an adaptive attacker decrypt RSA ciphertexts without the private key using ~1 million queries to a validating server.
RSA-OAEP is a direct encryption scheme — the decrypted output IS the DEK. No KDF step is needed. This step is skipped in the classical path.
The shared secret from ML-KEM.Encaps() is a 256-bit value that can be used directly as a shared secret key for symmetric cryptography. This demo applies HKDF with info="kms-envelope-v1" to bind the wrapping key to this protocol and version.
HKDF binds it to a context string (info="kms-envelope-v1") so the derived key is bound to that context, which may prevent the same keying material from being derived for other contexts (RFC 5869 §3.2).
AES-KW (RFC 3394), AES-KWP (RFC 5649), or AES-GCM (SP 800-38D) wraps the 32-byte DEK.
AES-KW: 40 B output — 8-byte A value (ICV, RFC 3394 §2.2.3, not a nonce) + 32 B; deterministic, no nonce management required; SP 800-38F §6.2 purpose-built for key wrapping.
AES-KWP: 40 B for the 32-byte DEK — 8-byte AIV (RFC 5649 §3: constant 0xA65959A6 + 32-bit length) + plaintext padded with zero octets to a multiple of 8; handles key lengths that are not multiples of 8 octets.
AES-GCM: 48 B output (32 B plaintext + 16 B auth tag embedded at the end) plus a 12-byte nonce stored separately (visible in the hex blobs above).
The 12-byte nonce is the SP 800-38D §5.2.1.1 recommended IV length for GCM. The 16-byte tag provides authenticated integrity — the ciphertext blob already contains it.
IV uniqueness is a requirement in GCM (SP 800-38D §8): if even one IV is ever repeated under a key, the implementation may be vulnerable to forgery attacks. Prefer AES-KW when nonce management is operationally risky.
Store the KEM ciphertext alongside the wrapped DEK.
Both paths recover the same 32-byte DEK. The byte-for-byte comparison of the DEK before wrapping and after unwrapping is the check that decides this result; the 3-byte KCV (CKA_CHECK_VALUE) is a separate diagnostic fingerprint, and two different keys can share one.
What rotation costs depends on what changes. Rotating the KEK means re-wrapping each existing DEK under the new KEK; the encrypted data blocks stay untouched. A new DEK protects only data written from then on: ciphertext already encrypted under the old DEK can be decrypted only with that DEK, so replacing the DEK that protects existing ciphertext means decrypting and re-encrypting that data.
That is envelope encryption's operational advantage at scale: KEK rotation touches small wrapped keys, not the data.

# Quantum Key Distribution — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) shares encryption keys using the fundamental laws of quantum physics—specifically the "no-cloning theorem"—rather than relying on difficult mathematical equations.

## Why It Matters

Standard Post-Quantum Cryptography relies on math problems that we _hope_ quantum computers cannot solve. QKD is entirely different: it offers "information-theoretic security" because measuring a quantum state physically disturbs it, immediately exposing any eavesdropper on the network.

## The Key Takeaway

Despite its immense security, QKD has severe physical limitations. Standard fiber optic cables max out at roughly 100 kilometers for QKD transmission. Extending this distance requires "trusted nodes" to relay the signal, but compromising any single node exposes all the keys.

This workshop is a classical mock: it draws one random value locally in place of the network call, so nothing here is quantum-generated. In ETSI GS QKD 014 each application (SAE) fetches the key from its own local key manager (KME) over HTTPS with mutual authentication (TLS 1.2 or higher), so the key material travels over a protected local transport, not between the two remote applications.
