• XMSS, XMSS^MT and HSS: no ACVP specification is published for them. The ACVP index at pages.nist.gov/ACVP lists LMS, ML-DSA, ML-KEM and SLH-DSA as its post-quantum entries (checked 23 October 2026). IG C.N, last modified 10 September 2024, says CAVP tests are “available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT”. IG C.O, of the same date, records that “Support for the LMS scheme was added to the ACVTS production server in April 2023” and that “the other schemes (including HSS) remain untestable by the CAVP as of the last modified date of this IG”.
• Every generated key pair also needs a pairwise consistency test. For SP 800-208 keys it “may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation”.
• LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) are listed for digitally signing firmware and software: “All parameters approved for all classification levels. LMS SHA-256/192 is recommended.” “The multi-tree algorithms HSS and XMSSMT are not allowed.” SLH-DSA “is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS”.
A certificate for a module that signs with LMS or XMSS rests on four checks. NIST publishes an algorithm test for LMS (key generation, signing and verification) but no ACVP specification for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS, and the test does not check whether a private key can be exported or a one-time key reused. The module also runs its own self-tests before first use. SP 800-208 requires key generation and signing to stay inside a validated hardware module with Level 3 or higher physical security and no export of private keys; a module that only verifies signatures does not have to meet those hardware rules. For national security systems, NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says a product that only verifies signatures needs algorithm testing (CAVP) alone, while a signer that is itself a national security system must use CMVP-validated hardware, with no waivers. NSA allows LMS and XMSS (all parameters, LMS with SHA-256/192 recommended), not HSS or XMSS^MT, and says SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in national security systems.
Generate real SLH-DSA keys, sign, and verify via PKCS#11 — compare stateless vs stateful.
The Stateful Hash-Based Signatures module covers LMS (Leighton-Micali Signature) and XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme), the most conservative post-quantum signature schemes standardized in NIST SP 800-208. These schemes derive security solely from hash function properties, requiring no new cryptographic hardness assumptions. The module explains Merkle tree signature construction, Winternitz one-time signatures (OTS), the critical state management problem, and the trade-offs between stateful schemes (LMS/XMSS) and stateless alternatives (SLH-DSA). CNSA 2.0 approves all parameters of LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) for digitally signing firmware and software in national security systems and recommends LMS SHA-256/192.
Stateful vs stateless comparison: LMS/XMSS require state tracking and have bounded leaf counts. SLH-DSA needs no persistent leaf counter, but the security claims for FIPS 205's 12 parameter sets assume at most 2^64 messages per key pair (§11). This analysis limit is not an LMS/XMSS-style counter requirement or a prediction of immediate failure beyond the limit. SLH-DSA has larger signatures (8-49 KB); performance depends on the parameter set and implementation.
XMSS, XMSS^MT and HSS: no ACVP specification is published for them (the ACVP index at pages.nist.gov/ACVP lists LMS, ML-DSA, ML-KEM and SLH-DSA as its post-quantum entries, checked 23 October 2026). FIPS 140-3 IG C.N, last modified 10 September 2024, says CAVP tests are "available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT". IG C.O (same date) records that "Support for the LMS scheme was added to the ACVTS production server in April 2023" and that "the other schemes (including HSS) remain untestable by the CAVP as of the last modified date of this IG".
Module self-tests (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A item 5, document updated 19 August 2026): cryptographic algorithm self-tests (CASTs) apply "prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm". A module that implements LMS (or HSS, XMSS, XMSS^MT) signature generation must also implement key generation and have CASTs for both; signature verification needs its own CAST; the HSS CASTs cover the LMS ones and the XMSS^MT CASTs cover the XMSS ones. A CAST for SHA-256 is required; for SHA-256/192 if implemented without SHA-256; for SHAKE256/256; for SHAKE256/192 if implemented without SHAKE256/256 (satisfiable inside the higher-level CASTs). Because testing cost depends on tree height, the CASTs need only exercise the smallest (or any single) supported parameter set, and "It is also not necessary to test both LM-OTS + LMS modes"; a CAST covering the different underlying SHA or SHAKE functions is still required. The pairwise consistency test for SP 800-208 keys "may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation".
CNSA 2.0 (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2, October 2026): LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) are listed for digitally signing firmware and software with "All parameters approved for all classification levels. LMS SHA-256/192 is recommended." HSS and XMSS^MT are "not allowed". SLH-DSA "is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS". Verifier and signer are validated differently. A product that only verifies signatures: "If your product is only verifying signatures, CAVP testing is all that is required." Signers that are NSS "are required to produce signatures according to NIST SP 800-208, which requires hardware validated by NIST's Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), or via other NSA guidance. Waivers for this will not be granted." Signers that are not themselves NSS (for example a commercial vendor's build environment) are "expected to use code in their signature generation processes that is at least at the same operational quality as the code being put on the device, but the only part NSA will validate is that the signature verification code on the device passes CAVP." For products evaluated under a NIAP Protection Profile where signing occurs outside the Target of Evaluation boundary, "if only signature verification is being performed only CAVP validation (not CMVP) will be expected to meet CNSA 2.0 for such products." The FAQ also says signing and state management should be implemented in hardware such as an HSM, and backup flows "must prevent state re-use".

SLH-DSA keeps no counter. A key pair is a very large set of few-time FORS keys; each signature hashes the message with a randomizer, uses part of the digest to select one of them, and authenticates it through the hypertree. A FORS key can be selected again, and its security degrades gradually; the parameter sets are designed for up to 2^64 signatures per key. Because SLH-DSA keeps no counter, a copy of the private key cannot cause the one-time key reuse that NIST SP 800-208 section 9.1 warns about for LMS and XMSS. Signatures made by all copies of a key still count towards the same limit of 2^64 signatures per key (FIPS 205 section 11). FIPS 205 gives no rules for backing up or replicating keys, so follow your module's key-management requirements.
SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, formerly SPHINCS+) signs with a Merkle hypertree whose path proof must be included in full — producing signatures of 7–49 KB depending on the parameter set, versus 1.3–9.3 KB for LMS. # SLH-DSA — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, **FIPS 205**) is NIST's hash-only signature scheme. It doesn't rely on lattices or elliptic curves: its security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions, as well as several related properties of the same hash functions (FIPS 205 section 1.1), and is based on nothing else (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4). If those hash properties hold, SLH-DSA holds.

## Why It Matters

Hash-based signatures were the first quantum-safe construction anyone trusted, but the early designs (LMS and XMSS, both **stateful**) had a brutal operational catch: the signer has to make sure no one-time key is ever used twice, so it must durably keep track of which keys it has already used. Lose that record, even briefly — accidental reboot, accidental restore-from-backup, accidental clone of a VM — and the whole key is compromised. SLH-DSA is **stateless**: the signer pseudorandomly selects a few-time signing key from the message digest instead of following a counter, so there is no leaf counter to persist, which suits distributed systems, serverless functions, and multi-instance HSMs (FIPS 205 section 3). That does not promise that a signing key is never selected twice: each few-time key can safely sign only a small number of messages, and the twelve parameter sets are designed for at most 2^64 signatures per key pair, so planned signing volume across all copies of a key still needs a limit. The price is signature size — anywhere from 8 KB to 50 KB depending on the parameter set — which makes SLH-DSA the bulky but conservative option compared with ML-DSA's lattice signatures of 2,420 to 4,627 bytes (FIPS 204 Table 2).

## The Key Takeaway

Reach for SLH-DSA when you want **the longest, most conservative security argument available** and you don't sign often: root CAs that issue once a year, firmware images stamped at the factory, code-signing certificates for ten-year-life embedded devices. (Note: SLH-DSA is not part of CNSA 2.0 — NSA's FAQ says it "is not approved for any use in NSS"; NSA's picks there are LMS/XMSS for firmware signing and ML-DSA-87 for general signing.) Reach for ML-DSA when signature size or throughput actually matters — TLS handshakes, JWTs, anything high-volume.

## What's Happening

FIPS 205 published in August 2024 with twelve parameter sets across NIST Levels 1, 3, and 5 (e.g. `SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f`). The `-s` variants are smaller signatures / slower signing; the `-f` variants are faster signing / larger signatures. Both the pure mode and the pre-hash mode (HashSLH-DSA) accept an optional context string of up to 255 bytes, and verification must use the same context that signing used. PKCS#11 v3.2 defines the SLH-DSA mechanisms (`CKM_SLH_DSA` and the `CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA` family), and the softhsmv3 build this module drives implements them. Support in other libraries varies by product and release, so check each one's own release notes. Our expectation (no source states it): the size cost makes SLH-DSA impractical at the TLS handshake layer, while it suits root-of-trust artifacts where you sign once and verify for decades.

## How It Is Tested

A validated SLH-DSA module is checked three ways. NIST's algorithm tests (ACVP) cover key generation, signing and verification, and a vendor registers options such as the parameter sets, internal or external interface, pure or pre-hash mode and, for signing, deterministic or hedged mode. The module also runs its own self-tests before first use: signing, verifying and key generation each get one, and if pure and pre-hash modes share the same code, testing one covers both. Finally the algorithm validation is only a prerequisite for the module certificate, not a substitute for it. This module's workshop replays eight published NIST verification cases (valid signatures, and ones NIST says must be rejected) through the in-browser engine; those are reference samples, not an official validation.

# SLH-DSA Module (FIPS 205)

The SLH-DSA module covers FIPS 205 (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard), NIST's standardized stateless hash-based signature scheme. Unlike stateful schemes (LMS, XMSS), SLH-DSA requires no per-key state tracking — it can be safely deployed in distributed, serverless, and multi-instance environments. Security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for the underlying hash functions (SHA-256, SHA-512, or SHAKE256) as well as several related properties of those functions (FIPS 205 §1.1). FIPS 205 §10.2 says that even if it is feasible to compute collisions on them, there is believed to be no adverse effect on the security of SLH-DSA, although applications that require message-bound signatures may be adversely affected if collisions on H_msg are feasible (§11). Likewise, if the input to the signing function is a digest of the content, then collisions on the function used to compute the digest can result in forged messages (§10.2, footnote 19). The module covers the full FIPS 205 specification: WOTS+ one-time signatures, FORS few-time signatures, hypertree construction, the twelve parameter sets from Table 2, context strings for domain separation, deterministic signing mode, and the HashSLH-DSA pre-hash variant.

## Key Concepts

Organizational-control example: set a maximum signing-key lifetime and rotate on schedule; inventory deployments, copies and backups; conservatively estimate aggregate signing volume over that lifetime and revisit changes; preserve the original retirement date after backup restore. These controls document expected use below the analysis bound, not an enforced exact count. This is practical planning guidance, not a FIPS 205-prescribed checklist or sufficient certification evidence by itself.

Keep planned use within the FIPS 205 analysis bound: even one billion signatures per second with the same key would take about 585 years to reach 2^64. Exact technical enforcement is difficult across key copies and devices: a local HSM counter is insufficient, and coordinated accounting must resist backup-restore resets and rollback. No HSM enforcement has been verified in this review. A practical planning approach is to conservatively bound total signing volume across all copies over the key lifetime, far below the limit; this is not a recommendation to add an LMS/XMSS-style per-signature counter.

- SLH-DSA is stateless (FIPS 205 §3): a key pair is a very large set of few-time FORS keys; each signature computes a randomized hash of the message, uses part of the digest to pseudorandomly select one FORS key, and authenticates it with a hypertree signature, so there is no leaf counter as in LMS/XMSS. The security of a FORS key degrades gradually as the number of signatures increases (§8), and the parameter sets are designed for at most 2^64 signatures per key (§11)
- WOTS+ (Winternitz OTS Plus): one-time signature component; signs a message digest by hashing chains of n-byte values; the Winternitz parameter lg_w=4 is fixed in FIPS 205; chain lengths balance signature size vs. hash-round cost
- FORS (Forest of Random Subsets): the few-time signature layer between WOTS+ and the hypertree; signs a k-subset of values using a-level hash trees; parameters (k, a) directly control signature size and security against multi-target attacks
- Hypertree: d layers of XMSS trees, each a Merkle tree of height h/d; the XMSS keys at the lowest layer sign FORS public keys, and the XMSS keys at every other layer sign the XMSS public keys at the layer below (FIPS 205 §7); the public key of the XMSS key at the top layer (PK.root), together with PK.seed, is the SLH-DSA public key (§3)
- The s vs. f tradeoff: -s (small) variants use fewer hypertree layers (lower d) producing smaller signatures but requiring more hash rounds per layer; -f (fast) variants use more layers for faster signing at the cost of larger signatures
- FIPS 205 Table 2 defines twelve parameter sets across three security levels (NIST Levels 1, 3, 5) and two hash families (SHA-2, SHAKE), with signature sizes ranging from 7,856 B (SHA2-128s) to 49,856 B (SHAKE-256f)
- Context strings (FIPS 205 §10.2): an optional byte string bound into the signature; provides domain separation between protocols; verification with a different context string produces CKR_SIGNATURE_INVALID even for a valid (SK, M) pair
- Deterministic versus hedged signing (FIPS 205 §9.2): identical key, message, context and settings produce identical deterministic signatures; hedged signing adds fresh randomness and normally produces different signatures. Both should verify. Comparing signatures demonstrates mode behavior, not random-generator quality or resistance to attacks. Deterministic signing still requires randomness for key generation. Internally opt_rand uses the public PK.seed value, not zeros.
- HashSLH-DSA (FIPS 205 §10.2.2, Algorithm 23): hashes the message with the selected pre-hash function and constructs M' = 0x01 || len(ctx) || ctx || OID_DER || H(M). Context strings of 0–255 bytes are permitted; verification uses the same context (§10.3, Algorithm 25). The live demo now exposes separate signing and verification contexts, empty by default, for pure and fixed-hash pre-hash modes. UTF-8 byte lengths are shown, whitespace is preserved, and overlong inputs are rejected. Tests of the shipped Rust WASM cover matching/mismatched contexts and length boundaries for SHA2-128f pure and SHA-256 pre-hash, plus an upstream pre-hash reference signature. This is not a full conformance claim for every parameter combination.
- Signing capacity: SLH-DSA needs no persistent leaf counter, but FIPS 205 §11 bases the security claims for its 12 parameter sets on at most 2^64 messages per key pair. This is an assumption of the security analysis, not a requirement to persist an LMS/XMSS-style counter, and not a prediction of immediate failure beyond the limit. Absence of a leaf counter does not remove key-management obligations.

## What the lab tests (validation)

The Learn tab (HashSLH-DSA Modes step) has a "What the lab tests" panel with these facts. A validated SLH-DSA module is checked in three separate ways: algorithm tests, the module's own self-tests, and the certificate path. Whether the algorithm may be used at all for national security systems is answered by CNSA 2.0.

- Algorithm tests (NIST ACVP, draft specification of 2 October 2026): SLH-DSA has three modes, keyGen, sigGen and sigVer, all against FIPS 205, each with one test type, AFT (Algorithm Functional Test). keyGen: generate a key pair from the provided seed and key values (SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed); the server provides at least 10 tests for each combination of capabilities. sigGen: generate a valid signature from the provided private key, message, context (external interface testing) and randomness (non-deterministic signing); at least 13 tests for each combination. sigVer: the server makes its tests by modifying a valid signature: a modified message, a modified signature (R, SIGFORS or SIGHT), a signature that is too long or too short, plus the valid case.
- ACVP capability options a vendor registers: parameterSets (any of the 12 names, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s through SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f); signatureInterfaces ("internal", "external"); preHash ("pure", "preHash", described as "Whether SLH-DSA or HashSLH-DSA are supported"), with hashAlgs used if preHash; deterministic (sigGen only), where "A value of 'true' indicates that deterministic signature generation is supported and a value of 'false' indicates that non-deterministic signature generation is supported"; messageLength (8 to 65536 bits, step 8) and contextLength (0 to 2040, step 8) as ranges. sigVer has signatureInterfaces and preHash but no deterministic field.
- Not tested by ACVP, in the specification's words: "that fresh seed values are used for fresh invocations of key generation, that approved deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs) are used with the correct security strengths, that sensitive data is destroyed, that key validation is performed, and that floating point arithmetic is not used."
- Module self-tests (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A item 16, document updated 19 August 2026): for each of signature generation, signature verification and key generation that the module implements, a cryptographic algorithm self-test (CAST) runs before the algorithm's first use in the approved mode. The signature generation CAST is a known-answer test with fixed values compared with a pre-computed signature (SIG); the verification CAST checks that a known signature verifies (returns true); the key generation CAST uses fixed SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed and compares the private key ("as the private key contains a copy of the public key"). Notes 27 and 28: if pure and pre-hash SLH-DSA signature generation (or verification) are both implemented and "they both share the same underlying cryptographic implementations, a CAST on either one of them is sufficient to meet the CAST requirements for both". Note 29: a module that supports both SHA2 and SHAKE parameter sets in the approved mode runs the CASTs on at least two parameter sets, one SHA2 and one SHAKE; a module with one family needs at least one; testing at least one "s" and one "f" set is recommended but not required. Note 30: the CASTs need only exercise the smallest parameter set (lowest height trees) the module supports. The pairwise consistency test for FIPS 205 keys "may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation".
- Certificate path (NIST CAVP page): "Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation." But "a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms." ACVTS testing "is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP", and CAVP "is not responsible for running those test vectors through the implementation". The CASTs are a FIPS 140-3 module requirement set by CMVP guidance (IG 10.3.A), separate from the ACVP tests.
- CNSA 2.0 status (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2, October 2026): "While SLH-DSA is hash-based, it is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS." For national security systems the list of deployment contexts where SLH-DSA's trade-offs are usually acceptable (code signing, firmware attestation) does not apply. The CNSA 2.0 algorithm table lists ML-DSA-87 for digital signatures and LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) for signing firmware and software; see the Stateful Hash Signatures module for how those are validated (verify-only products need CAVP testing alone, signers that are NSS need hardware validated by CMVP or, in the FAQ's words, "via other NSA guidance"; waivers are not granted).

## Workshop Activities

- **Step 1 -- Key Generation & Parameter Explorer**: Generate SLH-DSA key pairs across all twelve FIPS 205 parameter sets; observe how n, h, d, k, a determine key size, signature size, and the security-performance tradeoff
- **Step 2 -- Sign & Verify (Pure + HashSLH-DSA)**: Sign messages with Pure SLH-DSA (CKM_SLH_DSA) and HashSLH-DSA (CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA256); observe the PKCS#11 mechanism change and the pre-hash payload construction
- **Step 3 -- Context Strings & Deterministic Mode**: Demonstrate matching and mismatched contexts using separate fields; empty and a space differ. Expected signature rejection is distinct from an engine error. Explicit deterministic-required and hedged-required signing choices now drive the existing demo. “Sign twice and compare” signs identical inputs twice, compares full signature bytes and verifies both; expandable hex shows both signatures. Saved inputs/mode accompany results. This demonstrates behavior, not RNG quality, attack resistance or certification compliance.
- **Algorithm checks (workshop Steps 1-3)**: the panels are kept apart by the kind of evidence they give. Known-answer checks compare the engine with a value fixed in advance: a SHA-256 NIST sample, and a replay of eight published NIST ACVP sigVer cases (SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s test group 19, test cases 253, 256, 260, 262 and 266; SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s test group 25, test cases 338, 343 and 344; pure SLH-DSA, external interface; from the public NIST ACVP-Server repository, commit 975de31) through the in-browser engine. The valid signatures must be accepted and the ones NIST marks invalid (modified message, modified signature R or SIGFORS, signature too short or too long) rejected, as NIST's expected result says. The SLH-DSA sign-and-verify rows are functional round trips, not known-answer tests: the engine verifies its own output, so a pass shows the pieces work together and nothing more. The ACVP cases are public reference samples, not vectors issued by an ACVTS test session, so a pass establishes no validation. Pre-hash, internal-interface, key-generation and signature-generation vectors are not run in these panels. The intro of this demo points to Step 4 of this module for the comparison; the LMS checks live in the Stateful Hash Signatures module.
- **Step 4 -- LMS vs XMSS vs SLH-DSA Comparison**: Side-by-side comparison of all three hash-based signature families on key size, signature size, signing speed, state requirement, and deployment model. The size rows name their parameter sets (LMS_SHA256_M24_H10 / LMOTS_SHA256_N24_W4, XMSS-SHA2_10_192, SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s and -192f) and compare size classes, not equal security, because SP 800-208 assigns no NIST category to LMS or XMSS: LMS public key 48 B and signature 1,500 B (RFC 8554: public key 4 + 4 + 16 + m bytes, signature 12 + n(p + 1) + m*h bytes), XMSS 52 B and 1,492 B (RFC 8391), SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s 48 B and 16,224 B, -192f 35,664 B (FIPS 205 Table 2). CNSA 2.0 row (NSA FAQ version 2.2): single-tree LMS and XMSS are approved for firmware and software signing, HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed, and SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in NSS.

## Related Standards

- FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard, August 2024)
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, lattice-based alternative), SP 800-208 (LMS/XMSS stateful counterparts)
- PKCS#11 v3.2: CKM_SLH_DSA, CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA256, CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA384, CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA512, CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHAKE128, CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHAKE256
- CNSA 2.0 (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2, October 2026): "While SLH-DSA is hash-based, it is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS." The CNSA 2.0 algorithm table lists ML-DSA-87 for digital signatures and LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) for signing firmware and software.
- FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance 10.3.A (document updated 19 August 2026): self-test (CAST) requirements for SLH-DSA, item 16
- BSI TR-02102-1 (German Federal Office; recommends SLH-DSA-SHA2-192s or stronger for long-term security)
- ANSSI (PQC position of 2022 and PQC FAQ of 2025): the only post-quantum algorithms for which ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation are the hash-based signatures SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS; the 2022 position estimates they could be used today without hybridisation, however their potential application range is limited (low number of signatures queries or large signature sizes); for the regulated scope the FAQ says hybridisation is mandatory

The tradeoff: SLH-DSA signatures are significantly larger (7,856 to 49,856 bytes, FIPS 205 Table 2, against about 0.8 to 9 KB for LMS across the SP 800-208 parameter sets, by the RFC 8554 byte layout) and signing is slower due to the hypertree traversal. Not tested by ACVP, in the specification's words: “that fresh seed values are used for fresh invocations of key generation, that approved deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs) are used with the correct security strengths, that sensitive data is destroyed, that key validation is performed, and that floating point arithmetic is not used.”
For each of signature generation, signature verification and key generation that the module implements, IG 10.3.A requires a cryptographic algorithm self-test (CAST), run before the algorithm's first use in the approved mode. The signature generation CAST is a known-answer test: fixed values go in and the output is compared with a pre-computed signature (SIG). The verification CAST checks that a known signature verifies (returns true). The key generation CAST uses fixed SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed and compares the private key; the public key need not be compared, “as the private key contains a copy of the public key”.
A validated SLH-DSA module is checked three ways. NIST's algorithm tests (ACVP) cover key generation, signing and verification, and a vendor registers options such as the parameter sets, internal or external interface, pure or pre-hash mode and, for signing, deterministic or hedged mode. The module also runs its own self-tests before first use: signing, verifying and key generation each get one, and if pure and pre-hash modes share the same code, testing one covers both. Finally the algorithm validation is only a prerequisite for the module certificate, not a substitute for it. This module's workshop replays eight published NIST verification cases (valid signatures, and ones NIST says must be rejected) through the in-browser engine; those are reference samples, not an official validation.

SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, FIPS 205) is NIST's hash-only signature scheme. It doesn't rely on lattices or elliptic curves: its security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions, as well as several related properties of the same hash functions (FIPS 205 section 1.1), and is based on nothing else (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4). If those hash properties hold, SLH-DSA holds.
FIPS 205 published in August 2024 with twelve parameter sets across NIST Levels 1, 3, and 5 (e.g. `SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f`). The `-s` variants are smaller signatures / slower signing; the `-f` variants are faster signing / larger signatures. Both the pure mode and the pre-hash mode (HashSLH-DSA) accept an optional context string of up to 255 bytes, and verification must use the same context that signing used. PKCS#11 v3.2 defines the SLH-DSA mechanisms (`CKM_SLH_DSA` and the `CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA` family), and the softhsmv3 build this module drives implements them. Support in other libraries varies by product and release, so check each one's own release notes. Our expectation (no source states it): the size cost makes SLH-DSA impractical at the TLS handshake layer, while it suits root-of-trust artifacts where you sign once and verify for decades.

HashSLH-DSA (FIPS 205 §10.2.2, Algorithm 23): hashes the message with the selected pre-hash function and constructs M' = 0x01 || len(ctx) || ctx || OID_DER || H(M). Context strings of 0–255 bytes are permitted; verification uses the same context (§10.3, Algorithm 25). The live demo now exposes separate signing and verification contexts, empty by default, for pure and fixed-hash pre-hash modes. # Identity & Access Management PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Identity and Access Management (IAM) combines passwords, symmetric authenticators, public-key signatures, key exchange, and policy checks. Protocols such as SAML, JWT, and Kerberos use different combinations of these mechanisms.

## Why It Matters

Adversaries are actively capturing and storing these secure exchanges today. Kerberos is the highest priority risk: breaking a captured PKINIT exchange could expose that client's session key for as long as its ticket is valid; forging tickets for any account is a Golden Ticket, which needs the KRBTGT key and is a classical key-theft attack.

## The Key Takeaway

Public-key token signatures may need a post-quantum migration, but there is no universal rollout date or rule assigning ML-DSA parameter sets by token lifetime or application type. Choose algorithms and deployment profiles from applicable standards, vendor support, security requirements, interoperability, and measured size/performance constraints. HMAC-signed tokens have a different quantum-risk analysis.

## What's Happening

Our product catalogue records no post-quantum token signing for most of the identity providers this module lists, so Active Directory teams should plan the Kerberos PKINIT upgrade once Microsoft documents it; protect the KRBTGT key separately.

Identity and Access Management (IAM) systems decide who can access an organization's services and data. They combine several mechanisms, including passwords, symmetric authenticators, public-key signatures, key exchange, and policy checks.
The quantum risk depends on which mechanism is used. A sufficiently capable quantum computer could break widely used RSA and elliptic-curve signatures, enabling forged signed tokens or certificates. It could also break classical public-key key exchange, exposing recorded TLS traffic. These are different risks: forging an identity token is not the same as decrypting stored data. Symmetric mechanisms such as HMAC and AES need separate analysis and are not made equivalent to RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography. A migration plan should inventory protocols, token lifetimes, trust relationships, product support, and the data or access each mechanism protects.

LM-028.summary:
# Identity & Access Management with PQC

Module covering PQC migration for enterprise IAM systems including JWT/SAML token signing, Active Directory, and zero trust identity.

## Key Topics

- JWT, SAML, OIDC token signing migration to ML-DSA (FIPS 204)
- Active Directory, LDAP, Kerberos quantum vulnerabilities and quantum risk scores
- IAM vendor roadmaps: Okta, Microsoft Entra, PingFederate, ForgeRock, CyberArk, HashiCorp Vault, Keycloak
- Zero trust identity architecture with PQC across five pillars
- Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) risk for Kerberos PKINIT exchanges and the TLS channels that carry identity traffic; signed JWT, SAML and OIDC tokens carry a forgery risk, not an HNDL risk (NIST IR 8547)
- **Identity Proxy Architecture**: Bridging PQC-migrated Identity Providers (IdP) with classical Service Providers (SP) by translating SAML signatures (ML-DSA to RSA).

## Workshop Steps

1. IAM Crypto Inventory — audit 8 components by quantum risk level and migration priority
2. Token Migration Lab — compare RS256/ES256 vs ML-DSA-44/65/87 signature sizes and header changes
3. Directory Services Analyzer — AD/LDAP/Azure AD quantum risk scoring and attack scenario analysis
4. Vendor Readiness Scorer — score IAM vendors across token signing, MFA, API security, roadmap dimensions
5. Zero Trust Identity Architect — assign migration years to 5 identity pillars and generate a phased roadmap
6. Identity Proxy Simulator — test authentication flows by translating ML-DSA SAML assertions into classical RSA assertions for legacy downstream apps.

## Algorithms Covered

- ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204, NIST Level 2) — short-lived tokens, OAuth2 access tokens
- ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, NIST Level 3) — enterprise IAM, SAML, OIDC ID tokens
- ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204, NIST Level 5) — government/NSS, CNSA 2.0
- ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203) — hybrid TLS for LDAPS, MSAL, Kerberos PKINIT
- SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — stateless audit log signing

## Regulatory Context

- CNSA 2.0: the NSA FAQ (v2.2, October 2026) quotes CNSSP 15 as requiring CNSA 2.0 algorithms in all new NSS acquisitions by 1 January 2027 and mandating their use by 31 December 2031, unless otherwise noted; ML-DSA-87 is the signature algorithm for general signing, with LMS or XMSS for software and firmware signing
- NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026; systems that follow NIST standards): deprecates quantum-vulnerable RSA/ECDSA/EdDSA signatures at every key size of 112-bit security and up (RSA-2048 and RSA-3072, used to sign many IAM tokens, included) after 2030 and disallows them after 2035
- PCI DSS v4.0.1: cryptographic inventory required (Req. 12.3.3)
- DORA (EU): ICT risk management including IAM cryptographic risk

Module: iam-pqc
A CRQC recovers the PKINIT reply key from a recorded Kerberos exchange. PKINIT (RFC 4556) delivers that key either by Diffie-Hellman or by RSA encryption to the client public key; both can be broken by Shor's algorithm. The reply key decrypts one AS-REP, which carries that client's TGT session key, so the attacker can act as that one client only while the TGT is valid (10 hours by default in Active Directory). It does not reveal the KRBTGT key, so it does not by itself let the attacker forge tickets for other accounts or compromise the domain.
Illustrative future target, not a current setting: Microsoft lists Kerberos on its Windows post-quantum roadmap but gives no version or date for PQC in PKINIT, and we found no documented client or Group Policy setting for it. Windows Server 2025 offers ML-KEM and ML-DSA through its cryptography APIs; that is not PKINIT support. Before planning a rollout, check Microsoft documentation for the supported algorithms, how clients and domain controllers negotiate them, and validation evidence for the cryptographic module. Meanwhile, inventory PKINIT and smart-card logon dependencies.
NTLM challenge-response uses password-derived hashes and does not provide forward secrecy. Captured challenge-response material can support offline password guessing; that is a classical credential risk, not an RSA/ECC quantum break. A quantum computer does not directly reveal a password or domain credentials from an NTLM exchange.
Disable NTLM via Group Policy (Network Security: Restrict NTLM). Enforce Kerberos authentication exclusively. Use Protected Users security group for privileged accounts.
Golden Ticket via KRBTGT Key Theft
A Golden Ticket is forged with the KRBTGT account long-term key, which attackers obtain by classical means such as credential dumping on a domain controller. With that key they can create Ticket Granting Tickets for any user, including Domain Admins. This is a key-theft attack: a quantum computer adds no step to a key that is already stolen, and post-quantum PKINIT would not stop it.
Protect and monitor domain controllers and privileged accounts. After a suspected theft, reset the KRBTGT password twice and wait at least the maximum ticket lifetime (10 hours by default) between resets, as Microsoft guidance describes. Watch for anomalous ticket requests with your detection tooling.
When LDAP traffic uses LDAPS or StartTLS, the TLS key exchange and server authentication protect that session. If a recorded session used only quantum-vulnerable key establishment and is later decrypted, its directory data could be exposed. LDAP deployments that do not use TLS do not have this recorded-session HNDL scenario; their traffic is already exposed to network observers.
Configure and verify TLS according to the OpenLDAP build and TLS library actually deployed. Do not assume that upgrading to OpenSSL 3.x alone enables hybrid ML-KEM: hybrid key establishment depends on the TLS library, version, provider/build configuration, and peer support. Check the negotiated group with the library’s supported diagnostics and test both client and server paths.
An LDAP simple bind carries the bind distinguished name and the password as an OCTET STRING in the BindRequest (RFC 4511, RFC 4513). Nothing encodes or hides the password: without TLS it is readable on the network, and inside TLS it is protected only by that session. If the session was recorded and its key exchange is later broken, the bind credentials are exposed. HTTP Basic is different: it Base64-encodes user-id:password, and Base64 is a reversible encoding, not protection (RFC 7617).
Prefer SASL/GSSAPI (Kerberos-backed) over simple bind. Require StartTLS or LDAPS before any simple bind. Where no client needs them, disable anonymous and simple bind (slapd.conf: disallow bind_anon bind_simple).
JWT Token Forgery via RSA Key Recovery
A CRQC could derive a private signing key from the published public key material and forge identity tokens.
Watch for a Microsoft announcement of post-quantum Entra token signing (we found none). Short token lifetimes (for example 15-minute access tokens) limit how long a stolen token can be replayed, but do not stop forgery, because an attacker with a recovered signing key mints fresh tokens. Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) lets Entra tell a resource to stop honouring tokens of a real session after events such as account disablement; it is not a signature check and is not a defence against forged tokens.
Refresh tokens are bearer credentials whose lifetime and storage depend on the identity provider and client. For Microsoft Entra, defaults vary by client type; for example, refresh tokens last 24 hours for single-page applications and 90 days for other scenarios, and replacement tokens inherit the original expiration. Token theft or replay is an access-token security risk, not a consequence of decrypting a recorded TLS session; TLS key establishment is the HNDL exposure for the channel carrying tokens.
Enable refresh token rotation and revocation. Use device-bound tokens with TPM attestation (Windows Hello for Business). Monitor for anomalous refresh token usage via Entra ID Sign-in logs.
SAML 2.0 assertions signed with RSA-SHA256 can be replayed if the signature is quantum-forged. This would allow an attacker to authenticate as any user to all SAML federated relying parties.
Set assertion validity windows to the shortest duration compatible with clock skew and application behavior; there is no universal five-minute requirement. Enforce audience, recipient, NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter, and request correlation/replay checks as applicable. Changing from SAML to OIDC does not by itself provide a PQC migration path; both depend on the signing algorithms and TLS used by the deployment.
Analyze quantum vulnerabilities in Active Directory, OpenLDAP, and Azure AD / Entra ID. Understand quantum risk scores and migration paths for each service.

Open the Identity Proxy simulator (Step 6) and trace a PQC-signed SAML assertion from the IdP through the translation proxy to a legacy service provider. Identify which hop is protected by ML-DSA and where the quantum-safe trust boundary ends.

# Code Signing PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Code signing formally guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. As software supply chains grow increasingly complex with hundreds of open-source dependencies, verifying who built an update is critical to stopping injected malware.

## Why It Matters

A sufficiently capable quantum computer could use Shor's algorithm against exposed RSA or elliptic-curve public keys. If it recovered a trusted signing key, an attacker could forge signatures that relying systems might accept under their configured trust policies. This is a future forgery risk; it does not let an attacker instantly impersonate every publisher or bypass key rotation, revocation, and verifier policy.

## The Key Takeaway

PQC algorithms such as ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are designed to resist known quantum attacks on public-key signatures. For a concrete raw-signature comparison, ML-DSA-44 is 2,420 bytes and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s is 7,856 bytes, versus a 64-byte raw ECDSA P-256 signature: about 38× and 123× respectively. These ratios exclude certificates, container formats, and transparency proofs. Signatures may be checked at download, installation, boot, launch, or during transparency verification, so measure storage, bandwidth, and verification costs for the actual workflow.

## What's Happening

Sigstore's keyless flow binds a short-lived certificate to a developer identity, so developers do not manage a long-lived artifact-signing key. A post-quantum transition still involves signing clients, certificate issuance, artifact formats, transparency-log operations, trust-root distribution, and verifier support; upgrading a central service alone does not make existing artifacts or clients post-quantum.

Sources: [NIST FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final), [NIST FIPS 205](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final), [Sigstore documentation](https://docs.sigstore.dev/).

is the cryptographic mechanism that guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. Every operating system, package manager, and app store relies on digital signatures to ensure that binaries have not been tampered with after publication.
A compromised signing key is a skeleton key to every machine that trusts it.
Attackers compromised the Orion software build system, so a vulnerability shipped inside Orion updates released between March and June 2020; it was not present in the source code repository. CISA reports that the adversary added a malicious version of an Orion library to the software lifecycle and that it was then signed by the legitimate SolarWinds code signing certificate. SolarWinds believed fewer than 18,000 customers may have had an installation of the affected Orion products.
Mandiant found that 3CX’s network was first breached through malicious software downloaded from the Trading Technologies website: a tampered X_TRADER installer, signed with the subject “Trading Technologies International, Inc”. The attackers then distributed a trojanized 3CX DesktopApp (18.12.416 and earlier) that 3CX offered for download. Mandiant called it the first time it had seen one software supply chain attack lead to another.
A malicious party gained access to Codecov’s Bash Uploader script and modified it without authorization, so it exported CI-related information to a third-party server. That information could include API keys, deploy keys, passwords and authentication tokens.
These attacks exploited trust in code signing infrastructure. Post-quantum code signing must protect not only against today's threats but also against future signature forgery: once a quantum computer can derive private keys from public keys, an attacker could sign code that verifiers still accept. Unlike
, which concerns encrypted data recorded today, this risk needs nothing to be collected in advance, because public keys and certificates are already public.
Supply Chain Risk & the Quantum Amplifier
The attacks above are symptoms of deeper structural problems in modern
. As software composition grows more complex, the attack surface expands — and quantum computing threatens to break the cryptographic foundations that hold it together.
The Software Supply Chain Attack Surface
Applications pull in many transitive dependencies. Each dependency is a link in the trust chain — and each link is only as strong as its maintainer’s signing practices.
You audit your direct dependencies, but do you audit their dependencies? A malicious package five levels deep in the dependency tree can execute arbitrary code in your application.
Build systems, artifact registries, and deployment pipelines are high-value targets. The Codecov Bash Uploader attack shows that a script a pipeline downloads and runs can be modified at its source, and the modified script then runs in the CI systems that fetch it. The SolarWinds compromise shows that checking only the source repository is not enough, because the vulnerability came from the build system. Every step from source code to deployed binary is an attack surface.
An SBOM documents what goes into a build, but build provenance answers how it was built and who built it. Without cryptographically signed provenance, an attacker can substitute a tampered artifact that passes all hash checks.
Frameworks like SLSA and in-toto provide structured approaches to supply chain verification — defining security levels based on how much of the build pipeline is cryptographically attested. Their guarantees depend entirely on the strength of the underlying signatures.
How Quantum Computing Changes the Equation
Today, supply chain attackers get malicious code signed or distributed by compromising a build system, an identity or a signing key. A quantum-capable adversary would add another route: deriving a private key from its public key, without breaking into the key holder.
Today's attacks work through build-system or identity compromise as well as key theft (the SolarWinds and 3CX cases above). A quantum attacker running
could add a further route for any key whose algorithm it can break (RSA, ECDSA): deriving the private key from the public key, with no infiltration of the key holder. It would not remove the other routes.
Signed binaries and certificates carry only public keys, so nothing secret has to be harvested. The risk is future forgery: once a quantum computer can derive private keys, an attacker could create new signatures that chain to certificates verifiers still trust, or artifacts that appear signed by a publisher whose old key is still accepted.
is reserved for encrypted data. For signatures the controls are to stop trusting vulnerable keys in time, and to validate old signatures with timestamps and archive evidence that remain trustworthy.
An attacker holding the private key of a
or of an issuing CA could issue certificates for any subject that CA vouches for, and so sign software as
publisher under it. A publisher's own leaf key is scoped to that publisher, while an issuing CA key is scoped to everything the CA issues (limited only by constraints in the chain). If a quantum computer can break the CA's algorithm, that CA private key can be derived from its public key.
Scale: One Key vs a Shared Weakness
A stolen leaf signing key compromises one publisher, and a stolen issuing CA key compromises everything that CA vouches for. A quantum break of
: every key of that algorithm becomes derivable from its public key once a capable computer exists. That does not mean one event recovers all private keys — each key must still be attacked separately, at the attacker's cost — but migration cannot be limited to one publisher.
SCADA controllers, medical devices, avionics, and industrial infrastructure deployed today with classical signatures may stay in service for many years. Their signature verification is often hard to update, so they may still be running when a quantum computer can forge classical signatures. Until the verifier is updated, those signatures offer no protection against firmware forgery.

Whenever you download an app or a software update, your computer checks a hidden digital signature. Think of this signature like a tamper-evident wax seal from the software creator (like Microsoft or Apple). If the seal is unbroken, your computer knows the update is safe to install.
However, a sufficiently capable quantum computer could threaten the public-key algorithms used by some signing systems. If an attacker could recover a trusted publisher's private key from its public key, they could create a forged signature. Whether a device accepts that software still depends on its verification policy, trust store, revocation checks, and update controls.
Post-quantum signature standards such as ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are designed to resist known quantum attacks, but deployment requires compatible signing tools, formats, trust services, and verifiers. They reduce a cryptographic risk; they do not by themselves prove that software is safe or identify who created it without a trusted certificate and policy.

Code Signing PQC — In Simple Terms
Code signing formally guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. As software supply chains grow increasingly complex with hundreds of open-source dependencies, verifying who built an update is critical to stopping injected malware.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer could use Shor's algorithm against exposed RSA or elliptic-curve public keys. If it recovered a trusted signing key, an attacker could forge signatures that relying systems might accept under their configured trust policies. This is a future forgery risk; it does not let an attacker instantly impersonate every publisher or bypass key rotation, revocation, and verifier policy.
PQC algorithms such as ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are designed to resist known quantum attacks on public-key signatures. For a concrete raw-signature comparison, ML-DSA-44 is 2,420 bytes and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s is 7,856 bytes, versus a 64-byte raw ECDSA P-256 signature: about 38× and 123× respectively. These ratios exclude certificates, container formats, and transparency proofs. Signatures may be checked at download, installation, boot, launch, or during transparency verification, so measure storage, bandwidth, and verification costs for the actual workflow.
Sources: [NIST FIPS 204](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final), [NIST FIPS 205](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final), [Sigstore documentation](https://docs.sigstore.dev/).

Code Signing & Supply Chain Security
A forged signature on a software update is a supply-chain compromise at scale — code signing is one of the few PQC migrations where the attacker doesn't need to break today's crypto, just tomorrow's.

LM-029.summary:
# Code Signing & Supply Chain Security Module

This module teaches post-quantum code signing and software supply chain security. Code signing is the cryptographic mechanism that guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. Every operating system, package manager, and app store relies on digital signatures to verify that binaries have not been tampered with after publication. The module covers supply chain attack case studies (SolarWinds, 3CX, Codecov), the quantum threat amplifier for supply chains, PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS), certificate chain architecture, package manager signing status, Sigstore keyless signing, and secure boot/firmware signing with CNSA 2.0 timelines.

## Key Concepts

- **Supply chain attacks**: SolarWinds (2020, Orion software build system compromised; the vulnerability shipped in updates released March to June 2020 and was not in the source code repository; CISA reports the malicious Orion library was then signed by the legitimate SolarWinds code signing certificate; fewer than 18,000 customers may have had an installation), 3CX (2023, Mandiant: the compromise began with a tampered X_TRADER installer signed by Trading Technologies International, Inc, which led to a trojanized 3CX DesktopApp; the first software supply chain attack Mandiant had seen lead to another), Codecov (2021, Bash Uploader script modified without authorization to export CI-related information)
- **Quantum amplifier for supply chains**: Quantum computers transform supply chain risk from key theft to key forgery via Shor's algorithm; an adversary able to derive a publisher's private key from its public key could forge that publisher's signatures. Signed files are not encrypted, so harvest-now-decrypt-later does not apply to the signature; the risk is future forgery while the public key is still trusted (the update channel that delivers a file is assessed separately); a quantum-compromised Root CA key affects the entire ecosystem simultaneously
- **Classical vs PQC code signing algorithms**: ECDSA P-256 raw signature (64 B), RSA-4096 signature (512 B), ML-DSA-44 signature (2,420 B), ML-DSA-87 signature (4,627 B), SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signature (7,856 B). The 38–123× comparison is for these specific raw signature sizes versus raw ECDSA P-256 and excludes certificates, artifact framing, and transparency proofs. Verification frequency and performance depend on the consumer workflow; measure them rather than assuming one check per install.
- **Code signing certificate chains**: Root CA (ML-DSA-87, strongest), Intermediate CA (ML-DSA-65), end-entity Code Signing Certificate (ML-DSA-44, EKU OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.3, 1-year validity); PQC timestamping (RFC 3161) requires PQC-capable TSAs
- **Package manager signing**: RPM supports hybrid ML-DSA-87+Ed448 in RHEL 10.1. npm registry signatures use ECDSA P-256, while npm provenance and PyPI attestations use Sigstore. Sigstore ML-DSA identifiers remain experimental; its separate opt-in PQC public instance is targeted for mid-2027, not currently available.
- **Sigstore keyless signing**: Identity-based trust with short-lived Fulcio certificates and Rekor transparency entries. A PQC transition also requires compatible signing clients, certificate and artifact handling, transparency-log operations, trust-root distribution, and verifiers; central-service upgrades alone do not migrate clients or existing signatures.
- **Secure boot and firmware signing**: Trust chain from immutable root of trust (ROM/TPM) through UEFI Secure Boot, OS kernel, to runtime firmware; firmware keys have 10-20 year lifetimes making them priority PQC migration targets
- **CNSA 2.0 mandate**: NSA permits ML-DSA-87 or the stateful LMS/XMSS schemes specified by SP 800-208 for firmware/software signing in National Security Systems; NSA's 2022 category guidance says prefer CNSA 2.0 signing from 2025 and use it exclusively by 2030 (superseded for planning by the dates in NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2). FAQ version 2.2 mandates CNSA 2.0 algorithms for NSS by 2031 unless otherwise noted; 2035 is the separate NSM-10 objective.
- **LMS vs ML-DSA for firmware**: LMS offers compact signatures (2.5 KB) and tiny public keys (56 B), fast verification (~0.1 ms), CNSA 2.0 compliant, but requires stateful monotonic counter; ML-DSA is stateless but has larger signatures (3.3 KB) and public keys (1.9 KB)

## Workshop Activities

1. **Binary Signing**: Sign a file hash with ML-DSA and verify the signature interactively
2. **Certificate Chain Builder**: Build a complete PQC code signing certificate chain (Root CA, Intermediate CA, end-entity)
3. **Package Signing**: Simulate RPM-style ML-DSA-87+Ed448 hybrid package signing
4. **Sigstore Flow**: Walk through keyless signing workflow including OIDC authentication, Fulcio certificate issuance, and Rekor transparency log recording
5. **Secure Boot Chain**: Explore firmware signing trust chain with LMS, XMSS, and ML-DSA across boot stages

## Related Standards

- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
- NIST SP 800-208 (LMS/HSS and XMSS)
- NSA CNSA 2.0 guidance for firmware/software signing
- RFC 3161 (Internet X.509 PKI Time-Stamp Protocol)
- IETF composite signatures draft (hybrid classical + PQC)
- Sigstore (Fulcio, Rekor, Cosign)
- SLSA and in-toto supply chain verification frameworks

The developer logs in via GitHub/Google/Microsoft OIDC. The identity provider issues a JWT that Fulcio uses to bind an identity to a certificate. This step is algorithm-agnostic.
ECDSA P-256 keypair (ephemeral, in memory)
A short-lived keypair is generated in memory on the signing machine. The private key is destroyed shortly after signing. Private key: ECDSA P-256 = 32 bytes, ML-DSA-65 = 4,032 bytes. The ML-DSA-65 public key is 1,952 bytes.
X.509 cert with ECDSA P-256 public key
X.509 cert with ML-DSA-65 public key
Fulcio issues a certificate binding the OIDC identity (e.g., "name@example.com") to the ephemeral public key. The certificate is short-lived (valid for 10 minutes) and published to a certificate transparency log.
The artifact (e.g., container image, npm package) is hashed (SHA-256) and the hash is signed with the ephemeral private key. This is the core signing operation.
Rekor entry with ECDSA signature (~200 bytes total)
Rekor entry with ML-DSA-65 signature (3,309 B + ~300 B ≈ 3,600 bytes total)
The signature, certificate, and artifact hash are recorded in Rekor, an immutable, append-only transparency log. Each entry gets a unique log index and UUID. Once recorded, the entry cannot be modified or deleted.
The ephemeral private key is destroyed shortly after signing, so there is no long-term artifact-signing key to protect, rotate, or revoke. The certificate expires within minutes; the transparency log's signed timestamp lets a verifier check later that the signature was made while the certificate was valid.
Verify ECDSA sig + expected identity and issuer + cert chain to trust root + Rekor inclusion
Verify ML-DSA-65 sig + expected identity and issuer + cert chain to trust root + Rekor inclusion
Verification checks four things: (1) the signature is valid for the artifact hash under the public key in the certificate; (2) the certificate's identity and OIDC issuer match the identity and issuer the verifier expects, which the verifier must supply as policy (for example cosign's --certificate-identity and --certificate-oidc-issuer); (3) the certificate chains to Fulcio's root, taken from a trust root that verifiers must obtain and keep current (Sigstore distributes it, with Rekor's public key, using TUF); and (4) the Rekor entry carries an inclusion proof and a signed timestamp showing the signature was made while the short-lived certificate was valid. Keyless signing removes long-lived artifact-signing keys; it does not remove trust-root distribution or the need for an identity policy.
Step through the 7 stages of Sigstore keyless signing. Compare how classical ECDSA and PQC ML-DSA-65 differ at each stage.
Classical vs PQC Sigstore: Size Impact
The primary impact is on Rekor log storage (each entry grows ~18x). For individual developers, the difference is negligible — signing and verification remain sub-second.
What Sigstore Changes in a PQC Migration
Every developer manages long-term private keys, so PQC migration means generating new keys, updating signing configurations, and distributing new public keys or certificates.
Developers hold no long-term artifact-signing keys to replace, because each signature uses an ephemeral key. Migration is still not automatic: the signing client must generate keys and request certificates for the new algorithm, Fulcio and Rekor must support it, and verifiers must support it and obtain updated trust roots and an identity policy. Signatures already made stay as they were.
This walkthrough simulates the Sigstore keyless signing flow with realistic data structures. Sigstore is backed by the OpenSSF under the Linux Foundation. The ML-DSA-65 view illustrates how a post-quantum flow could look; check Sigstore's documentation for what it currently supports. The transparency log entries shown are for educational purposes only.

LM-030.curious:
### What This Is About

The eIDAS 2.0 regulation mandates that all 27 EU member states provide citizens with a European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet by 2026. These wallets use formats like mdoc and SD-JWT to allow selective disclosure of attributes (e.g., proving age without revealing a birthplace) across a pan-European trust framework.

### Why It Matters

The OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI specifications use classical ECDSA (P-256) signatures in most of their examples for issuing attestations and binding identities to devices. If an attacker leverages a quantum computer to forge these signatures, they can create perfectly valid but counterfeit credentials, enabling total identity impersonation and fraud across the entire European Union.

### The Key Takeaway

The text of eIDAS 2.0 and of the EUDI wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) that we checked contains no occurrence of “quantum.” FIPS 204 says ML-DSA is believed to be secure against adversaries with a large-scale quantum computer, and FIPS 205 says SLH-DSA is designed to resist attacks from one.

### What's Happening

The eIDAS 2.0 framework requires all 27 EU member states to deploy EUDI Wallets by 2026. As of October 2026, quantum-safe signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA) are not required, and ETSI says its cryptographic suites specification (TS 119 312 V2.1.1, June 2026) is incomplete for the EUDI Wallet, with an update in preparation.

eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation EU 2024/1183) mandates every EU member state issue an EUDI Wallet. Person Identification Data (PID) is the credential a national PID Provider issues after identity verification; other attestations do not require it. Two credential formats carry that data: mso_mdoc (ISO 18013-5, CBOR, proximity via NFC/BLE) and SD-JWT VC (RFC 9901 base SD-JWT, JSON, built for remote/online verification). Selective disclosure lets a holder reveal only chosen attributes — e.g. proving age without revealing a birthplace — which supports data minimisation; whether a request meets GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) still depends on what the verifier asks for and why, and unlinkability needs separate measures such as batch issuance. A Qualified Electronic Attestation of Attributes (QEAA) is an attestation issued by a qualified trust service provider (QTSP). A Qualified Electronic Signature (QES) is an advanced electronic signature created by a qualified signature creation device (QSCD) and based on a qualified certificate; it has the equivalent legal effect of a handwritten signature, and a QES based on a qualified certificate issued in one Member State is recognised in all others (Regulation (EU) No 910/2014, Articles 3(12), 25(2) and 25(3)). The OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI specifications use classical ECDSA P-256 in most of their examples, which a large-scale quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could forge.
EUDI Wallet: inspect a holder’s stored credentials, keys, and activity history. PID Issuer: authenticate as a citizen and receive an mso_mdoc PID credential. University Attestation: obtain an SD-JWT diploma attestation, gated on already holding a valid PID. Relying Party: present selective attributes to a bank to open an account, without the bank ever contacting the issuer. QES (illustrative): a fictional role flow that signs a sample document through a QTSP step and the CSC API. In production tools, look for a qualified certificate issued by a QTSP, a qualified signature creation device (QSCD, which can be a remote QSCD managed by a QTSP), evidence that the signatory has sole control of the signing key, and a qualified trust service doing the signing.

LM-030.summary:
# EUDI Digital Identity Wallet Module

The EUDI Digital Identity Wallet module simulates the European Digital Identity ecosystem established by eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation EU 2024/1183), which mandates all 27 EU member states provide citizens with at least one EUDI Wallet by December 2026. Learners experience the full credential lifecycle -- issuance, presentation, and qualified electronic signing -- through a five-step interactive workshop. The module covers the Architecture Reference Framework (ARF) attestation formats (mso_mdoc and SD-JWT VC, both mandatory, plus optional W3C VCDM v2.0), the layered trust framework (National Trusted Lists, QTSPs, eIDAS Bridge), privacy-by-design principles (selective disclosure, unlinkability, data minimization), and the post-quantum readiness roadmap for European digital identity.

## Key Concepts

- eIDAS 2.0 regulation: entered into force 20 May 2024; mandatory EUDI Wallets by December 2026; private sector acceptance by late 2027; five implementing regulations adopted 28 November 2024 and published in the Official Journal on 4 December 2024
- Person Identification Data (PID): the credential issued by a national PID Provider after identity verification; a Wallet Unit without a PID stays Operational and can still receive other attestations, but cannot present a PID
- Credential formats: mso_mdoc (ISO 18013-5, CBOR binary encoding, optimized for proximity via NFC/BLE) and dc+sd-jwt (the SD-JWT VC profile, draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc, built on base SD-JWT / RFC 9901, JSON text-based, optimized for remote/online verification; the media type was `vc+sd-jwt` until November 2024). In mso_mdoc, the holder's device proves possession of its key with either a device signature (for example ECDSA) or a MAC (HMAC 256/256 over an ECDH-derived key)
- Selective disclosure: only requested attributes are revealed to verifiers; all other claims remain cryptographically hidden, enforcing GDPR Article 5(1)(c) data minimization
- Wallet certification: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2981 requires the wallet's secure cryptographic device (WSCD) to be assessed against assurance level high as a prerequisite to certification under national schemes. When that hardware is provided, directly or indirectly, by the wallet solution and is needed to meet the desired level of assurance, the evaluation also includes a Common Criteria AVA_VAN.5 vulnerability assessment, unless it is duly justified to the certification body that the security characteristics of the wallet secure cryptographic application (WSCA) make a lower assessment level possible while the overall assurance level stays high. The Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA) is used when PIDs and attestations are issued, so that PID Providers and Attestation Providers can check that the wallet's secure cryptographic device meets the relevant requirements
- Qualified Electronic Attestations (QEAA): issued by certified QTSPs (Qualified Trust Service Providers), listed on National Trusted Lists; carry legal weight across all EU member states
- Qualified Electronic Signatures (QES): digital signatures with the legal equivalent of handwritten signatures under eIDAS 2.0; provided by QTSPs using the CSC (Cloud Signature Consortium) protocol
- Trust framework layers: National Trusted Lists (machine-readable registers of QTSPs per member state), QTSPs (issue QEAAs and provide QES), and the eIDAS Trust Framework bridge for cross-border mutual recognition
- Unlinkability: different presentations to different Relying Parties should not be correlatable; addressed through batch-issued credentials and pseudonymous identifiers
- Relying Party verification: banks, employers, and services verify credentials using selective disclosure and cryptographic proofs without contacting the issuer
- Post-quantum readiness: the OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI specifications use ECDSA with SHA-256 on a P-256 key in most of their credential-signing examples. The eIDAS 2.0 regulation text (Regulation (EU) 2024/1183) and the ARF text checked do not mention quantum computing; RFC 9901 leaves the choice of signature algorithm, including post-quantum algorithms "when they are ready", to the application, and ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) says it is incomplete for the EUDI Wallet, with an update in preparation. The EU PQC transition dates — national roadmaps by December 2026, high-risk migration by 2030, full transition by 2035 — come from the NIS Cooperation Group "Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography" (11 June 2025), which implements Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/1101; they are not specified by the EUDI ARF, and the roadmap does not name EUDI Wallets. ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are NIST-standardised post-quantum signatures that could replace ECDSA
- Large-Scale Pilots: Wave 1 (2023-2025) includes DC4EU (education/social security), EWC (travel/organisational identity), NOBID (payments), POTENTIAL (government, SIM registration, mDL, e-health, payments); Wave 2 (2025-2027) includes APTITUDE (travel credentials/banking) and WE BUILD (business identity)

## Workshop Activities

- **Step 1 -- EUDI Wallet**: View the wallet holder's credentials, cryptographic keys, and activity history
- **Step 2 -- PID Issuer**: Authenticate as a citizen and receive a Person Identification Data credential (mso_mdoc format) from the national PID Issuer
- **Step 3 -- University Attestation**: Obtain a Diploma attestation (SD-JWT format) from a university, which requires a valid PID credential as a prerequisite
- **Step 4 -- Bank (Relying Party)**: Present selective identity attributes to a bank to open an account, demonstrating privacy-preserving credential verification
- **Step 5 -- QTSP (QES)**: Sign a document using a Qualified Electronic Signature via a Trust Service Provider, producing a legally binding digital signature

## Related Standards

- `eIDAS-2-Regulation` — eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation EU 2024/1183): legal framework mandating EUDI Wallets for all 27 EU member states by late 2026
- `EUDI-Wallet-ARF` — EUDI Architecture Reference Framework: technical specification for attestation formats and the trust framework. It specifies no PQC migration roadmap — see `EU PQC Recommendation` for the transition dates
- `ISO-18013-5-mDL` — ISO/IEC 18013-5:2021: mso_mdoc credential format (CBOR binary, proximity via NFC/BLE) and the `org.iso.18013.5.1` namespace; the EUDI `eu.europa.ec.eudi.pid.1` doctype comes from the ARF PID Rulebook, not from ISO. Sold by ISO, so it carries access_type=paid — named and cited, but never presented as a free download
- `RFC-9901-SD-JWT-VC` — RFC 9901: Selective Disclosure for JWTs (base SD-JWT); the SD-JWT VC credential profile is the separate draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc (JSON text, optimised for online verification)
- `OpenID4VCI-Spec` — OpenID4VCI (Final): credential issuance protocol used by all EUDI PID and attestation issuers
- `OpenID4VP-Spec` — OpenID4VP (1.0 Final, July 2025): credential presentation protocol for relying party verification. Queries use DCQL; the earlier DIF Presentation Exchange syntax was removed before 1.0
- `CSC-API-v2-Spec` — Cloud Signature Consortium API (V2.2, November 2025): remote QES signing protocol used by QTSPs under eIDAS 2.0
- `ETSI-EN-319-411` — ETSI EN 319 411: QTSP requirements and audit scheme for qualified trust service providers. Note the server-signing/QSCD standards (EN 419 241 series, EN 419 221-5) are CEN deliverables, not ETSI
- `EU PQC Recommendation` — NIS Cooperation Group Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the PQC transition (11 June 2025), implementing Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/1101: the source of the Dec 2026 / 2030 / 2035 dates
- `FIPS 204` (ML-DSA) and `FIPS 205` (SLH-DSA): NIST post-quantum signatures that could replace ECDSA in credential issuance and QES signing. The workshop's known-answer tests for them are illustrative: the EUDI Architecture and Reference Framework and the OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP specifications define no post-quantum profile

The EU PQC transition dates — national roadmaps by December 2026, high-risk migration by 2030, full transition by 2035 — come from the NIS Cooperation Group "Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for the Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography" (11 June 2025), which implements Commission Recommendation (EU) 2024/1101; they are not specified by the EUDI ARF, and the roadmap does not name EUDI Wallets. ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are NIST-standardised post-quantum signatures that could replace ECDSA
`FIPS 204` (ML-DSA) and `FIPS 205` (SLH-DSA): NIST post-quantum signatures that could replace ECDSA in credential issuance and QES signing. The workshop's known-answer tests for them are illustrative: the EUDI Architecture and Reference Framework and the OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP specifications define no post-quantum profile

Use the QTSP provider (Step 5) to sign a document with a Qualified Electronic Signature. Note which algorithms the QTSP uses for signature creation. Then evaluate: why does QES require SCAL2 (Sole Control Assurance Level 2), and what makes a QTSP 'qualified' under eIDAS 2.0? Which ETSI standard governs QTSP requirements?
QES requires SCAL2 because the signing key must be under the sole control of the signatory — the QTSP must ensure no third party (including the QTSP itself) can sign on the user's behalf without their active authorisation. QTSPs that issue qualified certificates follow ETSI EN 319 411, while remote QES signing with SCAL2 is governed by the CEN standards for server signing (the remote QSCD combines a signature activation module under the CEN protection profile EN 419 241-2 with a cryptographic module certified against EN 419 221-5 — those standards come from CEN/TC 224, not ETSI); QTSPs are listed on National Trusted Lists. The CSC API v2 (Cloud Signature Consortium) standardises the remote signing protocol.

In a production EUDI Wallet, activation begins with the Wallet Provider issuing a WUA. This process: (1) generates a key pair in the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD), (2) binds the wallet instance to the user's device, and (3) proves to PID Providers and Attestation Providers that the wallet is genuine, unmodified, and running on certified hardware. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2981 requires the WSCD to be assessed against assurance level high as a prerequisite to certification under national schemes. When that hardware is provided, directly or indirectly, by the wallet solution and is needed to meet the desired level of assurance, the evaluation also includes a Common Criteria AVA_VAN.5 vulnerability assessment, unless it is duly justified to the certification body that the security characteristics of the wallet secure cryptographic application (WSCA) make a lower assessment level possible while the overall assurance level stays high. LM-031.curious:
### What This Is About

CI/CD pipelines use classical cryptography in some signatures, certificates, and key exchanges. Each has a different quantum risk and migration path; for example, TLS key exchange affects recorded-payload confidentiality, while artifact signatures affect long-term authenticity.

### Why It Matters

Some IaC configurations and software supply-chain signatures still use classical public-key algorithms. Post-quantum migration depends on support across the signing tool, identity or trust service, artifact format, and verifier; a signature change alone does not prevent every infrastructure compromise.

### The Key Takeaway

Automation is the only way to manage PQC correctly at scale. Platform teams should use Policy-as-Code via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno to block classical algorithms at cluster admission, and check which monitoring sources can report certificate algorithms (expiry metrics alone do not carry the key algorithm) to watch for algorithmic drift.

### What's Happening

Sigstore’s October 2026 architecture proposal describes a separate, initially opt-in PQC public service, with mid-2027 as a target. That proposal does not mean current cosign or Notation releases provide ML-DSA signing and verification; verify the specific tool and trust path before planning a migration.
