LM-054.curious:
# MLS — Group Messaging (Curious Explorer)

Signal made one thing famous: end-to-end encrypted chat. But Signal's
ratcheting math only works well for two people. Make it a group of 100,
and every message has to be encrypted 100 times. A group of 1000? Forget
it.

Messaging Layer Security (MLS) is a newer IETF standard (July 2023) that
solves this. Instead of a chain of pairwise locks, MLS arranges members
as leaves of a binary tree. Each branch holds a secret known only to the members below it. When you add a friend, or rotate a key, only the nodes on your path up the tree change, so the work grows with the logarithm of the group size — O(log N) — instead of with the group size.

The next chapter is post-quantum: ML-KEM and ML-DSA suites are in IETF
at draft -07 (November 2026), and the IESG has been asked to publish them.

This module covers:

- How TreeKEM gives forward secrecy + post-compromise security at scale
- How HPKE encrypts path updates between members
- How our OpenMLS provider keeps signature keys as PKCS#11 v3.2 token objects
  (softhsmv3 here, a software token in the same process; production deployments require hardware HSM isolation and assurance evidence) — returning opaque handles rather than raw key bytes to OpenMLS

Play with the TreeKEM visualizer in the Workshop tab and see how each
Add / Remove / Update operation lights up only the affected path.
LM-054.full:
Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420), which uses HPKE and provides efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and, conditionally, post-compromise security (once a committed fresh leaf key replaces the compromised one) for groups from two to thousands. In this module's illustration, an openmls provider holds signature keys as token objects of a PKCS#11 module (a software token in this sample).
Steps: treekem; provider-arch
lesson:
Group messaging at scale, with PQC custody
Asynchronous group key agreement via TreeKEM. Forward secrecy + conditional post-compromise security (once a committed fresh leaf key replaces the compromised one) with O(log N) Commit cost.
(1 November 2026) proposes eleven hybrid and pure ML-KEM cipher suites. The first eight retain traditional signatures. Their post-quantum confidentiality claim covers passive attackers.

When member i sends a Commit (add / remove / update operation), they refresh every node on their direct path with fresh HPKE keys and encrypt the new path secrets to the resolution of each node so the right subset of the group learns the new secrets.
Key schedule — from group secret to keys
Each AEAD application message uses a per-member, per-generation key derived from the encryption secret via a per-leaf hash ratchet. Lose any one message key, and the rest are still safe.
Cryptographically the schedule is RFC 9180-style HPKE labelled extract/expand. Every Extract is one HMAC; every Expand is iterated HMAC. In our PKCS#11 provider those HMACs all run inside the HSM.
How our HSM provider plugs into OpenMLS
OpenMLS — the only production-grade open-source MLS implementation in active use — talks to crypto through a single trait, `OpenMlsCrypto`. The trait has ~15 functions: hash, HMAC, HKDF extract/expand, AEAD seal/open, signature key generation, sign, verify, HPKE seal/open/setup/derive.
HPKE for the X25519 + SHA-256 + AES-128-GCM suite runs end-to-end through the HSM: ECDH via `CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE`, HKDF via PKCS#11 HMAC, AEAD via `CKM_AES_GCM`. Wire-interop with `hpke-rs` (the reference) is verified in both directions by integration tests.
A parallel path is the hybrid combiner: a traditional and a PQ MLS session run in parallel and combined through a PSK exported from the PQ session. This is the path most enterprise messaging vendors are watching, because it lets them ship MLS today and turn on PQ when their HSM fleet is ready, without re-keying.
Status snapshot (8 November 2026, from the drafts' datatracker pages): the PQ ciphersuite draft is an Active Internet-Draft at -07 (1 November 2026; the list of eleven suites is unchanged from -06) and its IESG state is "Publication Requested". The MLS extensions framework (`draft-ietf-mls-extensions`) is an active working-group draft at -11 (2 November 2026). As checked on 30 October 2026, the combiner draft (-02, 22 October 2025) is expired; its WG state is "Waiting for WG Chair Go-Ahead, Revised I-D Needed - Issue raised by WGLC". Check the datatracker pages for the current state.

LM-054/s:mls-overview.full:
The Messaging Layer Security protocol (RFC 9420) provides asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and, conditionally, post-compromise security (once a committed fresh leaf key replaces the compromised one) for groups from two to thousands. Our
MLS (RFC 9420) provides asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups from two to thousands, using TreeKEM: every member is a leaf of a binary tree, and a Commit that carries a path refreshes the sender's direct path with fresh HPKE keys, advancing a shared epoch secret that the whole group derives its next application keys from. Recovery from a compromised member is conditional: it starts only when the group processes a Commit that replaces that member's leaf key with a fresh one the attacker never saw. `draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites` (-07, 1 November 2026; datatracker on 8 November 2026: IESG state "Publication Requested") registers eleven ML-KEM cipher suites, hybrid and pure, the first eight with traditional signatures and the last three with ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87; `draft-ietf-mls-combiner-02` specifies a hybrid path — run a traditional and a PQ MLS session in parallel and combine them by importing a secret exported from the PQ session as a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) into the traditional session.
Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420, July 2023) is the IETF's protocol for efficient asynchronous group key establishment, giving groups from two to thousands of participants forward secrecy AND post-compromise security.
RFC 9420 describes the Double Ratchet as the common solution for two parties and sender keys as the common strategy for larger groups, where post-compromise security is difficult to achieve. MLS replaces both with a tree-based key encapsulation scheme — TreeKEM — that provides forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups from two to thousands.
Every member of an MLS group is a leaf of a left-balanced binary tree. Each internal node holds a key pair derived from the path of its descendants. A member knows the secret keys for every node on the path from their leaf to the root.
A Commit that carries a path derives a fresh commit secret from the root path secret and mixes it with the previous epoch's init secret to start the next epoch; application AEAD keys derive from that epoch's secrets (RFC 9420, section 12.4). A Commit that only adds members, injects a PSK or reinitialises may leave out the path; its commit secret is then the all-zero vector, so no fresh secret enters the key schedule.
Forward secrecy needs members to delete old keys: removing past ratchet-tree private keys protects earlier epochs, and deleting each message key after use protects earlier messages (RFC 9420, section 16.6). Post-compromise security is conditional. Suppose an attacker copies Bob's leaf and tree keys at one moment. A message sent by anyone only steps a one-way hash ratchet and adds no fresh randomness. A Commit by another member encrypts its new path secrets to nodes whose private keys Bob, and so the attacker, still holds, so an attacker who sees the Commit can follow it. Recovery begins when the group processes a Commit that replaces Bob's leaf with a fresh key pair whose private key the attacker never saw: Bob's own Commit with a path, or another member's Commit that includes Bob's Update proposal (an Update proposal has no effect until it is committed).
These guarantees model a one-time snapshot of a member's secrets. An attacker who keeps control of Bob's device, or who holds Bob's signature key, can keep reading the new secrets or can impersonate Bob: with the signature key the attacker can create LeafNodes and KeyPackages in Bob's name and, where the application allows external Commits, insert itself into the group. Groups can require a pre-shared key from joiners to raise that cost (RFC 9420, sections 16.5 and 12.4.3.2).
The MLS key schedule (RFC 9420) takes, among its inputs, the previous epoch's init secret, the current epoch's commit secret, and the current epoch's GroupContext object and runs them through a chain of Extract / Expand steps from the KDF to derive the encryption secret, exporter secret, and confirmation key.
MLS RFC 9420 registers seven fixed cipher suites (0x0001 to 0x0007), each pairing a specific DHKEM, KDF, AEAD, hash and signature scheme; MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_AES128GCM_SHA256_Ed25519 is the mandatory-to-implement suite.
Messaging Layer Security (MLS) is a newer IETF standard (July 2023) that solves this. Instead of a chain of pairwise locks, MLS arranges members as leaves of a binary tree. Each branch holds a secret known only to the members below it. When you add a friend, or rotate a key, only the nodes on your path up the tree change, so the work grows with the logarithm of the group size — O(log N) — instead of with the group size.

Each MLS leaf node carries an identity credential. The leaf_node is signed with ML-DSA-65 before being committed to the tree.

# PKI Enrollment Protocols — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Before a device, app, or person can use a digital certificate, it needs to enroll with a Certificate Authority. Enrollment protocols carry a request, public key, proof-of-possession or other authorization, and the issued certificate. Common protocols include **EST** (RFC 7030), **CMP** (RFC 9810), **SCEP** (RFC 8894), and **ACME** (RFC 8555); their workflows and supported key types differ.

## Why It Matters

Post-quantum migration changes key sizes, signature sizes, certificate encoding, and proof-of-possession. The amount of added data depends on the selected algorithms and encoding; it is not a fixed multiplier for every request or certificate. ML-KEM keys cannot sign a PKCS#10 request, so that format's signature proof-of-possession does not apply. RFC 9810 (July 2025) defines CMP methods for KEM-key proof-of-possession, including an encrypted-certificate method in which the client decapsulates, decrypts the issued certificate, and confirms its hash.

## The Key Takeaway

EST and CMP offer different enrollment workflows; SCEP and ACME address other deployment needs. RFCs define protocol mechanisms, while implementation and CA-profile support vary by product and version. The browser workshop exercises a local mock CA and does not establish interoperability with an external CA or production deployment readiness.

## What's Happening

Keyfactor's EJBCA 9.4.2 PQC guide says CMP `encrCert` proof-of-possession for ML-KEM is supported as of EJBCA 9.1; the EJBCA 9.6.2 algorithm table lists ML-DSA support via ACME, EST, and CMP. Verify version, edition, CA profile, and HSM support for a real deployment. Composite ML-DSA is specified by RFC 10073, with its security caveats. Composite ML-KEM remains an Internet-Draft at revision 23 (October 14, 2026), submitted to the RFC Editor queue as a Proposed Standard; it is not yet an RFC.

Sources: [RFC 10073](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10073.html), [Composite ML-KEM draft status](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem/), [EJBCA 9.4.2 PQC guide](https://docs.keyfactor.com/ejbca/9.4.2/post-quantum-cryptography-keys-and-signatures), and [EJBCA 9.6.2 supported algorithms](https://docs.keyfactor.com/ejbca/9.6.2/supported-algorithms).

# PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST and CMP)

## Overview

The PKI Enrollment Protocols module covers EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport, RFC 7030) and CMP (Certificate Management Protocol, RFC 9810, July 2025, which obsoletes RFC 4210 and adds support for KEM keys). These are the two protocols that actually carry a certificate request from a subscriber to a Certificate Authority and deliver the issued certificate back. The module covers what each protocol is, how they handle proof-of-possession for both signing keys and non-signing KEM keys, and how the standards have been updated for post-quantum cryptography. The workshop runs a real end-to-end CMP IR exchange in the browser: an in-process OSSL_CMP_SRV_CTX parses the CRMF cert template from the inbound IR, builds a fresh X509 with the requested ML-DSA-65 or ML-KEM-768 public key, signs it with the mock CA's ML-DSA-65 key, returns a real PKIMessage IP back through the same in-process transport. The separate key-update exercise sends KUR, recovers the encrypted KUP certificate, validates its key and issuing chain, and completes explicit certConf/PKIConfirm. A separate ML-DSA-65 signer authorizes that update; the ML-KEM key proves possession through recovery and confirmation. Both roles run locally with fictional materials and no external CA connection.

## Key Concepts

- **EST (RFC 7030, October 2013)** — Enrollment over Secure Transport; HTTPS-based; client POSTs a base64-encoded PKCS#10 CSR to `/.well-known/est/simpleenroll`; server returns base64-encoded PKCS#7 SignedData containing the issued cert; transport is TLS (TLS 1.1 or later in RFC 7030; RFC 8996 raises the minimum to TLS 1.2); proof-of-possession is the signed CSR itself (works for ML-DSA, does not work for ML-KEM)
- **CMP (RFC 4210, 2005 — obsoleted by RFC 9810 in July 2025)** — Certificate Management Protocol; HTTP-based with `application/pkixcmp` content type (RFC 9811, which obsoletes RFC 6712); richer state machine with Initial Request (`ir`), Cert Request (`cr`), Key Update Request (`kur`), Revocation Request (`rr`), General Message (`genm`)
- **CMP message structure** — PKIMessage = PKIHeader + PKIBody + PKIProtection; PKIHeader carries sender/recipient DN, transaction ID, sender/recip nonces, senderKID; PKIBody carries the actual request (CRMF for cert requests); protection follows RFC 9810 §5.1.3 (shared-secret MAC, DH key pairs, signature, key encapsulation or multiple protection); this module explains the shared-secret MAC and signature options
- **CRMF (Certificate Request Message Format, RFC 4211; updated for KEM POP by RFC 9883)** — the payload inside a CMP cert-request body; carries the CertTemplate (subject, publicKey, validity, extensions) plus proof-of-possession field
- **Proof-of-possession (POP)** — proves the requester actually holds the private key matching the public key in the request; RFC 9810 §5.2.8 defines `raVerified` (the Registration Authority vouches), a signature proof (POPOSigningKey) and, for keys that cannot sign, POPOPrivKey choices (`encrCert` and `challengeResp` as subsequent messages, `agreeMAC` and `encryptedKey`); this module demonstrates signature proof, encrypted-certificate recovery with explicit hash confirmation, and the separate pre-authorized raVerified initial-enrollment path
- **RFC 9810 (July 2025) — Internet X.509 PKI: Certificate Management Protocol (CMP)** — adds KEM-aware proof-of-possession via encrCert mode; obsoletes RFC 4210; enables CMP enrollment of ML-KEM and other KEM keys that cannot sign
- **RFC 9881** — Algorithm Identifiers for ML-DSA in X.509 PKI; defines the OIDs the CA uses in its signatureAlgorithm field when signing certs with ML-DSA
- **RFC 9935** — Algorithm Identifiers for ML-KEM in X.509 PKI; defines OIDs for ML-KEM-512/768/1024 in subjectPublicKeyInfo; makes pure ML-KEM certs spec-conformant
- **RFC 9909** — Algorithm Identifiers for SLH-DSA in X.509 PKI; companion to RFC 9881 for stateless hash-based signatures
- **RFC 9936** — Use of ML-KEM in CMS; downstream consumer of ML-KEM certs in S/MIME
- **RFC 9629** — KEM algorithms in CMS (KEMRecipientInfo); upstream of RFC 9936
- **Composite ML-DSA (RFC 10073)** defines composite signature algorithms for X.509/PKIX and includes a security caveat: not SUF-CMA secure against quantum adversaries. The **Composite ML-KEM** X.509 document is active Internet-Draft -23 (2026-10-14), submitted to the RFC Editor queue as a Proposed Standard, not yet an RFC. This workshop issues separate parallel certificates and does not create a composite certificate.
- **PBM-MAC protection (RFC 9810 §5.1.3.1)** — Password-Based Message Authentication Code; shared-secret protection mode where the requester and CA share a one-time secret; HMAC over the PKIMessage header + body
- **Signature-based protection (RFC 9810 §5.1.3.3)** — the sender possesses a signature key pair and signs the PKI message; PKIProtection contains the signature value and protectionAlg is a digital signature AlgorithmIdentifier
- **Implicit confirm vs explicit certConf** — CMP normally requires a second round trip where the EE confirms it received the cert; if both sides agree, this can be skipped via the `implicitConfirm` extension in the IR header
- **In-process server (workshop architecture)** — the workshop's `cmp_simulation.c` shim connects a real `OSSL_CMP_CTX` client to a real `OSSL_CMP_SRV_CTX` server via `OSSL_CMP_CTX_set_transfer_cb`; both ends run in the same WASM process exchanging real PKIMessages without sockets, mirroring how `tls_simulation.c` connects TLS client and server via memory BIOs
- **Mock CA root** — generated once per browser via `generate_mock_ca_root` C shim: `EVP_PKEY_Q_keygen` for the ML-DSA-65 keypair, then `X509_sign(cert, key, NULL)` for self-signing (NULL md because ML-DSA refuses hash-then-sign); the result is cached in IndexedDB for the initial-enrollment steps. The key-update exercise creates its own fresh fictional CA and signing identity, leaving that cached CA untouched
- **EJBCA product scope** — Keyfactor's 9.4.2 PQC guide says CMP `encrCert` POP for ML-KEM is supported as of EJBCA 9.1; the 9.6.2 supported-algorithms table lists ML-DSA over ACME, EST and CMP. Product/version/edition, CA profile and HSM support must be checked for each deployment.
- **Tested server capability** — EJBCA 9.6.3 interoperability covered ML-KEM-768 issuance and renewal using a separate ML-DSA-65 signing identity. Its acknowledgment accepted an incorrect certificate-confirmation hash in the test, so it is not used as proof of hash binding. The Hub exercise uses the opt-in modified CMP server that rejects incorrect confirmation; evaluate this behavior explicitly in production CA tooling.
- **Illustrative deployment pattern** — parallel chains: one PQC certificate (ML-DSA-65 EE → ML-DSA-65 root) + one classical certificate (ECDSA-P256 EE → ML-DSA-65 root), both for the same end-entity, a pattern this module uses while composite deployment and Composite ML-KEM (draft-23) adoption remain in progress; we found no source naming who deploys it. Both leaves chain to the ML-DSA-65 sample CA, so the ECDSA subject key does not make that chain usable by a classical-only validator

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 6 steps:

1. **Generate End-Entity Key** — uses `openssl genpkey` to create an ML-DSA-65 (or ML-KEM-768) keypair in the WASM filesystem; selected algorithm flows through to subsequent steps
2. **CMP Initial Request (ir)** — drives the real in-process CMP exchange via the `execute_cmp_simulation` shim: server callback parses the CRMF, builds a fresh X509 with the requested public key, signs with the CA's ML-DSA-65 key, returns a real PKIMessage IP; client validates protection and writes the issued cert to the FS; transcript shows every internal event from both sides
3. **EST simpleenroll** — exercises the EST-specific request/response shapes: PKCS#10 CSR via `openssl req`, mock CA signs via `openssl x509 -req`, response wrapped in PKCS#7 degenerate SignedData via `openssl crl2pkcs7`; transport is simulated (no real HTTP) because OpenSSL ships no EST client
4. **ML-KEM certificate key update** — provisions a fictional prior enrollment, a separately authorized ML-DSA-65 signing identity and a fresh ML-KEM-768 target key. The signed KUR names the prior certificate; the server checks that enrollment and subject, encrypts the new certificate to the new key, and accepts completion only after the client recovers it, validates it and confirms its hash. The alternative prior-enrollment case is rejected and failed operations return no certificate. This is actual CMP key update using the opt-in modified sample server, not a separate shared-secret comparison.
5. **Parallel certificate issuance** — issues a separate ECDSA-P256 subject certificate under the same ML-DSA-65 CA and compares it with the ML-DSA subject certificate. These are separate certificates, not a composite certificate; the ML-DSA issuer signature still requires a verifier that supports it. The sample helps learners distinguish subject-key choice, issuer signature and consumer compatibility. It links to RFC 10073 and the current -23 revision of the Composite ML-KEM Internet-Draft; the latter is in the RFC Editor queue, not yet published as an RFC.
6. **Inspect Issued Certificate** — decodes the issued cert with `openssl x509 -text -noout` and verifies the chain with `openssl verify -CAfile root.crt`; works for whichever cert (ML-DSA from Step 2 or ECDSA from Step 5) was issued last

It must be machine-readable and SIEM-integrated, ideally via API or automated feed — a Phase 1 architecture decision.

## Key Concepts

- **Use Case 1 — Hybrid Downgrade Detection** — SIEM correlation rules flag connections negotiating classical-only key shares (NamedGroups) when the registry expects hybrid; a TLS 1.3 session between two ML-KEM-capable systems should not complete using only ECDH. Severity High. Hybrid key exchanges are negotiated by IANA NamedGroup codepoints (ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, hybrid groups), not X.509 OIDs, so those codepoints must be added to traffic-analysis rules manually (1–2 weeks of custom engineering per platform as of mid-2026). The most common false positive is the organization's own middleboxes: legacy firewalls and SSL inspection proxies may discard fragmented handshakes or remove unrecognized extensions from oversized hybrid ClientHello messages, leading to a classical-only fallback that looks identical to an attack.
- **Use Case 2 — Cryptographic Drift Monitoring** — Migration is not a one-time event; systems drift via new microservices on classical libraries, pre-migration backup restores, vendor updates reverting to RSA, and shadow IT. Continuous network monitoring alerts when a migration-complete system negotiates a classical-only key share (Medium, escalating to High on repeat). Tracked as the "Cryptographic Migration Coverage" metric — % of monitored TLS sessions using PQC or hybrid, measured weekly, trending monotonically toward 100% with regressions investigated within 24 hours. Requires east-west (internal) traffic visibility, not just north-south perimeter flows.
- **Use Case 3 — Certificate Lifecycle Anomalies** — The wholesale transition to ML-DSA/SLH-DSA certificates, new intermediate CAs, and reconfigured chains creates elevated risk. Detection targets: failed PQC certificate chain validations (Medium), unauthorized issuance from the internal CA using a PQC signature algorithm not on the approved list (High), and CA signing-key access outside scheduled windows during the transition (Critical). Tooling gap: Certificate Transparency monitoring for PQC certificates is immature, so the SOC may need custom monitoring around internal CA logs.
- **Use Case 4 — TNFL & Signature Integrity Monitoring** — Trust Now, Forge Later enables present-tense exploitation once an adversary can forge signatures (forged software updates, fabricated financial instructions, impersonation) — unlike HNDL, which compromises past data. Heightened monitoring of code-signing, software-update authentication, and automated signature-verification trust decisions (firmware, financial authorization, identity federation). Alert Critical on unexpected signing keys/identities or unusual signing times and on any change to production signature-verification policy; alert High on signing volume more than two standard deviations above baseline. Metric: MTD-Signing under 15 minutes for production code signing, measured via red-team exercises. Challenge: signing telemetry is fragmented across dev, OT, and PKI teams.
- **Use Case 5 — Enhanced HNDL-Indicator Detection** — The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat is active today. This is existing exfiltration monitoring with quantum-informed reprioritization by data sensitivity and longevity: a slow exfiltration of archived diplomatic correspondence or pharmaceutical R&D outweighs a one-time transactional dump. Alert High on sustained outbound transfers from segments hosting 10+ year secrecy data (even below DLP volume thresholds) and on bulk archival access by accounts that do not normally touch those systems. The "HNDL Exposure Score" composites DLP coverage, detection latency, and classification completeness; target 100% coverage for 10+ year stores with detection under 4 hours. Hard dependency on information-governance data classification.
- **Three-Horizon Cyber Threat Intelligence** — Tactical (hours–days): triage liboqs CVEs, hardware ML-KEM side-channels, and cryptanalysis papers with implementation impact; TTAssess-PQC target under 4 hours for deployed implementations; sources include the NIST PQC mailing list, IETF pquip/lamps, CERT and vendor advisories. Operational (weeks–months): watch adversary collection shifts toward long-lived archives and PQC supply-chain probing — a watch-and-wait posture since no campaign is publicly attributed as of mid-2026. Strategic (months–years): track quantum hardware against the CRQC Quantum Capability Framework (error correction, logical gate operations, decoder performance, continuous operation, engineering scale) and national programs, producing a quarterly Quantum Threat Landscape Assessment for the CISO. Strategic CTI is scarce — most organizations should borrow it.
- **Four Incident-Response Playbooks** — Developed during Phase 0 governance setup, each with trigger, immediate actions, coordination, and drill metric. (1) PQC Algorithm Vulnerability Disclosure — distinguish full algorithm break from implementation bug, query the registry for affected systems, deliver impact assessment under 4 hours, emergency-patch or activate crypto-agility rotation; needs a named incident commander and pre-authorized change windows. (2) Confirmed Hybrid Downgrade Attack — isolate the path, preserve packet captures, determine mechanism and scope, escalate to the CISO. (3) Credible CRQC Announcement — crisis communications and emergency migration; prior preparation matters most. (4) Emergency Algorithm Rotation — the SOC must not mistake an authorized rotation (mass revocations, cipher-suite changes, KMS spikes) for an attack; rotation-drill false-positive rate under 10%.
- **Five Named Tabletop Exercises** — Run at least annually with the migration program office, CISO, GRC, and application owners, each producing an after-action report: (1) The Friday Afternoon CVE; (2) The Ambiguous Cryptanalysis Paper; (3) Silent Downgrade; (4) The CRQC Announcement; (5) Signing Key Compromise.
- **Skills & Tooling Gaps** — The protocol-parsing gap (2–4 weeks of custom Suricata/Zeek/SIEM engineering per platform plus maintenance), the CTI skills gap (tactical in-house, strategic contracted externally over 12–18 months), and the east-west visibility gap (a prerequisite for drift monitoring).

## SOC Metrics Summary

| Metric                           | What it measures                                               | Target                                                       |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cryptographic Migration Coverage | % of monitored TLS sessions using PQC or hybrid                | Monotonically increasing; regression investigated within 24h |
| Cryptographic Drift Incidents    | Systems reverting to classical-only after migration            | Zero; any non-zero value triggers investigation              |
| TTAssess-PQC                     | Time from PQC vulnerability disclosure to CTI assessment       | Under 4 hours for deployed implementations                   |
| Impact Assessment Speed          | Time from disclosure to identifying all affected systems       | Under 4 hours                                                |
| MTD-Signing                      | Mean time to detect unauthorized signing events                | Under 15 minutes for production signing keys                 |
| HNDL Exposure Score              | DLP coverage + detection latency + classification completeness | 100% coverage for 10+ year secrecy data stores               |
| Algorithm Rotation Drill FP Rate | False-positive rate during rotation exercises                  | Under 10%                                                    |

## SOC Implementation Roadmap

- **Phase 1 (0–3 months)** — Operationalize the posture registry for SOC access; stand up tactical CTI monitoring; draft the PQC Algorithm Vulnerability Disclosure playbook and run the first tabletop.
- **Phase 2 (3–9 months)** — Implement hybrid downgrade detection for priority segments; build/acquire PQC cipher-suite parsing; begin drift monitoring; run the first HNDL-focused data-classification/DLP review.
- **Phase 3 (9–18 months)** — Extend detection to full enterprise scope; integrate certificate lifecycle monitoring; implement TNFL signing-event monitoring; establish the quarterly Quantum Threat Landscape Assessment; run a full algorithm rotation drill.
- **Phase 4 (Ongoing)** — Refine rules from operational experience; update playbooks from exercise findings; report SOC quantum security metrics; adapt as implementations, standards, and the threat landscape evolve.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 5 interactive steps:

1. **Why It Matters** — the five detection use cases presented as threat impacts with example scenarios and severities, plus the posture-registry prerequisite as the urgency statement.
2. **What to Learn** — detection-engineering, threat-intelligence, and incident-response skill gaps mapped to target levels and cross-linked modules.
3. **How to Act** — a phased action plan mirroring the four-phase SOC Implementation Roadmap, with quick wins and the SOC metrics as KPIs.
4. **Detection Coverage Planner** — an interactive planner over the five detection use cases; each capability cycles Not started → Building → Operational and the SOC detection coverage score updates live with prioritization guidance.
5. **SOC Readiness Self-Assessment** — a nine-criterion checklist (posture registry, NamedGroup parsing, east-west visibility, unified signing view, data classification, tactical CTI, strategic CTI, drafted playbooks, tabletop run) producing a readiness band and next-step guidance.

## Related Standards

- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM — the key-encapsulation NamedGroups hybrid downgrade detection must parse)
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA — certificate and code-signing signatures behind certificate-lifecycle and TNFL monitoring)
- FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA — stateless hash-based signatures in the PQC certificate hierarchy)
- NIST SP 800-227 (Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms — hybrid configuration basis)
- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards — program context the posture registry derives from)
- RFC 9846 (TLS 1.3, obsoletes RFC 8446 — where hybrid key shares are negotiated by NamedGroup codepoints, not X.509 OIDs)

### What This Is About

PQC GRC is the governance, risk, and compliance machinery that makes a post-quantum migration measurable and auditable. Where the SOC detects and responds, GRC measures, reports, and governs — turning a multi-year migration into something a board can actually oversee.

### Why It Matters

Quantum risk has no historical incident base rate or reliable date for a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer. It is also a technology, compliance, strategic, and operational risk. Logging it as "low likelihood, review annually" is acknowledging the risk, not managing it. The fix is to give quantum risk the same structured treatment as any other top-tier risk.

NIST IR 8547 became final in October 2026. For federal high-value assets and high-impact systems, it identifies earlier targets for post-quantum key establishment (31 December 2030) and signatures (31 December 2031), mandated for federal civilian agencies under EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15 (which also directs a proposed FAR contractor rule). NIST plans to deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow it under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. Keep scopes separate: NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 governs National Security Systems (2027/2030/2031), EU Member States coordinate under the EU PQC Roadmap v1.1, and DORA/NIS2 impose cyber risk-management duties rather than fixed algorithm mandates. Other organizations must check their own applicable rules. The module recommends quarterly horizon review as a governance practice, not a universal legal requirement. [NIST IR 8547](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final)

### The Key Takeaway

Three instruments do most of the work: a Key Risk Indicator cascade that shows the board, the CISO, and operations the right metrics at the right cadence with thresholds that trigger specific action; a risk-appetite statement that lets the program make trade-offs without escalating every one; and a clean GRC-SOC handoff in which the exception register becomes the SOC's suppression list — so genuine cryptographic drift is not lost in alerts from systems that were legitimately deferred.

### What's Happening

Whether your insurer asks about quantum readiness at renewal is a question for your broker, but a documented, governed, measured migration program is easier to explain to an underwriter than a vague intention to migrate later. The organizations that maintain an evidence dossier can answer the attestation surge after any public quantum event with an export, not a project.

# PQC GRC

## Overview

The PQC GRC module teaches the Governance, Risk, and Compliance function that makes a post-quantum migration governable, measurable, and auditable. Where the SOC detects and responds, the GRC function measures, reports, and governs — producing the instruments the board uses to oversee the program, the CISO uses to manage it, and internal audit uses to verify it. The module is adapted from the GRC Implementation section of the Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework. It starts from why quantum risk breaks the standard ERM playbook (uncertain timing, no historical incidents, risk that straddles technology/compliance/strategic/operational categories) and shows how to give quantum risk the same structured treatment as any other top-tier risk rather than building a separate framework.

## Key Concepts

- **KRI Three-Level Cascade** — Key Risk Indicators cascade across three levels, each serving a different audience at a different cadence. **Board (quarterly):** Migration Completion Rate (variance >5pp triggers SteerCo review + board notification), HNDL Residual Exposure (must decrease each quarter), Regulatory Compliance Buffer (<12mo amber, <6mo red + board intervention), Third-Party Quantum Readiness (Tier 1 below "planning" triggers engagement), Material Developments Flag. **CISO (monthly):** Inventory Completeness (<80% = plan unreliable), Migration Velocity (<70% for 2 months = program review), Crypto-Agility Adoption (<95% = architecture review), Regulatory Horizon Tracker, Vendor Readiness Scores, Budget Consumption vs Plan (underspend >15% = review). **Operational (weekly/real-time):** Weekly Migration Throughput, Cryptographic Drift Count, Hybrid Downgrade Alerts, Certificate Transition Progress, Open Exceptions/Deferrals (>6 months without remediation plan = escalation), TTR-PQC.
- **Risk Appetite Statement** — operates at two levels: a strategic board-language sentence (complete migration of >10-year-secrecy data before earliest credible CRQC, with a 12-month regulatory buffer) plus measurable operational tolerances for HNDL, TNFL, regulatory compliance, and crypto-agility dimensions. Board-approved in Phase 0, reviewed annually.
- **Regulatory Horizon Report** — this module recommends quarterly review, with more frequent checks when sector rules or active proposals warrant them. This is a governance practice, not a universal legal minimum. Classify each development as Confirmed (enacted; immediate SteerCo assessment), Proposed (in process; impact assessment within 30 days), or Signaled (guidance/speeches; monitoring entry). Sources span NIST/NCCoE, NSA CNSA 2.0, EU NIS Cooperation Group, CISA, sector regulators, and standards bodies.
- **Current U.S. federal & EU horizon examples (as checked 18 November 2026)** — NIST IR 8547 is final (October 2026). Federal high-value assets and high-impact systems have earlier targets: post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and digital signatures by 31 December 2031 (mandated for US federal civilian agencies under EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15, which also directs a proposed FAR contractor rule). NIST plans to deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow it under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. Keep scopes distinct: NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 governs US National Security Systems (acquisitions 1 Jan 2027, phase-out 31 Dec 2030, mandated 31 Dec 2031), EU Member States coordinate under the EU PQC Roadmap v1.1, and DORA/NIS2 impose cyber risk-management duties rather than fixed PQC algorithm mandates. Do not transfer federal dates to other organizations without checking applicable rules. [NIST IR 8547 final page](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final) · [Full report](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8547)
- **Third-Party Quantum Readiness** — vendor tiering: Tier 1 migration-constraining (HSMs, CAs, cloud, payment processors, MSSPs) — an illustrative policy: ask for a CBOM (e.g. CycloneDX 1.6+) and a product-security review; Tier 2 cryptographic dependency require standard assessment; Tier 3 no dependency require none. Maintain substitution assessments to manage concentration risk; treat M&A as first-party crypto debt inherited at close.
- **GRC-SOC Handoff** — GRC produces four outputs the SOC consumes: the risk appetite statement (defines alert escalation thresholds), the compliance tracker (monitoring priority), vendor assessments (third-party connection treatment), and the **exception/deferral register as a dynamic suppression list** — without it, drift-detection rules drown in alerts from legitimately deferred legacy systems.
- **Audit, Insurance & Crisis Comms** — auditable artifact set (inventory with timestamps, quarterly CBOM snapshots, SteerCo minutes, board-approved appetite statement, Horizon Reports, vendor records, exception register); audit at <6 months, 18–24 months, then annually. Whether underwriters ask about quantum readiness is a question for your broker; no insurer's quantum-specific wording was found. GRC owns pre-drafted crisis-communication templates (customer, regulator, counterparty, market) with a named spokesperson and approval chain, exercised in tabletop exercises.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 2 interactive steps:

1. **KRI Cascade Builder** — assign each of 17 KRIs to a board / CISO / operational level and set a status (on track / watch / breach); validation warns when a level is empty (an audience is flying blind at its cadence) or when a board KRI is in breach (board-intervention threshold tripped); exports a board-ready cascade dashboard to the learning portfolio.
2. **Exception Register Triage** — classify deferral entries and decide which propagate to the SOC suppression list versus which escalate, applying the framework rule that an exception is safe to suppress only while ≤6 months old AND carrying a remediation plan; check-and-reveal scoring; exports the triaged register plus the derived SOC suppression list.

## Related Standards

- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards; final, October 2026)
- NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 (US National Security Systems)
- EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15 (US federal civilian agency transition requirements + directed FAR contractor rule)
- EU PQC Roadmap v1.1; DORA & NIS2 (EU cyber risk-management duties; no fixed PQC deadlines)
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
- NIST SP 800-208 (Stateful Hash-Based Signatures)
- CycloneDX 1.6+ / 1.7 (CBOM)
- ISO 27005 / ISO 31000 (risk management), COBIT (governance)

### What This Is About

A post-quantum migration is a multi-year program, and someone has to staff it. This module shows how to build the team: the core roles you need, how big the team should be, what to build in-house versus buy from outside, and how to train everyone.

### Why It Matters

The mix of skills PQC needs — deep cryptography, large-scale program management, and hands-on network/app/OT expertise — almost never sits in one person. Trying to hire a whole team of specialists is unrealistic. Instead, you build a small expert core, upskill the staff you already have, and bring in scarce specialists only where you must.

### The Key Takeaway

Team size follows your cryptographic estate, not your employee count. The rule of thumb is one dedicated person per 500 cryptographic "instances" (certificates, keys, TLS endpoints, HSMs) in the first couple of years, easing to one per 1,000 once tooling matures. A 50,000-person bank with a sprawling crypto estate needs a bigger team than a 200,000-person manufacturer whose crypto is concentrated in one platform.

### What's Happening

Leading programs designate a "crypto champion" on every platform team — web, mobile, data, infrastructure, OT, identity — so the program scales without every developer becoming a cryptographer. Champions sign off on crypto readiness in design reviews and shepherd library upgrades, and after migration they become a permanent network, much like long-running security champion programs.

# Building Your PQC Team (Skills & Team Structure)

## Overview

The Skills & Team Structure module teaches leaders how to staff a post-quantum cryptography (PQC) migration program. PQC migration demands a combination of skills that rarely coexists in one team: deep cryptographic knowledge (algorithms, protocols, PKI architecture), enterprise program management at scale, and domain-specific technical expertise (network, application, OT, cloud). The market for professionals who combine even two of these is thin. The recommended approach is to build a small core of cryptographic expertise, supplement it with upskilled existing security and IT staff, and augment with external specialists for capabilities that cannot be developed internally in the required timeframe. Source: Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework (Universal Edition 2.1), "Skills & Team Structure" section, pp. 160–164.

## Key Concepts

- **Seven core roles** — Quantum-Readiness Program Manager / QRPM (1.0 FTE), Cryptographic Architect (0.5–1.0), Security Engineers (PQC) (2–4), Application Security Lead (1.0), OT Security Specialist (0.5–1.0 if OT in scope), Vendor/Procurement Lead (0.5), PMO Analyst (0.5–1.0). Each role lists required skills and a recommended source. Role spine reused from `@/data/roleCrosswalk.ts` (`ROLE_CROSSWALK`).
- **Dedicated overhead** — QRPM, Cryptographic Architect, and PMO Analyst are staffed regardless of estate size.
- **Team-sizing heuristic** — one dedicated FTE per **500 cryptographic instances** in the CBOM for the first two years (discovery, CBOM, risk scoring, pilot), dropping to one per 1,000 during production rollout. Constant reused from `@/data/roleCrosswalk.ts` (`FTE_PER_CRYPTO_INSTANCES = 500`). Below 1,000 instances: part-time QRPM plus consulting. Above 10,000 instances: dedicated program office of 8–12 FTEs at peak. Team size tracks the cryptographic estate, not revenue or headcount.
- **Build / Borrow / Buy** — per-capability sourcing: Program management (Build), Cryptographic architecture (Build if possible, borrow for design), Discovery & inventory (Buy the tool, run internally), PKI modernization (Build, augmented), Vendor governance (Build), Strategic quantum CTI (Borrow).
- **Four training levels** — (1) Executive education (half-day to one day), (2) PQC foundations (3–5 days), (3) Deep technical (ongoing, lab-based), (4) Crypto Champion Program (standing).
- **Crypto Champion Program** — one champion per platform/application team (web, mobile, data, infrastructure, OT, identity). Champions attend foundations training, join quarterly crypto-agility briefings, liaise with the program, sign off on crypto readiness in design reviews, and shepherd PQC library upgrades. The model scales reach without making every developer a cryptographer; champions become a standing network after migration.
- **Skills matrix** — six skill domains mapped to primary roles and proficiency targets; a domain with no named owner is a program risk.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 2 interactive steps:

1. **Team Sizing Calculator** — enter cryptographic-instance count, select program phase (first-two-years 1/500 vs. production-rollout 1/1,000), and toggle OT-in-scope; computes an estimated program FTE count, classifies the estate band (small / standard / program-office), and exports a sizing plan plus the core-role table as Markdown (saved to the learning portfolio as a `skills-team-plan` document).
2. **Crypto Champion Roster** — assign a named champion per platform and track the four readiness commitments (foundations, quarterly briefings, design-review sign-off, library-upgrade shepherding); warns on unstaffed platforms and incomplete readiness; exports the roster as Markdown.

## Related Standards

- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards)
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), and planned FIPS 206 (FN-DSA; in development with no public draft)
- NSA CNSA 2.0 (algorithm suite and timelines)
- CycloneDX (CBOM format the team operates and maintains)

# Cryptography Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) is a machine-readable list of all the cryptography an organization actually uses — the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols, and where each one lives. It extends the idea of a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): the SBOM lists your software, the CBOM lists the cryptography inside it.

## Why It Matters

You cannot migrate to post-quantum cryptography what you cannot find. Most enterprises have a long tail of "ghost" cryptography — forgotten certificates, hardcoded algorithms, crypto buried in cloud services — that never appears in any inventory, and that is exactly where the risk hides. A good CBOM is built by combining the discovery tools you already run with targeted net-new scanning, then normalizing everything into one standard format you can query.

## The Key Takeaway

A CBOM only becomes useful when it is complete, normalized, and machine-verifiable: every cryptographic asset discovered across source code, binaries, the network, infrastructure and the cloud; named consistently despite the many competing standards; tied to a key you can identify and trace; and checkable by policy-as-code so you can prove what is quantum-safe and what is not.

Quantum computers will eventually break today's public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC). Before an organization can swap those out, it has to find them all — including the "ghost" crypto nobody tracks. # Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)

## Overview

The CBOM module teaches how to build, normalize, and operate a Cryptography Bill of Materials — a machine-readable inventory of every cryptographic asset (algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols and their configurations) and how they relate to software components. The CBOM extends the SBOM and is Phase 2 of the post-quantum migration lifecycle: cryptographic discovery (Phase 1) feeds it, and risk scoring (Phase 3) consumes it. The module covers format choice and governance, layered discovery including untracked "ghost" cryptography, key identity and provenance, the normalization of inconsistent mechanism nomenclatures, and machine-verifiable policy-as-code.

## Key Concepts

- **CBOM** — a machine-readable cryptographic inventory that extends the SBOM; the EU NIS Cooperation Group's Coordinated Implementation Roadmap v1.1 (11 June 2025) sets an end-2026 milestone for Member States whose First Steps include mature cryptographic asset management, recommending CBOM as the format. It is guidance to Member States, not a direct requirement on organisations.
- **Format landscape** — CycloneDX (OWASP; standardized as ECMA-424; current spec v1.7 with a Cryptography Registry) is the practical CBOM format because SPDX 3.0.1 (Linux Foundation; ISO/IEC 5962) has no dedicated cryptography object model yet. The PKI Consortium CBOM-Profiles Working Group (launched 8 June 2026) is building a neutral, open methodology mapping profiles onto both formats.
- **Ghost cryptography** — every cryptographic usage not in any inventory (shadow IT, forgotten certificates, hardcoded algorithms, embedded/OT crypto). "You cannot migrate what you cannot find."
- **Layered discovery** — five complementary layers: source code (sonar-cryptography / CBOMkit, IBM Quantum Safe Explorer), binary/container (CBOMkit-theia), network/traffic (passive handshake capture + active scanning), infrastructure/runtime (HSM/KMS, certificate lifecycle, CT logs), and cloud (KMS/cert APIs + CSPM). Reuse existing scanners and agents as sources; scan net-new only where blind.
- **Key identity** — assigned identifiers (PKCS#11 CKA_ID, KMIP Unique Identifier, KMS key-id, JWK kid) are local and don't correlate; content-derived identifiers (X.509 SKI/SPKI hash, KMIP Digest, JWK Thumbprint RFC 7638, KCV for symmetric keys) do. The SPKI fingerprint is the join key across systems.
- **Key provenance** — attestation proves a key was generated in hardware and is non-exportable (HSM/TPM attestation, Android Key Attestation, FIDO2/WebAuthn); record whether a key is software-, HSM-, or cloud-KMS-managed because it drives risk and migration feasibility.
- **Codification & normalization** — the same mechanism is named differently across OID, PKCS#11, KMIP, IETF/IANA (TLS/SSH/IPsec), JOSE/COSE and crypto libraries. PQC multiplies parameters per mechanism and proliferates OIDs (ML-DSA uses one OID per parameter set with parameters absent, RFC 9881); hybrid and composite ciphers add combination × nomenclature. Normalize onto a canonical model (CycloneDX Cryptography Registry) without over-collapsing security-relevant parameters.
- **Machine-verifiable** — policy-as-code (CBOMkit OPA/Rego) classifies each asset quantum-safe / quantum-vulnerable / na / unknown over a REST API. Secure the CBOM itself — it is a map of an organization's weakest cryptography.

## Standards & Sources

# Decommissioning & Program Closure — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

This is the end of a post-quantum migration: turning off the old, quantum-vulnerable cryptography and formally winding the program down. Both steps are surprisingly easy to skip — teams report systems as "done" on a ticket, and programs quietly drift on without ever closing.

## Why It Matters

A migration isn't finished when you add post-quantum cryptography — it's finished when the old RSA/ECC keys are actually gone, on a defensible schedule (under NIST IR 8547, final October 2026, classical public-key cryptography is set to be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035; US federal civilian agencies also follow EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15, US National Security Systems follow CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2, and EU entities coordinate under EU PQC Roadmap v1.1 alongside DORA/NIS2 cyber risk-management duties). And you only really know it happened if you can see it in the system's behaviour — for example, capturing the connection handshake and confirming it negotiated a post-quantum algorithm — rather than trusting a change ticket.

## The Key Takeaway

Close deliberately. Verify the highest-value systems completely and sample the rest; remove and then confirm-removed the old cryptography; and hand every ongoing responsibility (the crypto inventory, vendor monitoring, security detections, reporting) to a named permanent owner, accepting any leftover risk on the record. Then the program can formally end instead of fading away.

- **ACVP KAT Conformance vs. Module Boundary Validation**: NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify mathematical algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`). CMVP FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module against its security requirements (module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization, physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B); non-invasive (side-channel) requirements are currently N/A by default. Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates the product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims.
- **Evidence-Chain Verification vs. Sample Non-Equivalence**: When reading a production certificate, a useful check is: the certificate or module number and its status (active, historical or revoked); the exact module or product name and version; the tested operational environment or configuration (CMVP: Security Policy; CC: evaluated configuration in the certification report); the CAVP algorithm certificate numbers listed for the algorithms you rely on; and, for CC/EUCC, the Security Target and assurance level it claims. This is Hub practice guidance, not a certification-scheme requirement. A sample Hub exercise export or a vendor marketing datasheet is never certification evidence.

Decommissioning & Program Closure — For the Curious
Picture renovating a building: fitting new locks is only part of the job. You also need to account for old access paths, spare keys and the people who maintain them. A cryptography migration similarly needs clear retirement criteria, checks of remaining dependencies and an ongoing owner.
The risky assumption is that completing a removal task proves that every dependent copy is gone. A signing key can be removed while a verifier still trusts its old public key. A library can be replaced in one application while an older container still uses it. Your production tools need to find these remaining uses and show what their checks covered.
Using traditional and post-quantum algorithms together does not automatically make a migration incomplete. A documented hybrid construction combines components; a path that can use only the traditional algorithm is a different case. Check the required profile and whether the remaining path meets the intended security goal. Its transition schedule applies under NIST standards and guidelines; check the rules and earlier deadlines applicable to your organization rather than treating one date as universal.
Use the same reasoning with your own tools: look for discovery of active use, stored keys, trust settings and dependent copies; coverage and observation dates; and a way to retain exceptions and recheck after changes. Assign ongoing ownership of the inventory, monitoring and remaining work so retirement remains a maintained state rather than a one-time status label.

# Decommissioning & Program Closure

## Overview

This module covers the end of a post-quantum migration — two jobs that are routinely neglected: decommissioning classical cryptography on a defensible schedule, and closing the program into business-as-usual. The independently-sourced spine is the deprecation timeline (NIST IR 8547, final October 2026: deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key after 2030, disallow after 2035). Verification-by-observed-behaviour, the estate-scale sampling approach, and the PQC-specific closure detail are presented as practitioner guidance.

## Key Concepts

- **Decommissioning** — the migration is done when the classical cryptography is gone, not when PQC is added. Discipline: deprecate → remove → **verify removed** → log. Schedule anchored to NIST IR 8547 (deprecated after 2030 / disallowed after 2035) and SP 800-131A.
- **Verification by observed behaviour** (practitioner) — prove migration by capturing the handshake and confirming ML-KEM/ML-DSA was negotiated, not by trusting a change ticket. Reuse the Active PQC Scanner and passive handshake capture. Control basis: NIST CSWP 48 (draft) → CSF 2.0 / SP 800-53.
- **Coverage at estate scale** (practitioner) — verify business-critical systems fully, sample lower tiers per migration wave, widen the check on any sampled failure.

# CycloneDX Cryptography Registry — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Every tool that looks at your cryptography names it differently. An HSM calls something `CKM_ECDSA_SHA256`. A certificate calls the same thing an OID like `1.2.840.10045.4.3.2`. A login service calls it `ES256`. A network capture calls it `0x0403`. They're all the same signing mechanism — but nothing about the names tells you that.

The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry is a shared dictionary that fixes this: one canonical name for each cryptographic algorithm family (98 of them) and each elliptic curve (246 of them), each backed by a real standard. Once every tool's output is translated into this dictionary, you can finally ask questions like "which of our systems still use something quantum-vulnerable?" and get a real answer — because "ECDSA" means the same thing everywhere, instead of five different strings that happen to describe the same math.

## Why It Matters

Post-quantum readiness starts with knowing what cryptography you actually have. New algorithms like ML-KEM and ML-DSA are registered in this same dictionary right alongside RSA and AES, so checking "is this quantum-safe?" is a lookup, not a research project.

## Try It Yourself

The workshop in this module lets you type in a messy, real-world identifier — the kind a scanner or certificate would actually report — and watch it resolve to its canonical name, plus the standard that defines it.

# Software Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of software components within a product's stated scope, with fields such as component name, version, supplier or producer, and dependency relationships. Its coverage depends on how the SBOM is generated, reviewed and maintained; it should not be assumed to list every dependency automatically.

## Why It Matters

When a vulnerability is found in a widely-used library, teams need to determine whether it appears in their products and where. A current, sufficiently complete SBOM can make that search easier, but it does not prove that a vulnerable code path is reachable or that the inventory is complete. An SBOM is one useful input to a Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM), alongside crypto-scanner results, certificate and key inventories, runtime observation and manual investigation; it is not a mandatory prerequisite or a complete crypto inventory by itself.

## The Key Takeaway

A useful SBOM records consistent component identifiers, versions, provenance and dependency relationships for its stated scope, and is kept current. VEX adds product-specific status and justification to vulnerability findings; neither an SBOM nor VEX alone proves exploitability or non-exploitability. Treat an SBOM as an operational input that downstream disciplines can combine with other evidence, not as a one-off compliance checkbox.

## What's Happening

CISA's 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (version 2.1, published 29 July 2026 with NSA, FBI and international partner agencies) updates and replaces the 2021 NTIA baseline. It is not a strict superset. Ten elements are new: SBOM Author Signature, SBOM Data Format Name, SBOM Data Format Version, SBOM Generation Context, SBOM Tool Name, SBOM Tool Version, SBOM Version, Component Hash Value, Component Hash Algorithm and Component License. Several 2021 elements are renamed or redefined: Supplier Name became Component Producer, Author of SBOM Data became SBOM Author, Other Unique Identifiers became Component Identifiers, Version of the Component became Component Version, Depth became Coverage, Accommodation of Mistakes became Accommodation of Updates to SBOM Data, Known Unknowns became Explicitly Identifying Unknown Information, and Automation Support became Machine-Processable Data (with SWID tags dropped from the list of data formats). One element is removed as a stand-alone item: Access Control, whose considerations move into Distribution and Delivery. Timestamp now points to RFC 9557, and Component Name may have multiple entries.

# Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

## Overview

The SBOM module teaches general software-component inventory within a stated scope. Coverage depends on how the SBOM is generated and maintained; do not assume it lists every dependency. It is distinct from cryptographic-asset inventory (CBOM) and cross-tool cryptographic-mechanism name normalization (CycloneDX Cryptography Registry). The module covers SPDX and CycloneDX, NTIA and CISA minimum-element guidance, VEX for vulnerability-status communication, procurement and regulatory scope, and how SBOM data can contribute to broader crypto-asset discovery.

## Key Concepts

- **SBOM** — a machine-readable inventory of software components within a product's stated scope, with information such as names, versions, supplier or producer, and dependency relationships. It helps answer "what is in this build?"; it does not by itself identify all cryptographic assets.
- **Formats** — SPDX is an international open standard (ISO/IEC 5962:2021). CycloneDX is an OWASP community specification; CycloneDX 1.6 was published as ECMA-424. They have different schemas and tool support; neither should be described as universally more complete.
- **NTIA 2021 minimum elements** — seven data fields: Supplier Name, Component Name, Version of the Component, Other Unique Identifiers, Dependency Relationship, Author of SBOM Data, and Timestamp. NTIA's framing applies the first five to components; the author and timestamp describe the SBOM.
- **CISA 2026 update** — CISA published v2.1 on 29 July 2026 with NSA, FBI, and 15 international partner agencies. It revises or replaces several 2021 elements, adds ten (seven document-level and three per-component), clarifies existing fields, and removes Access Control as a standalone element. It is current CISA guidance, not a blanket legal requirement for every organization.
- **Generator selection** — output varies by tool release, ecosystem, lock file, and configuration. A format choice does not guarantee all required values or compliance. Inspect the generated artifact against the applicable CISA guidance and contract or regulation; use the module's linked tool documentation.
- **VEX** — Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange communicates product status and rationale for a vulnerability. OASIS CSAF 2.0 Profile 5 includes statuses such as known affected, known not affected, fixed, or under investigation. A VEX statement supports triage but does not prove exploitability or non-exploitability by itself.
- **Regulatory scope** — Executive Order 14028 directed federal software supply-chain security work, including the original NTIA elements. OMB M-22-18 says agencies may require SBOMs in solicitations based on software criticality or agency determination; it is not a blanket requirement for every federal software vendor. The EU Cyber Resilience Act applies to in-scope products and includes an SBOM in a commonly used machine-readable format covering at least top-level dependencies. Its general application date is 11 December 2027, with earlier dates for specified provisions.
- **SBOM-to-CBOM bridge** — an SBOM can contribute component and dependency data to crypto-asset discovery alongside scanner results, certificate and key inventories, runtime observation, and manual investigation. It is not a complete CBOM by itself or a mandatory single input.

## Standards & Sources

SPDX / ISO/IEC 5962:2021, CycloneDX 1.6 / ECMA-424, NTIA Minimum Elements for an SBOM (2021), CISA 2026 Minimum Elements for an SBOM v2.1, OASIS CSAF 2.0 (VEX Profile), Executive Order 14028, OMB M-22-18, and EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation EU 2024/2847).

LM-064.curious:
### What This Is About

DNSSEC signs DNS answers so resolvers can prove they weren't forged. IANA has assigned DNSSEC algorithm number 18 to ML-DSA-44, with resolver validation of ML-DSA-44 serving as one of the first deployment steps.

### Why It Matters

DNSSEC's PQC problem isn't cryptographic strength, it's size: an ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes, about 38x larger than the ECDSA P-256 signatures DNSSEC mostly uses today, and exceeds a common conservative ~1,232-byte UDP payload limit. Responses that large need another transport, normally TCP — a real operational cost that's one of several reasons this remains an individual IETF draft rather than a working-group standard.

### The Key Takeaway

Cloudflare's milestone proves a production resolver CAN validate ML-DSA-44 at scale, against a real signed zone. It does NOT mean any production zone is actually signed with a post-quantum algorithm yet. Resolver-side validation and authoritative-side signing are two different, still-separate steps.

### What's Happening

Cloudflare's own next steps are authoritative-side signing support and registrar DS-record support. Cloudflare's company-wide post-quantum security target is ~2029, but full end-to-end PQ DNSSEC also needs the root and other registries to adopt it. Separately, the RSA-to-RSA rollover to KSK-2024 began on 11 October 2026; ICANN's March 2026 proposal for the next classical algorithm rollover describes ECDSA key generation in 2027 and RSA key decommissioning in 2030, subject to community feedback. Verisign's 2023 comments describe a possible later PQ rollover in the mid-2030s, a conditional scenario rather than an ICANN plan or forecast.

LM-064.summary:
# DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures

## Overview

This module explains how DNSSEC — the DNS Security Extensions that sign DNS answers to prove authenticity and integrity — is moving to post-quantum signatures. It covers why DNSSEC's PQC motivation is forgery risk rather than harvest-now-decrypt-later (DNSSEC is signature-only, not confidential), the ML-DSA-44 mechanism behind IANA DNSSEC algorithm 18 (draft-westerbaan-dnssec-mldsa), Cloudflare's real 2026-09-10 deployment (1.1.1.1 validating by default against the dnstest.dev signed test zone), the signature-size problem that makes this an unusually hard PQC migration, and what remains before production zones can actually be signed.

## Key Concepts

- **DNSSEC basics** (RFC 4034, RFC 9364/BCP 237) — DS/DNSKEY/RRSIG resource records chain trust from the DNS root down through each delegated zone to the signed answer; signature-only, no confidentiality dimension
- **Forgery, not harvesting** — because DNSSEC has no ciphertext, the quantum threat is a future quantum computer forging RSA/ECDSA signatures the day it exists, not decrypting captured traffic later
- **ML-DSA-44 for DNSSEC** (current draft-westerbaan-dnssec-mldsa-04, an individual Internet-Draft, not an IETF standard) — defines DS/DNSKEY/RRSIG use of ML-DSA-44 (FIPS 204's smallest parameter set); IANA algorithm 18 (MLDSA44) currently has MAY values for use/implementation in signing and validation. IANA's reference is draft-03; draft-04 says it defines the same codepoint. Public key 1,312 bytes, signature 2,420 bytes
- **The size problem** — 2,420-byte ML-DSA-44 signatures are ~38x larger than ECDSA P-256's 64 bytes and exceed a common conservative ~1,232-byte UDP payload limit (RFC 9715 recommends up to 1,400 bytes), needing another transport, normally TCP; SLH-DSA alternatives run even larger (7,856+ bytes)
- **Downgrade risk** (RFC 6840 §5.11) — a lenient validator accepting any single valid signature path can be tricked into accepting a stripped classical signature if a zone is dual-signed; the fix is requiring algorithm 18 whenever the zone's DS record advertises it
- **Cloudflare's real pilot** (2026-09-10 blog post) — 1.1.1.1 validates ML-DSA-44 by default; dnstest.dev is a live, ML-DSA-44-signed test zone; this is resolver-side validation only, not production zone signing
- **What's missing** — authoritative-side signing support and registrar DS-record support are Cloudflare's own stated next steps; end-to-end PQ DNSSEC also needs the root and other registries to adopt algorithm 18, beyond what Cloudflare alone can deliver
- **Distinct dates and scenarios** — Cloudflare's ~2029 target is its own company-wide post-quantum security goal (not a DNSSEC-specific date). The RSA-to-RSA KSK-2024 rollover began 11 October 2026. Separately, ICANN's 2 March 2026 proposal for a classical algorithm rollover describes ECDSA key generation in 2027 and RSA key decommissioning in 2030; it invites feedback before execution. Verisign's December 2023 comments describe a possible later PQ rollover in the mid-2030s, a conditional scenario, not an ICANN plan or forecast.
- **Parallel size-mitigation drafts** — draft-sheth-pqc-dnssec-strategy surveys SLH-DSA-MTL/Falcon/XMSS/LMS candidates; the Fregly SLH-DSA-MTL draft -06 expired 1 October 2026; the Fregly and Kaizer individual drafts explore Merkle Tree Ladder mode with SLH-DSA and ML-DSA respectively. They are not IETF standards or working-group-adopted documents

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 3 steps:

1. **Signature Size Explorer** — compare RSA-2048, ECDSA P-256, Ed25519, ML-DSA-44, and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signature sizes against the ~1,232-byte DNS UDP ceiling; both PQ options shown exceed it
2. **PQ Validation Chain Walkthrough** — root → TLD → domain trust chain, toggling between "today" (algorithm 18 exists only at the dnstest.dev leaf) and "full deployment" (algorithm 18 at every level up to the root)
3. **Deployment Roadmap Tracker** — Cloudflare's own roadmap (resolver validation done → authoritative signing → registrar DS support → ~2029 company-wide PQ target) versus the DNS root's separate rollovers (the classical ICANN/IANA first rollover and Verisign's conditional mid-2030s scenario for a second)

## Related Standards

- RFC 4034 (DNSSEC resource records)
- RFC 9364 / BCP 237 (DNSSEC, consolidated)
- draft-westerbaan-dnssec-mldsa (ML-DSA-44 for DNSSEC, IANA algorithm 18)
- draft-sheth-pqc-dnssec-strategy (PQC strategy survey for DNSSEC)
- draft-fregly-dnsop-slh-dsa-mtl-dnssec (SLH-DSA Merkle Tree Ladder mode)
- draft-kaizer-dnsop-ml-dsa-mtl-dnssec (ML-DSA Merkle Tree Ladder mode)
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA)
- Cloudflare blog, "1.1.1.1 now supports post-quantum DNSSEC" (2026-09-10)

### What This Is About

Security products such as hardware security modules (HSMs) carry certificates: FIPS 140-3 in the US and Canada, Common Criteria internationally, EUCC in the European Union, and PCI approval for payment devices. This module explains what each certificate proves, why you read what a certificate covers before its level, and what happens when a certified product adds post-quantum cryptography. Three follow-on modules go deeper: into FIPS 140-3; into Common Criteria, EUCC and eIDAS; and into PCI.

### Why It Matters

A certificate covers something narrow: a defined product, at a specific version and configuration, checked against one scheme's rules. Adding new algorithms changes the product, and every scheme has its own route for handling that change. Reading a certificate wrongly leads to buying — or selling — protection that was never certified.

### The Key Takeaway

Read what a certificate covers before you read its grade. A deadline to move to post-quantum cryptography makes the work urgent, but it does not make certification faster or skip any step.

- **ACVP KAT Vector Conformance vs. Module Boundary Validation**: NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify mathematical algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`). CMVP FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module against its security requirements (module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization, physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B); non-invasive (side-channel) requirements are currently N/A by default. Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates the product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims.
- **Certificate Evidence-Chain Cross-Check vs. Sample Non-Equivalence**: When reading a production certificate, a useful check is: the certificate or module number and its status (active, historical or revoked); the exact module or product name and version; the tested operational environment or configuration (CMVP: Security Policy; CC: evaluated configuration in the certification report); the CAVP algorithm certificate numbers listed for the algorithms you rely on; and, for CC/EUCC, the Security Target and assurance level it claims. This is Hub practice guidance, not a certification-scheme requirement. A sample Hub exercise export or a vendor marketing datasheet is never certification evidence.

### What's Happening

As of November 2026, FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the CMVP Historical list in September 2026 while FIPS 140-3 itself is unchanged, NIST published final NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) deprecating quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them under NIST standards after 2035, the EU's EUCC scheme already lists post-quantum algorithms in its approved cryptography guidance (ECCG ACM v2), and PCI's newest HSM standard (PTS HSM v5.0) adds post-quantum definitions without naming a required algorithm or deadline.

A certificate covers something narrow: a defined product, at a specific version and configuration, checked against one scheme's rules. Adding new algorithms changes the product, and every scheme has its own route for handling that change. Reading a certificate wrongly leads to buying — or selling — protection that was never certified.
Read what a certificate covers before you read its grade. A deadline to move to post-quantum cryptography makes the work urgent, but it does not make certification faster or skip any step.
ACVP KAT Vector Conformance vs. Module Boundary Validation: NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify mathematical algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`). CMVP FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module against its security requirements (module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization, physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B); non-invasive (side-channel) requirements are currently N/A by default. Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates the product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims.
As of November 2026, FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the CMVP Historical list in September 2026 while FIPS 140-3 itself is unchanged, NIST published final NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) deprecating quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them under NIST standards after 2035, the EU's EUCC scheme already lists post-quantum algorithms in its approved cryptography guidance (ECCG ACM v2), and PCI's newest HSM standard (PTS HSM v5.0) adds post-quantum definitions without naming a required algorithm or deadline.

PQC does not replace the certification schemes or erase their process. It changes the cryptographic functions, implementation architecture, evidence, attack surface, test vectors, self-tests, operational constraints and change-control burden inside those processes.
Products still need a precisely defined boundary or TOE.
Vendors still produce design, lifecycle, test, guidance and vulnerability evidence.
Independent laboratories still evaluate against a declared standard or scheme.
Certificates still apply to specific versions and configurations.
Patches, algorithm additions, hardware revisions, compiler changes and new environments still need a change assessment.
Certification still does not replace secure deployment and operation.
New algorithm implementations and algorithm-validation dependencies
Each new function needs its own algorithm testing before a module can use it in approved mode.
New key, seed, signature, ciphertext, context and parameter formats
Import, export, wrapping and storage paths all change — and each is a place a lab looks.
Larger buffers, messages, certificates and persistent objects
ML-DSA signatures and ML-KEM ciphertexts are far larger than their classical counterparts.
Deterministic, hedged and randomized execution paths
Each variant is a distinct behaviour to document, test and self-test.
New approved-mode service definitions and APIs
A service is what the Security Policy or Security Target lists; new services change the evaluated interface.
Updated power-up and conditional self-tests, pairwise-consistency behaviour
FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance 10.3.A covers PQC self-tests, including a 19 August 2026 note on stored seeds.
New entropy and random-bit consumption patterns
Key generation draws on the RBG differently; entropy evidence may need re-examination.
Hybrid, classical and PQC negotiation and failure paths
Downgrade and fallback behaviour becomes security-relevant.
Constant-time and memory-handling work for new mathematical structures
Lattice and hash-based code leaks through different channels than RSA or ECC code.
Secure update and rollback during migration
A long transition means more firmware releases, each one a change to assess.
New operational environments, compilers, libraries or accelerators
Each needs certificate or change review, even if the algorithm code is unchanged.
Memory and bandwidth for larger keys, signatures and ciphertexts
An HSM sized for RSA and ECC transactions may need more of both.
Accelerator and datapath design for lattice and hash operations
New hardware paths are new implementations to evaluate.
New processor algorithm accelerators and implementation identities
FIPS 140-3 IG 2.3.C addresses processor algorithm accelerators (updated 27 February and 19 August 2026).
Power, electromagnetic, timing, cache and fault-injection leakage surfaces
Side-channel and fault analysis must be repeated for the new algorithms.
Random-number generation load and seed protection
More key generation and seed storage put more weight on the RBG and on seed confidentiality.
Non-volatile storage and zeroisation for new key formats
New objects must be stored and destroyed as reliably as the old ones.
Firmware authenticity and update capacity for long transitions
The firmware signature scheme itself may need a quantum-safe path.
Physical boundary and composition evidence when PQC runs in a coprocessor or FPGA
FIPS 140-3 IG 2.3.B allows multiple disjoint sub-chip cryptographic subsystems on one certificate only when Management Manual §7.8 is met (27 February 2026).

Throughput limits can shape which modes a product enables by default.
