# Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals

## Overview

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-065) distinguishes FIPS 140-3 module validation, Common Criteria product evaluation, EUCC scheme rules and PCI approval. Common Criteria supplies evaluation criteria; EUCC uses those criteria under an EU certification scheme. eIDAS is a separate legal context where applicable. The module explains certificate scope and what adding PQC changes, with links to LM-067 _FIPS 140-3 Certification_, LM-068 _Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification_ and LM-071 _PCI Certification_. It is written for product vendors, product-assurance leads, buyers and evaluators. It is labelled "Practitioner orientation — not laboratory training." Reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. It has not been reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. The context-separation correction was checked on 21 October 2026; other dated claims retain their individual source dates.

The module is a single ~95-minute route with no learn paths. Deeper material is kept as optional reference sections that do not count toward duration or completion. For the certification-engineer role, the box at the start of the Learn tab names three reader roles (lab tester, vendor engineer, scheme reviewer) and points next to LM-067 _FIPS 140-3 Certification_, then LM-066 _ACVP Lab Workflow_; no test vectors are run in this module.

## Key Concepts

- **Hybrid or standalone, by scheme (as of 22 October 2026)** — FIPS 140-3 approves ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA on their own; a hybrid KEM is allowed under IG D.S Scenario 2 conditions (approved key combiner, module-enforced fixed combinations); the IG has no hybrid-signature scenario. EUCC (ECCG ACM v2, unchanged in the v3 draft): (M)LWE mechanisms such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA should not be used standalone but combined with a classical mechanism; hash-based signatures may stand alone. BSI TR-02102-1 (2026-01) recommends PQC key agreement and (non-hash-based) signatures only in hybrid form, while hash-based signatures may in principle be used alone, provided their implementation security is carefully considered (BSI limits stateful schemes such as LMS and XMSS to special scenarios where error-free state management can be guaranteed); ANSSI's FAQ calls hybridisation essential, except for hash-based signatures. IETF Composite ML-DSA is approved and awaiting RFC publication but not yet named by FIPS IG or the ECCG mechanisms.

- **Standards, criteria and schemes have different roles** — FIPS 140-3 specifies module requirements validated through CMVP; CC provides product evaluation criteria; EUCC is a scheme using CC, not a separate alternative to CC. PCI addresses payment-device approval. Name the applicable scheme before applying its rules.
- **Words used in the scheme comparison table** — a short key above the "One question per scheme" table gives plain definitions of CSTL (Cryptographic and Security Testing Laboratory), CCRA (Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement), Security Target, Protection Profile, ITSEF (IT Security Evaluation Facility), PTS HSM (PIN Transaction Security Hardware Security Module), P2PE (Point-to-Point Encryption), KMO (Key Management and Operations, a PCI standard published as version 1.0 on 14 September 2026), QPA (Qualified PIN Assessor) and AVA_VAN (the Common Criteria vulnerability-analysis family, levels AVA_VAN.1 to AVA_VAN.5).
- **Scope before level** — a certificate covers a defined module, target or device at a version and configuration. The anchor is a fictional network HSM ("Orrin N7") sold as an appliance and as a multi-tenant cloud service into four markets.
- **What PQC changes in certification** — adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA changes the certified product, and each scheme has its own route for that change.
- **Reading a hybrid in a certificate's scope** — a hybrid KEM claim (IG D.S Scenario 2) is evidenced in different places: CAVP certificates for the ML-KEM half and the key combiner, the Security Policy's "KEM-Hybrid" or "KEM-Hybrid-Full" entry, and the lab's source-code review for the fixed combinations and the order the secrets are joined. A non-approved classical half such as X25519 must be enforced inside an approved hybrid by the module, and there is no end-to-end hybrid algorithm test yet. Under Common Criteria and EUCC the algorithm claims sit in the Security Target's cryptographic requirements.
- **Crypto agility versus certification latency** — a product can be agile in code and still wait on a scheme's change route.
- **A new platform, chip or accelerator: what carries over** — a validation covers the environments it was tested on. A moved module goes through vendor affirmation (VAOE, no CMVP statement on correct operation), an Operational Environment Update (OEUP, with CAVP testing on the new environment and ESV where applicable) or revalidation. A processor accelerator must be on the IG's "known" list and be tested with and without it; the list names no ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA accelerator. Under Common Criteria, a platform that breaks the Security Target's assumptions is a major change.
- **A market deadline creates urgency, not a shortcut** — it does not make a PQC addition eligible for a scheme's lighter change route. NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035 (supporting EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15), while CMVP moved FIPS 140-2 certificates to the Historical list on 21/22 September 2026; neither event bypasses CMVP submission routes.
- **ACVP KAT conformance vs. module boundary validation & certificate cross-check** — NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify mathematical algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`). CMVP FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module against its security requirements (module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization, physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B); non-invasive (side-channel) requirements are currently N/A by default. Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates the product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims. When reading a production certificate, a useful check is: the certificate or module number and its status (active, historical or revoked); the exact module or product name and version; the tested operational environment or configuration (CMVP: Security Policy; CC: evaluated configuration in the certification report); the CAVP algorithm certificate numbers listed for the algorithms you rely on; and, for CC/EUCC, the Security Target and assurance level it claims. This is Hub practice guidance, not a certification-scheme requirement. A sample Hub exercise export or a vendor marketing datasheet is never certification evidence.

A Processor Algorithm Acceleration (PAA) function is “simply a mathematical construct”; a Processor Algorithm Implementation (PAI) is a complete cryptographic algorithm in hardware. ### What This Is About

Before a cryptographic product can be sold to many governments and regulated buyers, its algorithms are tested by an automated NIST system and the whole product is examined by an accredited laboratory. This module explains, step by step, how that algorithm testing works and what each kind of test result does — and does not — prove.

### Why It Matters

"It passed the NIST tests" can mean very different things: a run against public sample data anyone can download, a run against test data issued to an accredited lab, or an official validation certificate. Mixing them up leads to claims nobody can back.

### The Key Takeaway

Every test result is evidence only for the exact test, settings, software build and machine it ran on. Only NIST publishes validations; running public samples, including on this site, never does.

- **ACVP KAT Vector Conformance vs. Module Boundary Validation**: NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`). CMVP FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module against its security requirements (module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization, physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B). Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates the product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims.
- **Certificate Evidence-Chain Cross-Check vs. Sample Non-Equivalence**: When reading a production certificate, a useful check is: the certificate or module number and its status (active, historical or revoked); the exact module or product name and version; the tested operational environment or configuration (CMVP: Security Policy; CC: evaluated configuration in the certification report); the CAVP algorithm certificate numbers listed for the algorithms you rely on; and, for CC/EUCC, the Security Target and assurance level it claims. This is Hub practice guidance, not a certification-scheme requirement. A sample Hub exercise export or a vendor marketing datasheet is never certification evidence.

### What's Happening

As of November 2026, NIST's ACVP protocol specification (`draft-ietf-acvp-spec-01`, 30 October 2026) and algorithm sub-specifications cover ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA using seed-driven `AFT` and `VAL` vector groups (distinct from classical `GDT` key-generation groups and SHA `MCT`/`LDT` groups). The PQC Today owner reviewed and signed off this module on 1 November 2026. No accredited laboratory or certification body has reviewed it. It explains how laboratory testing works; it is not laboratory training material.

LM-066.summary:
# ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence

**Status: reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. Not yet reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. Not a lab training resource.**

## Overview

Advanced module on how cryptographic algorithm validation testing actually runs and how to state a result at exactly the evidence level it reached. It separates algorithm validation (CAVP, run black-box through NIST's ACVTS) from module validation (CMVP, FIPS 140-3, tested by accredited CST laboratories), walks the ACVP lifecycle from capability registration to validation record, and shows where standard PKCS#11 v3.2 has no field for an ACVP test group's input and how this HSM accepts such inputs as optional test inputs outside the standard. It is the algorithm-testing companion to the pqc-testing-validation module.

## Key Concepts

- **Algorithm vs module validation** — CAVP validates algorithm implementations (NIST CAVP ACVP JSON test vectors verify algorithm conformance of an implementation under test (`IUT`)) and is a prerequisite of CMVP module validation (NIST CAVP page); CMVP validates modules to FIPS 140-3 (eleven requirement areas, four levels) covering module specification and boundary, interfaces, self-tests, key and SSP zeroization and physical security, with entropy sources validated separately under SP 800-90B. Common Criteria/EUCC evaluates a product against its own Security Target, and only what the ST claims. CMVP uses NVLAP-accredited CST labs; Common Criteria/EUCC uses ITSEFs and scheme certification bodies; labs must also confirm algorithm "shall" statements CAVP testing does not cover (CMVP Management Manual v2.7 §2.6.2)
- **Production certificate cross-check vs sample non-equivalence** — When reading a production certificate, a useful check is: the certificate or module number and its status (active, historical or revoked); the exact module or product name and version; the tested operational environment or configuration (CMVP: Security Policy; CC: evaluated configuration in the certification report); the CAVP algorithm certificate numbers listed for the algorithms you rely on; and, for CC/EUCC, the Security Target and assurance level it claims. This is Hub practice guidance, not a certification-scheme requirement. A sample Hub exercise export or a vendor marketing datasheet is never certification evidence.
- **Registration and vector sets** — the client registers algorithm/mode/revision capabilities; ACVTS generates matching test vector sets (vsId) of test groups (tgId) and test cases (tcId) (ACVP spec §3.2, §5.4); revision is part of the identity (ML-DSA sigGen FIPS204 vs FIPS204-tr1)
- **Lifecycle** — POST testSessions → GET vector set (prompt) → POST results (response) → GET results (disposition: passed/fail/incomplete/expired/missing/unreceived/error) → PUT testSessions (certify with module + OE) → validation id (ACVP spec §12.4); vector sets are one-time use for a validation authority (§14); ACVTS Demo is a sandbox, only Prod (accredited labs) creates CAVP certificates
- **Test types** — AFT (Algorithm Functional Test, including seed-driven ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA keyGen — in contrast to classical RSA/ECDSA GDT Generation-Driven Tests), VAL (ML-KEM decapsulation incl. implicit rejection; key checks), MCT (Monte Carlo Test) and LDT (Large Data Test) for SHA, plus ML-DSA rejection-path tests; minimum test counts per capability combination (usnistgov/ACVP sub-specifications)
- **Deterministic vs randomized** — FIPS 203/204/205 internal interfaces take randomness as input; tests that must supply the random input use them, and the current ACVP ML-DSA specification supports testing both internal and external interfaces (§6.1.2). Two correct ML-DSA implementations signing the same message in hedged mode can produce different signatures — check that both verify; in an ACVP sigGen test the test supplies the random input and the expected signature must match exactly; ML-DSA/SLH-DSA hedged vs deterministic variants; comparator policy (byte vs semantic)
- **PKCS#11 adapter boundaries** — standard PKCS#11 has no field for ML-KEM m, ML-DSA rnd, SLH-DSA addrnd, ECDSA k or the SLH-DSA internal interface; this HSM accepts each as an optional test input outside the standard (CKM_ML_KEM / CKM_ECDSA parameter; an extended signing structure with pRandom, ulRandomLen, messageEncoding), and every result that used one is labelled "test input supplied (outside the standard)"; FIPS 203/204/205 reserve such interfaces for testing and a validated module would keep them out of its approved mode; ML-DSA internal goes through the external-μ mechanism (0x403c, PKCS#11 v3.3 working draft) with μ = SHAKE256(tr ‖ M′, 64) computed by the harness; SHA2-512/224 and SHA2-512/256 pre-hash use the generic CKM_HASH_ML_DSA / CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA; ML-KEM key checks are not a PKCS#11 operation; deterministic sigGen via CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED
- **Negative testing** — ACVP sigVer modifications (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA incl. too long/short), ML-KEM modified ciphertexts and invalid keys; requirements ACVP does not test; API-level negatives
- **Evidence provenance** — the Hub's eight evidence classes and permitted claims, the nine-rung claim ladder (Hub policy), tested-scope rule, provenance by SHA-256 against a pinned ACVP-Server commit (not by the isSample flag), generated counts
- **Cross-implementation limits** — the two Hub engines share adapter code, so agreement is differential evidence, not independent validation; results bind to an operational environment
- **Contributing** — vector manifest workflow (scaffold, provenance, lineage, audit, generated counts), two-person review, never commit issued vectors

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

1. **Evidence Classifier** — classify ten test-log observations into the eight evidence classes or "not test evidence"; see the claim-ladder rung, permitted claim and the overclaim trap
2. **Vector Set Anatomy** — parse a public NIST ACVP-Server sample (ML-KEM encapDecap or ML-DSA sigVer) with the Hub's ACVP-format prototype parser and predict per test group whether standard PKCS#11 calls can answer it (Step 3 then shows what the engines' test-only inputs add)
3. **Response Artifact Lab** — save the public prompt, run it through the real ACVP-format prototype panel on the C++ or Rust engine (every test of both samples is answered; the answers are counted by how they were obtained: standard PKCS#11 v3.2 calls, calls to the vendor-defined external-μ mechanism with the μ NIST supplies, NIST's random value m as a test-only input, a value computed outside the engine, or the result of importing a key), download response.json + evidence.json, compare with NIST expectedResults.json, and audit evidence.json (a collapsed explanation covers every part of the file and why it exists)

## Related Standards

- ACVP JSON specification (draft-ietf-acvp-spec-01) and usnistgov/ACVP algorithm sub-specifications (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, SHA)
- FIPS 140-3, CMVP Management Manual v2.7, NIST SP 800-140C
- FIPS 203, FIPS 204, FIPS 205
- PKCS #11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard) and PKCS #11 Profiles v3.2

LM-066/s:prompt-response-lifecycle.full:
The prompt was issued to an authorized test session and executed unchanged, so the response is generated (rung 7). Acceptance (rung 8) needs the server disposition, and a validation record (rung 9) needs the certification step and NIST publication.
The prompt is not one of the pinned public NIST samples (its SHA-256 matched none of them) and nobody can show it was issued to an ACVTS session. There is no expected answer to compare with, so a fully answered response is not evidence of correctness at any rung. Only an ACVTS session can give it a verdict.
Lifecycle — POST testSessions → GET vector set (prompt) → POST results (response) → GET results (disposition: passed/fail/incomplete/expired/missing/unreceived/error) → PUT testSessions (certify with module + OE) → validation id (ACVP spec §12.4); vector sets are one-time use for a validation authority (§14); ACVTS Demo is a sandbox, only Prod (accredited labs) creates CAVP certificates

LM-066/s:test-types.full:
As of November 2026, NIST's ACVP protocol specification (`draft-ietf-acvp-spec-01`, 30 October 2026) and algorithm sub-specifications cover ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA using seed-driven `AFT` and `VAL` vector groups (distinct from classical `GDT` key-generation groups and SHA `MCT`/`LDT` groups). The PQC Today owner reviewed and signed off this module on 1 November 2026. No accredited laboratory or certification body has reviewed it. It explains how laboratory testing works; it is not laboratory training material.
Why can an application that talks to a token only through PKCS#11 v3.2 C_EncapsulateKey not answer an ML-KEM encapDecap AFT test group?
An ML-KEM VAL decapsulation test hands the implementation a modified ciphertext. What must the implementation return?
ML-KEM.Decaps_internal performs implicit rejection: on a re-encryption mismatch it returns a key derived from the secret rejection value z and the ciphertext. The ML-KEM sub-specification’s VAL decapsulation test expects k from either the valid path or the implicit-rejection path.
What does a SHA-2 Monte Carlo Test (MCT) exercise that an AFT does not?
The ACVP SHA sub-specification defines AFT (single operations), MCT (chained computations from a seed) and LDT (multi-gigabyte messages) as separate test types.

Comparator policy follows from the algorithm
You are comparing two implementations of ML-DSA, the post-quantum digital-signature algorithm. They sign the same message with the same key, context and settings. In normal hedged signing, each call uses fresh random input, so the signatures can differ without either implementation being wrong. Check that both signatures verify; different bytes alone do not establish a fault.
In an ACVP signature-generation test, however, the test supplies the random input as well as the other inputs. The implementation must use those inputs and produce the expected signature exactly. Successful verification alone is not enough to pass that test

ACVP builds negative cases into the vector sets. An implementation that answers “valid” to everything fails them:

Why rejecting a bad signature is a passing test
We deliberately give the module a bad signature. If it rejects that signature, the test passes—the module did its job correctly.
A failed internal self-test means something different: the module checked its own cryptographic implementation and that check failed. This does not prove it correctly examined our bad signature.
Therefore, our test must check why the operation failed—not treat every error as a correct rejection.
Implicit rejection is not an error path
You are testing a cryptographic implementation’s ML-KEM decapsulation operation: the step that uses the recipient’s private key and the received ciphertext to recover a shared secret. This ACVP test supplies a ciphertext of the correct length that triggers the algorithm’s internal rejection check, with otherwise valid inputs. The expected result is the fallback shared secret prescribed by FIPS 203—not an error and not an arbitrary random secret. The test passes only if the returned secret exactly matches the expected value. This test checks ML-KEM itself; it does not need to encrypt or decrypt application data. A wrong-length ciphertext is a separate input-error case
Run the ML-KEM tests in the
and compare two results. The row “PKCS#11 boundary · product-authored probe · C_DecapsulateKey with a … (1 short)” gives a ciphertext of the wrong length; the correct result is an input error. A row “Decapsulate · NIST encapDecap VAL … · modified ciphertext → implicit rejection k” gives a correct-length ciphertext that was altered; the correct result is success, with the returned secret equal to NIST’s expected fallback value. Both outcomes are correct: the first input breaks the rules before decapsulation starts, the second passes those checks and is handled by implicit rejection inside the algorithm.

Running the same case on two implementations or two platforms is valuable — a disagreement is always a finding. Agreement is weaker than it looks:
In the Hub’s ACVP-format prototype, the C++ and Rust engines are driven by one dispatcher and one response builder. LM-067.curious:
### What This Is About

A closer look at FIPS 140-3, the US and Canadian standard for cryptographic modules; the validation program behind it, the CMVP, is a joint effort of NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. It builds on the certification fundamentals module; payment approval (PCI) has its own module. A hands-on step reads the real algorithm and Security Policy records of two modules, side by side.

### Why It Matters

Passing algorithm tests is only the first step toward FIPS 140-3; the module certificate is a separate result. Adding post-quantum algorithms changes the module, so it needs a new validation route.

### The Key Takeaway

A listing on the Modules In Process list (voluntary, and not every module in review is shown) is a queue position, not a certificate; a module is validated only once NIST and CCCS issue a FIPS 140-3 certificate. Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA also requires module-internal cryptographic algorithm self-tests (CASTs) and pair-wise consistency tests (PCTs) under IG 10.3.A, not just external ACVP vectors.

### What's Happening

All FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the CMVP Historical list in September 2026 (still usable for existing systems, but not recommended for new federal procurements). Meanwhile, US Executive Order 14412 directs the Secretary of Commerce, through NIST's Director, to revise CMVP processes within 180 days (around 19 December 2026) to accelerate validations of cryptographic modules.

LM-067.summary:
# FIPS 140-3 Certification

## Overview

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-067) is a scheme deep dive split out of LM-065 _Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals_. It covers FIPS 140-3 and the CMVP: what a certificate proves, how to read one, and what adding post-quantum cryptography means for a validated module. PCI PTS HSM and the payment operating stack are covered in LM-071 _PCI Certification_. Version 1 is labelled "Practitioner orientation — not laboratory training." Reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. It has not been reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. Facts are as of 24 September 2026, except items that give their own later dates (such as the algorithm records, read on 23 and 24 October 2026).

One timed ~80-minute route. Deeper material is kept as optional reference sections.

## Key Concepts

- **Read the exact PQC capability** — KeyGen is key generation, SigGen is signing, and SigVer is signature verification. Follow the operation's algorithm-validation link for its capabilities and parameter sets, then check the module Security Policy for the approved service and configuration. A signing entry alone does not establish coverage of other operations or every parameter set. The existing certificate #5497 example links to A5631.
- **Three different ML-DSA checks** — external algorithm testing (ACVP/CAVP) checks supplied cases; a cryptographic algorithm self-test (CAST) checks the module's own implementation before first approved use (a known-answer test uses fixed inputs and an expected result, not every customer key); a pair-wise consistency test (PCT) checks that a generated key pair works together (required before first export or first operational use of a newly generated key pair/seed; reconstitution from a stored seed needs no new PCT per the 19 August 2026 IG update). They do not replace each other. Review test timing, failure reporting and required error-state restrictions; this explanation does not claim the Hub tested its HSM's failure handling. See IG §10.3.A for CAST and PCT requirements across ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.
- **Key export policy is not a blanket plaintext ban** — FIPS requirements for key entry/output depend on security level, module type and transfer method (IG §9.5.A). Consult the module’s Security Policy for covered services and protections. The linked PKCS#11 AES exercise checks a selected policy: plaintext reads refused, encrypted backup permitted, and protection retained on restoration. It does not establish FIPS validation.
- **Side-channel and fault attacks: what a certificate shows** — SP 800-140F, the publication that would set test metrics for non-invasive security, lists no requirements yet, so the Management Manual treats that area as N/A by default. A publicly documented countermeasure must still be addressed under "Mitigation of other attacks" (IG 12.A), but no published CMVP test metric sets how far the lab's verification goes. Common Criteria AVA_VAN analysis and penetration testing covers only what the Security Target claims, under its assumptions. The section separates sourced statements from the module's own analysis.
- **Algorithm validation is not the certificate** — CAVP/ACVP algorithm validation is the prerequisite stage, not a FIPS 140-3 module certificate. A module can be in progress without being listed: the Modules In Process and Implementation Under Test lists are voluntary, and the Management Manual (§4.2) says the list “doesn’t necessarily include all modules being tested or reviewed”. It is certified only with a FIPS 140-3 certificate.
- **Vendor-affirmed is not an algorithm test certificate** — vendor-affirmed means the vendor states that an algorithm meets the standard without an algorithm test certificate; NIST's FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance allows it only where a specific IG section permits it, for example IG C.O for HSS signatures.
- **Modules in Process is a queue, not an outcome** — a CMVP MIP entry is not evidence of validation.
- **FIPS 140-3 is unchanged** — no 2025–2026 draft revises FIPS 140-3 or Level 3. Executive Order 14412 §6(b) directs NIST to revise CMVP processes to accelerate validations, with a deadline of about 19 December 2026. FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the Historical list on 21/22 September 2026.
- **FIPS Level 3 is not a PCI approval** — a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM does not thereby hold PCI PTS HSM approval; whether a PCI operational standard accepts a FIPS certificate in place of a PTS approval is set in that standard’s own requirement text, which this module does not state.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

_Level and boundary planner_: choose the FIPS 140-3 security level and module boundary for the anchor HSM's appliance and cloud-partition variants.

_Read the algorithm records_ (about 15 minutes): read the records of two real modules, certificates #5497 (QASM Cryptographic Module, records as of 23 October 2026) and #5450 (Luna T7, records as of 24 October 2026), for the same operations. For each row the learner marks whether it is listed on the algorithm validation and whether it is listed in the Security Policy's Approved Algorithms table; the two deterministic-setting rows add a third mark for the Policy's function table (Security Function Implementations), because the Policy's two tables can differ. A last single-choice question asks what an algorithm validation can and cannot show. The step uses short quotes with page numbers and links to NIST's copies, names each vendor only as the source of its records, and does not rate or compare the modules.

LM-068.curious:
### What This Is About

A closer look at the certificates that matter most in Europe: Common Criteria, the EU's EUCC scheme built on it, and the eIDAS rules for qualified signature and seal devices. It builds on the certification fundamentals module.

### Why It Matters

A Common Criteria grade such as "EAL4+" only means something once you know which extra checks were added. A CC evaluation may support an EUCC certificate or form part of an eIDAS device-assessment chain, while international CCRA recognition remains a separate, conditional question.

### The Key Takeaway

"EAL4+" means nothing until its extra components are named, and EUCC is a legal scheme — not a Protection Profile. Certification engineers must also use the current mandatory CC:2022 errata, not only the base documents.

### What's Happening

As of November 2026, the EU's EUCC scheme (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482, succeeding SOG-IS national certificates across the EU) lists post-quantum algorithms in its applicable ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2 guidance and says lattice-based mechanisms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) should be combined with a classical mechanism, while US NIAP Policy #33 sets CNSA 2.0 cut-offs starting 1 January 2028 for products evaluated by NIAP or CCRA partners.

The lesson also includes Security Target source-reading cases (reviewed November 2026) and two collapsed reference panels: an invented example of how three post-quantum requirements could be written in a Security Target, and a box on how a laboratory might look at attacks on lattice-based code. No certification scheme or laboratory has reviewed either reference panel.

CC:2022 Part 5 describes EAL4 as “methodically designed, tested and reviewed”, and as the highest level at which it is likely to be economically feasible to retrofit an existing product line. Its components include:
Implementation representation of the TSF, mapped to the design for a sample

Flaw remediation is in no EAL; CC:2022 Part 5 notes it is often used as an augmentation
The notion of “augmentation” allows the addition of assurance components (from assurance families not already included in the EAL) or the substitution of assurance components (with another hierarchically higher assurance component in the same assurance family) to an EAL.
Listings shorten “EAL4 augmented” to “EAL4+”. The plus sign tells you something was added; it does not tell you what. The same headline can stand for one extra component or for five. A bare “EAL4+” is therefore incomplete — the claim only means something with its component list, as in “EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2, ALC_FLR.2 and AVA_VAN.5”.

The Cryptographic Module, which is the Target of Evaluation (TOE), generates and/or protects secret keys and other sensitive data, and allows controlled use of these data for one or more cryptographic services in support of TSP trust services.
The PP is deliberately generic: the TOE is “a set of configured software and hardware” — for example a PCIe card inside a server, or a dedicated module that client applications reach over a network — and client applications are always outside it. The TOE supports signing and sealing, certificate issuance and revocation, time stamping and authentication, and may support key backup. It is not, in general, aware of the context in which a function is used — enforcing sole control of a signing key is the client application’s job, with the TOE’s authorisation mechanisms.

FIPS 203, Section 7.1 (Algorithm 19, ML-KEM.KeyGen)
Name the parameter set. FIPS 203 defines three, and their key sizes differ: for ML-KEM-768 the encapsulation key is 1184 bytes and the decapsulation key is 2400 bytes. A claim that says only “ML-KEM” does not tell the laboratory which parameter set to test.
FCS_CKM.1 has three assignments and no selection. An ST author must complete every assignment.
One iteration is enough for one method, even with several key sizes. A later ML-KEM-1024 could be handled in two ways: the author can list both parameter sets and their key sizes in the assignments of this iteration, or write a second iteration. CC:2022 Part 1 leaves the choice to the author, who weighs whether one rationale covers the whole list or each value needs its own rationale and trace.
Key generation uses random bytes. FIPS 203 requires an approved random bit generator with at least 192 bits of security strength for ML-KEM-768. In CC terms that is the dependency of FCS_CKM.1 on FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, which the errata keep.
in accordance with a specified cryptographic algorithm
ML-DSA.Sign, hedged variant, parameter set ML-DSA-65
FIPS 204, Section 5.2 (Algorithm 2, ML-DSA.Sign)
For ML-DSA-65 the private key is 4032 bytes.
Put “hedged” in the algorithm assignment. FIPS 204 signs with fresh randomness by default and also allows a deterministic variant. The two variants differ in one step. A product that offers both can name both variants in the assignments of one iteration or write one iteration per variant. CC:2022 Part 1 requires every iteration to differ from the others in its completed assignments, selections or refinements, and leaves the choice between a list of values and separate iterations to the author.
FIPS 204 says the deterministic variant should not be used where side-channel attacks are a concern and cannot be otherwise mitigated. So offering the deterministic variant adds a question for the vulnerability analysis.
The hedged variant uses a fresh 32-byte random value, which FIPS 204 says should ideally be generated by an approved random bit generator. The errata say that random bits generated inside an operation should be covered by FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, through a dependency added to the operation or, where it applies, through the operation’s dependency on key generation, which itself depends on one of them. Here the second route applies, through the ML-DSA-65 key generation iteration that this excerpt leaves out.
This iteration covers signature generation only. Checking a signature, for example on a firmware update, is a different operation. CC:2022 Part 2 would let one iteration list both operations; this example gives checking its own iteration because it uses a different key (the public key) and a different algorithm entry (ML-DSA.Verify).
EN 419 221-5 requires that, if the TOE supports updates, the iterations cover the operations that check update signatures.
The classical half keeps its existing ECDSA or RSA iteration. ACM v2 says lattice mechanisms should be combined with a classical one, and that a hybrid signature can be a concatenation of signatures that must all verify. The excerpt does not show how the hybrid signature itself is claimed; see the note after the two panels.
The TSF shall derive cryptographic keys
the concatenation of the ML-KEM-768 shared secret and the ECDH P-256 shared secret in the fixed order of the combination; a salt; and a FixedInfo string that holds the name of the combination, the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key and ciphertext, and both ECDH public values
in accordance with a specified key derivation algorithm
two-step key derivation, with HMAC-SHA-256 for randomness extraction and HMAC-SHA-256 for key expansion (the HKDF construction of RFC 5869)
NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2, Sections 2 and 5; NIST SP 800-227, Section 4.6.2; RFC 5869
CC:2022 has a component for this step. FCS_CKM.5 is the key derivation component. It requires that the methods, standards and parameters for key derivation are specified. A CC 3.1 profile such as EN 419 221-5 has no such component. Its cryptographic support section lists FCS_CKM.1, FCS_CKM.4, FCS_COP.1 and FCS_RNG.1.
FCS_CKM.5 has five assignments: key type, input parameters, key derivation algorithm, key sizes and standards. The errata add the missing application notes for all five. The input parameters are where the design shows: which secrets go in, in what order, and what context is bound to the result.
NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2 allows a hybrid shared secret, which is the concatenation of a standard shared secret and a second secret. SP 800-227 approves applying SP 800-56C key-derivation methods to the shared secret of an approved KEM, and approves a key combiner built on them when at least one of the shared secrets comes from SP 800-56A, SP 800-56B or an approved KEM. With the two-step method, extraction is done on all the shared secrets together. HKDF, defined in RFC 5869, is a version of that two-step method that uses HMAC for both steps.
FIPS 203 itself says that further key derivation from the ML-KEM shared secret shall be done in an approved manner, as specified in SP 800-108 and SP 800-56C. Inside SP 800-56C, the functions of SP 800-108 are used in the key-expansion step of the two-step method. That is why the example lists SP 800-56C and not SP 800-108.
The FIPS 140-3 route asks for two related design choices: a fixed set of combinations and module control of the order in which the secrets are joined. There the step is called the key combiner.
FCS_CKM.5 depends on FCS_CKM.6, key destruction. CC:2022 reads that dependency in two directions, destruction of the key-derivation key and destruction of the derived keys, and asks the author to consider intermediate values from key establishment. In this example the destruction list could name the two shared secrets, the extracted key-derivation key, the session keys, and the ML-KEM key-generation seed if the product stores it; the sources do not prescribe the exact list.
SP 800-56C Rev. 2 says the extracted key-derivation key shall be destroyed after use. FIPS 203 says the key-generation seed is as sensitive as the decapsulation key. NIAP’s
says that key material includes seeds and other secret values used to derive keys, and that all such keys and keying material are subject to destruction in the first assignment of its key destruction requirement.

Annex I lists the EN 419 221-5 HSM interpretation under the security-box domain, and the security-box document has an annex with rating advice for hardware security modules. An HSM that claims EN 419 221-5, such as the Orrin N7, would therefore normally be assessed in that domain; the certification body confirms the domain for a given product.
The same attack path can get different points under the CEM, the security-box document and the smart-card document, because the factor values differ: for a difficult window of opportunity the CEM table gives 10 points, and the security-box document gives 4 for identification and 5 for exploitation. A total is read on the table of the domain that applies and is not carried to another table.
The security-box document scores the effort to find an attack (identification) and the effort to repeat it (exploitation) separately, then adds them.
The smart-card document adds that where cryptography is involved the certification body should be consulted. The attack types the documents already name are the ones behind the targets below: perturbation, power consumption, emanation and timing (security boxes); perturbation, key retrieval by fault analysis and side-channel attacks (smart cards).
Before rating an attack path, the evaluator determines whether it is applicable and reachable under the TOE boundary, the interfaces, the assumptions and the operational environment.
EN 419 221-5 assumes a protected environment that limits physical access to authorised administrators. Its OE.Env also lists inspections that detect attempts to reach side-channels, and protection against emanation attacks. The profile’s refinement of AVA_VAN.5 says that the protection which FPT_PHP.1 and FPT_PHP.3 must give against physical attacks is equivalent to the assessment in ISO/IEC 19790 at Security Level 3. Its rationale for AVA_VAN.5 (section 7.2.4) adds that, while the environment is meant to protect against physical attacks, a high level of protection against logical attacks, especially remote ones, is also necessary, and that this is why the vulnerability analysis is augmented to High attack potential. ENISA’s interpretation adds that physical attacks by other persons are not applicable, that no additional vulnerability analysis for physical attacks is needed, and that all kinds of administrator access must be taken into account, including logical access through interfaces that only administrators can reach. The security-box document describes power-consumption analysis as done through an external interface of the TOE, emanation analysis as done with an antenna outside the security-box boundary, and timing analysis as usually possible through the external interfaces. For an HSM under that profile, logical attacks reachable through interfaces, including timing and error behaviour seen from outside, therefore remain relevant.
Most of the published attacks below were shown on Kyber or Dilithium implementations. ML-KEM and ML-DSA are derived from those designs, and the standards list the differences in an appendix. NIST notes that exposure to side-channel attacks varies by application, so universal guidelines are unlikely to help.
The NTT and decapsulation in ML-KEM, masked or not.
Primas, Pessl and Mangard showed a single-trace attack on a lattice-based encryption scheme that uses leakage from the number-theoretic transform and can also attack masked implementations; they note that the attack can be adapted to other lattice-based constructions (CHES 2017).
Hamburg and co-authors attacked CCA2-secure Kyber with chosen ciphertexts, also against masked implementations, in a noisy leakage setting (TCHES 2021, issue 4).
Bos and co-authors built the first completely masked Kyber, with first-order masked decapsulation costing 3.1 million cycles on an Arm Cortex-M4F (TCHES 2021, issue 4).
Hermelink, Pessl and Pöppelmann combined a modified ciphertext with a fault that restores it during decapsulation, and say shuffling and Boolean masking do not stop the attack (INDOCRYPT 2021).
Bernstein and co-authors found that a division on secret data takes input-dependent time (KyberSlash), and recovered Kyber secret keys within minutes to a few hours on a Raspberry Pi 2 and an Arm Cortex-M4 (TCHES 2025, issue 2).
NIST SP 800-227 says KEM modules should have countermeasures against side-channel attacks, including constant-time code and protection of memory from leakage.
The rejection loop in ML-DSA signing.
ML-DSA signing repeats a loop until the checks pass, and FIPS 204 says each pass either produces a valid signature or an invalid one whose release would leak information about the private key.
Zhou and co-authors showed that leakage from rejected signing attempts gives the challenge and response of those attempts, from which an integer-programming step recovered Dilithium-2, -3 and -5 private keys in seconds or minutes; they measured the leakage as power consumption on an Arm Cortex-M4 (TCHES 2025, issue 4).
Zhao and co-authors used power traces from both rejected and final attempts, and report that the attack also works in the hedged mode (DATE 2026). Both attacks use power measurements.
FIPS 204 notes that deterministic signing leaks information about the message, not the private key, through timing, and advises hedged signing if the message must stay hidden.
Azouaoui and co-authors classify the steps of Dilithium signing by the protection they need, and report that the randomized variant can be much cheaper to protect than the deterministic one (TCHES 2023, issue 4).
Fault injection on ML-DSA signing, and on verification.
Signature verification takes only a public key, a message and a signature. Fault analysis that retrieves a key works from the difference between correct and faulty cryptographic outputs. So the fault target for key recovery is signing, not verification.
Bruinderink and Pessl showed that single random faults in deterministic Dilithium can cause nonce reuse and key recovery; with clock glitching on an Arm Cortex-M4, up to 65.2% of the execution time of Dilithium was vulnerable to an unprofiled attack that injects a random fault anywhere during signing (TCHES 2018, issue 3). FIPS 204 cites this paper among the reasons for the hedged default.
Ravi and co-authors injected electromagnetic faults into the deterministic Dilithium code of the pqm4 library and recovered an important portion of the secret key (AsiaCCS 2019).
Krahmer and co-authors showed key-recovery faults against hedged (randomized) Dilithium too: as few as 1024 and 512 faulty signatures for Dilithium2 in their two attacks, one of which faults the public matrix A (TCHES 2024, issue 3).
Azevedo-Oliveira and co-authors build a key-recovery attack on Dilithium for the case where the rejection step is weakened, and note that physically preventing one of the rejection tests gives two fault attacks (PKC 2025).
FIPS 204 says the missing randomness makes fault attacks on the deterministic variant harder to mitigate. So hedging makes fault attacks easier to mitigate, but published work shows it does not stop them.
A fault in verification does not recover a key, but it can change an accept or reject result: the smart-card document lists changing “the results of validation such as authentication” among the goals of faults. Calle Viera, Berzati and Heydemann examined the verification of the Dilithium reference implementation under randomizing, zeroizing and skipping faults, and describe how to forge signatures without the secret key by using faults in verification together with properties of the public parameters (CARDIS 2023). EN 419 221-5 has the evaluator test that only validly signed updates can be installed, so for a product with signed updates the check itself is a target.

Remote qualified signing on the Orrin N7 appliance
An EU qualified trust service provider (QTSP) wants to run remote qualified electronic signatures for its customers’ signatories. The signing keys will live in the fictional Orrin N7 network HSM. For this exercise, the buyer explicitly requests EUCC certification of the HSM against EN 419221-5. The vendor plans to add ML-DSA. Trace that selected evidence route; it is not a universal eIDAS route. Complete QSCD certification and qualified trust-service status remain separate questions.
Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 — Annex II requirements for QSCDs, Article 30 certification and Article 29a remote management
eIDAS 2.0 itself, which is the Protection Profile the HSM must conform to
CIR (EU) 2024/482 (EUCC), which obliges every QTSP to use EUCC-certified HSMs
EUCC is a certification scheme under the Cybersecurity Act. It says how a certificate is obtained, not who must obtain one. The duty to use a certified QSCD comes from eIDAS.
CIR 2025/1570, which defines the algorithms and Protection Profile for every certified QSCD
The QTSP’s remote-signing service and the HSM inside it are assessed differently. Which split is right?
Right. Two different assessments: a conformity assessment of the QTSP’s operations, and a product certification of the device. Neither substitutes for the other.
One EUCC certificate on the HSM covers the QTSP’s whole service
A product certificate covers a TOE — the device in its evaluated configuration. The QTSP’s key management, signatory authentication and operations are assessed as a trust service, not by the HSM’s certificate.
A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificate on the HSM satisfies both the service and the device requirement
FIPS 140-3 answers a different question (a US/Canadian cryptographic-module validation). It is neither a QSCD certification nor a trust-service conformity assessment.
Only where the product is covered by an Annex I technical domain or an Annex II certified PP (or, in exceptional and duly justified cases, once the authority approves or amends the proposed methodology) — and it is then assurance level “high”
Right. Article 7(3) allows AVA_VAN 4 or 5 where the product is covered by an Annex I technical domain or an Annex II protection profile and, in exceptional and duly justified cases, with the national cybersecurity certification authority’s approval (Art 7(3)(c), 7(4)); Article 4 maps AVA_VAN 3–5 to “high”. Annex II lists EN 419241-2 and EN 419221-5 for remote QSCDs.
Any ITSEF can evaluate any product at AVA_VAN.5; “high” just means EAL4 or above
“Substantial” is enough, because substantial means AVA_VAN.5
“Substantial” corresponds to AVA_VAN level 1 or 2 only. AVA_VAN.5 is always “high”.
EUCC (CIR 2024/482): level “high” (AVA_VAN 3–5, Art 4); AVA_VAN.5 via an Annex II PP (Art 7(3))
Which Protection Profile fits the Orrin N7 as the QTSP’s signing HSM?
EN 419221-5 (ANSSI-CC-PP-2016/05-M01), the TSP cryptographic-module PP — with EN 419241-2 covering the server-signing QSCD it sits in
Right. EN 419221-5 is the PP for a cryptographic module used by trust service providers (EAL4 augmented with AVA_VAN.5). EN 419241-2 covers the server-signing QSCD (signature activation). Both are the Annex II PPs for remote QSCDs.
EN 419211 (secure signature creation device PPs), listed in Decision 2016/650
PP: EN 419221-5:2018 (ANSSI-CC-PP-2016/05-M01), CC 3.1 R4, EAL4 augmented with AVA_VAN.5, strict conformance; with EN 419241-2 for the server-signing QSCD
EUCC Annex I lists a state-of-the-art document for this PP. What does it settle for the evaluator?
How the PP’s physical-protection (FPT_PHP) requirements are tested: meet the ISO/IEC 19790 Security Level 3 physical-security requirements; physical attacks by anyone other than authorised administrators are out of scope because the environment objective OE.ENV limits physical access
That a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificate replaces the physical-security evaluation
It points the evaluator at the ISO/IEC 19790 Level 3 physical-security requirements as the test basis. It does not accept a CMVP certificate in place of the CC evaluation.
ML-DSA is an agreed mechanism, preferably ML-DSA-87 or ML-DSA-65, and lattice-based schemes should be combined with a classical mechanism rather than used standalone
Right. ACM v2 lists ML-DSA and recommends the highest standardised parameter set (ML-DSA-87 or -65). Its Note 51 says these novel primitives “shouldn’t be used in a standalone way” — hybridise, for example by concatenating signatures that must all verify.
ACM v3 applies, so follow its PQC list
ACM v3 is a draft (public review until end of July 2026). As of 24 September 2026 the applicable version is ACM v2 (document dated April 2025; ENISA lists it on 6 May 2025).
Any parameter set NIST approved in FIPS 204 is agreed, standalone — ML-DSA-44 is fine
ACM is the EU’s own list. It recommends ML-DSA-65/87 and hybridisation; NIST approval does not import NIST’s parameter choices into EUCC.
How long does the QSCD certification hold?
At most five years, provided vulnerability assessments are carried out every two years; unremedied vulnerabilities cancel it
Right — eIDAS Article 30(3a), inserted by Regulation 2024/1183. Separately, an EUCC certificate may not exceed five years (Art 12) unless the NCCA approves a derogation.
Until the vendor stops selling the product
Certificates are time-limited. eIDAS caps QSCD certification at five years with a two-yearly vulnerability assessment.
Two years, then a new evaluation from scratch
Two years is the vulnerability-assessment interval, not the validity. The certification may last up to five years if those assessments are done.
Validity: QSCD certification ≤ 5 years with a vulnerability assessment every 2 years (eIDAS Art 30(3a)); EUCC certificate ≤ 5 years (Art 12)
The certified firmware gains an ML-DSA signing service. What happens to the EUCC certificate?
The holder submits an impact analysis report; the CB classifies the change. Adding a signature service changes the claimed SFRs, which is typically major → re-evaluation reusing prior results, then a new certificate
It is a minor change, so the CB issues a new certificate with the new version
Backwards on both counts. CIR 2025/2462 says a confirmed minor change gets a maintenance report and “no new certificate shall be issued”; and a new cryptographic service is not typically minor.
A market PQC deadline lets the CB treat it as minor
Deadlines create urgency, not shortcuts. Minor vs major depends only on the change’s impact on the assurance expressed in the certificate.
Change: IAR → CB classifies; new crypto service = SFR change → typically major → re-evaluation → new certificate (minor → maintenance report, no new certificate)

# Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification

## Overview

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-068) is a scheme deep dive split out of LM-065 _Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals_. It covers Common Criteria and the CC:2022 transition, EUCC as the EU scheme, eIDAS qualified devices and the Protection Profiles that connect them: what each claim proves and what adding post-quantum cryptography means for a certified product. Version 1 is labelled "Practitioner orientation — not laboratory training." Reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. It has not been reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. Facts are as of 24 September 2026.

Three distinct paths cover CC evaluation criteria (`cc`), EUCC scheme rules (`eucc`) and eIDAS device/service requirements (legacy URL `eucc-eidas` retained). EUCC uses CC, while eIDAS is a separate legal context, not the next mandatory stage. FIPS 140-3 remains separate. Shared PP examples are optional reference material. Existing section-progress identifiers are preserved.

## Key Concepts

Optional EN 419221-5 history explains the 2016 certification of draft v0.15 and ANSSI's 18 May 2020 maintenance report for published v1.0. ANSSI classified the reported editorial/standardisation changes as minor. This concerns a Protection Profile, not a PQC product update; it does not establish that adding ML-DSA qualifies for maintenance, that a product certificate is currently valid, or that no newer PP edition exists.

Guidance status checked 21 October 2026: ENISA lists ACM v2 as applicable and v3 as a draft for public review. ACM mechanism/parameter recommendations are not standalone certification verdicts or blanket legal requirements for every CC/eIDAS assessment. Check the construction, implementation, applicable scheme rules, PP and Security Target separately.

- **Common Criteria vs EUCC** — the Common Criteria path covers CC and the CCRA only; EUCC-specific rules appear there only as labelled "Under EUCC" pointers. An EUCC evaluation is a CC evaluation run under EU law: it takes the CC:2022 criteria, CEM, Security Target, Protection Profiles and assurance components, and adds two assurance levels (substantial = AVA_VAN 1–2, high = AVA_VAN 3–5; CIR 2024/482 Art 4), Annex I technical domains and Annex II protection profiles, the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (guidance, including PQC), no self-assessment (Art 6), at most five years' validity (Art 12), its own minor/major change rules (CIR 2025/2462) and a per-certificate route to the CCRA mark (CCMC-011). Adding PQC: under CC, new FCS_COP/FCS_CKM iterations are typically a major change and the certification body decides the route; under EUCC, the cryptography guidelines point evaluators to the ECCG ACM, which lists PQC mechanisms, and CC 3.1 revision 1–4 protection profiles required under eIDAS, Decision 2016/650 or the tachograph rules remain usable with no end date (CIR 2024/3144 Art 3(4)).
- **"EAL4+" is meaningless without its augmentations** — the named components are the claim.
- **EUCC is a scheme, not a Protection Profile** — EUCC's Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2 already lists ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS, and says (M)LWE-based mechanisms should be combined with a classical mechanism.
- **eIDAS assessment scope** — eIDAS sets legal device and service requirements. Identify the applicable Article 30 assessment basis and designated body; EUCC is not a universal route. Distinguish an HSM component certificate, certification of the complete QSCD and qualified trust-service status. The remote-signing exercise explicitly selects EUCC evidence for its HSM example.
- **One criteria, many schemes** — Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408) is the shared baseline, but certificates come from national schemes (in the EU, the EUCC scheme set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/482). The CCRA (36 countries: 18 issue, 18 recognise) mutually recognises only a collaborative PP or up to EAL2 + ALC_FLR; schemes in this module add their own cryptographic requirements (NIAP's CAVP requirement and PP-only policy, Canada's approved cryptography, Korea's KCMVP for listed product types, Malaysia's MyCV, the EU cryptography guidelines' pointer to the ECCG ACM), plus lighter national methods (CSPN, BSZ, LINCE) and procurement mandates. NIAP Policy #33 stops accepting products — certified by NIAP or any CCRA partner — that do not meet CNSA 2.0 from 1 January 2028. China (GB/T 18336), Russia (GOST R ISO/IEC 15408) and Kazakhstan use the CC text outside the CCRA, without mutual recognition.
- **NIAP and post-quantum cryptography** — the recent NIAP profiles offer post-quantum algorithms as choices; they do not mandate them. The Dedicated Security Component cPP v2.1 (17 November 2025) lists LMS, HSS, XMSS, XMSS-MT, ML-KEM and ML-DSA beside the classical algorithms as selections, and NIAP's Technical Decisions TD1011 (for this profile) and TD1010 (Network Devices v4.0) require at least one CNSA 1.0 or CNSA 2.0 selection for the Product Compliant List, so post-quantum is one allowed route, not the only one; the Application Software profile v2.0 (16 June 2025) has a CNSA 2.0 branch next to a CNSA 1.0 branch and says ML-DSA and ML-KEM are not usable yet. The push comes from a chain: CNSSP 11, CNSSP 15 and CNSA 2.0, NIAP Policy #33, the profiles, their test methods and those Technical Decisions, the Security Target's chosen branch, and CSfC. A CMVP module certificate is a separate ask from the NIAP certificate. A table lists 11 NIAP documents read on 23 October 2026 (8 profiles and 3 profile modules) that carry post-quantum choices beside the classical ones, with none requiring them, plus a list of further profiles reported but not yet read. The section ends with six questions to put to the lab. No NIAP profile written for HSMs was found.
- **Worked example and AVA_VAN.5 box (EUCC path, in "PQC under EUCC today (ACM v2)")** — two collapsed panels, each with a short summary that is always shown. The first is an invented Security Target excerpt for the fictional Orrin N7: FCS_CKM.1(ML-KEM-768) key generation, FCS_COP.1(ML-DSA-65 sign) signing and FCS_CKM.5(Hybrid) key derivation, worded to CC:2022 Part 2 with the mandatory errata v1.2, with a table of the dependencies each pulls in (FCS_CKM.2, FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, FCS_CKM.6) and a note on where NIAP profiles write ML-KEM encapsulation (FCS_COP.1/KeyEncap in three profiles, directly in FCS_CKM.2 in the VPN Client module). The second is orientation on AVA_VAN.5 for lattice-based code: what the CEM asks, which attack-potential table applies (CEM Table B.3, or the EUCC documents for security boxes and for smart cards, neither of which names a post-quantum algorithm), the scope check under EN 419 221-5, and three typical test targets with the published papers (the NTT and decapsulation in ML-KEM, the rejection loop in ML-DSA signing, fault injection on ML-DSA signing and verification). A visible note, "What this example does not settle", lists six open points that depend on scheme or laboratory practice, and a visible line points to the lessons PQC Network Testing & Validation and HSM & PQC Operations. The example is invented and has not been reviewed by any scheme or laboratory; the module's own reading is marked "Module analysis".

That is all an EAL measures: how much design evidence the developer provided and how hard the evaluator looked. An EAL is not a FIPS 140-3 security level, and there is no mapping between the two. FIPS 140-3 levels come from one fixed set of cryptographic-module requirements. EALs grade the assurance behind whatever SFRs an ST chooses to claim.

Collaborative PPs (cPPs) replace the EAL ladder with evaluation activities written for one product class. LM-068/s:cc-lifecycle.full:
Common Criteria (CC) is a framework for writing down security claims about an IT product and having an accredited laboratory check them. The criteria are published by the Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement (CCRA) participants as CC:2022, and by ISO/IEC as ISO/IEC 15408:2022. The evaluator follows the Common Evaluation Methodology, CEM:2022 (ISO/IEC 18045:2022). A certification scheme — for example France’s ANSSI or Singapore’s CSA — oversees the laboratory and issues the certificate. The CCRA then decides which certificates its member countries accept from one another.
CC:2022 Release 1 (November 2022) replaced CC 3.1 Revision 5. The CCRA transition policy,
The same policy lets a CC:2022 certification reuse CC 3.1 R5 life-cycle (ALC) results and CC 3.1 R5 platform certificates in a composite evaluation. PP maintainers must move their PPs to CC:2022; new or updated PPs published after 30 June 2024 must use CC:2022. All three certificates in this path’s workshop use CC 3.1 R5.

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-068) is a scheme deep dive split out of LM-065 _Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals_. It covers Common Criteria and the CC:2022 transition, EUCC as the EU scheme, eIDAS qualified devices and the Protection Profiles that connect them: what each claim proves and what adding post-quantum cryptography means for a certified product. Version 1 is labelled "Practitioner orientation — not laboratory training." Reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. It has not been reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. Facts are as of 24 September 2026.
Common Criteria vs EUCC — the Common Criteria path covers CC and the CCRA only; EUCC-specific rules appear there only as labelled "Under EUCC" pointers. An EUCC evaluation is a CC evaluation run under EU law: it takes the CC:2022 criteria, CEM, Security Target, Protection Profiles and assurance components, and adds two assurance levels (substantial = AVA_VAN 1–2, high = AVA_VAN 3–5; CIR 2024/482 Art 4), Annex I technical domains and Annex II protection profiles, the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (guidance, including PQC), no self-assessment (Art 6), at most five years' validity (Art 12), its own minor/major change rules (CIR 2025/2462) and a per-certificate route to the CCRA mark (CCMC-011). Adding PQC: under CC, new FCS_COP/FCS_CKM iterations are typically a major change and the certification body decides the route; under EUCC, the cryptography guidelines point evaluators to the ECCG ACM, which lists PQC mechanisms, and CC 3.1 revision 1–4 protection profiles required under eIDAS, Decision 2016/650 or the tachograph rules remain usable with no end date (CIR 2024/3144 Art 3(4)).
NIAP and post-quantum cryptography — the recent NIAP profiles offer post-quantum algorithms as choices; they do not mandate them. The Dedicated Security Component cPP v2.1 (17 November 2025) lists LMS, HSS, XMSS, XMSS-MT, ML-KEM and ML-DSA beside the classical algorithms as selections, and NIAP's Technical Decisions TD1011 (for this profile) and TD1010 (Network Devices v4.0) require at least one CNSA 1.0 or CNSA 2.0 selection for the Product Compliant List, so post-quantum is one allowed route, not the only one; the Application Software profile v2.0 (16 June 2025) has a CNSA 2.0 branch next to a CNSA 1.0 branch and says ML-DSA and ML-KEM are not usable yet. The push comes from a chain: CNSSP 11, CNSSP 15 and CNSA 2.0, NIAP Policy #33, the profiles, their test methods and those Technical Decisions, the Security Target's chosen branch, and CSfC. A CMVP module certificate is a separate ask from the NIAP certificate. A table lists 11 NIAP documents read on 23 October 2026 (8 profiles and 3 profile modules) that carry post-quantum choices beside the classical ones, with none requiring them, plus a list of further profiles reported but not yet read. The section ends with six questions to put to the lab. No NIAP profile written for HSMs was found.
Worked example and AVA_VAN.5 box (EUCC path, in "PQC under EUCC today (ACM v2)") — two collapsed panels, each with a short summary that is always shown. The first is an invented Security Target excerpt for the fictional Orrin N7: FCS_CKM.1(ML-KEM-768) key generation, FCS_COP.1(ML-DSA-65 sign) signing and FCS_CKM.5(Hybrid) key derivation, worded to CC:2022 Part 2 with the mandatory errata v1.2, with a table of the dependencies each pulls in (FCS_CKM.2, FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, FCS_CKM.6) and a note on where NIAP profiles write ML-KEM encapsulation (FCS_COP.1/KeyEncap in three profiles, directly in FCS_CKM.2 in the VPN Client module). The second is orientation on AVA_VAN.5 for lattice-based code: what the CEM asks, which attack-potential table applies (CEM Table B.3, or the EUCC documents for security boxes and for smart cards, neither of which names a post-quantum algorithm), the scope check under EN 419 221-5, and three typical test targets with the published papers (the NTT and decapsulation in ML-KEM, the rejection loop in ML-DSA signing, fault injection on ML-DSA signing and verification). A visible note, "What this example does not settle", lists six open points that depend on scheme or laboratory practice, and a visible line points to the lessons PQC Network Testing & Validation and HSM & PQC Operations. # Government & Defense PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Most organisations decide for themselves when to adopt post-quantum cryptography. US government systems do not. A stack of laws, executive orders and policies turns it into a requirement with dates attached — and the dates depend on which kind of system you run. National Security Systems follow one instrument with hard deadlines; federal civilian agencies follow a different set of rules: inventories, reports and migration plans, plus, since June 2026, their own dated deadlines for their most important systems (key exchange moved by the end of 2030, digital signatures by the end of 2031).

## Why It Matters

The deadlines reach much further than government itself. From 1 January 2027, CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new acquisitions for National Security Systems. Separately, the rules covering Controlled Unclassified Information reach contractors, universities and suppliers who never go near a classified system. A June 2026 executive order also directs a proposed rule that would require covered contractors to comply with NIST's Federal Information Processing Standards, including all applicable ones that cover post-quantum algorithms, by the end of 2030. If you sell to the US government, someone else's deadline has become yours.

## The Key Takeaway

Only the public-key half of the estate is being replaced. The NSA suite swaps out key exchange and digital signatures, but AES-256 encryption and the SHA hash functions carry on essentially unchanged. Budgeting to "replace all our cryptography" overstates the work considerably — the honest first step is finding out which half of your systems is actually affected.

## What's Happening

The dates are set: new purchases must use the new algorithms from January 2027, equipment that cannot be upgraded must be gone by the end of 2030 unless an exception is granted, and, unless otherwise noted, the new algorithms become mandatory at the end of 2031. One practical wrinkle catches people out — the 2022 advisory called the algorithms Kyber and Dilithium, while the October 2026 update calls the same things ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Because the two documents use different names for the same algorithms, searching your own estate for only one set of names will quietly miss half of what you have.
