LM-069.summary:
# Government & Defense PQC

## Overview

The Government & Defense module teaches the federal post-quantum policy layer — the instruments that turn post-quantum cryptography from an engineering preference into a procurement requirement. It covers the CNSA 2.0 suite and precisely what it replaces from CNSA 1.0, the dated CNSSP 15 milestones that bind National Security Systems, the National Security System versus federal civilian distinction that decides which deadline applies to a given system, the Federal PKI certificate profile pair (one published and classical, one draft and post-quantum), and how the requirement propagates outward through procurement to contractors who never touch an NSS. It carries genuine dated deadlines rather than advisory guidance: the CNSSP 15 dates for National Security Systems and, for federal civilian high value assets and high impact systems, the Executive Order 14412 dates.

## Key Concepts

- **CNSA 2.0 replaces every public-key line of CNSA 1.0 and almost nothing else.** Key establishment moves from ECDH P-384 / RSA-3072 to ML-KEM-1024 (FIPS 203); general-purpose signatures move from ECDSA P-384 / RSA-3072 to ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204); software and firmware signing moves to LMS or XMSS (NIST SP 800-208), with ML-DSA-87 also approved for it. AES-256 is unchanged and SHA-384 becomes SHA-384 or SHA-512. That asymmetry is the central budgeting lesson: "replace all cryptography" is the wrong model, because the symmetric half of the estate survives the transition intact
- **Level-5 parameters only.** CNSA 2.0 approves ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 exclusively. ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 are FIPS-approved but not CNSA 2.0-approved — an NSS-specific narrowing of the NIST standards, not a restatement of them
- **Firmware signing moved first, and NSA said why.** Three stated reasons: NIST had already standardised the algorithms, the use case is more urgent than others, and stateful hash-based signatures have the longest cryptanalytic history — so their performance costs matter least here. LMS and XMSS are the approved SP 800-208 schemes (all parameter sets; NSA recommends LMS with SHA-256/192) and the multi-tree variants HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed. Validated ML-DSA-87 is also approved for software and firmware signing, but NSA wants LMS and XMSS adopted now where possible because validated implementations have been available longer; ML-DSA can make sense when a signing strategy needs more signatures than a single LMS or XMSS key can reasonably provide, or in distributed signing environments
- **The dated CNSSP 15 milestones** (as stated in the CNSA 2.0 FAQ Ver 2.2, October 2026):
  - **1 January 2027** — CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new acquisitions for NSS
  - **31 December 2030** — all NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception; NSA also expects encryption to be broadly quantum resistant by default by this date
  - **31 December 2031** — CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted, to achieve full quantum resistance for NSS
  - **2035** — the goal set in NSM-10 for achieving quantum resistance; NSA intends that all NSS will be quantum-resistant well ahead of 2035
- **The advisory and the FAQ state different dates.** The September 2022 advisory carried a per-equipment-type timetable running from 2025 to 2033; the CNSA 2.0 FAQ (Ver 2.2, October 2026) says that the update to CNSSP 15 set several dates and states them as listed above. The FAQ does not restate the advisory's 2033 date
- **NSA does not require hybrids for NSS, and that is not a prohibition.** The FAQ states NSA "has confidence in CNSA 2.0 algorithms and will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes," while explicitly allowing that "product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions." This is routinely misreported as a ban. NSA also acknowledges some protocols may need hybrid-like constructions simply to carry the larger ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 objects
- **NSA's four stated objections to hybrids**: added protocol and library complexity (extra negotiation, error handling, modified APIs, more testing); interoperability becomes harder because every party must share both component algorithms _and_ the hybridisation method; it buys a second transition later when classical components are eventually dropped; and more security products fail from implementation flaws than from cryptanalysis, so added complexity is itself a risk. These are the strongest published arguments against the hybrid-by-default posture most of the commercial world has adopted — and the opposite of what ETSI specifies for European trust services
- **Naming drift is an inventory problem.** The September 2022 advisory names the algorithms CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium because FIPS 203/204 did not exist yet; the October 2026 FAQ (Ver 2.2) calls the same algorithms ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87. The two documents name the same algorithms differently. Estate inventory tooling must search both vocabularies, because a search for "Kyber" will not find documents written after standardisation
- **NSS and federal civilian are governed by different instruments.** CNSSP 15 carries the CNSA 2.0 dates and binds National Security Systems. Federal civilian agencies follow the Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act, OMB M-23-02 / M-26-15 and Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026): inventory, reporting and migration plans, plus **dated PQC deadlines for high value assets and high impact systems** — key establishment by 31 December 2030 and digital signatures by 31 December 2031 — which exclude National Security Systems, whose CNSSP 15 requirements and timelines NSA describes as comparable. Which stack applies to a system is the first question to answer, because it determines which dates apply
- **The federal mandate stack**:
  - **Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act (2022)** — Law. Federal civilian executive-branch agencies. Requires inventory of CRQC-vulnerable cryptographic systems and migration, with OMB reporting. The statute is what makes the rest of the stack enforceable rather than advisory
  - **OMB M-23-02** — To comply with NSM-10, directs agencies to submit a prioritised inventory of CRQC-vulnerable cryptographic systems (excluding National Security Systems) by 4 May 2023 and annually thereafter until 2035, or as directed by superseding guidance
  - **OMB M-26-15** — Implements the accelerated migration set by Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026), and fulfils OMB's responsibility under the QCCPA to issue guidance directing each agency to prioritise critical IT for migration to PQC and to plan that migration. Each agency submits a PQC migration plan within 120 days, phased from discovery (2026–2027) through pilots (2027–2028), prioritised key-establishment migration (2028–2030) and signature migration (2031) to full migration (2035). It does not apply to National Security Systems
  - **Executive Order 14306** — Sustains and amends prior federal cybersecurity direction, including the PQC provisions driving the CISA product-category work
  - **Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026)** — Section 4(b) directs OMB to require agencies to move all high value assets and high impact systems (not National Security Systems) to PQC for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. Section 6(c) directs the FAR Council to publish, within 180 days, a proposed rule requiring covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms; the order directs a proposed rule, it is not itself that rule
  - **CNSS Policy 15** — The instrument that actually carries the CNSA 2.0 dates, for National Security Systems
  - **NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3** — Reaches nonfederal systems processing Controlled Unclassified Information: contractors, universities and suppliers who never touch an NSS. NIST states that it supersedes Rev. 2 (February 2020), but DoD's CMMC briefing (cleared for open publication 21 January 2025) says CMMC assessments remain against Rev. 2 until DoD formally adopts Rev. 3 through rulemaking
- **Federal PKI has two certificate profiles, and only one is binding.** The Common Policy X.509 Certificate and CRL Profile is published, in force, and classical (RSA, SHA). A separate PQC profile dated **21 April 2026** is a **DRAFT**, adding ML-DSA and ML-KEM for CITE testing starting from v2.2 of the Common Policy profiles. A draft is not contractually bindable — teaching the pair side by side is crypto agility as an actual document lifecycle rather than a slogan. Separately, the Federal PKI page announced that the Federal Bridge Certification Authority (FBCA) G4 would be replaced by the FBCA G5 starting 27 August 2026 to meet federal cryptographic-strength requirements (applications may need new intermediate CA certificates in their trust stores), and under the Common Policy CA private keys must be held in cryptographic modules validated to at least FIPS 140 Level 3
- **The 1 January 2027 date is a requirement with exceptions, not an automatic ban.** CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new NSS acquisitions; the FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says that where no CNSA 2.0 compliant product meeting the need is available on 1 January 2027, a deployment may, if needed, be accepted on a vendor's contractual commitment to provide a CNSA 2.0 update, combined with a realistic deployment plan that prioritises partial quantum resistance and meets the 2030 deadline for full quantum resistance, and NIAP Policy Letter #33 (effective 1 January 2027) says government contracts must include language requiring products used in NSS to implement PQC or be updateable to implement PQC
- **The CSfC PQC Guidance Addendum is a draft.** Version 1.0 draft .5 (4 April 2025) sets out a planned timeline, subject to change, that aims for all CSfC solutions to implement post-quantum cryptography by 2030. NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says NIAP will begin archiving the certificates of partially quantum-resistant and quantum-vulnerable products generally within a year of fully quantum-resistant products coming on the market, that it expects this archiving to start in late 2027, and that products with archived certificates will not comply with CNSSP 11 and will not be appropriate for NSS
- **Algorithm support is not the only procurement gate.** CNSSP 11 requires commercial IA and IA-enabled IT products bought to protect information on NSS to comply with the NIAP program (agencies select evaluated products from the NIAP Product Compliant List) and, where applicable, the FIPS cryptographic validation programs; the CNSA 2.0 FAQ says NIAP and FIPS validation are required in most circumstances
- **The CISA PQC product category list is broader than CNSA 2.0.** It names ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and the stateful hash-based signatures of SP 800-208, and says organizations should acquire only PQC-capable products in the categories it lists as widely available; NSA does not approve SLH-DSA, HSS or XMSS^MT for National Security Systems

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 3 hands-on tools:

1. **CNSA 1.0 → 2.0 Suite Comparator** — which suite lines are replaced and which survive, with NSA's own stated rationale per line. Makes the "symmetric primitives survive" point concrete rather than asserted
2. **Federal Mandate Explorer** — pick a system type and see which instruments bind it, and critically, whether it has a dated deadline at all
3. **Federal PKI Profile Pair** — the classical certificate profile beside the draft PQC profile, and why a draft cannot be cited as binding

## Related Standards

CNSSP 15 carries the dates for National Security Systems. The QCCPA and OMB M-23-02 / M-26-15 carry inventory, reporting and migration-plan obligations for federal civilian systems, and Executive Order 14412 sets dated PQC deadlines for their high value assets and high impact systems (key establishment by 31 December 2030, digital signatures by 31 December 2031). NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 reaches nonfederal systems handling Controlled Unclassified Information (DoD's CMMC briefing, cleared for open publication 21 January 2025, says CMMC assessments remain against Rev. 2 until DoD formally adopts Rev. 3 through rulemaking), and Executive Order 14412 directs a proposed FAR rule requiring covered contractors to comply with NIST FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms, by 31 December 2030. CNSSP 11 requires commercial IA and IA-enabled IT products bought for National Security Systems to comply with the NIAP program and, where applicable, the FIPS cryptographic validation programs, and NIAP Policy Letter #33 sets the timeline for post-quantum requirements in NIAP evaluations. The Federal PKI Common Policy certificate profile is in force and classical; a draft profile dated 21 April 2026 adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM for CITE testing. Underlying algorithm standards are FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, named by the CISA list but not approved for NSS) and NIST SP 800-208 (LMS/XMSS). RFC 8603 profiles the earlier CNSA suite for X.509. Related guidance includes the NSA CSfC PQC Guidance Addendum (draft), the CISA PQC product category list (2026) and the CMMC 2.0 model.

Cross-reference: the **Hybrid Cryptography** module reaches a different default — hybrid recommended or mandated — and the **Trust Services** module covers ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1, which incorporates PQC transition requirements, including hybrid cryptographic schemes. Same algorithms, different authorities, different defaults. Which applies is a jurisdiction question, not a cryptography question.

Commercial Solutions for Classified (CSfC) layers two independent commercial encryption implementations to protect classified data without government-furnished cryptography. Its PQC guidance addendum is the document that tells integrators how the layers change under CNSA 2.0 — but the April 2025 edition (version 1.0 draft .5) is a draft whose planned timeline, subject to change, aims for all CSfC solutions to implement post-quantum cryptography by 2030. LM-070.curious:
# Trust Services & Signature Longevity — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

When you sign a mortgage, a will or a land registry entry electronically, that signature has to stay provable for decades. The certificate behind it expires in a year or two. The revocation records that prove it was good at the time disappear after a few more. And eventually the algorithm itself gets broken. This module is about how a signature stays believable long after everything that originally supported it has gone.

## Why It Matters

The answer is timestamping. A trusted authority signs a hash of your document together with the time, which fixes the moment the signature existed. That is what lets a court accept a signature made with a certificate that has since expired, or with an algorithm since broken — because the evidence points at the moment it was made rather than at today.

## The Key Takeaway

The deadline that matters is not the day quantum computers arrive. It is the day by which every signature you have _already_ made must be re-stamped using a quantum-safe algorithm. That work scales with the size of your archive, not with how many new documents you sign — and it has to be planned when the document is signed, because once the supporting evidence has aged out it cannot be recovered.

## What's Happening

Europe's rulebook has already moved. The ETSI cryptographic suites standard was updated in June 2026 to add the new quantum-safe signature algorithms and, importantly, hybrid modes where a classical and a quantum-safe signature must _both_ be valid. That differs from the American position for national security systems, where hybrids are not required. Same algorithms, two authorities, different defaults — which one applies to you depends on where you operate, not on the mathematics.

LM-070.summary:
# Trust Services & Signature Longevity

## Overview

The Trust Services module covers the part of the eIDAS world that has to plan in decades rather than in release cycles. It teaches qualified versus advanced electronic signatures, RFC 3161 timestamping as proof of existence, the five stages by which a signature degrades over thirty years, the ETSI cryptographic suites that gained post-quantum modes in June 2026, and why trust service provider conformity assessment makes migration slow even once the algorithms are settled. Its central argument is crypto agility demonstrated from documents rather than asserted from principle: the same ETSI standard, eighteen months apart, with and without a post-quantum path.

## Key Concepts

- **A qualified electronic signature carries legal equivalence to a handwritten one**, so the operative question is not "is this signature valid now" but "can a court establish that it was valid when it was made" — potentially decades later. That reframes migration from an algorithm-swap problem into an evidence-preservation problem
- **RFC 3161 time-stamp tokens are CMS SignedData, which is algorithm-agile, and that is the quiet hinge of the whole area.** The signature algorithm identifier is carried in the CMS signer information and the TSA certificate must carry a matching key, so the token format does not need redesigning for ML-DSA. A migration still needs a certified TSA key, TSA and HSM support, verifier support and interoperability testing, as well as trust-list and validation-policy changes
- **A timestamp is a proof of existence**: a TSA signs a hash of the data plus a time. That is what allows a signature made with a certificate since revoked — or with an algorithm since broken — to still be evaluated against the moment it was made
- **Long-term validation degrades in five stages**, each with a remedy that must be in place _before_ the stage arrives:
  - **Day 0 — signature creation.** No risk yet. Sign, and capture a qualified timestamp at the moment of signing
  - **1–3 years — certificate expiry.** The signing certificate expires; without evidence of when the signature was made, verification becomes ambiguous. The day-0 timestamp is what carries the signature past this point
  - **3–10 years — revocation data ages out.** CRLs and OCSP responses are no longer retrievable, so a verifier cannot establish the certificate was good at signing time. Archive revocation data alongside the signature (the LTV form)
  - **5–20 years — the signing algorithm weakens.** The original algorithm is deprecated or broken; a CRQC breaks RSA and ECDSA outright. Re-timestamp with a current algorithm before the old one becomes untrustworthy — each new timestamp attests to the whole previous structure, so the chain stays evaluable
  - **20–30+ years — archival horizon.** Land registries, notarial deeds and medical consent can outlive several algorithm generations. A repeated re-timestamping policy is the only mechanism that survives this, and it has to be planned at signing time; it cannot be retrofitted once the evidence is gone
- **The real deadline is not the CRQC date.** It is the date by which every signature already made must be re-timestamped under a quantum-safe algorithm — and that work is proportional to the size of the archive, not to the flow of new signatures. This is the single most under-estimated figure in the area
- **ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) supersedes V1.5.1 (December 2024).** The older edition lists only classical signature algorithms (RSA-PKCS#1v1_5, RSA-PSS, DSA, EC-DSA, EC-SDSA-opt); the newer adds ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS, XMSS and hybrid modes. Eighteen months apart, same standard, same committee — anything built against V1.5.1 has no post-quantum path in it at all, not because the design was wrong but because the suites document had not caught up
- **ETSI requires both halves of a hybrid signature to verify.** TS 119 312 V2.1.1 clause 6.4.1: implementations shall combine a classical signature and a post-quantum signature, and acceptance requires both signatures to be valid. This is a different default from NSA CNSA 2.0, which will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes (product availability and interoperability requirements may still lead to hybrid solutions in specific cases). Neither is wrong — they protect different things over different lifetimes, and which applies is a jurisdiction question rather than a cryptography one
- **TS 119 312 V2.1.1, Table 3.3 — the approved hybrid pairs**: RSA-PSS (≥ 3000 bit) with ML-DSA-65 for general purpose and certificates, or with ML-DSA-87 for high security and long term; ECDSA P-256/P-384 with ML-DSA-65, or P-384/P-521 with ML-DSA-87; EdDSA Ed25519 with ML-DSA-65, or Ed448 with ML-DSA-87; and ECDSA or EdDSA with SLH-DSA at Level 3 or 5 for the conservative hash-based option
- **A withdrawn standard is a live citation risk.** TS 119 312 V2.1.1 marks its predecessor explicitly: ETSI TS 102 176-1 is withdrawn and superseded by TS 119 312. It was the reference for years and is still widely linked, so citing it remains an easy mistake to make
- **ETSI EN 319 422 V1.1.1 (March 2016) is the timestamp profile the EU rules apply.** It profiles RFC 3161 and RFC 5816 for European qualified timestamps and names no algorithm itself, deferring to TS 119 312. Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929 (September 2025) applies V1.1.1 to qualified time-stamps and, in its version of the standard, replaces the profile’s algorithm clauses with clauses under which hash and time-stamp signature algorithms shall be compliant with the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms endorsed by the European Cybersecurity Certification Group. TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) still cites the 2016 edition
- **Conformity assessment is why this moves slowly.** Even once algorithms are settled, a qualified trust service provider's supervisory and audit regime governs how fast a change can actually be adopted in production
- **The hardware holding a provider's signing keys is certified, with a dated cut-off.** Commission Implementing Regulations (EU) 2025/1943 (qualified certificates) and 2025/1929 (qualified time-stamps) list reference standards, and supervisory bodies should presume that a provider that follows them complies, although a provider may still rely on other practices. Those standards require the secure cryptographic device that holds a provider's CA key, or a time-stamping unit's key, to be certified to Common Criteria or EUCC at EAL 4 or higher — or, until **31 December 2030**, to FIPS 140-3 level 3. In the text adopted on 29 September 2025, only the Common Criteria and EUCC routes remain after that date. This requirement covers the provider's own keys, not the signer's device
- **TS 119 312 V2.1.1 is not the last word.** The June 2026 edition says of itself that it is incomplete for the EU Digital Identity Wallet and for certain other trust services, including preservation and electronic registered delivery, with an update already in preparation, and it says that scheduling of the post-quantum migration is planned to be addressed in a separate document under development

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 3 hands-on tools:

1. **Signature Longevity Calculator** — pick a validity horizon and see which degradation stages apply, and when an existing archive must be re-timestamped
2. **Standards Supersession Explorer** — the same ETSI standard before and after PQC, with the superseded edition marked, including the TS 102 176-1 withdrawal
3. **Hybrid Suite Picker** — TS 119 312 V2.1.1 Table 3.3, filtered by use case

## Related Standards

ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) is the current cryptographic suites specification, superseding V1.5.1 (December 2024) and marking ETSI TS 102 176-1 withdrawn; it says of itself that it is incomplete for the EU Digital Identity Wallet and some other trust services, with an update in preparation. ETSI EN 319 422 V1.1.1 (March 2016) is the time-stamping protocol and token profile that Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929 applies to qualified time-stamps, replacing its algorithm clauses with clauses under which algorithms shall be compliant with the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms endorsed by the European Cybersecurity Certification Group. ETSI EN 319 411 governs policy and security requirements for trust service providers issuing certificates. RFC 3161 (August 2001, Standards Track) defines the Time-Stamp Protocol, updated by RFC 5816 for ESSCertIDv2. eIDAS (EU 910/2014) and eIDAS 2.0 (EU 2024/1183) are the governing regulations, with the Cloud Signature Consortium API v2 specification covering remote signing. Underlying algorithm standards are FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA).

Cross-reference: the **Government & Defense** module reaches a different hybrid default for US National Security Systems, and the **Hybrid Cryptography** module covers the combiner constructions themselves.

signature adds two things: it is created with a qualified signature creation device, and it rests on a certificate issued by a qualified trust service provider. Only the qualified form carries automatic legal equivalence to a handwritten signature across the Union.
A qualified trust service provider is not simply a CA with good intentions — it is an audited entity on a national trusted list, assessed against the ETSI EN 319 4xx series. That audit relationship is what makes a migration in this sector slow: changing signing algorithms means re-establishing conformity, not just deploying software.
The practical sequence for a TSP is therefore: the suites document gains PQC modes (done — TS 119 312 V2.1.1), the timestamp and policy standards have to follow (EN 319 422 dates from 2016 and defers algorithm choice to the suites document, although for qualified time-stamps Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929 lists a version of EN 319 422 in which those clauses are replaced by clauses under which hash and time-stamp signature algorithms shall be compliant with the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms endorsed by the European Cybersecurity Certification Group), conformity assessment schemes absorb the change, and only then can a qualified service issue post-quantum signatures under audit. ### What This Is About

A closer look at PCI approval for payment hardware security modules (HSMs), together with the rules for the companies that operate them. It builds on the certification fundamentals module; FIPS 140-3 has its own module.

### Why It Matters

For payment devices, the device approval and the rules for the companies operating it are different things, and both matter. A FIPS 140-3 certificate is not a PCI approval.

### The Key Takeaway

A PCI listing's post-quantum flag only says that support exists — it does not approve a specific algorithm.

### What's Happening

As of November 2026, PCI PTS HSM v5.0 adds post-quantum definitions without naming a required algorithm or deadline, PCI KMO v1.0 (published 14 September 2026) consolidates key-management operations requirements, P2PE v3.2 applies to new submissions from 1 January 2026, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 is the only active PCI DSS version. This lesson covers PTS HSM and its operating stack (PIN, P2PE, KMO), not PTS POI terminals.

# PCI Certification

## Overview

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-071) is a scheme deep dive split out of LM-065 _Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals_ (via LM-067). It covers PCI PTS HSM with the payment operating stack (PIN Security, P2PE, KMO): what a device approval proves, how to read one, and what adding post-quantum cryptography means for a payment HSM. FIPS 140-3 and the CMVP are covered in LM-067 _FIPS 140-3 Certification_. Version 1 is labelled "Practitioner orientation — not laboratory training." Reviewed and signed off by the PQC Today owner on 1 November 2026. It has not been reviewed by an accredited laboratory or certification body. Facts are as of 30 October 2026.

This lesson covers four PCI programmes: PTS HSM, PIN Security, P2PE and key management operations. It does not cover PTS POI, card production and provisioning, 3-D Secure, or MPoC and CPoC.

One timed ~60-minute route. Deeper material is kept as optional reference sections.

## Key Concepts

- **PCI device approval is not entity assessment** — in this module’s reading, a PTS HSM approval is about the device (independent laboratories evaluate HSMs; PCI SSC approves and lists them), while PIN Security, P2PE and KMO are about how HSMs are operated and the solutions built on them. A PCI listing’s PQC notation records that PQC support exists; the implementation details are in the device’s security policy.
- **A FIPS certificate is not a PCI approval** — a FIPS 140-3 certificate and a PTS approval are separate evidence under separate schemes, each tied to versions; which HSM evidence a PCI standard accepts is set out in that standard, which this module does not read.
- **PCI DSS v4.0.1 and PTS POI boundary** — PCI DSS v4.0.1 is the only active PCI DSS version (v4.0 retired 31 December 2024; v4.0 future-dated requirements effective 31 March 2025). This module covers PTS HSM plus PIN Security, P2PE (v3.2 mandatory for new submissions from 1 January 2026) and KMO v1.0 (published 14 September 2026); PTS POI is outside this module's scope.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

_Payment HSM evidence review_: review a payment HSM's evidence — PTS listing, Security Policy, FIPS certificate and KMO/PIN assessment scope.

## Source Currency

This module states only what public PCI SSC pages state: PCI Perspectives blogs, the P2PE and PTS HSM program pages, the Document Library feed (titles and dates only) and the PTS listing field definitions. The PTS HSM v5.0 requirements, the Device Testing and Approval Program Guide, the KMO standard and the P2PE standard are not read, so their content is not taught. The v5.0 announcement names no post-quantum algorithm and no deadline. PCI SSC announced P2PE v3.2 on 30 June 2025 as a minor revision; from 1 January 2026 all new P2PE submissions, including reassessments of listed products, must comply with it, and validations already done to P2PE v3.0 or v3.1 are not affected (P2PE v3.2 announcement).

## Related Standards

- `PCI-SSC-Blog-Publishes-PTS-HSM-v5-0`
- `PCI-PTS-Listing-Field-Definitions`
- `PCI-SSC-Blog-KMO-v1-0-Published`
- `PCI-SSC-P2PE-Program-Page`
- `PCI-DSS-v4-0-1-Requirements-and-Testing-Procedures`
- `NIST-CMVP-140-2-to-140-3-Transition-Timeline`

LM-072.curious:
### What This Is About

This module compares ways to speed up post-quantum signatures — wider CPU instructions, built-in hash instructions, graphics cards and custom chips (FPGAs and ASICs) — and examines whether AI accelerators support the required workload. This module explains each one with an everyday analogy, and checks the claims against our own measurements across Apple M4 Pro/M5 Max, NXP i.MX95, AMD Kria KV260, Ventuno Q and an AMD AI X1 Pro, plus focused KV260 FPGA experiments.

### Why It Matters

The two main post-quantum signatures spend their time in completely different places. ML-DSA is mostly arithmetic and is already fast; SLH-DSA is mostly hashing and can take seconds on a small chip. So on our KV260 board the FPGA gave only +29% on ML-DSA, but took an SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signature from 2.12 seconds on the board's own CPU to 69 milliseconds.

### The Key Takeaway

Speed comes from matching the accelerator to where the time actually goes — and from moving the work cheaply. Moving data to an accelerator and back often costs more than the work itself, one accelerator is shared by all the processor cores, and a chip can own a fast instruction that the software never uses. The X1 tests make this concrete: AVX-512/IFMA helped the measured RSA path, but explicit VAES candidates were correct and slower, so they were not deployed.

### What's Happening

Newer Arm cores (like Apple's M4) add SHA-3 and SHA-512 instructions that older cores lack; x86 has AVX2, AVX-512/IFMA, AES-NI and SHA-NI but no SHA-3 instruction. The common benchmark also measures ML-DSA + ECDSA hybrid signatures and ML-KEM + X25519 hybrid KEMs directly inside the HSM. Chip vendors are adding fixed post-quantum engines to secure elements and roots of trust, while GPU libraries such as NVIDIA cuPQC target very large batches of operations in data centres.

The model-fit exercises compare actual measured GPU batches where the CPU wins and where the GPU wins. A separate exact arithmetic example reconstructs a large number from three bytes: small arithmetic units do not make the mathematics impossible, but the chosen backend still needs working kernels and an efficient way to move and recombine the data. The i.MX95 PQC NPU discussion is a desk assessment, not a measured cryptographic implementation.

lesson:
1. Which Measured GPU Batch Wins?
Open the GPU model and change the measured key-generation batch from 256 to 4,096 and 65,536. Compare throughput against the all-core CPU.
The retained Metal ML-DSA-65 key-generation study gives GPU/CPU throughput ratios of 0.54× at 256, 5.87× at 4,096 and 9.27× at 65,536. The CPU wins the first batch and the GPU the other two. These are not single-signature latency results; an operation can contain parallel work.
2. Kernel Support, Cost or Representation?
Open the NPU model, compare the three failure categories, then run “Recompose the 23-bit example”. Check the byte limbs and the modular result.
Keeping only one byte loses the value, but three base-256 limbs reconstruct 8,380,416 exactly; nine byte-pair products give (q − 1)² mod q = 1. This establishes representation correctness, not a supported or fast NPU kernel. Missing operators, data movement and arithmetic costs require separate checks.
3. Check Montgomery Reduction by Hand
In “Building blocks”, follow the decimal example 4321 → 5000 → 50 with N = 97 and R = 100. Verify that 50 × 100 ≡ 4321 (mod 97).
50 × 100 = 5000 = 51 × 97 + 53, and 4321 = 44 × 97 + 53 — the same remainder. The only “division” was dropping two zeros, which in binary is a free shift.
In the dated 27 September 2026 four-worker comparison, the i.MX 95 A55 CPU signs SHA2-128s at 10.87/s and SHAKE-128s at 0.94/s: about 11.6× the throughput. The KV260 SHAKE result (13.0/s) uses its FPGA, while its SHA-2 result (5.09/s) uses its CPU; that reversal is not an A53 CPU-only comparison. Choose an allowed variant using the actual implementation, operation and measured path on your target.
5. When Software Beat Our FPGA
6. Close Timing at 250 MHz
In “FPGA limits”, move the clock slider from 200 to 260 MHz and watch where the clock period crosses the 4-lane engine’s critical path.
At 250 MHz the period is 4.000 ns and our routed path was 4.010 ns — 10 picoseconds too long. Shipping at 240 MHz (4.167 ns) cost 4% throughput; the alternative was a redesign.
7. Can Any Batch Pay Back the Trip?
At 58.7 µs per job the accelerator is slower than the A53 for every batch size — the fixed cost can never be earned back. Only when the per-job cost drops below the CPU’s does a break-even batch size appear.

In plain English: constant-time vs masked
means the circuit takes exactly the same time and follows the same steps whatever the secret key is, so a stopwatch learns nothing. It is cheap.
goes further: every secret value is split into random pieces (“shares”) that are processed separately and only recombine at the end, which is designed to reduce the leakage that power and electromagnetic analysis can use. How much it helps depends on the masking order (how many shares) and on the leakage model and assumptions the design was analysed and tested under; it is not a blanket guarantee, and implementation flaws, attacks of a higher order than the one tested, or leakage nobody modelled can still defeat a masked design. Every share has to be carried, refreshed with fresh randomness and recombined carefully, which costs extra area, randomness and time, and the cost grows with the number of shares. Being built as an ASIC does not by itself show that a design resists physical attacks.
Can an ASIC be reprogrammed? Partly — it depends where the “recipe” lives
: fixed hardware (multipliers, Keccak, memories) follows a stored list of steps, like a kitchen following a recipe card. If that card is in writable memory, a signed update can change the step order, the parameter sets or fix a bug — but never add hardware the chip lacks. Accelerate shared building blocks, not whole algorithms
Offload whole operations only where the win is decisive
A whole-signature engine avoids the round trip and can be many times faster — but it only knows one algorithm and a few parameter sets.
Always keep a software path for every algorithm
Hardware is an optimisation, never the only implementation: if the accelerator is missing, busy or does not know the parameter set, the CPU does the work.
Route by configuration, not by code change
A routing table decides which algorithm goes to which accelerator, so a new standard or a broken parameter set is a configuration change.
Reprogram the hardware when the workload changes
An FPGA can swap whole images (profiles) or single slots (partial reconfiguration). An ASIC cannot — which is why ASIC PQC engines fix their parameter sets up front.
Prefer general instructions over fixed engines on the CPU
A SHA-3 or SIMD instruction helps every algorithm that uses the primitive, now and later — the most agile acceleration there is.
NEON code gave ML-DSA ~4×; SHA-3 instructions gave SHAKE ~20% — for every SHAKE user at once.

Building blocks are small (5–20k LUTs); whole-operation engines are large (24–55k LUTs) because they carry control, buffers and the algorithm’s own logic.
Plumbing is not free: control, DMA and interconnect took about 33k LUTs in the ML-DSA image — more than one whole signer.
Memory often runs out before logic: the ML-DSA image used 95% of block RAM but 81% of LUTs.
A SHA-2 core cost about as much as a Keccak lane (~33k LUTs) and was slower than the CPU’s SHA-256 instructions — so we left SHA-2 on the CPU.
Put N copies of the engine on the chip so N cores can use one each at the same time. Throughput grows with N — until the chip is full or something else becomes the bottleneck.
Make one engine faster by giving it internal lanes that work on the same operation at once. Every request gets the speed-up, but requests still go one at a time.
Share one engine with a queue — and fall back
All cores send requests to one engine; a scheduler queues them (or sends overflow back to the CPU). Cheap in area, but the engine becomes a shared resource.
Match the design to the bottleneck: duplicate when the engine is saturated and area allows; add lanes when single-request latency matters; queue when requests are bursty and area is tight — and always keep the CPU as the overflow path.

Every approach above is a mix of three ways to share one FPGA. (1) Swap the whole image — simplest, but everything stops during the swap. (2) Swap slots (partial reconfiguration) — a fixed shell keeps running while one slot changes, at the cost of fixed slot sizes and a harder design. (3) Put several engines in one image and share them in software — no swap time at all, but everything must fit on the chip at once. And they all split the chip the same way: fixed “plumbing” (memory, DMA, host link) that never changes, plus swappable accelerators — the shell-and-role pattern.
For crypto, sharing matters: Zynq UltraScale+ can authenticate and decrypt full and partial images before loading them, but researchers have shown that a circuit placed next to a victim on the same FPGA can act as a power probe and attack an RSA module on the same chip. Loading one trusted image at a time (time-sharing) is the safer pattern than placing untrusted designs side by side.

In software, first-order masking costs roughly 3–7× the time for Kyber and Dilithium, and the cost climbs steeply with each extra order (Kyber768: 3.5× at first order, over 100× at third).
In hardware the bill can be paid in area as well as time, and it depends on the version and the operation: for Adams Bridge the 2.1-era documentation says arithmetic masking adds no cycles to ML-DSA and at most 2 to ML-KEM (two parallel NTT engines, so the cost is area), while its masked Keccak adds latency (about 15% for ML-DSA key generation and 9–11% for signing, 8–11% for ML-KEM; one ML-DSA-87 signing round 58 → 63 µs), and a security presentation (version not stated) reports 37% for signing and 10% for ML-KEM — while masked Keccak in OpenTitan more than doubles the round logic.
Masking a design that was not built for it can be disastrous: one first-order ML-DSA FPGA design added only 13–20% area but ran 378× slower.
Always ask which attacks a “protected” product covers: constant-time (timing), SPA, or DPA/masking — and at what order.

“mod N” without ever dividing by N.
Dividing by an awkward number like 97 is slow, even for a computer. Dividing by 100 is trivial — you just drop the last two digits. Montgomery’s trick adds a carefully chosen multiple of 97 so the number ends in 00, then drops the zeros. The answer is still correct “mod 97”, and no division by 97 ever happened.
Computers do the same thing in binary: “dropping digits” is a free shift. So a modular multiplication becomes a few ordinary multiplications and a shift — which is why it sits inside RSA, elliptic curves and every ML-DSA coefficient multiply (FIPS 204 Appendix A).
The fastest way to schedule those multiplications depends on the exact core. On our Cortex-A55 a crypto library picked a kernel tuned for server chips, and plain scalar code beat it by 22–62%.
RSA and ECC big numbers; ML-DSA coefficient arithmetic (mod 8,380,417)
Fast multiply-high instructions; NEON/AVX2 doing 4–8 reductions at once; AVX-512 IFMA for RSA
Change the viewpoint and polynomial multiplication becomes element-by-element.
Multiplying two 256-term polynomials the school way means every term times every other term — 65,536 multiplications. The Number-Theoretic Transform is a change of viewpoint, like describing a song by its notes instead of its waveform. In the new view, multiplying is just “each note times the matching note” — 256 multiplications — and you transform back at the end.
The transform itself is a network of “butterflies”, each taking two numbers and producing their sum and difference with a twist. For 256 coefficients that is 8 layers of 128 butterflies. Doing forward, pointwise and inverse costs about 3,300 multiplications instead of 65,536.
Every butterfly needs a modular reduction, and layers must finish in order. ML-KEM’s smaller modulus (3,329) only allows 7 layers, so it finishes with 128 small 2-term products instead of 256 single ones.
ML-DSA (q = 8,380,417, 8 layers) and ML-KEM (q = 3,329, 7 layers)
SIMD butterflies (NEON 4, AVX2 8, AVX-512 16 lanes); GPUs across thousands of polynomials; FPGA/ASIC butterfly pipelines
Shuffle a 1,600-bit block 24 times — using only XOR, AND, NOT and rotate.
Picture a 5×5 grid of 64-bit tiles. Each round mixes every column into its neighbours, rotates each tile, moves the tiles to new positions, scrambles each row, and flips a few bits with a round constant. Repeat 24 times and the block looks completely random.
It uses no arithmetic and no lookup tables — only bit operations — so it is naturally constant-time and very cheap to build in hardware. The Armv8 SHA-3 instructions (EOR3, RAX1, XAR, BCAX) fuse several of these steps into single instructions.
It is 25 × 64-bit lanes wide. A core without SHA-3 instructions spends many instructions per round shuffling them, and our A53/A55 boards have none — so every SHAKE call there is software.
Armv8.2 SHA-3 instructions; SIMD running 4 states side by side (x86 has no Keccak instruction); FPGA/ASIC Keccak cores
A sponge: soak up the message, squeeze out a fixed-length fingerprint.
SHA3-256 uses a 1,600-bit state split into 1,088 bits of “rate” (the cup) and 512 bits of capacity (the sealed part). It always returns exactly 256 bits.
A bigger capacity means more security but a smaller cup, so more permutations per byte. SHA3-512 is slower than SHA3-256 for exactly that reason.
ML-KEM (SHA3-256, SHA3-512 for its internal hashes); general-purpose hashing
The same sponge, with a tap you can leave running.
SHAKE is SHA-3’s sponge with an open tap: after soaking up the input you can keep squeezing for as much output as you like — 32 bytes, or tens of kilobytes of random-looking data from one short seed.

LM-072.summary:
# PQC Hardware Acceleration

## Overview

This module explains how post-quantum signature algorithms are accelerated and why the same accelerator helps ML-DSA and SLH-DSA very differently. It covers seven acceleration models (scalar CPU, SIMD vector units, dedicated crypto instructions, GPU, FPGA, ASIC/secure element, NPU), the five primitives they target (Montgomery reduction, the NTT, the Keccak permutation, SHA-3, SHAKE), and the practical limits of offloading (area, clock, CPU↔accelerator round trip, sharing one engine between cores, batch vs latency). Its current common CPU/PKCS#11 measurement covers AI X1 Pro, i.MX95 Pro, i.MX95, KV260 CPU, Ventuno Q, M4 Pro and M5 Max; its focused Arm/KV260 FPGA experiments remain visibly separate.

## Key Concepts

- **Where the time goes** — ML-DSA: NTT polynomial arithmetic mod 8,380,417 plus SHAKE sampling inside a rejection loop (~4–5 attempts per signature); SLH-DSA: almost pure hashing (about two million Keccak permutations per SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signature); RSA/ECC: Montgomery big-integer arithmetic
- **Montgomery reduction** — modular multiplication without trial division (Montgomery 1985; FIPS 204 Appendix A)
- **NTT** — 256-coefficient polynomial multiplication in ~3,300 instead of 65,536 multiplications; ML-DSA uses a full 8-layer NTT, ML-KEM (q = 3,329) a 7-layer one
- **Keccak / SHA-3 / SHAKE** (FIPS 202) — 24-round bitwise permutation of a 1,600-bit state; SHA3-256 and SHAKE256 use rate 1,088 / capacity 512, SHAKE128 rate 1,344 / capacity 256
- **Instruction sets** — Arm FEAT_SHA256/AES (optional since Armv8.0) and FEAT_SHA512/FEAT_SHA3 (Armv8.2 extension; EOR3, RAX1, XAR, BCAX); Cortex-A53/A55 have AES and SHA-256 but not SHA-512 or SHA-3; Apple M4 has both. x86 has AES-NI and SHA-NI (SHA-1/SHA-256 only), SHA-512 instructions only from Arrow Lake-S/Lunar Lake, and no SHA-3/Keccak instruction
- **Measured: the instruction set picks the variant** — on today's engine SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signs 9–12× faster than SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s on every CPU (M4 Pro 124 vs 13.5/s, i.MX 95 10.9 vs 0.94/s), while the KV260's FPGA reverses it (SHAKE-128s 13.0/s = 96% of the whole M4 Pro CPU's 13.49/s, which does not yet use its SHA-3 instructions); SHA-256 runs ~3× faster than SHA-512 on those cores
- **Measured: owning an instruction is not using it** — AES ran in software until a build flag was set (7–13× after); SLH-DSA's Keccak did not use the M4's SHA-3 instructions, and switching them on (A/B on the M4 Pro) gave only 1.17–1.21×; an AWS-LC Montgomery kernel tuned for server cores was 22–62% slower than scalar code on the A55
- **Measured: AWS-LC NEON on vs off (M4 Pro)** — ML-DSA sign/verify about 4×, ML-DSA-65/87 keygen 7.7–8.3×, ML-KEM-768 decapsulation 1.5×
- **Measured: Ventuno Q CPU path** — Qualcomm QCS8275 (4× Cortex-A78C + 4× Cortex-A55) measured ML-DSA-65 signing at 3,996.64 TPS with one active worker and 18,972.13 TPS with eight workers; GPU/NPU is not part of that result
- **Measured: AI X1 Pro AMD64 dispatch** — the VM exposes AVX2, AVX-512F/IFMA, VAES, AES-NI and SHA-NI. AWS-LC IFMA RSA-PSS-2048 signing measured 2.08× faster at one worker and 1.99× whole-platform than its masked control. Extra AVX2 ML-KEM gave no saturated whole-platform gain; correct VAES-256/512 candidates were slower and rejected
- **Measured: hybrid mechanisms** — Scenario 39 measures ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 signing and ML-KEM-768 + X25519 encapsulation directly through PKCS#11 v3.3, with component secrets combined inside the HSM. They are not arithmetic sums of their pure-operation TPS results
- **Measured: KV260 FPGA on vs off, same board** — SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signing 0.46 → 13.0/s (28.4×); the KV260's lead over the i.MX 95 on SLH-DSA-SHAKE is entirely the fabric
- **Measured: board engine update (2026-09-27)** — RSA-OAEP decrypt 2×, AES-GCM 16 KiB 6–7.6×, small-AES multi-core scaling 3.2–5×, on both the KV260 and the i.MX 95 Pro
- **Measured: FPGA outcomes** — KV260 ML-DSA-65 with two FPGA signers: 404.45 → 522.50 sign/s (+29.2%), capped by ARM-side work (key decode, ExpandA, copies, cache sync, PKCS#11); SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s with a 4-lane Keccak engine at 240 MHz: 2.12 s on the board's CPU → 69 ms per signature on the FPGA (the shipped software engine measured 12.3 s before the CPU work)
- **Measured: software can overtake hardware** — after the engine moved ML-DSA onto AWS-LC's NEON assembly, the KV260's A53 alone signed ML-DSA-65 at 2,675/s (2026-09-26), about five times the older FPGA-assisted figure
- **FPGA: narrow but powerful** — built for one workload (SLH-DSA-SHAKE signing), the KV260's FPGA is 13–15× faster than the i.MX 95 CPU and reaches 84–97% of a whole Apple M4 Pro CPU; on every other workload it adds nothing
- **FPGA limits** — LUTs, flip-flops, DSP slices and block RAM (KV260: 117,120 LUTs, 144 BRAM tiles); the clock is set by the design's critical path (the 4-lane engine missed 250 MHz by 0.010 ns and ships at 240 MHz); per-call round-trip cost (first Keccak engine: 1,481 µs fixed + 58.7 µs per hash vs ~12 µs on the A53); one engine shared by all cores
- **GPU** — measured batching, not a universal latency verdict: our Metal ML-DSA-65 key generation lost to the CPU at a batch of 256 and won 9.3× at 65,536; NVIDIA cuPQC's published ML-KEM figures (175×/120×/135× vs one CPU core) were measured on an H100 (Hopper), but cuPQC also supports Ampere GPUs including the embedded Jetson Orin (compute capability 8.7)
- **ASIC** — same bus and sharing limits as an FPGA, plus fixed parameter sets at tape-out (Caliptra's Adams Bridge documents ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 only; Tessera's accelerator comes from an open hardware design with no silicon or product in the sources read; its hardware repository's parameter package says the core implements every ML-DSA and ML-KEM parameter set, selected at run time (the package uses Adams Bridge's abr naming and the repository does not say how the two relate, so reading them as separate designs is our inference). The Tessera Chip Requirements say Tessera "MUST have a Caliptra 2.2 subsystem root of trust", while the Adams Bridge figures here come from the Caliptra 2.1 documentation; Microsoft's 13 October 2026 post says Caliptra 2.2, "scheduled for release in December", adds "a smaller, fully masked Adams Bridge post-quantum cryptography accelerator" — see Step 6 of Architect Quantum Impact, /learn/arch-quantum-impact?tab=workshop&step=5); OpenTitan verifies boot images with SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s on its SHA-256 block
- **Cost of side-channel masking in Adams Bridge (documented figures for a named version, not silicon measurements)** — the Adams Bridge v3.0 columns of the Caliptra 2.1 documentation (RTL simulation at 600 MHz) say arithmetic masking adds no cycles to ML-DSA and at most 2 cycles to ML-KEM, with its cost in area, and that the masked Keccak adds latency: ML-DSA-87 one signing round 58 µs unprotected vs 63 µs protected (35,012 vs 38,036 cycles), about 15% for key generation and 9–11% for signing, ML-KEM-1024 decapsulation 11,144 vs 11,986 cycles; area 909,602 vs 1,398,044 gate equivalents. A security presentation for Adams Bridge (version not stated) reports 6× area, 37% more latency for ML-DSA signing and 10% for ML-KEM. The cost depends on the version and the operation, so masking is not free in time.
- **NPU** — the i.MX95 combines CPUs and an eIQ Neutron NPU. PQC offload was desk-assessed, not prototyped or benchmarked. The workshop executes exact base-256 reconstruction and nine byte-pair products for q − 1 = 8,380,416; correctness of representation does not establish an implemented or fast NPU kernel. Missing software operators, inefficient partition/data movement and an impossible single-byte representation are distinct cases. TensorFHE’s historical GPU tensor-core decomposition is not an i.MX95 implementation.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 5 steps:

1. **Acceleration Models, Explained** — seven models, each with an everyday analogy, an animated mechanism diagram and a fit grid (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, single op, big batch)
2. **Building Blocks, Explained** — Montgomery (worked decimal example), NTT butterfly network, Keccak round steps, SHA-3 and SHAKE sponges
3. **Our Measurements** — current seven-platform classical, pure-PQC and hybrid CPU/PKCS#11 comparison, followed by the historical M4 Pro/i.MX95/KV260 signature and FPGA experiments
4. **FPGA Limits Lab** — resource budget, clock-vs-critical-path slider, anatomy of the +29% ML-DSA result
5. **Offload, Sharing and Batching** — round-trip break-even calculator, shared-engine concurrency, GPU batch crossover

## Related Standards

- FIPS 202 (SHA-3 / SHAKE)
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM)
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA)
- FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
- CRYSTALS-Dilithium (TCHES 2018) — AVX2 implementation results
- SPHINCS+ (CCS 2019)

Unlike an ASIC, the fabric can be rewritten in the field. Our KV260 ships one complete image; we also tested swapping whole images at runtime (“profiles”: ML-DSA signers ⇄ SLH-DSA hash engine, live on the board, with the crypto services restarting). AMD’s modular alternative — partial reconfiguration, which swaps one slot while the rest keeps running — we documented but did not use.
A real system never runs one algorithm. It runs ML-KEM and ML-DSA for new sessions, SLH-DSA for long-lived signatures, RSA and ECC for everything not yet migrated, and AES and SHA-2 for the traffic — and the list will change as standards evolve. Acceleration has to follow that list without being rebuilt every time.

The two main post-quantum signatures spend their time in completely different places. ML-DSA is mostly arithmetic and is already fast; SLH-DSA is mostly hashing and can take seconds on a small chip. So on our KV260 board the FPGA gave only +29% on ML-DSA, but took an SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signature from 2.12 seconds on the board's own CPU to 69 milliseconds.
One Keccak engine serves ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA-SHAKE; one NTT engine serves both lattice schemes. A new algorithm built from the same blocks gets faster for free.
Our SLH-DSA engine signs the SHAKE “s” sets 26–31× faster on the same board, and does nothing for the SHA-2 or “f” sets.

An FPGA has a fixed amount of logic and memory. Our ML-DSA image alone uses 81% of the KV260’s logic and 95% of its on-chip memory; the SLH-DSA image uses 55% of the logic. Together they would need roughly 159k LUTs on a 117k-LUT chip — so they cannot be loaded at the same time. Every extra algorithm you want in hardware makes this worse, which is what forces a loading model: swap whole images (profiles), swap slots (partial reconfiguration), or keep only small shared building blocks resident.

LM-072/s:where-time-goes.full:
The practical checklist: find where the time actually goes; check which instructions the core really has
Speed comes from matching the accelerator to where the time actually goes — and from moving the work cheaply. Moving data to an accelerator and back often costs more than the work itself, one accelerator is shared by all the processor cores, and a chip can own a fast instruction that the software never uses. The X1 tests make this concrete: AVX-512/IFMA helped the measured RSA path, but explicit VAES candidates were correct and slower, so they were not deployed.
Tessera’s accelerator comes from an open hardware design, with no silicon or product in the sources read: its hardware repository’s parameter package says the core implements every ML-DSA and ML-KEM parameter set, selected at run time (ML-DSA-44/65/87 and ML-KEM-512/768/1024), where Adams Bridge’s documentation lists ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 only. The package uses Adams Bridge’s abr naming and the repository does not say how the two relate; reading them as separate designs is our inference, so do not read them as the same engine. The Tessera Chip Requirements say Tessera “MUST have a Caliptra 2.2 subsystem root of trust”, while the Adams Bridge figures on this page come from the Caliptra 2.1 documentation; Microsoft’s 13 October 2026 post says Caliptra 2.2, “scheduled for release in December”, adds “a smaller, fully masked Adams Bridge post-quantum cryptography accelerator”.
ML-DSA and SLH-DSA spend their time in completely different places, so on our KV260 board the FPGA gave +29% on ML-DSA signing and about 28× more SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signatures per second (13.0 against 0.46). Choosing hardware, parameter sets and hash variants for a device — or judging a vendor’s acceleration claim — needs an honest picture of where the time goes and what moving it costs.
Where the time goes — ML-DSA: NTT polynomial arithmetic mod 8,380,417 plus SHAKE sampling inside a rejection loop (~4–5 attempts per signature); SLH-DSA: almost pure hashing (about two million Keccak permutations per SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signature); RSA/ECC: Montgomery big-integer arithmetic
A sponge. You pour the message in one cupful at a time, and after every cup you wring the sponge (one Keccak permutation). Part of the sponge — the “capacity” — is sealed inside and never touches the message or the output directly; that hidden part is where the security comes from.

LM-073.curious:
### What This Is About

You don't need to understand the mathematics to talk about post-quantum cryptography — but you do need to get the facts right. This module is for anyone who has to say something about it at work: in sales, marketing, communications, procurement, policy or the press. It covers what is true today, which deadlines are real and who they apply to, what a security certificate actually proves, and which popular words don't hold up.

### Why It Matters

Customers, buyers and journalists can now check a quantum claim against public records: the standards are published, the government deadlines are written down, and certificate numbers can be looked up. A sentence that overstates a deadline or a certificate costs more trust than it ever wins.

### The Key Takeaway

Say what the record shows, and point to it. Name the standard (for example ML-KEM, FIPS 203), the version of the product, and the evidence — a certificate number or a public roadmap — instead of "quantum-proof" or "fully compliant".

### Try It Yourself

The workshop gives you six real-sounding claims and four customer questions. Pick the most accurate answer and see straight away why it holds up and the others don't.

The arrival date of a code-breaking quantum computer is an estimate, and experts disagree. The risk to data copied today (“harvest now, decrypt later”) does not depend on the exact year.
“NIST will ban RSA in ${NIST_DEPRECATION.deprecateClassical}.”
NIST will ban RSA in ${NIST_DEPRECATION.deprecateClassical}.
In NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026), NIST deprecates today’s quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms, such as RSA and ECDSA, after ${NIST_DEPRECATION.deprecateClassical} and disallows them under NIST standards and guidelines after ${NIST_DEPRECATION.disallowClassical}.
NIST IR 8547 is NIST guidance, not a ban. “Deprecated” means still allowed, with a risk the user accepts; “disallowed” comes later, and applies under NIST standards and guidelines.
A customer asks: “Are you quantum-safe?”
Quantum is not a real risk yet, so it does not matter.
Here is what is protected today, what is planned and when, and the evidence for each: our roadmap page and our certificate numbers.
A good answer splits the product into what is done, what is planned and what is unknown, and links evidence for each part. A single “yes” cannot be checked, and dismissing the risk contradicts published government guidance.
A buyer asks: “Is your product FIPS-validated for PQC?”
Our FIPS 140-3 certificate number covers a specific version. The certificate gives the validated module name and version number, plus its tested operational environment, so let us check it together.
FIPS does not apply to post-quantum cryptography.
A certificate covers a specific version and configuration. Post-quantum algorithms added later are only covered once a validation that includes them is complete.
A customer asks: “Do we need to replace everything now?”
Yes, immediately, or you will be breached.
Start by finding where you use cryptography. Replacements roll out over years, starting with data that must stay secret for a long time.
No, wait until quantum computers exist.
Finding the cryptography is usually the longest step. Panic overstates the risk, and waiting ignores data being copied today.
Someone asks: “What does hybrid mean?”
A halfway step that is less secure than full PQC.
It is just a marketing term.
It uses a traditional and a post-quantum algorithm together, so the connection stays protected as long as either one holds.
Hybrid is a deliberate design that many standards bodies recommend during the transition, not a compromise. It is a good word to use once you have explained it.

LM-074.curious:
### What This Is About

Smart meters, sensors, wearables and gateways run on tiny chips with a few kilobytes of memory and slow radios. This module looks at how post-quantum cryptography fits on them: which algorithms they can run, how their software updates are signed, and how their networks carry the larger keys.

### Why It Matters

A device sold today may still be working in 15 years. If its update signatures can be forged by a future quantum computer, an attacker could install anything on it — and many devices can only be fixed by replacing them.

### The Key Takeaway

Small devices mostly check signatures rather than make them, and checking is much cheaper. Many post-quantum algorithms fit when built for low memory; signing and heavy handshakes are best left to servers and gateways.

### What's Happening

New laws such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act require secure updates for years after sale, and chip makers have started shipping security chips with post-quantum algorithms built in.

Each collector finishes its radio exchanges in about 16 minutes (2,472 B per meter, 7.5× today’s 328 B), but the head-end HSM needs about 1.1 hours for 4 million operations — the HSM is the bottleneck. The ML-DSA-87 signature is 2.9% of the update. Unicast needs about 45 hours of downlink and misses the 24-hour window — but the same update signed with ECDSA needs about 44 hours and misses it too. Billions of small connected devices — electricity meters, building sensors, fitness trackers — check a digital signature before they accept a software update. That signature is what stops a stranger from taking over the device. A future quantum computer could forge today's signatures, so these devices need new, quantum-safe ones.
The new signatures are bigger, and these devices have very little memory and slow radios. The good news is that checking a signature is cheap even when making one is not, so most small devices can do their part while the heavy work happens on servers. Engineers are choosing those algorithms now, because a device built today may stay in service for 15 years.
