qa.answer: Each collector finishes its radio exchanges in about 16 minutes, sending 2,472 B per meter (7.5× today's 328 B), but the head-end HSM needs about 1.1 hours for 4 million operations, so the HSM is the bottleneck rather than the power-line link. Collectors work in parallel while every key update passes through the same HSM. Switching to a high-throughput HSM moves the bottleneck back to the network (model estimate).
qa.question: In the Fleet Key Manager's default scenario (2 million smart meters, 1,000 per collector, G3-PLC, ML-KEM-768, standard HSM), what limits a fleet-wide key rotation?

qa.answer: RFC 7228 gives Class 0 devices well under 10 KiB of RAM (≪ 10 KiB) and well under 100 KiB of code (≪ 100 KiB); they are too constrained to talk to the Internet securely on their own and rely on a gateway or proxy. RFC 7228 defines only Classes 0–2 (Class 1 ~10 KiB RAM, Class 2 ~50 KiB). Classes 3 (~100 KiB) and 4 (~300–1000 KiB) come from draft-ietf-iotops-7228bis.
qa.question: How does RFC 7228 size a Class 0 constrained device, and which device classes come from draft-ietf-iotops-7228bis rather than RFC 7228?

qa.answer: NIST SP 800-232, final in August 2025, standardises the Ascon family for devices too small for AES-GCM. It is symmetric cryptography: AES and SHA-2 stay too, since a quantum computer weakens them only modestly. PQC replaces the public-key parts, key establishment and signatures.
qa.question: Which NIST publication standardises the Ascon lightweight cryptography family, and which part of a device's crypto does it address?

qa.answer: A classical DTLS 1.3 handshake with an ECDSA certificate chain is about 1,374 B (20 radio frames). With ML-KEM-768 and an ML-DSA-44 chain it grows to about 13,146 B: 13 IPv6 datagrams and 171 IEEE 802.15.4 frames, where each 127-byte frame has about 80 bytes of payload once link security is on. These are model estimates from the Constrained Handshake step (constrained-handshake).
qa.question: How large is a DTLS 1.3 handshake over CoAP and 6LoWPAN before and after PQC, in the module's model?

qa.answer: Interval readings reveal when a home is occupied, and meters stay installed 15 years or more, so metering traffic recorded today could be decrypted once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. DLMS/COSEM Suite 1 (P-256) and Suite 2 (P-384) meters agree keys with ECDH, which is the harvestable part. Suite 0 meters use symmetric key wrap only and have no public-key exchange to break.
qa.question: Why is smart-meter data a harvest-now-decrypt-later target, and which DLMS/COSEM security suites expose a public-key exchange?

qa.answer: FrodoKEM-640 needs 72,408 B (about 72 KB) of stack to decapsulate in the pqm4 benchmark and has 9,616-byte public keys. In the module's fit model it is too large for Class 1 key establishment and is out of reach below Class 4 (~300–1000 KiB RAM, draft-ietf-iotops-7228bis). By contrast, ML-KEM-768 decapsulation needs 2,844 B in pqm4's stack-optimised build.
qa.question: How much RAM does FrodoKEM-640 need on a Cortex-M4, and which device classes can run it?

qa.answer: CNSA 2.0 accepts only ML-DSA-87 or LMS/XMSS (per NIST SP 800-208) for firmware and software signing. NSA's 2022 category guidance had such signing prefer CNSA 2.0 algorithms from 2025 and use them exclusively by 2030; for current planning NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2) mandates CNSA 2.0 algorithms for national security systems by 31 December 2031 unless otherwise noted. ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 are fine for commercial FIPS 204 products but not for national security systems.
qa.question: Under CNSA 2.0, which signature algorithms are accepted for firmware and software signing in national security systems, and by when?

qa.answer: A TLS or DTLS server sends its leaf and intermediate certificates and leaves the root out (RFC 9846 §4.5.1, formerly RFC 8446 §4.4.2), and each certificate carries its subject's key plus its issuer's signature (RFC 5280). Under that model an ECDSA P-256 chain sends 856 B, while an all-ML-DSA-65 chain sends 11,122 B, about 13× as much and larger than a Class 1 device's whole RAM. ML-DSA-44 sends 8,064 B and FN-DSA-512 3,726 B.
qa.question: How many bytes does a certificate chain put on the wire with ML-DSA-65 compared with ECDSA P-256, in the module's model?

qa.answer: LMS/HSS (RFC 8554) has a 60 B public key and a 2,512 B signature (H10/W4 as HSS L = 1); XMSS (RFC 8391) has a 68 B public key and a 2,500 B signature (SHA2_10_256). Both are stateful, covered by SP 800-208, and accepted by BSI TR-02102-1. In the Cortex-M4 benchmark LMS verifies in 2.66 M cycles against 13.07 M for XMSS (4.9×), a gap that comes from the reference code. LMS is still not the fastest verifier: FN-DSA-512, ECDSA P-256, ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 all verify in fewer cycles.
qa.question: How do LMS and XMSS compare for firmware signing on a constrained MCU?

qa.answer: Every extra byte on air and every extra million cycles costs battery, and a PQC handshake adds both: DTLS 1.3 with ML-KEM-768 and an ML-DSA-44 chain is about 13,146 B versus 1,374 B classically (model estimate). PSK resumption sends no certificate after the first handshake. The same energy argument favours verifying on the device while signing elsewhere.
qa.question: Why does the module favour session resumption over repeated full handshakes on battery-powered devices?

qa.answer: draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs replaces the CA signature with an inclusion proof of 32 bytes per tree level and drops the intermediate certificate. In the Certificate Chain step (cert-chain) an MTC with a 20-level proof sends 2,892 B where a full ML-DSA-65 chain sends 11,122 B. It works only if the relying party already holds current trusted tree heads, distributed out of band, so a device that is offline for months needs a fallback chain.
qa.question: How do Merkle Tree Certificates shrink the certificate bytes a constrained device receives, and what condition limits their use?

qa.answer: FN-DSA-512 signatures are 666 B in Falcon v1.2's padded, fixed-length format; FIPS 206 is not yet published, so the module labels these sizes pre-standard. On a Cortex-M4, FN-DSA-512 verifies with 2,976 B of stack and is the fastest verifier benchmarked (0.40 M cycles), but signing needs 41,952 B of stack and the full scheme is 103,789 B (~104 KB) of code. Verify on the device; sign on a server.
qa.question: Which post-quantum signature in the module has the most compact signatures, and why is it verified on the device but signed elsewhere?

qa.answer: Symmetric crypto stays: AES and SHA-2 are weakened only modestly by a quantum computer, and Suite 0's symmetric key wrap has no public-key exchange to break. What PQC replaces is the ECDH key agreement of Suite 1 (P-256) and Suite 2 (P-384). The Fleet Key Manager takes today's key establishment (DLMS Suite 0/1/2) and an ML-KEM parameter set as inputs, and its known-answer tests cover NIST ACVP ML-KEM-768 decapsulation, NIST CAVP AES-256-GCM decryption and an ECDH P-256 round-trip for the classical baseline.
qa.question: A utility is planning PQC for a DLMS/COSEM smart-meter fleet. Which parts of its cryptography change, and how does the Fleet Key Manager (fleet-key-manager) model them?

qa.answer: LMS produces a 2,512-byte signature that verifies in the browser's SoftHSM, the one-bit-tampered manifest is rejected, and the token's remaining-signature counter (where the engine publishes one) reads one less than 1,024. Signature plus SUIT/COSE is about 0.97% of the 256 KiB update. ML-DSA-44 gives 2,420 bytes but is not accepted by CNSA 2.0, which allows only ML-DSA-87 or LMS/XMSS. In the verification ranking LMS is fifth, behind FN-DSA-512, ECDSA, ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65.
qa.question: In Firmware Signing (firmware-signing), Exercise 2 signs a smart-meter update with LMS and then with ML-DSA-44. What does the step show?

qa.answer: LoRaWAN 1.1 has no public-key exchange on the air: it uses AES-128 root keys (AppKey/NwkKey) and AES-CMAC/CTR session keys, so the radio link is not a Shor target. The quantum exposure is the backend, meaning join-server and network-server TLS, and how the root keys were provisioned. With 51–222 B per uplink (EU868) and a 1% duty cycle, large updates go by multicast with fragmentation.
qa.question: You are adding post-quantum protection to a LoRaWAN 1.1 deployment with 51–222 B uplink payloads. Where is the quantum exposure?

qa.answer: An IEEE 802.1AR initial device identifier (IDevID) is a certificate and key installed in the factory; NIST SP 1800-36B shows it anchoring trusted network-layer onboarding. FIDO Device Onboard 1.1 transfers ownership late with an ownership voucher, and EST-coaps (RFC 9148) enrols operational certificates over CoAP. Each of these is a long-lived signature key that PQC must replace, and an IDevID baked into silicon today cannot be swapped later.
qa.question: A manufacturer is deciding how its devices will prove their identity over their whole service life. Which identity and onboarding mechanisms does the module describe, and why must the PQC decision be made before manufacture?

qa.answer: Using the fastest benchmarked build of each: FN-DSA-512 0.40 M < ECDSA P-256 0.98 M < ML-DSA-44 1.42 M < ML-DSA-65 2.42 M < LMS 2.66 M < ML-DSA-87 4.19 M < XMSS 13.07 M cycles. LMS is not the fastest verifier; its case is the tiny 60-byte public key and hash-only security assumption. Firmware Signing (firmware-signing) shows the same verification-cost ranking.
qa.question: A battery-powered sensor must verify OTA update signatures as cheaply as possible. How do the candidate signatures rank for verification cost on a Cortex-M4?

qa.answer: The full chain sends 11,122 B (leaf + intermediate; the root stays on the device), more than the 10 KiB budget. In this model, compression saves about 300 B: it assumes half of the non-key, non-signature bytes in each certificate compress, because PQC keys and signatures are high-entropy and do not compress. RFC 8879 states no such fraction. C509 saves 320 B. A raw public key (RFC 7250) needs 1,982 B and a Merkle Tree Certificate with a 20-level proof 2,892 B, each with its own trust caveat, while PSK resumption sends nothing.
qa.question: In Certificate Chain (cert-chain), Exercise 4 tries to fit an ML-DSA-65 chain on a 10 KiB device. What does each delivery mode achieve?

qa.answer: For verification, ECDSA P-256, LMS (H10/W4) and FN-DSA-512 fit, while XMSS and all three ML-DSA sets are tight; ML-DSA-44 peaks at 6,444 B, 63% of 10 KiB. For key establishment ECDH P-256 fits, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 are tight, and FrodoKEM-640 is too large. With speed-optimised builds every ML-DSA set is too large (ML-DSA-44 needs 12,644 B), and signing with FN-DSA-512 needs 41,952 B of stack, so signing belongs on a server.
qa.question: In the Algorithm Explorer (constrained-algorithm), what can a Class 1 device (~10 KiB RAM) do with stack-optimised builds for signature verification and for key establishment?

qa.answer: In the gateway-mediated model, field devices keep symmetric or classical crypto to a nearby gateway, which runs PQC or hybrid to the cloud. That protects the long-haul link without touching the devices. The device-to-gateway link stays classical, so its traffic remains harvestable unless it is symmetric-only; Class 0 devices fit none of the PQC algorithms and need a gateway in any case.
qa.question: An enterprise runs Class 0 sensor tags and Class 1 meters it cannot upgrade. What does gateway-mediated PQC protect, and what does it leave exposed?

qa.answer: SUIT is three documents: RFC 9019 is the firmware update architecture, RFC 9124 the manifest information model, and draft-ietf-suit-manifest the CBOR manifest format itself. The manifest carries the image digest and conditions and is signed with COSE: HSS-LMS is registered by RFC 8778 (COSE alg −46) and ML-DSA by RFC 9964 (−48/−49/−50), while SLH-DSA and FN-DSA are still drafts. Firmware Signing (firmware-signing) signs such a manifest for real and shows the COSE_Sign1 layout.
qa.question: Which documents make up SUIT, and which COSE registrations let a SUIT manifest carry a post-quantum signature?

qa.answer: TrustZone-M is isolation, not a secure element: the Armv8-M security extension separates secure and non-secure software on the same core, so PQC code in the secure world uses the same RAM, flash and cycles and gains no capacity or acceleration. Secure elements with on-chip PQC now exist; Infineon reports Common Criteria EAL6 certification for an ML-KEM implementation on its TEGRION controllers, and Samsung's S3SSE2A received an ANSSI Common Criteria certificate in 2025 (its published Security Target Lite lists an optional ML-DSA library among the functions included in the TOE). ECC-only parts such as Microchip's ATECC608B cannot offload ML-KEM or ML-DSA, so a device built around one needs PQC in MCU firmware or a new part.
qa.question: Does ARM TrustZone-M accelerate PQC on a Class 2 device, and what can secure elements offload?

qa.answer: In the Constrained Handshake model (constrained-handshake), DTLS 1.3 with ML-KEM-768 and an ML-DSA-44 chain is about 13,146 B (171 IEEE 802.15.4 frames), 9.6× the 1,374 B classical handshake. EDHOC (RFC 9528) with credentials sent by reference needs about 7,141 B (92 frames) because no certificate chain crosses the air; classically EDHOC is about 216 B. Post-quantum EDHOC suites are specified in draft-ietf-lake-pqsuites, and every byte saved on air saves battery.
qa.question: For a battery-operated Class 1 device on a 6LoWPAN mesh, how does EDHOC compare with DTLS 1.3 once PQC algorithms are used?

qa.answer: None of them names a PQC algorithm; what they require (secure updates over a support period, state-of-the-art protection, vulnerability handling) decides whether a later PQC migration is possible. The EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) applies its reporting obligations from 11 September 2026 and its essential requirements from 11 December 2027, and RED Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 sets cybersecurity requirements for internet-connected radio equipment, with EN 18031-1/-2/-3 as harmonised standards that Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/138 cites with restrictions. The UK PSTI Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1007) ban universal default passwords and require a vulnerability disclosure policy and a stated minimum security-update period, while the US Cyber Trust Mark (FCC 24-26) is a voluntary label.
qa.question: A consumer-IoT vendor sells into the EU, the UK and the US. Which security regulations apply, and do any of them name a PQC algorithm?

qa.answer: X25519MLKEM768 stays secret as long as either component is unbroken. The X25519 half adds 32 bytes in each direction, and its ECC routine (at most 2,048 B of stack in the benchmark) runs before or after ML-KEM rather than on top of its peak, so hybrid does not double the cost. Native hybrid suits Class 2 and up (Class 1 with stack-optimised builds); gateway mediation is for Class 0–1 devices, whose link to the gateway stays classical.
qa.question: A Class 2 gateway will run hybrid key exchange to the cloud. What does X25519MLKEM768 add on top of ML-KEM-768, and when is gateway mediation used instead?

LM-074.summary:
# IoT & Embedded Device PQC

## Overview

This advanced Applications module (LM-074, 90 minutes) covers post-quantum cryptography for constrained IoT and embedded devices. It was split on 2026-10-01 from the former IoT/OT and Energy & Utilities modules: industrial control systems (SCADA, PLCs, IEC 62443 zones and conduits, sector deep dives) moved to LM-075 _OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC_; vehicle networks to _Automotive PQC_; boot-time verification to _Secure Boot PQC_. Smart-meter key management and RF-mesh airtime moved in from Energy & Utilities and were generalised to device fleets and LPWAN.

Numbers in the module are of three kinds and are labelled that way: exact sizes from the standards (FIPS 203 Table 3, FIPS 204 Table 2, RFC 8554, RFC 8391, Falcon v1.2); Cortex-M4 benchmarks with a named source (pqm4 benchmarks.md at commit 90bfb63 of 2025-05-22, pqm4 at 33de42d of 2021-09-06 for FrodoKEM, Campos et al. IACR ePrint 2020/470 for LMS/XMSS, the Emill P256-Cortex-M4 library for ECDSA/ECDH); and model estimates computed from those.

## Learn sections

1. **Why IoT is different: device classes** — RFC 7228 Classes 0–2 (≪10 KiB / ~10 KiB / ~50 KiB RAM) and Classes 3–4 from draft-ietf-iotops-7228bis (~100 KiB; ~300–1000 KiB). An IEEE 802.15.4 frame is 127 bytes with about 80 bytes of payload once link security is on. Lifetimes, radio cost, energy. Ascon (NIST SP 800-232, final August 2025) for lightweight symmetric crypto. Industrial IoT in a plant: NIST SP 800-82r3 §5.4.2 routes the IIoT platform tier through the industrial DMZ border firewall (level 3.5 of the plant network); a device that connects straight to the cloud skips that boundary (see `ot-pqc`, section `attack-surface`).
2. **Algorithm selection: verify vs sign** — devices mostly verify. Stack RAM on Cortex-M4 (pqm4): ML-KEM-768 decapsulation 2,844 B in the stack-optimised build vs 6,452 B speed-optimised; ML-DSA-44 verify 2,712 B / sign 5,080 B (stack build), verify 8,912 B in the speed build; FN-DSA-512 verify 2,976 B but sign 41,952 B with ~104 KB of code; LMS H10/W4 verify 1,044 B (reference code); FrodoKEM-640 decapsulation ~72 KB. FIPS 206 is not yet published; FN-DSA-512 signatures are 666 B in Falcon v1.2's padded format.
3. **Firmware and update signing (SUIT, COSE)** — LMS/HSS (60 B key, 2,512 B signature as HSS L=1), XMSS (68 B / 2,500 B), ML-DSA (stateless). Stateful counters must never roll back. Verification cost on Cortex-M4, fastest build of each: FN-DSA-512 0.40 M < ECDSA P-256 0.98 M < ML-DSA-44 1.42 M < ML-DSA-65 2.42 M < LMS 2.66 M < ML-DSA-87 4.19 M < XMSS 13.07 M cycles — LMS is not the fastest verifier. CNSA 2.0 accepts only LMS, XMSS and ML-DSA-87 for national-security-system firmware, not HSS, XMSSMT or SLH-DSA; its FAQ v2.2 dates are new national security system acquisitions from 1 January 2027, unsupported equipment phased out by 31 December 2030, and CNSA 2.0 mandated by 31 December 2031. SUIT = RFC 9019 (architecture) + RFC 9124 (information model) + draft-ietf-suit-manifest (CBOR format). COSE: HSS-LMS in RFC 8778, ML-DSA in RFC 9964; SLH-DSA and FN-DSA still drafts. Devices that cannot update their signature-checking code: RFC 9019 recommends that unchangeable bootloader code in ROM use post-quantum secure signature schemes such as hash-based signatures, because RSA and ECC signatures may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated key extraction, and a bootloader author has to weigh the product's service lifetime against that risk; NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) says such devices should be designed to require quantum-resistant signatures on the executable code if they may still be in use once cryptanalytically relevant quantum computers exist.
4. **Constrained protocols** — CoAP + DTLS 1.3 (RFC 7252, RFC 9147, RFC 7925 and the TLS 1.3 IoT profile draft); EDHOC (RFC 9528) + OSCORE (RFC 8613) with PQ suites in draft-ietf-lake-pqsuites; MQTT 5 (maximum packet 268,435,455 B over TCP/TLS); LwM2M; Matter (PASE with SPAKE2+, DAC → PAI → PAA attestation, CASE; Matter 1.6 defines no PQC suites yet, and a note in its onboarding payload table says PQC Phase 1 will likely soon replace the AttestationCryptoInfo mechanism with an equivalent mechanism using the Operational Credentials cluster); Bluetooth Mesh (P-256 provisioning in PB-ADV segments, certificate-based provisioning in Mesh Protocol 1.1); LoRaWAN 1.1 (symmetric AES-128 air interface — the quantum exposure is backend TLS and root-key provisioning). Model: classical DTLS 1.3 ≈ 1,374 B; ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-44 ≈ 13,146 B in 13 IPv6 datagrams and 171 802.15.4 frames; EDHOC with credentials by reference ≈ 216 B classical, ≈ 7,141 B with the same PQC algorithms.
5. **Certificates and device identity** — each certificate holds the subject key and the issuer's signature (RFC 5280); TLS/DTLS sends leaf + intermediate and omits the root (RFC 8446 §4.4.2). Model chain bytes sent: ECDSA 856 B, RSA-2048 1,624 B, FN-DSA-512 3,726 B, LMS 5,744 B, ML-DSA-44 8,064 B, ML-DSA-65 11,122 B, ML-DSA-87 15,038 B. Mitigations: RFC 8879 compression (only the structured bytes compress), C509 (draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert), RFC 7250 raw public keys, PSK resumption, Merkle Tree Certificates (draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs: 32-byte hashes per tree level; needs current trusted tree heads at the relying party). Identity: IEEE 802.1AR IDevID (NIST SP 1800-36B), FIDO Device Onboard 1.1, EST-coaps (RFC 9148).
6. **Fleet key management and LPWAN** — in the Fleet Key Manager's default fictional smart-meter scenario (2,000,000 meters, 1,000 per cell running in parallel, G3-PLC modelled at 34 kbit/s with 60% usable, ML-KEM-768 at 2,472 B per device = 1,184 B public key + 1,088 B ciphertext + 200 B modelled framing, two head-end HSM operations per device), the illustrative 1,000 ops/s HSM takes about 66.7 minutes against about 16.2 minutes of radio time per cell, so the HSM time is the larger figure; at the illustrative 10,000 ops/s rating the HSM takes about 6.7 minutes and the radio time is larger. This is an incomplete comparison: network time excludes the signature bytes that the HSM count includes, so it does not establish the full rotation time or the actual bottleneck. These are model assumptions, not fleet or vendor measurements. Harvest-now-decrypt-later risk applies to metering data; DLMS/COSEM Suite 0 (symmetric only), Suite 1 (P-256), Suite 2 (P-384); Wi-SUN FAN 1.1 (FSK 50–300 kbit/s, OFDM up to 2.4 Mbit/s), LoRaWAN (51–222 B per uplink in EU868, 1% duty cycle), NB-IoT (Cat-NB1 ≈ 26 kbit/s downlink, 62.5 kbit/s uplink). A PQC signature is a few percent of a firmware update (ML-DSA-87: 2.9% of a 150 KiB image); unicast vs multicast decides whether a cell can be updated.
7. **Hardware support** — secure elements with on-chip PQC (Infineon reports its TEGRION SLC27 is Common Criteria EAL6+ certified with an ML-KEM and ML-DSA library, and that in January 2025 it received the first EAL6+ certificate for a security controller comprising a post-quantum algorithm (ML-KEM); Samsung S3SSE2A, which received an ANSSI Common Criteria certificate in 2025 (its published Security Target Lite lists an optional ML-DSA library among the functions included in the TOE); STMicroelectronics ST54M); ECC-only parts such as Microchip ATECC608B cannot offload PQC; TrustZone-M is isolation on the same core, not a secure element; Infineon says two OPTIGA TPMs (SLB 9672, SLB 9673) use XMSS for firmware updates and its PSoC Control C3 family accelerates post-quantum secure boot in hardware; The TCG PC Client Platform TPM Profile v1.07 (23 March 2026) makes ML-KEM (768 or 1024) and ML-DSA (65 or 87) mandatory for PC-client TPMs (Infineon says its OPTIGA TPM SLB 9678, designed to be fully PQC-ready, will be coming in 2027); PSA Certified / SESIP / EN 17927 assurance.
8. **Hybrid on constrained hardware** — X25519MLKEM768 stays secret if either component is unbroken; the classical half adds 32 bytes each way, so hybrid does not double the cost. Gateway-mediated (Class 0–1) vs native hybrid.
9. **IoT security regulations** — EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847: reporting from 11 September 2026, essential requirements from 11 December 2027; from that date critical products listed in Annex IV, including smartcards or similar devices, including secure elements, must demonstrate conformity through a European cybersecurity certification scheme or, where the conditions of Article 8(1) are not met, through one of the Article 32(3) procedures: EU-type examination, full quality assurance, or a certification scheme at assurance level "substantial" or higher); ETSI EN 303 645; RED Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/30 with EN 18031-1/-2/-3 (cited with restrictions by Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/138); US Cyber Trust Mark (FCC 24-26); UK PSTI Regulations 2023 (SI 2023/1007); NIST IR 8259r1 (April 2026, supersedes NIST IR 8259; mentions quantum-safe approaches as future-proofing) and NIST IR 8259A. None requires a PQC algorithm.

## Workshop Steps

1. **Algorithm Explorer** (`constrained-algorithm`) — choose a device class (0–4), a role (verify, sign, key establishment) and a stack- or speed-optimised build; each algorithm's peak RAM is its Cortex-M4 benchmark stack plus the keys/ciphertext/signature it holds, with cycles, code size and the benchmark source. The summary of what fits is generated from the same model.
2. **Firmware Signing** (`firmware-signing`) — hash a firmware image, build a SUIT-style manifest and sign it for real in the browser's SoftHSM with ML-DSA-44/65/87 or LMS (HSS L=1, H10/W4, with the token's remaining-signature counter); a one-bit-tampered manifest is shown to fail. XMSS, FN-DSA-512 and ECDSA are size-only and labelled. Shows the COSE_Sign1 layout (COSE alg −46 HSS-LMS, −48/−49/−50 ML-DSA), CNSA 2.0 status, update overhead on the device's link, and a verification-cost ranking. Known-answer tests: NIST ACVP ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-87 sigVer, and RFC 8554 Appendix F Test Cases 1–2 through the same CKM_HSS verifier (with a tampered-signature negative check).
3. **Constrained Handshake** (`constrained-handshake`) — DTLS 1.3 vs EDHOC message sizes for a chosen KEM (X25519, ML-KEM-512/768, X25519MLKEM768) and signature (ECDSA, ML-DSA-44/65, FN-DSA-512), with IPv6 datagrams and 802.15.4 frame counts; a BLE Mesh / Matter provisioning view counts PB-ADV segments for PQC keys and sizes the DAC + PAI chain.
4. **Certificate Chain** (`cert-chain`) — pick root, intermediate and leaf algorithms; certificates carry the issuer's signature; the root is stored, not sent; delivery modes: full chain, RFC 8879 compression, C509, raw public key, Merkle Tree Certificate (adjustable tree depth), PSK resumption — each with its caveat — against a device RAM budget.
5. **Fleet Key Manager** (`fleet-key-manager`) — fleet type (smart meters, asset trackers, building sensors), fleet size, devices per cell, link (NB-IoT, G3-PLC, Wi-SUN, LTE-M, LoRaWAN), today's key establishment (DLMS Suite 0/1/2), ML-KEM parameter set, rotation frequency and HSM rating; outputs per-cell network time, HSM time, the bottleneck, share of the rotation period and yearly traffic. Known-answer tests: NIST ACVP ML-KEM-768 decapsulation, NIST CAVP AES-256-GCM decryption, and an ECDH P-256 round-trip for the classical baseline.
6. **LPWAN Airtime** (`lpwan-airtime`) — deliver a signed firmware image over Wi-SUN FAN 1.1 (FSK or OFDM, with mesh hops), NB-IoT or LoRaWAN (frame-by-frame time on air and a 1% duty cycle), unicast or multicast, and compare the result with the same update signed with ECDSA.

has no public-key exchange on the air (AES-128 root keys and session keys), so its radio link is not a Shor target. The exposure is the backend: join server and network server TLS, and how root keys were provisioned.
Rotating keys on millions of devices is a scheduling problem. Devices sit in thousands of cells or collectors that work in parallel, but every key update passes through the same head-end HSM. In the step 5 default —
None over the air: AES-128 root keys (AppKey/NwkKey) and AES-CMAC/CTR session keys
No public-key key establishment over the air: LoRaWAN 1.1 derives session keys from AES-128 root keys at join. Rotation means re-join; a KEM would need several frames per exchange.
New keys travel wrapped under a key-encryption key. There is no public-key exchange for Shor’s algorithm to break; the exposure is how the KEK was provisioned.
Wraps the global keys when they are replaced (AES key wrap). Never sent in clear; its provisioning is the root of a Suite 0 system.
Suite 1/2 only: ECDSA keys for signing and ECDH keys for key agreement, bound to certificates — the part a PQC migration replaces.
PQC for constrained devices — algorithm fit by device class, firmware signing, constrained handshakes, certificate size, fleet keys and LPWAN airtime.
A device shipped today may still be in the field when a quantum computer can forge its update signatures. Whether it can verify a PQC signature, fit a PQC handshake in its radio frames and rotate keys across a fleet is decided now, in hardware and protocol choices that cannot be patched in later.
This advanced Applications module (LM-074, 90 minutes) covers post-quantum cryptography for constrained IoT and embedded devices. It was split on 2026-10-01 from the former IoT/OT and Energy & Utilities modules: industrial control systems (SCADA, PLCs, IEC 62443 zones and conduits, sector deep dives) moved to LM-075 _OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC_; vehicle networks to _Automotive PQC_; boot-time verification to _Secure Boot PQC_. Smart-meter key management and RF-mesh airtime moved in from Energy & Utilities and were generalised to device fleets and LPWAN.
RFC 7250 raw public key: no chain at all. The key has to be bound to its owner out of band (RFC 7250 names DANE, pre-configured keys, and keys provisioned in firmware and updated by software updates), and the status of that binding has to be checked. This workshop assumes the simplest binding, a key pinned at provisioning: then there is no CA or revocation service, and changing the key means updating the device. Other bindings change those limits; they are not limits of the protocol itself.

An IEEE 802.15.4 frame is 127 bytes with about 80 bytes of payload once link security is on. Lifetimes, radio cost, energy. Ascon (NIST SP 800-232, final August 2025) for lightweight symmetric crypto. Industrial IoT in a plant: NIST SP 800-82r3 §5.4.2 routes the IIoT platform tier through the industrial DMZ border firewall (level 3.5 of the plant network); a device that connects straight to the cloud skips that boundary (see `ot-pqc`, section `attack-surface`). 2. Algorithm selection: verify vs sign — devices mostly verify. Stack RAM on Cortex-M4 (pqm4): ML-KEM-768 decapsulation 2,844 B in the stack-optimised build vs 6,452 B speed-optimised; ML-DSA-44 verify 2,712 B / sign 5,080 B (stack build), verify 8,912 B in the speed build; FN-DSA-512 verify 2,976 B but sign 41,952 B with ~104 KB of code; LMS H10/W4 verify 1,044 B (reference code); FrodoKEM-640 decapsulation ~72 KB. FIPS 206 is not yet published; FN-DSA-512 signatures are 666 B in Falcon v1.2's padded format. 3. Firmware and update signing (SUIT, COSE) — LMS/HSS (60 B key, 2,512 B signature as HSS L=1), XMSS (68 B / 2,500 B), ML-DSA (stateless). Stateful counters must never roll back. Verification cost on Cortex-M4, fastest build of each: FN-DSA-512 0.40 M < ECDSA P-256 0.98 M < ML-DSA-44 1.42 M < ML-DSA-65 2.42 M < LMS 2.66 M < ML-DSA-87 4.19 M < XMSS 13.07 M cycles — LMS is not the fastest verifier. LM-075.curious:
# OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Power grids, pipelines, water plants, railways, factories and big buildings are run by industrial computers — controllers that open breakers, move valves and set temperatures. This module is about keeping those systems trustworthy once quantum computers can break today's public-key cryptography.

## Why It Matters

In these systems the scariest quantum attack is not reading old messages. It is forgery: a quantum computer could fake the digital signatures that tell a controller "this software update really came from the manufacturer" or "this command really came from the control room". Controllers stay in service for 20 years or more, so the keys they trust have to be replaced long before that becomes possible.

## How Attackers Get In

There are three ways into these systems. Most attacks start in the company's office network and work their way down into the plant, so protecting the office side protects the plant too. Others come in through remote connections, such as vendor support links and internet-connected sensors, which should all pass through one guarded entry point. The last way is physical: someone on site or nearby, where most of the equipment checks nothing at all about who is sending it commands.

## The Key Takeaway

The fastest messages — like the 3-millisecond trip signals inside a substation — are already protected with symmetric codes that quantum computers don't break, so they stay as they are. The work is in the slower parts around them: the keys that sign firmware and configurations, the certificates that identify devices, and the remote-access links into the plant.

## What's Happening

IEC 62443 is a paid standard, so we could not read it to check whether it addresses post-quantum cryptography, and in the documents we hold we found no quantum-safe option for protocols like OPC UA, BACnet/SC and DNP3. Post-quantum work on the IEC 62351 power-grid security standards has started, but further refinements are needed. Operators are starting with an inventory, moving their signing keys to new schemes such as LMS and ML-DSA, and protecting remote access with hybrid key exchange while the standards catch up.

The computers that run power grids, water plants, railways and factories stay in service for decades. They only accept software updates and commands that carry a valid digital signature — a kind of tamper-proof seal from the manufacturer or the control room.
A powerful future quantum computer could fake those seals. That is why operators are already moving the keys that sign updates and commands to new quantum-safe schemes, and protecting the remote connections into their plants, while leaving the ultra-fast safety signals — which already use quantum-safe codes — exactly as they are.
Attackers usually get in through the company's office network, through remote connections such as vendor links and internet-connected sensors, or by being on site, where most plant equipment accepts commands from anyone. Each route needs its own fix.

OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — In Simple Terms
Power grids, pipelines, water plants, railways, factories and big buildings are run by industrial computers — controllers that open breakers, move valves and set temperatures. This module is about keeping those systems trustworthy once quantum computers can break today's public-key cryptography.
In these systems the scariest quantum attack is not reading old messages. It is forgery: a quantum computer could fake the digital signatures that tell a controller "this software update really came from the manufacturer" or "this command really came from the control room". Controllers stay in service for 20 years or more, so the keys they trust have to be replaced long before that becomes possible.
There are three ways into these systems. Most attacks start in the company's office network and work their way down into the plant, so protecting the office side protects the plant too. Others come in through remote connections, such as vendor support links and internet-connected sensors, which should all pass through one guarded entry point. The last way is physical: someone on site or nearby, where most of the equipment checks nothing at all about who is sending it commands.

OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — Module Summary
Firmware and project signing (`firmware-project-signing`): vendor firmware and engineering-workstation project signing; NERC CIP-010-4 R1.6 (software source and integrity verification — not CIP-007); IEC 62443-4-1 and 4-2 CR 3.4; CNSA 2.0 lists LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for software/firmware signing and ML-DSA-87 as its signature parameter set; NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2: new national security system acquisitions from 1 January 2027, equipment that cannot support CNSA 2.0 phased out by 31 December 2030 (exceptions possible), CNSA 2.0 algorithms mandated by 31 December 2031 unless otherwise noted. LMS is stateful (counter must never repeat; SP 800-208 requires hardware modules that prevent state cloning); ML-DSA is stateless.
`iot-pqc` — constrained devices, smart-meter fleets, LPWAN
`stateful-signatures` — LMS / XMSS state management
`secure-boot-pqc` — bootloader verification of PQC firmware signatures
`hsm-pqc` — where signing keys and LMS state live
`migration-program` — programme governance for critical infrastructure

qa.answer: The roadmap has six phases: inventory, boundary, signing roots, supervisory, site rollout and legacy. With the defaults (energy, medium programme, 50 sites, US, CRQC planning year 2033) it takes 60 months, ends in 2030 and finishes signing roots in 2027. At 400 sites the site rollout alone runs 192 months and the programme ends in 2043, while signing roots still finish in 2027, which is why they are scheduled early. These are model estimates and no costs are shown.
qa.question: In the Sector Roadmap (sector-migration-roadmap), how long does a SCADA migration programme take with the default settings, and what changes at 400 sites?

qa.answer: Not entirely. A one-way data diode has no key exchange to break, but the files and updates it passes still need PQC signature checks. In OT the main quantum threat is forgery of the RSA or ECDSA signatures controllers use to accept firmware and project downloads, and forgery needs no harvesting. Overlays and inline appliances protect the wire, not the device's own firmware trust, so a controller that still verifies firmware with an RSA key eventually needs a firmware update or replacement.
qa.question: An isolated Level 1 control network receives updates only through a data diode and cannot be patched remotely. Does that make it safe from quantum attack?

qa.answer: IEC 62443 groups assets with the same security needs into zones and treats every communication path between zones as a conduit with its own controls. Each zone carries a target (SL-T), capability (SL-C) and achieved (SL-A) security level from SL 1 to SL 4. SR 4.3 (IEC 62443-3-3) and CR 4.3 (IEC 62443-4-2), both titled 'Use of cryptography' and applying from SL 1, ask for cryptography that follows commonly accepted (SR 4.3) or internationally recognized and proven (CR 4.3) security practice; neither names an algorithm or PQC, so PQC enters through risk assessment and procurement rather than through the standard's text.
qa.question: How do IEC 62443 zones, conduits and security levels frame a PQC migration, and what does the standard say about quantum-safe cryptography?

qa.answer: IEC 61869-9 defines Sampled Value rates including 4,000, 4,800 and 14,400 samples per second, a frame every 250, 208 and 69 µs. A 1,776-byte LMS or 4,627-byte ML-DSA-87 signature on every frame is neither needed nor practical, because the symmetric MAC already protecting the stream is quantum-safe. The PQC work goes into key distribution, firmware and the boundary; substation time sync is secured by IEEE 1588-2019 Annex P, not NTS.
qa.question: Why should PQC authentication not be inserted into the real-time path of IEC 61850 Sampled Values from a merging unit?

qa.answer: A protection relay or PLC typically lasts 15–25 years, rail signalling 25–40 and substation primary plant 30–50, so a device installed today may still run in the 2040s. Forgery of the signatures these devices trust needs no harvesting and starts the day a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, so their signing roots have to be migrated first. Changing crypto in a safety-related device can mean re-testing a protection scheme, re-running a SIL assessment or re-opening a rail safety case, far more than a software update.
qa.question: How do 20–50-year OT asset lifecycles affect PQC decisions made today?

qa.answer: ML-KEM is defined in FIPS 203 and ML-DSA in FIPS 204. In OT, ML-KEM goes into the key exchange of TLS, VPN and SSH at the boundary, for example hybrid ML-KEM in front of jump hosts, or a hybrid ML-KEM group added to BACnet/SC, which already uses TLS 1.3. ML-DSA, alongside LMS/HSS, replaces RSA and ECDSA for firmware and project signing, where an ML-DSA-87 signature is 4,627 B. OPC UA's RSA and ECC SecurityPolicies have no published PQC policy yet.
qa.question: Which NIST FIPS standards define ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and where does each land in an OT network?

qa.answer: IEC 61850-5 puts GOOSE trip messages in transfer-time class TT6, 3 ms or less (Torres et al., ICREPQ 2024, Table I). The module's Substation Planner, not the standard, assigns budgets by substation type: it plans on TT6 for transmission, sub-transmission and generation, and on a 10 ms budget for distribution as a planning assumption (Torres Table I gives 10 ms to class TT5, which covers releases and status changes, not trips).
qa.question: Which transfer-time class does IEC 61850-5 set for GOOSE trip messages?

qa.answer: CIP-012-2, effective 1 July 2026, requires a documented plan to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of Real-time Assessment and Real-time monitoring data between Control Centers; CIP-012-2 adds availability. It is technology-neutral: encryption is one listed way to meet it, not a mandate. Where encryption is used, its key exchange is a harvest-now-decrypt-later target.
qa.question: What does NERC CIP-012-2 require for communications between Control Centers, and does it mandate encryption?

qa.answer: IEC 62351-6 (2020) protects GOOSE and Sampled Values with profiles that include HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC, symmetric MACs that a quantum computer does not break. Their group keys come from a key distribution centre over GDOI (IEC 62351-9, RFC 8052), not from RSA certificates. The quantum exposure is therefore in key management: the GDOI registration channel and the PKI behind it, which are open to both forgery and harvest-now-decrypt-later.
qa.question: How does IEC 62351-6 protect GOOSE and Sampled Values, and where is their quantum exposure?

qa.answer: DNP3 SAv5 uses an HMAC challenge-response, wraps session keys with AES key wrap, and keeps update keys pre-shared by default; where they are changed remotely, the default method is symmetric (AES-256 key wrap plus HMAC-SHA-256), so all three are quantum-safe. Only the optional RSA/DSA update-key change methods are exposed. IEEE moved 1815-2012 to inactive status in 2023, the P1815 revision runs to 2027, and "SAv6" is unpublished. The Protocol Analyzer (protocol-security-analyzer) checks HMAC-SHA-256 against a NIST ACVP vector and AES-256 key wrap against RFC 3394 §4.6.
qa.question: Which part of DNP3 Secure Authentication v5 is actually exposed to a quantum computer?

qa.answer: For NSS, FAQ version 2.2 requires compliant new acquisitions from 1 January 2027, equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 to be phased out by 31 December 2030 unless excepted, and CNSA 2.0 algorithms by 31 December 2031 unless otherwise noted. Earlier category guidance places exclusive CNSA 2.0 use for software and firmware signing and traditional networking at 2030. CNSA 2.0 does not generally mandate hybrid constructions, and AES-256 remains part of the suite. Firmware signing uses ML-DSA-87 or the stateful LMS/XMSS schemes specified by NIST SP 800-208.
qa.question: What dates does CNSA 2.0 set for equipment an OT supplier delivers to US national security systems, and does it mandate hybrid?

qa.answer: No. In OT the bigger risk is authenticity: a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could forge the RSA or ECDSA signatures that controllers use to accept firmware, project downloads, certificates and commands. Forgery needs no harvesting, it starts the day such a machine exists, and the devices that trust the old keys stay in service for decades. Harvest-now-decrypt-later still matters at remote-access and inter-site boundaries, where sessions carry credentials, topology and settings.
qa.question: For SCADA systems that stay in service for decades, is harvest-now-decrypt-later the main quantum risk?

qa.answer: Each zone has three settings: firmware and project signing, command authentication and traffic protection. Forgery uses the stronger of the two authentication settings, harvest-now-decrypt-later is scored separately, and each zone is ranked by the larger. With the defaults, IIoT & cloud connectors, Remote & vendor access and the Industrial DMZ (L3.5) rank first at 100, driven by HNDL; Basic control and the SIS (L1) come next at 90, driven by firmware and project-signing forgery, followed by Process / field devices 80, Enterprise 70, Supervisory control 64 and Site operations 50. L1 and L0 commands default to unauthenticated, which the planner flags as a present-day gap rather than a quantum risk. An HNDL-only view would have put Level 0–1 last.
qa.question: How does the Zone & Conduit Planner rank Purdue zones by default, and why does Level 1 outrank the enterprise zone?

qa.answer: The PI PROFINET Security Whitepaper (V1.05, 2019, a release candidate for advisory board review) defines three classes. Class 1 adds robustness, including integrity and authenticity of the GSD device-description files. Class 2 protects cyclic traffic against unauthorized modification and ensures the integrity and authenticity of acyclic services. Class 3 adds confidentiality for all services and is meant for cases where reading cyclic IO data would reveal company secrets. The whitepaper states that most applications can operate on classes 1 and 2.
qa.question: What do PROFINET security classes 1, 2 and 3 add, and which class do most plants need?

qa.answer: SD Pipeline-2021-02G is in force from 3 May 2026 to 2 May 2027 and supersedes 02F with no substantive change. Among its measures, OT services may not traverse the IT system unless the OT content is encrypted in transit, and access to Critical Cyber Systems needs multi-factor authentication or controls that give equivalent risk mitigation. It names no cryptographic algorithm and does not mention quantum computing, so post-quantum migration is the operator's choice inside a technology-neutral directive.
qa.question: What does TSA Security Directive Pipeline-2021-02G require for pipeline OT, and does it name an algorithm or mention post-quantum cryptography?

qa.answer: SUBSET-137 (v1.0.0, 2015) has the Key Management Centre and KMAC entities talk over mutually authenticated TLS with X.509 v3 certificates from the KMS's own PKI. Every client and server must support TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and PKI client and CA public keys are 3072 bits. The keys it distributes, KMACs, are 24-byte symmetric authentication keys defined in SUBSET-114. The ECDHE key exchange and RSA authentication are breakable by a quantum computer; the symmetric KMACs are not, but they travel inside that TLS channel. The FFFIS allows other cipher suites only if ENISA recommends them for 'Future System Use', a hook for a later post-quantum suite.
qa.question: What cryptography does UNISIG SUBSET-137 fix for ERTMS/ETCS online key management, and which parts are quantum-vulnerable?

qa.answer: IT-to-OT lateral movement starts on the business network (L4/5), crosses the industrial DMZ (L3.5) and spreads into site operations (L3) and supervisory control (L2). Enterprise identity, PKI and Active Directory trust vouch for every hop, so migrating the IT side to PQC is part of protecting OT; NIST SP 800-82r3 also asks for separate OT accounts and a monitored DMZ. Remote access and connected devices (vendor VPNs, jump hosts, IIoT platforms) should end at L3.5; hybrid ML-KEM on those links is the first PQC step, after phishing-resistant MFA and private links. Physical or local access reaches L1/L0 directly, where most installed field protocols still trust anyone with access (CISA, 2026); that is a present-day gap fixed with classical authentication or an authenticating gateway, and PQC goes into firmware signing and key distribution.
qa.question: What are the three paths into an OT network, and what fixes each one?

qa.answer: In NIST SP 800-82r3's reference architecture (§5.4.2), communication from the IIoT platform tier is routed through the DMZ border firewall, so IIoT gateways and cloud connectors belong on their own L3.5 segment; a direct cloud link from L1 or L2 is a DMZ bypass that changes the boundaries the zone model relies on (§5.3.7). In the December 2015 Ukraine attack (CISA IR-ALERT-H-16-056-01), spear phishing put BlackEnergy on the companies' networks, probably to obtain legitimate credentials (IT-to-OT); breakers were then operated remotely through VPN connections and ICS client software (remote access); and serial-to-Ethernet devices at substations were rendered inoperable by corrupted firmware (field level).
qa.question: Where should IIoT platforms connect in a Purdue-based plant, and how did the 2015 Ukraine grid attack use the three paths?

qa.answer: WAN / control-centre links come first (91), then the station bus (88) and engineering access (87), with IED firmware signing at 70. The process bus scores only 34 because GOOSE and SV keep their symmetric MAC and only the GDOI key channel needs work, even though it is the highest-complexity zone; PTP time sync scores 21. Zones are scored by forgery and HNDL exposure weighted by NERC CIP impact, and complexity changes effort only (model estimate).
qa.question: In the Substation Planner (substation-migration-planner), which zones of a high-impact transmission substation (80 IEDs, utility fibre, full IEC 62351) should be migrated first?

qa.answer: The gas pipeline starts at 46 (high): its DNP3 SAv5 commands are symmetric, so its exposure is firmware signing, and with LMS / ML-DSA signed firmware it falls to 9 (low). The hydro dam spillway scores 90 (critical) because no independent safety layer bounds the outcome. The scorer weighs consequence severity, people affected, command and firmware authentication, an independent safety layer (IEC 61511) and asset life; it is a model estimate, not a SIL determination.
qa.question: In the Safety & Consequence Scorer (safety-consequence-scorer), what happens to the gas pipeline compressor station score when controller firmware is PQC-signed, and why does the hydro dam spillway stay critical?

qa.answer: An LMS H10 tree holds 1,024 signatures, so used for project signing at 5,000 signatures a year it is exhausted after 0.2 years, and keeping a stateful counter consistent across engineering workstations is hard. ML-DSA-87 is stateless (no counter, no exhaustion) at the cost of a 4,627-byte signature, so the usual split is LMS or HSS in a vendor HSM for rare firmware releases and ML-DSA for high-volume project signing. NERC CIP-010-4 R1.6 requires verifying the software source and integrity before a baseline change on high and medium impact systems, and CIP-013-2 is the contractual lever for asking vendors for PQC firmware signing.
qa.question: A utility wants PQC signatures for vendor firmware and for PLC project downloads. What does the Firmware & Project Signing Lab (firmware-project-signing-lab) show about LMS versus ML-DSA, and which NERC CIP requirements apply?

qa.answer: There are four options, from least to most disruptive: a firmware update where the device has the CPU, memory and vendor support for PQC; a VPN overlay of hybrid ML-KEM tunnels between sites or zones; a bump-in-the-wire inline appliance that adds authentication and encryption in front of the device or serial link; and replacement with devices whose firmware signing and certificates are PQC-ready, written into the procurement contract. Overlays and appliances protect the wire, not the device's own firmware trust. A controller that still verifies firmware with an RSA key therefore needs a firmware update or replacement eventually.
qa.question: A legacy PLC cannot take new firmware. What brownfield retrofit options does the module give, and what does each protect?

qa.answer: Power-up runs in two phases. In phase 1 the IO controller or supervisor and the IO device use public keys and certificates (a manufacturer certificate plus the operator's own) to authenticate each other and negotiate symmetric keys; that is the quantum-vulnerable part, along with signed GSD files, and where PQC certificates, a KEM and ML-DSA or LMS signatures belong. In phase 2 every cyclic frame carries a MAC computed with those symmetric keys and a sequence counter (HMAC-SHA256 performed best in testing; no final choice was made), so the sub-millisecond real-time path needs no PQC change. The Protocol Security Analyzer step marks the cyclic MAC layer accordingly.
qa.question: In a PROFINET class 2 or 3 installation, which parts need post-quantum cryptography and which can stay as they are?

qa.answer: The directive allows OT traffic to cross IT only if it is encrypted in transit, so that tunnel is a required control. It does not say which algorithms protect it. Recorded tunnel traffic is exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later if the key exchange is classical, so the tunnel is a natural early place for a hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, as in the module's VPN overlay retrofit option. The directive neither requires nor forbids this, and it is renewed annually, so the operator should track each renewal for changes.
qa.question: A US pipeline operator carries SCADA traffic across its corporate IT network in an encrypted tunnel to meet SD Pipeline-2021-02G. Where does post-quantum migration fit?

qa.answer: The attack path it models is a forged KMC identity: once a quantum computer breaks the RSA and ECDH that authenticate the Key Management Centre, an attacker can distribute keys to ETCS entities. The consequence chain is forged key-management messages reaching trackside equipment, authenticated movement authorities that can no longer be trusted, lines falling back to degraded operation under safety rules, and network-wide disruption with a safety-case reassessment. The scenario carries severity 'catastrophic' and a 30-year lifecycle, so the harm is to safe operation, not to secrecy.
qa.question: Why does the Safety Consequence Scorer treat ETCS key management as a forgery risk with a catastrophic ceiling rather than a data-confidentiality problem?

LM-075.summary:
# OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — Module Summary

## Overview

Advanced module (90 min, 10 learn sections, 6 workshop steps) on post-quantum cryptography for operational technology (OT) in five sectors: energy, water and wastewater, rail and transit, manufacturing and process, and building automation. OT ranks safety first, then availability, integrity and confidentiality. The main quantum threat in OT is authenticity — a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) could forge the RSA/ECDSA signatures that controllers use to accept firmware, project downloads, certificates and commands — rather than harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL), which matters mostly at remote-access, IIoT and inter-site boundaries. OT is reached along three paths: IT-to-OT lateral movement, remote access and connected devices ending at L3.5, and physical or local access at L1/L0. Assets can stay in service for decades (NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3: the lifespan of an OT system can exceed 20 years), and changing crypto in a safety-related device can mean re-testing a protection scheme, a SIL assessment or a rail safety case. Smart meters, AMI and RF mesh are covered in the IoT module (`iot-pqc`).

## Learn sections

- **Why OT is different** (`why-ot`): safety > availability > integrity > confidentiality; forgery vs HNDL; long lifecycles (NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3: the lifespan of an OT system can exceed 20 years; the Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework: OT systems (SCADA, PLCs, RTUs) often have 15–25 year lifecycles). The module's typical lives are its own illustrative figures, not values from a standard: SCADA/HMI servers 7–15 years, relays, PLCs and safety instrumented systems 15–25, RTUs 15–20, rail signalling 25–40, substation primary plant 30–50; recertification cost.
- **Purdue, zones and conduits** (`architecture`): Purdue levels L0–L5 grouped into IEC 62443 zones and conduits; SL-T (target), SL-C (capability), SL-A (achieved). CR 4.3 (IEC 62443-4-2), 'Use of cryptography', is quoted by Siemens (Fries, ITU-T X.509 Day, September 2025) as requiring cryptographic security mechanisms according to internationally recognized and proven security practices and recommendations; that wording names no algorithm or PQC. IEC 62443-3-3 (SR 4.3) is not among the documents the module holds, so its wording is not described.
- **OT attack surface: three paths in** (`attack-surface`): (A) IT-to-OT lateral movement, L4/5 → L3.5 → L3 → L2: enterprise identity, PKI and Active Directory trust vouch for every hop, so migrating the IT side is part of protecting OT (CISA PQC considerations for OT; NIST SP 800-82r3 asks for separate OT accounts and a monitored DMZ; CISA/FBI/EPA/DOE Primary Mitigations 2025; CISA AA21-131A, where ransomware on a pipeline operator's IT network led it to disconnect OT systems). (B) Remote access and connected devices ending at L3.5: vendor VPNs, jump hosts and IIoT platforms; NIST SP 800-82r3 §5.4.2 routes the IIoT platform tier through the DMZ border firewall, and a direct cloud link from L1–L2 is a DMZ bypass (§5.3.7); hybrid ML-KEM on the link is the first PQC step. (C) Physical or local access at L1/L0 (sometimes called close access): CISA concludes that secure versions of industrial protocols remain underutilized in OT environments, and its 2026 study "Barriers to Secure OT Communication" found many systems built today still trust anyone with access, and SP 800-82r3 §5.3.6 says many Level 0 devices cannot be authenticated; that is a present-day gap fixed with classical authentication or a gateway, and PQC goes into firmware signing and key distribution. Worked example: Ukraine, December 2015 (CISA IR-ALERT-H-16-056-01), which used all three paths.
- **OT protocol native security** (`ot-protocols`): IEC 62351-6 (2020) protects GOOSE and Sampled Values with profiles that include HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC; group keys come from a GDOI key distribution centre (IEC 62351-9, RFC 8052), not RSA certificates. MMS uses IEC 62351-3 TLS; IEC 62351-3:2023 adds a TLS 1.3 profile and now lists the mandatory TLS 1.2 cipher suites itself; it profiles conventional TLS cipher suites and does not specify PQC key-exchange or signature algorithms. An industry presentation (Siemens, ITU-T X.509 Day, September 2025) reports that the PQC transition for IEC 62351 has started in IEC TC57, with further refinements needed, and cites IEC 62351-90-4 for guidance on migrating from one cryptographic algorithm to another. DNP3 SAv5: HMAC challenge-response, AES key wrap of session keys, and pre-shared update keys by default; where they are changed remotely, the 2011 IEEE 1815 working draft makes the symmetric method (AES-256 key wrap plus HMAC-SHA-256) the default and the asymmetric methods, which use RSA and DSA, optional. IEEE SA lists IEEE 1815-2012 as an Inactive-Reserved standard (inactivated 30 March 2023) and lists a P1815 project that would supersede it; the documents the module holds describe no revision named "SAv6". IEC 60870-5-104 uses IEC 62351-3 TLS and IEC 62351-5 authentication. OPC UA SecurityPolicies use RSA or ECC. CIP Security (EtherNet/IP) uses TLS/DTLS with certificates or PSKs across five profiles. PROFINET Security Classes 1–3. Modbus/TCP Security wraps Modbus in mutual TLS; plain Modbus has none. BACnet/SC uses TLS 1.3 with elliptic-curve crypto only. DLMS/COSEM suites 0/1/2 use AES-GCM, ECDH/ECDSA P-256 or P-384 — no RSA. IEC 62351 part scopes: Part 3 TLS, Part 4 MMS, Part 5 IEC 60870-5 and DNP3, Part 6 IEC 61850, Part 8 RBAC, Part 9 key management, Part 14 security event logging (syslog/TLS, so quantum-exposed).
- **Safety-critical timing** (`safety-timing`): IEC 61850-5 puts GOOSE trip messages in transfer-time class TT6 (3 ms or less). IEC 61869-9 SV rates include 4,000, 4,800 and 14,400 samples/s (250, 208 and 69 µs apart). PQC stays out of the trip path; the symmetric MAC is already quantum-safe. PTP security is IEEE 1588-2019 Annex P (not NTS). IEC 61511 Ed.2 clause 8.2.4 requires a security risk assessment that includes the SIS (per Derbyshire; the standard text is not held).
- **Firmware and project signing** (`firmware-project-signing`): vendor firmware and engineering-workstation project signing; NERC CIP-010-4 R1.6 (software source and integrity verification — not CIP-007); IEC 62443-4-1 and 4-2 CR 3.4; CNSA 2.0 lists LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for software/firmware signing and ML-DSA-87 as its signature parameter set; NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2: new national security system acquisitions from 1 January 2027, equipment that cannot support CNSA 2.0 phased out by 31 December 2030 (exceptions possible), CNSA 2.0 algorithms mandated by 31 December 2031 unless otherwise noted. LMS is stateful (counter must never repeat; SP 800-208 requires hardware modules that prevent state cloning); ML-DSA is stateless.
- **Remote access and boundaries** (`remote-access`): industrial DMZ, jump hosts, IIoT platforms on their own segment routed through the DMZ, data diodes (no key exchange to break, but passed files still need signature checks), NERC CIP-005-7 R2 (Interactive Remote Access through an intermediate system with encryption and MFA) and R3 (vendor remote access for EACMS and PACS). For IPsec/IKEv2 VPNs: RFC 8784 (Standards Track) stirs an additional shared secret into the IKEv2 key derivation, so that, where the two ends share a long secret key, the exchange is quantum secure without waiting for new key-exchange algorithms; RFC 9370 lets IKEv2 add a post-quantum key exchange alongside the classical (EC)DH one; as of 21 August 2026 (version 12), post-quantum signature authentication for IKEv2 was specified in an IETF Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth.
- **Sector deep dives** (`sectors`): Energy (substations; NERC CIP-012-2 effective 2026-07-01 adds availability and is technology-neutral; TSA SD Pipeline-2021-02G for TSA-designated pipelines; for IEEE 2030.5 distributed energy resources the SunSpec/Sandia workgroup recommends TLS 1.3 for all DER communications (SAND2022-1118), and a 2025 conference abstract reports a hybrid quantum-safe prototype of OCPP for EV charging that names no algorithm). Water (EPA's 2023 sanitary-survey cybersecurity move was withdrawn the same year; AWIA §2013 risk assessments and voluntary EPA/AWWA guidance remain). Rail (UNISIG SUBSET-137 KMC names RSA and ECDH; FRMCS / ETSI TS 103 764 names no algorithm — its security is layered, with a TLS-backed, mutually authenticated Local Binding between applications and the On-Board FRMCS or Trackside Gateway, and the transport and service layers defer to 3GPP security specifications; 49 CFR Part 236 Subpart I names no algorithm). Manufacturing and process (PLC/DCS, OPC UA, CIP Security, PROFINET, IEC 61511 SIS). Building automation (BACnet/SC).
- **Brownfield retrofit** (`retrofit`): firmware update, VPN overlay, bump-in-the-wire / inline appliance, replacement. Overlays protect the wire, not the device's own firmware trust.
- **Key regulations** (`regulations`): IEC 62443; NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 (no mention of quantum computing); CISA PQC considerations for OT; NIS2 Art. 21(2)(h) and the EU coordinated PQC roadmap (start by end of 2026, high-risk use cases by end of 2030, as much as feasible by 2035); NERC CIP-002, CIP-005-7, CIP-010-4, CIP-012-2, CIP-013-2, CIP-015-1; TSA SD Pipeline-2021-02G (3 May 2026 – 2 May 2027; operational-technology services may not traverse the IT system unless their content is encrypted while in transit); CNSA 2.0's earlier category preferences (firmware signing 2025, networking equipment 2026) plus the current FAQ version 2.2 milestones (new NSS acquisitions from 2027, unsupported equipment and services phased out by the end of 2030, CNSA 2.0 algorithms mandated by the end of 2031 unless otherwise noted). The separate 2035 date is the broader NSM-10 quantum-risk objective, not the current CNSA 2.0 algorithm mandate. CNSA 2.0 does not generally require hybrids, and AES-256 has no stated sunset.

## Workshop steps

1. **Protocol Analyzer** (`protocol-security-analyzer`): 14 OT protocols (IEC 61850 GOOSE, SV and MMS; DNP3 SAv5; IEC 60870-5-104; ICCP/TASE.2; OPC UA; CIP Security; PROFINET Security Classes; Modbus/TCP Security; BACnet/SC; DLMS/COSEM; IEEE 2030.5; IEEE 1588 PTP), each split into crypto layers tagged forgery, HNDL, both, symmetric (quantum-safe) or no crypto, with a sector filter and illustrative component or directional TLS group-share sizes. A KAT panel checks HMAC-SHA-256 against a NIST ACVP HMAC-SHA2-256 sample (FIPS 198-1) and AES-256 key wrap against RFC 3394 §4.6.
2. **Zone & Conduit Planner** (`zone-conduit-planner`): nine IEC 62443 zones on the Purdue model, including IIoT & cloud connectors as a separate L3.5 segment. Each zone has three settings: firmware and project signing, command authentication, and traffic protection. Forgery uses the stronger of the two authentication settings, HNDL is scored separately, and the zone is ranked by the larger; an unauthenticated setting is flagged as a present-day gap, not scored as quantum risk. L1, SIS and L0 default to unauthenticated commands with classically signed firmware. Defaults: IIoT & cloud connectors, Remote & vendor access and Industrial DMZ 100 (HNDL), Basic control and SIS 90 (forgery), Process / field devices 80, Enterprise 70, Supervisory control 64, Site operations 50. Ten conduits with PQC actions, each tagged with its attack path (A IT-to-OT, B remote access and connected devices, C physical or local access) and filterable by path; the IIoT-to-site-operations conduit is marked as a DMZ bypass. Model estimate.
3. **Substation Planner** (`substation-migration-planner`): six substation zones (WAN / control-centre links, station bus MMS, engineering access, IED firmware signing, process bus GOOSE/SV, PTP time sync) scored by forgery and HNDL exposure weighted by NERC CIP impact; complexity changes effort only. A high-impact transmission substation on fibre with 80 IEDs ranks WAN 91, station bus 88, engineering 87, IED firmware 70, process bus 34, time sync 21, with a 3 ms (TT6) trip budget. Model estimate.
4. **Safety & Consequence Scorer** (`safety-consequence-scorer`): eight scenarios across five sectors, scored on consequence severity, people affected, command and firmware authentication, independent safety layer (IEC 61511) and asset life. Defaults: hydro spillway 90, rail ETCS 72, chemical SIS 63 (critical); water treatment 59, gas pipeline 46, transmission SCADA 44 (high); hospital building automation 33 (medium); assembly line 14 (low). With PQC firmware signing the gas pipeline drops to 9. Model estimate, not a SIL determination.
5. **Sector Roadmap** (`sector-migration-roadmap`): six phases (inventory, boundary, signing roots, supervisory, site rollout, legacy) driven by sector, programme size, budget pace, jurisdiction, site count and CRQC planning year. Defaults (energy, medium programme, 50 sites, US, 2033): 60 months, ending 2030, signing roots done 2027. At 400 sites the rollout runs 192 months and the programme ends in 2043. No costs are shown. Model estimate.
6. **Firmware & Project Signing Lab** (`firmware-project-signing-lab`): LMS H10–H25 and HSS L=2 (sizes computed from RFC 8554; H20/W8 = 1,776 B signature, 60 B public key), XMSS (size only) and ML-DSA-65 / ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204; ML-DSA-87 = 4,627 B). Shows signatures per HSM, years until the key is exhausted and state-management warnings; an LMS H10 tree used for project signing at 5,000 signatures a year is exhausted after 0.2 years. ML-DSA is checked by NIST ACVP ML-DSA sigVer KATs; LMS and XMSS rows are labelled simulated (no signature computed).

LM-075/s:attack-surface.full:
Zones say what is at stake; they do not say how an attacker gets there. OT is reached along three paths, and each needs a different fix. Step 2 of the workshop tags every conduit with its path.
OT attack surface: three paths in (`attack-surface`): (A) IT-to-OT lateral movement, L4/5 → L3.5 → L3 → L2: enterprise identity, PKI and Active Directory trust vouch for every hop, so migrating the IT side is part of protecting OT (CISA PQC considerations for OT; NIST SP 800-82r3 asks for separate OT accounts and a monitored DMZ; CISA/FBI/EPA/DOE Primary Mitigations 2025; CISA AA21-131A, where ransomware on a pipeline operator's IT network led it to disconnect OT systems). (B) Remote access and connected devices ending at L3.5: vendor VPNs, jump hosts and IIoT platforms; NIST SP 800-82r3 §5.4.2 routes the IIoT platform tier through the DMZ border firewall, and a direct cloud link from L1–L2 is a DMZ bypass (§5.3.7); hybrid ML-KEM on the link is the first PQC step. (C) Physical or local access at L1/L0 (sometimes called close access): CISA concludes that secure versions of industrial protocols remain underutilized in OT environments, and its 2026 study "Barriers to Secure OT Communication" found many systems built today still trust anyone with access, and SP 800-82r3 §5.3.6 says many Level 0 devices cannot be authenticated; that is a present-day gap fixed with classical authentication or a gateway, and PQC goes into firmware signing and key distribution. Worked example: Ukraine, December 2015 (CISA IR-ALERT-H-16-056-01), which used all three paths.

OT protocol native security (`ot-protocols`): IEC 62351-6 (2020) protects GOOSE and Sampled Values with profiles that include HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC; group keys come from a GDOI key distribution centre (IEC 62351-9, RFC 8052), not RSA certificates. MMS uses IEC 62351-3 TLS; IEC 62351-3:2023 adds a TLS 1.3 profile and now lists the mandatory TLS 1.2 cipher suites itself; it profiles conventional TLS cipher suites and does not specify PQC key-exchange or signature algorithms. An industry presentation (Siemens, ITU-T X.509 Day, September 2025) reports that the PQC transition for IEC 62351 has started in IEC TC57, with further refinements needed, and cites IEC 62351-90-4 for guidance on migrating from one cryptographic algorithm to another. DNP3 SAv5: HMAC challenge-response, AES key wrap of session keys, and pre-shared update keys by default; where they are changed remotely, the 2011 IEEE 1815 working draft makes the symmetric method (AES-256 key wrap plus HMAC-SHA-256) the default and the asymmetric methods, which use RSA and DSA, optional. IEEE SA lists IEEE 1815-2012 as an Inactive-Reserved standard (inactivated 30 March 2023) and lists a P1815 project that would supersede it; the documents the module holds describe no revision named "SAv6". IEC 60870-5-104 uses IEC 62351-3 TLS and IEC 62351-5 authentication. OPC UA SecurityPolicies use RSA or ECC. CIP Security (EtherNet/IP) uses TLS/DTLS with certificates or PSKs across five profiles. PROFINET Security Classes 1–3. Modbus/TCP Security wraps Modbus in mutual TLS; plain Modbus has none. BACnet/SC uses TLS 1.3 with elliptic-curve crypto only. DLMS/COSEM suites 0/1/2 use AES-GCM, ECDH/ECDSA P-256 or P-384 — no RSA. IEC 62351 part scopes: Part 3 TLS, Part 4 MMS, Part 5 IEC 60870-5 and DNP3, Part 6 IEC 61850, Part 8 RBAC, Part 9 key management, Part 14 security event logging (syslog/TLS, so quantum-exposed).

Advanced module (90 min, 10 learn sections, 6 workshop steps) on PQC for operational technology across energy, water, rail, manufacturing and building automation. In OT, safety and availability come first, and the main quantum threat is authenticity — forged commands, firmware and project files — rather than harvest-now-decrypt-later, which matters mostly at remote-access, IIoT and inter-site boundaries. OT is reached along three paths: IT-to-OT lateral movement (L4/5 → L3.5 → L3 → L2), remote access and connected devices ending at L3.5, and physical or local access at L1/L0, where most installed field traffic has no authentication at all. Assets can stay in service for decades (NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3: the lifespan of an OT system can exceed 20 years) and crypto changes can trigger safety recertification.
The fastest messages — like the 3-millisecond trip signals inside a substation — are already protected with symmetric codes that quantum computers don't break, so they stay as they are. The work is in the slower parts around them: the keys that sign firmware and configurations, the certificates that identify devices, and the remote-access links into the plant.
IEC 62443 is a paid standard, so we could not read it to check whether it addresses post-quantum cryptography, and in the documents we hold we found no quantum-safe option for protocols like OPC UA, BACnet/SC and DNP3. Post-quantum work on the IEC 62351 power-grid security standards has started, but further refinements are needed. Operators are starting with an inventory, moving their signing keys to new schemes such as LMS and ML-DSA, and protecting remote access with hybrid key exchange while the standards catch up.

Advanced module (90 min, 10 learn sections, 6 workshop steps) on post-quantum cryptography for operational technology (OT) in five sectors: energy, water and wastewater, rail and transit, manufacturing and process, and building automation. OT ranks safety first, then availability, integrity and confidentiality. The main quantum threat in OT is authenticity — a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) could forge the RSA/ECDSA signatures that controllers use to accept firmware, project downloads, certificates and commands — rather than harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL), which matters mostly at remote-access, IIoT and inter-site boundaries. OT is reached along three paths: IT-to-OT lateral movement, remote access and connected devices ending at L3.5, and physical or local access at L1/L0. Assets can stay in service for decades (NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3: the lifespan of an OT system can exceed 20 years), and changing crypto in a safety-related device can mean re-testing a protection scheme, a SIL assessment or a rail safety case. Smart meters, AMI and RF mesh are covered in the IoT module (`iot-pqc`).
Remote access and boundaries (`remote-access`): industrial DMZ, jump hosts, IIoT platforms on their own segment routed through the DMZ, data diodes (no key exchange to break, but passed files still need signature checks), NERC CIP-005-7 R2 (Interactive Remote Access through an intermediate system with encryption and MFA) and R3 (vendor remote access for EACMS and PACS). For IPsec/IKEv2 VPNs: RFC 8784 (Standards Track) stirs an additional shared secret into the IKEv2 key derivation, so that, where the two ends share a long secret key, the exchange is quantum secure without waiting for new key-exchange algorithms; RFC 9370 lets IKEv2 add a post-quantum key exchange alongside the classical (EC)DH one; as of 21 August 2026 (version 12), post-quantum signature authentication for IKEv2 was specified in an IETF Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth.
`vpn-ssh-pqc` — hybrid key exchange for remote access and overlays

IEC 61869-9 SV rates include 4,000, 4,800 and 14,400 samples/s (250, 208 and 69 µs apart). PQC stays out of the trip path; the symmetric MAC is already quantum-safe. PTP security is IEEE 1588-2019 Annex P (not NTS). IEC 61511 Ed.2 clause 8.2.4 requires a security risk assessment that includes the SIS (per Derbyshire; the standard text is not held).

LM-075/s:sectors.full: Sector deep dives (`sectors`): Energy (substations; NERC CIP-012-2 effective 2026-07-01 adds availability and is technology-neutral; TSA SD Pipeline-2021-02G for TSA-designated pipelines; for IEEE 2030.5 distributed energy resources the SunSpec/Sandia workgroup recommends TLS 1.3 for all DER communications (SAND2022-1118), and a 2025 conference abstract reports a hybrid quantum-safe prototype of OCPP for EV charging that names no algorithm). Water (EPA's 2023 sanitary-survey cybersecurity move was withdrawn the same year; AWIA §2013 risk assessments and voluntary EPA/AWWA guidance remain). Rail (UNISIG SUBSET-137 KMC names RSA and ECDH; FRMCS / ETSI TS 103 764 names no algorithm — its security is layered, with a TLS-backed, mutually authenticated Local Binding between applications and the On-Board FRMCS or Trackside Gateway, and the transport and service layers defer to 3GPP security specifications; 49 CFR Part 236 Subpart I names no algorithm). Manufacturing and process (PLC/DCS, OPC UA, CIP Security, PROFINET, IEC 61511 SIS). Building automation (BACnet/SC).

LM-076.curious:
### What This Is About

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) lets a server do calculations on data that stays encrypted the whole time. The server returns an encrypted answer that only the data owner can open. Unlike a trusted-hardware enclave, it relies on mathematics instead of trusting a chip.

### Why It Matters

Whoever holds the secret key can open everything, and the public keys that make the computation possible are huge. Where the secret key lives, and who may ask for a decryption, decides whether the scheme protects anything.

### The Key Takeaway

FHE keeps data hidden from the server, but it is much slower than ordinary computing and suits some kinds of data better than others. Its secret key is best kept inside a hardware security module, and whoever is allowed to ask that module to decrypt can, in principle, recover the key from the answers, so who may ask decides how well the data is protected.

### What's Happening

Standardisation of FHE is very active, for example under ISO/IEC 28033, though performance is still a concern for some applications.

lesson:
What “fully homomorphic” promises, and what it does not
Gentry proposed a fully homomorphic encryption scheme, “a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt” (Gentry, STOC 2009). “Fully” means there is no limit on which circuit can be evaluated: with bootstrapping, additions and multiplications can be chained without end. It is a statement about what is possible, not about precision, speed, integrity or who sees the result. The name invites expectations that the sources qualify:
CKKS was built as “a homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic” (Cheon, Kim, Kim & Song 2017). A real value is multiplied by a scaling factor and rounded to an integer polynomial before encryption, which preserves its precision despite the rounding. Values must stay small compared with the ciphertext modulus, and the last bits of every result carry error.
