1. CKKS single-HSM custody — find the heaviest step and what limits it
The relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are public, but each one encrypts something derived from the secret key, so only the HSM can make them. A bootstrappable CKKS set is 7.87 GB, 3.94 GB as exported (measured): too large for an HSM to hold, so it streams the set out in 1,001 bounded PKCS#11 calls with a token peak of about 16 MiB. What limits the step is CPU time, not memory or the PKCS#11 interface: 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core, 42–44 s on one Mac core, with the network adding about 5 %. Letting the token cache work between calls cuts it to 214 s on one MX95 core and 72–84 s on six MX95 Pro cores, at the cost of more token memory (65–124 MiB). It is a one-time cost per key set, paid again on rotation or recovery.
2. Why TFHE custody fits an HSM — compare key sizes with the CKKS scenario
Select "TFHE single-HSM custody" and compare what the HSM creates and exports at each step with the CKKS scenario. Note which keys stay inside the HSM and which are published.
Every key the HSM creates is kilobytes to tens of megabytes: the secret is a few hundred bytes of key bits (tens of KB as stored), the server key is tens of MB compressed and generated in seconds, and decryption is a dot product. The trade-off is that TFHE computes on bits and small integers, so heavy numeric workloads run slower than with CKKS.
3. Threshold FHE — no single party can decrypt
Open "Threshold: OpenFHE BFV (3-of-3)" and then "Threshold: Lattigo BGV (2-of-3)". For each, note how the key is generated, who must contribute to a decryption, and what replaces bootstrapping keys.
OpenFHE's threshold extension with BFV uses additive key shares and chained key generation, and every party must contribute a partial decryption. Lattigo's multiparty protocols with BGV use t-of-N shares and collective key generation, with an interactive refresh among the key holders instead of bootstrapping keys, so no GB-scale bootstrapping keys are generated. Each party still produces a full-size share of every Galois key the application needs.
Select "What can run in the HSM?" and note, for each FHE operation, whether it fits inside an HSM, fits only when streamed, or does not fit.
5. Transciphering with Kreyvium — why upload the stream cipher, not FHE ciphertexts
Select "Transciphering: TFHE-rs Kreyvium". Follow the data from the client to the server and note what the client uploads, what the server runs, and what it gets back.
The client uploads data encrypted with the Kreyvium stream cipher, plus its Kreyvium key encrypted under FHE once. The server runs the keystream inside FHE and ends with FHE ciphertexts it never saw in the clear. Uploads stay at plaintext size instead of FHE size, which can be a thousand times larger or more. Use Kreyvium's 128-bit key: Trivium's 80-bit key falls below the federal minimum of 112 bits of security strength for applying cryptographic protection before Grover.
6. Read a noisy CKKS result — decide what precision to report
The last digits of a CKKS result are noise, so report it rounded to a precision you trust: rounded to 20 bits (multiples of 2^-20 ≈ 0.00000095) it reads 3.141593 to six decimals. Rounding removes low-order noise bits but cannot recover bits the noise has already destroyed. If the result goes to others, rounding alone is not enough: decrypted CKKS results seen by others can lead to key recovery, and the research countermeasure, noise flooding, costs further precision. At the default parameters flooding for third parties leaves no correct bits (−12.8 bits in the noise-study emulation, and the token refuses the release); a second parameter set with higher-precision bootstrapping keeps 11.1–11.4 bits against a bar of 10 bits, measured with the corrected flood width on a Mac and with the token on both MX95 boards: a thin margin, set by the published sizing.
7. Pick a scheme for three use cases
Using "Which scheme for which data" in the Learn tab, pick a scheme for each: (a) counting how many encrypted records match a condition, exactly; (b) running a machine-learning model on encrypted real-valued measurements; (c) comparing encrypted values and branching on the result, or evaluating a lookup table.
(a) BFV or BGV: exact integer arithmetic; Microsoft SEAL notes that where exact values are necessary these schemes are more suitable. (b) CKKS: approximate arithmetic on real numbers, suited to evaluating machine-learning models; read the results to a trusted precision. (c) TFHE: it evaluates functions through lookup tables during bootstrapping, while with BFV, BGV and CKKS encrypted comparison is in most cases not feasible.

Key rotation without decrypting stored data
After an incident the response is to stop decryption and move to a new key. Decrypting every stored ciphertext and encrypting it again would send the data through the path under suspicion. Instead the token streams one key-switching key from the old secret to the new one, and the FHE server applies it to each stored ciphertext; no plaintext appears.

A general FHE path first explains the promise and limits, BFV/BGV/CKKS/TFHE scheme fit, noise, levels, precision, circuits, performance, parameters, quantum exposure, standards and implementations. An advanced path for developer, architect, researcher, certification-engineer and operations roles adds HSM custody, controlled decryption, key rotation, threshold operation and evidence boundaries. FHE protects plaintext from the evaluator but does not by itself provide result integrity or hide timing, traffic, access patterns, circuit shape, dimensions and implementation leakage.

Imagine handing someone a locked box with a glove-port, so they can work on what is inside without ever being able to open the lid. That is homomorphic encryption: a cloud service can add up, compare or analyse your data while it stays locked, and hands the result back still locked. Only you hold the key.
The mathematics behind it is the same family used in the new quantum-safe standards, and no one knows how to break it with a quantum computer. The parts around it, such as how the keys are sent, still need to be upgraded.

Whoever holds the secret key can open everything, and the public keys that make the computation possible are huge. Where the secret key lives, and who may ask for a decryption, decides whether the scheme protects anything.
FHE keeps data hidden from the server, but it is much slower than ordinary computing and suits some kinds of data better than others. Its secret key is best kept inside a hardware security module, and whoever is allowed to ask that module to decrypt can, in principle, recover the key from the answers, so who may ask decides how well the data is protected.
Standardisation of FHE is very active, for example under ISO/IEC 28033, though performance is still a concern for some applications.

FHE lets a server compute on data it only ever sees encrypted: the trust moves from hardware to mathematics.
“Fully” means any computation can in principle be evaluated, not that every computation is exact, fast or verified.
Each scheme fits a data type: BFV/BGV for exact integers, CKKS for approximate real numbers, TFHE for comparisons and lookup logic.
CKKS works like fixed-point arithmetic: every result carries noise and is correct only to a number of bits, so read it by rounding.
FHE is in production for private lookups; most other uses are peer-reviewed studies, pilots or research.
GPUs, FPGAs, purpose-built chips and better algorithms reduce it; reported speedups use different baselines and do not multiply.
One small secret key, and public evaluation keys that can reach gigabytes and need integrity protection.
The parts around the scheme (key exchange, signatures on the key set) are usually still classical and need a post-quantum fix.
No FHE scheme is FIPS-approved, CNSA-approved or Common Criteria-certified, and ISO/IEC 28033 is not yet published (not sourced in the Library).
What can be validated today is the conventional cryptography around FHE, not FHE itself.
An HSM can hold the FHE secret key, stream out even a multi-GB evaluation-key set in bounded pieces, sign it and decrypt under policy; it cannot run the homomorphic computation.
Whoever may ask the HSM to decrypt can recover the key, so decryption policy, compensating controls or threshold decryption carry the security model.
The HSM’s own CKKS key export now runs in OpenFHE as it is, and a reference service scores encrypted credit records with the token’s keys at the same ranking quality as plaintext, in about 200 ms per 32,768 customers on a Mac (277 ms on an x86 virtual machine, 4.29 s on an MX95 Pro board).
Any computation can run on encrypted data
Depends on the scheme. CKKS is “a homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic” (Cheon, Kim, Kim & Song 2017): results are close to the true value, correct to a number of bits. BFV, BGV and TFHE return exact integers as long as the noise stays within bounds.
Whoever holds the secret key, or may ask for decryptions, decides who sees results (section 8).
It runs at a usable speed
At a cost. The ICO describes HE as “several thousand times slower than processing plaintext”; DARPA estimated in 2021 that it was “about a million times slower” to compute in the FHE world; NIST SP 800-226 says that in most cases secure computation “is several orders of magnitude slower than native execution” and that “its performance is improving quickly” (section 4) (not sourced in the Library).

Integers modulo a plaintext modulus t. Batching treats a plaintext as 2 × (N/2) matrices of integers modulo t, and operations act on every element at once.
Exact modulo t. A result that exceeds t wraps around silently: “overflow cannot be detected in encrypted form” (SEAL), so t must be chosen larger than any intermediate value.
The message is shifted “to the most significant bits” and the noise sits in the low bits. Bits of padding above the message absorb carries: an addition consumes padding. Larger integers are radix blocks, e.g. “8-bit integers … 4 shortint blocks that store 2 bits of message each”; propagating carries between blocks is “costly” (TFHE-rs).
Exact. Integer operations wrap around; overflow-detecting operations return an encrypted flag for the client to check.
“In Concrete, everything needs to be an integer”: floats are quantized to integers before encryption, in the clear (post-training quantization or quantization-aware training). Concrete ML works with “integers of maximum 16 bits”.
Dequantize to floats after decryption; Concrete ML does both steps for the user.
“FHE computations are, by definition, data-independent” (SoK). An if/else computes both branches and selects the result with arithmetic: “any conditional branching on a ciphertext can be converted into a ‘mux’” (Coyote).
“any loop with known (plaintext) bounds can be fully unrolled” (Coyote); a loop whose bound depends on encrypted data “quickly becomes infeasible” (SoK).
Noise “limits computations to a (parameter-dependent) number of consecutive multiplications” (SoK). Rewriting reduces depth: SEAL computes 4(x+1)^2(x^2+1) at depth 2.

SCALES WHEN STREAMED: GB EVAL KEYS
An HSM cannot hold a bootstrappable CKKS key set, but it can produce one as a stream of bounded calls. Measured with Lattigo v6.2.0’s default bootstrappable set (N = 2¹⁶): 51 keys, 7.87 GB in full and 3.94 GB as exported (the other half of each key is re-expanded from a public seed). A software token on an MX95 board streamed it in 1,001 PKCS#11 calls of 4 MB each, in 473 s on one Cortex-A55 core with a 16.7 MiB peak (498 s when sent to the Mac over SSH); one Mac (M4 Pro) core takes 42–44 s. With the token caching work between calls, one MX95 core generates the set in 214 s and six MX95 Pro cores in 72–84 s, with a 65–124 MiB peak. This is the heaviest step of the scenario, a one-time cost per key set that is paid again on rotation or recovery. Homomorphic evaluation itself still does not fit in an HSM. TFHE (a 30 MB server key) and Lattigo’s interactive refresh (threshold scenario, no bootstrapping keys) avoid this volume altogether.
Think of a sealed glovebox. The cloud can reach in and work on your data through the gloves, but it cannot see inside. The only key that opens the box sits in a vault: the HSM.
With a TEE you trust the chip the computation runs on. Here the cloud is untrusted by design, and the HSM never computes on your data. It only creates the key and opens the final result.
The HSM becomes the one place that can decrypt anything. If it decrypts whatever it is sent, an attacker can use it as an oracle to learn the key, so decryption needs a policy.
Generate the FHE secret inside the HSM
The HSM DRBG produces a 32-byte seed, stored as a non-extractable key: it leaves only through the vendor replication capability, to an authenticated peer or an enrolled backup HSM. The FHE secret key s (a small polynomial) is derived from it inside the mechanism with an SP 800-108 KDF and never leaves the HSM.
Stream the evaluation keys: the heaviest step
The relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are public, but each one encrypts something derived from s, so only the HSM can make them. A bootstrappable set is GBs, too large to hold in an HSM, but it never has to be held: the HSM produces it one bounded piece at a time. Each PKCS#11 call derives a few limbs (one limb is one residue polynomial of 512 KB) of one key digit as a public session object; the host reads it, destroys it and asks for the next. Memory stays bounded, every piece is deterministic, and the receiver checks a hash per piece against a signed manifest. Measured: 3.94 GB in 1,001 calls of 4 MB, 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core with a 16.7 MiB token peak, 42–44 s on one Mac (M4 Pro) core. With the token caching work between calls: 214 s on one MX95 core and 84 s on six MX95 Pro cores (65–94 MiB peak). On the board the CPU, not the link, is the limit: the fastest run reaches 54 MB/s, about half of 1 Gb/s.
Give the data owner the public key
The client checks the HSM signature before trusting the public key. A swapped public key would let an attacker read everything encrypted under it.
The data owner encrypts on its own device
The data owner encodes its values and encrypts them with the FHE public key on its own device. No secret is needed to encrypt. From here on the data never leaves the data owner in the clear.
Upload ciphertexts to the third party
EvalAdd · EvalMult · EvalRotate · EvalBootstrap
Return the encrypted result to the data owner
The third party sends the result back still encrypted. It never held a key that could open it.
The data owner asks its HSM to decrypt
The data owner (or its authorized application) sends the encrypted result to its own HSM over an authenticated channel. Only the data owner can ask; the third party has no access to the HSM.
Policy first, then decryption. This policy is not defined by ISO/IEC 28033 or by OpenFHE; it is the HSM’s deployment layer. (1) Only the data owner’s authenticated session may ask. (2) The HSM checks the ciphertext’s metadata (slot count, level, scale) against an allowed result shape before decrypting; this limits how much one release can reveal, not where the ciphertext came from. (3) It decrypts inside the HSM, adds noise flooding (OpenFHE NOISE_FLOODING_DECRYPT) so the approximate output does not leak the key, and releases the value only if it fits the allowed range; a refusal still counts against the rate limit. (4) Rate limit and audit. The HSM cannot verify which computation produced a ciphertext.
Only the authorized party gets the plaintext result.

KB KEYS · MB SERVER KEY · µs DECRYPT
Fits an HSM. The secret is a few hundred bytes of key bits (tens of KB as stored), the server key is tens of MB compressed and generated in seconds, and decryption is a dot product. The trade-off is that TFHE computes on bits and small integers, so heavy numeric workloads run slower than with CKKS.
Same vault, smaller tools. With TFHE the "instruction manual" the cloud needs (the server key) fits on a USB stick instead of a hard-drive shelf, so the vault can write it itself.
CKKS packs thousands of numbers per ciphertext and needs GB of rotation keys to move them around. TFHE encrypts small integers one block at a time and refreshes them with a bootstrapping key and a key-switching key, so there are no rotation keys at all.
TFHE has leveled operations, which add noise and use up carry space without a bootstrap, and bootstrapped operations that reset the noise and clear carries. Which operations bootstrap depends on the API and the parameters: an unchecked addition is leveled, but the default flavour of an operation clears the carry afterwards with programmable bootstraps, and comparisons, multiplications and carry propagation use them too. A complex integer operation can use several programmable bootstraps and key switches (the library has a counter that shows how many), so wide arithmetic (64-bit multiplies, big matrix maths) is costly. TFHE suits comparisons, lookups and business logic, not large-scale ML training.
Generate the TFHE client key inside the HSM
The HSM keeps a 32-byte seed. A KDF inside the mechanism derives TFHE-rs’s 128-bit Seed from it, which expands into two binary secrets: an LWE key (918 bits) and a GLWE key (2,048 bits). That is a few hundred bytes of key bits, tens of KB as TFHE-rs stores them: an ordinary HSM-sized object.
Generate the server key inside the HSM
The bootstrapping key is about 1,800 GLWE encryptions of the LWE key bits; the key-switching key is about 8,200 small LWE encryptions (2,048 coefficients × 4 levels). That is seconds of work and tens of MB, returned in one size-checked export (PKCS#11 asks for the length, then fills the buffer) and hashed for the signed manifest. The token does not store it.

Leveled operations only add noise and use up carry space, so they need no bootstrap. When a non-linear step is needed, or the carry has to be cleared, the library runs a programmable bootstrap, usually paired with a key switch, which resets the noise and can apply any lookup table. How many bootstraps an operation uses depends on the API flavour, the operation and the parameter set, and a complex integer operation can use several. Comparisons, branches and table lookups are natural, and because bootstrapping resets the noise there is no fixed depth limit.

N-OF-N · LEAD / MAIN / FUSION
Three keyholders each own a slice of one key. The lock only opens when all three turn their slice: any one of them alone, or any two, can do nothing.
Nobody, not even an HSM, ever holds the whole secret. Each party’s HSM keeps only its own slice and produces a partial decryption; the data owner fuses them.
N-of-N means every party must be online for every decryption: one unavailable HSM blocks everything. OpenFHE’s example uses leveled evaluation (no bootstrapping keys).

Party C completes the joint public key
Party C does the same with s₃. The final joint public key encrypts under s = s₁ + s₂ + s₃, which no party ever holds.
Each party contributes a key-switching share; the shares are added, multiplied by each party’s secret in turn, and added again to give one joint evaluation-multiplication key.

FITS · STREAMS · DOES NOT FIT
An HSM is a safe with a small calculator inside. It is perfect for minting and using a key. FHE evaluation is more like a factory floor that needs warehouse-sized key tables and a lot of compute, on CPUs, GPUs or FPGAs.
Even "public" evaluation-key generation needs the secret, so it has to happen inside the HSM. The output is huge and must be streamed out.

CPU / GPU / FPGA cluster
A seed and one small polynomial take kilobytes and milliseconds. This is exactly what an HSM is for.
CKKS evaluation-key generation: streams, the heaviest step
The math (NTTs, polynomial multiplication) fits; the volume is what matters. A bootstrappable CKKS set is 3.94 GB as exported, too large to hold in an HSM, so the HSM streams it in bounded pieces instead: measured 1,001 PKCS#11 calls with a 16.7 MiB token peak, 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core (214 s with the token caching work between calls, 84 s on six MX95 Pro cores). It is a one-time cost per key set, paid again on rotation or recovery. TFHE, whose server key is 30 MB, and threshold refresh (Lattigo), which needs no bootstrapping keys, avoid the volume altogether. The seed itself never leaves the HSM. The same chunk mechanism serves the other CKKS key sets: the second parameter set (registry ID 3, scale 2^90) is 4.41 GB in 1,201 calls, generated in 96.9 s on the MX95 Pro and 99.2 s on the MX95, and a rotation key from an old secret to a new one is one 31.5 MB key that only the security officer may ask for. The generator (version 1) is frozen, so the same seed always yields the same bytes and the receiver checks every piece against the token-signed manifest.
Homomorphic evaluation in the sample HSM profile: does not fit
The cluster needs only public evaluation keys and ciphertexts, so it can sit outside the trust boundary. It can be CPUs, GPUs or FPGAs: TFHE-rs, for example, documents a default CPU backend, a CUDA GPU backend and an FPGA-based HPU backend, and the speed-up differs by operation. Which is cheaper or faster depends on the scheme, the parameters and the batch size, so measure with your own workload.
The application asks the HSM to decrypt
The application, acting for the data owner, sends the encrypted result to the HSM over an authenticated channel. The accelerators have no access to the HSM.
Decryption fits easily: microseconds to milliseconds. The policy around it matters more: only the application’s authenticated session may ask, only allowed result types or shapes are decrypted, and the plaintext must fit the allowed form before release.
Same policy and noise-flooding rules as single-HSM custody.

Move stored ciphertexts to a new key without decrypting them: the security officer, the token and the server, and what the token refuses.
SO ONLY · 31.5 MB KEY · 8 REFUSALS
A rotation key is one key-switching key at the lower levels stored ciphertexts use: 31.5 MB (15.7 MB streamed in 4 calls of 8 limbs, token peak 51.4 MiB), not the 157 MB of a bootstrapping-level key and not the 3.94 GB key set. Measured on a Mac with the software token in a container: 0.14 s to stream it, 10–37 ms per ciphertext at the server. The new key set must still be streamed once.
Changing the lock on a warehouse without opening the sealed crates: a one-way adapter converts each crate’s seal from the old lock to the new one, and nobody reads what is inside.
Decrypting every stored ciphertext and encrypting it again would send the data through the very path that is under suspicion after an incident. Here the token produces one small key and the server does the conversion on ciphertexts.
The adapter has a price: whoever holds the new secret and the adapter can compute the old secret, so it is used once and deleted. Whether someone who holds the old secret can read a converted ciphertext without having kept the original is not established.
CKM_PQCTODAY_FHE_DERIVE_PUBLIC, parameter version 3, kind 3 (rotation descriptor)
The security officer starts the rotation
Only a security-officer session may run a rotation. The token checks the session before it looks at any key: a user session is refused with CKR_USER_TYPE_INVALID and a public session with CKR_USER_NOT_LOGGED_IN. The security officer names the old and the new seed by lineage and never holds a handle to either. Pick who starts it, and what the new secret is, in “Try to start a rotation” below.
The token generates the new secret itself
The new seed is made inside the token with the same mechanism as any FHE seed, never supplied or imported by the caller. A switching key toward a secret the caller knows would hand over the old secret, so a seed that was imported, or that arrived as a copy from another token (even one that made it), is refused as the new secret. Both seeds must belong to the same parameter set, and the new seed’s decryption policy must be equal to or stricter than the old one’s.
Stream the rotation key with a signed manifest
One key-switching key from the old secret to the new one, at the lower levels stored ciphertexts use: 31,457,872 B, of which the token streams the b half, 15,728,640 B, in 4 calls of 8 limbs. The a half is re-expanded by the receiver. The token signs a manifest of the pieces once every digit has been sent exactly once. Measured: all 30 limbs matched Lattigo’s own rebuild from the two seeds.
The server switches each stored ciphertext
The server applies the key to every stored ciphertext; the result decrypts under the new secret and no plaintext appears. Measured on a Mac: 36.5 ms at the top level (9) and 10.1 ms at level 0, with precision 28.7 → 27.1 bits and 28.6 → 27.3 bits, a loss of about 1.3–1.6 bits.
The owner fetches a switched ciphertext
The server returns a switched ciphertext still encrypted, now under the new secret. It never held a key that could open it.
The new secret decrypts it; the old one no longer does
The new seed decrypts the switched level-0 ciphertext under its own policy: released rounded to 20 bits it keeps 20.99 bits. Under the old key a switched ciphertext gives noise: −27.8 bits at level 0 and −387.8 bits at level 9. Not established: whether a holder of the old secret can read a switched ciphertext without the original; until it is, the server deletes the rotation key and the old seed is retired.
The security officer retires the old secret
Only after the rotation manifest was signed, and after the server reports that every stored ciphertext was switched; the token cannot check that itself. The token first commits a signed retirement record to its retirement ledger, a public token object marked not modifiable, not copyable and not destroyable (the PKCS#11 attributes CKA_MODIFIABLE, CKA_COPYABLE and CKA_DESTROYABLE) that names both lineages, the parameter hash and the time, and links to the rotation manifest by its descriptor hash. Only then does it destroy the old seed. Those attributes stop calls through the token API; keeping the record through a restored backup or snapshot, a replaced token or a storage-level change, and retaining it for as long as policy requires, are separate production capabilities that this model does not demonstrate.
The server deletes the rotation key

Each token streams 4.10 GB of key shares (the single-token stream is 3.94 GB) in the existing chunk format for 50 of the 51 keys, and downloads 157 MB of the aggregated first round for the relinearization key. The time was not measured on the boards; the study extrapolates about 222 s on one MX95 core and 75–87 s on six MX95 Pro cores. The sums and the decryption are cheap: a decryption share is 0.5 MB and took 1.9 ms on a Mac.
A vault that needs two keys turned at once, held by two different people. Neither can open it alone, and a thief who steals one key gets nothing.
With one token, an unrestricted or insufficiently checked decryption interface can become a key-recovery oracle. With two shares, one stolen or compromised token is no longer enough, and decryption needs two genuinely independent approvals.
It protects only if the two approvals really are independent: a crafted request sent to one token returned that token’s whole share, so one application holding both approvals gets both shares. Flooding the shares for third parties still fails at the default parameters.

Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody
This Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-076) was split out of LM-019 _Confidential Computing & TEEs_. It covers fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) as the way to protect data in use by trusting mathematics instead of hardware and, on an optional advanced route, how an HSM can hold the FHE secret key and what its decryption policy can and cannot protect. TEEs, remote attestation and the TEE-HSM channel stay in LM-019.
Which scheme for which data — BFV/BGV for exact values (counting, matching, private lookups), CKKS for real numbers and machine-learning inference, TFHE for comparisons and lookup-table logic (Microsoft SEAL README).
Cost and acceleration — reported overheads range from thousands of times (ICO) to about a million times (DARPA estimate, 2021). GPUs, FPGAs, simulated and fabricated accelerator chips and better algorithms report large speedups, each against its own baseline; no source shows DARPA DPRIVE's within-ten-times goal met. TEEs, MPC, differential privacy and federated learning trade cost against different trust assumptions.
One small secret key, many large public keys — the secret key can be regenerated from a 32-byte seed; the public encryption, relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are large and need integrity protection. There is no standard encoding yet: no PKCS#11 or KMIP object type and no X.509 OID.
The HSM as FHE key custodian — generate a non-extractable 32-byte seed in the HSM, derive the secret key inside it, sign the parameter set and evaluation-key hashes with ML-DSA, decrypt under policy with an audit log, and back the seed up only HSM to HSM. The HSM can run key generation and decryption but not homomorphic evaluation. A bootstrappable CKKS evaluation-key set (3.94 GB as exported) streams out of the token in 1,001 bounded calls: measured 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core with a 16.7 MiB token peak, and 213.8 s on one core or 84.0 s on six MX95 Pro cores once the token caches work between calls (64.5–123.6 MiB peak; about 16 MiB at about twice the time with the cache off). On the board the CPU, not the 1 Gb/s link, is the limit (54 MB/s at best). This is a deployment pattern; no FHE library or paper defines an HSM role. No standard PKCS#11 mechanism exists.
The decryption-oracle limitation — an unrestricted or insufficiently checked HSM decryption interface can become a key-recovery oracle, and decrypted CKKS results seen by others can leak key information even from honest computations. Single-HSM decryption therefore trusts the authorized release path and relies on a decryption policy (approved result shapes, rounding, noise flooding for CKKS, budgets, audit) plus compensating controls; BFV, BGV and TFHE need negligible decryption-failure probability. Measured: the flood width follows the published analysis (Li, Micciancio, Schultz and Sorrell 2022, Corollary 2: log2 sigma = s/2 + 1/2 log2(24 q n) + log2 B, q = (replicas + 1) x maximum decryptions; the first version was 10.3 bits narrower and counted one copy of the key). At CKKS default parameters, flooding for 30 bits of statistical security over 10,000 releases and four replicas needs sigma = 2^43.1 and leaves -12.8 bits in the noise-study emulation, and the token refuses the release. A second parameter set (META-BTS bootstrapping twice per refresh, scale 2^90, sigma = 2^69.1) keeps 11.10, 11.25 and 11.34 bits at program depth 0, 1 and 3 end to end on a Mac, and with the token on the boards 11.37, 11.20 and 11.26 bits (MX95 Pro) and 11.19, 11.14 and 11.32 bits (MX95), within 0.3 bits of the Mac, against a bar of 10 bits: a thin margin of about 1.1-1.4 bits, set by the paper's exact sizing, at about twice the bootstrap time, 3 multiplications between refreshes instead of 9 and a 12 % larger key set. Each board generated the 4.41 GB key set in 96.9 s (MX95 Pro) and 99.2 s (MX95), with every limb equal to the reference. The earlier board runs at the narrower width (22.78 bits on the MX95 Pro, 22.59 on the MX95) are kept as records of that run. The noise is drawn with floating-point Box-Muller and rounded: the time of one draw depends on the value drawn (about 21 ns of 230-390 ns, measured on both MX95 boards), the time of a whole release showed no measurable dependence, the noise is a rounded continuous Gaussian rather than the discrete Gaussian of the published analysis, and a constant-time sampler is a tracked next-development item. Threshold decryption removes the single point of trust at the cost of more parties and ceremony.
Threshold FHE — split the key across several parties so no single decryptor exists. OpenFHE (BFV, N-of-N) and Lattigo (BGV, t-of-N) implement it. For CKKS, a 2-of-2 Lattigo prototype at the real parameters works (joint keys bootstrap at 24.3–24.5 bits; 4.10 GB of shares per party), but flooding for third parties at the default parameters fails as with one token (the corrected width is wider, so it fails by more), and a crafted request sent to one party returns that party's whole share, so each token needs its own independent approval. One share alone decrypts nothing (-27.8 bits); the joint secret has about 384 non-zero coefficients against 192; a decryption share at level 0 is 0.5 MB (1.05 MB switched to the owner's public key). Key-recovery attacks have been reported on t-of-N threshold decryption (IACR ePrint 2026/031, preprint); t-of-N such as 2-of-3 is not recommended, and whether the attacks apply to a fixed 2-of-2 split is not established.
Key rotation without decrypting stored data — the token streams one key-switching key from the old secret to a new token-generated one (31.5 MB, byte-identical to Lattigo), and the FHE server switches stored ciphertexts to the new key (precision 28.7 → 27.1–27.3 bits). Security officer only; the old seed is retired after the rotation manifest is signed, and the token commits a signed retirement record before it destroys it; the server deletes the rotation key. The token refuses a user or public session, the same seed, a different parameter set, a copy of a token-made key as the new secret, going back from new to old, a second target for the same old secret, and a looser decryption policy. One switch took 36.5 ms at the top level and 10.1 ms at level 0 on a Mac. Not established: whether a holder of the old secret can read switched ciphertexts without the original.
Cross-checks with other libraries — OpenFHE v1.6.0 CKKS at N = 2^16 (128-bit-checked settings): 80 keys, 13.26 GB, one bootstrap at 13.3 bits; That run counted one test rotation; the keys bootstrapping needs are 79, 13.09 GB. Lattigo-layout keys ran in OpenFHE with equal precision through a format bridge. The HSM's own key export now runs in OpenFHE as it is: a third parameter set (registry ID 4) takes OpenFHE v1.6.0's primes, digits and key list at its 128-bit-checked settings; the token streamed all 79 keys (6.56 GB) in 17.8 s on an M5 Max with an 83.5 MB peak, 0 mismatches over 12,483 evaluation-key limbs, and OpenFHE bootstrapped once, its default refresh, with only the token's keys at 13.28 bits against 13.20 with its own; owner release only. OpenFHE's iterative bootstrapping (two rounds: EvalBootstrap with numIterations 2 and a precision argument) works with the same 79 keys, nothing changed on the token, and raises the precision: one round 13.2 bits; two rounds 21.1 bits at the setting OpenFHE's example recommends (precision 8, the measured bits minus 5) and 31.7 to 31.8 bits at the best settings found (precision 19 to 20; a freshly encrypted ciphertext is 32.1 bits in the earlier run); through the token's owner release 30.5 bits when the ciphertext's true scale is applied and 27.0 bits when the release is read at face value, because OpenFHE's scale after a bootstrap differs from 2^52 by 6 to 7 parts in a billion and the token's input carries the scale only as a power of two. Below precision 19 the result is about 13.2 plus the precision; above 20 it falls (28.0 at 22, 24.2 at 24; not investigated); the best setting came from a sweep, not from a documented rule. The token's keys and OpenFHE's own agree within 0.4 bit. The cost is about twice the time (about 6 s against 3.2 s on a shared Mac) and one level (7 left instead of 8; keeping 8 needs a chain depth that OpenFHE refuses at N = 2^16; it asks for N = 2^17); peak memory is unchanged at 16.6 GiB. One Mac, no board, one seeded input, four runs per setting up to precision 15 and two above, the variant that raises the modulus first only. The token's export of this set was also generated on both MX95 boards in 145 s (MX95) and 142 s (MX95 Pro), about 2.4 minutes each, and streamed to a Mac in about 3 minutes (181 s and 178 s), with all 1,565 pieces matching the reference and the token-signed manifest; OpenFHE itself ran only in a container on a Mac, not on a board. Lattigo reproduces Microsoft SEAL v4.1.2 CKKS decryptions exactly. TFHE-rs 1.8.1 published test vectors: 28 of 36 byte-identical on a Mac and both MX95 boards; the 8 FFT outputs differ from upstream bytes but are identical across our platforms and decrypt correctly.
_FHE concepts, hands-on_: six interactive views, the first three on both routes (noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, programs as FHE circuits) and the last three on the Advanced HSM custody route only (key streaming and chunk size, key rotation without decrypting, shared 2-of-2 decryption). In the key-rotation view the user picks who starts a rotation and what the new secret is and sees what the token refuses; in the shared-decryption view the user toggles independent approvals and flooding and sees the measured outcome.

It cannot get an answer from the second token without that token’s own approver.
One application or person approves both tokens, so a compromised requester can send a crafted request to each: each returns its whole share (${m.craftedRecovered} of ${m.craftedTotal} coefficients) and the two shares add up to the secret. This is back to single-token trust.
Flooded at the 2^31.6 width of the earlier sizing, the result keeps ${m.floodBits} bits at the default parameters: nothing usable. The corrected width is wider (2^43.1 for one token), so it fails by more. A smaller flood of 2^20 keeps ${m.smallFloodBits} bits but is narrower than 30-bit statistical security over 10,000 releases needs.
Without flooding the result keeps ${m.noFloodBits} bits, but a partial decryption that is not flooded leaks like a whole key when results are seen by others, so releases to third parties are not safe.
Each token floods at the full width, because it must protect itself against the receiver colluding with the other token; the total is about half a bit worse than one token.
Two designs are open: shares re-encrypted to the owner’s public key (policy limited to authorization, counters and flooding), or one combining token that applies the full decryption policy and accepts the combiner-plus-requester risk. Both are still open.
More than two parties (for example 2-of-3) is not recommended: key-recovery attacks are reported on the t-of-N threshold decryption of Mouchet et al. (ePrint 2026/031, a preprint). Whether they apply to a fixed 2-of-2 split is not established.
LM-076.summary:
# Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody

## Overview

This Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-076) was split out of LM-019 _Confidential Computing & TEEs_. It covers fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) as the way to protect data in use by trusting mathematics instead of hardware and, on an optional advanced route, how an HSM can hold the FHE secret key and what its decryption policy can and cannot protect. TEEs, remote attestation and the TEE-HSM channel stay in LM-019.

Two routes. The FHE foundations route (about 60 minutes; for anyone evaluating, designing, implementing or operating an FHE workload) has eight learn sections in learning order (what FHE is and promises; schemes, data types and noisy results; where FHE is used; the cost and how it is being reduced; keys, operations and AES data; the quantum threat; standards and compliance; open-source implementations), three exercises (read a noisy CKKS result, pick a scheme, check a compliance claim) and one workshop step, the FHE concepts lab with three views (noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, programs as FHE circuits). The Advanced HSM custody route (about 105 minutes; offered to the developer, architect, researcher, certification-engineer and operations roles, and the default for certification engineers) adds a ninth learn section after the open-source implementations, the HSM as key custodian, plus five custody exercises (eight in all) and a second workshop step, the HSM custody lab with eight flow scenarios; its concepts lab adds three more views (key streaming and chunk size, key rotation without decrypting, shared 2-of-2 decryption).

## Key Concepts

- **FHE trusts mathematics, a TEE trusts hardware** (not sourced in the Library) — the server computes directly on ciphertexts and never sees input or output, and there is no enclave to attest. The cost is speed (orders of magnitude slower than computing in the clear). FHE does not prove the result is correct: ciphertexts are malleable.
- **What "fully homomorphic" promises** — Gentry (STOC 2009): a scheme "that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt". It does not promise exact results (CKKS is approximate), speed (the ICO: "several thousand times slower than processing plaintext"), integrity (NCSC: FHE provides "only confidentiality"), or that decrypted results can be shared freely.
- **Four schemes in ISO/IEC 28033 (drafts)** — BGV and BFV (exact integers, ISO/IEC 28033-2), CKKS (approximate real and complex numbers, 28033-3) and TFHE/CGGI with FHEW (bits and small integers, 28033-4; the part is titled look-up-table evaluation). The Library records ISO/IEC 28033 as under development; the current stage of each part is not sourced in the Library. Every ciphertext carries noise that grows with each operation; bootstrapping refreshes it. CKKS is fixed-point approximate arithmetic: read results by rounding to a trusted precision.
- **Which scheme for which data** — BFV/BGV for exact values (counting, matching, private lookups), CKKS for real numbers and machine-learning inference, TFHE for comparisons and lookup-table logic (Microsoft SEAL README).
- **Where FHE is used** — in production for private lookups (Apple, BFV) and Microsoft Edge's password breach check (SEAL); peer-reviewed for private set intersection, genome-wide association studies, biometric search and AI inference; small, slow AI training; pilots for official statistics; a regulator sandbox for cross-border financial-crime intelligence. The sources show it used where a small query or simple computation can wait seconds to hours and the data could not otherwise be shared.
- **Cost and acceleration** — reported overheads range from thousands of times (ICO) to about a million times (DARPA estimate, 2021). GPUs, FPGAs, simulated and fabricated accelerator chips and better algorithms report large speedups, each against its own baseline; no source shows DARPA DPRIVE's within-ten-times goal met. TEEs, MPC, differential privacy and federated learning trade cost against different trust assumptions.
- **Standards and compliance** — FHE is not among FIPS 140-3 approved security functions, has no generally approved CNSA 2.0 solution and no Common Criteria certification; only the conventional cryptography around it can be validated. The HomomorphicEncryption.org Security Standard v1.1 (2018) is a community standard. Under the GDPR, encryption is not anonymisation (EDPB draft Guidelines 02/2026).
- **One small secret key, many large public keys** — the secret key can be regenerated from a 32-byte seed; the public encryption, relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are large and need integrity protection. There is no standard encoding yet: no PKCS#11 or KMIP object type and no X.509 OID.
- **FHE does not work directly with AES** — an AES ciphertext has no structure a server can compute on. Transciphering runs the symmetric cipher's decryption inside FHE; TFHE-rs ships it for Kreyvium and AES-128-CTR.
- **Quantum threat** — lattice-based FHE has no known quantum break (it rests on the (Ring-)Learning With Errors family behind ML-KEM). The parts around the scheme, such as classical key exchange and signatures on the key set, are usually still classical and need a post-quantum fix.
- **The HSM as FHE key custodian** — generate a non-extractable 32-byte seed in the HSM, derive the secret key inside it, sign the parameter set and evaluation-key hashes with ML-DSA, decrypt under policy with an audit log, and back the seed up only HSM to HSM. The HSM can run key generation and decryption but not homomorphic evaluation. A bootstrappable CKKS evaluation-key set (3.94 GB as exported) streams out of the token in 1,001 bounded calls: measured 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core with a 16.7 MiB token peak, and 213.8 s on one core or 84.0 s on six MX95 Pro cores once the token caches work between calls (64.5–123.6 MiB peak; about 16 MiB at about twice the time with the cache off). On the board the CPU, not the 1 Gb/s link, is the limit (54 MB/s at best). This is a deployment pattern; no FHE library or paper defines an HSM role. No standard PKCS#11 mechanism exists.
- **The decryption-oracle limitation** — an unrestricted or insufficiently checked HSM decryption interface can become a key-recovery oracle, and decrypted CKKS results seen by others can leak key information even from honest computations. Single-HSM decryption therefore trusts the authorized release path and relies on a decryption policy (approved result shapes, rounding, noise flooding for CKKS, budgets, audit) plus compensating controls; BFV, BGV and TFHE need negligible decryption-failure probability. Measured: the flood width follows the published analysis (Li, Micciancio, Schultz and Sorrell 2022, Corollary 2: log2 sigma = s/2 + 1/2 log2(24 q n) + log2 B, q = (replicas + 1) x maximum decryptions; the first version was 10.3 bits narrower and counted one copy of the key). At CKKS default parameters, flooding for 30 bits of statistical security over 10,000 releases and four replicas needs sigma = 2^43.1 and leaves -12.8 bits in the noise-study emulation, and the token refuses the release. A second parameter set (META-BTS bootstrapping twice per refresh, scale 2^90, sigma = 2^69.1) keeps 11.10, 11.25 and 11.34 bits at program depth 0, 1 and 3 end to end on a Mac, and with the token on the boards 11.37, 11.20 and 11.26 bits (MX95 Pro) and 11.19, 11.14 and 11.32 bits (MX95), within 0.3 bits of the Mac, against a bar of 10 bits: a thin margin of about 1.1-1.4 bits, set by the paper's exact sizing, at about twice the bootstrap time, 3 multiplications between refreshes instead of 9 and a 12 % larger key set. Each board generated the 4.41 GB key set in 96.9 s (MX95 Pro) and 99.2 s (MX95), with every limb equal to the reference. The earlier board runs at the narrower width (22.78 bits on the MX95 Pro, 22.59 on the MX95) are kept as records of that run. The noise is drawn with floating-point Box-Muller and rounded: the time of one draw depends on the value drawn (about 21 ns of 230-390 ns, measured on both MX95 boards), the time of a whole release showed no measurable dependence, the noise is a rounded continuous Gaussian rather than the discrete Gaussian of the published analysis, and a constant-time sampler is a tracked next-development item. Threshold decryption removes the single point of trust at the cost of more parties and ceremony.
- **Threshold FHE** — split the key across several parties so no single decryptor exists. OpenFHE (BFV, N-of-N) and Lattigo (BGV, t-of-N) implement it. For CKKS, a 2-of-2 Lattigo prototype at the real parameters works (joint keys bootstrap at 24.3–24.5 bits; 4.10 GB of shares per party), but flooding for third parties at the default parameters fails as with one token (the corrected width is wider, so it fails by more), and a crafted request sent to one party returns that party's whole share, so each token needs its own independent approval. One share alone decrypts nothing (-27.8 bits); the joint secret has about 384 non-zero coefficients against 192; a decryption share at level 0 is 0.5 MB (1.05 MB switched to the owner's public key). Key-recovery attacks have been reported on t-of-N threshold decryption (IACR ePrint 2026/031, preprint); t-of-N such as 2-of-3 is not recommended, and whether the attacks apply to a fixed 2-of-2 split is not established.
- **Key rotation without decrypting stored data** — the token streams one key-switching key from the old secret to a new token-generated one (31.5 MB, byte-identical to Lattigo), and the FHE server switches stored ciphertexts to the new key (precision 28.7 → 27.1–27.3 bits). Security officer only; the old seed is retired after the rotation manifest is signed, and the token commits a signed retirement record before it destroys it; the server deletes the rotation key. The token refuses a user or public session, the same seed, a different parameter set, a copy of a token-made key as the new secret, going back from new to old, a second target for the same old secret, and a looser decryption policy. One switch took 36.5 ms at the top level and 10.1 ms at level 0 on a Mac. Not established: whether a holder of the old secret can read switched ciphertexts without the original.
- **Cross-checks with other libraries** — OpenFHE v1.6.0 CKKS at N = 2^16 (128-bit-checked settings): 80 keys, 13.26 GB, one bootstrap at 13.3 bits; That run counted one test rotation; the keys bootstrapping needs are 79, 13.09 GB. Lattigo-layout keys ran in OpenFHE with equal precision through a format bridge. The HSM's own key export now runs in OpenFHE as it is: a third parameter set (registry ID 4) takes OpenFHE v1.6.0's primes, digits and key list at its 128-bit-checked settings; the token streamed all 79 keys (6.56 GB) in 17.8 s on an M5 Max with an 83.5 MB peak, 0 mismatches over 12,483 evaluation-key limbs, and OpenFHE bootstrapped once, its default refresh, with only the token's keys at 13.28 bits against 13.20 with its own; owner release only. OpenFHE's iterative bootstrapping (two rounds: EvalBootstrap with numIterations 2 and a precision argument) works with the same 79 keys, nothing changed on the token, and raises the precision: one round 13.2 bits; two rounds 21.1 bits at the setting OpenFHE's example recommends (precision 8, the measured bits minus 5) and 31.7 to 31.8 bits at the best settings found (precision 19 to 20; a freshly encrypted ciphertext is 32.1 bits in the earlier run); through the token's owner release 30.5 bits when the ciphertext's true scale is applied and 27.0 bits when the release is read at face value, because OpenFHE's scale after a bootstrap differs from 2^52 by 6 to 7 parts in a billion and the token's input carries the scale only as a power of two. Below precision 19 the result is about 13.2 plus the precision; above 20 it falls (28.0 at 22, 24.2 at 24; not investigated); the best setting came from a sweep, not from a documented rule. The token's keys and OpenFHE's own agree within 0.4 bit. The cost is about twice the time (about 6 s against 3.2 s on a shared Mac) and one level (7 left instead of 8; keeping 8 needs a chain depth that OpenFHE refuses at N = 2^16; it asks for N = 2^17); peak memory is unchanged at 16.6 GiB. One Mac, no board, one seeded input, four runs per setting up to precision 15 and two above, the variant that raises the modulus first only. The token's export of this set was also generated on both MX95 boards in 145 s (MX95) and 142 s (MX95 Pro), about 2.4 minutes each, and streamed to a Mac in about 3 minutes (181 s and 178 s), with all 1,565 pieces matching the reference and the token-signed manifest; OpenFHE itself ran only in a container on a Mac, not on a board. Lattigo reproduces Microsoft SEAL v4.1.2 CKKS decryptions exactly. TFHE-rs 1.8.1 published test vectors: 28 of 36 byte-identical on a Mac and both MX95 boards; the 8 FFT outputs differ from upstream bytes but are identical across our platforms and decrypt correctly.
- **An encrypted risk-scoring service** — a reference service scores 32,768 customers per request on CKKS ciphertexts made under the token's keys (logistic regression on the UCI credit-default dataset, CC BY 4.0; a cubic in place of the sigmoid, 3 multiplications, no refresh). On 6,000 held-out rows: AUC 0.717298 encrypted against 0.717299 in plaintext and the same decision on all 32,768 slots; about 200 ms of server time per batch on an M5 Max, while encrypting a batch takes the data owner 3.6 s. The same service, built as a static binary for each processor, also ran on an x86-64 virtual machine (12 virtual CPUs of an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, token in a container on the Mac: 277 ms per batch, median of three repetitions, 273-305 ms over all 8 jobs; server peak 1,311 MiB; key set admitted with 40 ms to verify and 100 ms to assemble; about 13,000 requests an hour by server time alone; whole run 47 s) and on an MX95 Pro board (6 Cortex-A55 cores, 15.4 GiB) with the token on the base MX95 board, which exported its 4.41 GB key set in 124 s (35.7 MB/s, 83 MiB peak): 4.29 s per batch (median of three, 4.16-4.66 s over all 8 jobs), about 21 times the Mac; server peak 1,870 MiB; key set admitted with 170 ms to verify and 497 ms to assemble; 600 requests an hour one at a time with the 184 MiB upload and 840 by server time alone; whole run 202 s. The scores were identical on all three machines (21.00 bits against the plaintext cubic, the same decision on every slot at 0.5 and 0.25, AUC 0.717298 against 0.717299). The service admits keys only with the token's ML-DSA-65-signed manifest, needs only the relinearization key, speaks TLS 1.3 with X25519MLKEM768 and a client certificate, and refuses about 40 tested bad inputs; only the owner can decrypt a score (owner release). Limits: classical test certificates, one tenant, memory only, 3 multiplications and one batch size, one run per machine; the first virtual machine run and the board run use the published test seed (a third run, on the virtual machine with the token on the MX95 Pro reached over KMIP, used a random seed generated in the token and gave the same accuracy) (the secret key is public, so they measure time, memory and correctness, not secrecy), the x86 run is a virtual machine whose cores were not pinned, and the board's service listens on loopback behind an ssh tunnel with TLS inside it.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

_FHE + HSM Flows_ (the Advanced HSM custody route only): step through eight scenarios (CKKS and TFHE single-HSM custody, OpenFHE and Lattigo threshold FHE, what fits in the HSM, Kreyvium transciphering, CKKS key rotation, and CKKS shared 2-of-2 decryption). Each step shows who holds which key and which data state, and a quantum overlay marks the links a quantum computer breaks.

_FHE concepts, hands-on_: six interactive views, the first three on both routes (noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, programs as FHE circuits) and the last three on the Advanced HSM custody route only (key streaming and chunk size, key rotation without decrypting, shared 2-of-2 decryption). In the key-rotation view the user picks who starts a rotation and what the new secret is and sees what the token refuses; in the shared-decryption view the user toggles independent approvals and flooding and sees the measured outcome.

LM-076.topic:
**Scope.** Explore fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) as data-in-use protection that trusts mathematics instead of hardware, covering the contrast with TEEs (root of trust, side channels, speed, integrity of the result), the four schemes in the ISO/IEC 28033 drafts (BGV, BFV, CKKS, TFHE/CGGI with FHEW), noise and bootstrapping. Covers the FHE key set (one small secret key, large public encryption, relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys), who runs each operation (client, server, key holder) and how AES data enters FHE through transciphering (Kreyvium, AES-128-CTR in TFHE-rs). Covers FHE against the quantum threat (lattice-based, no known quantum break; the classical parts around the scheme still need a PQC fix). Covers the HSM as FHE key custodian (non-extractable seed, secret key derived inside the HSM, ML-DSA signature over the parameter set, decryption under policy, HSM-to-HSM backup), threshold FHE (OpenFHE, Lattigo), why an HSM must not be a raw decryption oracle, and the open-source implementations (TFHE-rs, OpenFHE, Lattigo, Microsoft SEAL). Out of scope: commercial FHE products, GPU or FPGA acceleration details, and a PKCS#11 or KMIP standard for FHE objects (none exists today).

**Sub-topics keywords:** FHE fully homomorphic encryption, ISO/IEC 28033, BGV, BFV, CKKS, TFHE, CGGI, FHEW, noise, bootstrapping, ciphertext, relinearization key, Galois key, evaluation key, transciphering, Kreyvium, threshold FHE, LWE, RLWE, lattice, HSM key custody, non-extractable seed, decryption oracle, noise flooding, TFHE-rs, OpenFHE, Lattigo, FIPS 203 204, PKCS#11.

LM-076/s:fhe-cost.full:
A pattern runs through the deployments above, offered as a reading of the sources rather than a rule. The query or computation is small or simple (a lookup, a match, a count, a linear model). A response in seconds to hours is acceptable: Mastercard notes that “for now, FHE is more suited to needs requiring a response measured in seconds rather than milliseconds”. And a legal or trust barrier keeps the data from being shared in the clear, such as cross-border rules on financial data or a service that must not learn what a user looks up. The UK NCSC advises organisations to “first consider whether traditional cryptography will solve your data processing problem”.

LM-076/s:fhe-quantum.full:
each speedup is measured against that paper's own baseline, often a single CPU thread, so the figures cannot be compared with each other or multiplied together. DARPA's DPRIVE programme set the goal of bringing FHE “within a factor of ten of unencrypted computations”; none of the sources above shows that goal met.
The UK ICO says the security of most HE schemes rests on hard mathematical problems “that are currently considered to be secure even against quantum computers”. NIST and the NSA make no such statement: the NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says that neither NSA nor NIST has produced standards for these areas, and it lists homomorphic encryption among areas with “no generally approved solutions” (in its “Future cryptographic algorithms” section).
Lattice-based FHE has no known quantum break.
ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signatures replace the quantum-vulnerable ones. They show who signed a key or ciphertext and that it was not altered afterwards, provided the verifier already trusts the signer’s public key. They do not show that the computation was correct: an evaluator can sign a wrong result. Correctness against a malicious evaluator needs a verifiable-computation proof (research) or an application-specific check
Only ciphertexts leave the data owner. The third party stores and computes on them but cannot read them. The FHE layer is post-quantum; the TLS session around it often is not.
Quantum threat — lattice-based FHE has no known quantum break (it rests on the (Ring-)Learning With Errors family behind ML-KEM). The parts around the scheme, such as classical key exchange and signatures on the key set, are usually still classical and need a post-quantum fix.

In the Learn tab, open "Schemes, Data Types and Noisy Results" and find the illustration under "Reading a noisy CKKS result: rounding". The encrypted input was 3.14159265 and decryption returned 3.1415926481. Decide how many digits you would report, and what changes if the result goes to someone other than the key owner.
Results are rounded to multiples of 2^-precisionBits before release; the HSM never releases raw noisy coefficients
Decryption results are noisy: what that means and how to read them
decrypted CKKS results leak the key even when every computation was honest, if people other than the key owner see them (Li & Micciancio 2021). Exact schemes leak the same way through decryption failures when the failure probability is not negligible (Cheon et al. 2024; Checri et al. 2024).
Not without care. Decrypted CKKS results seen by others can lead to key recovery (Li & Micciancio 2021); the countermeasure, noise flooding, costs precision (Li, Micciancio, Schultz & Sorrell 2022). Exact schemes need a negligible decryption-failure probability (Cheon et al. 2024).
SEAL names CKKS for applications such as “summing up encrypted real numbers, evaluating machine learning models on encrypted data”; results are approximate.
The Library records ISO/IEC 28033 as under development (Part 1, general, at Draft International Standard) and lists its other parts as the BGV/BFV, CKKS and look-up-table (TFHE) schemes. The EPC cryptography guidelines (v16.0.1) say that standardisation of FHE is very active, naming ISO/IEC 28033 as an example. The current stage of each part is not sourced in the Library; check the ISO project pages.
Checri, Sirdey, Boudguiga, Bultel. On the practical CPAD security of “exact” and threshold FHE schemes and libraries. CRYPTO 2024, IACR ePrint 2024/116.
Policy first, then decryption. This policy is not defined by ISO/IEC 28033 or by TFHE-rs; it is the HSM’s deployment layer built on TFHE-rs building blocks. The serialized ciphertext carries no access-control metadata (no owner, purpose or recipient, and nothing in it is authenticated), so control comes from the HSM’s policy object and the requester. (1) Only the data owner’s authenticated session may ask. (2) A conformance-checked type gate (TFHE-rs safe_deserialize_conformant) refuses a ciphertext whose type, block count or parameter set is not an allowed result type, before decrypting. Marking input types as never releasable stops a raw input being released whole, but not a slice of it: the HSM limits how many bits each release can reveal, and the rate limit caps the total. (3) After decrypting inside the HSM, the value must fit the allowed shape (a yes/no, a score from 0 to 100) or nothing is released; a refusal still counts against the rate limit, because refusing is itself an answer. (4) Rate limit and audit. Decryption itself is a 2,048-term dot product per block: microseconds. The HSM cannot verify which computation produced a ciphertext; only verifiable-computation proofs could, and those are research.
Two routes. The FHE foundations route (about 60 minutes; for anyone evaluating, designing, implementing or operating an FHE workload) has eight learn sections in learning order (what FHE is and promises; schemes, data types and noisy results; where FHE is used; the cost and how it is being reduced; keys, operations and AES data; the quantum threat; standards and compliance; open-source implementations), three exercises (read a noisy CKKS result, pick a scheme, check a compliance claim) and one workshop step, the FHE concepts lab with three views (noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, programs as FHE circuits). The Advanced HSM custody route (about 105 minutes; offered to the developer, architect, researcher, certification-engineer and operations roles, and the default for certification engineers) adds a ninth learn section after the open-source implementations, the HSM as key custodian, plus five custody exercises (eight in all) and a second workshop step, the HSM custody lab with eight flow scenarios; its concepts lab adds three more views (key streaming and chunk size, key rotation without decrypting, shared 2-of-2 decryption).
What "fully homomorphic" promises — Gentry (STOC 2009): a scheme "that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt". It does not promise exact results (CKKS is approximate), speed (the ICO: "several thousand times slower than processing plaintext"), integrity (NCSC: FHE provides "only confidentiality"), or that decrypted results can be shared freely.
Four schemes in ISO/IEC 28033 (drafts) — BGV and BFV (exact integers, ISO/IEC 28033-2), CKKS (approximate real and complex numbers, 28033-3) and TFHE/CGGI with FHEW (bits and small integers, 28033-4; the part is titled look-up-table evaluation). The Library records ISO/IEC 28033 as under development; the current stage of each part is not sourced in the Library. Every ciphertext carries noise that grows with each operation; bootstrapping refreshes it. CKKS is fixed-point approximate arithmetic: read results by rounding to a trusted precision.

Standards and compliance — FHE is not among FIPS 140-3 approved security functions, has no generally approved CNSA 2.0 solution and no Common Criteria certification; only the conventional cryptography around it can be validated. The catch is that the key is everything. Anyone allowed to ask the key-holder to open boxes could piece the key together from the answers. So the key is best kept in a dedicated security device that only opens a box when the rules say so, and the rules on who may ask matter as much as the device. The glove-port also makes the work slow, so it is used where keeping the data locked is worth the wait.
The sources show it used where a small query or simple computation can wait seconds to hours, and the data could not otherwise be shared.
In principle yes, but each scheme favours a data type. Microsoft SEAL: “For applications where exact values are necessary, the BFV and BGV schemes are more suitable”, CKKS suits real numbers, and with these schemes “encrypted comparison, sorting, or regular expressions, are in most cases not feasible”. TFHE handles comparisons and lookup logic, on small integers.
“in most cases not feasible” (SEAL README); comparisons need binary circuits, where TFHE fits better (SoK on FHE compilers).

# Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A content-protection system can bind its keys to a particular device and revoke devices that have been compromised. In consumer content protection a compromised device is part of the threat model, so asking whether the system is quantum-safe has to be done link by link. This module reads the actual specifications behind some of those systems — the AACS system, whose specification covers keys held on media and the exchange between a drive and a host, the CI Plus system, which protects content where it leaves a conditional-access module and re-enters the host device, the MovieLabs ECP specification, and the C2PA standard that attaches signed "content credentials" to media — and asks one precise question of each: where does it use public-key cryptography, the kind that a large quantum computer would break?

## Why It Matters

Public-key cryptography does two jobs in these systems: it signs things (a block of keys, a certificate, a media file's credentials) and it lets two devices agree on a shared key. NIST's transition plan says that quantum-vulnerable signature and key-agreement schemes will be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed in NIST standards after 2035. That is NIST's schedule for NIST standards. None of the media specifications read here sets a deadline of its own.

## The Key Takeaway

A specification that does not mention quantum computers is not the same as an organisation that has no plan. The first is a fact about a document; the second would need a different kind of evidence. Reading each link precisely — which kind of cryptography it uses, who can change it, who can revoke a compromised device — is more useful than a general statement that "media is vulnerable".

## What's Happening

In the editions read here, the key tree and the content cipher use symmetric cryptography (AES-128 in AACS; DES-56 or AES-128 in CI Plus), while the signatures and key exchanges use ECDSA, RSA and Diffie-Hellman. The C2PA standard allows ECDSA, RSA and EdDSA signatures for new credentials and lists no post-quantum algorithm; separate IETF documents describe how to carry a post-quantum signature in the same format. For streaming, a hybrid key exchange for the web's encryption layer was published in August 2026 as RFC 10024, while a 2023 research paper reported an absence of post-quantum security in three widely used DRM systems.

The specification distinguishes three mechanisms of revocation for host devices whose security has been compromised: Host Service Shunning, revocation by the CA system, and Host Revocation. Revocation by the CA system is defined by a particular CA system and is out of scope for the specification.
Host Revocation is revocation by denial of service: the CICAM stops CI Plus operation, withholding Content Control services from the host. Revoked hosts are listed in a Service Operator Certificate Revocation List (SOCRL), and a Service Operator Certificate White List (SOCWL) undoes a revocation. A SOCRL is created by the Root-of-Trust on request of a Service Operator for its own operation, so a host can be revoked for one operator and still work for others. # Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC

## Overview

The Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC module (60 minutes, intermediate, Industries track) reads four editions as they are written and asks, link by link, which public-key primitive each uses and what its text says about quantum computing: the AACS Introduction and Common Cryptographic Elements Book (Revision 0.953, 26 October 2012), the CI Plus Specification v1.3.2 (March 2015), the MovieLabs Specification for Enhanced Content Protection, Version 1.4 (August 2024), and the C2PA Technical Specification, Version 2.4. It adds a 2023 paper on three streaming DRM systems, RFC 10024 for hybrid key agreement in TLS 1.3, and NIST IR 8547 (October 2026). Other editions and generations of these schemes are not covered.

## Key Concepts

- **Threat model.** A compromised device is part of the threat model. ECP describes ripping software as enabled by "hack one, hack all" scenarios: breaking protection on one device can break it on a wide class of devices. ECP is a set of high-level specifications from MovieLabs, and each studio decides which practices it requires.
- **What ECP asks for.** Limiting a compromise to one platform, binding license keys to a device, revoking and renewing clients and revoking devices or classes of devices, a content cipher of AES 128 or better, a secure media pipeline from decryption to protected output, support for a requirement of HDCP 2.2 or better for specific content, forensic watermarking, separate content keys and keeping content off public CDNs until needed, the ability for operators to restrict content when devices stop receiving security updates, and certification by third parties and trusted implementers.
- **AACS key ladder.** Device Keys (128 bits each) are given to a device at manufacture; subsidiary Device Keys and Processing Keys come from the AES-G3 function; AACS LA generates the Media Key Block; a device recovers the 128-bit Media Key with AES-128D under a Processing Key. An updated Media Key Block revokes compromised Device Keys. All digital signatures use ECDSA (ANSI X9.62, FIPS 186-2) with SHA-1; the Bus Key in drive authentication is derived from exchanged elliptic-curve points. Implementing the specification requires a license from AACS LA LLC.
- **CI Plus.** The specification addresses content protection after conditional access protection is removed, where content leaves the CA module and re-enters the host. Authentication signatures are RSASSA-PSS with 2048-bit RSA and SHA-1 (MGF1 with SHA-1, 20-byte salt); key negotiation is Diffie-Hellman with 2048-bit values, with the parameters held in the CI Plus Licensee Specification; the scrambler is DES-56 in ECB mode (mandatory) or AES-128 in CBC mode (optional for the CICAM, mandatory for HD hosts); SHA-256 is used for derived values such as the UCK. Host Revocation is revocation by denial of service, through a Service Operator Certificate Revocation List created by the Root-of-Trust at a Service Operator's request.
- **Streaming.** RFC 10024 (IETF Standards Track, August 2026) defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. Cloudflare reported in the last week of October 2025 that the majority of human-initiated traffic with Cloudflare was using post-quantum encryption. A 2023 paper (arXiv preprint, version 3, 3 August 2023) identifies an absence of post-quantum security in Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady and urges the transition to post-quantum algorithms for license distribution and authentication.
- **C2PA.** Version 2.4 allows ES256, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512 and EdDSA (Ed25519 only) for new claim signatures; the deprecated list is empty. The claim signature is a COSE_Sign1_Tagged structure; time-stamps (RFC 3161, sigTst2) are optional; a C2PA Trust List and a TSA Trust List are kept; validation checks credential revocation information. RFC 9964 specifies COSE serializations for ML-DSA; the SLH-DSA equivalent is an Internet-Draft.
- **Central distinction.** The text of each edition read does not mention quantum computing. That is a statement about a document; it says nothing about what any organisation plans.
- **NIST IR 8547.** NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035 (Tables 2 and 4 list ECDSA, EdDSA, RSA, Diffie-Hellman and MQV, and RSA key establishment). These dates are NIST's schedule for NIST standards; the media documents read here state no deadline of their own.

## Workshop Activities

1. **Key Ladder Explorer** — walk the AACS or CI Plus ladder and see which rungs use a public-key primitive of a kind NIST IR 8547 lists
2. **Spec vs Quantum** — compare what four editions specify and what their text says about quantum computing
3. **Provenance Algorithm Check** — test candidate algorithms against the C2PA 2.4 allowed list

1. Trace an AACS revocation: which keys change, and which signature carries it
Open the Key Ladder Explorer on AACS. A set of Device Keys has been compromised. Walk rungs 1 to 6 and write down, for each rung, whether it changes when AACS LA releases an updated Media Key Block, and which primitive protects the new block.
Rungs 1 to 4 (Device Keys, Processing Keys, the Media Key, the revocation itself) are built from 128-bit keys and AES-based functions. Rung 5, the signature on the Media Key Block, uses ECDSA, and rung 6, the Bus Key exchange, uses an elliptic-curve exchange signed with ECDSA. The document says the block of a subset-difference system is of the same order in size as a public-key certificate revocation list.
The ladder below runs from the secret keys a device is given at manufacture to the key exchange between a drive and a host. For each rung the lesson shows the primitive the specification names, and, for the public-key rungs, which NIST IR 8547 table lists that kind of primitive. The pairing with NIST is this lesson’s, not the specification’s.
All digital signatures in AACS use the ECDSA digital signature scheme defined in ANSI X9.62 and FIPS 186-2. The Media Key Block signature and the drive and host signatures in the Bus Key exchange all rest on that one scheme.
The Device Key tree, the Processing Keys and the Media Key are built from AES-128. The public-key operations in this edition are the ECDSA signatures and the Bus Key exchange. Forging a Media Key Block signature would need the AACS LA signing key, so an attacker who could derive an ECDSA key from a public key could do that. The lesson draws no conclusion about the effect of a quantum computer on AES.
Public-key cryptography does two jobs in these systems: it signs things (a block of keys, a certificate, a media file's credentials) and it lets two devices agree on a shared key. NIST's transition plan says that quantum-vulnerable signature and key-agreement schemes will be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed in NIST standards after 2035. That is NIST's schedule for NIST standards. None of the media specifications read here sets a deadline of its own.
Each compliant device is given a set of secret Device Keys when it is manufactured. The keys come from AACS LA and are 128 bits each.
AACS LA generates the Media Key Block. A device decrypts one or more elements of it with its Device Keys to extract the 128-bit Media Key: AES-128D of the encrypted key data under a Processing Key, combined by XOR with a mask built from the uv number. The encrypted key data is in the Media Key Data Record of the block.
If a set of Device Keys is compromised, an updated Media Key Block can be released that stops devices with those Device Keys from calculating the correct Media Key. The block of a subset-difference tree system is of the same order in size as a public-key certificate revocation list, which the document says makes it equivalent in revocation power to a public-key system (an informative section).
Devices are required to check the signature on the Media Key Block. The End of Media Key Block record carries the AACS LA signature on the data in the block.

# Software Supply Chain PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

When software or a firmware update reaches a device, a digital signature is one of the main ways the receiver can check that what arrived is what was sent. This module reads the documents that govern those signatures, one link at a time, and asks a precise question of each: what does it say about signatures that a large quantum computer could not break, and where is it silent?

## Why It Matters

The documents differ. Some specify post-quantum and hash-based signatures for common formats such as CMS, X.509 and COSE; some are still drafts; one registry marks the post-quantum entries experimental; and two documents that govern signing, the CA/Browser Forum code signing requirements v3.11 and the UEFI Specification Release 2.11, contain no post-quantum term in the editions read here.

## The Key Takeaway

A document that does not mention quantum computers is a fact about that document, not about anyone's plans. Reading each link precisely — which document, which edition, what it says — is more useful than a general statement that the supply chain is vulnerable.

## What's Happening

Update frameworks such as TUF and Uptane spread trust across several roles and keys, and require a threshold of signatures for a role to be trusted. SLSA and in-toto describe provenance and attestations but name no signature algorithm in the pages read here. For a verifier that has already shipped, the documents describe carrying two signatures during a change, combining algorithms, and, for unchangeable boot code, recommending hash-based signatures.

Software reaches a device through a series of hand-offs, and at each hand-off some control is meant to tell the receiver that what arrived is what was sent. Many of those controls are signatures. When software or a firmware update reaches a device, a digital signature is one of the main ways the receiver can check that what arrived is what was sent. This module reads the documents that govern those signatures, one link at a time, and asks a precise question of each: what does it say about signatures that a large quantum computer could not break, and where is it silent?
A document that does not mention quantum computers is a fact about that document, not about anyone's plans. Reading each link precisely — which document, which edition, what it says — is more useful than a general statement that the supply chain is vulnerable.

The useful skill is reading each link from its own document and knowing which role, threshold and verifier a change would have to go through.
