It reads the documents that govern them: the Sigstore algorithm registry, the CA/Browser Forum code signing requirements v3.11, the UEFI Specification Release 2.11, the SUIT manifest draft, the RFCs that carry ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and HSS/LMS in COSE, CMS and X.509, RFC 9980 for OpenPGP, ETSI TS 119 312, the TUF and Uptane update frameworks, the SLSA v1.2 Build pages and the in-toto Statement, and RFC 9019 for bootloaders that cannot change.
Each link is read from its own document and labelled by what that document says: specified in an RFC, a draft, experimental, a requirement, recommended, or silent. In the held editions the Sigstore algorithm registry marks ML-DSA as experimental, and the CA/Browser Forum code signing requirements v3.11 and the UEFI Specification Release 2.11 contain no post-quantum term. TUF and Uptane spread trust across roles that need a threshold of signatures. SLSA v1.2 and the in-toto Statement describe provenance and attestations but name no signature algorithm.
Many software and firmware updates are protected by a digital signature, a bit of maths that lets your device check who sent the update and that nobody changed it on the way. That check is only as good as the rules behind it: who is allowed to sign, how many keys must agree, and what the device does when something looks wrong.
Update frameworks such as TUF and Uptane spread trust across several roles and keys, and require a threshold of signatures for a role to be trusted. SLSA and in-toto describe provenance and attestations but name no signature algorithm in the pages read here. For a verifier that has already shipped, the documents describe carrying two signatures during a change, combining algorithms, and, for unchangeable boot code, recommending hash-based signatures.
Uptane's threat model includes attacks on update systems such as rollback (install an older valid revision), freeze (keep sending a properly signed but old bundle), endless data, and partial bundle installation, and it assumes an attacker who may compromise and control a Director or an Image repository server and its keys, but not both.

### What This Is About

Adding post-quantum cryptography to a hardware security module or cryptographic library is only half the work — proving it through formal product certification is often the longest bottleneck. Certification engineers, lab testers, and scheme reviewers must navigate FIPS 140-3, ACVP algorithm testing, entropy source validation (ESV), EUCC, NIAP Policy #33, and PCI boundaries without conflating what each certificate actually proves.

### Why It Matters

Active FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the CMVP Historical List in September 2026, so PQC upgrades now run through FIPS 140-3 and congested laboratory queues. Meanwhile, PQC algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) introduce seed-driven ACVP `keyGen` test vectors, mandatory IG 10.3.A CAST/PCT self-tests, and SP 800-90B/90C ESV entropy dependencies. At the same time, separate regulatory clocks are active: CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 sets 2027/2030/2031 National Security System gates (aligned with NIAP Policy #33), and EO 14412 / OMB M-26-15 sets 2030 key-establishment and 2031 signature dates for US federal civilian HVAs and high-impact systems.

### The Key Takeaway

Never equate a CAVP algorithm certificate (or ACVP validation record) or a Modules in Process (MIP) listing with an active FIPS 140-3 module certificate. Verify exact firmware versions, operating environments, ESV linkage, and regional scheme boundaries (FIPS 140-3 vs. EUCC vs. PCI PTS HSM v5.0 / PCI DSS v4.0.1) in primary registries — and mark anything unverified as Unknown.

### What's Happening

Final NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms by 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards after 2035. NIST finalized SP 800-90C in September 2025 alongside mandatory CMVP ESV validation, EUCC operates under CIR (EU) 2024/482 with ACM v2 PQC guidance, and PCI SSC separates PTS HSM v5.0 device approvals from PCI DSS v4.0.1 operational assessments.

Your validation scoping, evidence discipline, and scheme boundary decisions determine whether PQC products ship with defensible assurance or stall in lab queues.
FIPS 140-2 Historical List Transition & CMVP Queue Pressure
Active FIPS 140-2 certificates transitioned to the CMVP Historical List on 21 September 2026. Adding PQC algorithms to legacy modules requires FIPS 140-3 submissions through a congested Modules in Process (MIP) queue, making submission-route planning (new validation vs. 1SUB/3SUB/5SUB) critical.
A product team assumes an existing FIPS 140-2 Level 3 HSM certificate can be patched with ML-KEM-768 in six weeks. In reality, the FIPS 140-2 certificate is Historical, federal procurements require FIPS 140-3, and a new CMVP submission plus CSTL testing requires multi-quarter lead time.
ACVP Seed-Driven AFT keyGen & CAST/PCT (IG 10.3.A)
PQC algorithm validation introduces deterministic seed-driven Algorithm Functional Tests (AFT) for keyGen alongside encapsulation/decapsulation and signing/verification vectors. Inside the module, FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A requires pre-operational Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Tests (CASTs) and conditional Pairwise Consistency Tests (PCTs) for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA.
A vendor exposes only randomized ML-DSA key generation through its PKCS#11 interface. When the CSTL runs ACVP AFT keyGen vectors, the harness cannot inject deterministic 32-byte seeds, forcing a firmware test-harness redesign and re-audit of the module boundary.
Entropy Source Validation (ESV / SP 800-90B / SP 800-90C)
FIPS 140-3 modules require validated entropy sources under NIST SP 800-90B via the CMVP Entropy Source Validation (ESV) program, and RBG constructions must align with NIST SP 800-90C (finalized September 2025). PQC key generation (especially ML-KEM and ML-DSA seed material) depends on full-entropy seeding and documented health tests.
An HSM firmware team integrates ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 using a new hardware noise source, but forgets to schedule an independent ESV submission. CMVP rejects the module package until an active ESV certificate is linked to the exact OE and conditioning component.
EUCC (CIR (EU) 2024/482) & NIAP Policy #33 CNSA 2.0 Cut-Offs
Common Criteria evaluations now split across regional schemes with distinct PQC rules: the EUCC scheme under CIR (EU) 2024/482 references the EUCC Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (ACM v2) for PQC parameter guidance, while US NIAP CCEVS Policy Letter #33 enforces CNSA 2.0 algorithm cut-offs for National Security System Protection Profiles.
A network appliance vendor targets both US NSS buyers (under NIAP cPP Network Devices + Policy #33) and European qualified signature deployments (under EUCC + EN 419 221-5). Assuming a single Common Criteria evaluation covers both schemes fails because Protection Profile claims, PQC parameter sets, and assurance continuity rules diverge.
PCI PTS HSM v5.0 vs. PCI DSS v4.0.1 Scope Boundaries
Payment security separates device approval (PCI PTS HSM v5.0) from operational environment compliance (PCI DSS v4.0.1, PIN Security v3.1, P2PE, KMO v1.0). PCI SSC has published PQC preparation guidance but has not yet mandated PQC algorithms in PTS HSM v5.0 — conflating PCI DSS cryptographic inventory duties with HSM device-approval rules creates costly scoping errors.

# Certification Engineer Quantum Impact

## Overview

The Certification Engineer Quantum Impact module (`cert-quantum-impact`, `LM-079`) equips CSTL/ITSEF lab testers, cryptographic module vendor engineers, and scheme/procurement reviewers with the decision framework needed to scope, plan, and verify post-quantum product certifications. It covers six certification-engineering impacts, a nine-criterion Certification Evidence Scope checklist (Yes/No/Unknown), a phased action plan, and three applied decision scenarios. All exercises are educational and do not perform formal laboratory testing or issue certificates.

## Key Concepts

- **FIPS 140-2 Historical List Transition & CMVP Queue Pressure** — active FIPS 140-2 certificates moved to the CMVP Historical List on 21 September 2026; adding PQC algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) requires FIPS 140-3 submissions through a congested Modules in Process (MIP) queue, making submission-route planning (new validation vs. 1SUB/3SUB/5SUB) and lab scheduling critical.
- **ACVP Seed-Driven AFT `keyGen` & `CAST`/`PCT` (IG 10.3.A)** — PQC algorithm testing under ACVP requires deterministic seed-driven Algorithm Functional Tests (AFT) for `keyGen` alongside encapsulation/decapsulation and signing/verification vectors; inside the module boundary, FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG 10.3.A) mandates pre-operational Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Tests (CASTs) and conditional Pairwise Consistency Tests (PCTs).
- **Entropy Source Validation (ESV / SP 800-90B / SP 800-90C)** — FIPS 140-3 modules require validated entropy sources under NIST SP 800-90B via CMVP ESV, and Random Bit Generator (RBG) constructions must align with NIST SP 800-90C (finalized September 2025). PQC key generation depends on full-entropy seeding and documented health tests bound to the target operating environment (OE).
- **EUCC (CIR (EU) 2024/482) & NIAP Policy #33 CNSA 2.0 Cut-Offs** — Common Criteria evaluations diverge across regional schemes: EUCC under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482 references EUCC Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (ACM v2) for PQC parameter guidance and eIDAS QSCD Protection Profiles, while US NIAP CCEVS Policy Letter #33 enforces CNSA 2.0 algorithm cut-offs for National Security System Protection Profiles.
- **PCI PTS HSM v5.0 vs. PCI DSS v4.0.1 Scope Boundaries** — payment security separates hardware device approval (PCI PTS HSM v5.0, listed by PCI SSC without a current PQC algorithm mandate) from operational environment compliance (PCI DSS v4.0.1, PIN Security v3.1, P2PE, KMO v1.0). Conflating device approval with operational cryptographic inventory causes scoping errors.
- **Avoiding ACVP-vs.-CMVP & Marketing-Claim Conflation** — an ACVP validation record proves only algorithm vector conformance on a specified OE; a MIP listing proves only queue entry; neither is an active FIPS 140-3 module certificate. Reviewers must check exact firmware versions, OEs, and Security Policies in primary registries and record `Unknown` where evidence is missing.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 4 interactive steps:

1. **Why It Matters** — reviews six certification-engineering impacts with severity, timeframe, and concrete lab/vendor scenarios.
2. **What to Learn** — self-checks validation skill gaps and links to deep-dive modules (`crypto-product-certification`, `fips-140-3-certification`, `acvp-lab-workflow`, `entropy-randomness`, `cc-eucc-certification`, `pci-certification`, `cbom`, `hsm-pqc`, `standards-bodies`).
3. **How to Act** — generates a phased validation-readiness plan across This Week, 30 Days, 90 Days, and 6 Months, with quick wins, example KPIs, and Markdown export.
4. **Certification Evidence Scope** — nine Yes/No/Unknown questions that identify applicable validation drivers and evidence gaps without treating unanswered items as low exposure.

## Related Standards

- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) — August 2024 NIST PQC standards
- FIPS 140-3 & FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG 10.3.A; FIPS 140-2 Historical List transition September 2026)
- NIST ACVP (Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol)
- NIST CMVP ESV, NIST SP 800-90B, and NIST SP 800-90C (final, September 2025)
- NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards — final, October 2026: 2030 deprecation, post-2035 disallowance)
- NSA CNSA 2.0 & CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2 (October 2026: 2027 new acquisitions, 2030 phase-out, 2031 NSS mandate)
- EO 14412 (22 June 2026) & OMB M-26-15 (24 June 2026: 2030 key establishment, 2031 digital signatures for US federal civilian HVAs/high-impact systems)
- EUCC CIR (EU) 2024/482 & EUCC ACM v2
- NIAP CCEVS Policy Letter #33
- PCI PTS HSM v5.0 & PCI DSS v4.0.1

## Cross-References

- `hsm-pqc` — HSM firmware architecture and PKCS#11 PQC mechanisms
- `standards-bodies` — NIST, ENISA, NIAP, and PCI SSC governance landscape

### What This Is About

Moving your apps and data to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, or SaaS does not automatically make them quantum-safe. Cloud providers manage the physical servers and underlying HSMs, but your team still controls TLS policies, origin connections, KMS key types, key-import workflows, and SaaS vendor checks.

### Why It Matters

Small blind spots in the cloud create big security gaps. A CDN might negotiate hybrid post-quantum TLS (`X25519MLKEM768`) with a browser while the connection to your origin server stays classical. A cloud KMS might support ML-KEM keys in most regions while excluding others, or still wrap imported BYOK keys with classical RSA. And an unanswered SaaS vendor questionnaire hides risk rather than proving safety.

### The Key Takeaway

Map every cloud surface by who controls it and what protected asset it guards, verify live behavior with provider CLI commands and TLS probes instead of relying on marketing claims, and treat every unknown SaaS or multi-account control as an active evidence gap.

### What's Happening

As of late 2026, hybrid TLS 1.3 (`X25519MLKEM768`, RFC 10024) is widely supported at major cloud edges, AWS KMS offers both ML-DSA (June 2025) and ML-KEM (October 2026) keys, Google Cloud KMS offers GA ML-DSA/SLH-DSA signing and Preview HPKE key import, and NIST moved FIPS 140-2 certificates to Historical status in September 2026 — making active FIPS 140-3 verification essential across cloud and SaaS estates.

- Late-2026 GCP PQC posture: Cloud Load Balancing / Cloud Armor hybrid TLS (X25519MLKEM768); Cloud KMS ML-DSA and SLH-DSA signing GA (July 2026); quantum-safe HPKE (RFC 9180) key import in Preview for software-protected keys; verify ML-KEM/X-Wing GA vs. Preview status per region

2. Edge, CDN & Origin TLS (RFC 9846 & RFC 10024)
CDN-to-origin pools, API gateways, and cross-region service meshes (Envoy/Istio) are configured independently. An external scanner showing
at the CDN does not verify the origin leg.
Hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846 and RFC 10024, led by X25519MLKEM768 codepoint 0x11EC) mitigates harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) risk on public and inter-region traffic. Enabling hybrid TLS on a CDN or load balancer only protects the client-to-edge leg; origin-leg TLS, API gateways, service meshes, and middleboxes that truncate oversized ClientHello messages must be tested and verified independently.
Moving your apps and data to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, or SaaS does not automatically make them quantum-safe. Cloud providers manage the physical servers and underlying HSMs, but your team still controls TLS policies, origin connections, KMS key types, key-import workflows, and SaaS vendor checks.
Small blind spots in the cloud create big security gaps. A CDN might negotiate hybrid post-quantum TLS (`X25519MLKEM768`) with a browser while the connection to your origin server stays classical. A cloud KMS might support ML-KEM keys in most regions while excluding others, or still wrap imported BYOK keys with classical RSA. And an unanswered SaaS vendor questionnaire hides risk rather than proving safety.

### What This Is About

Even when post-quantum algorithms like ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA are mathematically strong, real-world software and hardware implementations can still leak secret keys through execution timing, CPU caches, power draw, electromagnetic emissions, or voltage glitches.

### Why It Matters

A single variable-time division instruction (like KyberSlash), an early-exit loop during ML-DSA signing, or returning an error message when ML-KEM decapsulation fails can give an attacker enough signal to recover a private key. On smart cards, embedded devices, and HSMs, physical side channels and fault injection require dedicated masking and verification defenses that carry real cycle, memory, and randomness costs.

### The Key Takeaway

Passing mathematical correctness tests (ACVP) is only the starting line. Verify constant-time behavior on compiled binaries, enforce FIPS 203 implicit rejection without error oracles, budget masking around non-linear bottlenecks (Keccak and A2B/B2A conversions) plus redundant verification for faults, and demand concrete TVLA, FIPS 140-3, and EUCC AVA_VAN evidence rather than marketing claims.

### What's Happening

Following the September 2026 transition of FIPS 140-2 to Historical status, cryptographic module evaluations center on FIPS 140-3 (ISO/IEC 19790 / NIST SP 800-140F / IG PQC) and EUCC (`AVA_VAN.4`/`AVA_VAN.5`), making reproducible side-channel and fault-resistance evidence essential for production PQC deployments.

FIPS 203 ML-KEM.Decaps relies on the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform to achieve IND-CCA2 security. After decrypting c to candidate message m′, decapsulation re-encrypts m′ to c′ and compares c against c′ in constant time. On mismatch, ML-KEM.Decaps must NOT return an error code or abort early; instead it uses a constant-time conditional move (cmov) to return a pseudorandom key K̄ = J(z || c) derived from the secret implicit-rejection seed z. Any timing delta, early-exit memcmp, or distinct API error turns decapsulation into a chosen-ciphertext oracle.

Vulnerable: Compiler emits variable-time DIV / SDIV instruction
// Vulnerable C pattern during ML-KEM message decoding / compression // On many x86, ARM, and RISC-V cores, integer division latency depends on operand magnitude. uint16_t compress_1_vuln(uint16_t coeff) { uint32_t t = ((uint32_t)coeff << 1) + 1665; return (uint16_t)((t / 3329) & 1); // LEAK: secret-dependent dividend in hardware DIV }
Hardware integer division units often terminate early when the dividend is small or has leading zeros. During ML-KEM decapsulation, the intermediate polynomial coefficient depends on secret key s; timing the division across chosen ciphertexts recovers secret coefficients (as shown in KyberSlash1 and KyberSlash2).

# PQC Implementation Security & Side-Channel Resistance

## Topics Covered

- Constant-time pitfalls in FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA): KyberSlash-class variable-latency division (`t / q` with `q = 3329` vs. Barrett/Montgomery constant-time multiply-shift reductions), ML-DSA rejection-sampling early-exit branching (`||z||_∞`, `||r0||_∞`, `||ct0||_∞`), non-constant-time `memcmp` in FO comparison, and secret-dependent memory/cache indexing
- Compiler and binary verification: per-ISA disassembly checks banning `DIV`/`SDIV`/`UDIV` on secret paths, `dudect` statistical timing tests, and `Timecop`/`ctgrind` taint tracking
- Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transform implicit rejection in FIPS 203 (`ML-KEM.Decaps`, Algorithm 18): unconditional computation of `K̄ = J(z || c)`, full-length constant-time comparison of `c` vs. `c'`, branchless `cmov` selection without returning error codes, and immediate zeroization of `m'` and `r'`
- Hardware/embedded masking & fault-injection defenses: linear NTT masking vs. non-linear bottlenecks (A2B/B2A conversions, masked rejection sampling, and FIPS 202 Keccak/SHAKE Chi step), quadratic fresh-randomness demand at higher masking orders, operation shuffling against single-trace horizontal attacks, and redundant verification (verify-after-sign) against voltage/clock glitches and laser faults on FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
- Evaluation evidence and certification scoping: TVLA (`Welch's t-test`, `|t| > 4.5` threshold and key caveats — TVLA detects leakage rather than proving exploitability or ruling out higher-order/template attacks), FIPS 140-3 non-invasive attack mitigation (ISO/IEC 19790:2025, ISO/IEC 17825, NIST SP 800-140F, FIPS 140-3 IG PQC, post-Sept 2026 FIPS 140-2 Historical transition), and EUCC CIR (EU) 2024/482 (`AVA_VAN.4` / `AVA_VAN.5` bound to exact TOE firmware and silicon revision)

1. Timing Leak Inspector — Interactive side-by-side code-pattern triage comparing vulnerable vs. constant-time ML-KEM and ML-DSA snippets with production verification tooling
2. FO Implicit Rejection Lab — Interactive 5-stage `ML-KEM.Decaps` walkthrough contrasting valid ciphertext, 1-bit tampered ciphertext (implicit rejection returning `K̄ = J(z || c)`), and a broken explicit-error/early-exit `memcmp` oracle

Masking & Fault Cost Explorer — Interactive masking-order (`Unmasked`, `1st-Order`, `2nd-Order`) and fault-countermeasure (`None`, `Redundant Verify`, `Shuffling + Redundancy`) trade-off explorer across ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-65, NTT, and Keccak/SHAKE (illustrative educational profiles, not vendor benchmarks)

1. Constant-Time Pitfalls in ML-KEM & ML-DSA
instructions on many x86, ARM, and RISC-V cores. Replace divisions with constant-time Barrett or Montgomery multiply-shift reductions and enforce disassembly gates in CI.
Lookup tables indexed by secret noise or message bits expose cache-line access patterns to co-resident Prime+Probe or Flush+Reload attackers. Use bitsliced or arithmetic formulas (e.g., Hamming-weight subtraction for CBD sampling) or full-table constant-time scans.
A constant-time pass on one compiler version or CPU architecture does not carry over automatically when flags, compilers, or target ISAs change.
On HSMs, smart cards, secure elements, and embedded MCUs where adversaries can capture power consumption or electromagnetic (EM) traces — or inject voltage/clock glitches and laser pulses — constant-time software alone is insufficient. Defense-in-depth combines
Post-quantum lattice schemes introduce distinct timing side channels compared to RSA and ECC. KyberSlash demonstrated that compiling a seemingly harmless division by q = 3329 during ML-KEM message compression/decompression into variable-latency hardware division instructions (DIV/SDIV) leaks secret key bits across decapsulation calls. In ML-DSA signing, branching early on rejection-sampling norm bounds or indexing lookup tables with secret polynomial coefficients leaks masking vector y and ultimately secret vectors s1/s2. Constant-time Barrett or Montgomery multiply-shift reductions, branchless bound masks, and disassembly-level compiler verification are mandatory.
Embedded targets, HSMs, and smart cards exposed to physical power, electromagnetic (EM), or fault-injection (FI) adversaries require countermeasures beyond constant-time software. Linear operations such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) mask cheaply with arithmetic shares, whereas non-linear steps — arithmetic-to-Boolean (A2B/B2A) conversions, centered binomial sampling, rejection checks, and the Keccak/SHAKE (FIPS 202) Chi layer — dominate cycle, RAM, and fresh-randomness budgets. Redundant verification (re-verifying ML-DSA/SLH-DSA signatures or checking decapsulation invariants) and random operation shuffling defend against clock/voltage glitches and laser faults.
Constant-Time: Barrett multiply-shift reduction (no division instruction)
// Constant-Time Barrett-style multiply-shift for q = 3329 // Uses fixed-latency multiply + shift; verify assembly emits no DIV/SDIV/UDIV. uint16_t compress_1_ct(uint16_t coeff) { uint32_t t = ((uint32_t)coeff << 1) + 1665; // floor(2^28 / 3329) = 80635; exact for all valid reduced inputs uint32_t q_approx = (t * 80635u) >> 28; return (uint16_t)(q_approx & 1u); }
Replace all secret-dependent `/` and `%` operations with constant-time Barrett or Montgomery multiply-shift reductions, and inspect compiled object code for `div`, `idiv`, `sdiv`, or `udiv` instructions across every target ISA and compiler optimization flag.
Constant-Time: Branchless absolute value + full-vector mask accumulation
// Constant-time infinity-norm check across all coefficients // Only the final single-bit rejection decision (publicly visible as retry count) is branched on. uint32_t check_norm_ct(const int32_t *z, size_t len, int32_t bound) { uint32_t fail_mask = 0; for (size_t i = 0; i < len; i++) { int32_t sign = z[i] >> 31; // arithmetic shift: 0 or -1 int32_t abs_val = (z[i] ^ sign) - sign; // branchless |z[i]| // High bit set if (bound - 1 - abs_val) < 0, i.e., abs_val >= bound fail_mask |= (uint32_t)(bound - 1 - abs_val) >> 31; } return fail_mask & 1u; }
Constant-time software norm checks stop timing leaks of failing indices, but single-trace power/EM attacks during `y` generation or `c * s1` still require hardware masking or shuffling.
Non-Constant-Time memcmp & Branch in FO Re-Encryption Check
Constant-Time: Bitwise OR diff + branchless cmov selecting K or K̄
// Constant-time FO ciphertext verification and implicit-rejection selection // Always computes both K and K_bar = J(z || c), then selects without branching or error codes. void decaps_select_ct(uint8_t *out_k, const uint8_t *k_valid, const uint8_t *k_reject, const uint8_t *c, const uint8_t *c_prime, size_t c_len) { uint32_t diff = 0; for (size_t i = 0; i < c_len; i++) { diff |= (uint32_t)(c[i] ^ c_prime[i]); } // mask = 0xFFFFFFFF if diff != 0 (mismatch -> select k_reject), else 0x00000000 uint32_t mask = (uint32_t)(-((diff | (~diff + 1u)) >> 31)); for (size_t i = 0; i < 32; i++) { out_k[i] = (uint8_t)((k_valid[i] & ~mask) | (k_reject[i] & mask)); } }
Compare the entire ciphertext byte-by-byte with bitwise XOR/OR, derive a full-width constant-time bitmask, select between `K` and `K̄ = J(z || c)` via constant-time `cmov`, and always return success without exposing whether re-encryption matched.

LM-082.curious:
### What This Is About

Power grids run on equipment designed to last 15 to 25 years, from high-voltage substation protection relays to millions of smart meters. Moving energy infrastructure to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is not a simple software swap — protection relays must trip in under 4 milliseconds, and narrowband smart-meter radios cannot carry multi-kilobyte quantum-safe signatures on every packet.

### Why It Matters

If a utility tries to drop large post-quantum signatures straight into real-time substation links, protection messages miss their timing budgets. At the same time, waiting 20 years for field equipment to retire leaves long-lived grid topology records, control-center links, and customer metering archives exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later interception.

### The Key Takeaway

Keep fast symmetric cryptography (`HMAC-SHA-256` and `AES-256`) on real-time protection and constrained meter links, move key distribution and WAN gateways (`TLS 1.3` RFC 10024 and `IKEv2` RFC 9370) to hybrid `ML-KEM-768` first, and build PQC firmware verification (`LMS-SHA256` or `ML-DSA`) into every new equipment RFP now.

### What's Happening

NIST finalized NIST IR 8547 in October 2026 (2030 classical deprecation, 2035 disallowance), while energy regulations remain layered: NERC CIP and EU NIS2 govern cybersecurity risk management without setting standalone PQC algorithm deadlines, whereas the non-binding EU PQC Roadmap v1.1 targets 2030/2035 milestones and US federal power systems follow EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15.

Power grids combine harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) confidentiality exposure on long-lived control-center and topology data with high-consequence integrity and availability risks on firmware signing and telecontrol authentication. Always distinguish operational grid services (such as the SCADA telemetry/control service, AMI head-end collection service, and substation firmware-update service) from protected assets (long-lived grid topology records, customer metering histories, and field IED root-of-trust keys).
IEC 62351 secures IEC 61850 substation communications, but GOOSE and Sampled Values (SV) protection-relay frames operate under strict <4 ms real-time latency budgets and ~1,500-byte Ethernet MTUs where 2,420-byte ML-DSA-44 signatures cannot sit in the tripping loop. Instead, substations keep symmetric HMAC-SHA-256 / AES-256-GCM on the real-time data plane while migrating out-of-band key distribution (GDOI RFC 8052 / TLS 1.3 RFC 9846 + RFC 10024) and SCADA WAN gateways (IKEv2 RFC 9370) to hybrid PQC. Similarly, DNP3-SA (IEEE 1815) uses symmetric HMAC-SHA-256 per-message authentication with PQC-protected update-key distribution.
Regulatory obligations in energy are layered rather than uniform. NERC CIP (CIP-005, CIP-007, CIP-010, CIP-011, CIP-012, CIP-013) governs North American Bulk Electric System (BES) cyber security controls and supply-chain risk management without setting a standalone PQC algorithm deadline. In the EU, the NIS2 Directive establishes cybersecurity risk-management duties for critical energy entities and does not set a fixed PQC deadline; 2030/2035 transition targets come from the non-binding EU NIS Cooperation Group PQC Roadmap v1.1. US federal power marketing administrations and covered federal civilian systems follow EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15 alongside NIST IR 8547 (final October 2026).
FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), NIST SP 800-208 (LMS/XMSS), NIST IR 8547 (final Oct 2026), NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 (OT Security), IEC 62351-6 (IEC 61850 security), IEC 62443-4-2 (IACS components), IEC 62056-5-3 (DLMS/COSEM), RFC 8052 (GDOI for IEC 62351), RFC 9370 (IKEv2 multiple key exchanges), RFC 9846 & RFC 10024 (TLS 1.3 hybrid), NERC CIP-005/007/010/011/012/013, NIS2 Directive & EU PQC Roadmap v1.1, EO 14412 & OMB M-26-15.

If a utility tries to drop large post-quantum signatures straight into real-time substation links, protection messages miss their timing budgets. At the same time, waiting 20 years for field equipment to retire leaves long-lived grid topology records, control-center links, and customer metering archives exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later interception.
Keep fast symmetric cryptography (`HMAC-SHA-256` and `AES-256`) on real-time protection and constrained meter links, move key distribution and WAN gateways (`TLS 1.3` RFC 10024 and `IKEv2` RFC 9370) to hybrid `ML-KEM-768` first, and build PQC firmware verification (`LMS-SHA256` or `ML-DSA`) into every new equipment RFP now.
NIST finalized NIST IR 8547 in October 2026 (2030 classical deprecation, 2035 disallowance), while energy regulations remain layered: NERC CIP and EU NIS2 govern cybersecurity risk management without setting standalone PQC algorithm deadlines, whereas the non-binding EU PQC Roadmap v1.1 targets 2030/2035 milestones and US federal power systems follow EO 14412 and OMB M-26-15.

# Custody Key Threats & Controls — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Keeping a digital-asset private key locked inside hardware does not stop theft if an attacker can trick people or software into signing the wrong transaction. This module shows who can actually make a custody system sign today, how real incidents succeeded without stealing a raw key, and which combinations of controls stop them.

## Why It Matters

Standard hardware security module APIs such as PKCS#11 `C_Sign` sign whatever 32-byte digest an authorized session sends them — they do not read blockchain smart-contract calls or judge whether a payee is safe. Meanwhile, browser screens can be tampered with, pre-signed authorizations can stay valid long after an emergency shutdown, and AI agents can be tricked into spending funds unless limits sit inside the signing boundary.

## The Key Takeaway

Security comes from putting transaction decoding, policy checks, and quorum approvals inside a protected boundary, and from stating exactly which authorities — signers, approver screens, recovery quorums, and upgrade keys — an attacker must not control.

## What's Happening

In the interactive labs, you test blind signing against clear signing plus policy enforcement in a browser HSM emulator, gate a classical signature behind post-quantum `ML-DSA-65` quorum approvals with nonce and expiry checks, run a live 2-of-3 RFC 9591 FROST threshold signature where parties enforce independent local policies, and scope an AI agent wallet against prompt injection and runaway loops.

Keeping a digital-asset private key locked inside hardware does not stop theft if an attacker can trick people or software into signing the wrong transaction. This module shows who can actually make a custody system sign today, how real incidents succeeded without stealing a raw key, and which combinations of controls stop them.
Standard hardware security module APIs such as PKCS#11 `C_Sign` sign whatever 32-byte digest an authorized session sends them — they do not read blockchain smart-contract calls or judge whether a payee is safe. Meanwhile, browser screens can be tampered with, pre-signed authorizations can stay valid long after an emergency shutdown, and AI agents can be tricked into spending funds unless limits sit inside the signing boundary.

Compromised requester / host API abuse

A compromised requester can still drain funds within configured velocity caps or to already-allowlisted addresses.
MPC with Shares in HSMs Across Separate Trust Domains
t-of-n threshold shares are generated via DKG (never by a dealer) and isolated in HSMs operated in distinct trust domains.
Threshold t > 1; key was generated via DKG (not imported from a dealer); NO shared orchestrator or policy service can instruct all >= t parties; attacker holds < t HSM credentials/sessions and uncorrupted protocol proofs.
A shared un-verified orchestrator feeding identical forged payloads to all parties defeats threshold separation; protocol bugs (BitForge) require patched implementations.
MPC + Attested Enclave Policy Co-Signer
One signing participant or mandatory co-signer runs policy evaluation inside an attested TEE enforcing admin-approved rules.
If remaining parties can form t without the policy co-signer, policy is advisory only; TEE microarchitectural or bus attacks (TEE.fail / Battering RAM) break single-TEE guarantees.
Enclave Policy + KMS/HSM Signer vs Key Release to Enclave
Pattern (i): Enclave evaluates policy while HSM/KMS retains key and signs. Pattern (ii): HSM/KMS releases exportable key into attested TEE memory (AWS KMS / Azure SKR).
Unattested host access to KMS keys
Pattern (i): KMS/HSM IAM policy admin, attestation verifier, and enclave build authority are not compromised; key stays in HSM. Pattern (ii): Key is marked exportable — cloud/hardware TEE isolation (and vendor endorsement PKI) must hold against host/physical attacks.
Pattern (ii) places raw key material in TEE memory during use; both patterns inherit cloud/hardware attestation trust roots and availability assumptions.
Cross-Cutting Controls: Timelocks, Approval Expiry, Nonce Binding & Quorum Allowlists
Time-delayed execution, bounded approval TTLs, single-use nonce consumption, and quorum-protected allowlists layered onto signing boundaries.
Durable-nonce / pre-signed approval replay (Drift pattern)
Instant drain & silent allowlist tampering
Attacker cannot disable or shorten timelocks, forge fresh nonces, or edit allowlists without a separate admin quorum; monitoring exists during the timelock window.
Emergency response during a timelock requires an independent freeze/cancel authority that does not rely on the compromised quorum; off-chain shutdown alone does not revoke on-chain EIP-7702/permit grants.

HSM holds wrapping key or encrypted share at rest; MPC daemon on host OS holds decrypted share during signing.
Often only in host application or external policy service — must be reinforced inside each party’s boundary.

Inside the HSM physical boundary (never exported to host RAM).

Shares distributed across distinct technologies & operators (e.g., custodian HSM + attested TEE co-signer + client hardware device).
Each share executes inside its own operator’s isolated boundary (HSM, TEE, or client hardware).
Independently inside each trust domain’s boundary (not solely in one shared orchestrator).

On-chain multisig (e.g., Safe.sol threshold) combines distinct owner keys: e.g., one HSM-held owner key + MPC-held owner keys.
Off-chain MPC shares sign for Owner 1; HSM key signs for Owner 2; on-chain contract verifies t-of-n owners.

# Custody Key Threats & Controls

## Overview

The Custody Key Threats & Controls module (35 minutes, intermediate, Industries track, LM-083) examines who can make a digital-asset custody system sign and which control combinations mitigate unauthorized signing today. It complements Digital Assets (LM-045), which covers foundational curves, RFC 6979 nonces, HD wallets, and the five custody layers, without repeating them. It covers keys versus signing authority, nine exfiltration and misuse paths, a nine-row adversary model, AI agent spend authority, chronological case studies (Bybit, Drift, Binance), technical limits of HSMs, MPC, and confidential computing enclaves, control combinations with Rule G1 authority assumptions, and five hybrid MPC + HSM architecture variants. Educational simulations do not verify or certify production custody deployments.

## Key Concepts

### Keys vs signing authority and exfiltration paths

- Possessing a key inside an HSM or MPC cluster does not guarantee funds cannot move if an attacker controls transaction construction, the signing screen, pre-collected off-chain authorizations (EIP-2612 `permit`, Permit2, Solana durable nonces, EIP-7702 persistent `0xef0100` delegations), or an authenticated signing-service session.
- Safe.sol `checkSignatures` enforces a nonzero stored threshold before calling `checkNSignatures`, whereas calling `checkNSignatures` directly relies on caller-supplied threshold and `executor` values.
- Address poisoning (arXiv:2501.16681) requires no victim private key; the attacker generates lookalike vanity addresses with its own keys.
- CertiK recorded 52 verified physical coercion ("wrench attack") incidents globally in H1 2026 (+33.3% YoY, $124.1M recorded exposure, including 20 home invasions and 16 kidnappings).

### AI agent spend authority

- CSA AP2 guidance recommends hardware-backed keys, decentralized allowlists, and bounded Intent Mandate TTLs against mandate spoofing and agent coercion; Coinbase CDP / Wallet MCP illustrates Nitro Enclave isolation and expiring scoped signing grants (early deployment).
- An individual Internet-Draft specifies binding Falcon-1024 and ML-DSA-65 credentials to x402 agentic payments (research, no working-group adoption).
- Prompt-injected agents are treated as compromised requesters: spend caps, allowlists, and human approval thresholds must sit inside the HSM or enclave signing boundary.

### Case studies (victim statements, investigator findings, government attribution separated)

- **Bybit (21 Feb 2025):** Victim statement (26 Feb) and Safe Foundation statement (28 Feb) report compromised Safe{Wallet} developer credentials/machine; Sygnia and NCC Group (10 Mar) detail malicious frontend JavaScript masking a `delegatecall` proxy upgrade; FBI PSA I-022625-PSA (26 Feb) attributes ~$1.5B theft to North Korea ("TraderTraitor").
- **Drift (1 Apr 2026):** Drift's 16 April update states $295M in outstanding user losses and mandates dedicated clear-signing devices; Chainalysis (9 Apr, $285M estimate) explicitly marks the durable-nonce social-engineering account as relayed from Drift's unverified post-mortem while identifying Tornado Cash staging on 10–11 March 2026.
- **Binance (29 Oct 2026):** Imported from the canonical incident record (`canonicalBinanceIncident.ts`) separating Binance's 3 November 2026 initial findings report (Engineer A tampered Homebrew installation, Engineer B fake-recruiter `pyenv` script replacement, 20 October use of an internal AI tool to pivot, 29 October container/signing-service exploitation and 50 EIP-7702 delegations on `Binance14` MPC hot wallet, ~$6.34B impacted / ~$2.85B frozen, 30 October 00:10 UTC zero-address revocation) from the FBI's 31 October 2026 (updated 2 November) "TraderTraitor" attribution (> $6B).

### Limits of HSMs, MPC, and confidential computing

- **HSMs:** OASIS PKCS#11 v3.2 `C_Sign` signs caller-supplied data and defines no transaction parser, transaction-level policy, or MPC/threshold signing mechanism (whereas KMIP 2.1 and KMIP 3.0 CSD02 model Split Key objects). NIST FIPS 140-3 IG distinguishes physical boundaries (IG 1.A/1.B), Excluded Components (IG 2.3.D), Approved Security Service Indicators (IG 2.4.A/C), and Software/Firmware Loading (IG 10.3.F).
- **MPC:** RFC 9591 specifies two-round threshold Schnorr (FROST). Missing zero-knowledge proofs in GG18/GG20 enabled key extraction in BitForge (2023-08-09, 16 to 1B signatures) and `GHSA-h24c-6p6p-m3vx` (`tss-lib <= 1.3.5` small-factor Paillier modulus `N`, fixed with CGGMP21 proofs); ePrint 2023/1234 summarizes four key-extraction attacks (`10^6`, `256`, `16`, and `1` signature).
- **Enclaves / TEEs:** NIST IR 8320E (ipd) notes attestation proves measured state under vendor endorsement PKI; CCC v1.3 marks DoS and invasive physical attacks out of scope. Demonstrated attacks include Foreshadow (SGX), ÆPIC Leak (Intel CPU MMIO affecting SGX), BadRAM (bypassed AMD SEV-SNP; TDX/scalable SGX alias checks resisted), Battering RAM (DDR4 interposer breaking Intel Scalable SGX and AMD SEV-SNP, not TDX), and TEE.fail (DDR5 interposer breaking Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP).

### Hybrid MPC + HSM variants (a)-(e)

- **(a)** Share wrapped by HSM at rest, unwrapped into host RAM during signing (weakest; vulnerable to host root; Dfns documents wrapped-key HSM signing as an alternative to MPC).
- **(b)** Share and policy execute inside HSM boundary via vendor firmware extensions (Entrust CodeSafe / Thales Luna FM; check FIPS 140-3 IG Excluded Components & loading validation).
- **(c)** Mixed trust domains across custodian HSM, enclave co-signer, and hardware approver device (no single vendor/cloud signs; e.g., Google Cloud Confidential Space + Cloud KMS/HSM reference architecture).
- **(d)** HSM as ceremony and recovery anchor (operational details in Module A2, optional further reading).
- **(e)** Layered on-chain multisig / smart account (`Safe.sol`) combining HSM and MPC owner keys.

## Workshop Activities

1. **Blind vs Clear Signing (HSM)** — Compare raw `CKM_ECDSA` blind signing, parse-only warnings, and parse-plus-policy blocking on a hidden `delegatecall` payload in browser SoftHSMv3.
2. **Quorum Approvals (ML-DSA-65 + secp256k1)** — Require 2-of-3 HSM `ML-DSA-65` approvals over decoded payload, nonce, and expiry before `CKM_ECDSA` signing, with tamper, expiry, and replay fault injection.
3. **Threshold Signing (RFC 9591 FROST)** — Run 3-round DKG and 2-of-3 `secp256k1_FROST` signing in page JS with HSM `ML-DSA-65` party authentication, independent per-party policy refusals, and the §5b host-RAM vs in-HSM conceptual diagram toggle.
4. **Control Combination Builder** — Combine HSM, MPC, enclave, trusted display, and timelock controls across three account types to inspect mitigated incidents, Rule G1 assumptions, and residual risks.
5. **Agent Wallet Scoping** — Configure spend caps, signer allowlists, human approval thresholds, grant TTLs, and key isolation against three agent mistake scenarios.

## Related Standards

- IETF RFC 6979, RFC 9591 (FROST), IETF RATS `draft-ietf-rats-pkix-key-attestation-08`
- OASIS PKCS#11 v3.2, OASIS KMIP 2.1 & KMIP 3.0 CSD02
- NIST FIPS 140-3 IG (2026-08-19), NIST IR 8320E (ipd), Confidential Computing Consortium v1.3
- Ethereum EIP-2612, EIP-7702, ERC-7730, ERC-8176, Safe.sol

# Custody Key Lifecycle Operations — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Keeping a digital-asset key safe on day one is only the beginning. This module explains how custody keys are created in ceremonies, refreshed or rotated when people leave, watched for misuse, recovered after a lost device or outage, and retired safely without burning incoming funds.

## Why It Matters

Unlike a website TLS certificate, an ordinary Bitcoin or Ethereum key cannot be "revoked" by publishing a list — as long as coins sit at that address, anyone with the key can spend them, and pausing withdrawals off-chain does not cancel existing on-chain token allowances or EIP-7702 delegations. Meanwhile, rushed disaster-recovery restores can bring back an attacker's foothold, and destroying a retired key too early can permanently trap late customer deposits.

## The Key Takeaway

Every lifecycle stage — generation, refresh, recovery, monitoring, access control, backup, and destruction — carries the same authority assumptions as live signing. Safe custody depends on pre-planned sweeps, separated signing and admin paths, rehearsed canary restores, and verified retirement before destruction.

## What's Happening

In the seven interactive workshops, you classify twelve custody items between revoke, rotate, reshare, and sweep; stress-test recovery and inheritance plans against five real disruptions; audit a key-ceremony script for eight planted defects; triage twelve custody alerts across pre-signing, mempool, and confirmed stages; spot eight effective-permission conflicts in a custody access matrix; run three disaster-recovery drills; and sequence safe key decommissioning.

An EOA key cannot be revoked. You must sweep all liquid funds to pre-generated destination keys and revoke any active ERC-20 allowances or EIP-7702 delegations; locked or staked assets cannot be swept until transferable, and future deposits to the old address remain at risk.

Safe OwnerManager.sol allows the remaining 3-of-5 quorum to call swapOwner or removeOwner on-chain without moving funds (assuming no attacker-controlled module, guard, or upgrade key bypasses the owner quorum).
Healthy remaining quorum, verified replacement owner key, and audited module/guard configuration.

Scheduled rotation of the HSM wrapping key that protects encrypted backup envelopes.
Rotating a wrapping key in envelope encryption normally re-wraps each data key rather than re-encrypting the underlying data — and provides the operational window to move backup envelopes to a stronger wrapping scheme.

The Custody Key Lifecycle Operations module (38 minutes, intermediate, Industries track, LM-084) explains how digital-asset custody keys are created, guarded, watched, recovered, and retired in daily operation. Building on Module A1 (Custody Key Threats & Controls, LM-083) and linking foundational coverage in Digital Assets (LM-045) and KMS & PQC (LM-016), it covers eight lifecycle domains: threshold key lifecycle (§5a), rotation and revocation (§5e), recovery and inheritance (§5f), key ceremonies (§5g), monitoring and alerting (§5h), access control and path separation (§5i), backup and disaster recovery (§5j), and destruction and decommissioning (§5k), plus a takeaways matrix (§9A). Educational simulations do not verify or certify production custody deployments.
Distributed Key Generation (DKG) avoids a single-point dealer, whereas dealer import briefly materializes the full secret.
Proactive share refresh (Herzberg et al. CRYPTO 1995; CGGMP21 ePrint 2021/060) refreshes shares of the same secret to resist mobile adversaries and supports membership change, while identifiable abort attributes protocol-blocking faults. NISTIR 8214 notes that threshold systems add protocol complexity and can increase the attack surface.
ERC-20 allowances (`approve`, EIP-2612 `permit`, Permit2) and EIP-7702 delegations (`0xef0100 || address`) must be revoked explicitly on-chain — suspending off-chain withdrawals does not invalidate existing on-chain authorizations (illustrated by the 29 October 2026 Binance incident record).
Smart accounts (Safe `OwnerManager.sol`, ERC-4337 accounts) rotate owners on-chain without moving funds, subject to Rule G1 assumptions on modules, guards, and upgrade keys.

# Custody Key Lifecycle Operations

## Overview

The Custody Key Lifecycle Operations module (38 minutes, intermediate, Industries track, LM-084) explains how digital-asset custody keys are created, guarded, watched, recovered, and retired in daily operation. Building on Module A1 (Custody Key Threats & Controls, LM-083) and linking foundational coverage in Digital Assets (LM-045) and KMS & PQC (LM-016), it covers eight lifecycle domains: threshold key lifecycle (§5a), rotation and revocation (§5e), recovery and inheritance (§5f), key ceremonies (§5g), monitoring and alerting (§5h), access control and path separation (§5i), backup and disaster recovery (§5j), and destruction and decommissioning (§5k), plus a takeaways matrix (§9A). Educational simulations do not verify or certify production custody deployments.

## Key Concepts

### Threshold key lifecycle (§5a)

- Distributed Key Generation (DKG) avoids a single-point dealer, whereas dealer import briefly materializes the full secret.
- Proactive share refresh (Herzberg et al. CRYPTO 1995; CGGMP21 ePrint 2021/060) refreshes shares of the same secret to resist mobile adversaries and supports membership change, while identifiable abort attributes protocol-blocking faults. NISTIR 8214 notes that threshold systems add protocol complexity and can increase the attack surface.

### Rotation and revocation (§5e)

- Ordinary Bitcoin UTXO and Ethereum EOA keys have no revocation mechanism; rotation requires sweeping funds to pre-planned destination keys, which cannot move locked/staked assets or stop future deposits.
- ERC-20 allowances (`approve`, EIP-2612 `permit`, Permit2) and EIP-7702 delegations (`0xef0100 || address`) must be revoked explicitly on-chain — suspending off-chain withdrawals does not invalidate existing on-chain authorizations (illustrated by the 29 October 2026 Binance incident record).
- Smart accounts (Safe `OwnerManager.sol`, ERC-4337 accounts) rotate owners on-chain without moving funds, subject to Rule G1 assumptions on modules, guards, and upgrade keys.
- Proactive MPC refresh does not change the public key or protect a compromised key, and assumes erasure of old-epoch shares.
- Control-plane credentials rotate with KMS tools and X.509 certificates use CRL/OCSP (RFC 5280, RFC 6960 — certificate status, not on-chain key status); ERC-7730 defines versioned descriptor schemas without expiry/revocation, while ERC-8176 adds EAS revocation and `expirationTime`.

### Recovery and inheritance (§5f)

- Compares SLIP-0039 Shamir shares, HSM M-of-N backup cards (vendor pattern, e.g. Thales Luna Backup HSM 7), client-held MPC recovery kits (vendor pattern, e.g. Fireblocks Recovery Utility), Bitcoin timelocks (BIP-68/BIP-112 relative timelocks capped at 65,535 blocks or ~388 days; BIP-65 absolute timelocks for multi-year delays; BIP-379 Miniscript), and smart-account guardian recovery (Safe{RecoveryHub}, ERC-4337).
- Recovery paths are an attack surface: mitigate social engineering, forged incapacity claims, and coercion with delays, veto windows, independent guardian channels, and rehearsals. Inheritance guidance covers technical patterns only (not legal/estate advice).

### Key ceremonies (§5g)

- Separates ceremony administrator, key custodians, operators, independent witnesses, and auditor (citing ICANN Root Zone KSK DPS 8th Edition §4.2.2, IANA Root KSK Ceremonies, NIST SP 800-57 Part 2 Rev. 1, CCSS v9.0 Level 3, and CA/B Forum TLS BR v2.2.9 §6.1.1.1 — which allows either a Qualified Auditor witness OR a video recording of the whole generation).
- Contrasts custody root ceremonies with automated per-vault MPC DKG and with zero-knowledge trusted-setup ceremonies (Ethereum KZG Ceremony) whose goal is secret destruction.

### Monitoring and alerting (§5h)

- Organizes signals across signing paths, key infrastructure (e.g. Azure Cloud HSM audit-log tutorial as one vendor example), governance changes (Safe `ModuleManager.sol` / `GuardManager.sol` events), and on-chain activity (ERC-20 `Approval` events; EIP-7702 type-4 authorization lists / account code, which emit no dedicated log).
- Distinguishes pre-signing (can block), mempool (seconds to minutes), and confirmed-chain (can only protect later activity) stages; frames with NIST CSF 2.0 Detect/Respond, SEAL 911 (industry resource), and Tenderly Web3 Actions (vendor pattern).

### Access control (§5i)

- Separates signing path from administration path; enforces separation of duties (NIST SP 800-53 AC-5/AC-6) in the boundary.
- Quotes PKCS#11 v3.2 & Usage Guide (`CKU_SO` vs `CKU_USER`, `CKA_ALWAYS_AUTHENTICATE` / `CKU_CONTEXT_SPECIFIC`, noting SO PIN-reset authority under Rule G1), NIST SP 800-63B-4 (synced passkeys at AAL2, hardware-bound non-exportable keys at AAL3), NIST SP 800-207 / 800-207A zero-trust workload identities, and Thales Multifactor Quorum Authentication (vendor pattern).

### Backup and disaster recovery (§5j)

- Covers key material, policy/quorum configuration, audit logs, and chain-side operating state (derivation indexes, nonces, pending transactions).
- Applies NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 (RTO/RPO/testing), ISO 22301:2019 (catalogue reference), and vendor patterns (AWS CloudHSM cross-region backups, Luna Backup HSM, Fireblocks Recovery Utility).
- Enforces canary/drill-key restore testing, authoritative inventories against rollback, and restore-after-compromise rules (known-good backup + authenticated replay + chain reconciliation before signing resumes).

### Destruction and decommissioning (§5k)

- Chain keys: sweep -> revoke allowances/delegations/owners -> announce & monitor -> cold retention window -> destroy, so late deposits are not permanently burned.
- HSMs & KMS: PKCS#11 `C_DestroyObject` (`CKA_DESTROYABLE` / `CKR_ACTION_PROHIBITED`, single object only), KMIP v2.1 state transitions (deactivate/revoke before Destroy), FIPS 140-3 IG / ISO/IEC 19790:2012 SSP zeroisation, NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (Clear, Purge / cryptographic erase, Destroy + verification), and Entrust nShield decommissioning (vendor pattern).
- Preserves audit logs, ceremony/destruction evidence, and retired public keys/addresses.

## Workshop Activities

1. **W9. Revoke or Rotate Matrix** — Classify 12 custody items across revoke, rotate in place, reshare, sweep funds, revoke allowances, and nothing possible.
2. **W10. Recovery & Inheritance Planner** — Configure recovery mechanisms, delays, guardians, and heir paths for a custody desk, family office, and individual across five disruption events.
3. **W12. Ceremony Script Review** — Audit a 10-step ceremony script to flag eight planted defects without misflagging valid BR §6.1.1.1 practices.
4. **W14. Custody Alert Triage** — Assign severity and response (log / page / auto-pause) to 12 replayed custody events and compare stage finality.
5. **W15. Access Matrix Review** — Inspect a 10-role permission matrix for eight effective-permission conflicts across groups, service identities, and break-glass accounts.
6. **W16. Disaster Recovery Drill** — Choose backup source, restore order, quorum presence, and tier resume plan across three outage/compromise scenarios.
7. **W17. Decommission Checklist** — Order retirement steps and keep-vs-destroy decisions for a hot-wallet address, HSM model, and departed approver share.

5g. Key Ceremonies (Procedure, Evidence & Failure Modes)
introduces what a key ceremony is. Here we focus on operational procedure, verifiable evidence, and failure modes — distinguishing physical root-key ceremonies from automated per-vault MPC DKG and from zero-knowledge trusted-setup ceremonies.
Keeping a digital-asset key safe on day one is only the beginning. This module explains how custody keys are created in ceremonies, refreshed or rotated when people leave, watched for misuse, recovered after a lost device or outage, and retired safely without burning incoming funds.
The ICANN Root Zone KSK Operator DNSSEC Practice Statement (8th Edition) enumerates separated trusted roles for HSM smart-card and safe ceremonies: System Administrators, Crypto Officers, Recovery Key Share Holders, Safe Security Controllers, Internal Witnesses, and Ceremony Administrators.
CryptoCurrency Security Standard (CCSS) v9.0 covers Key/Seed Generation (1.01) and Wallet Creation (1.02) and requires independently witnessed key ceremonies at Level 3.
Zero-knowledge trusted-setup ceremonies (such as the Ethereum KZG Ceremony) are a distinct ceremony class whose sole security goal is destroying every participant’s secret ("toxic waste") rather than preserving a usable custody key.
Separates ceremony administrator, key custodians, operators, independent witnesses, and auditor (citing ICANN Root Zone KSK DPS 8th Edition §4.2.2, IANA Root KSK Ceremonies, NIST SP 800-57 Part 2 Rev. 1, CCSS v9.0 Level 3, and CA/B Forum TLS BR v2.2.9 §6.1.1.1 — which allows either a Qualified Auditor witness OR a video recording of the whole generation).

Custody Key Lifecycle Operations — In Simple Terms
Proactive share refresh (resharing) gives every party new shares of the same secret, defeating a mobile adversary who collects shares across epochs. It does NOT change the public key or protect a key whose threshold was breached, and requires verified erasure of old-epoch shares.
Removing a person requires both revoking their device/API credentials AND removing them from the quorum via a protocol-specific membership-change reshare (or on-chain owner removal / HSM approver-key removal), then verifying remaining threshold and separation rules.
CGGMP21 (IACR ePrint 2021/060) specifies a UC-secure proactive threshold ECDSA protocol with periodic key-share refresh and identifiable aborts so honest parties can detect and attribute protocol-blocking faults.
NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 (final) defines key-lifecycle states, cryptoperiod selection factors, and guidance for key rotation, backup, archival, and destruction.
§5.3.6 Cryptoperiods & §7 Key Management Lifecycle
NIST SP 800-57 Part 2 Rev. 1 defines split knowledge and dual control as organizational safeguards so no single person can generate, copy, or take away a usable cryptographic key during sensitive lifecycle procedures.
Custody failures happen across the entire key lifecycle, not only during signing: unrevoked token allowances or EIP-7702 delegations outlive withdrawal pauses, untested recovery paths become attack paths, rushed restores re-enable attacker footholds, and premature key destruction permanently burns incoming funds.

# Custody PQC Migration — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A future quantum computer capable of breaking elliptic-curve cryptography does not just threaten blockchain addresses — it also threatens the encrypted channels, backup envelopes, and hardware attestation chains that surround a custody platform. This module explains what changes for HSMs, MPC clusters, enclaves, Shamir seed backups, hardware wallets, and smart accounts, and which parts a custodian can migrate today without waiting for blockchains to upgrade.

## Why It Matters

None of today’s custody architectures is quantum-safe on its own. Classical threshold MPC still outputs an ordinary elliptic-curve signature, share backups encrypted under RSA or ECDH can be harvested today and decrypted later, and no NIST-standardised post-quantum threshold signature exists yet. Waiting for Bitcoin or Ethereum to adopt post-quantum consensus leaves platform-controlled secrets and long-lived recovery envelopes unnecessarily exposed.

## The Key Takeaway

Separate your custody stack into three clocks: **platform-controlled** (channels, share backups, approval signatures — fix harvest-now-decrypt-later risks today with hybrid ML-KEM and move control-plane signing to ML-DSA), **account-controlled** (smart accounts can test hybrid PQ verification while watching residual classical keys), and **chain-controlled** (track protocol proposals without betting on unfinalised dates).

## What's Happening

In the interactive labs, you inspect what a quantum attacker breaks first across HSM, MPC, and enclave stacks, classify 15 custody components into migration phases and export a CSV/Markdown plan, explore how Shamir secret sharing compares to SLIP-39 encoding and hybrid KEM-DEM backup envelopes, and dissect hardware wallet "quantum-ready" claims into four distinct parts.

# Custody PQC Migration

## Overview

The Custody PQC Migration module (40 minutes, intermediate, Industries track, LM-085) answers what a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) changes for digital-asset custody and how custodians plan migration across platform-, account-, and chain-controlled layers. It builds on Digital Assets (LM-045) and Custody Key Threats & Controls (Module A1, LM-083) without repeating them, focusing on HSM/MPC/enclave quantum deltas, post-quantum threshold signing research, SLIP-39 and Shamir seed-backup internals, hardware wallet claim decomposition, post-quantum smart accounts, phased migration planning, and quantum views of custody operations. All workshops are educational simulations using fictional data and do not certify or validate deployed custody systems.

## Key Concepts

### Quantum limits delta (HSM, MPC, Confidential Computing)

- **HSM delta:** Beyond Shor recovery of exposed on-chain EC keys (LM-045), channels into HSM clusters carry confidential shares, policy updates, and backup material under classical key exchange — an immediate harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) target.
- **MPC delta:** Threshold ECDSA/EdDSA produces ordinary classical signatures (RFC 9591 FROST; CMP ePrint 2020/492; CGGMP21 ePrint 2021/060). Paillier and Strong-RSA assumptions inside CMP/CGGMP21 and classical party-to-party channels are quantum-vulnerable. As of November 2026, no NIST-standardised threshold variant of a standardised PQ signature exists; NIST IR 8214C leads to a characterization report rather than a competition selection.
- **Confidential computing delta:** Platform attestation chains remain classical today — Intel SGX DCAP ECDSA, AWS Nitro COSE ES384, AMD SEV-SNP VCEK ECDSA P-384, and Intel TDX DCAP — and attested TLS uses classical key exchange unless configured hybrid.

### Evolution & PQ threshold MPC research

- **Standards & firmware:** CAVP-validated ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA firmware exists (CAVP validates algorithm conformance, not full CMVP module validation); OASIS PKCS#11 v3.2 defines ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA mechanisms; RFC 10024 standardises PQ/T hybrid key agreement for TLS 1.3; TPM 2.0 Library V185, DMTF SPDM 1.4.1, and Caliptra 2.1 advance PQ attestation while PQ RATS (`draft-elekula-rats-pqc-attestation-00`) is an individual draft and FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware authenticators do not yet show widespread PQ deployment despite RFC 9964 COSE identifiers.
- **Threshold PQ signing (all research, not standardised):** ML-DSA rejection sampling and secret nonces complicate thresholdization. Two research families exist: (i) FIPS 204-compatible threshold ML-DSA (Quorus ePrint 2025/1163, Mithril ePrint 2026/013, TALUS arXiv 2603.22109, Shamir-nonce DKG arXiv 2601.20917) and (ii) threshold-friendly non-FIPS-204 variants (Threshold Raccoon ePrint 2024/184, TRaccoon ePrint 2025/849, Hermine ePrint 2026/419, Ringtail ePrint 2024/1113). SLH-DSA has early research (Aker ePrint 2026/2899; threshold FHE/CKKS ePrint 2026/2360). Custody alternatives include separating ML-DSA/SLH-DSA member authentication from quorum authorization (arXiv 2607.08226), smart-account verification, and hybrid classical-threshold + PQ backup keys.

### Shamir seeds (SLIP-39) & PQ hardware wallet claims

- **SLIP-39:** Replaces BIP-39 mnemonics with byte-wise GF(256) Shamir sharing, a four-round PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 Feistel passphrase layer, and an RS1024 checksum. Ideal Shamir reveals zero information below threshold `t`, while SLIP-39 interpolates a 4-byte digest with the secret for reconstruction validation. Quantum reaches seed custody via exposed derived EC keys, BIP-32 non-hardened xpub + child-key parent recovery (hardened derivation avoids this), RSA/ECDH share envelopes (fix with hybrid KEM-DEM / `draft-ietf-hpke-pq`), and Feldman/Pedersen VSS limits. Deriving ML-DSA (`ξ`) or ML-KEM (`d, z`) seeds from a wallet seed via hardened HMAC is a proposed construction, not FIPS behaviour; no standard PQ HD derivation path or xpub equivalent exists as of November 2026.
- **Hardware wallets:** Split any "quantum-ready" claim into four parts — (1) device integrity & attestation (e.g. Trezor Safe 7 SLH-DSA-128 firmware + ML-DSA-44 attestation), (2) transaction signing accepted by a chain (e.g. announced Freedom Factory PQ1 vendor-defined SPHINCS+ C10 for EVM smart accounts), (3) seed & derivation, and (4) host channel & clear-signing display for larger PQ signatures (ML-DSA-44: 2,420 B; SLH-DSA-128s: 7,856 B; SLH-DSA-128f: 17,088 B). Separate Blockstream hash-based timing benchmarks from Ledger Donjon secure-element RAM/flash and side-channel analyses.

### PQ smart accounts & phased custody migration path

- **PQ smart accounts:** On-chain policy boundaries hold against a compromised custodian stack only under explicit Rule G1 authority assumptions (no single stack holds signer, guardian, recovery, or upgrade authority). No PQ precompile is live on Ethereum mainnet as of November 2026 (drafts: EIP-8051, EIP-8052, EIP-8355, EIP-7932, EIP-8141; prototypes: ZKNOX ETHDILITHIUM / ETHFALCON; contrast Algorand Falcon). Separate residual classical **authorization** dependencies (EIP-7702 persistent delegation and legacy `ecrecover`/`permit` paths unless revoked via draft EIP-7851, classical guardians, upgrade keys, L2 bridge keys) from **liveness/fee** dependencies (ERC-4337 bundlers, L2 sequencers).
- **Migration phases (0–4):** Phase 0 CBOM splits platform-controlled, account-controlled, and chain-controlled dependencies and separates confidentiality (HNDL) from future forgery (authentication). Phase 1 executes no-regret platform controls now (RFC 10024 hybrid TLS, hybrid KEM-DEM backup re-wrapping, CAVP/CMVP-scoped HSM firmware, ML-DSA control-plane approvals, address hygiene). Phase 2 tracks chain proposals (BIP-360 P2MR, BIP-361, Ethereum, Solana) and downtime/fee budgets. Phase 3 manages interim MPC/threshold designs. Phase 4 enforces crypto-agility (NIST CSWP 39), ACVP evidence, and regulatory alignment (NIST IR 8547 2030/2035, MAS, HKMA, BIS Paper 158, ASC X9, CISA/NSA/NIST; MiCA and DORA carry no explicit PQC mandate as of November 2026).

## Workshop Activities

1. **Quantum Limits & HNDL Check (W5)** — Identify what a CRQC breaks first in each custody combination and which party-to-party channel messages are exposed to HNDL under classical key exchange.
2. **Custody Migration Planner (W7)** — Classify 15 custody components by control plane, migration phase, and HNDL exposure; evaluate account-type residual classical dependencies (EOA, ERC-4337 hybrid, EIP-7702 EOA, PQ-only smart account) and recovery-material CRQC horizon assumptions; export CSV or Markdown.
3. **Shamir Seed & Envelope Demo (W8)** — Compare ideal GF(256) Shamir t-1 uniformity against SLIP-39's 4-byte digest encoding, inspect RSA/ECDH vs hybrid KEM-DEM share envelopes, and test ceremony metadata binding.
4. **HW Wallet Claim Reader (W13)** — Sort hardware wallet statements across the four decomposition layers, assign maturity labels, and apply the five evaluation questions.

## Related Standards

- NIST FIPS 203, FIPS 204, FIPS 205, NIST IR 8547, NIST IR 8214C, NIST CSWP 39, NIST NCCoE SP 1800-38B
- OASIS PKCS#11 v3.2, IETF RFC 10024, RFC 9591 (FROST), RFC 9334 (RATS), RFC 9711 (EAT), RFC 9964, RFC 4998 (ERS), RFC 10033, `draft-ietf-hpke-pq`
- TCG TPM 2.0 Library V185, DMTF SPDM 1.4.1, Caliptra 2.1, W3C WebAuthn
- BIP-32, SLIP-0039, Bitcoin BIP-360 / BIP-361 (drafts), Ethereum ERC-4337, EIP-7702, EIP-2612, EIP-7851 / 7932 / 8051 / 8052 / 8141 / 8355 (drafts)

5c. Shamir Secret Sharing for Seeds (SLIP-39) & VSS Deltas
SLIP-0039 replaces BIP-39 mnemonics with byte-wise GF(256) Shamir secret sharing, a four-round PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 Feistel passphrase layer, an interpolated 4-byte digest, and an RS1024 checksum.
SLIP-39: Replaces BIP-39 mnemonics with byte-wise GF(256) Shamir sharing, a four-round PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 Feistel passphrase layer, and an RS1024 checksum. Ideal Shamir reveals zero information below threshold `t`, while SLIP-39 interpolates a 4-byte digest with the secret for reconstruction validation. Quantum reaches seed custody via exposed derived EC keys, BIP-32 non-hardened xpub + child-key parent recovery (hardened derivation avoids this), RSA/ECDH share envelopes (fix with hybrid KEM-DEM / `draft-ietf-hpke-pq`), and Feldman/Pedersen VSS limits. Deriving ML-DSA (`ξ`) or ML-KEM (`d, z`) seeds from a wallet seed via hardened HMAC is a proposed construction, not FIPS behaviour; no standard PQ HD derivation path or xpub equivalent exists as of November 2026.

# Custody Governance & Assurance — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Buying an HSM, holding a SOC 2 report, or showing a crime-insurance certificate does not automatically prove a digital-asset custodian can stop unauthorized transfers. This module explains how to test a custody architecture with six practical evaluation questions, how major jurisdictions actually regulate key management, and what insurance, audits, and proof-of-reserves reports do and do not prove.

## Why It Matters

Governance teams often face bold vendor claims ("policy enforced in hardware", "fully insured", "audited proof of reserves") and overlapping regulatory acronyms across the EU, Hong Kong, Dubai, New York, Singapore, Japan, and Switzerland. Without separating binding statutes from supervisory guidance, accounting rules, and broker-reported market practice, decision-makers can miss real signing-authority gaps or rely on reports whose scope never tested key management.

## The Key Takeaway

Judge custody governance by three tests: (1) where transaction parsing, policy checks, and recovery authority actually sit under explicit Rule G1 assumptions; (2) which regulatory texts legally apply to your entity and licence — quoted verbatim or explicitly marked "not stated"; and (3) whether an audit or insurance policy actually covers the signing boundary rather than merely reporting on a narrow perimeter or capping financial loss after a breach.

## What's Happening

In the interactive Regulation & Assurance Control Mapper (W11), you pick a built-in custody architecture preset, apply applicability gates (entity type, licence, binding force), and compare two or more jurisdictions side by side alongside market-practice insurer questions and auditor tests — with US federal accounting and permissibility texts separated into their own context band and no fabricated compliance verdicts.

When a vendor claims "policy is enforced in hardware", does the signing boundary itself evaluate transaction rules, or does a host broker check policy before calling a policy-free signer?
Policy rules (spend limits, allowlists, quorum thresholds) are evaluated inside the signing boundary (HSM firmware/enclave/co-signer) before producing a signature.
Enough indispensable threshold or multisig signers independently enforce the policy, or an on-chain verifier contract enforces it.
A host application or API broker sitting in front of a policy-free signer is bypassable if the host, container, or API credential is compromised.
Who can modify the policy-engine code, firmware, or configuration, and what quorum gates that change?
Module A1 §5 (Control combinations & signing boundaries)
Does the signer see the full transaction or only a hash?
Can the signing boundary decode the full transaction calldata and recipient, or does it blind-sign a 32-byte digest supplied by a browser or backend?
The signing boundary parses the full raw transaction it signs, or verifies a decoded form cryptographically bound to the exact bytes being signed.
Independent verifier devices decode the raw calldata locally before co-signing; clear-signing descriptors (such as ERC-7730) display human-readable fields on a trusted screen.
Blind-signing a hash lets a compromised UI or frontend substitute a malicious delegatecall or approval while displaying benign details.
Who controls the transaction parser, ABI metadata, and clear-signing descriptor registry (ERC-7730 registry trust)?
Module A1 §5 & W1 (Clear signing); Module B §5d (hardware-wallet PQ specialisation — optional further reading)
Who can change the policy, and is that change checked inside the boundary?
If an attacker cannot bypass the spending policy directly, can they lower the quorum, add their own address to the allowlist, or swap a contract module?
Policy changes require the same or a higher quorum than spending, enforced inside the signing boundary with a mandatory time delay and out-of-band governance alerts.
On-chain timelocked governance with independent guardian veto for smart-account policy updates.
A single admin console user, vendor support role, or unmonitored upgrade key can silently weaken rules before initiating a transfer.
Can a contract-upgrade key, smart-account module, vendor master key, or admin role bypass the policy-change quorum?
Module A2 §5h (Governance-change monitoring) & §5i (Separation of duties)
Are approvers’ keys in attested hardware with a trusted display?
How does the signing boundary know an approval came from a genuine, unrevoked human approver who saw the real transaction?
Approver keys live in attested hardware verified by the signing boundary or an independent verifier, with approvals bound to decoded transaction content and clean revocation.
Independent hardware security keys plus out-of-band transaction verification on a separate device where full trusted-display hardware is not deployed.
Device attestation alone proves neither display correctness nor that the signed approval matches the decoded content shown to the human.
Can a single operator, IT admin, or vendor enrol a new approver device or substitute attestation root certificates?
Module A1 §5 (Approver devices); Module A2 §5e (Approver revocation) & §5i (Enrolment)
How are state, replay, and expiry enforced?
What stops an attacker from replaying an old approval, rolling back a daily spend counter, or abusing a long-lived pre-signed transaction?
Approvals carry fresh nonces and short expiries; replay state (monotonic counters, velocity limits) lives inside the signing boundary, in bound on-chain state, or in distributed consensus state. No long-lived pre-signed transactions.
Authenticated external state anchored by monotonic hardware counters or on-chain nonces when signing hardware itself is stateless.
A stateless HSM cannot hold durable monotonic counters without authenticated state, and host-stored counters or VM snapshots can be rolled back.
Who can reset replay counters, restore a VM snapshot to roll back rate limits, or extend approval expiry?
Module A1 §5; Module A2 §5j (No rollback of counters/nonces); Module B §5d (optional further reading)
How do recovery, rotation, and time locks work?
If operational keys are lost or rotated, does the recovery path become a weaker backdoor than day-to-day spending?
Time locks and veto windows are enforced inside the signing boundary or on-chain; recovery has its own independently satisfiable trigger; key rotation never bypasses the operational quorum.
Geographically distributed offline key-share recovery ceremonies with dual-custody physical vaults and independent witness logs.
An opaque vendor recovery backdoor, unmonitored guardian quorum, or unauthenticated rotation procedure undermines every operational control.
Who holds recovery shares, guardian keys, and upgrade authority, and could they collude to bypass the operational quorum?

Preset A: Single-cluster policy-free HSM + host broker (hot)
Private keys sit in a single PKCS#11 HSM, but transaction parsing, allowlists, and approvals run in a host web service; no cold-storage split, no segregated client wallets, and no formal key-destruction or DR drill.
Illustrates why an HSM alone leaves major control gaps across segregation, cold/hot split, multi-party quorum, recovery, third-party oversight, and resilience testing.
Preset B: Mixed-domain MPC + enclave co-signer + 98/2 cold-hot split
Mixed trust-domain MPC + hardware enclave policy engine with attested clear-signing approvers, 98% offline cold storage / 2% hot cap, client wallet segregation, MFA, daily monitoring, and tested recovery — but no formal key-destruction procedure or sub-custodian register.
Strong operational stack that still surfaces targeted gaps on key destruction (DORA RTS Art. 7) and third-party/sub-custodian governance (DORA Arts. 28–30 / NYDFS Sept 2025).
Preset C: Air-gapped cold vault + witnessed ceremonies + full lifecycle
Offline HSM key generation and storage, M-of-N witnessed ceremonies, legally and operationally segregated client vaults, 98%+ cold split, MFA + least privilege, tested recovery/DR, documented rotation/destruction, sub-custodian due diligence, and annual pen-test/audit.
Preset D: Omnibus sub-custodian + browser multisig UI
Client assets pooled at an external sub-custodian behind a browser multisig interface; basic MFA and backup exist, but no independent clear-signing verifier, no client-level segregation records, no hot/cold split cap, and no sub-custodian audit rights.
