Regulatory silence on an algorithm or architecture does not validate a design; check who holds signing, policy-update, and recovery authority under Rule G1.
Assurance scope depends on management’s system description; verify whether frontend transaction builders, signing-service APIs, upgrade keys, and recovery quorums were actually inside the tested boundary.
Q1 (Where is policy checked?): Strong pattern — policy is evaluated inside the signing boundary (HSM/enclave/co-signer) before signing. Acceptable alternatives — enough indispensable threshold/multisig signers enforce it independently, or an on-chain verifier enforces it. Residual risk — a host broker sitting in front of a policy-free signer can be bypassed if compromised.
Rule G1 check: Who can modify the policy-engine code, firmware, or configuration, and what quorum gates that change?
Q2 (Full transaction or hash only?): Strong pattern — the signing boundary parses the full transaction it signs, or verifies a decoded form cryptographically bound to the raw transaction bytes. Acceptable alternatives — independent verifier devices decode the raw calldata before co-signing. Residual risk — blind-signing a 32-byte digest allows UI/proxy substitution.
Rule G1 check: Who controls the transaction parser, ABI metadata, and clear-signing descriptor registry (e.g., ERC-7730 registry trust)?
Q3 (Policy-change governance): Strong pattern — policy changes require at least the same or a higher quorum than spending, enforced inside the signing boundary with a time delay and out-of-band alerting (Module A2 §5h, §5i). Residual risk — a single admin or vendor support role that can lower thresholds or add allowlist entries collapses spending controls.
Rule G1 check: Can a contract-upgrade key, smart-account module, vendor master key, or admin role bypass the policy-change quorum?
Q4 (Attested approver hardware & trusted display): Strong pattern — approver keys live in attested hardware checked by the signing boundary or an independent verifier, with approvals cryptographically bound to decoded transaction content and revocable cleanly (Module A2 §5e). Residual risk — device attestation alone proves neither display correctness nor that the approval matches the decoded content.
Rule G1 check: Can a single operator, IT admin, or vendor enrol a new approver device or substitute attestation root certificates?
Q5 (State, replay, and expiry): Strong pattern — approvals carry fresh nonces and short expiries, with replay counters and rate limits held inside the signing boundary, in correctly bound on-chain state, or in distributed consensus state (Module A2 §5j); no long-lived pre-signed transactions. Residual risk — a stateless HSM cannot hold durable monotonic counters without authenticated external state, and host-stored state can be rolled back.
Rule G1 check: Who can reset replay counters, restore a VM snapshot to roll back rate-limit state, or extend approval expiry?
Q6 (Recovery, rotation, and time locks): Strong pattern — time locks and veto windows are enforced inside the signing boundary or on-chain; recovery uses an independently satisfiable trigger (Module A2 §5f); key rotation does not bypass the signing quorum (Module A2 §5e). Residual risk — an opaque recovery backdoor or unmonitored guardian set undermines day-to-day quorum controls.
Rule G1 check: Who holds recovery shares, guardian keys, and upgrade authority, and could a subset collude to bypass the operational quorum?

# Custody Governance & Assurance

## Overview

The Custody Governance & Assurance module (30 minutes, intermediate, Industries track, LM-086) answers how a digital-asset custody design is evaluated, regulated, insured, and audited. It builds on the controls taught in Custody Key Threats & Controls (Module A1) and operational lifecycle procedures (Module A2), while linking Module B as optional further reading for long-term evidence and post-quantum supervisory roadmaps. All regulatory, insurance, and audit statements are educational — never legal advice — and every cell either cites an admitted Library text with its edition/as-of date or explicitly states "not stated".

## Key Concepts

### 6. Six custody evaluation questions (Q1–Q6) with Rule G1 authority checks

- **Q1 (Where is policy checked?):** Strong pattern checks policy inside the signing boundary; acceptable alternatives use indispensable signers or an on-chain verifier. Residual risk: a host broker in front of a policy-free signer is bypassable. Rule G1: who can alter policy code or configuration?
- **Q2 (Full transaction or hash only?):** Strong pattern parses the full transaction inside the boundary or verifies a decoded form bound to the raw bytes. Rule G1: who controls the parser and clear-signing descriptors (ERC-7730 registry trust)?
- **Q3 (Policy-change governance):** Strong pattern requires the same or higher quorum than spending, enforced inside the boundary with a delay and alerting (Module A2 §5h). Rule G1: can an upgrade, module, or admin key bypass it?
- **Q4 (Attested approver hardware & trusted display):** Strong pattern checks device attestation inside the boundary or an independent verifier and binds approvals to decoded content, with revocation (Module A2 §5e). Attestation alone proves neither display correctness nor decoded-content binding. Rule G1: can one person or vendor enrol a new approver?
- **Q5 (State, replay, and expiry):** Strong pattern binds approvals to nonces and short expiries, storing counters/rate limits in-boundary, on-chain, or in distributed state (Module A2 §5j); no long-lived pre-signed transactions. Stateless HSMs cannot hold durable monotonic counters without authenticated external state. Rule G1: who can reset counters or roll back state?
- **Q6 (Recovery, rotation, and time locks):** Strong pattern enforces time locks and veto windows in-boundary or on-chain, gives recovery an independently satisfiable trigger (Module A2 §5f), and ensures rotation does not bypass the quorum (Module A2 §5e). Rule G1: who holds recovery, guardian, and upgrade authority?

### 6b. Jurisdiction-scoped regulatory control map & applicability gates

- **EU:** MiCA (Reg. 2023/1114, Art. 75 safekeeping & custody policy, Art. 70), MiCA CASP authorisation RTS (EU 2025/305), ESMA First-Package Final Report, DORA (Reg. 2022/2554, Art. 2(1)(f) CASP scope, Arts. 17–19, 24–30), DORA ICT Risk RTS (EU 2024/1774, Arts. 6–7 cryptographic key lifecycle including generating, renewing, storing, revoking, and destroying keys), and EBA/GL/2025/02.
- **Hong Kong:** SFC VATP Guidelines (§10.6 98% cold-storage "should" expectation; §10.8(a) offline generation / HSM with "appropriate certification") and SFC Circular 25EC44 (15 Aug 2025) on minimum custody obligations and monitoring (Module A2 §5h).
- **Dubai:** VARA Custody Services Rulebook (v2) and Technology and Information Rulebook (v2) — neither names FIPS 140 or Common Criteria; insurance sits in the VARA Company Rulebook (Part VI.D).
- **New York:** NYDFS 23 NYCRR Part 500 Amendment 2 (access privileges §500.7, MFA §500.12, audit trails §500.6, pen-testing §500.5, 72-hour incident notice §500.17), 23 NYCRR §200.9 (BitLicense customer asset protection), and the updated 30 September 2025 Custodial Structures Guidance (superseding Jan 2023).
- **Singapore:** Binding Payment Services Regulations 2019 (Regs. 18B–18C statutory trust safeguarding; Reg. 18G security of DPT instruments and segregation of duties) separated from non-binding guidance in MAS PS-G03 (19 Sept 2024) and MAS TRM Guidelines (Jan 2021).
- **Japan:** Payment Services Act (Art. 63-11) and Cabinet Office Order No. 7 of 2017 (cold-wallet segregation, matching proprietary assets in cold storage for hot-wallet customer holdings, and external audit).
- **Switzerland:** DEBA Art. 242a and Banking Act Art. 16(1bis) / Art. 37d for insolvency segregation; FINMA Guidance 08/2023 is scoped specifically to staking, not general custody.
- **US Federal Context Band (excluded from W11 control cells by instrument-type gate):** SEC SAB 121 (rescinded 23 Jan 2025 by SAB 122, directing ASC 450-20 / IAS 37 loss-contingency accounting) and OCC Interpretive Letters 1170 & 1184 (national bank custody permissibility).
- **International / Industry:** IOSCO FR11/2023 (policy recommendations) and CCSS v9.0 (voluntary industry standard, not regulation).
- **Algorithm-neutral vs architecture-neutral:** Held texts rarely name algorithms, MPC vs HSM, or PQC (quantum supervisory roadmaps like NIST IR 8547, BIS Paper 158, MAS Quantum Advisory, and HKMA Blueprint are optional further reading in Module B §8c), but several explicitly constrain architecture (cold-storage ratios, segregation, statutory trusts).

### 6c. Insurance, audit, and proof of reserves

- **Insurance:** Covers described in broker material (Aon 2025, WTW 2023) include crime/specie (often split cold vs hot), cyber, and D&O, with underwriting scrutiny of key generation, quorum, cold-storage ratios, ceremonies, and exclusions (insider collusion, social engineering / authorised-push transfers, hot-wallet sub-limits, coercion). Statutory hooks: MiCA Art. 75(8) liability cap & Art. 67 prudential own funds/insurance; SFC §10.22–10.23 compensation arrangement (50% cold / 100% hot "should"); VARA Company Rulebook Part VI.D. Insurance caps or transfers loss after the fact; it does not reduce the attack surface.
- **Audit & assurance:** SOC 1 and ISAE 3402 cover internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR); SOC 2 evaluates AICPA Trust Services Criteria; ISAE 3000 (Revised) is a general assurance standard (limited or reasonable assurance against any suitable criteria, not an "international SOC 2"). Type II covers a period over a service-organization-chosen scope and does not inherently test custody key management. DORA TLPT RTS (EU 2025/1190) Art. 2 / Recital 3 sets authority-assessment criteria for TLPT scoping rather than automatically sweeping in every CASP.
- **Proof of Reserves:** Merkle-tree / Provisions (ePrint 2015/1008) cryptographic asset/liability proofs are one construction. Per the PCAOB Investor Advisory (8 March 2023), PoR reports are not audits and may omit complete liabilities, beneficial ownership, encumbrances, or continuing control after the snapshot.

## Workshop Activity

- **W11 — Regulation & Assurance Control Mapper:** Select a built-in custody architecture preset (or mirror a design from Module A1 W4), apply applicability gates (entity type, licence, jurisdiction, effective version, exemptions, binding verb), and compare multiple jurisdictions side by side — never as cumulative mandates — across key-management controls, a separate US federal context band, and market-practice insurer/auditor columns. Unmapped controls report "no mapped control found (reviewer analysis)" rather than "non-compliant".

- Singapore MAS TRM, PS-G03 & Payment Services Regulations 2019; Japan PSA & Cabinet Office Order; Swiss DEBA Art. 242a, Banking Act Art. 16(1bis) & FINMA 08/2023

# AI as an Attacker of Cryptography — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

As artificial intelligence tools become part of software engineering and security testing, organisations ask a straightforward question: can AI break our encryption or steal our keys? This module looks at the actual published evidence across five layers—keys stored in software, bugs in cryptographic libraries, physical side-channel leaks, key-management policies, and the underlying mathematics—and labels every finding as demonstrated, reported, or still hypothesised.

## Why It Matters

Headlines often blur together very different results. In published research through November 2026, AI tools have helped discover real software bugs in cryptographic libraries (such as wolfSSL CVE-2026-5194 and OpenSSL CVE-2026-45445) and weakened an unstandardised candidate signature scheme called HAWK (which its authors promptly withdrew) as well as a reduced 7-round version of AES-128 that requires an impractical 2^105 chosen plaintexts. Meanwhile, AI has NOT broken standardised FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), or full-round AES.

## The Key Takeaway

The immediate practical risk from AI is not a sudden collapse of post-quantum or symmetric mathematics—it is faster discovery of software bugs, insecure code written with AI assistants, and stolen developer or cloud credentials. Nothing in the reviewed evidence justifies delaying or altering standards-based post-quantum migration deadlines (NIST IR 8547 and NSA CNSA 2.0).

## What's Happening

Defenders protect cryptographic systems against AI-assisted attackers with disciplined engineering: pre-commit secret push protection and short-lived workload identity, fast patching of cryptographic libraries (especially new PQC-enabled builds), human-in-the-loop review around AI coding tools, immutable non-exportable HSM key policies, and attack-based side-channel evaluation for embedded targets.

People often ask whether artificial intelligence can suddenly crack the locks that protect our banking, cloud accounts, and software updates. Looking closely at the real tests published so far gives a clear, calmer answer: AI has helped researchers find bugs in encryption software and weaken an experimental signature proposal before it ever became a standard, yet it has not broken the main encryption or post-quantum standards we rely on today.
Where AI actually changes day-to-day security is around the edges—where keys sit in developer files, where programmers accept buggy code from an AI assistant, or where attackers write convincing fake job lures and phishing messages faster. In real incidents, criminals mostly use AI as a helper for social engineering or searching files, rather than an autonomous robot cracking cryptography on its own.

AI as an Attacker of Cryptography — In Simple Terms
Headlines often blur together very different results. In published research through November 2026, AI tools have helped discover real software bugs in cryptographic libraries (such as wolfSSL CVE-2026-5194 and OpenSSL CVE-2026-45445) and weakened an unstandardised candidate signature scheme called HAWK (which its authors promptly withdrew) as well as a reduced 7-round version of AES-128 that requires an impractical 2^105 chosen plaintexts. Meanwhile, AI has NOT broken standardised FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), or full-round AES.
The immediate practical risk from AI is not a sudden collapse of post-quantum or symmetric mathematics—it is faster discovery of software bugs, insecure code written with AI assistants, and stolen developer or cloud credentials. Nothing in the reviewed evidence justifies delaying or altering standards-based post-quantum migration deadlines (NIST IR 8547 and NSA CNSA 2.0).

Cloud KMS / Managed HSM Policy
Setting CKA_EXTRACTABLE=true without CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED=true and a strict CKA_WRAP_TEMPLATE allows an authorised session with wrap access to wrap the key under an untrusted wrapping key (the classical attribute-policy flaw analysed by Tookan via formal model checking in AI-5.1; AI automating such API search remains hypothesised in AI-5.4).
Set CKA_EXTRACTABLE=false and CKA_SENSITIVE=true at key generation for signing keys, or enforce CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED=true plus immutable CKA_WRAP_TEMPLATE constraints.
Template B: Cloud KMS App Role with Wildcard Policy
Even when the HSM keeps raw key bytes non-extractable, combining operator key-use permissions with policy-administration permissions lets a stolen session mutate key policies, bypass dual control, and operate without tamper-evident signed audit records.
Separate IAM key-policy administration from operational callers, require dual control for policy changes or key deletion, and enable signed HSM operation audit logs (AI-5.3).
Template C: PKCS #1 v1.5 Unwrap Enabled Without OAEP/AES-KW
Allowing unrestricted key-import/unwrap templates without modern authenticated wrapping (AES-KW / OAEP) risks exposing historical padding-oracle behaviour on import error paths (AI-5.5 classical baseline, non-AI) and permits unconstrained unwrapped key attributes.
Restrict CKA_UNWRAP_TEMPLATE / CKA_WRAP_TEMPLATE to approved mechanisms (e.g., AES-KW or RSA-OAEP / ML-KEM envelope wrapping) with uniform error handling.
Template D: Hardened Non-Exportable Governance Key
All seven configuration controls are aligned: raw key material is non-extractable inside a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 boundary, policy mutation requires separated dual control, and management actions emit signed audit logs. Caveat: if an authorised application identity itself is stolen, the HSM will still sign authorised requests for that caller.

# AI as an Attacker of Cryptography

Intermediate-level module (50 min, 5 workshop steps) in the Foundations track (`ai-crypto-attacks`, `LM-087`).

## Overview

AI as an Attacker of Cryptography evaluates how AI changes threat models across five cryptographic layers as of 2026-11-21: (1) keys and secrets in software, (2) implementation and protocol flaw discovery, (3) deep-learning side-channel analysis, (4) KMS/HSM key policies, and (5) mathematical cryptanalysis. Every claim is classified under a capability rubric (`demonstrated`, `reported`, or `hypothesised`) separating discovery, reproduction, patch, successful exploitation, and independent replication.

## Key Concepts

- **Two Threats (Quantum vs AI):** Quantum computers target algebraic hardness (RSA/ECC via Shor's algorithm, taught in `quantum-threats` LM-002); reviewed AI results primarily impact implementations, software secrets, and lab side-channel evaluation.
- **Keys & Secrets in Software:** Google Cloud Threat Horizons H1 2026 distinguishes the executive headline from incident detail (`QUIETVAULT` prompted an endpoint LLM to attempt filesystem enumeration while malware stole the GitHub PAT and `UNC6426` pivoted via OIDC). The 29 October 2026 Binance incident (`canonicalBinanceIncident.ts`) assigns local AI causal roles across three preparation branches (`none shown`, `not stated`, `tool-mediated`). Pearce et al. (S&P 2022) and Perry et al. (CCS '23) demonstrate insecure classical crypto code written with early Codex assistants (pre-FIPS 203–205).
- **Finding Flaws in Crypto Code:** wolfSSL `CVE-2026-5194` (`>= 3.12.0, < 5.9.1`, affecting ECDSA/ECC verification when EdDSA or ML-DSA is also enabled—a PQC-enabled build defect, not ML-DSA math) and OpenSSL `CVE-2026-45445` (`AES-OCB IV Ignored on EVP_Cipher() Path`) show AI-assisted vulnerability discovery with zero reported in-the-wild exploitation, alongside Big Sleep, DARPA AIxCC, and OSS-Fuzz benchmarks.
- **Side Channels:** Profiled CNN/MLP deep-learning SCA defeated hardware AES clock jitter (Cagli et al. 2017) and 1st/2nd/3rd-order bitsliced masked Kyber-768 on ARM Cortex-M4 (`STM32F415RGT6`, B2A leakage, `3 × k` chosen ciphertexts, 5 profiling devices; Wang et al. 2023), while non-profiled DL-SCA (Timon 2018/196) still requires physical target traces. NIST SP 800-140F defines no approved non-invasive mitigation test metrics.
- **KMS & HSM Policies:** Classical formal model checking (`Tookan`, Bortolozzo et al. CCS 2010—not AI) and padding oracles (Bardou et al. 2012) show API/attribute exposure; AI automating KMS/HSM API search remains `hypothesised` as of 2026-11-21.
- **AI Cryptanalysis & Bounded Negative Finding:** Claude Mythos Preview reduced unstandardised HAWK (withdrawn 29 Jul 2026) and sped up a 7-of-10-round AES-128 meet-in-the-middle attack (`2^105` chosen plaintexts, `200–800×` faster); Gohr (Speck32/64) and SALSA/PICANTE/VERDE/FRESCA target reduced-round or small/sparse-secret plain LWE. No reviewed AI attack breaks FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), or full-round AES as of 2026-11-21; NIST IR 8547 and NSA CNSA 2.0 migration deadlines remain unchanged.

## Workshop Activities

1. **Secret Hunt (CI & Repo Hygiene)** — inspect dummy `EXAMPLE_FAKE_` leaks across config, Git history, logs, crash dumps, and CI workflows and compare deterministic regex hits against missed leaks.
2. **KMS & HSM Key-Policy Review** — review PKCS #11 v3.2 attributes (`CKA_SENSITIVE`, `CKA_EXTRACTABLE`, `CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED`, wrap templates) and IAM separation without generating call sequences or exporting keys.
3. **Synthetic Trace Learning Lab** — vary synthetic jitter, masking order, and trace count on in-page waveforms to compare template vs shift-tolerant indicators.
4. **Claim & Rubric Sorter** — classify 12 AI-and-crypto statements into demonstrated/reported/hypothesised and full vs reduced scope.
5. **Layered Defence Planner** — select layered defences across three sample systems and inspect residual risk boundaries.

## Related Standards

- NIST FIPS 203, FIPS 204, FIPS 205, NIST IR 8547, NSA CNSA 2.0 & FAQ Ver. 2.2
- OASIS PKCS #11 v3.2, NIST SP 800-140F, FIPS 140-3 IG §12.A
- CVE-2026-5194 (wolfSSL), CVE-2026-45445 (OpenSSL), OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

# The PQC Algorithms: How They Work and How to Choose — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

This module explains the standardised post-quantum algorithms in the words of the documents that define them. FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism that is believed to be secure even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer. FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA, a set of algorithms for generating and verifying digital signatures that is believed to be secure even against adversaries with a large-scale quantum computer.

## Why It Matters

Every sentence in the lesson names the document, the edition and the place it comes from, so a choice of algorithm can be traced to its source.

## The Key Takeaway

In FIPS 203, a key-encapsulation mechanism is a set of algorithms that two parties can use, under certain conditions, to establish a shared secret key over a public channel. FIPS 204 specifies three main ML-DSA algorithms covering key generation (ML-DSA.KeyGen), signature generation (ML-DSA.Sign), and signature verification (ML-DSA.Verify).

## What's Happening

In a KEM, the receiving party begins by running KeyGen to generate a public encapsulation key and a private decapsulation key. Using the encapsulation key, the other party runs Encaps to produce a copy of the shared secret key and an associated ciphertext, then sends the ciphertext back. The first party completes key establishment by running Decaps with the decapsulation key and the received ciphertext to produce a copy of the shared secret key.

qa.answer: NIST IR 8547 states that existing symmetric-cryptography standards, including hash functions, are significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than public-key standards, and NIST does not expect to transition away from them. NIST IR 8547 reports that symmetric primitives with at least 128 bits of classical security are believed to meet at least Category 1, while 112-bit symmetric standards will be disallowed in 2030.
qa.question: Do we need to replace AES and other symmetric algorithms for post-quantum security?

qa.answer: NIST SP 800-227 states that most applications need authentication to prevent machine-in-the-middle attacks, which typically requires additional cryptographic elements such as digital signatures and certificates. NIST SP 800-227 requires that a party using another party's static encapsulation key must have assurance of key ownership, such as through a certificate authority or proof of possession.
qa.question: Does a KEM handle authentication, or do you also need digital signatures?

qa.answer: NIST IR 8413 states that NIST aims to standardize schemes from different cryptographic families so a single advance in cryptanalysis does not leave the world without a viable standard. NIST IR 8413 explains that NIST selected hash-based SPHINCS+ so its signature standards do not rely entirely on lattices, providing a fallback against unforeseen cryptanalytic attacks.
qa.question: Why did NIST standardize post-quantum algorithms from more than one cryptographic family?

qa.answer: In March 2025, NIST IR 8545 reported that HQC was the only fourth-round key-establishment candidate selected for standardization to augment NIST's key-establishment portfolio. On March 11, 2025, NIST announced that HQC, like ML-KEM, is a key encapsulation mechanism, built around error-correcting codes rather than structured lattices. NIST's announcement states that NIST plans to release a draft HQC standard for public comment in about a year, followed by a 90-day comment period and a finalized standard in 2027.
qa.question: What is HQC and when does NIST plan to finalize its standard?

qa.answer: FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism that is believed to be secure even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer. In FIPS 203, a key-encapsulation mechanism is a set of algorithms that two parties can use, under certain conditions, to establish a shared secret key over a public channel. FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM's security is based on the presumed hardness of the Module Learning with Errors (MLWE) problem, which rests on computational problems in module lattices.
qa.question: What is ML-KEM and what hard problem is its security based on?

qa.answer: FIPS 203 specifies three ML-KEM parameter sets in order of increasing security strength and decreasing performance: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024. FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM-512 is claimed for security category 1, ML-KEM-768 for security category 3, and ML-KEM-1024 for security category 5. FIPS 203 states that NIST recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set because it provides a large security margin at a reasonable performance cost, while other parameter sets may be used when needed.

# The PQC Algorithms: How They Work and How to Choose

## Overview

The PQC Algorithms: How They Work and How to Choose module (40 minutes, intermediate, Foundations track) reads the standardised post-quantum algorithms from the documents that define and guide their use, one sentence at a time. Each sentence below comes from a named document; the lesson shows the document, its edition and the place in it beside every sentence. The workshop runs ML-KEM and ML-DSA in the browser and compares sizes.

## Key Concepts

### Two jobs, new tools

**Key establishment and key derivation**

- NIST SP 800-227 explains that after a KEM establishes a shared secret key, an application may use key derivation to produce multiple symmetric keys from that initial key.
- NIST SP 800-227 states that when an application needs a different amount of keying material than a KEM outputs, the shared secret key may be supplied to an approved key-derivation method from SP 800-108 or SP 800-56C.
- NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2 requires that derived keying material be computed in full before output and used only as secret keying material, such as symmetric keys for data encryption or message integrity.

**Authentication and digital signatures**

- NIST SP 800-227 states that most applications require authentication and cryptographic integrity checking, for example to prevent machine-in-the-middle attacks, typically using additional elements such as digital signatures and certificates.
- NIST SP 800-227 requires that an encapsulating party obtaining another party's static encapsulation key have assurance of the other party's ownership before or during key establishment, such as from a trusted party like a certificate authority or from proof of possession combined with verification of real-world identity.
- According to FIPS 204, digital signatures detect unauthorized modifications to data, authenticate the signatory's identity, and provide non-repudiation by giving recipients evidence for a third party that the claimed signatory generated the signature.

**Symmetric algorithms in the transition**

- NIST IR 8547 states that existing symmetric-cryptography standards, including hash functions, are significantly less vulnerable to known quantum attacks than public-key standards; NIST does not expect to need to transition away from them as part of the PQC migration, although applications should move away from 112-bit symmetric standards.
- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ specifies the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with 256-bit keys and Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA) SHA-384 or SHA-512 for all classification levels.

### The families at a glance

**Mathematical families**

- NIST IR 8413 states that NIST aims to standardize schemes from different cryptographic families so a single advance in cryptanalysis does not leave the world without a viable standard.
- NIST IR 8413 explains that NIST selected hash-based SPHINCS+ so its signature standards do not rely entirely on lattices, providing a fallback against unforeseen cryptanalytic attacks.
- NIST IR 8413 describes CRYSTALS-Kyber as a module-learning-with-errors-based KEM and notes that CRYSTALS-Dilithium and Falcon are both based on structured lattices.
- NIST IR 8413 describes SPHINCS+ as a stateless hash-based signature scheme whose cryptographic security relies only on the security of its underlying hash functions.
- NIST IR 8413 explains that the learning with errors (LWE) problem for public-key encryption relates quantum security to the worst-case hardness of finding short vectors in lattices, known as the approximate Shortest Vector Problem (SVP).

**FALCON and HQC**

- Although Dilithium and Falcon are based on structured lattices, NIST decided to standardize Falcon as well because some applications cannot work as designed when signatures and signed data exceed one internet packet.
- On March 11, 2025, NIST announced that HQC, like ML-KEM, is a key encapsulation mechanism, built around error-correcting codes rather than structured lattices.
- NIST's announcement explains that HQC will serve as a backup to ML-KEM using different mathematics in case a weakness is discovered in ML-KEM, while ML-KEM remains the recommended choice.
- NIST's announcement states that NIST plans to release a draft HQC standard for public comment in about a year, followed by a 90-day comment period and a finalized standard in 2027.
- NIST IR 8547 states that NIST is developing a FIPS specifying a digital signature algorithm derived from FALCON as an additional alternative to its other digital signature standards.

### ML-KEM (FIPS 203)

**What ML-KEM is and how KEMs compare to classical methods**

- FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism that is believed to be secure even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer.
- FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM is derived from the round-three version of the CRYSTALS-KYBER KEM submitted in the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization effort.
- FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM's security is based on the presumed hardness of the Module Learning with Errors (MLWE) problem, which rests on computational problems in module lattices.
- In FIPS 203, a key-encapsulation mechanism is a set of algorithms that two parties can use, under certain conditions, to establish a shared secret key over a public channel.
- NIST SP 800-227 explains that in key agreement such as Diffie-Hellman both parties contribute to the shared secret key, whereas in key transport one party selects the key and transmits it.
- NIST SP 800-227 notes that a KEM can be viewed as either key agreement or key transport depending on its encapsulation function; ML-KEM's shared secret depends on both Bob's randomness and Alice's encapsulation key.

**How key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation work**

- NIST SP 800-227 states that using a KEM should produce a shared secret key that is random, unknown to adversaries, and identical for both parties with high probability.
- In a KEM, the receiving party begins by running KeyGen to generate a public encapsulation key and a private decapsulation key.
- Using the encapsulation key, the other party runs Encaps to produce a copy of the shared secret key and an associated ciphertext, then sends the ciphertext back.
- The first party completes key establishment by running Decaps with the decapsulation key and the received ciphertext to produce a copy of the shared secret key.
- In FIPS 203, when a re-encrypted ciphertext does not match the provided ciphertext, decapsulation performs an implicit rejection and outputs a hash of the ciphertext with a secret random value.

**Parameter sets and sizes**

- FIPS 203 specifies three ML-KEM parameter sets in order of increasing security strength and decreasing performance: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024.
- FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM-512 is claimed for security category 1, ML-KEM-768 for security category 3, and ML-KEM-1024 for security category 5.
- In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-512 uses an 800-byte encapsulation key, a 1632-byte decapsulation key, and a 768-byte ciphertext.
- In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-768 uses an 1184-byte encapsulation key, a 2400-byte decapsulation key, and a 1088-byte ciphertext.
- In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-1024 uses a 1568-byte encapsulation key, a 3168-byte decapsulation key, and a 1568-byte ciphertext.
- In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 all produce a shared secret key that is 32 bytes long.

**Input checks, rejection handling, and key formats** (for developers)

- FIPS 203 requires that ML-KEM.Encaps must not run with an unchecked encapsulation key; checking verifies its byte length and that its encoded integers fall in the valid range.
- FIPS 203 requires that ML-KEM.Decaps must not run unless both the decapsulation key and ciphertext have been checked, and ciphertext checking must be performed on every execution.
- FIPS 203 requires implementations to destroy the implicit-reject comparison flag before decapsulation terminates and prohibits returning that flag as an output in any form.
- FIPS 203 permits storing the key-generation seed (d, z) for later expansion with ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal, and requires that it be protected with the same safeguards as a decapsulation key.
- NIST SP 800-227 states that a cryptographic module may store, import, or export keys in alternative formats, such as a short seed or an expanded format that allows faster computations.

**Randomness and intermediate data requirements** (for validation engineers)

- FIPS 203 requires random bytes to be generated using an approved RBG with at least 128 bits of security strength for ML-KEM-512, 192 bits for ML-KEM-768, and 256 bits for ML-KEM-1024.
- FIPS 203 requires implementers to destroy intermediate data as soon as it is no longer needed and, except for specified storage exceptions, retain only the designated output in memory after an ML-KEM algorithm terminates.

### ML-DSA (FIPS 204)

**What ML-DSA is and how it works**

- FIPS 204 specifies ML-DSA, a set of algorithms for generating and verifying digital signatures that is believed to be secure even against adversaries with a large-scale quantum computer.
- After three rounds of evaluation and analysis, NIST selected four algorithms for standardization, and FIPS 204 states that ML-DSA is derived from one of those schemes, CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM.
- FIPS 204 states that ML-DSA's security is based on the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem and SelfTargetMSIS, a nonstandard variant of the Module Short Integer Solution (MSIS) problem.
- FIPS 204 specifies three main ML-DSA algorithms covering key generation (ML-DSA.KeyGen), signature generation (ML-DSA.Sign), and signature verification (ML-DSA.Verify).
- Only the user who possesses the private key can generate a signature that verifies under the corresponding public key, while anyone can verify the signature using the signatory's public key.

**Parameter sets and sizes**

- FIPS 204 defines three ML-DSA parameter sets with different claimed security strength categories: ML-DSA-44 in category 2, ML-DSA-65 in category 3, and ML-DSA-87 in category 5.
- In the names ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, FIPS 204 explains that the numerical suffix refers to the dimensions of the matrix A, such as a 6 × 5 matrix in ML-DSA-65.
- In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-44 has a private key of 2560 bytes, a public key of 1312 bytes, and a signature size of 2420 bytes.
- In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-65 has a private key of 4032 bytes, a public key of 1952 bytes, and a signature size of 3309 bytes.
- In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-87 has a private key of 4896 bytes, a public key of 2592 bytes, and a signature size of 4627 bytes.
- NIST IR 8413 reports that structured lattice finalists for KEMs and signatures could replace existing public-key algorithms in widely used protocols like TLS, IPSec, and SSH, and in certificates, with relatively small or no performance loss.
- NIST IR 8413 notes that some applications will not work as currently designed if a signature and signed data cannot fit in a single internet packet, so modifying them for Dilithium’s larger signature size may create a transition barrier.

**Hedged and deterministic signing** (for developers)

- By default, FIPS 204 specifies a hedged signing variant that uses both fresh signing-time randomness to help mitigate side-channel attacks and precomputed randomness to protect against flaws in the signer's random number generator.
- For hedged signing in ML-DSA and HashML-DSA, FIPS 204 states that the signing randomness should ideally be generated by an approved RBG, though other methods for generating fresh random values may be used.
- FIPS 204 also permits a fully deterministic signing variant when the signer has no access to fresh randomness at signing time, and states that implementing only the hedged variant suffices for interoperability because the same verification algorithm verifies both.
- Because the lack of randomness in deterministic signing makes side-channel attacks, particularly fault attacks, harder to mitigate, FIPS 204 states this variant should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and cannot be otherwise mitigated.

**Context strings, pre-hashing, and seed storage** (for developers)

- In FIPS 204, both ML-DSA signing and verification take a context string as input, encoded as a byte string of 255 or fewer bytes.
- By default in FIPS 204, the context string is the empty string, though applications may specify a non-empty context string, which should be indicated by the signature's identifier or by the application.
- FIPS 204 defines a pre-hash variant called HashML-DSA that signs a message digest with domain separation information rather than signing the message directly, though FIPS 204 states that pure ML-DSA is generally preferred.
- HashML-DSA is domain-separated from ML-DSA and shares the same ML-DSA.KeyGen algorithm for key generation, but adds a pre-hashing step before signing through its separate HashML-DSA.Sign and HashML-DSA.Verify algorithms.
- To reduce private-key storage space, FIPS 204 notes that an implementation can store only the 32-byte key-generation seed, which is sufficient to generate the other parts of the private key.
- Because the seed generated during ML-DSA.KeyGen can be stored for later expansion into the private key, FIPS 204 requires that it be treated with the same safeguards as a private key.

### Hash-based signatures in brief

**SLH-DSA**

- FIPS 205 specifies SLH-DSA, a stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm used to detect unauthorized modifications to data and authenticate identity.
- FIPS 205 bases SLH-DSA on SPHINCS+, which was selected for standardization as part of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization process.
- The security of SLH-DSA relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions and related hash-function properties, and it is designed to resist attacks from a large-scale quantum computer.
- In FIPS 205 parameter set names, the suffix 's' indicates relatively small signatures, whereas 'f' indicates relatively fast signature generation.

**LMS and XMSS**

- NIST SP 800-208 specifies two stateful hash-based signature schemes, the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS), along with their multi-tree variants, HSS and multi-tree XMSS.
- RFC 8391 states that XMSS can sign a potentially large but fixed number of messages, using a tree of height h to produce a key pair that can sign 2^h messages.
- NIST SP 800-208 states that stateful hash-based signature schemes are not suitable for general use because they require careful state management that is often difficult to assure.
- NIST SP 800-208 says stateful HBS schemes are primarily intended where a signature scheme is needed soon, the implementation will have a long lifetime, and post-deployment transition is impractical; constrained-device firmware-update authentication may fit this profile.

**SLH-DSA parameter sets and signature sizes** (for developers)

- FIPS 205 approves 12 parameter sets for SLH-DSA, instantiated using either the SHA2 or SHAKE hash function family.
- In FIPS 205 Table 2, the parameter set SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s has a 32-byte public key and a 7,856-byte signature.
- In FIPS 205 Table 2, the parameter set SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f has a 64-byte public key and a 49,856-byte signature.

**Validation and hardware-module requirements** (for validation engineers)

- FIPS 205 states that parameter sets with n = 16 are claimed to be in security category 1, those with n = 24 in category 3, and those with n = 32 in category 5.
- NIST SP 800-208 requires that key and signature generation be performed in hardware cryptographic modules that do not allow secret keying material to be exported.

### How standards bodies map use cases to algorithms

**Security categories**

- NIST IR 8547 explains that post-quantum security is described using broad security categories, each defined by a symmetric-cryptography reference primitive whose security serves as a floor.
- In NIST IR 8547 Table 1, Categories 1, 3, and 5 correspond to key search on block ciphers with 128-bit, 192-bit, and 256-bit keys, exemplified by AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256.
- In NIST IR 8547 Table 1, Categories 2 and 4 correspond to collision search on 256-bit and 384-bit hash functions, exemplified by SHA-256 and SHA3-384.

**NIST**

- NIST IR 8547 gives its document number as NIST IR 8547, lists its publication date as October 2026, and records NIST Editorial Review Board approval on 2026-10-21.
- FIPS 203 states that NIST recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set because it provides a large security margin at a reasonable performance cost, while other parameter sets may be used when needed.
- For post-quantum digital signatures, NIST IR 8547 names FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), and SP 800-208 for stateful hash-based signature schemes, and notes a Falcon-based FIPS is under development.

**NSA CNSA 2.0**

- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ document is dated October 2026 and marked as Version 2.2 in its page footer.
- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ states that CNSA 2.0 requirements are for National Security System (NSS) owners, operators, and vendors, and are not mandated outside NSS, though they may serve as guidance.
- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ lists ML-KEM (previously CRYSTALS-Kyber) as the asymmetric algorithm for key establishment, using ML-KEM-1024 for all classification levels.
- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ lists ML-DSA (previously CRYSTALS-Dilithium) for digital signatures in any use case, using ML-DSA-87 for all classification levels.

**BSI**

- BSI TR-02102-1 identifies itself as Version 2026-01, dated January 23, 2026, and its version-history table lists 23.01.2026 in the Date column for version 2026-01.
- BSI TR-02102-1 recommends ML-KEM with the parameter sets ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024, corresponding to NIST Security Strength Categories 3 and 5, for long-term protection of confidential information.
- BSI TR-02102-1 recommends the hedged variant of ML-DSA with parameter sets ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87, corresponding to NIST Security Strength Categories 3 and 5.

**ANSSI**

- ANSSI's follow-up paper, titled ANSSI views on the Post-Quantum Cryptography transition, states a date of December 21, 2023 on its first page.
- ANSSI's 2023 follow-up paper does not give a closed list of recommended algorithms, and names CRYSTALS-Kyber (ML-KEM) and FrodoKEM as appropriate post-quantum KEMs, preferring NIST security level 5 or level 3.
- In its non-exhaustive list of post-quantum digital signatures, ANSSI's 2023 follow-up paper names CRYSTALS-Dilithium (ML-DSA), Falcon (FN-DSA), XMSS/LMS, and SPHINCS+ (SLH-DSA) as appropriate choices.

**UK NCSC**

- The UK NCSC white paper states that it was originally published in November 2023, updated in August 2024, and published on 14 August 2024.
- The UK NCSC white paper states that ML-KEM and ML-DSA are suitable for general-purpose use and recommends ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 for most use cases.

**TLS 1.3**

- RFC 10024 defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3—X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, and SecP384r1MLKEM1024—that combine post-quantum ML-KEM with ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE).
- The draft-ietf-tls-mlkem-11 specification defines standalone ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 as NamedGroups in the IANA TLS Supported Groups registry for post-quantum key establishment in TLS 1.3.

### Implementation considerations

**Pre-standard Kyber and Dilithium differences**

- FIPS 203 lists differences between CRYSTALS-KYBER and ML-KEM that change input-output behavior, including fixing the shared secret key to 256 bits and no longer including a hash of the ciphertext in ML-KEM.Encaps’s shared-secret derivation.
- FIPS 203 also adds explicit input checking that was not part of the third-round specification, and introduces domain separation in K-PKE.KeyGen to prevent a saved seed from being misused across security levels.
- Unlike Version 3.1 of the CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM submission, where signing was deterministic by default, FIPS 204 makes ML-DSA signing hedged by default by incorporating a 256-bit random string.
- Compared with CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM Version 3.1, ML-DSA increases tr to 512 bits and c-tilde to 384 and 512 bits for ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87; the final standard also adds direct-versus-pre-hash domain separation.

**KEM key confirmation and ephemeral key handling**

- NIST SP 800-227 recommends using key confirmation during KEM usage because confirming successful establishment of the shared secret key can address transmission or decapsulation errors.
- NIST SP 800-227 requires that an ephemeral KEM key pair be used for only one key-establishment execution and destroyed as soon as possible afterward.

**Stateful key reuse and compliance pitfalls** (for developers)

- NIST SP 800-208 says that signatures on two messages using one OTS key make forgery computationally feasible; if the private key is stored in nonvolatile memory, its state must mark that OTS key unavailable before its signature is exported.
- The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ states that only ML-KEM and ML-DSA are in CNSA 2.0, and any algorithm called CRYSTALS-Kyber or CRYSTALS-Dilithium that does not adhere to FIPS 203 or 204 is not CNSA 2.0 compliant.

## Workshop

ML-KEM Round Trip: generate a key pair, encapsulate, decapsulate, then change one byte of the ciphertext and decapsulate again.

ML-DSA Sign and Verify: generate a key pair, sign in the hedged or deterministic mode with or without a context string, and verify against the same or a changed message or context.

Size Comparator: compare key, signature and ciphertext sizes from the algorithm registry next to the sentences that state them.

After three rounds of evaluation and analysis, NIST selected four algorithms for standardization, and FIPS 204 states that ML-DSA is derived from one of those schemes, CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM.
FIPS 204 states that ML-DSA's security is based on the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem and SelfTargetMSIS, a nonstandard variant of the Module Short Integer Solution (MSIS) problem.
FIPS 204 defines three ML-DSA parameter sets with different claimed security strength categories: ML-DSA-44 in category 2, ML-DSA-65 in category 3, and ML-DSA-87 in category 5.
In the names ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87, FIPS 204 explains that the numerical suffix refers to the dimensions of the matrix A, such as a 6 × 5 matrix in ML-DSA-65.
In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-44 has a private key of 2560 bytes, a public key of 1312 bytes, and a signature size of 2420 bytes.
In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-65 has a private key of 4032 bytes, a public key of 1952 bytes, and a signature size of 3309 bytes.
In FIPS 204, ML-DSA-87 has a private key of 4896 bytes, a public key of 2592 bytes, and a signature size of 4627 bytes.
By default, FIPS 204 specifies a hedged signing variant that uses both fresh signing-time randomness to help mitigate side-channel attacks and precomputed randomness to protect against flaws in the signer's random number generator.
For hedged signing in ML-DSA and HashML-DSA, FIPS 204 states that the signing randomness should ideally be generated by an approved RBG, though other methods for generating fresh random values may be used.
FIPS 204 also permits a fully deterministic signing variant when the signer has no access to fresh randomness at signing time, and states that implementing only the hedged variant suffices for interoperability because the same verification algorithm verifies both.
Because the lack of randomness in deterministic signing makes side-channel attacks, particularly fault attacks, harder to mitigate, FIPS 204 states this variant should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and cannot be otherwise mitigated.
In FIPS 204, both ML-DSA signing and verification take a context string as input, encoded as a byte string of 255 or fewer bytes.
By default in FIPS 204, the context string is the empty string, though applications may specify a non-empty context string, which should be indicated by the signature's identifier or by the application.
FIPS 204 defines a pre-hash variant called HashML-DSA that signs a message digest with domain separation information rather than signing the message directly, though FIPS 204 states that pure ML-DSA is generally preferred.
To reduce private-key storage space, FIPS 204 notes that an implementation can store only the 32-byte key-generation seed, which is sufficient to generate the other parts of the private key.
Because the seed generated during ML-DSA.KeyGen can be stored for later expansion into the private key, FIPS 204 requires that it be treated with the same safeguards as a private key.
FIPS 205 bases SLH-DSA on SPHINCS+, which was selected for standardization as part of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization process.
FIPS 205 approves 12 parameter sets for SLH-DSA, instantiated using either the SHA2 or SHAKE hash function family.
In FIPS 205 Table 2, the parameter set SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s has a 32-byte public key and a 7,856-byte signature.
In FIPS 205 Table 2, the parameter set SLH-DSA-SHA2-256f has a 64-byte public key and a 49,856-byte signature.
Unlike Version 3.1 of the CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM submission, where signing was deterministic by default, FIPS 204 makes ML-DSA signing hedged by default by incorporating a 256-bit random string.

LM-088/s:ml-kem-fips-203.full:
FIPS 203 standardizes ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation mechanism that is believed to be secure even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer.
FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM is derived from the round-three version of the CRYSTALS-KYBER KEM submitted in the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization effort.
FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM's security is based on the presumed hardness of the Module Learning with Errors (MLWE) problem, which rests on computational problems in module lattices.
In FIPS 203, a key-encapsulation mechanism is a set of algorithms that two parties can use, under certain conditions, to establish a shared secret key over a public channel.
In FIPS 203, when a re-encrypted ciphertext does not match the provided ciphertext, decapsulation performs an implicit rejection and outputs a hash of the ciphertext with a secret random value.
FIPS 203 specifies three ML-KEM parameter sets in order of increasing security strength and decreasing performance: ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024.
FIPS 203 states that ML-KEM-512 is claimed for security category 1, ML-KEM-768 for security category 3, and ML-KEM-1024 for security category 5.
In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-512 uses an 800-byte encapsulation key, a 1632-byte decapsulation key, and a 768-byte ciphertext.
In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-768 uses an 1184-byte encapsulation key, a 2400-byte decapsulation key, and a 1088-byte ciphertext.
In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-1024 uses a 1568-byte encapsulation key, a 3168-byte decapsulation key, and a 1568-byte ciphertext.
In FIPS 203, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 all produce a shared secret key that is 32 bytes long.
FIPS 203 requires that ML-KEM.Encaps must not run with an unchecked encapsulation key; checking verifies its byte length and that its encoded integers fall in the valid range.
FIPS 203 requires that ML-KEM.Decaps must not run unless both the decapsulation key and ciphertext have been checked, and ciphertext checking must be performed on every execution.
FIPS 203 requires implementations to destroy the implicit-reject comparison flag before decapsulation terminates and prohibits returning that flag as an output in any form.
FIPS 203 permits storing the key-generation seed (d, z) for later expansion with ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal, and requires that it be protected with the same safeguards as a decapsulation key.
FIPS 203 requires random bytes to be generated using an approved RBG with at least 128 bits of security strength for ML-KEM-512, 192 bits for ML-KEM-768, and 256 bits for ML-KEM-1024.
FIPS 203 requires implementers to destroy intermediate data as soon as it is no longer needed and, except for specified storage exceptions, retain only the designated output in memory after an ML-KEM algorithm terminates.
FIPS 203 states that NIST recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default parameter set because it provides a large security margin at a reasonable performance cost, while other parameter sets may be used when needed.
FIPS 203 lists differences between CRYSTALS-KYBER and ML-KEM that change input-output behavior, including fixing the shared secret key to 256 bits and no longer including a hash of the ciphertext in ML-KEM.Encaps’s shared-secret derivation.
FIPS 203 also adds explicit input checking that was not part of the third-round specification, and introduces domain separation in K-PKE.KeyGen to prevent a saved seed from being misused across security levels.
