LM:quiz.full: Test your knowledge across all PQC topics — algorithms, standards, compliance, migration, and more.

PAGE:algorithms.manual:
PQC Algorithms

Learn how post-quantum algorithms differ, explore candidate transition paths, inspect evidence, and run scoped implementation checks.

Transition Tab: Shows candidate migration paths from classical algorithms (RSA, ECDH, ECDSA) to post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and others). Each row shows the classical algorithm on the left and a candidate migration path on the right, with region, publication status and transition timing. A row is educational context, not a drop-in replacement or a compliance determination.

Detailed Comparison Tab: Deep-dive into algorithms in a sortable table covering security levels, key/ciphertext/signature sizes, catalogue estimates, and reviewed use cases. Toggle Browse ↔ Compare mode. Baselines help explain size differences; they are not universal performance rankings. Filter by crypto family, function group, or security level.

Compare Panel: Select up to 3 algorithms to compare side-by-side. Click the compare icon on algorithm cards to add them to the comparison bar at the bottom of the page. The panel shows a detailed table comparing all properties.

URL Parameters: Deep link to specific views: ?tab=transition|detailed|support|landscape|validation, ?family=, ?fn=, ?level=, ?region=, ?status= and ?q= to filter, ?quickview=nist-picks|final-nist-standards|none (the older fips-validated value still opens Final NIST standards), ?mode=compare for the Detailed tab, ?section=attacks|kat|coverage for the Validation tab, ?protocol=<id> to open a Protocol Support row, ?industry= for the Landscape tab, ?highlight= to highlight algorithms, ?transition=<row> to open and highlight one Transition Guide row, ?compare= for pre-selected comparisons. On the Protocol Support tab: ?matrixView=detailed, ?matrixQ=, ?matrixStatus=, ?matrixAvailability=, ?matrixSort=key:direction. Use the Share button to copy a link to your current selection.

Tips:
- Use the Detailed tab filters to quickly narrow down algorithms by security level or standardization status.
- The compare panel is great for preparing algorithm selection reports.
- Toggle Browse ↔ Compare mode on the Detailed tab, or open the Validation tab for implementation attacks and live KAT tests.

PAGE:compliance.manual:
Compliance Frameworks

Use this educational reference to learn which rules, standards and certification records may be relevant to a country and sector, why they were included, what their sources say about post-quantum cryptography, and the dates they state. It is not a GRC system, legal advice, an applicability decision or proof of compliance. The page has eight views: Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices, Progress, Products, Landscape, Product Records, For You and CSWP.39 Agility.

Eight Views: The tab bar has eight views: Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices, Progress, Products, Landscape, Product Records, For You and CSWP.39 Agility. Rules & Standards opens first for most roles, and operations roles open on Progress. A link that carries a certificate, a source passage, a product or a CSWP.39 reference opens the view it belongs to. On a narrow screen the tab bar scrolls sideways.

Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices and Progress: Rules & Standards lists instruments associated with the selected country and sector, why each one was included, and what its source says about post-quantum cryptography. Each item carries a tier (Binding, Relevant / recognized, Cross-border, Advisory, Related via IR 8477 or Informational) from the same educational applicability model as For You. Binding requires a reviewed binding status and a stated basis; an issuer match alone is not enough, and the site does not decide whether an instrument applies to a real organisation. Sources & Practices shows machine-extracted source passages, where they appear and which model extracted them. Verify the primary passage and obtain the appropriate legal or assurance review before treating it as an obligation. Progress compares dates stated by scoped sources; a date does not by itself prove implementation is overdue.

Products and Product Records: Products maps the inventory you keep on Migrate to reviewed evidence. It distinguishes NIST CAVP/ACVP algorithm validation, FIPS 140 module validation, and algorithms named in evaluated-product documentation; those evidence classes are not interchangeable. Product Records is a searchable snapshot of NIST CMVP module validations, NIST CAVP algorithm validations, NIST entropy source validations (the Entropy (ESV) tab), Common Criteria and EUCC certificates, and ANSSI CSPN certificates. Search by product, vendor or type, filter by source and status, and use the source and freshness fields before relying on a record. A link with ?cert= opens one specific record.

Landscape: Landscape lays the field out as a chain of three groups. Standardization Bodies define the algorithms and publish the standards. Certification Schemes (FIPS 140-3, ACVP, Common Criteria, EUCC) test that products implement them correctly. Compliance Frameworks (for example CNSA 2.0, NIS2 and DORA) set the requirements and deadlines. Switch between the three groups at the top, filter by organization, industry or search, and sort by name, deadline or finish date.

For You and CSWP.39 Agility: For You presents standards, threats, library documents and timeline milestones associated with the selected industry, country and region, tuned by the role selected in the top bar. The executive CSV is a learning worksheet, not an audit or management register. CSWP.39 Agility presents a PQC Today learning sequence based on NIST CSWP 39, with links to the source PDF and related Learn module; its steps are not NIST’s section structure.

Framework Details: Click any framework to open its details drawer: source and trust information, a Learn this link, the traceability chain, deadline phases, and related and overlapping frameworks.

Tips:
- Framework entries cross-reference both Library documents and Timeline milestones.
- Old links still work: ?tab=standards, ?tab=certification and ?tab=compliance open Landscape.
- URL params: ?tab=obligations|requirements|progress|products|foryou|records|cswp39 chooses a view; ?framework=<id> opens a framework, ?cert=<id> a certification record, ?reqfw=<id> a framework in Requirements, ?prod=<id> a product, ?evref= a CSWP.39 reference; ?org=, ?ind=, ?q= and ?mcat= filter.

PAGE:faq.manual:
Frequently Asked Questions

Browse common questions about post-quantum cryptography, the PQC Today platform, and how to get started with your migration planning.

Category Navigation: Questions are organized by category with quick-link pills at the top. Select a category pill to jump to that section. Each question opens when you select it.

Search: Use the search bar to filter questions across all categories. A question is shown only if it contains every word you type, in the question or in its answer.

Your Role: When you have picked a role, a "Start here" block above the categories leads with the three questions that role asks first, and role-matching questions float to the top of their category with a "For you" tag. Nothing is hidden: the full list is always below.

Learn More Links: Each open answer ends with a Learn more link to the page or module where the topic is covered in depth.

Tips:
- Can't find your answer? The Assistant tab in the right-hand panel opens the PQC Assistant; the button at the bottom of this page opens the About page, which describes it.

PAGE:leaders.manual:
Community

An evidence-linked directory of people and organizations named in post-quantum research, standards, policy, patent and open-source sources. Inclusion is not an endorsement, a ranking or a certification.

Curated profiles and document contributors: The directory opens on the hand-curated profiles. "Show all contributors" adds the document-contributor profiles, created from the author lists of documents in the Library (the link form is ?all=1). The page shows the current count of each.

Filters and views: Filter by category, region and country, or sector (Public, Private, Academic), or search by name, role, organization or bio. Three views show the same results: Sector Stack (people grouped by sector; choose a sector to narrow the list), Cards, and Table (sortable columns, including Category). Name order ignores titles such as "Dr." and "Prof.", and people with no recorded country sort last.

What a profile links to: Open a card or a table row to read the full role, organizations and bio, and the cited evidence: "Cited in the Library" opens each document in the Library, "External sources" opens the cited pages, "View patents" opens the person's patent records, and catalog products open in Migrate. "Events from <country>" appears when the Timeline has events for that country.

Links you can share: ?leader=<id> opens one profile (old links to merged or renamed profiles forward to the current one). Filters are kept in the address too: ?cat=, ?region=, ?country=, ?sector=, ?q=, ?mode=stack|cards|table, ?layer= (a Sector Stack sector) and ?sort=.

Reading a profile critically: A profile is a starting point, not a verdict. The recorded source details (institutions in source metadata, review flags, "profile sources checked" dates) say what was recorded, not that anyone endorsed the person or their work. Check the claim in the linked primary source, and check its date and version.

Tips:
- Profiles are compiled from cited public sources and from people who ask to be listed; anyone listed can ask for a correction or removal from the page.
- Export CSV includes each profile's Library refs, external sources, patents and catalog products, so you can check them in bulk.

PAGE:learn.manual:
Learning Center

Structured PQC education: 85 modules in nine tracks, from foundations through protocols, infrastructure, governance and industry topics, with hands-on workshops where a module has them. The Practice quiz is a separate entry.

Finding a Module: The Learn page has four views. Your journey holds your objectives, their steps and your role map, and keeps them on this device. Recommended order shows a sequence tuned to the role you picked in the top bar. All modules lists every module and can be narrowed by track, search, status and saved modules, in a grid or a list. Guided routing asks about your migration situation and points to a first module or page, with a framework crosswalk. The Practice quiz button opens the quiz.

Module Tracks: Modules are organised into nine tracks: Role Guides, Foundations, Strategy, Protocols, Hardware Infrastructure, Software Infrastructure, Applications, Governance & Risk and Industries. All modules shows a chip for each track with its module count.

Module Tabs: Each module opens on Learn (the lessons). Depending on the module it also has Visual, Workshop (hands-on exercises), Exercises, References and Tools & Products tabs.

Progress Tracking: Inside a module, a progress panel lists its lesson sections with checkmarks and shows a percentage, plus workshop progress where the module has a workshop. Your progress is saved in this browser (local storage) and survives a refresh on the same device.

Navigation: On a module's Learn tab, Mark as Read marks every lesson section done. On the Workshop tab, use Previous Step and Next Step (or the step chips) to move through the exercises; the last step offers Complete Module. When all of a module's workshop steps are done, a prompt links to the next module in your role's path if there is one.

Achievements: Badges are awarded for learning activity such as workshop steps, modules and tracks, and also for using other parts of the Hub; a toast appears when you unlock one. The badge collection is shown on the Home page score card and at the top of Role map in Learn › Your journey.

Tips:
- Start with the Foundations track if you are new to PQC, or pick a role first so Your journey and Recommended order can order the modules for you.
- Workshop exercises that use WebAssembly cryptography run locally in your browser.
- The Practice quiz draws on questions across many topics, filtered by your role and the difficulty you choose.

PAGE:library.manual:
PQC Library

Search and browse post-quantum cryptography standards, drafts, RFCs, guidance and research from NIST, IETF, ETSI and other organizations. Each record says what the document is, where it stands in its lifecycle, and links to the official source.

Where to start: Three purpose doors (Learn, Reference, Plan migration) narrow the catalogue by why you are here. With a role selected, Start here suggests three documents for it, and the New & updated strip lists documents added or revised recently.

Search & Filters: Type in the search bar to search titles, summaries, reference IDs and tags. The left rail filters by quick view (All, New & updated, Certification starter set, Bookmarked), by the 13 categories and by lifecycle status; the toolbar adds organization, geography, sector, trust tier, algorithm family and research topic. With a role selected, the list starts narrowed to that role's focus areas; "Show all documents" turns that off.

View Toggle: Switch between Card view and Tree Table view in the toolbar. Card view shows document summaries; the Tree Table lists the documents that match your filters, with sortable columns and nests, under each document, the documents that build on it.

Document Details: Open any document to see its catalogue summary, status and dates, the documents it builds on, earlier revisions, the catalogue's classification tags, the Learn modules that use it, and a direct link to the source.

Export: Export the filtered list as CSV, or export citations for the filtered list or your bookmarks as BibTeX or CSL-JSON.

Tips:
- Use ?ref=REFERENCE_ID to deep-link directly to a document; a retired ID opens the document that replaced it.
- URL params: ?purpose=, ?cat=, ?org=, ?geo=, ?sector=, ?tier=, ?algo=, ?topic=, ?lifecycle=, ?cswp39=1, ?q=, ?sort= and ?view=cards|table combine into shareable filtered views.
- On other pages, ?spec=REFERENCE_ID opens a document in place without leaving the page.

PAGE:migrate.manual:
Migration Workbench

Browse the catalogue of software products, each with its own PQC status, organized across 9 infrastructure layers with certification cross-references and migration planning tools.

Infrastructure Layer Stack: Products are organized across 9 layers: Cloud, Network, Application Servers, Libraries & SDKs, Security Software, Database, Security Stack, Operating Systems, and Hardware & Secure Elements. Click a layer to filter. The stack shows readiness counts per layer.

Product Search & Filters: Search by product name or vendor. Filter by infrastructure layer, category, sub-category, vendor, verification status, and migration step. Persona-based recommendations highlight relevant layers. URL params: ?product=<product id> opens one product, ?productIds= lists several, ?tab=replace|plan|roadmaps|vendorrisk picks a tab, and ?tab=roadmaps&vendor=<vendor id> opens a vendor roadmap.

Product Details: Click any product to see its full migration profile: current PQC support, migration timeline, certification status (FIPS 140-3/CAVP/CC cross-references), vendor links, and product briefs.

My Products & Comparison: Add products to your comparison list using the bookmark icon. The "My Products" panel lets you compare up to 3 products side-by-side via the sticky compare bar.

View Modes: Three view modes: Stack (grouped by infrastructure layer, default), Cards (flat grid), and Table (sortable columns). Hidden products can be managed via the settings icon.

Tips:
- Hidden products can be managed via the settings icon — useful for excluding irrelevant entries.
- Certification cross-references link directly to the Compliance page for each product.
- Community members can submit product update requests via the contribution cards.

PAGE:navigate.manual:
Navigate: the knowledge graph

A 3D map of how the hub’s records connect. Each node is a record from one of the hub’s data sets and each line is a relationship recorded in that data. The graph teaches how standards, algorithms, protocols, compliance frameworks, products and vendors refer to each other; it does not validate any of them.

Twelve kinds of record: Nodes are coloured by category: Trusted source, Crypto mechanism, Industry, Use case, Compliance, Standard, Glossary, Product, Protocol, Patent, Community and Vendor. A bigger, darker node has more recorded connections in this graph. That is a count of links in the data, not a measure of importance, trust or maturity.

Zooming and labels: Labels change with distance. From far away you see the category names, closer in the sub-category names, and close up the names of single records. The Labels slider sets how many labels can show at once; labels never overlap.

Filters and the node count: Filters turns categories and sub-categories on and off. The Nodes slider sets how many records are drawn; each category contributes its most-connected records first, so a record that is not drawn is not missing from the data. The line under the sliders shows how many records and links are drawn out of the whole graph.

Finding a record: Search (or the search box at the top of Filters) finds any record by name across the whole graph, including records the node count or the filters leave out. Picking one draws it, opens its details and flies the camera to it. List view (keyboard) lists the drawn records for keyboard and screen-reader use and does the same.

Spotlight: Click a category or sub-category label to spotlight it: the camera frames it and every other record is hidden. The chip at the top names the spotlight; Show all or Escape returns to the whole graph. Clicking empty space also ends it, but releasing a drag does not.

Record details: Clicking a record opens its details: what it is, links to its page in the hub (and to Learn modules or tools that cover it), and its connections grouped by relationship. A connection marked "name match" was found because one record’s text uses the other’s name; "family match" means a source named an algorithm family and the link goes to every parameter set of it. Unmarked connections come from a field that cites that exact record.

Guided tour and motion: Spin turns the graph slowly. Tour visits each category and then its most-connected records, with a caption naming each one and, on a wider screen, its details panel open (on a phone the panel would cover the tour controls, so only the caption shows). Pause, Previous and Next control the tour; dragging the view also pauses it, and Resume carries on from the current stop.

Sharing a view: The address bar follows what you have open: ?node= for a record, ?type= and ?sub= for a spotlight. The Share button in the top bar copies that link, and opening it shows the same record or spotlight.

Tips:
- A link records a reference in the dataset, not a validation. Before relying on one, open the cited document or the official register (for example CMVP for FIPS 140-3 certificates).
- If the canvas feels busy, spotlight one category or lower the Nodes slider, then follow connections from the details panel.

PAGE:patents.manual:
PQC Patents

An educational catalogue of US patent records that touch post-quantum cryptography. Use it to see which algorithms, protocols and hardware the claims describe and who holds them. It records what each filing discloses and claims; it does not tell you whether a patent is valid, enforceable against you, or licensed, and it is not legal or IP advice.

Scope: PQC & hybrid or All crypto: The page opens on records that use post-quantum or hybrid cryptography. All crypto adds the remaining records, including ones that are quantum-safe without a PQC algorithm (AES-256 or SHA-2/3 strength, lattice homomorphic encryption, quantum key distribution) and classical-only ones. Records outside the patents scope were retired from the catalogue, not deleted. A shared link to a record outside your current scope widens it (with Undo on a computer).

Granted patents and published applications: A granted patent has been examined and its claims allowed on the grant date. A published application (an 11-digit US number beginning with the year) is an application the patent office has published; the publication alone gives no current prosecution status. The patent office record records any subsequent grant or abandonment. The Granted / pub. column, the detail panel and the export say which each record is.

Impact level and PQC migration score: Each record has a 1–10 PQC migration score with a one-sentence reason, shown in the detail panel. The Hub impact score (0–100) takes half from what the record names (FIPS 203/204/205 standards, protocols, hardware, application domains, data types protected) and half from the migration score; High is 72 or more (about the top fifth of the catalogue), Medium 35–71, Low below 35. Both are reading aids for this catalogue, not measures of patent value.

Explore, Insights and Search: Explore lists the records with filters for filing office, agility, impact and domain; More filters adds assignee, PQC algorithm, protocol, classical algorithm, hardware, NIST status, publication type and, under All crypto, quantum-safe basis. Algorithms named by their filing-era name (Kyber, Dilithium, SPHINCS+, Falcon) are counted and filtered together with their FIPS name. Insights charts the corpus; clicking a bar opens Explore filtered to it. Search finds records by meaning as well as words.

What a record does not tell you: The catalogue records assignees, claims and dates. It records no licensing terms, patent-pledge commitments or history of assertion, and it is not a complete search of patent offices. Treat the holders it lists as people to ask, and take questions of freedom to operate to your own counsel.

Tips:
- In the detail panel, click an algorithm, protocol or hardware tag to see every record that names it; a standard the Library holds opens there.
- The role panel above the list links a holder to /migrate only when the holder is a vendor in the Migrate catalogue.

PAGE:playground.manual:
Interactive Playground

Generate real post-quantum cryptographic keys, encrypt data, and sign messages directly in your browser using WebAssembly. 34 workshop tools, an interactive crypto lab, and a full PKCS#11 HSM emulator — all running locally.

Workshop Grid: The main /playground view shows a searchable catalog of 34 workshop tools across 7 categories: HSM / PKCS#11, Entropy & Random, Certificates & Proofs, Protocol Simulations, Blockchain & Digital Assets, Digital Identity, and OpenSSL Studio (includes TLS 1.3 Simulator). Persona-aware filtering highlights recommended tools with difficulty badges (beginner/intermediate/advanced).

Interactive Crypto Lab: The /playground/interactive route provides 7 tabs: Key Store (keypair generation), Data (hex editor), KEM & Encrypt (ML-KEM + X25519 ECDH), Sym Encrypt (AES/ChaCha), Hash (SHA/SHAKE), Sign & Verify (PQC + classical), and Logs (operation history). Use ?tab= to deep-link to specific operations.

HSM Playground: The /playground/hsm route emulates a PKCS#11 v3.2 HSM via SoftHSMv3 WASM in four modes. Learn runs guided lessons in three tracks: PKCS#11 Foundations, v3.2 & the PQC transformation, and PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft). Operate has seven panels: KEM, Symmetric Encrypt, Key Wrap / Unwrap, Hashing, Sign & Verify, Key Agreement and KDF. Build holds the test suites (standard KATs, selected NIST ACVP-Server reference samples, conformance, and v3.3). Inspect shows the mechanism list, the call log and the keys on the token. Supports C++, Rust, and Dual engine modes with parity cross-check.

KMIP Control Plane: The /playground/cacp route is a KMIP 3.0 key-management control plane running in the browser, with Learn, Policy, Operate, Inspect, Dev and Migration Estate tabs. Switch a crypto-agility policy and watch new keys and operations move to post-quantum algorithms.

Individual Tools: Each workshop tool has its own route at /playground/:toolId with lazy-loaded components, breadcrumb navigation, and community endorse/flag buttons. Step-based tools open at a given step with ?step=N (counting from 0), and the TPM 2.0 Playground keeps its open tab in ?tab=.

Command Palette: On a laptop, press ⌘K (Ctrl-K) or / on the /playground page to search every tool, task and full playground by name, algorithm or keyword. Algorithm nicknames such as Kyber, Dilithium and SPHINCS find the standard ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA tools.

Tips:
- All generated keys are for educational purposes only — not for production use.
- The Logs tab records every operation with timestamps for review.
- Use the HSM Playground to understand how real HSMs handle PQC operations via PKCS#11.

PAGE:threats.manual:
Quantum Threats

Explore industry-specific threat analysis showing which cryptographic assets are at risk from quantum computers and the recommended PQC replacements.

Industry Filters: Filter threats by industry using the multi-select dropdown — select multiple industries simultaneously (e.g., Finance + Healthcare). Each industry shows its specific threat landscape and affected cryptographic protocols. A persona-aware summary card highlights the most impactful threats for your role.

Criticality & Search: Filter by criticality level (Critical, High, Medium-High, Medium, Low) to focus on the most urgent threats. Use the search bar to find threats by keyword across all fields.

Threat Details: Click any threat card to expand full details: affected algorithms, at-risk protocols, timeline to quantum risk, recommended PQC replacements, trust score badges, and references to compliance frameworks.

Sort Options: Sort threats by industry, threat ID, or criticality level. The default view groups threats by industry with the most critical items first. URL params: ?industry= (comma-separated), ?criticality=, ?q=, ?sort=, ?dir=, ?id=.

Tips:
- Use Endorse/Flag buttons to provide community feedback on threat assessments.
- Threats link to related compliance frameworks — click through to see requirements.

PAGE:timeline.manual:
Global Migration Timeline

Compare published post-quantum migration records — standards, guidance, policy and deadlines — across countries and international bodies, each linked to its source.

Region & Country Filters: Use the region dropdown, or a Coverage-by-region tile, to show Americas, EU (the Europe group, including the UK, Norway and Switzerland), MENA, APAC or Global (international bodies such as the G7, IETF, ITU-T and ETSI). Pick a country to narrow further and to open its Documents panel. Filters are kept in the URL (?region=, ?country=, ?q=) so a filtered view can be shared.

Gantt Chart: Each country has one row per phase type: Discovery, Testing, POC, Migration, Standardization, Guidance, Policy, Regulation, Research or Deadline. Bars are phases with a start and end year; flags are dated milestones, with a number when one year holds several, and a thin line when a milestone states a span. The Organization column names the body behind each row. Click a bar or flag to open that year's record; when a row groups several records, the popover lists them all so each can be opened.

Search & Quick Filters: Search matches countries, issuing bodies and each record's title, description and identifiers (for example "FIPS 203" or "TR-02102"). The phase and type dropdowns narrow the chart (?phase=, ?etype=), and Deadlines (?deadlines=1) shows deadline records only. A deadline that states a range counts at its end year.

Records, Binding Force & Evidence: A record shows who issued it, its period, how binding the source is (binding, mandatory in scope, official target, recommendation, draft or informational), its HARD/SOFT mandate label where one has been reviewed, its evidence score, its review history, and links to the Library documents and compliance frameworks that cite it. In the Documents panel, switch between Cards and Table (?docview=table). A link to one record is /timeline?event=<record id>; a link to a retired record opens the record that replaced it when the dataset names one.

Export & Sharing: Export (in the header or the chart toolbar) downloads one CSV row per record in the current view, with its issuer, dates, source, mandate label and binding force. The operations view also offers a calendar (.ics) export of the same records. Years are year-level: a calendar entry marks the year, not a day.

Endorsements & Flags: Use Endorse or Flag on a country row or a record to send feedback about its accuracy.

Tips:
- Bookmark a filtered URL to quickly return to a specific region view.
- A country-level record does not establish that a milestone applies to your organization; open its source to check scope.

PL:kmip3:async.full:
Enqueue an op as a real background job, then Poll its correlation value.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:certificate-services.full:
Certify / Re-certify / Validate — pure Rust, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA chains included.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:hbs.full:
SLH-DSA has no classical predecessor — a conservative addition, not a replacement.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:honesty.full:
Inspect lifecycle and refusal outcomes, and understand what they do not establish.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:hybrid.full:
X25519MLKEM768 — one op, two algorithms, secure if either survives.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:kem.full:
ECDH → ML-KEM-768 — same goal, a completely different wire shape.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:provision.full:
CreateKeyPair → Activate — the object model everything else builds on.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:sign.full:
RSA-3072 / ECDSA → ML-DSA-65 — the biggest visible size jump under PQC.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:splitkey.full:
Split a key into 5 shares where any 3 recover it — and 2 honestly cannot.
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:kmip3:symmetric.full:
The shortest lesson here, on purpose — the answer is "nothing changes."
Playground label: KMIP 3.0

PL:openssl-studio:capstone-tls.full:
Every artifact so far has stayed inside the Workbench's virtual filesystem. This lesson generates one final certificate, then points to the Studio's TLS Simulator — a separate tool that runs a real TLS 1.3 handshake in WASM using its own bundled sample certificates — so you can see a certificate used on the wire. The Simulator does not pick up the files made here by itself; the notes say how to import them by hand.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:cert-issuance.full:
req -new produces a CSR for a CA to sign; req -x509 -new skips straight to a self-signed certificate. Both classical and PQC keys go through the identical req command.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:config-files.full:
openssl.cnf quietly supplies defaults every req/x509 call in this curriculum relied on. openssl configutl (new in OpenSSL 3.6) parses and re-dumps a config file so you can see exactly what it resolves to.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:first-keypair.full:
genpkey generates both eras of key with the same command shape — only the -algorithm value changes. Watch what changes (and what stays the same) between an RSA-2048 key and an ML-DSA-65 key.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:honest-lms.full:
This Studio's LMS/HSS panel generates, signs and verifies via a separate WASM engine, not openssl itself — because upstream OpenSSL does not support LMS/HSS key generation or signing, and this openssl build has no LMS at all. Don't take that on faith: try it yourself and read the real error.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:kdf-choice.full:
openssl kdf (added in OpenSSL 3.0) exposes HKDF, PBKDF2, SCRYPT and more behind one command. Each expects different -kdfopt keys — mixing them up is the most common way to get a useless key silently.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:key-establishment.full:
ML-KEM has no drop-in classical equivalent in this Studio — it's a genuinely new operation shape (encapsulate/decapsulate) rather than a PQC repaint of an existing one. This lesson runs the full round trip and checks the recovered secret really matches.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:pkcs12-packaging.full:
pkcs12 bundles a key + certificate (+ chain) into one password-protected file — the format most browsers and app servers actually import. Classical and PQC keys bundle identically.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:randomness.full:
Every key this Studio has generated so far leaned on openssl rand under the hood. This lesson calls it directly and looks at what it actually promises.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:sign-verify.full:
Classical keys sign through dgst (hash-then-sign, hash chosen explicitly); ML-DSA and SLH-DSA sign through pkeyutl instead, hashing internally. The Studio's own Workbench already branches on this — this lesson shows why.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:openssl-studio:symmetric-myth.full:
AES and SHA-256/SHA3 are NOT what post-quantum migration is about. Grover's algorithm only halves their effective security — a bigger key fixes it. Shor's algorithm breaks RSA/ECC/DH outright, which is why THOSE need new algorithms, not bigger keys.
Playground label: OpenSSL Studio

PL:pkcs11-v32:authenticated-wrap.full:
C_WrapKeyAuthenticated is one of the 12 new v3.2 functions — AEAD key wrapping with a per-wrap IV and an authentication tag. The lesson alters one byte of an AES-GCM blob and of an AES-KW blob (RFC 3394, which also checks integrity on unwrap) and shows both unwraps refused.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:hash-based-signatures.full:
SLH-DSA has no classical predecessor to compare against — its whole point is resting on nothing but hash-function security, the most conservative assumption available.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:hedged-signing.full:
This walkthrough signs the same message twice with Preferred hedging and twice with deterministic signing, then compares the output bytes.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:inspecting-policy.full:
Read back the existing CKA_ALLOWED_MECHANISMS key policy, then query the separate v3.2 session validation indicator.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:kem-api.full:
C_EncapsulateKey/C_DecapsulateKey are a genuinely new call SHAPE, not just a new algorithm — no classical PKCS#11 call works this way.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:migration-capstone.full:
Inventory the sample token, create a PQC signing key alongside a classical signing key, then delete the local legacy private key and keep its public key.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:policy-pinning.full:
CKA_ALLOWED_MECHANISMS pins a key to an explicit allow-list at creation time — the token enforces it on every later call, independent of what it otherwise supports.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:signing-goes-lattice.full:
RSA-3072 and ML-DSA-65 both sign and verify. Only the sizes tell you which one just quietly stopped being safe against a quantum adversary.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:trust-wrapping-policy.full:
CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED pins a key so only a CKA_TRUSTED wrapping key may ever wrap it out — and CKA_TRUSTED itself is the one attribute you can never set yourself, not even as the token administrator, once a key already exists.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v32:whats-new.full:
Discover an existing standard profile object, then query the session validation indicator introduced in v3.2.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.2

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-composite-mldsa.full:
One key, two signatures: an ML-DSA-65 signature and an ECDSA P-256 signature over the same message representative M′. Both must verify.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-composite-mlkem.full:
Two KEMs, one key, one 32-byte secret. The key teaching moment: the same two component secrets give a different result in a TLS hybrid group than in a composite KEM, on purpose.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-external-mu.full:
ML-DSA signs µ, a 64-byte digest of the public key, the context and the message. Compute µ where the message is, and send only µ to the HSM.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-keys-remaining.full:
A stateful hash-based key can sign only so many times. CKA_KEYS_REMAINING tells you how many are left, and now covers XMSS too.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-renamed-deprecated.full:
v3.3 marks some names deprecated and some historical. No value changes, so nothing breaks — but some code should change.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11-v33:v33-what-is-v33.full:
There is no published PKCS#11 v3.3. There is an OASIS working draft whose new codepoints are already approved. This lesson asks the engine what it actually implements.
Playground label: PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft)

PL:pkcs11:agreement-derivation.full:
ECDH lets two parties who've never met agree on a shared secret over a public channel. HKDF then turns that raw shared secret into a well-formed key.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:certificate-discovery.full:
Listing every certificate on every slot — slot ID, CKA_LABEL, CKA_SUBJECT, CKA_ID — is the first thing most PKCS#11 clients do. The same answer can cost a few dozen calls or twice as many, depending on how the client talks to the token.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:cryptoki-model.full:
Every PKCS#11 call happens through a session, opened against a token, that lives in a slot. This walkthrough boots the real engine and shows what each layer actually is — then deliberately breaks one to show what an honest failure looks like.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:digest-random.full:
Two stateless building blocks used everywhere else in this curriculum: hashing and random-number generation.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:key-wrap.full:
Moving a key off a token requires wrapping it under another key — and PKCS#11 refuses to wrap a key that was never marked extractable, no exceptions.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:mechanism-discovery.full:
A token doesn't support every algorithm — it advertises exactly which mechanisms it implements, and C_GetMechanismInfo is how you check before you commit to one.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:objects-attributes.full:
Every key on a token is an object described by attributes. Two of those attributes — CKA_SENSITIVE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE — decide whether its value can ever be read back, and PKCS#11 enforces that decision permanently.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:sign-verify.full:
The private key signs, the public key verifies — and verification is a real cryptographic check, not a formality.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:pkcs11:symmetric-encryption.full:
AES-GCM is authenticated encryption — it detects tampering, not just decrypts. This walkthrough encrypts, decrypts successfully, then tampers the ciphertext and watches decryption honestly refuse it.
Playground label: PKCS#11 foundations

PL:tpm:attestation.full:
Quote platform state with a classical restricted RSA AK, then with ML-DSA — reusing everything the track taught: restricted keys, pinned schemes, PCRs, signatures, and ticket semantics.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:boot-discover.full:
The TPM booted when this page loaded. These steps interrogate the live chip: self-test, then the algorithm table — where RSA (0x0001) and ML-KEM (0x00A0) sit side by side — and finally a deliberate rule-break to see what an honest TPM refusal looks like.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:create-keys.full:
Create an RSA-2048 key and an ML-KEM-768 key in the live TPM and read back what each actually produced. The hierarchy seeds, deterministic derivation, and non-exportability are identical — the public key grows from 256 bytes to 1184.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:honest-tpm.full:
Inspect bridge status, check known placeholder patterns and compare a selected response with the pinned reference. These are bounded sample checks, not complete cryptographic or TPM conformance verification.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:key-establishment.full:
Run classical RSA-OAEP key transport and ML-KEM encapsulation back to back — then corrupt a ciphertext in each system and watch them fail in OPPOSITE ways. OAEP refuses loudly; ML-KEM “succeeds” with a useless secret (implicit rejection).
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:sign-verify.full:
Sign with RSA through the classic TPM2_Sign, then with ML-DSA through the NEW TPM2_SignDigest — and notice V1.85 gave PQC signing its own command surface, its own signature layout, and its own verified-ticket type.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:streaming.full:
Classical TPMs hash-then-sign: stream chunks into a hash sequence, sign the 32-byte digest. Pure ML-DSA signs the MESSAGE — hashing first changes the security claim — so V1.85 streams chunks into the signing operation itself. Run both flows.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PL:tpm:v27-ek-certs.full:
This TPM was provisioned at “manufacture” (page load) with six V2.7 PQC Endorsement Keys and X.509 certificates in well-known NV slots. Find them with live queries — persistent handles first, then the DER certificate bytes themselves.
Playground label: TPM 2.0

PRD:age-plugin-pqctoday.full:
An age recipient plugin implementing X-Wing draft-06 (X25519 + ML-KEM-768). The default backend performs the construction in software. With the pkcs11 feature, long-term private keys are generated as sensitive, non-extractable token objects; the plugin reads the two component shared secrets and combines them with SHA3-256 on the host. Therefore token-held private keys do not imply that every intermediate secret remains inside the token. The resulting secret protects the age file key using HKDF-SHA256 and ChaCha20-Poly1305. SOPS can use this recipient through its age integration; SOPS itself does not implement X-Wing.

PRD:applivery-uem-pqc.full:
Applivery states it is the first UEM to deploy post-quantum cryptography across managed Apple devices (a vendor claim, not independently verified). Its announcement of September 16, 2025 says the implementation secures key exchange in MDM communication and describes it as Post-quantum Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) leveraging X25519MLKEM768, with Apple's quantum-secure TLS 1.3 APIs on iOS 26, macOS 26 and iPadOS 26, TLS 1.3 via OpenSSL 3.5.0 on the server side, and Cloudflare configured between clients and servers to use X25519MLKEM768. X25519MLKEM768 is a TLS 1.3 hybrid key-agreement group (RFC 10024) and HPKE is a separate public-key encryption scheme (RFC 9180); the announcement does not say how the two are combined, so the exact mechanism is the vendor's wording only. The announcement says AES-256 is the minimum symmetric key size and that Android and Windows support is on the roadmap.

PRD:berten-mlke-b135.full:
BERTEN MLKE-B135 is a FIPS 203-compliant ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism, derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber) IP core for FPGA, SoC, and ASIC implementation, portable to AMD (Xilinx), Intel (Altera), and Microchip (Microsemi) device families. It supports all three NIST ML-KEM parameter sets: ML-KEM-512 (Security Category 1), ML-KEM-768 (Category 3), and ML-KEM-1024 (Category 5). The core integrates a dedicated sequencer, a Polynomial Arithmetic Unit, and high-performance SHA-3/SHAKE functions, exposing four AXI4-Stream data interfaces plus one AXI4-Lite register-map interface (user-programmable to select ML-KEM operation and parameter set) and a status-notification port. At 300 MHz the vendor reports throughput of up to 87,050 key-generation, 70,500 encapsulation, and 52,300 decapsulation operations/second at ML-KEM-512, scaling to 36,500/32,200/25,600 ops/s at ML-KEM-1024, with target-specific resource units: AMD devices use 8.6K-9.0K LUTs, while the Intel table reports 17.4K LE or 7.4K-7.5K ALM depending on family; register counts are 7.4K-8.0K. Countermeasures include resistance to timing and Simple Power Analysis (SPA) side-channel attacks, FIPS 203 input validation, and automatic/on-demand zeroization of internal memories and registers. Deliverables under a perpetual site license (12 months support) include an encrypted netlist, design constraints, simulation model, user manual, and ANSI C drivers.

PRD:bouncy-castle-c-java.full:
Official, NIST-standardized PQC support (ML-KEM/FIPS 203, ML-DSA/FIPS 204, SLH-DSA/FIPS 205) has shipped in Bouncy Castle's mainline JCA/JCE provider (Java) and BouncyCastle.Cryptography (C#/.NET) since Java 1.79 / C# 2.5.0 (Dec 2024), replacing the earlier pre-standardization Kyber/Dilithium implementations — this is mainline official library functionality, not a third-party demo/concept-study app built on an old version. Java and C# are separately versioned, independently maintained codebases (bc-java vs bc-csharp) with their own release cadence. Subsequent releases (Java 1.81/C# 2.6.1, Jun 2025, through current Java 1.85.2/LTS 2.73.12/C# 2.7.0, Aug 2026) added standardized PKCS#8 key encodings interoperable with OpenSSL 3.5+, ML-KEM TLS 1.3 cipher suites (KEM-only and hybrid) in JSSE/(D)TLS, ML-DSA/SLH-DSA support in CMS SignedData, and Java keytool compatibility. Both editions' own package descriptions also list additional NIST PQC Standardization Process candidate algorithms — Falcon, Classic McEliece, FrodoKEM, NTRU, NTRU Prime, Picnic, SABER, and BIKE — explicitly labeled 'EXPERIMENTAL and subject to change or removal' by Bouncy Castle itself, a designation distinct from the finalized ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA. SIKE and Rainbow are not offered, consistent with their removal from the NIST PQC process.

PRD:cisco-ios-xr.full:
Cisco IOS XR is the service-provider routing OS for ASR 9000, NCS, and 8000 platforms. Separately from the ML-KEM/ML-DSA (NIST-PQC) roadmap, which is not yet GA, IOS XR has shipped a distinct quantum-safe mechanism since Release 24.1.1 on the Cisco NCS 1004 optical platform: RFC 8784 Postquantum Preshared Keys (PPK) for IKEv2/OTNsec encryption, available as manual PPK or dynamic PPK via the Cisco Secure Key Integration Protocol (SKIP) against an external key source (e.g. QKD). PRD:evolutionq-basejumpqdn.full:
Software platform for building a Quantum Delivery Network (QDN) that unifies Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) and Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) in a single control plane. Each BasejumpQDN node runs a crypto-agile key agent that delivers QKD-derived keys, PQC-derived keys (ML-KEM for key establishment, ML-DSA for authentication), or Multimodal hybrid keys (QKD + PQC + symmetric), with automatic fallback to PQC/hybrid key establishment if the QKD key supply is interrupted. Extends key delivery across fiber distances beyond QKD's natural range limit using trusted repeater nodes (evolutionQ's product page states 'a few hundred kilometers'; a 2025 evolutionQ/Nokia joint paper cites '~100-125 km' for current QKD technology — no evolutionQ source states '~300 km'). Vendor-neutral — validated with over 10 QKD vendors via ETSI GS QKD 014, including ID Quantique and Toshiba by name, preventing lock-in. Includes BasejumpSIM cloud-based simulation tool for modeling QDN deployments before physical rollout. Used by Nokia and ID Quantique in a live network trial for Proximus (Belgian telecom) — 'Europe's first live hybrid quantum encryption key trial,' completed June 2023 between Brussels and Mechelen; both evolutionQ and ID Quantique describe this as a trial/demonstration, not an ongoing production deployment.

PRD:google-cloud-cdn.full:
Cloud CDN has no independent TLS stack: per Google's Cloud CDN docs, it 'works with the global external Application Load Balancer or the classic Application Load Balancer to deliver content' — that Load Balancer handles TLS termination. Google's Load Balancing documentation (last updated 2026-10-26) describes post-quantum hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768/ML-KEM) as disabled by default and enabled only when set to ENABLED, with a planned rollout of enabled by default after October 2026 (disabled when set to DEFERRED) and always enabled after October 2027; the page does not state that the default has changed. OPA is a general-purpose policy engine using the Rego policy language for unified authorization across cloud-native stacks. In the PQC migration context, OPA enforces cryptographic policies — blocking Kubernetes deployments that use RSA-2048, flagging TLS configs without ML-KEM, or failing CI pipelines that include quantum-vulnerable algorithms in their CBOM. OPA itself has no crypto; it is the policy enforcement layer above crypto discovery tools.

PRD:openbao.full:
OpenBao is an open-source fork of HashiCorp Vault (donated to LF Edge / OpenBao project, Apache-2.0). OpenBao 2.7.0 (released September 23, 2026; newest release 2.7.2, October 26, 2026) introduced ML-DSA (FIPS 204). The Transit secrets engine can generate, import and export keys of type mldsa-44, mldsa-65 and mldsa-87 and can create and verify pure ML-DSA signatures. The PKI engine supports ML-DSA for all CA, CSR and leaf actions; Go's OCSP implementation does not support ML-DSA, so OCSP is unusable with ML-DSA typed issuers. Server, agent and proxy listeners accept tls_key_exchange_preferences with SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024, X25519MLKEM768 and MLKEM1024, and can use ML-DSA certificates; outbound TLS connections can reach servers using those key exchanges or presenting an ML-DSA server or CA certificate. Suitable for OSS-only deployments requiring open-source secrets management.

PRD:pqc-flow.full:
Passive analyzer that detects post-quantum and hybrid key exchange in live network traffic and PCAP captures and keeps what a handshake offered apart from what was negotiated. SSH detection (production): a custom parser extracts the kex_algorithms name-list from SSH_MSG_KEXINIT and the tool reports a negotiated key-exchange algorithm in ssh_kex_negotiated (the client-offered list ssh_kex_offered comes from nDPI and may be empty); sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com (OpenSSH 9.0+) is detected, while mlkem, kyber and ntruprime SSH variants are pattern-ready but NOT yet implemented (roadmap item). TLS 1.3 detection: a custom ClientHello/ServerHello parser reads the supported_groups and key_share extensions and reports the group the server selected in tls_negotiated_group (groups the client offered are in tls_supported_groups, nDPI JSON, limited), recognizing X25519Kyber768 (Chrome 0x11ec), X25519Kyber768Draft00 (Cloudflare 0xfe31/0x6399) and NIST ML-KEM draft group codes (0x2001+). These are key-exchange groups, not cipher suites or signature algorithms. QUIC detection is a partial implementation (nDPI classification plus the TLS extension parser applied to the TLS-in-QUIC handshake; limited testing; the README also lists QUIC as limited/nDPI-only with a custom QUIC Initial parser on the roadmap). IKE/IPsec via nDPI classification (limited metadata support, not extensively tested). Post-quantum signature detection (ML-DSA/Dilithium, SLH-DSA/SPHINCS+, Falcon) is roadmap-only, not yet implemented; it requires future TLS certificate parsing. The PQC flags bitmask tracks KEM presence, signature presence, hybrid negotiation, offered-only and session resumption states (value 9 means PQC offered but the server chose a classical exchange). No nDPI patches required for SSH/TLS PQC extraction.

PRD:pqcscan.full:
Open-source PQC readiness scanner written in Rust. Two scan modes: tls-scan (probes HTTPS/TLS endpoints for standardized PQC/hybrid key-exchange groups using final NIST names — e.g. X25519MLKEM768, SECP384R1MLKEM1024, MLKEM768, MLKEM1024 — plus TLS version and cipher suite) and ssh-scan (probes SSH servers for PQC key-exchange (KEM) algorithm support, e.g. ml-kem-*, sntrup761x25519-*, mlkem768x25519-*; the server's host-key/signature algorithm list is captured and reported but is NOT classified against a PQC signature database — the tool currently ships no ML-DSA/SLH-DSA/Dilithium/SPHINCS+ list for SSH host keys or TLS signature schemes). Algorithm matching is done by name against bundled JSON tables (kex_algos.json, tls_groups.json, tls_cipher_suites.json, tls_sig_schemes.json), not by OID. Outputs JSON with HTML report generation. Binary releases for Linux, macOS, Windows. Developed by Anvil Secure. Both released versions (0.7.0, released 2025-07-02; 0.8.0, released 2025-11-08) postdate FIPS 203/204/205 finalization (Aug 2024) and use final NIST algorithm names.

PRD:rosenpass.full:
Rosenpass is a Rust post-quantum-secure VPN key-exchange daemon. It performs a handshake that combines Classic McEliece 460896 (static keys) and Kyber-512 (ephemeral keys), the NIST competition Round 3 versions rather than FIPS 203 ML-KEM, and rotates the WireGuard pre-shared key roughly every 2 minutes, giving WireGuard tunnels post-quantum forward secrecy. In the sandbox it replaces the prior fake-PQC WireGuard script (which used SHA-256 of an ML-KEM public key as the PSK). Architectural note: Rosenpass uses its own internal liboqs PQC backend, NOT the pqctoday-hsm PKCS#11 backend — the only sandbox scenario with this exception, disclosed in the scenario JSON.

PRD:tor-browser.full:
Tor Browser 15.0.x is rebased on Firefox ESR 140 (15.0.23 on 140.16.0esr). In Tor Browser's own source at that branch, security.tls.enable_kyber defaults to true and, when set, the TLS layer offers the mlkem768x25519 hybrid group first, so website TLS 1.3 connections use hybrid ML-KEM by default. Tor Browser adds no override of this pref and publishes no documentation of it. Separately, the Tor network's circuit-extension handshake has no post-quantum protection; Tor Proposal 355 only explores candidate ML-KEM designs.

PRD:xmss-reference.full:
Official C reference implementation of XMSS and XMSS^MT per RFC 8391, originally written by two of the RFC's five authors (Andreas Hülsing and Joost Rijneveld). Selects the parameter set at run time through a 32-bit OID prefix on keys. The parameter-name table in params.c lists the RFC 8391 sets (SHA2-256, SHA2-512, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 variants) and the sets that NIST SP 800-208 adds: XMSS-SHA2_{10,16,20}_192, XMSS-SHAKE256_{10,16,20}_256 and XMSS-SHAKE256_{10,16,20}_192, with the matching XMSSMT names. SP 800-208 approves only the SHA-256, SHA-256/192, SHAKE256/256 and SHAKE256/192 sets, so the RFC 8391 sets that use SHA2-512, SHAKE128 or 64-byte SHAKE256 output are not among the approved sets. The README documents RFC 8391 coverage and states no test results for the SP 800-208 sets. Includes key generation, signing, verification, and state persistence. Repository has had no commits since 2021-03-16 and multiple open issues (some dating to 2019) remain unaddressed, indicating it is effectively unmaintained rather than actively maintained. Historically used as a canonical cross-validation reference for other XMSS implementations.

PRD:zscaler-zero-trust-exchange.full:
Zscaler Internet Access (part of the Zero Trust Exchange) performs real-time inline SSL/TLS inspection of PQC traffic, using hybrid post-quantum key exchange built on the NIST-standardized ML-KEM algorithm (FIPS 203) combined with classical ECDHE. PQC negotiation between the client and Zscaler is independent of the destination server's capabilities (Zscaler always offers PQC to the server, but the server decides whether to accept it), giving administrators session-level visibility via logged TLS version and key-exchange group, and protecting the client-to-Zscaler hop against "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" attacks. Zscaler also supports post-quantum-resistant IPsec VPN tunnels via Pre-Shared, Post-Quantum Keys (PPK, per RFC 8784). Deployment requires no changes to existing customer configurations or hardware.

PRD:zscaler-zte.full:
Zscaler Internet Access (part of the Zero Trust Exchange/ZTE) provides real-time inline inspection of PQC traffic via hybrid PQC key exchange in TLS 1.2/1.3, auto-detecting ML-KEM (FIPS 203, finalized August 2024) and Open Quantum Safe groups alongside classical elliptic curves. This PQC negotiation between the client and Zscaler is independent of the destination server's capabilities — Zscaler always offers PQC to the server, but the client-to-Zscaler leg is protected from 'Harvest Now, Decrypt Later' attacks regardless of whether the server supports PQC. Supports IPsec with Pre-shared Post-Quantum Keys (PPK) per RFC 8784 to protect IKE key derivation against quantum attacks without requiring full PQC algorithms in the exchange.

QZ:aero-004.full:
DO-178C ties verification objectives to the Design Assurance Level. At DAL A these include MC/DC structural coverage, requirements-to-code traceability and independence in verification, and they apply to software that is added or changed, such as a PQC cryptographic library. FIPS 140-3 validates a cryptographic module; it does not replace the airborne-software objectives. Recertification effort and cost depend on the system, how much software changes, the certification authority and the supplier, so any published cost or schedule is an estimate for a stated project, not a value set by the standard.

QZ:aisec-002.full:
Model collapse is the degradation reported when models are trained recursively on model-generated content. Shumailov et al. found that indiscriminate use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in which the tails of the original content distribution disappear. It is conditional, not inevitable: Gerstgrasser et al. found that replacing real data with each generation's synthetic data tends toward collapse, while accumulating synthetic data alongside the original real data avoided it in their experiments. Records of where training data came from help a team choose what to train on; a valid signature on content shows which signer vouched for it, not that it is human-made or of good quality.

QZ:aisec-003.full:
C2PA (Content Credentials) defines signed manifests with claims and assertions about content, such as its signer, creation tool and edits. A consumer can check that the signed parts of the content have not changed since the manifest was produced and decide whether to trust the signer. The C2PA trust model is concerned with trust in the signer's identity; the consumer uses that identity, along with other trust signals, to decide whether the assertions made about an asset are true. A valid signature therefore does not show that content is human-made or accurate, and provenance records alone do not prevent model collapse. FIPS 203 defines a key-encapsulation mechanism, FIPS 204 a signature algorithm and RFC 8446 TLS 1.3.

QZ:aisec-004.full:
True. The model file is encrypted under a symmetric data key, and ML-KEM does not wrap that key by itself: encapsulation produces a fresh shared secret and a ciphertext, which is 1,088 bytes for ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203, Table 3). A wrapping key derived from the shared secret can then wrap the data key; for a 32-byte key, AES key wrap (RFC 3394) adds 8 bytes, giving 40. The stored envelope in this module's model is therefore about 1,128 bytes, negligible next to a 140 GB model file. If the data key is instead derived directly from the shared secret, only the 1,088-byte ciphertext is stored.

QZ:aisec-014.full:
Envelope encryption encrypts data with a data encryption key (DEK) and then encrypts the DEK under another key, so the top-level key encryption keys (KEKs) are what a KMS or HSM has to protect, while wrapped DEKs can be stored with the data. That separation is what scales: data is encrypted once under DEKs (AES-256-GCM in this module's model) and only the smaller set of KEKs protects them. ML-KEM does not wrap a DEK by itself: a common construction encapsulates to the KEK's public key, derives a wrapping key from the shared secret and wraps the DEK with it, so each stored DEK carries a 1,088-byte ML-KEM-768 ciphertext plus the wrapped key. How many DEKs to use is a design choice, and unwrapping a DEK still needs an operation with its KEK.

Difficulty: advanced

QZ:algo-029.full:
The Falcon specification says its signing procedure uses floating-point arithmetic with 53 bits of precision, which poses no problem for software implementations but can be a major limitation on constrained devices without a floating-point unit (those need emulation with integer operations). Signing also relies on discrete Gaussian sampling, and the specification notes that constant-time implementations of that step and of the whole scheme have been published. The specification itself names a delicate implementation as Falcon's main shortcoming. The challenge is therefore getting a correct, constant-time implementation on each platform and compiler, not an outright ban on floating point. FIPS 204 requires that ML-DSA implementations not use floating-point arithmetic, which removes this concern for ML-DSA. FN-DSA's advantage is smaller keys and signatures: for example Falcon-512 has an 897-byte public key and a 666-byte signature, against 1,312 and 2,420 bytes for ML-DSA-44.

The specification itself names a delicate implementation as Falcon's main shortcoming. The challenge is therefore getting a correct, constant-time implementation on each platform and compiler, not an outright ban on floating point. FIPS 204 requires that ML-DSA implementations not use floating-point arithmetic, which removes this concern for ML-DSA. FN-DSA's advantage is smaller keys and signatures: for example Falcon-512 has an 897-byte public key and a 666-byte signature, against 1,312 and 2,420 bytes for ML-DSA-44.

QZ:aqi-007.full:
A cross-certificate is a CA certificate in which the issuer and subject are different CAs. Here the existing classical root signs a certificate for the new PQC root's key. A client that does not yet have the new root in its trust store, but trusts the classical root and can verify the new signature algorithm, can build a path to the PQC root through the cross-signed certificate. A client that already holds the new root as a trust anchor can trust it directly. Cross-signing does not add algorithm support: path validation requires each certificate's signature to be verified with the issuer's key and algorithm, so a client that cannot verify ML-DSA cannot validate certificates issued under the PQC root, even through a cross-signed path. Such algorithm-unaware clients need a compatible classical certification path or another migration arrangement.

QZ:cbom-010.full:
Attestation proves only what its verified fields state. The validated chain and certified public key tie the evidence to that key, the challenge ties it to the verifier's request, and the security level says where the key is held (in Android key attestation, attestationSecurityLevel is the security level of the location where the attested key is stored). Nothing here states an export or backup policy, so non-exportability is not shown: hardware residency is a different property (PKCS#11 wrapping a key out of a token needs its CKA_EXTRACTABLE attribute to be true). Attestation can also be absent: in WebAuthn it defaults to none, and a backup-eligible credential is a multi-device credential.

The initial public draft of NIST IR 8320E covers remote attestation: it gives cryptographic evidence that a VM is running on hardware equipped with TEE capabilities and that the VM's memory and state are isolated and protected from other tenants and the hypervisor. QZ:cda-014.full:
Rust. In safe Rust, memory is managed through ownership rules that the compiler checks: if a rule is violated, the program does not compile. Java, Python and Go reclaim memory at run time instead, with garbage collection or reference counting. The guarantee has limits: code in unsafe blocks and calls into C libraries are not checked by the compiler for memory safety, so PQC bindings that wrap C code inherit its risks (the pqcrypto crate wraps PQClean's C implementations, and its maintainers now mark it unmaintained and advise against using it in new projects). Ownership rules also say nothing about timing: side channels depend on the deployed system, so constant-time behaviour still needs review and testing. Choose a language by requirements, library maintenance and validation status, and testing, not by a ranking.

FIPS 140-3 is the security standard that the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) validates cryptographic modules against. NIST states that FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3 requirements apply to all US Federal agencies and that "if cryptography is required, then it must be validated." So where validated cryptography is required, implementations of FIPS 203, 204 and 205 need to be inside a validated module. FIPS 140-3 does not define PQC algorithm parameters (the FIPS 203/204/205 documents do) and does not mandate quantum key distribution.

QZ:comp-022.full:
KpqC selected two signature algorithms, HAETAE and AIMer, and two KEMs, SMAUG-T and NTRU+, and does not rank them. HAETAE's security rests on the hardness of the module versions of the lattice problems LWE and SIS, the same family of problems as NIST's ML-DSA, although the designs differ. AIMer is a signature scheme built with the MPC-in-the-head paradigm, and its security depends on symmetric primitives, not lattices. SMAUG-T is based on module lattice problems too, but it is a KEM, and NTRU+ is a KEM based on the NTRU problem, so neither is a signature scheme.

QZ:comp-030.full:
A crypto-agile deployment fits both markets. FIPS 203, 204 and 205 are published NIST standards, and US federal policy is moving toward them: Executive Order 14412 directs OMB guidance requiring agencies to move high-value assets and high-impact systems (excluding national security systems) to PQC key establishment by December 31, 2030 and PQC digital signatures by December 31, 2031, and directs the FAR Council to publish a proposed rule that would require covered contractors to comply by December 31, 2030 with NIST's FIPS, including FIPS with PQC algorithms (a proposed rule is not yet a final requirement). On the Korean side, the KpqC group selected four algorithms in January 2025, published final specifications in January 2026 and says it supports their national standardization; the pages read give no date by which Korean government systems must use them. A crypto-agile design lets the organization add KpqC algorithms if a Korean customer or regulator requires them. Disregarding Korean requirements (a) risks non-compliance, separate stacks (b) duplicate effort, and waiting (d) is hard to square with the EO 14412 dates.

Each approved function on a FIPS 140-3 certificate carries its CAVP reference for exactly this reason (not sourced in the Library). Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7 (9 April 2026).

QZ:cpc-004.full:

Under the amended assurance-continuity rules the certification body — not the vendor — decides minor versus major. For a confirmed minor change “no new certificate shall be issued”: the holder gets a maintenance report. Adding a signature service changes the claimed security functional requirements, which CCRA assurance-continuity guidance (CCDB-014) lists as a typical major change, leading to re-evaluation and a new certificate. A deadline does not change the classification. Source: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2462.

QZ:cpc-014.full:
A FIPS 140-3 certificate comes from the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP). A PTS HSM approval is a separate scheme: PCI SSC assigns the approval number to a device at the time of approval, and the number remains the same for the life of the device’s approval. A FIPS certificate is therefore not a PTS approval. Which HSM evidence a PCI standard accepts is set out in that standard, which this lesson does not read. Source: PCI SSC, Approved PTS Devices listing, field definitions.

The certified lane stays valid while the PQC candidate goes through the scheme’s route; an algorithm standard is not a validation, and a MIP entry is a queue position. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7, §7.1.12 (as of 24 September 2026).

QZ:cryp-010.full:
FIPS 205 approves 12 SLH-DSA parameter sets. For each of six sets of values the hash functions may be instantiated with either SHAKE or SHA-2, which gives the SLH-DSA-SHA2-* and SLH-DSA-SHAKE-* parameter sets. The parameter-set name also shows the security parameter and whether the set is designed for small signatures ('s') or fast signing ('f'). FIPS 205 does not state a preference for one family; the choice is made by the profile or policy you follow and by your implementation. SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature scheme, so its security rests on hash functions.

QZ:csig-002.full:
Sigstore keyless signing uses an ephemeral key pair and a short-lived certificate bound to an OIDC identity: Fulcio signs X.509 certificates that are valid for 10 minutes. The private key is discarded shortly after signing, and the signing event, including the certificate, is recorded in the Rekor transparency log. This removes the need to store and protect a long-lived signing key, which is the main advantage over traditional certificate-based code signing. It does not remove every risk: identity owners are expected to monitor the log for unexpected signing events under their identity.

QZ:csig-007.full:
False. LMS/HSS (NIST SP 800-208, RFC 8554) is stateful — each one-time key in the Merkle tree can only be used once. The signer must maintain a counter tracking which one-time keys have been consumed. If state is lost or the same key is reused, security is catastrophically compromised. State management typically uses an HSM or TPM with a monotonic counter.

QZ:dep-002.full:
TDE uses a two-layer architecture: the DEK (AES-256-GCM) encrypts the actual data, and a certificate/asymmetric key wraps the DEK. AES-256-GCM with 128-bit post-quantum security (after Grover) remains computationally infeasible to break. The vulnerability is in the DEK wrapping: RSA-OAEP or ECDH key derivation for the DEK protection is broken by Shor's algorithm. An adversary who harvests the encrypted DEK today can decrypt it in the future to expose all TDE-protected data.

Difficulty: beginner
Quiz mode: both
Type: multiple-choice

The vulnerability is in the DEK wrapping: RSA-OAEP or ECDH key derivation for the DEK protection is broken by Shor's algorithm. An adversary who harvests the encrypted DEK today can decrypt it in the future to expose all TDE-protected data.

This eliminates cloud-provider key exposure but introduces latency for every database decryption operation.

QZ:dep-004.full:
SQL Server TDE's crypto weakness is in the certificate key: RSA-2048 is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. The AES-256 DEK is already post-quantum resistant (128-bit security after Grover), so it needs no algorithm change. SQL Server secures the DEK with a certificate or an asymmetric key, so the migration is to re-wrap the DEK under a different protector once SQL Server supports a post-quantum one: only the DEK wrapper changes, not the encrypted data. ML-DSA cannot be that protector: it is a signature algorithm and cannot wrap a DEK.

ML-DSA cannot be that protector: it is a signature algorithm and cannot wrap a DEK.

QZ:dep-005.full:
Oracle Wallet PKCS#12 uses RSA for the MEK protection. The migration path via OKV provides: (1) Centralized key management with HSM backing, (2) ML-KEM-768 capable HSMs (Entrust nShield and Thales Luna) can provide PQC-resistant MEK wrapping (AWS CloudHSM documents ML-DSA but no ML-KEM command), (3) OKV's REST API supports plugin-based KMS integration. Re-encrypting tablespaces with AES-512 is not a real option (no Oracle TDE supports AES-512) and would require full offline re-encryption of all data.

CSFLE encrypts data in your application before it is sent to MongoDB. Fields are protected by Data Encryption Keys, and a Customer Master Key encrypts and decrypts those DEKs. MongoDB's documentation lists AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, KMIP and a local key provider; with the cloud KMS providers the KMS remotely encrypts and decrypts the DEK, so the CMK is never exposed to the application. The way the DEKs are wrapped is therefore provider-specific, and that is the layer to review with your provider. If a provider does not document post-quantum support, record it as unknown. QZ:dep-007.full:
CLE has two layers: a symmetric key (SymKey) encrypts the column values, and an asymmetric key or certificate protects the SymKey. The public-key layer is the part exposed to Shor's algorithm when it uses RSA (NIST IR 8547 lists RSA as quantum-vulnerable). ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is a digital signature algorithm, so it cannot be used to protect a key; a key-encapsulation mechanism such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is used to establish shared keys. SQL Server's CREATE ASYMMETRIC KEY documentation lists only RSA key sizes (RSA_512 to RSA_4096, plus RSA-HSM_2048 and RSA-HSM_3072 from SQL Server 2022), so a post-quantum option in this layer is hypothetical until Microsoft documents it. If one existed, completing the migration would mean re-protecting every SymKey under the new key (if several SymKeys share the old key, each must be handled); the column values themselves would not change.

If one existed, completing the migration would mean re-protecting every SymKey under the new key (if several SymKeys share the old key, each must be handled); the column values themselves would not change.

QZ:dep-008.full:
With customer-managed TDE, Microsoft documents the TDE protector as a key stored in Azure Key Vault or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM that secures the database encryption key (DEK). A customer can import a key from an on-premises HSM into one of those services (bring your own key), but the server then sends each database's DEK to the key vault to be encrypted, and the encrypted DEK is stored in the user database. For a quantum-risk review this means: check which key type backs the protector (Microsoft lists RSA keys of 2,048 or 3,072 bits, and AES keys in preview); an RSA-protected DEK that is stored or captured today is exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later if RSA is later broken, because NIST IR 8547 lists RSA as quantum-vulnerable; and ask Microsoft what it documents for the connection between the server and the key service.

QZ:dep-009.full:
LUKS2 is the practical interim solution: AES-256-XTS encrypts the block device containing PostgreSQL data files. LUKS2 keyslots can be bound to an external KMS using the clevis/tang framework or custom KMS integration. The LUKS2 master key is wrapped by the KMS using ML-KEM-768. This provides BYOK semantics with PQC-resistant key wrapping. SEV-SNP addresses memory encryption (not storage at rest). pgcrypto ML-DSA would be signing, not encryption. PostgreSQL native TDE has been planned for many versions and has no committed ML-KEM date.

QZ:dep-010.full:
SQL Server TDE migration is an online operation: it does not lock tables or prevent application access. However, the database engine re-encrypts all data pages in the background, generating sequential read and write I/O across all data files. For a 100TB database, this represents significant I/O load over 4-12 hours (depending on I/O throughput). Transaction logs grow proportionally during the migration. The operational risks are storage capacity exhaustion (log files) and I/O saturation causing application performance degradation.

Logical replication + online batch re-encryption is the safest approach: (1) New PostgreSQL is provisioned with PQC-capable crypto configuration. This approach provides near-zero downtime and allows rollback if issues arise.

To manage descriptor trust lifecycle, ERC-8176 binds ERC-7730 descriptors to Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS) attestations with uint64 expirationTime (where 0 never expires and relies on eas.revokeOffchain(uid), while bounded future expirations are recommended).

QZ:diga-023.full:

Under NIST FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance, CAVP validates an algorithm implementation rather than the cryptographic module, and code inside the enclosure may be an Excluded Component (IG 2.3.D) outside the validated boundary; reviewers must check the Approved Security Service Indicator (IG 2.4.A/C) and Software/Firmware Loading rules (IG 10.3.F).

QZ:diga-024.full:
Decoding and logging warnings on an untrusted host refuses nothing unless policy enforcement sits inside the signing boundary (HSM or attested enclave). QZ:diga-025.full:
In Pattern (ii) (key release to an attested TEE), the key is marked exportable and enters TEE DRAM during use. Recent physical interposer research breaks single-TEE isolation under physical datacenter access: Battering RAM (IEEE S&P 2026) breaks Intel Scalable SGX and AMD SEV-SNP via DDR4 interposers (not Intel TDX), while TEE.fail (IEEE S&P 2026) breaks Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP via DDR5 interposers even with Ciphertext Hiding enabled. Pattern (i) keeps the long-term key inside the HSM/KMS boundary.

Difficulty: advanced

Pattern (i) keeps the long-term key inside the HSM/KMS boundary.

options.b: Pattern (ii) places the released key inside TEE DRAM, where interposer attacks have extracted secrets—Battering RAM against Intel Scalable SGX and AMD SEV-SNP (DDR4, not Intel TDX) and TEE.fail against Intel TDX and AMD SEV-SNP (DDR5)—whereas Pattern (i) keeps the long-term signing key inside the HSM.
options.c: Battering RAM breaks Intel TDX on DDR5, whereas TEE.fail only affects Intel SGX on DDR4.
options.d: Pattern (i) exposes the raw private key in host RAM every time the enclave verifies PCR measurements.

How do physical datacenter memory-bus interposer attacks affect these two patterns?

QZ:diga-026.full:

options.a: Any threshold above 1 guarantees safety even if one dealer generated and split the key, one orchestrator triggers all parties, and the GG18 library is unpatched.
options.b: Only the coordinator node needs to verify transaction policy, because MPC shares automatically enforce EVM calldata rules.
options.c: Shares must be created via Distributed Key Generation (never imported by a dealer), implementations must be patched against missing ZK proof / small-factor Paillier modulus flaws (such as BitForge / GHSA-h24c-6p6p-m3vx in GG18/GG20), and no shared orchestrator may unilaterally instruct >= t parties.
options.d: Switching from threshold 2-of-3 to 1-of-3 removes the need for zero-knowledge proofs during Paillier key setup.

QZ:diga-027.full:
Storing an encrypted share at rest and unwrapping it into host RAM during signing (Variant a) protects disk backups, not a compromised MPC host OS. Stronger designs run MPC state inside HSM firmware extensions (Variant b, vendor-specific such as CodeSafe or Luna FMs) or across mixed trust domains (Variant c). OASIS PKCS#11 v3.2 contains zero MPC or threshold-signing mechanisms, whereas KMIP 2.1 (Standard) and KMIP 3.0 CSD02 (draft) model Split Key objects (Create Split Key / Join Split Key).
